Second Part. Editor: Kevalānandasarasvatī. Vijayā Daśamī, Saturday, Śaka 1875.
The Publisher’s Note: This is indeed auspicious news that the second volume of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsākoṣa*, compiled by the venerable Kevalānandasarasvatī, has come into the light of publication.
We shall consider ourselves fortunate only when we are able to bring all six volumes to completion.
This undertaking depends upon a great expenditure of wealth; it could only reach completion through the patronage of the state and the wealthy.

We most heartily thank those who have assisted us by contributing five hundred rupees for the printing of this volume from the Bombay Education Society, one thousand rupees from the Poona Education Society, and especially ten thousand rupees from the Central Department of Education of the Government of India, which has helped to lighten the financial burden of publishing this treasury. We deeply appreciate their kindness.
Vijayā Daśamī, Śaka 1875.

(The meaning of the statement regarding possessive suffixes: For in cases such as "gomān" (possessor of cows), when the cows have already been denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the possessive suffix *matup* must denote the sense of "possessing that"; first of all, a relationship (*sambandha*) is necessarily required there.
It should be mentioned first. Why? Because one who is not connected with cows is not called "possessor of cows" (gomān).
Therefore, in that case, the qualification is accepted as being the relationship [with the preceding].
It has been established (in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*) that, as a general rule, the qualifier is always denoted first;
and here, it is the relationship [that is the qualifier].

The qualifier refers to what is intended, not to "cow" in general, because it would convey [the meaning] in relation to things that are unconnected. If "cow" in general were the qualifier, then the suffix would express the qualified object after those [cows] have already been denoted by the nominal stem.
In the case of a relation,
moreover, that [relation] must necessarily be denoted by something as a qualifier. No.
Furthermore, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is its denoter, because it denotes only the generic form (*ākṛti*).

Nor is the meaning of the nominal stem the indicator (*gamaka*, i.e., the signifier) [of the individual], since it is applicable even without a relation, as is evident when the word "cow" (*go*) is uttered in isolation.
And it is attained;

And for this reason, even the statement "for when that [cause] arrives, that [effect] is seen" (4.1.1; 5.15) establishes that [the cause] is the meaning of the suffix.
Furthermore, that which resides in the substantive must take up a qualifier that is proximate to it.

Furthermore, the nominal stem (prātipadika) does not denote the qualified object (viśeṣya), such that it would require the relation which serves as its qualifier. Rather, it is the suffix (pratyaya) that denotes it, and thus it is what is required. If that [suffix] is present, the cognition of the relation is established by that very [suffix].
The denotation of the qualified object occurs because it is the object to be understood through the power of the denotative word.
Nor does the cognition of the relation arise from the cognition of the qualified object, because prior to the relation, the status of being a qualified object does not exist.

And once the status of being a qualified object is established and the relation is [already] known, there is no further purpose served; thus, it follows that this [relation] would simply not be cognized.
Therefore, from the very first suffix, the meaning of the suffix is the relation (*saṃbandha*). For this reason as well, the meaning of the suffix is the relation:
"For the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is desired [to denote] the cause of the occurrence of a word."
In the expression "Devadatta’s possession of cows" (*devadattasya gomattvam*), both the state of being a cow (*gomattva*) and the relation are perceived.

Just as in the case of "Śāleya’s cowness" (*śāleyasya gotvam*), where the genus (*jāti*) serves as a qualifier and is expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) as extracted from its substrate, that very [genus] is intended as the denotation; so too, when it is said "Devadatta’s possession of cows," since there is no cognition of the cow itself, but rather a perception of the accomplishment of a relation, that relation alone is determined to be the meaning of the abstract suffix.
And that which is the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is the cause (*nimitta*) for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as it occurs in its referent (*viśeṣya*).
And that which is the cause, because it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), is the primary denotation (*mukhyam abhidheyam*); the referent (*viśeṣya*) is secondary (*lākṣaṇika*).

And if the relation is expressed by the possessive suffix (*matup*), then, according to the principle that "the base and the suffix together express the meaning of the suffix," the abstract suffix is produced from the nominal stem *gomat*.
It is capable of denoting a relationship in no other way;
therefore, for this reason as well, the meaning is the relationship. By this, all derivative (yaugika) words [are explained].

In the case of primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa), [the suffixes] have already been explained. For in every instance, an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) denotes a relation, as in *rājapuruṣatvam* (the state of being the king's man), *aupagavatvam* (the state of being Upagu’s descendant), and *pācakatvam* (the state of being a cook).
Therefore, these are derivative (*yaugika*) because they function by means of that [etymological] cause.
(Thus ends the discussion on the sense of possessive suffixes.
Consequently, since the *bahuvrīhi* has as its object the sense of a possessive suffix (*mattvartha*), [it applies here].
By words such as *ekahāyana* ("one-year-old"), the relation is expressed. Furthermore, in that case where the *bahuvrīhi* compound is prescribed with respect to another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*),
there too, because it is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the relation holds the status of the primary element.
The meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is indicated by the suffix *pratyaya* in the expression *ekaṃ hāyanaṃ asyāḥ*.
Furthermore, because the meaning of the suffix is the referent of the compound *pañcayathasya*, it possesses predominance (*prādhānya*) here;
the use of the pronoun (*sarvanāma*) is solely for the purpose of demonstrating that specific form.
Because a case-ending alone cannot be connected [to another word], and because the meaning of a pronoun is not perceived [in that way],

it is well known that the relationship— whether it be the relationship between the five cases (*pañcamy-artha*) or the relationship between *syāt* and *syāmi*, or the relationship with *ka* and *idā*— must be expressed; therefore,
the expression of this relationship is achieved by the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
"Nor is the universal (jāti) determined to be the meaning of another word [in the compound],

for its connection with 'tawny eyes' (piñjākṣi) does not belong to it, nor does its being 'one-year-old' (ekavarṣā). These— such as 'she whose eyes are tawny' (piñje akṣiṇī asyāḥ), 'she who is one year old' (ekaṃ hāyanaṃ asyāḥ), and 'variegated cows' (citā gāvaḥ)— are properties of the individual (vyakti)."

Furthermore, because those individuals are infinite, a relationship [between word and object] cannot be apprehended, and due to the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it has been stated that the word is not expressive [of the individual].
Indeed, there could be no first usage of a word for a brown-eyed woman born of a brown-eyed mother;
therefore, some universal (*sāmānya*) must necessarily be posited as the denotable object.
And nothing other than a relationship is logically possible here. Furthermore, even if the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is not subject to being enjoined as a specific age-stage,
nevertheless it is understood that this is merely a quality (*guṇa*) and not a substance (*dravya*).

(Thus ends the prima facie argument [pūrvapakṣa] regarding the primary significance of words denoting substances through their etymological derivation. (By this very reason, the entire section [adhikaraṇa] is rejected: Therefore, since no word here exists that denotes a substance, there is no illustrative example [anudāharaṇatva].
Nor is another example possible, because there is an absence of any word that directly denotes a substance.

For in all cases, established words denote a genus; even in the case of derivative words, such as *bhāva* (being), they would be so called because of their status as causes for [the application of] qualities like redness.

And the word *puruṣa* does not receive a different designation such as "the state of being that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*). Therefore, the suffix denoting a state (*bhāvapratyaya*) relies upon a relationship that is implied by the sense, according to the principle: "Because of its lack of purpose [in the primary sense], it [applies] to its constituent parts" (Pāṇini 5.1.119). Furthermore, since it possesses the characteristic of being a real entity (*vastu*), even in the absence of a denotable cause, one resorts to this [interpretation] thinking, "Let that [characteristic] at least be grasped."
Therefore, this is the view of those who hold the etymological (yaugika) position regarding the assumption of the power to denote a relationship:
"And thus, just as by the word *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) it is the possessor of the relation [the staff] that is expressed,
so too it is by etymological words such as the term *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed one) and others."
Furthermore, the fact that the relation is a positive entity must be explained regarding those [relations] as before;
in this case, the possessive compound (bahuvrīhi) denotes a substance, not its quality.

As for the claim that "one year of his" (*ekahāyana asya*) is also not the meaning of the compound because the genitive sense predominates and thus it is a *bahuvrīhi* expressing a relationship—this is addressed as follows:
"It is said that the expressed meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* is [the possessor];
nevertheless, it is perceived as being equivalent to a word ending in the nominative case."

If, however, the meaning of another word were to be the related member only when it is in the locative case, then—just as in the expression "king’s man" (*rāja-puruṣaḥ*), where the king is the qualifier of the man because he is in the genitive case, and the man is the primary element to be compounded because he is in the nominative case—in the same way, by words such as *citragu* ("having brindled cows"), only the cows qualified by Devadatta and others would be understood, and not Devadatta and others qualified by brindled cows.
Therefore, the *bahuvrīhi* compound functions to express the intended meaning: "this belongs to the brindled cows."
Even if the analysis (*vigraha*) were otherwise, nevertheless, because such a meaning is observed at a later time, the analysis must be performed in this very way.
Consequently, the meaning of the compound is understood as "qualified by the related denotata," that is, "qualified by Devadatta and so forth."

Just as in the expression "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), when the genitive case is employed, the relation is expressed as the primary element; yet when a compound is formed and the case-ending has ceased, because the two constituent words (*pūrva-pada* and *uttara-pada*) abandon their fitness for separate usage, and because the relation to be expressed is already established through the cognition of a qualified meaning derived from proximity, the compound does not have the relation as its primary referent—in exactly the same way, even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, there is no primacy of the relation solely due to the use of a nominal stem.

And since that [meaning] belongs neither to the meanings of the preceding nor the subsequent members, nor even to either one of them, there is a determination of the predominance of the substance (*dravya*) which constitutes the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*). (This is the investigation of the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. And that "meaning of the other member" is understood, by the force of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*), as being one among genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*).
For example: "This is a spotted cow-individual; this [cow] is a genus-substance possessing various qualities."
A quality has multiple substrates, whereas this action has but a single substrate.

And in all cases, because of their mutual fitness (*yogyatva*), a specific meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is understood as being conveyed by words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Thus, in this instance, since the universal (*jāti*) is beginningless, it cannot be connected with the qualifier "having one year" (*ekaṃ hāyanamasyāḥ*); therefore, the individual (*vyakti*) is resorted to.
But was it not stated that individuals cannot be denoted due to their infinity and the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)?
This is not a fault:
"Even though things are infinite, a single instance serves as a defining characteristic; thus, the relationship of the word is easily established, and it will not be subject to deviation."

In cases where the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is indicated by the genus (*jāti*) itself, then the individuals thus indicated—being grasped once and for all by that single [genus]—will be denoted along with their locations and other attributes; thus, the relationship [between word and meaning] is easily understood. Nor is there an application elsewhere of what is indicated by that [genus]; therefore, there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*). But where individuals themselves qualify other individuals, even there the genus is accepted as the fundamental indicator (*mūlopalakṣaṇa*).
In every case, even when a qualifier follows at a distance, the perception of a relationship is established because there is no difference from the first definition;
for it is precisely the very first relationship that is derived from the word's meaning.
However, as for internal [qualifiers], they are not denotable because their relationship is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And thus, by means of the two [qualities] "tawny-eyed" (*piṅga-akṣa*), the qualities and parts are indicated; by those [qualities and parts], the substance possessing the parts (*avayavin*) is indicated, and that [substance] becomes the primary referent (*samāsārtha*). (This concludes the investigation into the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Furthermore, is this [primary referent] directly denoted (*abhidheya*) or merely indicated (*lākṣaṇika*)?

It is perceived as the primary element; for it is remembered [in Pāṇini’s rule] "multiple [words] in the sense of another word-meaning" (*anekaṃ manyapadārthe*, Pāṇini 2.2.24), and it is thought that it is denoted just like [words ending in] patronymic suffixes (*taddhita*) such as those expressing divinity or abstract nouns (*bhāvārthīya*).

Others, however, say: It is logical that the *taddhita* suffixes denoting deities express the meaning of another word (the compound), because they have no other purpose and because there is an increase in the number of words. Furthermore, in those cases, that meaning cannot be indicated by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as it is not cognized from the nominal stem by itself.

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, however, since both the preceding and following members exist, and there is no other verbal element (*śabdāvayava*) intervening, the cognition of the substance is established through the qualities of "tawny" and "eyes" alone; therefore, it is impossible to postulate [the existence of] a further denotable object.
However, this cannot be established by way of pervasion (*vyāpitva*).
For this [pervasion] would apply in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, since in that case the basis for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is established in every respect.

But here, in cases such as "citraguḥ" (the one possessing brindled cows), because the words "citra" and "go" denote objects that are entirely distinct, there is no figurative indication through direct denotation (*śruti*) with respect to Devadatta and the like.
Alternatively, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "forest" (arūṇyāni) is possible;
furthermore, since the meaning of the other word is already perceived even before the word "Devadatta" and so forth, it cannot be assumed that this is the meaning of the sentence as a whole.
Furthermore, it is not only the two word-meanings determined at the time of the compound that belong to the deity; for otherwise, Devadatta would be the meaning of the sentence.
Therefore, because it must necessarily be understood, one must accept that the "other referent" (anyapadārtha) is what is expressed by this [compound].
And in this way, its predominance will not be contradicted.

And therefore, since one observes that in such cases as these the *bahuvrīhi* has the power to denote an external referent (*anyapadārtha*), even where a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) might somehow be possible, it is nevertheless determined that there is denotation of the primary meaning itself, because the previously established definition [of the compound] does not lose its force. (This concludes the investigation into the figurative nature of the denotation of the *bahuvrīhi* meaning.
Consequently, it is logically established that words such as *piṅgākṣī* denote a substance (*dravya*).
As for the claim that *ekahāyanī* denotes age, that is untenable.
Because age is understood through its characteristic marks: for words such as *ukṣan* (bull) and others denote age itself.
On the other hand, words such as *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old female) denote a substance associated with a particular period of time; while denoting the substance, they function by indicating age.
For in the expression "she has one year (*ekaṃ hāyanaṃ asyāḥ*)," it is not the age that is being designated, but rather the substance.
For in this case, "one year" refers to the age of the animal at birth, not its current age.

(Thus ends the critique of the theory that words denote substances through their derivative [yaugika] meanings. [From here on follows the analysis of the Bhāṣya: Therefore, it is logical that this doubt arises from the effort to understand a substance qualified by a quality mentioned as a part of the compound *āruṇaikahāyanī*: does the redness (*aruṇā*) enter into the context as a subordinate element for the purchase and other rites occurring within the ritual section, or rather, because it resides in the same sentence, its denotation is restricted solely to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*)?

Here too, there is an objection similar to that regarding the *uddanā* (summary verse): since they are heard in syntactical connection (*saṃyukta*), it follows that they belong to three separate purposes; he refutes this.
This is the merit: because of being mentioned in the same sentence with either the purchase (*kraya*) or the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), it is connected [to them].

In that case, since the connection with the substance is even less open to doubt due to the mention of the case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*), the connection with the purchase would occur by virtue of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
Furthermore, this [connection] is not possible for a quality that is inactive because it is formless (*amūrta*).

If, however, out of necessity, a connection with the substance is resorted to, then even there, in the case of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), there would be a discrepancy between the purchase and the redness (*aruṇimā*) due to their being related to different purposes, according to the principle: "When there is a single connection, they serve the purpose of another" (PMS 2.4.18).

Moreover, a connection with a distinct case-meaning must be admitted for this [quality], because a connection with an action is accomplished by a kāraka-case ending, whereas a connection with a quality depends on the fifth [genitive] case.

And for this reason, it is suspected that because the syntactic connection within the sentence lacks compatibility (*ayogyatā*), [the term *aruṇā*], being impossible [to apply] to the primary subject of the context (*prakaraṇin*), would instead pertain to everything. If that were so, then this very meaning would be determined; thus, the connection with the purchase (*kraya*) would not even be suspected. To address this, he says: "A word that has become a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-bhūta*) will not express an impossible meaning. Furthermore, by this very fact—the inclusion within the same sentence and the indication through the instrumental case-ending—there arises a firm cognition that [the redness] is a qualifier of the *krayahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow used in the purchase).
Therefore, because of the authority of the word and because of the non-discrepancy with the actual state of things, a doubt arises as to what is consistent and what is inconsistent.
In that regard, due to its primacy, [the author] first presents the connection with action based on the meaning of the words;
for there is no excessive burden upon the Vedic word.

In this matter, by the force of the application (*viniyoga*) and because of the actual existence of the thing's inherent capacity (*vastusāmarthya*), we shall endeavor to act. If it is possible in some way [to connect it] with the purchase (*kraya*), then we shall certainly accept its inclusion therein. But if it cannot be established in any manner whatsoever, then even disregarding the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), we shall determine it to be a property of the context (*prakaraṇadharma*). (In the original text, however, the opening of the sentence begins with "But if, by those who are not being negligent... it is not being accomplished," whereas the portion beginning with "not in any way whatsoever" is the same.)

And there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here, because [the sentence] ends with a suffix denoting a gerundive (*pratyayānta*), which implies insignificance. What then? It is a division (*vibhāga*). The meaning is: having accepted a division of the purchase-sentence characterized by such a separation.

Alternatively, the term "is divided" (*bhidyate*) may be understood as a passive-reflexive construction (*karmakartari*). In this way, it is the word *aruṇā* itself that is understood to cause the division of the sentence.

"Vākya-bheda" (splitting of the sentence) means that a separate statement causes a division. Such a [division] results in the conclusion that the quality belongs to the context (*prakaraṇa*), which is understood through the water-carrying [vessel]. This is what is meant: as long as the *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) and the *vākya* (syntactical connection) are operative, there is no status of being a quality belonging to the context.

But when, due to a discrepancy with the actual object (*vastu*), those [means] whose capacity has been enjoined become devoid of operation, then there is application by context (*prakaraṇa-viniyoga*). (Now, the prima facie view: What, then, is the initial position? To this he says: "But that which is enjoined should be a universal duty (*sarvadharma*), because of the lack of distinction in its connection and because of the contradiction with the context" (3.1.4.8). (In the original text, however, the portion of the sūtra *vihitastu sarvadharmaḥ syāt* is not recited here. This is because both direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) remain indifferent due to their incapacity [to apply it].
But how is it that a quality (*guṇa*), which is non-active by nature, is grasped through the context (*prakaraṇa*) when it already exists? It is said:
here, the context is not intended as the "grasper" (i.e., the applicator).

How then? In the word *aruṇā*, by means of the instrumental case-ending, the instruments—namely the Soma and so forth, which are the means for the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma characterized by the context—are referred to, and the meaning of the nominal stem *aruṇā* is enjoined [in relation to them].
And for this reason, it is the word itself that is divided by the sentence:
[the word] whose individual instance is enjoined as the instrument for the accomplishment of the *apūrva*.
Thus, one should accomplish that which is characterized by the quality of being reddish;
for if it is thus, then even that which is great is the action and the instrument that is reddish.

Therefore, all instruments must be reddened. Furthermore, regarding another cause that has been prescribed by Brahmā and others, this quality is not a subordinate part of it; rather, its purpose is determined to be universal.

(The inquiry: Is the word *aruṇa* expressive of a quality (*guṇavacana*) or expressive of a substance (*dravyavacana*)? Bhāṣya (p. 681): Now, this is certainly not expressive of a quality; rather, it is expressive of a substance. Why? Because of its connection with the feminine gender.

For these are indeed specific substances: female, male, and neuter. A feminine suffix is applied to that nominal stem which denotes a female; and we perceive the feminine suffix in the word *aruṇayā*.

Therefore, the word *aruṇā* denotes a substance. This [position] is not sound; for it is that very same substance which, being delimited by redness (*aruṇimā*), acquires the status of being denoted by the word *aruṇā*.
Therefore, this word "atom" (aṇu) is not able to denote another quality;
this word does not deviate from the property of redness (aruṇimā), whereas it does deviate from the substance.
And that which is non-deviating is the basis for the designation of being a cause.
Therefore,
its [the substance's] status is inherent;

for when color and other qualities are denoted by their own inherent nature, the substance is expressed as the qualifier, whereas in the case of "white" and so forth, it is expressed as the qualificand.
And for this very reason, because this definition has been established since beginningless time, it follows through the elision of the possessive suffix *-mat*.
However, that which has a beginning and is not universally established is not followed by the treatise in its destruction;
even without inference, it is sometimes perceived as possessing a more excellent relationship.

For example, in the expression "sweet taste is unctuous, cold, and heavy," because qualities such as unctuousness and coldness are specific instances of other qualities, they have no direct connection with "taste" itself; rather, they are connected with the substance characterized by that taste.

Therefore, since there is no connection extending to the limit of the potency (*śakti*), there is neither the elision of the suffix *matup* nor its presence. By this, the rule governing the presence or absence of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), and the distinction between grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), is explained.

Because this [quality] possesses the quality that constitutes its substantive base as extracted by the abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya), such as "whiteness" (śuklatva) and so forth, it is eternally related through a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya), just like smell. However, there is this much distinction here: even in this case, the qualifier is indeed the substantive; in the case of "whiteness," it is the white substance that is the substantive.
Subordinate to the substance, residing within its own nominal stem,
such [a quality] is subsequently extracted from the substance by means of the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth.
Therefore, this [color] possesses two forms, whereas odor and the like possess only one form;
likewise, the word "white" has its two forms in yet another way.

Sometimes a quality alone is expressed, while at other times it is perceived as belonging to a possessor of that quality. In the expression "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*), the quality is presented as something abstracted and dependent [on a substance], being subordinate to the substance denoted by the word ending in the genitive case (or its corresponding case-ending).
In the expression "the cloth is white," however, that which is inherent in the substance is being denoted.

Furthermore, among grammarians, the word *vacana*—referring to gender, number, and so forth—is used when the substance (*dravya*) is predominant, because it functions by expressing a quality (*guṇa*) and then referring to the possessor of that quality (*guṇin*).
For the grammarians do not enumerate qualities as the Vaiśeṣikas do.
What then? The conventional usage of "quality" and "possessor of quality" is based on the relationship between the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*).

Furthermore, words such as "white" (*śukla*) and the like denote only that which has become subordinate (*upasarjana*), whereas words for color and so forth do not; thus there is no confusion regarding gender and number. (This concludes the section on the theory of denotation and indication.)

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, keeping this very solution in mind, stated: "For even that which expresses a quality may possess neuter gender, as in the case of the words *karuṇā* and *buddhi*" (though it is read in the root-text as *yathā karuṇā buddhiḥ*). These two [words, *karuṇā* and *buddhi*], although similar to words such as *gandha* [which denote qualities], were cited because they serve merely as illustrative qualifiers. What is meant is this: even those words expressing qualities where the quality itself is primary are somehow joined with gender and number; how much more so, then, those in which the substance is primary?
Thus, by this reasoning, "aruṇā" is a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).

Bhāṣya (p. 685): Now, if it is not connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys), but is instead connected with the word *ekahāyanī* within that same sentence, there will be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
That is not so.
For the word *aruṇā* denotes only a quality (*guṇa*), not both substance and quality;

and the word *ekahāyanī* denotes only a substance, not [a substance] accompanied by a quality. Thus, without a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to express their relationship, how could that relationship be understood? [The opponent] says: Even without the genitive, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is understood from the indication of a single case-ending.
As in the case of "a blue lotus" (*anīlotpala*). That is appropriate.

By implication from the form [of the word], the term *aruṇā* denotes a quality; however, because of its connection with a single case-ending and its proximity to the word *ekahāyanī*, one must assume a single syntactical unit and thus accept its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ekahāyanī*.
And a sentence is not stronger than an indicative mark (liṅga).
Therefore, that [objection] is incorrect.
To this, it is replied:

When a word, functioning as a mere expression of quality (*guṇavacana*), does not obtain a connection with anything else, then—in order to avoid the consequence of meaninglessness due to its lack of syntactic capacity—it attains the status of referring to a substance (*dravyaparatā*). In that state, by entering into a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*) through proximity with the word *ekahāyanī* (a one-year-old cow) which bears the same case-ending, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises.
And having done so, the expression "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*) becomes logically possible.
And this word *aruṇā* functions in that particular state;
for it does not denote its own primary meaning [in isolation].
Even when separated from this [context], it possesses significance within the ritual context (*prakaraṇa*).

Why? For the very same reason that an immaterial object (*anāmṛta*) cannot be connected with the act of buying (*krīṇāti*), nor can it become an instrument (*sādhana*) for an action through other instruments of action; and because it is not the case that "a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) merely by relying [on another] denotes a substance (*dravya*)," that same reason applies even when there is a connection with the context (*prakaraṇa*). Even in that case, being connected, it must be connected either with actions or with the substances that are their instruments. To claim otherwise—that it is somehow inherently connected—is untenable.
Therefore, out of a desire to avoid meaninglessness, the word *aruṇā* (red) is connected with the proximate word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old), and there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
This is not so;
for this word *aruṇā* cannot serve as a qualifier of the *ekahāyanī*.
What is the reason? This [word] is uttered with the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇa-vibhakti*, third case).
Therefore, by virtue of the hearing of the instrumental case, it must function as an adverbial adjunct (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) to the action;
for the connection of *kārakas* (factors of action) is with the action, not with a substance.
This very [term] is an adverb by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*), whereas it is an adjective qualifying the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) by virtue of syntactical connection (*vākya*);
and direct statement is more powerful than syntactical connection.
Therefore, it has no connection with the *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow). [Objection:

It is said that the word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) is not connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (to buy); however, the opponent replies: "But if it is not connected with *krīṇāti*, then it must be connected with the *ekahāyanī*."

For it is possible to establish a relationship between a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) and a substance (*dravya*). However, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādī*), having heard the statement regarding the relationship with an action, explains that the relationship with a substance—being characterized by syntactical connection (*vākyalakṣaṇa*)—is sublated because of its weakness, by saying: "In that case, [the word] does not denote the quality alone. For the relationship of words is indeed twofold: either through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
In that regard, when both [words] denote both meanings [i.e., substance and quality], then grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs.
However, when a word denoting a substance is uttered in the genitive case, the connection is one of non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Therefore, in this instance, because the words *aruṇā* (red) and *kathāyanī* (belonging to Kathāyani) denote qualities alone, there exists at least coreferentiality based on direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Nor is there an explicit mention of the genitive case.
Therefore, because the force of the explicit mention of the instrumental case is stronger, there is no connection between the substance and the quality.

Thinking that this [author] states the refutation of the connection based on strength [of grammatical markers] with the intention that it is necessarily rendered invalid by a lack of authoritative evidence, he says: "Because of the employment of a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktiyogāt*; in the original text, it is *ekavibhaktinirdeśāt*).
"That is untenable" refers to the demonstration of relative strength and weakness.

First of all, from its own direct denotation (*sva-śruti*), it is understood that the nominal stem *aruṇā* expresses a quality (*guṇavacanatva*); furthermore, because of the proximity of another word, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This constitutes the strength [of the direct statement].
Regarding this, he says: "Even though the state of being solely characterized by redness is understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*)."
Nevertheless, due to the lack of any other recourse, one must resort to the function of indication (lakṣaṇā) based on the statement.
Now, because the third [case-ending] is stronger by virtue of its scriptural authority, it demonstrates a connection with a substance rather than a connection with an action.

Bhāṣya (p. 686): But surely, since a quality has no connection with an action, the case-ending expressing the kāraka is not intended to be significant; thus, this connection with the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) remains established. Even so, this is not tenable.

If the expression of the case-role (kāraka) is not intended to be conveyed, and it is sought to denote the substance by this word *aruṇā*, then, because there is no deviation from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the nominative case-ending would result.

Indeed, a word ending in the third case is not capable of expressing that relationship. Nor can another meaning be postulated for it on the grounds of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*), since there is no other meaning of this word that remains unaccounted for.

Just as when it is said, "The boy stands in the fire," since [standing] is impossible in the flame itself, one does not conceive of it as being in a horse or a cow; rather, it is determined to mean "in the vicinity of the fire"—so too here, the word *apramathyataḥ* cannot in any way apply to a meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is distinct [from its own primary sense]. Therefore, let it be admitted that it is purposeless; its connection with the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) is not necessarily established.
Or—(p. 686)—even there, Agastya offers this rebuttal: "But surely, because a quality has no connection with an action..."
The reply to that is: because it would entail the consequence of [the suffix] having a third meaning.
For it is not possible to convey a meaning that is not denotable by the word *agastya*.

And here, even by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the third case ending is not meaningful in the same way as the second case, because a general agent (*kāraka*) is also not intended [as the primary meaning].
Bhāṣya (p. 687): He says, "We do not say that the agent is not denoted by the word *aruṇā* (red).
Clearly, the agent qualified by the quality of redness is denoted by this [word]."

Sometimes something is the object of an injunction (*vidhi*), while sometimes that which is subordinate (*upasarjana*) is the object of an injunction and that which is primary (*pradhāna*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

For example, in the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī*), the word is understood as having the person as its primary referent with the staff being subordinate. Sometimes, however, when the person is already established, it is uttered for the purpose of enjoining the quality of the staff, as in: "The staff-bearer leads the way.
This is like the statement: "The priests proceed wearing red turbans."

Similarly here as well, even if the quality *aruṇī* (red) is subordinate and the *kāraka* (grammatical factor) is primary, nevertheless, a statement is appropriate for the purpose of enjoining the quality of redness with respect to the *kāraka* that has already been restated.
Therefore, the connection with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is established, and there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
This [argument] is not sound.
For here, this word *ekahāyanī* is uttered in order to make known the relationship between [the cow] and the act of purchasing (*krīṇāti*), a relationship not yet understood.
How, then, can this very word be connected with the word *aruṇā*?
This point, though already stated, is being questioned again and again.

(The word *ekahāyanī* is syntactically connected with the verb *krīṇāti*, not with the word *aruṇā*). But how is it that, when the word *ekahāyanī* occurs in the same utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with both the verb *krīṇāti* and the quality of redness (*aruṇaguṇa*), its connection must be accepted with the verb *krīṇāti* and not with that which is called "redness"?
[The answer is: Because of the authority of the word (*śabdaprāmāṇyāt*).

For there is indeed a case-ending that expresses a connection with an action, which is applied following the word *ekahāyanī*, but it does not express a connection with a quality. What, then, is that which expresses a connection with an action, and what expresses a connection with a quality? When a connection with an action characterized by a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is intended to be expressed, the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others occur.
Furthermore, when a kāraka is not intended to be expressed and only the mere relationship is intended to be expressed, the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) is used;
yet we do not see the sixth case here.

Indeed, we observe a third [element]; therefore, we accept its connection with the verb "to buy" (*krīṇāti*), and not with the word "ruddy" (*aruṇā*). The word *ekahāyanī* [is connected], not the word *aruṇā*.
How, then, does the connection "the blue lotus" arise here?
It is said:
it does arise, but not by way of direct audition (śruti); rather, it is by way of syntactical connection (vākya).

In proximity to a word that functions as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the word "blue" depends upon it; thus, accepting syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with it, it enters into a relationship while being uttered—not by abandoning its own primary meaning, but by being intent on denoting a specific secondary indicator. [Objection: But here too, just like that, a relationship characterized by a sentence would be joined with the eight-year-old cow.
[Reply: We say, "No."
For direct assertion (śruti) is stronger than syntactical connection (vākya). And direct assertion expresses a connection with the action, not a connection with a quality.

If, however, a connection with the action were accepted on the strength of direct assertion, then a connection with the quality would also follow from their forming a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva).
This is not possible.
For when one [term] is stated to have a connection with another, that other [term], even if it has already reached [the first], does not deserve to be connected with it.
Just as in the expression "the king’s wife, the man of Devadatta," the word "king," which is uttered for the purpose of qualifying the wife, is not connected with the man.

Therefore, in this context, the word *ekahāyanī*, being uttered as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) for the sake of the action, cannot enter into a syntactic relationship with the word *aruṇā*.

But another [teacher] says: "Just like gender and number, the meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadikārtha*) enter into the case-role (*kāraka*) by means of their substratum (*āśraya*), and thus they remain as objects of the injunction.

For there is indeed this view as well: that even from words denoting qualities (*guṇaśabda*), accusative and other case-endings occur because they serve as qualifiers of the case-role, even in the absence of a distinct word expressing the case-role itself.
"This is not the essence.

Even if, in some way, the word *aruṇayā* ("by means of the red one") were capable of being connected with the *ekahāyanī* ("the one-year-old cow"), nevertheless, since the one-year-old cow is dependent upon the action, its connection with the quality is set aside by the stronger connection with the purchase (*kraya*), according to the principle "In the case of a single substance serving another purpose" (*aikadhanye parārthavat*, PMS 1.4.18).
For here, unlike the case of a case-ending indicating a connection with an action, no genitive case-ending—which would indicate a connection with a quality—is observed.

However, in the case of the *nīlotpala* (blue lotus), because there is no contradiction with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), even a relationship characterized by *vākya-lakṣaṇa* (sentence-indication) is understood; thus, there is a disparity [between the two cases].

As for those alternative views regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), we shall explain them all under the section on the Sūtra: "The restriction is due to unity of meaning" (*niyamo vaikāthyaṃ hi*, 6.8.10.35).
In every respect, coreferentiality based on indication (*lakṣaṇaka*) is weak.

Nor is the case-ending of the subordinate elements (*guṇa*) a "kāraka" case-ending simply because it is a kāraka case-ending; rather, it is so precisely because they possess the status of being kārakas.
This point will also be discussed in the section concerning the intention to express the singularity of a word (Pāṇini 6.1.1–2). Bhāṣya (p. 688): He says, "This is indeed true."
In the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not a cause [of syntactic unity].
However, the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is established only when the meanings of the individual words have been made known, and not otherwise.
For a word functions with reference to a general sense (*sāmānya-vṛtti*), whereas a sentence functions with reference to a specific sense (*viśeṣa-vṛtti*).
If there is a subsistence in a remainder of those word-meanings that have been generally touched upon, that is the sentence-meaning.

This is what was stated [in the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "The recitation of those [words] which have become [part of a sentence] is for the sake of the action, because the purpose is caused by that" (1.1.25).
In that regard, the word-meaning is perceptible, whereas the sentence-meaning is inferential.

Let this be understood: a word that functions solely for its own meaning is *anupadeśa* (non-instructive) [in isolation], and thus it enters into a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with another proximate word, but not otherwise.

Therefore, in this case, although the word *hāyanī*—being connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (buys)—has fulfilled its purpose and does not require a connection with another word, the word *aruṇā*, however, being without a connection to another word and thus being meaningless, enters into a single syntactical unit with the word *ekahāyanī*. [Objection: But surely, its purpose is to connect with the action, not to connect with the word *aruṇā*.
He said: "We say that the word *aruṇā* is for the purpose of connecting both [the quality and the substance], in order to avoid its meaninglessness.
Even that which is performed for one purpose is capable of serving another purpose as well.
For example, when [channels] are prepared for the sake of rice, water is both drunk from them and collected."

In the same way here as well, the word *ekahāyanī*, being uttered for the purpose of connecting with the act of purchase, is connected with the word *aruṇā*; nothing is faulty in this. Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
[The opponent] says: "True, this is so"—yet he again strives solely to avoid the contradiction with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

How so? [It is argued: "When both are connected by a single syntactical unit (*tantra*), a contradiction arises; but when there are two [meanings] in one incidental context (*prāsaṅgika*), how will there be a contradiction? [Objection:
"But since the meaning of a word is understood everywhere, what is this proposal? It is replied:
"In every respect, the independence of word-meanings has been refuted;
therefore, even if multiple relations are postulated, there is no fault.
The word *aruṇā* must necessarily be connected with some possessor of the quality."

The word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) also has its independence removed due to its connection with an action; even when it is connected with another word, since it occurs only once, there is as much strain on the direct Vedic text (*śruti*) as there would be from a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), according to the principle that "what occurs only once cannot be burdened by a subordinate element. Therefore, it should be connected with the word denoting the quality as well.
(Now, the presentation of the primary prima facie view: Bhā—(p. 689) This is not so.
Even if this word *aruṇā* were connected with the *ekahāyanī* so that it might not be meaningless, nevertheless, it ought to be excluded from the entire context.
Furthermore, the word "he buys Soma" (*somaṃ krīṇāti*) is not capable of qualifying it.

For this [word] is not uttered as a qualifier; what then? This is enjoined as something previously unknown (*apūrva*). Or—(p. 689)—having accepted that there is no connection between the substance and the quality, [the word is used] because the root *krī* (to buy) excludes a connection with a different substance.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction here due to the simultaneous occurrence of both an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restatement (*anuvāda*).
However, where all [elements] are qualifiers of the action (*kriyā*), there is no difficulty because of the prescription of a qualified [action].

But where an action is enjoined as well as something regarding a substance (*dravya*), it is said that there is an absence of restriction, having accepted a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) characterized by the repetition of the suffix.
For a qualification must be something already well-known;

however, the purchase (*kraya*) in its state of being enjoined is not well-known. Therefore, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence that it applies only to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).

But which other one-year-old cow exists within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma? In any case, the accessory (*guṇa*) is obtained for her as well through syntactical connection (*vākya*); if, however, she is not present, what can be done?
But there will be some sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) either for the Anubrūyā [offering] or else; or rather,

because it is being pointed out as the object, and because only the name "one-year-old" (ekahāyanī)— characterized by the power of ignorance— is grasped, the term "one-year-old" should not be applied even to the Savanīya or the Agnīṣomīya [cows].
Or rather, that [objection] will apply to other similar examples.

For instance, in the case of "these ten cows for the Sudhīrmi," there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even though Soma is measured, the number ten would also apply to the *ahargaṇa* sacrifices, the *nirvāpa*, and so forth.
Bhāṣya (p. 690): But surely, even when something new (*apūrva*) is being enjoined, it will be connected with the other [element], just as in the case of the word *ekahāyanī*.

How so? For a word being uttered for a specific purpose is understood as serving that very purpose, and it becomes present in the mind. Thus, by means of what is present in the mind, a word possessing expectancy can be connected [with its object].
This is not so.
For that which, when connected, becomes meaningful is what is to be connected, and not anything else.
Why is this so? Because if it were connected [to something else], the general term would fail to convey the specific meaning;
in that case, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would be contradicted by the syntactical connection (*vākya*).

And this [word], not being connected with the verb "to buy" (krīṇāti), does not become meaningless; it will be connected with those [elements] contained within the context. But was it not said that even in the context, its connection is untenable? It is not untenable.
In a single sentence, one meaning being enjoined is not connected with another because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*).
For the mode of expression is different for that which is being enjoined, and different for that which is being connected with a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, the meaning being enjoined is understood as something unknown, whereas that which is restated (*anūdyate*) for the sake of connecting it with a subordinate quality is understood as something already known.
Furthermore, that which is being uttered only once cannot simultaneously be both known and unknown;

for instance, the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), while being enjoined in connection with the purchase (*kraya*), would be unknown [as a factor of the act], yet it would be known [as a quality] when connected with the word *aruṇā* (red).
However, there is no fault if there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

In the context (prakaraṇa), however, actions and other substances are obtained through other sentences; by means of those, what is enjoined in one sentence is connected [with what is obtained]. Thus, it becomes logical that in one case something is enjoined, while in another sentence something else is enjoined.

Therefore, because there is no distinction in its connection [with the substance] and because of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is to be applied to all substances within that context.

The opponent (*paraḥ punaḥ*), however, who maintains the position that the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is indeed red, offers a concise argument: "But surely, even when something new (*apūrva*) is being enjoined, as it revolves in the mind, it is qualified by implication (*prasaṅgāt*) itself.
To this, the reply is: "It is not so."

For as much as a thing is qualified, to that same extent there is a disruption of the natural flow of the scriptural statement. Therefore, one must accept that once a thing has been qualified by one [attribute] through a single application [of the word], it may be qualified by another as well;
nor is this redundant, because it possesses meaning within the context.
If it is argued that the relationship there is likewise the same,
we say no;
for if one were to enjoin a quality by way of restating a substance already obtained from another sentence, it would result in the fault of syntactical dissimilarity (*vairūpya*).

Even in the case of the "bhāvapakṣa" (the view that the action is primary), when the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is enjoined with respect to the purchase (*kraya*) in its own form, yet is mentioned as a qualifier with respect to the substance (*dravya*), there arises a dual nature (*vairūpya*).
Thus, the one-year-old cow cannot be connected at all due to this dual nature with respect to both the purchase and the quality.
The previous [authorities], however, accepted it merely as a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).
Now, that very point is refuted so that no fault may be attributed to the opponent;

therefore, this [objection] should be disregarded, as it would result in the absence of a basis for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by making this logic logically consistent with being an integral part of the purchase.
Therefore, according to the previous method, the insertion of the *āruṇya* (redness) occurs throughout the entire section; this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
[Bhāṣya, p. 611] This being the case, we reply:
when there is a single purpose, there is a designation of the substance and the quality as performing a single function.
Regarding the term "satya":

where the unity of purpose is heard between a substance and a quality, there the substance and the quality should be restricted to a single object. Why? Because of their oneness of purpose—that is, because they share a single function.
For a single purpose is heard for both the substance and the quality: their connection with the act of purchase.

How is this understood? From syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*). How is there syntactical unity? Because the meaning of "the red, the one-year-old [cow]" is not complete due to its expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), as the denotation has not yet been fully realized.
However, "he buys Soma" reaches completion, because those two [the substance and the quality] are mutually independent [in that context].
Or—(p. 611)—this being the position reached, it is replied:
"Where the identity of substance and quality is understood from the scriptural statement itself, there a mutual restriction between the two exists, as in the case of 'Being' (sat) and so forth."
The phrase "unity of purpose" (*arthakatva*) is an indication of a specific type of sentence;
furthermore, the term "because of being one" (*aikakarmyāt*) is taught as the reason for that very same thing.
Alternatively, the meaning is that syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is possible only when there is unity of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

In this regard, there is a single injunction for a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) qualified by all the qualifiers; because one achieves the fulfillment of purpose by performing it in such a manner, a universal restriction (*sarvaniyama*) arises through that inclusion.

Just as when it is said, "Devadatta cooks rice with wood," all [the factors] have the single act of cooking as their objective, so too here, since there is no performance of substance or quality alone, they are not enjoined individually.
A subsequent suffix is not capable of establishing a connection with another action;
however, in the case of a connection with a substance, injunctions are everywhere capable [of doing so].

For we shall explain in the subsequent section that, in every case, there is no operation of an injunction regarding an additional element that serves as a qualifier of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

And because of the third [type of] indication, it is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*) that there is a relationship between both the *aruṇā* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), which depend upon each other and require only the action to be accomplished, within that same location.

Why? Because the case-factor (*kāraka*) is heard in the sacred text; where does it perform the action? And it performs it toward the action. Therefore, a certain case-factor has a relationship with the substance.

Because there is no difference in their being already established, they do not depend upon one another; furthermore, because the qualities (*guṇas*) are themselves categories (*padārthas*), there is no relation between them due to their equality. Nor does an injunction operate toward their mutual connection.
The conceptualization of a relationship between actions [is expressed as] "we sing that" and "we [are those who sing]";
yet even action is not accomplished by anyone without certain factors of action (*kāraka*).
The connection between action and its factors of action occurs through the relation of the already-existent (*bhūta*) and the yet-to-be-accomplished (*bhavya*).

And just as they accept a substance as the means for accomplishing actions, so too do they accept a quality; thus, even in the case of the *araṇya* (wilderness), there is no connection with anything else.

Just as, because an action is impossible without a substance, the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is taken for the purchase, so too is a substance taken by way of a specific quality as long as it remains uncharacterized.
To that extent, a quality (*guṇa*) is required for the accomplishment of an action (*kriyā*);
therefore, that too is understood as being subordinate to the action.
And thus, in the rule "In the case of substances, qualities, and preparatory acts" (*dravyaguṇasaṃskāreṣu*, 3.1.13), the mention of "quality" (*guṇa*) was made.

[Objection: Since qualities are performed through the apprehension of the substance by way of invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*), and because there is no separate effort [required for them], there is no dependence on qualities as there is on the substance. For it is said: "Activity in an action is not intended to proceed without having taken up a substance;
but once the substance has been previously apprehended, its quality follows along. [Reply: It is said in response:
"Even when the action has been previously performed, there is no requirement for a substance;
if there were a prior requirement for a substance, that same requirement should be understood to apply to the accessory as well.

For just as by the mention of a substance those two [the substance and its accessory] are already included, such that a separate mention of the accessory is not required, so too upon the mention of the action, some substance is already implied, and thus [a substance] need not be further expected.

If, however, prior to the acquisition of the substance there is a requirement for a specific quality, then in the other case as well, prior to the acquisition of the substance, there should likewise be a requirement [for a quality], such as: "What qualities does the substance possess that I shall take?

In every respect, however, this much is the distinction here: even after the time of the question, the substance is pervaded by the action, whereas the quality, because it is already known, is not pervaded separately from the substance; for its purpose is fulfilled by that much alone.
Nor does that which is thus pervaded become something else, since the modes of operation are manifold.

However, at the time of delimitation (*pariccheda*), the predominance of this [quality’s] operation is distinguished. For it is said: "When an action is to be accomplished by a substance and is known [as such], then an expectation regarding what kind [of quality] it possesses is also sought in the quality."
Therefore, in this case, if the Veda provides some specific distinction in this manner, then [the word] will be determined by that;

but if it does not provide one, then—given the understanding that whatever is based on the meaning will be authoritative—it follows that the subsidiary element being enjoined, such as the quality of redness (*aruṇa*), becomes [part of the injunction].

And everywhere, because of the word, when a matter is not explicitly enjoined, the exclusion of ignorance is observed through the principle: "Or, [an injunction] is inferred from the sense, because of the location" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.4.25). When it is clearly enjoined that "the action is accomplished by means of redness," since there is no room for supplying words from another source or other such means, and since the principle "as far as one is able" is applicable, it is determined only this much: "by one who delimits the substance that serves as its means. Why? Because "it is established everywhere that such is the very nature of qualities."

It is not so, because of its being for sale and because of the specific favor [of the injunction]. First of all, the injunction pertaining to the purchase does not, in any way, relinquish the redness brought forward by the third [case-ending];
nor can that [redness] attain the status of being a part of that [purchase] through any other means.
Nor is the status of being a means (sādhanatā) for all [factors] of an unbroken nature;
nor is it accepted that action—whether consisting solely of motion or of transformation—is inherent only in its own substrate in every case;
nor [is this true] of the principal action.
In every case, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are directly [effective], because the relationship [between the means and the result] depends upon intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*).

And since redness (*aruṇā*) and the like are capable [of such operation], they are understood to perform their own function precisely through the delimitation of the substance (*dravyapariccheda*), because they possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) therein.
In other instances, they will possess the status of instrument (*karaṇatva*).
From that word *aruṇā* (red), this much is understood: "The purchase is to be accomplished by means of the quality of redness which delimits some substance.

Likewise, from the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old female cow) as well, since there is the possibility of its being a means in another way, only this much is required: "My delimitation must be performed by means of some quality.
In that context, the quality begins by requiring some substance to be delimited as its substratum, and the substance likewise requires some quality.
The relationship between the two characteristics is quickly established because it depends on both;
moreover, in this sentence, no mutual dependence among the qualities of the two other things is perceived.
Therefore, even without the substance of a naked horse, the relationship belongs to these two alone.
Furthermore, because there is no reason to override what is already established, it is understood that the singing (*geya*) must indeed be performed here.
Moreover: "The quality (*guṇa*) of a substance (*dravya*) obtained through the mention of its purchase is recognized as primary;
even if one does not desire it, the *citra* sacrifice restricts that quality to the substance."

Just as a quality (*guṇa*), because it cannot otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*), brings along a substance (*dravya*) even though it is not explicitly mentioned (*aśruta*), so too does the explicitly mentioned one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) bring along [the substance] that is not explicitly mentioned. However, the act of purchase (*kraya*) itself—because its quality is already heard in the text (*śruta*)—does not desire that [unmentioned substance], since its quality is already established. For if this [purchase] were to have an indefinite substance and quality, then anything whatsoever being brought along would suffice.

But precisely because of the specific, independent substance and quality, the purchase as enjoined would not be performed with both [indeterminate] qualifications; furthermore, there would result the repetition of what is already primary (*pradhāna*), which is not mentioned in the text.
Alternatively, in the case of an option (*vikalpa*), a specific injunction is stated;
and precisely because of the predominance of these two qualities, it precludes the purchase from another substance that does not possess those qualities.
Or, according to the maxim of the one who eats from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyabhojinī-nyāya*), even a subordinate element might prevent an unrestricted option, let alone one that is primary.

Nor is there an assumption of what is not heard (aśruta-kalpanā) without a logical inconsistency (anupapatti), because the two [terms] that are already heard become complete through their mutual connection.
In this way, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) found within its own sentence will also be justified.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with what is heard (śruti) here, as he will state: "The meaning of the sentence is not something other than what is heard."
For instance: "This very relationship, which is required by the act of purchase, is established once again;
and here, even a weak secondary sense (*vṛtti*) that is compatible is not contradicted."

For indeed, when purchasing a substance (*dravya*), one considers thus: "What quality (*guṇa*) will determine this? And when purchasing a quality, one also considers: "What substance will be its substrate?
Thus, although those two attain mutual compatibility by virtue of the purchase, there is no state of knowing or not knowing one another between them.

As for the one who thinks that because a quality (guṇa) is a delimiting factor, its subsistence in a substance (dravya) is understood, he should be told: since it is impossible to accomplish the purchase otherwise, the quality also attains subsistence in the substance, and thus it is called "anointing" (añjana). Therefore, it should be understood that while both [the substance and the quality] are auxiliary to the purchase, their mutual assistance—which occurs as an inseparable concomitant—brings about the state of being "anointing. Furthermore, as for the one who maintains that it belongs within the context (prakaraṇa), it must be stated by what means the quality is enjoined therein.
First of all, no connection with the act of purchase is intended;
however, the injunction of performance requires something that has the nature of an action,
and the word *aruṇa* (red) does not possess such injunctive power.
Although substances are perceived as factors of action (*kāraka*), nevertheless, those words [denoting them] are like non-injunctive sentences.
Even those injunctions which have actions related to them as their object are already exhausted;
they are not capable of enjoining [the substance] even though it is being perceived at present.
Nor do these have a function as qualifiers of a substance;
therefore, they cannot in any way be included in the context, for it would contradict the principle that "things serving a single purpose should be treated as options" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.1.4.10).
Nor is there a distinction [in their status as causes], for they have a single effect; rather, there is a difference in their capacities.
For a substance directly assists the action, whereas a quality qualifies the instrument.
If this is so, then the quality does not bring about the action itself, since it is merely a qualifier of the instrument.
This is not so.

It is precisely this capacity that belongs to a quality (*guṇa*) when it brings about an action: that it qualifies the instrument (*sādhana*). Furthermore, the action requires a qualifier of its instrument;
for a quality, serving as a mark, indicates the instrument.

In the absence of a mark (cihna), it could not be discerned which means belongs to which action; consequently, one would not determine the action to be performed. Thus, the quality (guṇa) serves as the means for the action. And this being so, there is no optionality (vikalpa) as there is in the case of the locus (adhikaraṇa) or the agent (kartṛ) and so forth.
For the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) sustains the agent (*kartṛ*) and the other factors;

if they were not sustained, they would be unable to bring about the action. Likewise, the agent gathers the agent and the other factors together; if they were not gathered together, they would be unable to accomplish their respective purposes.
However, when another means is prescribed for that very same assistance toward the accomplishment of the effect, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
For example: "One should sacrifice with rice" and "One should sacrifice with barley.
Both are intended for the purpose of producing the rice-grains.
Or—(p. 614)—he speaks without having grasped that there is a plurality of purposes due to intermediate operations, asking: "Why does the fact of having a single purpose not result in an option?
But the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) says: "It is not by this [argument] that the position of incapacity is refuted;
rather, either the inclusion within the entire context is established, or the connection with the purchase (*kraya*) is set aside."

Therefore, because it constitutes a refutation of another established doctrine (siddhāntāntara), it is a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna). As for the statement, "And there is no alternative [explanation], because there are various effects," this was said with reference to intermediate operations (avāntaravyāpāra). However, the opponent, thinking that what was stated refers only to the primary effect itself, says: "But was it not just now stated..."
"Nevertheless—[it is] contradictory" that which was stated previously, namely, that because it is immortal, [the Self] is devoid of action (*niṣkriya*).

Now, one might object: "The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) stated that; now the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*) does not say it has activity. Thus, the presentation of a contradiction is appropriate. It is replied: "A doubt is raised by everyone when situated upon a common ground."
In that regard, it would contradict even the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "it is formless.
Alternatively, it was stated as a reason by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*);
and a reason must be one that is accepted by both parties.
If this [reason] were unestablished (*asiddha*), it would have been pointed out at that very moment;
since it was not pointed out, it is therefore accepted.
Thus, if one now asserts its efficacy by stating it as if it were established, a contradiction arises for one who maintains its causal activity.
"This is not contradictory, nor is there any inconsistency," because there is no intermediate operation caused by a difference in capacity [between the substance and the quality].
He demonstrates this: "The substance is the direct means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), while the quality is for the purpose of defining that [substance].

But the opponent, thinking that the quality exists for the sake of the substance—just as in the expression "the other is for its sake"—says: "If it is so, then [the quality] does not at all bring about the action."

"'This is not so'—this [statement] first shows that the substance is merely a door [to the injunction]. Bhāṣya (p. 616): If that is the case, then it follows that there is an injunction of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) and the quality red (*aruṇa*) as its qualifier. In that case, the same fault would follow, namely, the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*)."
We do not say that the substance "red" (aruṇa) is connected with the word "one-year-old cow" (ekahāyanī).
What then? It is connected with the verb "to buy" (krīṇāti) itself.
For it is heard thus: "One should accomplish the purchase by means of the quality of redness."
And just as it is brought about by that [means], so must one strive;
moreover, since a quality does not accomplish an action through an unqualified means, it follows by implication that there must be qualifiers of the means.

Just as in the case of "one should cook in a pot," when the pot is indicated as the instrument for the action, one employs the pot for pouring and holding by implication—so too here is the case with the substance (*dravya*).
And therefore, there arises the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). [Vārttika, p.

619]—In this section, not seeing the fact of the matter—that the state of being the means (*dvāratva*) [of the redness] pertains to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*)—the author raises the objection regarding the resulting dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) caused by the sentence itself having to establish both the connection with the door and the connection with the purchase: "If that is so...
He shows that the mention of the one-year-old cow is brought about by the inherent capacity [of the word], stating: "We do not say that the word *aruṇā*..."
Bhāṣya (p. 616): But even so, would the sentence not be split?
How? Because it is observed that the completion of a sentence occurs with each [individual].
For example, in the statement "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra should be fed," the act of eating is completed with each person individually.
And just as in the case of the statement, "He whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma," so too here in the case of "He buys [the Soma] with a reddish one; he buys it with a one-year-old cow.
This does not constitute a sublation of what is impossible to accomplish.
Even so, it establishes the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) only in the act of purchase (*kraya*), not throughout the entire context.
Or rather—[the author] says this in order to refute the restriction [that the sentence must apply to the whole context], even while acknowledging its connection with the purchase:

"Even though there is a connection with the purchase, because the action differs for each factor (*kāraka*), the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) caused by a difference in meaning occurs only when [the connection with the purchase] is absent."
And thus, two examples are seen in common worldly usage and in the Veda:

in each case, the eating of Devadatta and others, or the fact that one's father or grandfather was not a Soma-drinker, when stated as the cause for the gift of a Prātya animal, is established through the intention to express their collective association (*sāhitya*).
In this context, the connection is "one should not [conclude] thus.
The presentation of the lack of connection follows from the very alternative position that "this is not a sublater of what is impossible to accomplish.

Bhāṣya (p. 616): True, this fault does not occur; however, the purchase would also result [as being possible] by means of a one-year-old cow that is not red, and also by means of a multi-colored cow that is red.
In that regard, the claim made—that there is a restriction between the substance and the quality—is abandoned.

If so, we do not say that there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). How so? For it is the substance and the redness (*aruṇimā*) that are enjoined for the purchase (*kraya*), and not the purchase for those two.
Furthermore, the primary element does not differ with each subordinate element; rather, it is the subordinate element that differs with each primary element.

Moreover, this illustration—that the completion of the sentence occurs with respect to the aggregate—is well-known, as in the case of "Let the Gargas be fined a hundred," or likewise, "Having pressed [the Soma] and offered [it], they consume [it]."
Therefore, the purchase qualified by both attributes is enjoined.
But how, given that other example, is it determined with certainty that the completion of the sentence occurs only in the aggregate and not in each individual part?
To this we reply:
In this case, both the substance and the quality of redness are perceived as connected to the action, yet they are not connected to each other.
The purchase, too, is perceived as qualified by both the substance and the quality of redness, and not by either one alone.

Therefore, if this statement intends the substance as its primary object and the quality of redness as secondary, then the connection with the purchase follows undoubtedly from the two distinct suffixes.
Now, the procedure for the purchase is being stated: since this [cow] is qualified by being one-year-old, and likewise qualified by being red, a necessary connection with both must be admitted.
Furthermore, in this context, neither the substance nor the redness is the desired end;
rather, it is the act of purchase that is desired.
Therefore, the substance for the Jyotiṣṭoma, namely Soma, is obtained.
Since both the substance and the quality of redness (aruṇimā) would be desired as being for the purpose of purchase, and not otherwise,
the act of purchase is thus enjoined.
And since it is not perceived as qualified by either one individually, the completion of the sentence occurs in the aggregate.
This is certain here.

And thus, at that time, there is no means of purchase other than the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), nor is the quality of redness (*aruṇa*) a qualifier of the means; therefore, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is established.
(Regarding the prima facie view: Here we reply:

if the quality enters into a connection as a means for the purchase (*kraya*), then, even though the sentence is divided, because it serves as a means for the purchase, the redness (*aruṇā*) is not to be applied to any other substance.
For what purpose, then, is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) established with such effort?
This is now explained:
