for when the sentence is split, the purchase (*kraya*) having the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) as its means is understood as one thing, and the purchase having the red color (*aruṇā*) as its means is understood as a different purchase altogether; it is not the case that the red color is enjoined within that very same purchase which has the one-year-old cow as its means.
In that case, since there is a separate purchase qualified by the quality of redness, another means would necessarily follow by implication.
Even that [objection] would be heard as a fault because of the quality of being reddish;
however, if there is syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), that is avoided. Therefore, it is rightly said.
"In the case of a single purpose, there would be a rule of syntactic unity (*aikakarmya*) between the substance and the quality.
To this, the opponent replies: "True, this is not a fault.
However, when the action is primary, the completion of the sentence occurs within the collection of qualifiers produced by that substance."
The resolution is that it is like the case of the staff, the giving, the sacrificial offering, the pressing, and the consuming.
Now, one might object: since the staff is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the staff, its repetition should occur for each individual [person], just as in the case of eating and so forth.
This is not a fault.
Where corporal punishment is prescribed, there each individual is distinct;
however, the fine of confiscation of gold is completed upon the collective group.
For when the offense is the cause, the number "one hundred" is not specified as a distinction.
The livelihood of those kings who perform that [duty] is now prescribed.

Just as for the *adhvaryu* and other priests, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is for the purpose of hiring because of its connection to the ritual act, so too for kings, the fines for wealth constitute their occasional livelihood derived from protection.
And since these [fines], such as the hundred *paṇas* and so forth, are levied upon various offenses as specific occasions, they are intended to have a singular number.

Just as that offense committed by the Gargas is performed by a single agent, or perhaps by many agents, it serves as the cause for the king to take a hundred [coins] as a fine. At that time, since the king stands as the recipient of the fine from the offenders, it is understood that "the king must collect a hundred from the entire group of Gargas. If the collection were made individually, once the offense had been expiated by one person with a hundred, the remainder would constitute an unscripted seizure of a Brahmin's property; furthermore, the number would result in an increase.

Therefore, the completion of the sentence occurs in the aggregate. However, the opponent, even though the specific reason has been stated, raises a doubt based on two examples. Because the comparison of the purchase (*kraya*) with the means of sacrifice serves as an illustration, and because it possesses the status of an injunction according to the principle of the simultaneous mention of "what has been" (*bhūta*) and "what is to be eaten" (*bhakṣya*), it is primary; furthermore, since substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) are the reverse of the previous reasons, the other [view] achieves the result of establishing syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*).

Regarding this, another says: "In every respect, since the restriction is established even for two things enjoined by separate sentences through the assumption of what was not previously heard, there is no purpose in [assuming] syntactical unity.

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) replies: "If there were a division of sentences, then based merely on the cognition of a purchase qualified by both attributes, and when the performance of the purchase occurs according to the individual connections as they were heard, it would follow that any substance whatsoever might be taken by means of the quality, and any quality whatsoever might be taken by means of the substance."

For at that time, there is no capacity for mutual proximity to imply or restrict [the object]; nor could a single action be capable of accepting both a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*). Indeed, since the purchase characterized by the quality of redness (*aruṇa*) has an unrestricted substance, why should it not take up some substance whatsoever established by the quality? Or why should the purchase of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) not take up some quality whatsoever?

Even if it were argued that the quality applies only to those substances for purchase already enjoined by other sentences, even so, it would apply to all ten [substances], beginning with the cloth (*vāsas*).
Therefore, for the sake of establishing a single act of purchase (*kraya*), syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) must be asserted;
and thus, it is established that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Śābarabhāṣya: "Because it is formless (*amūrtatva*), a quality (*guṇa*) is not at all capable of accomplishing an action."
"Therefore, because it has been purchased, its occurrence [in connection with the purchase] is not possible through syntactic unity.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"The instrumental case [ending] expresses the instrumentality of the accessory (guṇa) itself with respect to the purchase."
That [redness] is clearly understood, and it is logically connected by way of the substance (*dravya*).
As for the statement "he buys with the *araṇī*," it is either a case of confusion or it shares a single [grammatical] function (*kyai-kabhāk*).
Because of its connection with the act of buying (*kraya*), the redness resides in all the substances used in the purchase.
Furthermore, when there is a purchase by means of a substance, there is again a connection with its constituent part;
this follows the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow) and is illustrated by the example of Arundhatī.
The modification (*ūha*) is established.
*Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 1.1.9: "With the yoking of the chariot, he begins the *Māhendra* hymn. Here, the chariot is something visible, and its sound serves to set aside the [ordinary] mantra.
And thus, the expression "the sound is not [like] that of a chariot" is like "the sound is not [like] that of a chariot.

Nor should it be argued: "Since the two are understood through the copulative compound (*dvandva*) to be mutually concomitant, and since they are mutually restricted according to the principle of the 'ruddy one-year-old cow' (*aruṇaikahāyanī*), why is it not said that 'the sound is [only] of a chariot'?

For, in whatever manner the relationship between the meanings of those two terms is understood when two such qualifying words (*upapada*) are used in close proximity—even down to cowherds and women—it is precisely in that manner that the relationship between their meanings is understood.
In other cases, there is a dual objective consisting of two sides.

For this very reason, in the case of the *aruṇā-ekahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow), the relationship between the qualifier (*paricchedaka*) and the qualified (*paricchedya*) itself has a dual objective consisting of two sides.
[This is] according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the phrase "vasānau" (10.4.2), both masculinity and duality are understood as denotable meanings through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
In that context, because they are mutually restrictive according to the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow), the establishment of masculinity follows.

(Pūrvapakṣa: According to Ratna. 6|1|522, varṇaka 2, even though it is derived from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by means of a common suffix (*samānapratyaya*), the meaning of the nominal stem *aruṇā*—being more closely proximate and being the primary factor (*pradhānabhūta*) among the case-factors (*kāraka*)—is disregarded; rather, it is understood as a subordinate member of the action (*kriyāṅga*), and having been presented by the sentence (*vākya*) as a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), it is subsequently connected by implication with the word *ekahāyanī* through the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as its qualifier, according to the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* [rule].

Śā. 4.1.10: Even for those qualities that qualify Brahman, there is a distinct purpose consisting in the form of meditation, according to the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow). Parimala 3.1.188: [This is] because the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* is inapplicable here, since the subject matter concerns the taking up of something qualified (*viśiṣṭādāna*).

Su. p. 104: In that mental realization (*bhāvanā*) where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*), those [qualities], being independent of any other entity, subsequently receive the connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) obtained through the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī*.
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.6.1643, page 1069: "The word *aruṇa* (red) is connected only with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys).
And since a quality (*guṇa*) does not accomplish an action without specifying its instrument (*sādhana*), it follows by implication that it functions as a qualifier of that instrument."

Mā. 3|1|612, p. 696: The word *aruṇā* denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*). Since it is possible for it to express its status as an instrumental factor (*kārakatva*), syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the verb *krīṇāti* ("to buy") is established; therefore, it does not apply to all [ritual] elements (*sarvadharmatva*).
The justification for the connection of the word *aruṇā* with the word *ekahāyanī*, rather than with anything else,
is to be found in the section of the Bhāṣya concerning the "Aruṇā-nyāya.
Regarding the justification for the connection of the word *aruṇā* with the verb *krīṇāti* (to buy), this is to be seen in the Pūrvapakṣa under the "Aruṇā-nyāya" in the Bhāṣya and other works.
The investigation into whether the word *aruṇā* (red) denotes a quality (*guṇavacana*) or a substance (*dravyavacana*) is to be seen in the section of the *Bhāṣya* known as the "Aruṇā-nyāya.

[The view of] Ke. is that, by accepting the word *aruṇā* as denoting a substance qualified by a quality through primary denotation (*śakti*) or well-established secondary indication (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*), there is an injunction of a qualified factor (*viśiṣṭa-kāraka*) in reference to the act of purchase (in the passage: "He buys with the red one," *aruṇayā krīṇāti*).

If, by virtue of the mention of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-nirdeśa*), the *aruṇā* (the red cow) and the *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow)—which, being independent of each other, require only their respective primary actions—are understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*) to be related to that specific act of purchase (*kraya*), [then the following applies].

Just as there is a mutual restriction (*itaretara-niyama*) between "red" (*aruṇā*) and "one-year-old" (*ekahāyanī*)—such that the red one is not any other [animal] but specifically the one-year-old, and the one-year-old is not any other [color] but specifically the red one—so too, in the case of the word "two [men] shall put on [the garment]" (*avasānau*), there is a mutual restriction between duality and masculinity; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

And just as with the red cow and the one-year-old, because of this mutual restriction, there is a lack of universal applicability (*asarvaviṣayatva*) [of the grinding rule] in the case of the grinding for Pūṣan (*pauṣṇapeṣaṇa*). (Ratna., 6.1.522).
Or [it is] like the case of the *aruṇā* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow).

Now, an objection is raised: "Even if there is an injunction for the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant, since both are equally non-distinctive qualifiers of the act (*kṛtvā*), their mutual restriction is established—just as in the case of the *aruṇā* and the *ekahāyanī*—and thus it contradicts the cognition based on their syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*).
(Sudhā, p. 684).
In cases such as "aruṇaikahāyanī" (a one-year-old red cow), the relationship of qualifier and qualified is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
[Śabara-bhāṣya] Sūtra, p. 409:
The quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) is to be applied only to the act of purchase (*kraya*), not to the entire context (*prakaraṇa*).
"The connection of redness with the purchase is our position," Bhāṣya 3.6.162, p. 696. "The connection of redness with the purchase is our position," Bhāṣya 3.6.162, p. 694.
Arundhatī is the wife of Vasiṣṭha. Pāṇini-vārttika 3.4.19. The maxim of the observation of Arundhatī (arundhatīkṣaṇanyāya).
Because one who perceives only gross objects must, by the maxim of the observation of Arundhatī, eventually come to perceive the subtle;
as stated in the Siddhāntadarśana, Nirañjanabhāṣya 2.2.18: "The maxim of the illustration of Arundhatī."

In the illustration of Arundhatī, when these stars—which are merely folds [of light]—are shown as Arundhatīs, that other star which is pointed out becomes the primary Arundhatī; likewise here too, because the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the innermost of all, it possesses the status of the primary Self (*ātman*).
(Śāṃbhā. 1.1.12, Basu, p.
623) "Arka" means the sun; "artha" means capacity or efficacy.
In the statement "he takes the *arka*," a cup named *arka* is prescribed for the day of the equinox (*viṣuvat*).
Its combination with the archetypal cups (*prākṛta-graha*) occurs; there is no sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal ones.
However, the doubt concerns whether it is a different act of taking [the soma].
Bhāṭṭa 10.4.3:

"If one should find honey on the *arka* tree, why would he go to the mountain? What wise person would exert effort for the sake of achieving that which is already accomplished? This is the maxim (*nyāya*).
"Arkaḥ arka arkaṃ arkate"—this is the fourfold reading.
In that context, "arkaṃ arkaṃ" refers to the angle of the planet Mercury (*gṛhṇakoṇa*).
"Arka" is a specific type of Mercury (*budhaviśeṣa*).
—Near the sun.
This is the established meaning of the term *nyāya*. A compendium.
(For further details, see page 6 of the *Mīmāṃsākośa*).
If the goal were achieved through knowledge alone, why would they perform other means, namely ritual actions? This follows the maxim: "If one has the sun [right there].

(*Śāṃbhā.* 3.1413; *Vas.*). Just as those traveling on a path who pass by honey in a tree branch might not reach the mountain by that very same path if they disregard it—such indeed is that [attainment].

Moreover, they say: "If one should obtain honey from an *arka* tree. (Bhāṣya 1.2.14). For if a result equal [in magnitude] were to arise from both a small and a great action, then, by the very logic of "if one should obtain honey from an *arka*," no one would ever engage in the greater [action] when the goal could be accomplished by the smaller.
In that case, it would be so because of the power of the injunction:
There is a Sāman named Arkagrīva consisting of eight [verses].
Fool! On page 72:
Since Arjuna is a Kṣatriya, drinking *paiṣṭī* (liquor distilled from flour) is indeed forbidden for him;
however, drinking *mādhvī* (liquor made from honey or molasses) is not forbidden.
Su. pṛ. 195. [This refers to] Arjuna;
it should be consulted under the section "Vāsudeva-Arjunayoḥ.
*Artha* (purpose): Even when there are multiple things to be adopted (*upādeya*), they are understood as being connected with the primary element, even if separated by an interval;

for "purpose" (*artha*) is stronger than separation, according to Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 6.1.62, p. 1445. *Artha* (cause of happiness): What is the purpose? That which leads to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others, according to [Tantravārttika] 1.1.212, p. 18. *Artha* is an authority (*pramāṇa*) that indicates the sequence [of performance].
Maṇi, p. 13. Meaning (object):

[Ślokavārttika, Śūnyavāda 59].

All forms, such as a corpse and so forth, exist within a woman; however, a wandering mendicant or others perceive only certain forms according to their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and not everyone perceives all of them.
For a latent predisposition, which conforms to the two types of affectionate cognitions, intensifies the cognition that serves as its own cause.
The meaning is that it produces a cognition of exactly the same kind as the one by which it was produced.

Therefore, this [consciousness] serves as the cause for determining a form previously practiced with respect to an external object; it does not, however, conceptualize a form that was not previously [experienced].
For even one who has never before encountered an end does not, upon seeing a jar, see it as a woman, nor as its middle part.
(Ślokavārttika, Śūnyavāda, verse 184). The meaning is that the object is distinct from cognition.

Just as falsity is not possible when an object exists, so too the arising of cognition is not possible in the absence of an object. Therefore, for the sake of the arising of cognition, the object must also be admitted. (Rjuvimalā, p. 55). An object (the denotatum), in whatever form it is understood at the time of the word, is connected with that very same form by the subsequent word.

In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, during the *Mahāpitṛyajña*, it is stated: "To the *Barhiṣad* ancestors, parched grains (*dhānāḥ*).

Regarding those parched grains, threshing must be performed; however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a reversal of the order is accepted, such that threshing is done first to produce flour (*saktu*), and subsequently roasting is performed to produce the parched grains.
This is stated as being "for the sake of the purpose," meaning for the purpose of generating the parched grains.

Even if a reversal of the natural order—where threshing comes first and roasting afterwards—is accepted, because that reversal is for the sake of that [roasting] and because the purpose is the production of roasted grains (*dhānā*), the result would indeed be only roasted grains;
the sprouts would simply not be produced.
Therefore, the reversal must be accepted.

In the section concerning the revealed scripture (*śruta-śastra-adhikaraṇa*), it was shown that there is a conflict between indicative mark (*liṅga*) and order (*krama*), according to the principle: "It should be drawn away by the purpose" (*arthena tatprakṛṣyeta*, 2.1.14).
Thus [it is said].

Vārttika 3.3.14, p. 826. Oṃ. In the section concerning the sublation of the order [of recitation] by the purpose (*arthena pāṭhabādhaḥ kramakopādhikaraṇe*, 5.1.14), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding such passages as "He offers the *agnihotra* oblation" and "He cooks the gruel" is as follows: Bālakrīḍā, p. 137. Oṃ. Where a function is accomplished by the purpose (*artha*), there the word serves the purpose of indicating that meaning.

Furthermore, where the word itself is the effect, there the word itself conveys [the meaning] for the sake of the connection with the effect: Vi. 10.1.14. "By implication, that which is performed by the *codaka* is not obtained. Bhā. 12.1.12. "And from the sense."

Just as the sequence is established by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), so too is the sequence established by the purpose (*artha*), that is, in accordance with the objective. For instance, "He offers the *agnihotra*" [is stated] before "He cooks the gruel (*yavāgū*). Because the cooking of the gruel serves the purpose of the oblation, first there is the cooking of the gruel, and subsequently the offering of that very gruel. Thus, the meaning is that the authority of the purpose (*arthapramāṇa*) is to be combined with the authority of the scriptural statement (*śrutipramāṇa*).
Oṃ. That which is implied by the sense is set aside by what is directly stated in the Vedic text; likewise also that which is expressed indirectly.
Vārttika 2.1.3.12, p. 566. Oṃ. That which is obtained through the force of the sense is performed only where it serves a purpose.
Bhāṣya 3.1.18:
"Or rather, [the number] is to be supplied from the sense, because it is a part of the same context.
It is heard in scripture: "He cuts with the *sruva* ladle, he cuts with the *svadhiti* knife, he cuts with the hand."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should all substances—whether liquid, meat, or solid—be cut with the *sruva* ladle; likewise, should all be cut with the *svadhiti* knife or with the hand? Or is there a distribution according to the nature of the substance: liquids with the *sruva*, meats with the *svadhiti*, and solids with the hand?
Here, Prabhākara has described this as a distinct section (*adhikaraṇa*) out of a desire for systematic connection.
In this matter, it is understood from scripture that the *sruva*, the *svadhiti*, and the hand are, without distinction, the instruments for cutting.
Furthermore, the substances to be offered consist of a collection of meats;

yet it is not possible for all of them to be offered indiscriminately by means of the *sruva* and other implements. Thus, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the [Vedic] statement lacks authority because it contradicts the nature of the material objects and because the logical connection (*anvaya*) fails.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that [the application of the implements] occurs according to their capacity, as explained in the Bhāṣya.
That is appropriate.

If it is argued that "it exists" because a determination (*adhyavasāya*) is possible precisely through the lack of restriction (*avyavasthā*) according to the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) to be stated hereafter— just as the section (*adhikaraṇa*) is introduced in accordance with the *Vārttika*—

then, having established that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves to resolve doubt, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) is now established by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*) as a means of resolving doubt as well.
In this regard, the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:
It is understood from the verbal testimony that the *sruva* ladle and other implements serve as the means for the act of cutting portions (*avadāna*) without distinction.
Nor should it be argued that this is impossible because the *sruva* and other implements lack the capacity to serve as the means for cutting portions of meat.

Since it is possible for something to function as a means of proof by establishing its capacity even through a non-simultaneous relationship with the object solely by virtue of being a word, there would be total lack of restriction, such that everything would be understood by everyone at all times.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
this would indeed be so if capacity were not the determining factor here.
Indeed, in all cases, an injunction proceeds by depending upon the capacity of that which is to be enjoined;
for it is impossible to enjoin even by means of a hundred injunctions that which lacks the capacity.

In those instances where there is no established capacity that serves as the basis for the application, an application is made by the injunction itself through another means, having brought about the capacity [as indicated by the variant reading shown in the manuscript: "an application of the means is made by postulating the capacity"].

Furthermore, where a previously established capacity already exists, since the determination [of the meaning] is possible through the observation of that [capacity], the assumption of a disjunction (*viccheda*) is made precisely in accordance with it. As it has been said: "Now, where there is doubt and no supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) is found, there the decision is reached by means of the force of the injunction established through semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*)."
Thus [it is said] (Vārttika 1.4.14, p. 358).

Therefore, those three sentences—“he cuts with the *sruva* ladle,” “he cuts with the *svadhiti* knife,” and “he cuts with the hand”—possess the nature of being parts of a single whole as established by their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
This is because they are understood as parts through their respective purposes; or rather, it is an *adhikaraṇa* (topic/section) based on purpose. 625. Or rather, it is based on purpose.
[This applies] to those things that are combined.
As it has been said: "Just as the literal recitation is a means for comprehension, so too is the inherent capacity of the Vedic texts.
For this very reason, these [texts] do not record [the combined meanings]; they would record but a thousandth part [of what is actually possible]."
(Vārttika 1.4.14, p. 369) The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), everything must be understood by everyone;
however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is only through the aforementioned restriction.
As for the Sūtra: "From the sense" (*arthāt*) means from the capacity (*sāmarthyāt*); thus, the restriction is to be inferred.
Even by implication, [the word] serves as the cause for postulating the location of the sound, because it is a single part of the heard sound.

"Whoever, having understood an object of knowledge, speaks of it as something other than what it is, or does so himself—he would imitate the nature of a monkey; may he be rebuked by the loss of his fame and so forth, and may he undergo hundreds of births."
Thus ends the twentieth section on capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Thus concludes the section on Names (*nāmadheya-pāda*) in the *Tautātitamatatilaka*, the work of the Great Teacher Śrī Bhavadeva, whose other name is Bālavalabhībhujaṅga (in some manuscripts, the reading is *Bhujaṅgadra*).
Oṃ. Or rather, [the word] is derived from its meaning, because it is a part of the conceptualization.
It is heard in the scripture: "He cuts with the knife," "He cuts with the hand," and "He cuts with the ladle.
In that context, a conceptual construction must be made based on the sense or the capacity [of the words]. The construction should be understood through the capacity of the ladle.

The power of the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) lies in the taking up of two substances; the power of the hand lies in the giving of rice and the like; the power of the axe (*svadhiti*) lies in the giving of meat.
Having observed the power in each respective case, the application should be made accordingly.
Furthermore, that capacity should be understood as being merely a part of the injunction (*vidhi*).
"The capacity of verbs expressing their meaning is an auxiliary factor"—this is indeed the principle here.

In some cases, the determination [of meaning] arises from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), and in other cases, the determination arises from the context of the purpose (*artha*); such is the eightfold power of words.

Oṃ. From the sense of the passage and from the remainder of the sentence, the determination of the meaning of names whose meanings are doubtful is the best [method]. Oṃ. Or, from the sense, there is the topical section (adhikaraṇa).
The section on purpose;
the section on settled rule;
the section on capacity.
Or [the rule is determined] by implication, because it pertains to a specific portion of the conceptualization.

The Bhāṣya states: "It is heard in the scripture: 'He cuts with the *sruva* ladle,' 'he cuts with the *svadhiti* knife,' and 'he cuts with the hand. Or is there, by implication, a fixed distribution: liquids with the *sruva*, meats with the *svadhiti*, and solid masses with the hand?"
"Since there is no specific designation, there is a fixed rule.
This being the position reached, we reply: "The determination is from the sense; it is a determination based on capability.
One should take the portion with the *sruva* ladle, as follows:
Because it is possible [to speak] in that way, and because it belongs to that which is possible;
for those who speak of the meaning of verbs and nouns, capacity is the auxiliary factor.
If this is so, then a systematic arrangement according to capacity ought to occur.
Likewise, [the text says]: "Having offered once with the *añjali*, one performs the oblation.
The *añjali* is the joining of both hands; it must be opened, as is implied by the sense, for in that way the oblation can be accomplished.

For example, when it is said, "he ate on a mat" or "he ate from a bronze vessel," it is understood by implication that he ate while sitting on a mat and having placed the rice in a bronze vessel. Or: "Now, where there is doubt because no supplementary part of the sentence exists, the determination is made through the force of the context."

In rites such as the prayer for the grace and protection of the deities, *añjali* consists merely of the joining of the hands together; however, in cases such as "one should not drink water with the *añjali*," it is open.

When there is an injunction for a single oblation (*homacodanā*), whether or not there is doubt regarding the word, one must resort to the open form because the remaining part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) would otherwise be inconsistent.

But, by this very logic, since the remaining part of the sentence says "as far as possible" (*yathāśaktyā*), there would follow an eligibility for ritual action even for those lacking food, clothing, and so forth.
No;

because there is no doubt. Such an assumption arises only for the purpose of resolving a doubt. Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding the qualification [for the rite], because of the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa): "One should perform it in such a way that it is endowed with all its constituent elements as far as possible."
Furthermore, there exist such agents as Cakṣuṣmat and others; thus, the application of the injunction is not otherwise inexplicable.

However, in cases such as the "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīva) injunctions, where [the agent] will indeed exist, we certainly understand that even if the capacity [to perform it] were otherwise, the deficiency therein would be overlooked because the primary element has been enjoined.

Therefore, as long as an injunction is obtained with its own indicator (liṅga), so long is it considered Vedic; but once that is established, the assumption of it [as being authored by a person] lacks authority due to the theory of human authorship, since the establishment of the supplementary portion of the text depends upon [the speaker's] capability.
And it is said: "Just as the literal text is a means for comprehension, so too is the inherent power (*sāmarthya*) of the Vedic revelations.
For this very reason, these [texts] do not prescribe even a thousandth part [of what they imply]; rather, they would prescribe [the full meaning].

Thus, [the Veda] is constructed with great care through mantras, injunctions, and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), surrounded by the moat of tradition (*smṛti*), and concealed within the fortress of the Vedas.
Having entered the difficult terrain of the Dharma, which is capable of being invincible, he now masters the contemplation of the purposeful meaning.

Śā—Now, even in the determination of a doubtful matter, it is the capacity alone of an injunction (*vidhi*) whose authority has been established that is demonstrated as its authority. Therefore, the injunction itself, aided by power (*śakti*), determines the object to be enjoined according to its capacity.

"In the case of liquids and the like, [the pouring] of ladles and such [is implied]; and in the case of groats, the act of 'opening' [the vessel].
Because of the necessity of the purpose (*arthāpatti*), it is therefore established that there is a fixed rule."

Since the sentence is in the form of an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), its authority is established by way of its being commendatory; just as in that case, so too here, since it is not merely injunctive, its authority is demonstrated through another mode as well—namely, its being in the form of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Regarding the term *vyākośa*: the prefix *ā* is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*), thus *ā-kośaḥ* means "slightly opened," resembling a bud that has slightly blossomed, but not something to be completely set aside like [objections] in the context of prayers for the propitiation of a deity and so forth.
The connection [of this section] is due to the refutation following the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: by virtue of *sāmarthya* (contextual capacity), there may be the assumption that the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) has a fixed meaning, because that which is established through *sāmarthya* constitutes a part of the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*).
Here, the word “*saṃdigdhe*” (when there is doubt) from the preceding sūtra should be supplied;
therefore, where no doubt exists, a fixed determination should not be assumed on the basis of *sāmarthya*.

And likewise, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, according to the principle to be stated in the eleventh [book], since the scope of the root *iṣ* (to sacrifice) pertains to the ritual action as qualified by all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), there is no contradiction between the two meanings; therefore, first the rice must be cooked.

However, the *praiṣa* (the command) and the meaning of the *praiṣa* are recorded in reverse order; these two must therefore be performed in reverse order. [The opponent] objects: "In the previous section (*pūrvatantra*), since there was no other thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it was appropriate for the text to enjoin a meaning that was somehow already present; but here, because there exists another thing to be enjoined, that is not the case. This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). By the word "and" (*ca*) in the sūtra, the predicate from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*apakarṣa*).

Regarding the statements "He performs the Agnihotra" and "He cooks the gruel," the sequence [of actions] may be determined either by the order of recitation (pāṭha) or by the purpose (artha); however, it is established by the order of recitation, since that is observed in all cases.
First, the cooking of the sacrificial substance is understood;
since the status of *yavāgū* as the sacrificial substance is explicitly stated in the scripture, the sequence follows from the sense of the matter.

Bhaṭṭa: "Artha" means purpose (*prayojana*). And that [purpose], being otherwise impossible (*anupapadyamānatvāt*) due to a reversal of sequence, is the authority for the [correct] order. For example, in the case of "He offers the *agnihotra*" and "He cooks the gruel (*yavāgū*)," the cooking of the gruel must come first because of the order of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). This is because the purpose established by the scriptural statement "He offers the *agnihotra* with gruel"—namely, the act of offering—is not accomplished if the gruel has not been prepared by cooking; and furthermore, although cooking does produce the gruel, that gruel cannot serve as the purpose [of the offering] if it remains unutilized. Since this would otherwise be impossible, cooking comes first and the offering follows.

Nor does the grammatical rule "And the third case [is used] after *hu* in the Veda" (*Pāṇini* 2.3.2)—which means that the third case is used for the object of *hu*, and by the word "and" (*ca*), the second case as well—imply that because the third case in the sentence "He offers with gruel" (*yavāgyā juhoti*) indicates that the gruel is the object, the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) is not established. Even if that were so, since there is no utility for the gruel itself, one must accept a disruption of the application (*viniyoga-bhaṅga*) within the very sentence concerning the oblation, according to the principle of the single instance (*sakṛnnaya*, *Jaiminisūtra* 2.1.12).
However, since cooking has a visible purpose, it is indeed a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*).

In reality, however, the primary expressive power (*śakti*) of the third case-ending lies only in instrumentality (*karaṇatva*); as for objecthood (*karmatva*), it is merely a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on contextual necessity.
And in this context, there is no such necessity.

Therefore, this traditional rule (smaraṇa) is intended only for those cases where, as in the instance of the "fourfold portion" (*caturavatta*) and the like, there is actually a functional utility; only in such cases does the cognition of objecthood arise even when a sentence such as "he offers with the fourfold portion" exists.
And here, the purchase (kraya), which is presented by the sense of the text, is enjoined by the injunction of performance (prayogavidhi) itself;
thus, it is also to be understood from the very recitation (pāṭha).

Like other subsidiaries, its application (viniyoga) occurs through a syntactical connection (śruti) imagined from the sense, while its mere performance (prayogamātra) is established by the injunction of performance—this too can be asserted.

In reality, however, it should be understood that when the performance of ritual items (*padārtha*) is enjoined by virtue of a specific purpose (*prayojana*), the sequence (*krama*) is merely incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*); therefore, there is no injunction for that sequence itself. Furthermore, it must be recognized that "purpose" (*artha*) is also a regulator of sequence. In fact, in cases where the sequence follows the order of recitation (*pāṭha*) without contradicting the purpose, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), because the sequence is obtainable through other means.

Furthermore, in cases where there is a conflict in the textual order, it should also be understood that this serves as an indicator of that very same *apūrva*. Maṇḍana [states]: "In the case of cooking and the *agnihotra*, that sequence exists by virtue of the purpose (*artha*)."
Śaṅkara says: "Only in the case of cooking and the Agnihotra sacrifice. This is the authority for the sequence.

Regarding the fourfold objects—since people in the world consider their purpose fulfilled by the mere production of a cognition, they disregard the discrimination between the fourfold objects consisting of the denoted, the implied, the fit, and the contextual.
Vārttika 3.4.4.13, p. 132: The meaning that is denoted (*abhidheya*) by words such as *go* (cow) is the genus (*jāti*); the meaning that is understood (*gamyamāna*) is the individual (*vyakti*);
the meaning that is manifested (*dyotya*) by prefixes (*upasarga*) such as *pra* is the action of going (*gamana*), and so forth.

for words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus") which possess both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) meanings, the referent is "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*), because it is the substratum of the single property co-inherent [with the action] that consists in being the agent of production from mud (*paṅkajajanana-kartṛtva*).

Mīmāṃsā: For all these words, worldly usage is accepted as the means for knowing their meaning. Bhāṣya 6.1.1.1, p. 1347. [This is] a sūtra of the Siddhānta (conclusion), because it establishes that when there is a conflict between two meanings, or in the absence of the substance, since the production [of the effect] arises from that [substitute], substances are subordinate to the purpose; thus, even when the primary substance is available, one must take only a substitute due to the incapacity of the [primary] task.
*Artha* means purpose;
*dravya* is the means for accomplishing it.
When a conflict between these two arises, it should be understood that *artha* is the more powerful.

In the absence of the substance—meaning, when the primary substance capable of performing the function is unavailable—a substitute must be sought for its production. Indeed, the non-availability of the primary substance capable of performing the function is the reason for taking a substitute. This is because substances are subordinate to the purpose; for a substance is the means that accomplishes the purpose, which is the goal.
However, when the purpose cannot be achieved, it is not proper to employ even the primary substance that has already been obtained.
Therefore, in such a case, only a substitute (pratinidhi) should be accepted;
for if one were intent on the purpose, the abandonment of the substance would result.
Thus, it should be understood that there is a contradiction between these two.

For example, when the primary *nyagrodha* tree intended for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is obtained, it is incapable of the consecrations such as carving and so forth, and is also unfit for the tethering of the animal; whereas the substitute (*pratinidhi*), the *kadara* tree, is capable of the carving and so forth, and is fit for the tethering of the animal.
[This illustrates] the injunction of two purposes, which constitutes the efficient force of meaning (*arthabhāvanā*).
It is possible [to obtain it].
This being the case, only a substitute (*pratinidhi*) should be accepted, and not even the primary substance (*mukhya*),
because it would be a fault to enjoin two distinct meanings by means of a single sentence.
For the connection with the *adhyā* and other [mantras] occurs through the medium of the meaning (*artha*), not by relying on the literal form of the text. (Vārttika 3.1.1.1, p. 649).

According to the principle that "when the purpose is distinct, [the mantra] is repeated" (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 1.1.39), there is a repetition of the mantra at each instance [of the rite], such as in the pouring of the materials (*saṃbhāranivapana*) during the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*).

and this [capacity] exists in both the primary and the secondary sense in some manner or other.

Vārttika 3.1.2.16: For factors such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, when obtained by implication, do not become the actual denotata of the word.

But these [prohibitions] do not result from the meaning [of the injunction]; therefore, they constitute the literal meaning of the words. Bhāṣya 3.4.1.3, p. 927. Regarding that which is obtained through the sense—just as in common worldly usage, when a prohibition applies to something already obtained through its own nature, such as: "Poison must not be eaten," "One must not step on what is smeared by snakes and the like," or "A thorn must not be stepped upon with the foot"—in such cases, there is no option (vikalpa) regarding that matter; it is simply fire [to be avoided]. Therefore, we consider that between an injunction and a prohibition, the prohibition is the stronger.

*Mā.* 10.8.12.12: Regarding the statement "If it is argued that it is like what is obtained through the sense" (10.8.12), it will be stated there that when something is established as being obtained through the sense of the words, a prohibition that is encountered even while an injunction or permission is being obtained becomes more powerful.
*Vā.* 12.1.2, p. 107: *Arthabhāvanā*.
"But another [bhāvanā], the objective bhāvanā (*arthabhāvanā*), is understood in all verbal suffixes."

For when the *bhāvanā*—expressed by the verbal root and consisting in human effort—is understood as following all finite verbs (*ākhyāta*), then those [meanings] situated therein, which are expressed by specific words internal to the general category of finite verbs, are perceived through injunctions, prohibitions, the past, the future, and so forth;
as in: "he cooks," "he cooked," "he will cook," "he should cook," and "let him not cook."

Vārttika 2|1|1|1, p. 378: "The object of desire (*icchādyartha*) is that which is desired (*arthyate*). From the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of the root, when there is a desire to express the agent, the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3|1|56 (*erac*: the suffix *ac* occurs after a verbal root ending in *i*). Thus, by the application of the suffix *ac*, the person who desires (*arthin*) is identified with the object (*artha*), because of the superimposition of non-difference between them. Furthermore, since the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*) is a property of the person, and because there is no absolute difference between a property and its possessor (*dharmadharmiṇoḥ*), identity (*tādātmya*) is intended. Therefore, the analysis (*vigraha*) should be made as: "the mental disposition whose essence is the object" (*arthātmā cāsau bhāvanā ca*). Alternatively, as stated in the Vārttika, it may be analyzed as "the mental disposition whose essence is the object" (*arthātmabhāvanā*). However, this [mental disposition] is distinct from the other [mental dispositions].

Su. P. 560: In the Mīmāṃsaka school, the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is precisely the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) in the form of being qualified by its causal factors (*kāraka*).
Bāla. P. 73: The objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) alone is the content of the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*).

Maṇi. P. 91: Furthermore, the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) is expressed by every finite verb (*ākhyāta*), as it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "to do" (*karoti*), as in "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*).

*Bāla.*, p. 74: The objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*), presented by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), requires these three factors in succession—*what*, *by what*, and *how*. When the expectancy arises, "What desired thing should one bring about?", the answer is that the sacrifice (*yāga*) is to be performed as the instrument (*karaṇa*), not as something yet to be accomplished (*asādhyatayā*), in the sense that "one should bring about something else by means of the sacrifice. Then, when the expectancy arises, "What is this other thing?", the objective productive energy accepts as its object (*bhāvya*) heaven itself—which is supplied by the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*)—precisely because it is not yet established (*asiddhatayā*) and thus stands in need of being brought about.

For, by the primary function of the word (*śrutivṛttyā*), the state of being the object to be brought about (*bhāvyatva*)—which primarily belongs to the "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) as the referent of the term—is restricted to the specific qualification within the cognition of the particular [injunction].

Thus, the result is: "One should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice. The resulting cognition is: "An activity (effort) which has sacrifice as its instrument and heaven as its fruit is the object of the instigation (*pravartanā*)."

Where the fruit is mentioned in close proximity [to the injunction], there it is understood through the mention of another factor (*parakaraṇa*) and so forth; in the absence of even those, it is understood through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that depends on the injunction (as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifices); and in the absence of that, a specific fruit is postulated according to the principle of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice.

Although the sacrifice is not the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that culminates in human exertion, nevertheless, there is a metaphorical designation of "instrument" for the sacrifice when it serves as the instrument with respect to the qualification of the productive activity delimited by the fruit. Thus, in this context, being the object of the volition that impels one toward the fruit is precisely what constitutes its status as the "instrument."
In common worldly usage as well, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is exactly the same in expressions such as "he makes a jar with a stick.
Regarding the question "by what?", others hold that the answer is "the act of becoming possessed of some wealth is the means for attaining heaven.
On this point, the ancients maintain that there is a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by the instrumentality of the sacrifice.
In reality, the syntactic meaning of the sentence is that the sacrifice possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) or a relation;
thus, the connection of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) between the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth with that [instrumentality] is uncontradicted.

And in this way, when the realization arises as to how heaven can be brought about by a sacrifice that has perished, the conclusion is reached that it is done "by producing the *apūrva* in the interim."

Thereupon, the collection of procedural requirements (*itikartavyatājātam*), which is connected as the "manner of performance" (*itthambhāvena*) to the production of the unseen potency (*apūrvabhāvanā*)—in response to the question "How is the unseen potency to be accomplished by means of the sacrifice?"—is said to be "prompted by the unseen potency" (*apūrvaprayuktam*).

Then, when there is a requirement for the specific mode [of performance], through the syntactical unity of their respective prescriptive contexts (*svādhikāraikyavākyatayā*) with such injunctions as "He offers the *samidh* oblation," which expect specific sacrifices, it is understood that "By means of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, he accomplishes this unseen potency through these productions consisting of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Once this is understood, the *prayāja* offerings and others are subsequently construed as being for that purpose (*tādarthyena*), and their status as a "contribution" (*upakāratvam*) is inferred.
Thus, in the view of Bhaṭṭa, this [injunction] is the communicator:
"The sacrifice, which has as its locus one who desires heaven, has heaven as its fruit.
[This is] the Arthavāda; [this concludes] the section on Arthavādas.

The purpose of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) must be determined through the interpretation of those explanatory passages. Since the taking [of the animal] has been enjoined, there must be an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the female donkey; thus, it must be stated that the passage culminates in a meaningful purpose characterized by such an exclusion.
And that object is obtained; such is the meaning of the second sūtra.
[With the words] "O wide one, spread yourself out," [he spreads] the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
Discourses are of two kinds:
those supplementary to injunctions and those supplementary to prohibitions.
In that regard,
"prathasva" (spread out) is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the injunction "he spreads" (*prathayati*).
"One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," and so forth, refers to the specific objects of the injunction.
The inclusion of the word "mantra" [is for emphasis]. The particle "vā" has the sense of "eva" (only/indeed).
Such is the meaning of the third sūtra.
Its purposefulness lies in its being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*).

[Examples such as] "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam*) and so forth are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Even though they lack [independent] primary purport (*tātparya*), they function as indicators of praise (*stuti-lakṣaka*).

And regarding the prohibitions and the remaining explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*), they [serve] by virtue of being sentences that convey the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*);
that is, through the authority of the sentence itself.
This is because they consist of the censure of the prohibited act.
And for this reason, the excellence of the *lakṣaṇā* (indicative power) is designated separately by means of *arthavādas* (explanatory passages);
however, in reality, it does not exist as a separate form of sentence.

The *arthavādakalpa* (the assumption of an injunction from an explanatory passage) is as follows: "The [oblation] remains unfailing on the new moon and full moon days in the pot-sherd," which is like an injunction.

An example of the *arthavādakalpa* as a supplement to another injunction is: "Therefore, let only forest [food] be resorted to. By means of this supplement to the injunction, the prohibition of beans (*māṣa*) is inferred through the passage, "Indeed, these do not take beans as an oblation," which is like the injunction, "For he holds [the ladle] above for the gods."

*Bālapriyā*, page 30: The assumption of an injunction (*vidhi*) based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is of two kinds: that which is assumed from an independent explanatory passage, and that which is assumed from an explanatory passage subordinate to another injunction.

The former is also threefold: that which is assumed from an explanatory passage concerning a result (*phala*), that which is assumed from an explanatory passage concerning an established fact (*siddhavṛttānta*), and that which is assumed from an explanatory passage consisting of a narrative (*upākhyāna*). The latter is also twofold: that which is based on a narrative having a single agent, and that which is based on a narrative having multiple agents.

Among these, that which is to be inferred from a statement of result (*phalārthavāda*) is, for example: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report. That which is to be inferred from a statement of established fact (*siddhavakīrtana*) is, for example: "Three, indeed, are the bellies of the sacrifice—the *gāyatrī*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *triṣṭubh*; for in them they pour in, and from them they draw out. That which is to be inferred from a traditional report (*parukti*) is, for example: "To those two he offered this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma at the full moon," because [the agent] is connected as the performer of the action.

That which is to be inferred from a past model (purākalpya) is, for example: "In former times, one sacrificed with the Agniṣomīya [animal] at the full moon using ghee, silently and with the dust [of the altar].

That which is to be inferred from an explanatory passage (arthavāda) supplementary to another injunction is, for example: "For he holds it above for the gods" (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 5.3.9, p. 198). A name occurring within an explanatory passage does not constitute a basis for extended application (atideśa). Furthermore, each individual word within an explanatory passage does not individually indicate commendation (*prāśastya*); if that were the case, other words would become redundant. Rather, it is the entire sentence of the explanatory passage that indicates it.
Soma. 10|8|518. The reference to the *aṣṭākapāla* and other offerings in the *vaiśvānara-hetu* is found within an *arthavāda*. Vi. 4|4|12.
The mention of the *upavīta* and the duty (*dharma*) regarding the two types of *pretāgnihotra* is found within an *arthavāda*. 3|4|4.

That even a mantra possesses the status of an *arthavāda* is stated by the sūtra, "The *arthavāda* is meaningful because it has that [mantra] as its purpose" (4|4|124), and by the commentary on that [sūtra]: "In this way, the mantra-*arthavāda*—'Thus the youth, well-dressed and adorned, has come around'—will become meaningful."
Thus, regarding other Vedāntic passages such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," Bhaṭṭa Someśvara stated that this too is merely "typical" (*prāyika*) (p.

435). He further remarked that [the example] "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" and so forth is intended as an illustration (in the *Sudhā* commentary on the aforementioned sūtra; however, this specific line is not found in the text available to me).

Thus, the "vidvadvākya" (the statement concerning the one who knows), namely, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day," serves to establish the existence of a collective [of rites] for the purpose of supporting the injunction "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," just as the statement "he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva" does. It is like the illustrative arthavāda (explanatory passage) regarding an existing fact, which serves to establish a collective for the purpose of supporting the injunction "with the Vaiśvadeva [offering] on ground sloping toward the east.
Another example is: "Holding the fuel-stick below, he follows; for he holds it for the gods."

In this third [section], it is stated that even for the *uparicaraṇa*, there is an injunction (*vidhi*) by means of the exclusion of the word "hi" (indeed). By this much, the threefold nature of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) has been explained. Furthermore, the *arthavāda* is of eight kinds, beginning with the *aṣṭi*.
Blessing (*āśīḥ*): "He desired, 'May I create offspring.
Raving (*pralāpa*): "And we do not know this: whether we are Brahmins or non-Brahmins.
Lamentation (*paridevana*): "Those who were mocking me have now mocked me in return."

Similarly, there is that which has the form of lamentation (*paridevana*). For instance, in the *Vārtika* on the section concerning "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), it says: "He who, being one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), performs the *agnihotra* but does not perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, makes those deities who partake of the oblations go astray. This is of the nature of lamentation. It has been stated that this is an *arthavāda*. (Regarding this, the line from the *Vārtika* reads: "Being one who has maintained the sacred fires, when [the performance of] initiation and giving and so forth are prohibited, [this statement] becomes an *arthavāda* in the form of lamentation for the sake of praising another injunction.")
629) The command (*praiṣa*) is: "Bring the immortal Soma.
The search (*anveṣaṇa*) is: "He is here, he is there."
Question: "The Veda is a glowing iron image with ears.
Answer: "We know it indeed. Supplement:

"If one were to scratch [the head] with [one's own] hand, offspring would be afflicted with scabies; if [one were to scratch] with truth, they would be free from scabies; therefore, one should scratch with a black antelope horn."
In this context, regarding the phrase "O brothers of the sky," the word "progeny" (*prajāḥ*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

Thus, there is an abundance of ritual injunctions: "The exponents of Brahman deliberate, 'Should one suspend [the rites], or should one not suspend them? Regarding this they say: 'One should indeed suspend them; on the new moon and the full moon days they should be suspended, for these two carry the sacrifice,' yet they also say, 'They should not be suspended by those who perform the intermediate sacrifice.

Thus say the followers of the Upaniṣads: "'On the impulse of the god Savitṛ'—he takes up the *sphya* [sacrificial wooden sword] on the impulse"—this is the remainder of the injunction concerning the purpose of the action.

"He says, 'By the arms of the Aśvins,' for the two Aśvins were the Adhvaryu priests among the gods; he says, 'By the hands of Pūṣan,' because of that. This is in the form of a narrative: "The gods indeed sacrificed a man as an animal; from him, once sacrificed, the sacrificial essence (medhas) departed and entered the horse; therefore the horse is the sacrificial essence, and [the sacrifice] is called Aśvamedha. From that he fashioned the sacrificial essence, which became a Kimpuruṣa. They sacrificed the horse; from the horse, once sacrificed, the sacrificial essence departed and entered the cow," and so forth.

Explanations based on cause (*hetu-vākya*): for instance, "He offers with curd" (*śarpeṇa juhoti*), and as a supplementary statement to that injunction, "For by that, the purpose is accomplished" (*tena hyaṃ kriyate*).
An etymological explanation (*nirvacana-rūpa*): "Because he ate that, therefore it is called *dadhi* (curd)" (*tadenamadhināt tadabhno dadhitvam*).
A declamatory passage expressing censure (*nindārthavāda*): "The Brahmin does not sing the *Sāman* chants," which is a declamatory passage for the sake of a prohibition.
"Indeed, the gods have passed by him who is without the *upavīta*.
This is a praise: "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity.

Although the purpose of praise is uniform across all *arthavādas* except for those intended as censure, nevertheless, there is a distinction: here, through the praise of Vāyu, there is a praise of the enjoined sacrifice to Vāyu involving a goat (*vāyavyapaśuyāga*), whereas in other cases it is not so.

An explanatory statement based on doubt (*saṃśayārthavāda*) is: "It should be offered into the *gārhapatya* fire; it should not be offered. An alternative injunction (*vidhikalpaka*) is: "The *audumbarī* post is to be of a height equal to the sacrificer.

A report of another's action (*parakṛti*) is: "'Thus indeed said Baṭu Kurmaṇipāna, "I cook for a great [purpose]"'; therefore, one should resort only to forest food"—this is a supplement to an injunction.

The ancient legend (*purākalpa*)—"In former times, he [Indra] struck down the Asuras and Rakṣasas at the assembly with firebrands"—and the injunction "Therefore, having churned the fire-drills of the householder, they should offer [the oblation]" do not establish the mere generic class (*jāti*) of being a *puroḍāśa* cake.
This too is established by the very principle: "In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (*sūtra* 1.4.29).
An injunction regarding a genus (*jātividhi*) is as follows: "Therefore, one should sacrifice with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone, not with water, silently (*upāṃśu*) on the full moon day.

This too, because its purpose is to enjoin the time of the full moon which was not previously established, is not an injunction of the genus *ājyatva* (the state of being clarified butter). Indeed, it is stated in the tenth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the genus already established by the text, "That which is the clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice," which serves to delimit the substance of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
According to the author of the Vārttika, the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is: "He places [it] well-steadied" (*sudhīrupadadhāti*).

The Commentator [Kumārila] maintains that there is neither a prescription for the mere act of placing (*upadhāna*) nor a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the mantra; rather, since faults would arise from prescribing the mere act of placing and faults would likewise arise from prescribing the mantra alone, and since a specific prescription would entail the application of only those primary mantras possessing the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the injunction of the number seventeen is established through secondary indication (*gauṇī*) based on the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*): "That he places seventeen.
This very point was clearly explained by Bhaṭṭa Someśvara in *Bhūmā* (JS 1.4.12–13).

A quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) of the same form [as a mandatory injunction] is: "When it is on one potsherd, the *gāyatrī* purifies him with Vedic splendor. This is because it has the nature of an injunction for an existing class of things.

This very point was discussed in the section concerning Vaiśvānara (1.4.12). An injunction regarding action (*kriyāvidhi*) is: "While holding the fuel-stick below, he should run after [the oblation]," the remainder of which sentence is: "For he holds it above for the gods."

Regarding that which was stated in the third [section] (3.4.15), since the phrase "from the gods" is used, it is understood that in the *daiva-agnihotra*—the fire sacrifice performed while one is alive—the practice of placing the ladle over the fire (*uparidhāraṇa*) is not established by custom or other means; therefore, a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) is inferred by abandoning its connection with the [preceding] context.

The nature of the injunction regarding the action (*kriyāvidhi*) is as follows: "That which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti; that which is undercooked belongs to Rudra; that which is well-cooked belongs to the Sadās. Therefore, it must be cooked by one who burns it for the sake of the Sadās. This statement, intended for the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, is cited by the Author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) in the *Audumbara* section under the sūtra: "And when [an injunction] is possible within the context (*prakaraṇa*), an alternative (*pakṣa*) is not to be assumed, for [the assumption of such an alternative] would render the injunction purposeless with respect to that context" (1.4.24). He explains: "But in the case of an injunction [of a specific quality], it would be brought in wherever there is something belonging to Nirṛti; if that were so, the context would be sublated. Thus, this is based on an injunction regarding the action itself.

Thus [it is said]. The rule regarding the occasion (*nimittavidhi*) is heard further on: "If one who has maintained the Aśvamedha for a year builds the fire-altar, it is just as if a fetus were miscarried prematurely; he would meet with calamity. Therefore, he should first offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara."

In this regard, in the fourth section (4.1.6), under the heading "The Vaiśvānara sacrifice should be obligatory," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the mention of "sustaining [one's family] for a year" is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), and thus the sacrifice is obligatory. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the word "whoever" (*yaḥ*) is in grammatical apposition with the agent, it establishes that sustaining [one's family] for a year is the occasioning cause; therefore, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is contingent upon that occasion.

An example of a rule based on a sign (*nimitta-vidhi-sarūpa*) is as follows: it is heard in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, "Whatever deity the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer have omitted, they fall short of her; when he takes the curd-cup (*dadhi-graha*) dedicated to Prajāpati, it indeed pacifies him."

In the section (4.1.5) beginning with "The curd-offering (*dadhighraha*) is occasional because of its connection with a scriptural statement," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that the intervention of another deity is the occasion because of the word *yat*. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) asserts that since the word *yat* standing in grammatical apposition with the agent does not convey the status of being an occasion, the mention of the intervention is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); thus, the curd-offering is obligatory (*nitya*).

The injunction regarding the agent: In the sixth [book], the recitations (*japa*) and oblations (*homa*) enjoined for the sake of human ends by means of the mantras designated as *caturhotṛ* were the subject of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the passages "one should employ the *caturhotṛ*" and "one desiring offspring should offer with the *caturhotṛ*. It was argued that the oblations should be performed in the *āhavanīya* fire; however, the statement "this indeed belongs to one who has not established the sacred fires" is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), intended to show the equality [of the rites] with recitation (*japa*), since the word *iṣṭi* is used here to denote recitation: "that action consisting of recitation which belongs to one who has not established the sacred fires is the *iṣṭi*."

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: to avoid the redundancy of the scriptural statement and to exclude the characteristics of an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, the nature of these acts is that of an oblation (*homa*) performed through the medium of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), based on the direct mention of the genitive case.

This is similar in form to the injunction regarding the agent found in the sixth book (*Ṣaṣṭha Adhyāya*, 6.1.12): "Thus said Baṭuka Vārṣṇi: 'Cook beans for me today. The cooking of beans is to be performed by a Vṛṣṇi or a Gaura, and not by others.
Having thus raised this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is refuted.
This has been considered after formulating an alternative interpretation of the procedure for cooking the beans (*māṣapāka*).
Regarding the rule for time: "One should sacrifice with the *āgneya* and *aindrāgna* [offerings] of clarified butter alone, not silently (*nāupāṃśu*), on the full moon day.
This very point was stated in the tenth book (*daśama*) under the section concerning the *upāṃśu*.

The rule regarding time is of the same form: "The seasons are indeed free from blemish; whenever one may come, at whatever time, when [the texts] have been studied, then one should sacrifice. This is a supplementary statement (*śeṣa*) to the injunction of the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*.
Therefore, in the *Vaiṣuvatī* sacrifice, there is no injunction for a season other than spring; for that injunction is established by the very rule "whenever one may come."

And this was stated by implication in the fifth [book], in the section (5.1.5) titled "It should be at its own time because of the prohibition of what has been omitted," where, in the discussion of that [passage], it was explained that the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa statement beginning with "When at any time... prescribes another season for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; thus, the fact that the remainder of that passage is an injunction regarding time was stated as a matter of course. As for the injunction regarding place: in the Tāṇḍaka [Brāhmaṇa] it is said, "They undergo initiation at the Vanashana of the Sarasvatī; the Adhvaryu hurls the wooden pin (śamyā); where it falls, that is the site of the Āgnīdhra shed; from there he strides thirty-six steps, which is the site of the Āhavanīya fire. They proceed upstream, [starting] from the eastern wing."
The varieties of *arthavāda* (639): The section on *arthavāda*.

Having enjoined, "They proceed after having offered the *caru* oblation to Aponaptrīya," the remainder of the sentence states, "The seasons depend upon the movement [of the sun]; Sarasvatī flows from the Vinaśana until the Pralavaṇa.
This prescribes that as much as is given should be used for the journey.

For this very reason, its source has been summarized [in the following passage]: "When they come to the Plakṣa Pralavana, then is the rising; for the sake of coming to the Plakṣa Pralavana, others perform the sacrifice for their desired object; having given the mother-cow and the first milch-cow, they go toward Kārapacava and descend into the Yamunā for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
However, in the Vārttika, another scriptural text stating "thirty-four *avanī* measures" is mentioned in the section on Grammar (PMS 3.4.8).

The *deśavidhisarūpa* (that which has the form of an injunction regarding location) is as follows: "Thirty-six steps toward the east, thirty toward the north, twenty-four in front"—this is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction for measuring the great altar (*mahāvedi*) of the Soma sacrifice, namely, "In this much space we shall perform the sacrifice. This very point was stated by Bhaṭṭa Someśvara in the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) [of the *Tantravārttika*], under the sūtra "And because of the connection with the desire to build" (3.1.3).

Regarding the rule of prohibition (*niṣedhavidhi*): In the *Aitareya-brāhmaṇa*, within the narrative of Hariścandra, there is the injunction for the recitation of the Śunaḥśepa story, which serves both the purpose of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*)—as seen in the phrase "O you who dwell in Hiraṇyakaśipu" uttered by the Hotṛ priest—and the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—as seen in "Those desiring sons should have [the story] told. In the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of this injunction, it is stated that they "did not find anyone to employ them" and "did not find anyone to banish them," expressing the acquisition [of the story] through Sāman chants. Furthermore, it describes their engagement out of greed with the words, "I will give another hundred; I shall release him. In this context, the general prohibition "one should not harm" (*na hiṃsyāt*) applies to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) regarding their own specific duty. Even though the priests are touched by the general injunction related to the Sāman—which pertains to another’s duty (*parādhikārika*) and concerns the agent as such—their engagement remains uncontradicted. For this very reason, the author of the Vārttika stated in the third book, under the section "And the Śamitṛ [is distinct], because of the difference in terms" (3.1.13), "Therefore, they censure the office of the officiating priest. Nevertheless, the specific prohibition exists as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of indicating the fault [of violating the general rule].
An example of that which has the form of both a prohibition and an injunction is: "Now, moreover, they say: 'The *jatilā* and *gavedhukā* grasses are indeed not offerings (*anāhuti*').

For in the tenth [book], having raised as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) the assumption of a prohibition based on the phrase "not an offering" as a censure, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached: "For a censure does not proceed for the sake of censuring, but rather for the sake of praising what is to be enjoined. Thus, by the principle of "the mention of another scriptural passage" (*śāstrāntara-karaṇa*), it is established that since this is a supplement to the injunction regarding milk—"That which one offers the *agnihotra* with milk"—there is no assumption of a prohibition.

That which determines the meaning of a doubtful injunction is, for example, in the injunction "May you two become possessed of Sarasvatī," the statement: "This indeed is the divine pair, namely Sarasvatī and the waters."

In this context, the doubt arises as follows: "Sārasvata" may mean "that which has Sarasvant as its deity," or another [possibility] is that there is yet another [deity]. Thus, one could be a *taddhita* derivative meaning "that which has Sarasvant as its deity," while the other is a *taddhita* derivative meaning "that which has Sarasvatī as its deity"; since both are reduced to a single form (*ekaśeṣa*), the conclusion is reached from this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that this [offering] belongs exclusively to the male-female pair of deities, and not to two male deities.
This very point was stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* under the fifth chapter, in the section (5.1.7) beginning with "Or by the order of the principal [deity], because of the lack of knowledge."

That which indicates the power of a meaning that is doubtful is the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction "He sprinkles the *udumbara* post with barley-grains," namely: "When these plants die, then these [grains] grow rejoicing.
This has been stated in the section on the aphorism "And the scripture [is authoritative], because it is based on that" (1.3.6).

An illustrative explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of analogy is: "Just as a hawk swoops down, so does he who performs this rite with the two-fold [offering] swoop down upon his hateful enemy."

This has been stated in the section concerning names (*nāmadheya-pāda*) under the heading "And because there is designation as such" (*tadvyapadeśaṃ ca*) at 1.4.14. [End of] Bālakrīḍā, page [blank]. Now begins the section on explanatory passages (*arthavāda-adhikaraṇa*).
Those devoid of meaning.
The section concerning the authoritative status of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

(The subject matter of the section on *arthavāda* is stated: "Now, the utility of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras is being discussed in every respect regarding the Veda, which has already been established as a means of valid cognition with respect to *dharma*."
The general authority of the Veda having been established, its specific application is now set forth by way of division.

Alternatively, since the authority of the Veda as a whole has already been determined, the utility of its constituent parts—namely injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras—with respect to *dharma* is now explained according to their respective classifications.

"Because the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) has action as its purpose, those portions which do not have that [action] as their purpose are therefore said to be non-eternal (in their direct application)."

The Commentary states: "He wept; because he wept, that is the nature of Rudra"; "Prajāpati extracted his own omentum"; "The gods, having failed to determine the place of sacrifice, did not know the directions"—such sentences do the Samāmnātāras (those who recite the collections) transmit.
Regarding these, there is an inquiry as to whether they establish some dharma or not. To this, it is replied:
How is action to be sought? To understand that, the reciters transmit sentences;
those sentences which [concern] action constitute the section on explanatory passages (arthavāda).

They do not convey anything connected with an action; rather, they merely report what has already occurred, such as "Rudra wept," "Prajāpati cut out his omentum," or "The gods, indeed, did not know the directions. What dharma could such [statements] establish? Now, if it is argued that some meaning will be inferred through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), modification (*vipariṇāma*), supplying a missing word (*vyavahitakalpatā*), supplying a restrictive particle (*vyavadhāraṇakalpatā*), or supplying a secondary attribute (*guṇakalpatā*), then what kind of thing would be so inferred? [For example, from] "Rudra wept" (*rudraḥ kila ruroda*), one might infer: "Therefore, others too must weep."
Prajāpati cut out his own omentum; therefore, another might also cut out his own omentum.
At the time of preparing the sacrificial ground, the gods did not know the directions; therefore, another might also fail to know the directions.
But such a thing is impossible.

That which is the liberation of a Brāhmaṇa by one who is struck down by separation from what is dear is called "weeping"; yet that does not occur for one who desires [the goal]. Nor could anyone, having cut out their own omentum and struck themselves with it, be able to sacrifice with that hornless animal standing up.
Furthermore, at the time of settling upon the sacrificial ground for the gods, no one would become confused about the directions;
therefore, these [other] statements are purposeless.
Consequently, such types of sentences are said to be non-injunctions (*anitikāni*).
And even though they are eternal, they nevertheless do not perform an eternal purpose.
This is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of only a portion of the sentence, not of the entire sentence.

[Objection: But surely a collection of words that is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) due to a missing portion and so forth is not sufficient for the purpose of attaining heaven; therefore, it must indeed be implied.
It is not so.
For there exists a certain collection of words which enjoins some matter even without the explanatory passages (arthavādas).
However, those [words] which function toward a different meaning by being joined with them are included by the inclusion of one part.

Alternatively—the intention of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: From the opening statement, "Dharma is a purposeful matter characterized by an injunction" (1.1.2), through the reference [in the middle], "Its knowledge is derived from instruction" (1.1.5), and up to the conclusion, "The collection of words denoting existing things is for the sake of action" (1.1.25), it has been established that authority belongs solely to injunctions and prohibitions.
