Furthermore, there is no means of knowing Dharma and Adharma other than being cognizable through verbal testimony (*śabda*). Nor, as has already been stated, does a word have any function other than making known an object not previously apprehended.

Therefore, let there be authority for only those [Vedic elements] that are included within injunctions and prohibitions by virtue of being integral to the goal, the means, and the procedure; however, those which are additional—
such as the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and mantras that merely follow the [injunctions],

namely "He wept," "For strength thee," "For vigor thee," "O you who have risen," and so forth— even though they are of non-human origin and possess the capacity to denote meaning, they are not authoritative regarding *dharma* and *adharma*, because their purpose is not that.
First, because the reason (*hetu*) for those things grasped exactly as they were heard is unestablished (*asiddha*);
and consequently, [there is no connection] between the moon and the sun throughout the night and day.

It becomes the cause of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for even though the eye and other [senses] are not themselves [the direct cause], praise is also not [considered] non-existent because it serves to establish their status as causes, since they are perceived.
Or rather, this lack of determination (*anavadhāraṇā*) is that even when [the object] is separated by an intervening memory, it is still postulated as being in contact with the sense faculty.

Alternatively, "The sun is the light" refers to perception following the day; this has been established. "Not suddenly"—this mantra is for the morning, while "Agni is the light" is for the evening. Thus it is said.
It is not directly perceived by everyone; therefore, even for those who observe with great precision, the non-retention of the two mantras is not established.
Alternatively, the entire Veda is authoritative;
this has already been stated regarding direct perception as well.
The intention is that this restriction—that [the soul] exists for the purpose of seeing the Self-luminous—is not established.
There is a contradiction with the scripture;
he himself will state [this] as "saṃśrava" (1.2.113).

Nor is there a twofold contradiction with what is perceived; furthermore, as for the contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures, perception does not lose its status on account of that alone. That which exists according to the logic of "the mountain peak and the real object" is not challenged by a different sequence; that is the resolution.
If it is grasped after having mounted [the vehicle], that is not perceptible.
Nor is there any deviation from the sequence of the Sūtras on the part of women.
"And we do not know this," says Āpeya.
Because deviation is observed everywhere, it is proper to assume that what is intended is merely the remainder of the non-contradiction with worldly usage;
and this [remainder] is expressed through its connection with the action,
since no other means of proof is possible.

For those born of noble lineage protect themselves with distinguished effort; [the scripture] is not an authority because it has that [body] as its object, for the body is not coextensive with a Brāhmaṇa.
For this very reason, kings and Brahmins employ various reversals in ritual action according to some specific part [of the requirement].
Nor is it for the sake of extending the lineage through one's own father, grandfather, and so forth.
Praise that contradicts direct perception is to be rejected;
nor can it be established by independent non-Brahmins.
And likewise, because one follows after qualities and defects according to what is agreeable or disagreeable, there is validity in the communication of knowledge corresponding to that.
But how is this a contradiction regarding substance? [The answer is:
Engagements and withdrawals are observed.

Nor does the distinction of caste arise from the transgression of the husband; for when individuals possess identical physical forms, the classification as "Brāhmaṇa" is determined solely by the scriptures, and not by [the occurrence of] sexual confusion (saṃkara).
Indeed, it is observed that even those who have committed transgressions are nonetheless ascertained [as Brāhmaṇas] based on the scriptures alone.

This is not the subject of the treatise, because it is well known in the world. Their birth is caused by their own husbands; their transformation into trees and so forth is caused by the husbands' offenses.
But how is this well-known to the world? We reply: it is through perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There would be the experience of unpleasant results, but there is no mixing of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) among those who are not born [of such unions].
Thus we say.
Why, moreover, are they not aware of their connection with their mother and father? And why is there no necessary (or mandatory) transgression with those of other castes?
Why do they not realize their own future state among human beings who are in close proximity to their eyes?
And for one begotten by a man of the same caste (*savarṇa*), there is no possibility of falling into another caste (*varṇāntara*), because such a mixture (*saṃkara*) is impossible;
just as the nature of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) remains even before its specific designation is established. It is not thus [in the case of different castes].
Furthermore, regarding those who have been born [into a different caste], their elevation or degradation occurs equally in the seventh or the fifth generation;

this attainment of another caste is declared to happen through the agency of the ancestors, even before [the individual] has reached the state of being a tree, by means of the performance of a ritual for a specific purpose (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.96).
In that case, however, it is not seen that [the universal] is cut off from its own individuals while persisting in the form of being possessed of scripture and so forth;

rather, only this much should be accepted as based on tradition (*āgamika*), for this [scriptural status] is not the same as the [universal] "Brāhmaṇahood" (brāhmaṇatva) regarding the number of persons. Furthermore, even one who has mastered words [does not possess it] due to a cause...
The rule is cognizable through worldly means of valid knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*).
Therefore, even though there is similarity, it is not understood from within [the text] alone;
nor is the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the study of the Veda, and so forth, the cause [of its cognition].

Just as the knowledge of the distinction between male and female cuckoos and the like arises from some specific sign, because [the color] is common to all three castes; likewise, even teaching and so forth— though they are objects of perception aided by a tradition of seeing and remembering— are doubtful, because they stand in a relationship of opposition to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas of distinct conduct, and Vaiśyas.
And since [qualities] such as being estimable (*saṃbhāvya*) exist among those with wrong faith (*duṣṭaśraddha*),
there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) regarding the statement that it is "unknown" (*ajñāna*);
for [the statement] is not certain because it lacks validity (*amānatva*).
For whom [the status of being a Brahmin] is established precisely without investigation;

even for those for whom Brahminhood and so forth are caused by conduct, that [status] would have to be perceived through direct observation. Then, even one who perceives mother-of-pearl as silver might purchase it.
Indeed, there is a contradiction in this very [position].
But this is not a fault, for there is no such rule regarding the grasping of any particular caste based on conduct, marks, or complexion; nor is there any authority whatsoever for such a distinction.
For it has already been explained that the status of being a Brahmin and so forth is established through the Siddhānta (the final conclusion).
Therefore, just as light, the sense organs,
and conduct are prescribed [as means of knowledge], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*) in those cases.

The practice of [the term] "Brāhmaṇa" consists in the recollection of the word "anekapiṇḍānusyūti" (the continuity of many individual bodies), as well as its manifestation, magnitude, and location; by virtue of that, there are those such as Brāhmaṇas. That very same thing—namely, the specific ear-shape and so forth—is the cause for the apprehension of other castes (*anyajāti*) in exactly the same way.
A Brahmin at the time of performing virtuous conduct, and again a Śūdra at the time of performing non-virtuous conduct—herein lies the recollection of one's birth as a progenitor.
And this [status] arises from the means of its production;
thus, there is instability.

Likewise, through a single effort, there is a connection with the suffering of others; this is directly perceived by the mother herself, whereas for others who perform acts such as inference, acceptance, or support, there is simultaneously a contradiction between their being Brāhmaṇas and their non-grasping [of that status].
The place and so forth, as understood, serve as the cause.
Nor is it necessarily the case that [this] is understood through direct perception alone; rather, it is established by these arguments. It is not [established] by means of austerity and so forth.
Brahminhood is a collection [of qualities], not a refinement produced by that [birth], nor something distinct from it, because it would otherwise be purposeless.
Caste is not established through etymological derivation; rather, it is designated by the names of one's mother and father.
The Bhāṣya states: "By the final oblation, one obtains all desires"—this is to be understood through direct perception.
Therefore, by this very logic, the distinction between the social classes (varṇa) is established.

"An offerer of the animal sacrifice conquers all worlds," "He crosses over death, he crosses over [the world] established [in duality]," "In a month he becomes a Śūdra"—such are the statements regarding ritual action (*karma*).

Furthermore, there are words of censure such as, "He who performs the horse-sacrifice for the sake of killing a Brāhmaṇa, and he who knows this [sacrifice] in that way," or else, statements demonstrating the loss of caste and ritual efficacy.
Thus [it is said].
If it were a mere restatement of what already exists, it would be purposeless; otherwise, it must be said that it is for the sake of a result.
And as before, perception is authoritative here as well because it is possible.
If it were a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), the repetition would be purposeless;
for an option with an injunction of ignorance—such as "having smeared [the ladle]" or "offering the full oblation"—is not possible.
Nor is there [an option] here.

The Agnihotra and other rites are performed, yet one does not perform them without having first sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma; moreover, while that might be possible there because it consists of ritual performance, it is not so here.
They sacrifice with Soma, and they do not sacrifice with the Aśvamedha without having studied [the Veda].
This is because things that exist as real entities cannot be subject to alternative options.
"For who indeed,

having abandoned honey produced on a nearby path, would— desiring that very honey— not go by that same path, knowing it as they did before? Such is that [Veda], which is free from ignorance, doubt, and error."

Moreover, they say: [The Smṛtis are] useless because they contradict the Veda. And by those who have ascertained the authority of the Veda: "If one should find honey on an *arka* tree, why would he go to the mountain?"
Since the desired goal is not manifold and because duality is known to be an end, even the pursuit of one's own self-interest is useless;
for what wise person would exert effort toward the mere accomplishment of such an object?
Thus [it is said].

And the absence of alternative options (*vikalpābhāva*) follows from what was stated immediately prior. Or rather (*vā*): because the statements regarding the fruits, such as the *pūrṇāhuti*, have already been explained by the preceding [passage], there is an absence of fruit [in this case].
Having established those [points], another fault is stated by way of the theory of means (abhyupāyavāda).
The Bhāṣya, referring to the *Gargatrirātrabrāhmaṇa*, says: "It is beautiful..."

Because the *pūrṇāhuti* is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), and because the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)— in the passage "The Jyotiṣṭoma is the mouth of him who knows thus"— is either a restatement of an established fact (*bhūtānuvāda*) and thus lacks utility, or because the knowledge of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is itself a purificatory rite, [the statement] is not purposeful. If, on the other hand, it is a restatement of the fruit of study (*adhyayanaphala*), then it would be a false assertion (*asadadvāda*).

The status of being an injunction for a fruit is clear. If, however, it is maintained that a fruit will arise at another time when other purposes have been fulfilled, there is no evidence for this here.
Even regarding actions that yield the same result, there are those which are independent of one another.
If it is argued that this must be an injunction (*vidhi*), we reply: no, for this is not intended as an injunction. [Regarding] "substance" (*dravya*)—
They are performed because they are carried out according to one's inclination; thus, they do not have any other purposelessness.
This will be considered under the sūtra "saṃskāram astu" (4.3.11).

However, regarding the Pūrṇāhuti and the Paśubandha, since the other rites would be incomplete if these two were not performed, the question arises as to whether this [mention of results] is a prescription of a fruit (*phalavidhi*) or a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

In this context, by the rule "Or the first [word] should be restricted" (11.1.43), it must be determined whether it is a restatement of an existing fact (*bhūtānuvāda*) or for the purpose of enjoining an action (*kriyārtha*).
Therefore, it is not an injunction of a result (*phalavidhi*).

Since there is no necessity for the performance of subsequent rites once the fruit has been obtained through logic (*nyāya*), the investigation of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is useless here for one who has already been refuted;
thus, that [investigation] is purposeless.
And so too is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"By that very same path, the seeker of food is born as a victor for one who knows thus"—
this is an example [of a case] where there is another path to the mountain for those seeking honey;
even though they go there, they do not go by that very same path.
Therefore,
rather than rendering useless many established injunctions that are auspicious, it is better to [accept] the non-existence [of the result];
nor can it be said— [namely], if [it were argued] that there is knowledge of the *gargatrirātrabrāhmaṇa* and the *vedānumantraṇa*...

The subsequent rites are for one who desires specific fruits, because they tend toward non-distinction [of fruit]. This is not so; for it is only the root-beauty and the production of offspring that exist at the time [of the primary rite] which are mentioned. Indeed, when the scriptural revelation (*śruti*) is equal, a specific fruit that is not directly perceived cannot serve as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the merit (*dharma*) of the rite.
But if they were non-existent,
then it would be possible to conceive of a distinction;
yet praise is not [possible] even in its own sense because of their unreality.
Furthermore, because the teaching concerns the present time, there is a contradiction with direct perception;
thus it remains established.
Since the purification through knowledge (*vidyā-saṃskāra*) serves as an instrument for a person capable of performing ritual acts, it belongs to the stage of one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*).
Because it consists of bathing and other such acts, and because it is self-sufficient, its status as an injunction of a result will be refuted;
and also because of the prohibition of [receiving] a share.
In that case, because of the tautology, this must be examined here; thus he says.

The Bhāṣya states: "He should not mix it on the earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in heaven"—this prohibits a matter that was not subject to prohibition [previously], since its status as an injunction of results has been refuted, and its purpose here is merely as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
"Consciousness is reflection.
Furthermore, there can be no praise for that which is unreal;
for this very reason, it is said that "Agni is piled in the intermediate space and in heaven."
It remains exactly as it was established.
Furthermore, because there is a prohibition of the piling (cayana), whatever statement there may be, that is solely for the purpose of prohibiting the piling.

Now, if it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this contradiction does not arise. How can that be a valid means of knowledge which, while confounding another injunction, is itself confused? And this is not the case, as in the instance: "Having deposited gold, one should think."

Alternatively—these three statements regarding earth and the other elements negate an object that is not characterized by non-existence. Since [the elements] exist in the intermediate space and in heaven, they are not objects of negation;
and because they are thus excluded [by implication], this is not a case of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
For since piling [of the altar] is already established as occurring eternally in the intermediate space, in heaven, and on earth, the injunction for it would be purposeless.
Even if it were a restatement of what is eternal, it would still not have the function of enjoining action.
Furthermore, both the prohibition and the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of piling on earth are impossible, as they would contradict the injunction for piling itself.
Furthermore, if there were sublation (bādha), the injunction would be purposeless;
even in the case of an option (vikalpa), there is sublation in one of the two alternatives.
Moreover, because of its connection with a specific desire (kāma), it is optional (pākṣika) only for this [Agni] sacrifice.

Furthermore, a prohibition is difficult to establish when there is a state of being the earth (pṛthivīparatva), because it would have to be assumed as a secondary application (kalpyatva) of the piling (cayana).

This very thing constitutes its own internal inconsistency. It would further create confusion with other injunctions, such as "having placed gold, one should pile" and "one piles the fire-altar with bricks."
However, no intention to provide an inducement (*prarocanā*) is perceived,
because of the connection with impermanence (*anitya*). Regarding this,
the *Bhāṣya* states that the objection concerning the connection with impermanence— namely, "But [the word] is merely due to the commonality of the sound" (JS 1.1.8)— has already been refuted.
Now, another objection arises regarding certain portions of the Veda that rely [on such stories], namely: "Varuṇa desired a son of Prāvāhaṇa.

[The opponent argues: Since it is possible for all such narratives to have a different purpose (anyaparatva) rather than establishing the actual nature [of the deity], there is a connection with what is non-eternal (anityasaṃyoga).
And while the entire Veda possesses authority, how could this [objection] be somehow refuted?

But when, just as among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) sound is one, and among those the Veda is a means of valid cognition, so too within the Veda injunction alone is postulated on the basis of reason, then—just like other parts [of the Veda]—the validity of certain portions of its content would result in being non-eternal because they are not accepted as they are heard; what could prevent this?
Therefore, for such [passages], disregarding their meaning, a fruit must be postulated from mere study alone.
Alternatively, just as these have disregard as their fruit, so too direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) should be understood as having the opposite result.

Now, why is it not employed at the time of performance according to the context, as is the case with mantras? Because of a lack of functional capacity. For the application of mantras does not occur through mere recitation; rather, it occurs through their inherent capacity. And that [capacity] is not present here.
Alternatively, just as in their prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) only the mere form [of the words] is accepted because there is no other purpose, so let it be here as well.
That which the author of the Sūtras stated regarding impermanence was with reference to its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), not to its lack of utility (*aprayojyatva*).
For, because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they serve the purpose of praising the injunctions.

Commentary: This is handed down in the sacred tradition: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he (Vāyu) leads him to prosperity.

Although no action nor anything connected to an action is understood from the statement "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," it is nonetheless authoritative because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunctive portion.
The injunctive statement ends with the words "one desiring prosperity" (*bhūtikāmaḥ*). With that, the passage beginning with "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" forms a single syntactical unit.
How is there this unity of a single sentence? Because the words possess mutual expectancy, the injunction and the praise constitute a single sentence:
"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice."
Why? Because wind is the swiftest.
This connection—that "one desiring prosperity should sacrifice it"—is not intended.
How then? That "one should sacrifice it, because from that [wind] comes prosperity."
There would be a split in these two meanings, and if both were expressed, the sentence would be split.

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of the praise?", [the answer is: so that it might be pleasing; otherwise, it would not be performed. But surely, prior to the statement of praise, the performance is already established by the words ending in "desirous of prosperity"; therefore, the statement of praise is useless.
No.

When there is proximity to words of praise, then the injunction is by the former [word] alone; when there is connection with words of praise, then the taking up (*ālambha*) of one desiring prosperity is not enjoined.
Just as in the case of "the cloth comes into being" (*paṭo bhavati*), the meaning is "the cloth is produced"; and these two words are each complete in themselves (*nirākāṅkṣa*).

And when another word, "red," is heard in reference to that very same object, then the meaning is that there is a connection with passion (attachment); and indeed, there arises an expectancy toward the red.
Thus, when there are no words of praise, the incitement occurs through the injunctive word itself; when there is a statement of praise, it occurs through that eulogy.
Now, if this is the case, what is the use of the statement of praise? Let it not exist, for even in its absence, one will be incited by the prior injunction alone.
True, even without that [injunction], the incitement would be established; however, it does exist.
When that is present, the meaning of the sentence is understood. Praise is the purpose of those two.
"When that [injunction] exists, there is an incitement (prarocana) by means of the rule.

Now, even though there are words of praise, because the preceding [portion] has the form of an injunction, it would be the injunction that is intended, and the connection with the words of praise would not be intended to be expressed.
To this he replies: "For the words of praise are meaningless, non-expressive, and expectant [of something else]."

If it is argued that they should be meaningless, we reply: when the meaning is already being understood, they cannot be considered as having unintended meanings. That which is the injunctive statement (vidhyuddeśa) is capable of enjoining the matter independently, and it is also capable of serving as the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) for the words of praise.
The state of being a supplement to a sentence is directly perceived;
therefore, from this injunction, we understand its praise.
But surely, we shall understand it even from an independent injunction?
It is indeed so; when this is the case, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
However, when there is a connection with words of praise, it is impossible to intend the injunctive meaning [of the mantra].
For a sentence is that which prescribes a connection.

If one were to establish two distinct relationships—namely, "one desiring prosperity should sacrifice" and "by means of the sacrifice, this [prosperity] will become a subordinate quality (guṇa)"—then, in that case, the sentence would be split. Furthermore, as for what was said—that no action is understood, nor anything connected with it—it is because "they [the words] exist for the purpose of praising the injunctions.
Words of praise, by praising and creating an incentive for performers, will assist the ritual action.
Thus, all these words—ending in the suffix -śat (present participles)—either enjoin or praise;

therefore, such types of passages are indeed authoritative, as in: "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity. [Objection: Since the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is to be stated regarding the very same sentences cited under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), for what purpose is the sentence concerning Vāyu introduced here? Some say: because they follow the same logic, this one is included there, and those others were cited here as representative examples.
Even though this is so, nevertheless, regarding the unprecedented example, another intention is required;
that is now stated.
In all the previously cited examples, even when one's own meaning is true, it is not accepted.

In this regard, since it would be unreasonable for anyone to voluntarily accept the affliction of being led astray at the very outset, the citation of the *Vāyavya* passage is intended to establish that it serves as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) to the means of knowing Dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*), by way of praise through its status as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with those [passages] whose meaning is well-known to be true.
Regarding this, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* state that its utility lies in praise precisely because of its established status as a single syntactical unit.

(Vedavākyānām ekavākyatvād apratipādanopayogaḥ) First, this must be addressed here: for what purpose is it asserted that the Veda, by virtue of its unity of meaning despite differences in form, serves the human goal?
If it is argued that this is because such is observed in worldly sentences, to that we reply:
in the world, since the meaning of a sentence is accessible through other means of knowledge, it is reasonable to conceive of it otherwise [than as a mere injunction].

In this case, however, because [the subject matter] is entirely beyond the reach of the senses, any deviation—even slightly—from what is heard would result in a total lack of validity. Furthermore, even in the world, those things whose objects are not accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) become authoritative for listeners by the mere fact of their being traditionally accepted; regarding these, no assumption of error can be entertained.
In this regard, some say: "And the traditional [teaching] is equal [to perception]" (Sūtra 1.1.18), as he will state later; therefore...
It is established that the entire Veda has human purpose as its goal;
for rational persons would not have preserved it with such effort if it were not beneficial to themselves.
And even if some individuals might be ignorant, nevertheless, the assumption of negligence on the part of numerous previous investigators who preceded us is without any basis in evidence.

Therefore, in whatever way a thing serves the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*), in that very way it is explained—even by breaking its formal structure—though not exactly as it was stated [in the original].
Why? Because it would follow that the validity of the scripture would be dependent upon the person.

For if a meaning not even recorded in the syllables were to be postulated by Asada and others simply because we preserve it with effort, then its status as a human goal [would follow]. In that case, validity would have to be accepted as being dependent upon the cognition of a person. If, on the other hand, it is argued that it is the preservation by other persons [that establishes it], even so, it depends on them; and since they too must preserve it based on yet others, and so on through an infinite succession, there would be reliance on another for everyone, and thus no explanation of validity would ever be established.
For everywhere there is the cognition, "This person knows thus," and not, "This object is thus.

Therefore, although it may be inferred that the intention of those students was surely that they considered the Veda to be for the sake of man (*puruṣārtha*), nevertheless, because that [intention] lacks a foundation, it is unestablished by that alone.
Consequently, as long as the Veda itself does not establish its entire self as being for the sake of man, it remains non-authoritative.
That too is stated as follows:
First, for the entire Veda, the injunction regarding the cultivation of study (*adhyayana-bhāvanā*) is enjoined by the rule, "One's own Veda is to be studied.

In that context, when the expectation arises as to "what should one cultivate," although "study" presents itself, it is excluded from that part [of the injunction] because the single injunction, which possesses the power to impel a person toward action, would lack the capacity to impel one toward a cultivation whose object is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Thus, it is set aside.
And thus, because there is no contradiction with the act of study and due to its proximity, [the injunction] enters into the instrumental aspect [of the action].
When the expectation arises as to "what is to be done by that," one recites "the grasping of syllables" (akṣaragrahaṇa), following the connection with the word "will be stated" (vakṣyate).

Nevertheless, because that [grasping of syllables] does not have the human goal as its purpose, the phrase "the determination of words" (padāvadhāraṇa) presents itself in response to the question "what is to be done by that."

From that [knowledge of words], there arises the knowledge of the meaning of individual words (padārtha); from that, the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (vākyārtha); from that, the performance of the action (anuṣṭhāna); and by means of that performance, the attainment of results such as heaven. When this much has been established, the injunction becomes free of further expectancy. Thus, all injunctions possess purposefulness prior to the attainment of a human goal. Nor is it the case that, because no other result is seen, the injunction immediately postulates heaven or the like as its fruit.
For, by virtue of fitness (*yogyatā*), when an operation is observed to follow immediately after something in a certain case, that alone is determined to be its effect.

In that regard, if the action itself attains the result within the temporal sequence (*adhvan*) in accordance with that very [fitness], then no intermediate [operation] deserves to be postulated. This is because of the causal efficacy of the succession (*pāraṃparya-prayoga*).

The meaning is that even for ordinary people, [the status of being a wife] is established through the application of scriptural injunctions (*śruti-vidhi*), by way of *arthāpatti* (presumption) based on the impossibility of otherwise.
When it is asked "How so?", [the answer is: because the husband is restated (*anuvāda*) by means of establishing the agent who exists for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*).
But where the effect is seen immediately after [the cause], and not by itself [independently]—
so it has been said.
Thus [ends the section].
However, O Pārtha, the application of both the mantra and its name occurs within the context of the ritual authority (*adhikāra*);
nor does one attain it through mere tradition, as in the case of the *homa*,
which will be explained below.
Therefore, it is established that all [results] are included within the process of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Whether it be the attainment of what is desired or the reduction to ashes, in those cases, [the result occurs] directly through that sequence;
thus, the postulation of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) applies to the action alone.
And this is to be observed everywhere:

that the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) fall within the three constituent parts of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). However, where an enjoined act requires a fruit, it pertains to a series of effects consisting of that [fruit].

As for the fact that explanatory passages fall within the three constituent parts of the *bhāvanā*, when there is something intermediate—whether for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtu*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—[they serve that purpose].
Regarding the statement "there is no apprehension," it is replied:

It is true that nothing additional is apprehended; rather, it is urged that in that case, that very [act] is the means for that [result], while for the preceding injunction, it is included therein. However, it is indeed contained within.

How so? For here, in sentences containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, the final purposeful realization lies in the sense of an action (*kārya*). As for those effects of the subsequent injunction, two types of efficient force (*bhāvanā*) are understood in the sentences: the verbal (*śabdārthikā*) and the objective (*arthātmikā*). Prior to that, because they have not been enjoined as being in a relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), they are not [independently] connected.

And therein, those *arthavādas* consisting of meaning are not required, whereas those consisting of sound are accepted as being for the purpose of praise, just as [the mention of] burning and so forth [is accepted] in the case of wood and other materials in previously enjoined rituals.

For that [injunction] proceeds in this manner: it is to be understood as consisting merely of the activity of reciting and studying one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*). However, where there is no [direct] injunction through tradition, all others are to be rested; and because of the instruction regarding *svādhyāya*, the Self (*ātman*), which is internal consciousness (*cidantarā*), is enjoined. In that case, having made all [other elements] its own activity, it is that which is to be enjoined.
"One is enjoined" means "one should cultivate.

In that context, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth possess the status of an instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*), just as the sacrifice itself possesses the status of being the means to its own fruit.
In that regard, as for those [injunctions] such as the *ṛtu* and *kalpa*...
The person is that which is to be impelled.

When the question arises as to "by what means," it is heard [in the scriptures] that there are injunctions (*vidhi*) which proclaim the means for accomplishing the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) intended to be realized, and these are what impel the person toward them.

But rather, by virtue of their inherent capacity (*yogyatā*), actions as far as the production [of results]—which are the objects of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—are led by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) toward the person; thus it is said that [the injunction] "should impel. When the question "What then? arises, it is expected that [it impels] the person. Since the fact that [the action] possesses a fruit is already known, it is not [the case that] until that is heard [is there any need for further instruction].

And although, because they are insentient, the *liṅ* suffixes and others are understood in this way [as instigators], those which are recited as their instruments (*karaṇa*) are likewise [insentient]. Thus, such a form of instigation (*prayojakatva*) is not possible; nevertheless, [the process] proceeds from the person's apprehension of the syllables and so forth, up until the point of making known the meaning for one's own sake. It does not [proceed otherwise].
Because it is untenable for the body to be the motivator (*prayojaka*), [the organs] become knowers of the result directly by means of the consciousness residing therein.
Why? How? Because the status of being a motivator does not belong to those [organs] whose function is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*).
And if it were not conceived in this way, there would be no non-dependence on excellence regarding the syllables and so forth resulting from the study performed;
rather, there would be a requirement for these [syllables] to possess the nature of being prescriptive.
Now, as for the question "by what?", it is simply the action enjoined by that [injunction] which is taken up by way of its purpose.
Since it depends upon the prior experience of that meaning through the cognition of the injunction (*vidhi*), there is no contradiction.
Therefore, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) become equal to the principal sentence (*pradhānavākya*). It is thus explained.
"How so? [It is] by means of this [injunction], through the favor of the knowledge of its excellence.
Why? Because those other scriptural passages are even more external than the study [of the Veda] and so forth.
Thus it is.

Why is this? For men who act with prior deliberation do not engage [in an action] as long as they do not understand that this [action] is praised, [namely] the mere fruit of the purification (*saṃskāra*) of rice and so forth resulting from sentences concerning sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the like. In that regard, the injunctive suffix (*vidhibhakti*) is more remote from the primary [result] due to the intervention of the two examples given, such as the rice-grains and the flour.
It falters; knowledge of its excellence supports it.
And that [excellence] consists in its connection with a person.
In this very way, there is the statement of a desire for a form studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*).
Since the performance of everything that has an object as its purpose occurs spontaneously by itself, how could [such] injunctions be applied?
In that regard, however, this much is certain:
because it is already well-known, it does not depend on what arises from the Veda.

The distinction regarding the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is as follows: because it does not reside within a specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇasthatvāt*), the primary [injunction] does not touch upon the syllables [of the mantra].

However, since there is no application of a person's duty (*puruṣaniyoga*) toward that which is to be performed, excellence (*prāśastya*) is understood only through knowledge; thus, it is heard as being for that very purpose.
As for those sentences concerning the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and so forth—
It is required for the sake of accomplishment.
As for the question "By what would that be supported?", those [injunctions] also— being dependent on the means for accomplishing the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *grahavatīya* and other vessels,

which possess results— would either be restricted by the word denoting the result, or they would be rendered free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣīkriyante*) by the distant result itself, as this [result] is already established as desirable.

Because it has prosperity as its fruit; or rather, because by the injunction itself all suspicion of defects is removed—thus, by means of establishing the agent for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*), the lack of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) of the Upaniṣads is explained (as stated in the *Sudhā*: "Even the Upaniṣads, like the sentences concerning the *āghāra* libation and so forth, have their lack of expectancy fulfilled by the distant fruit of the rite"). Or else, because they are endowed with specific materials, deities, and procedures (*itikartavyatā*)—in that regard, the words denoting the fruit and so forth [are satisfied] by another purpose [namely, the fruit of the ritual].
Furthermore, due to this connection, it is not logical for its application to extend elsewhere;
this expectancy lasts only as long as a flash of lightning, whereas the placement of the word "fruit" (*phala*) and so forth occurs earlier.
Therefore, it is not produced by them either; moreover, a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is postulated for these [words],
and the purpose [of that indication] is to be understood solely from the sentence containing the censure.
And for this reason, it is not logical to assume a single sentence when the literal meaning is possible;
furthermore, there would be a simultaneous contradiction between two Vedic texts.
Thus, the status of being a single sentence is established.

Furthermore, if [the passage] were eternally the object of an injunction, then, due to the sequence of the sentence and the verbal root, if it were intended for the purpose of praising, the results and so forth would not exist;
for [injunctions] do not have another purpose.
Thus, the remaining [passages], such as praise and censure, are determined [as being for the sake of the injunction].

The section concerning explanatory passages (arthavāda). Regarding the section on explanatory passages: [it is established] by means of an explanatory passage, while others [establish it] by means of a great [explanatory passage].
The undertaking is precisely this: that the mind of all [beings] must be grasped.
In that regard, some mental injunctions and prohibitions are rooted in the Veda (*śruti*); some are easily obtained through worldly purpose and are rooted in the world (*loka*).
Likewise, some explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are purely Vedic, some are purely worldly, and some are composed by themselves according to the principles of poetry (*kāvyanyāya*).

And all [such passages] are authoritative by virtue of their being praise. However, those which do not function as supplements to a statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), some of them—such as the descriptions of the fragrance of the Gandhamādana and so forth—spontaneously generate delight when heard. Those, however, which are descriptions of battle, produce enthusiasm in all, both the brave and the timid; they are useful for kings.

Where nothing visible is perceived, there an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated by means of the praise of a specific deity or other such factors; this is the general direction [of the argument]. (This is the *Bhāṣya-yojanā* according to the opinion of some, followed later by his own view: "Because of being a single syntactical unit with the injunctive statement" (*vidhyuddeśena ekavākyatvāt*).

Some say: "If it is asked what the purpose of the praise is, [the answer is: so that [the action] might be found pleasing (in the case of a prescription), or so that it might not be performed (in the case of a prohibition). Thus, through praise and censure, there is the production of engagement or desistance, while the denotation [of the meaning] occurs through the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers.
Therefore, there is an identity of purpose [between the two].
And there is no combination (*samuccaya*) of things that have the same purpose.

In this regard, for those injunctions (*liṅgādi*) that are devoid of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), as well as for those explanatory passages themselves that are devoid of them, their capacity to either prohibit or impel is established according to their respective domains without contradiction.

But where there is a convergence of multiple [indications], since the purpose is accomplished by either one, it is proper that the greater number of factors should be favored within the constituent parts.
Thus, as in the saying "one should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family," the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) is discarded.

Because there is no usage of the bare verbal root (*prakṛti*) alone, it proceeds by way of restating the injunction of a light rule (*laghuvihitavidhi*) and providing encouragement (*prarocanā*) for the sake of favoring that [root].

Just as in the case of "Having performed the *satra*, they should sacrifice with the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*," it will be stated that [the latter clause] is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of what has already been established by the suffix *-ktvā*. Therefore, only that which is obtainable through effort is intended here. And that very injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), after the connection with the result and so forth has occurred, is praised; thus, the injunctive statement ends with the words "one who desires prosperity" (*bhūtikāmaḥ*).
This is what is stated by this [commentary].
Otherwise, however, the mention of the *uddeśa* would be entirely purposeless.
Since syntactic unity with that which is stated in the Sūtra is not possible according to the prescribed rule, one must bypass that and adopt its subject matter.
And thus he says: "This is not the intended meaning.

By negating the connection with a specific injunction, he expresses the intended connection with the nature of praise in the words, "Whatever prosperity [arises] from that. And that very [praise] is the cause of prosperity.
The interpretation (*yojanā*): The previously mentioned connection, namely "these two are non-different," expresses [the meaning].
[If it is asked: "For what purpose is there praise? [it is as follows].
If the conviction (*pratyaya*) has already arisen, then what is the use of praise for that which is not being enjoined?
Alternatively, he speaks with the thought in mind: "Whatever is accomplished by this [praise] will be accomplished by the conviction itself.

But the Teacher, even when the conviction has arisen, maintains that the attainment of that purpose comes from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) alone, and considering that both [conviction and praise] may be possible, yet the explanatory passage is more significant, he says: "How could it be pleasing? (*kathaṃ roceta*).
The other [opponent] clarifies the intention behind the question, [arguing that] since [the fact of the Veda’s authority] is already established, the statement of praise is purposeless.
The word "na hi" (for not) marks a break in the text.
In all cases, intermediate sentences within great sentences do not constitute independent authorities; they exist merely as intermediate numbers within great numbers.
But when those very [words] are employed alone, they constitute a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because of their independence,
as in the case of "there is a cloth.
And it is not the case that because a lack of expectancy is observed in some instances where completion occurs through this much alone, there is a lack of expectancy in all cases.

For all sentences reach their completion through the cognition of other words that are appropriate [to the context]. Otherwise, however, even when there is no additional word heard, a requirement for one might arise even for a subtle observer;
and that requirement is removed by non-perception.
And thus, wherever they are perceived, they will attain syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). Otherwise, even upon their utterance, that [unity] would not exist.
Therefore, in this case, the intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākya*) is authoritative only in the absence of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*).
But when that [subordinate sentence] exists, [the main sentence] does not [function as such]; this he expresses with the words, "When there are no words of praise. [Objection:

"But if this is so," [then it is appropriate only where the fruit of the larger sentence and the subordinate sentences differ, as in the cases of the production of a cloth and the production of dyeing]. However, here the fruit is not distinct; this he expresses by saying: "In the presence of which [subordinate sentence], the intermediate sentence becomes non-injunctive—let that [intermediate sentence] not be a 'larger sentence' (mahāvākya)."
"Even without that [author], it is true.

For if there were indeed an author of the Veda, he alone would be subject to such an inquiry: "Since the goal is accomplished by a simpler means, why do you practice such voluminous texts? And because such an author does not exist, the objection [of redundancy] does not apply.
There may be an excess of fatigue from traveling along the path,
but there is no failure to understand the meaning;
moreover, this is observed among those of such a kind due to their great respect.

Just as they express that very same meaning by the word "enough" (*alam*) alone, even though it is already established, yet they do not incur dullness [of intellect] by using words such as "space" (*ākāśa*) and so forth;
likewise, here too, they grasp from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) a meaning that is already established by means of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) and other criteria.
And this can be said: just as in the case of a mantra which possesses many means and auxiliary parts...
The Section on Arthavādas (Exegetical Passages).

It is recorded that an arthavāda being performed brings about prosperity; likewise, even when a rule is established by another means, that which is enjoined by a rule propounded in an arthavāda is also effective.
"Now, [it is said] that Sarasvatī resides in words of praise. Where a heavy syllable (*guru*) is resorted to without employing a light one (*laghu*), there it may indeed be so;
but here, a lighter syllable has already been employed previously, and it is more capable.

Therefore, just as when the word "space" (*kha*) is employed, words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) are not employed at that very same time, so too, since this injunction exists, the laudatory passages (*stuti*) should not be discarded.
In that case, because they would require a subsequent referent, the laudatory words would be meaningless.
If it is argued, "Let them be [meaningless]," we reply: no, for by the aforementioned reasoning, since they possess meaning, it is not proper to claim they have no intended meaning.
For when both are possible, since there is a direct perception of the word's location, it is logical that the favoring of the meaningful [word] should occur.
[Objection: Since this has already been covered by the phrase "nanu sarasv api," the phrase "nanu nirapekṣatvāt" need not be stated. To this it is replied:

In that case, it was stated for the sake of abandoning the status of being a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); however, let there now be a connection with praise. Nevertheless, the connection with the injunction regarding the nature of the previously mentioned *rāmasasya* must not be sublated.
If its capacity were removed in even one instance, then, due to the absence of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), the consequence would be a total incapacity in all cases.
To this, it is replied:
Let it be that the injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) belongs to the preceding [word], yet this [power] is not obstructed by anything else; having manifested at some time, it manifests everywhere.
However, in cases where another purpose such as praise (*stuti*) is not employed, there the manifested power initiates its effect.
But where there is the manifestation of another obstructing power (*apavādabhūtaśakti*), it remains concealed beforehand due to the consequence of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
This very syntactical split mentioned previously is referred to here by way of question and answer.
Therefore, because they share a single purpose, the injunction here occurs solely through incitement. As it is said: "Those who are being incited [to act]..."

Why does the status of *saṃpradāna* (recipient) apply [to the word "people"] according to Pāṇini 1.4.33, which states: "One who is being pleased by those for whom something is intended (*havyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ*)"? If you argue that this is because *prarocayate* ("he incites") is a different verbal root (*prakṛtyantara*), we say no; for even there, the connection with the act of pleasing (*ruci*) remains subordinate (*pallava*). If it is argued that the genitive case is used in its general sense, even that is difficult to maintain when a specific relation is already expressed. Therefore, the relationship is between the action and the performers. When the expectation arises as to "for whom is he inciting?", these two [the performers and the action] are understood from the context itself.

Furthermore, the connection is: "and yet they will be beneficial to the performers. The word "kriyāyāḥ" is in the ablative case; for it is from the action itself that those [injunctions] are inciting.
Alternatively, the suffix may be understood as having the sense of "for the sake of the action" (*kriyārthe*).

The form *ke cidarthe stuvanti* contains a present participle (*śatṛ*-anta). It enjoins either "someone" (*kaṃ cit*) as the object to be enjoined (Mīmāṃsākośa 82), or someone related to that [person], or it enjoins an action or something related to that [action], and it does so by means of praise (*stuti*).
Thus, the authority of the *arthavāda* is established by way of the production of conviction (*pratyaya*).
[The author now refutes the commentary on the Bhāṣya as stated according to the opinion of some: However, they do not accept this interpretation;
for if there were the production of conviction, then by whom would the praise be required?
To begin with, there is no such thing as the operation of the verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā).
Even if one were to assume a requirement for the question "Why?", that too would concern only the injunction and its procedure, since it serves to assist them.
Only the mere instruction by means of different words varies.
Furthermore, that [commendation] occurs only for a person who is being enjoined, not merely from hearing the action itself.

For when it is said, "The white animal is to be sacrificed to Vāyu," one does not require [an answer to] whether it is praiseworthy or blameworthy prior to the statement of its being something to be done or not to be done.
And since they do not depend on that, the explanatory passages (arthavādas) do not convey their meaning by means of the scriptural statement alone.

Furthermore, there is no connection or dependence between the mind and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), because everything is subject to mental construction (*bhāvanā*). Since mental construction is removed by means of the exclusion of conditions (*pratyaya*), what would it depend upon?
Therefore, due to the cutting off of those three doors, there is no "coming-to-be" as a result, no sacrifice as an instrument (*karaṇa*), and no procedure (*itikartavyatā*) whatsoever for the mind.

Furthermore, even if predominance (*prādhānya*) has been stated, since the question "Why? is not required, once it is determined merely that "this is praiseworthy" (*praśasta*), the cognition of what ought to be done (*kartavyatābuddhi*) would not arise at all unless [the word] "because it is praiseworthy" (*praśastatvāt*) is supplied. Or, if such a cognition were to arise, it would be restricted solely to that [quality], just as in the cases: "This is praiseworthy and ought to be done," or "The cloth is red and ought to be made. If an injunction (*vidhi*) is not postulated, there would be nothing but meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*).

To set aside a directly perceived injunction (*pratyakṣa-vidhi*) and instead accept it through an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is an unprecedented mode of expression.
Nor is there any occasion for such a hypothesis, because [the injunction] is established by other means.
For an injunction would only be inferred from an explanatory passage when it is not explicitly stated and cannot be accounted for otherwise.
Because it is established by direct perception and valid cognition, there is no lack of logical necessity [for its existence].
Likewise, even an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), if it were useless for the purpose of generating interest through narratives and the like, would be cast far aside;
however, since it serves to generate interest according to the aforementioned principle, it does not go elsewhere.
Furthermore, if the incitement (*prarocanā*) were established from another source because it is something to be understood, then there would be no dependence on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

However, since that [incitement] has no other basis, it relies upon that very [explanatory passage]. Moreover, in every Vedic matter, a word would have to be inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and from that, the meaning would be established; thus, by means of the incitement, the injunctive word itself would be inferred, not the meaning.

And at the time of that conceptualization, just as in the case of the sentences concerning the [cups] for Indra-Vāyu and others, when the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" is present— as in the *Arthavāda* section (6.50)— no other [independent] sacrificial act is postulated; in exactly the same way, by the word "should take hold of" (*ālabheta*), there is a preclusion of the inference of another [act].
Furthermore, sublation (*bādha*) and option (*vikalpa*) occur between two [statements] that have the same meaning.

However, in the case of the statement regarding the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) and the statement regarding the ritual injunction (*vāda*), because their objects are entirely distinct—as being respectively the beneficiary (*anugrāhya*) and the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*)—there is a combination (*samuccaya*) due to the difference in meaning;
thus, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

And if there were a manifestation of the *pratyaya*, then there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of distinctions such as the agent (*kartṛ*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and voice (*upagraha*), as well as whether the fruit of the action is for one's own sake or for the sake of another.
This might be argued:
"By not intending to express merely the injunctive force (*vidhi-lakṣaṇa*), but by intending to express the remainder, the [distinctions of] agent, number, and so forth, are obtained."

And this is impossible, because even for that purpose, the suffix (pratyaya) employed by its very capacity (sāmarthyāt) necessarily expresses an injunction (vidhitva). Furthermore, there are only two possibilities for that which is already understood: either it is touched by an injunction, like the *mṛṣṭaka* [rite], or it is a mere restatement (*anuvādakatva*), like the *indriyakāma* oblation.
There is no such thing as the "non-injunctive nature" of an injunction.
Nor is it a restatement (anuvāda), because that meaning has not been previously established.

For it is not possible [to say], "This which is to be performed—the touching of the animal dedicated to Vāyu—is praiseworthy"; rather, it is possible [to say], "It is to be performed because it is praiseworthy.

As for the argument regarding the *udavasānīya* sacrifice, there too it must be accepted that the injunctive force rests solely on the action itself, without depending on the suffix *-ktvā* for either injunction or prohibition.

Furthermore, if there were an intention to express an injunction (*vidhi*), then the meaning of the verbal root *prayāsya-* would fall solely within the sphere of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and thus it would be fruitless.
(He begins to explain according to his own view: Therefore, there is syntactic unity with the injunction through the non-destruction of the Sūtra.
And so the author of the Bhāṣya says that [the passage] ending with "one desiring prosperity" (*bhūtikāmaḥ*) is indeed accompanied by an injunction: "a pure place."
Otherwise, he would have simply stated that "the meaning of the verbal root [is the object].
Furthermore, it is not possible to say here that the mere action itself is the pure location.
Therefore, it is the suffix (pratyaya) alone which, by virtue of being the agent of the act of knowing (*vid-bhi*), constitutes the pure location.

However, since it is possible for [the injunction] to form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive sense (*vidhyartha*), the mention of the subject (*uddeśa*) occurs beyond the scope of the sūtra.

Furthermore, the phrase "ending with 'one desiring prosperity'" (*bhūtikāma ityevamantaḥ*) is intended to demonstrate the occasion for praise (*stuti*) at a time subsequent to the connection with the result (*phala*) and so forth.

Now, one might object: since there is no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in cases where the present tense is used as an indicator (*vartamānāpadeśa*), the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) cannot be connected [to the injunction].
It is exactly so.

Nevertheless, because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it, the connection with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) occurs in some cases through an injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*), such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālo bhavati*); in some cases through the optative suffix (*pañcamalakāra*), as in "He performs the *upāṃśu* sacrifice elsewhere" (*upāṃśuyājam anyatrā yajati*); or else, when an injunction is inferred from the fact that what is heard cannot otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*). Even where an injunction is understood solely from the observation of a result, there too, the sole recourse is the principle of "otherwise being unaccountable."

[This is] because we observe that [passages such as] "To those two, he offered this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma at the Full Moon sacrifice" (TS 2.5.3.1) function as *arthavādas* (explanatory passages).
Furthermore, when a [more parsimonious] possibility exists, it is not appropriate to assume excessive complexity (*atigaurava*). (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 49)

As for the objection that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in this view because two relationships are not heard [simultaneously], that is refuted by the fact that it is possible for there to be a single flow [of meaning] in the form "one should sacrifice because it is praiseworthy. For it is only that which is being sought (*vicīyamāna*) that has a requirement for praise; thus, due to this lack of disparity (*avaiṣamya*), the status of being a common factor (*tantratva*) is established. Moreover, if a sentence were split by such differences in relationship, then it would also have to be split by the relationships between the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Therefore, the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "this connection is not intended" is to be interpreted as follows: it is not intended that the injunction for the constituent parts (*sāṅga*) reaches its conclusion in the preceding [sentence] alone; for if one were to assume an incentive (*prarocanā*) based on the fact that it is an injunction, there would be the fault of excessive prolixity (*atigaurava*) resulting from a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). The question "What is the purpose of the praise? arises from the misconception that the incentive is already established by the preceding [injunction]. The statement "How would it be pleasing? is an explanation of the grasping of the injunction.
The phrase "nanu prāk" (but previously) is a recapitulation of what was said before.

As for "na hi" (for not), this means that in the absence of praise (*stuti*), the two-fold capacity of that [word] is attributed only out of necessity (*agatyā*), and not even by way of a connection; thus he says that the injunction (*vidhi*) of the *bhūti* [mantra] is then completed. The example "yathā paṭaḥ" (just as a cloth) has its meaning already explained.
"The incitement [occurs] at that time by means of the word of injunction"—thus has the plurality of functions of the injunction (*vidhi*) and the eulogy (*stuti*) been explained.
To the objection, "But if it is so," [the response is: "If there is the power even to incite, why is anything else required? [The reply is:
"True. Therefore, when that [power] exists, and not when it is absent, the intended meaning is understood.
And what is this? It means that "praise is the purpose of those two," and not [the purpose] of that [injunction] alone, nor even of the preceding one.
Furthermore, because it provides a specific form of praise, the injunction itself is designated as having praise as its purpose;
for praise cannot occur without an object.
But in the absence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), one will have to accept the burden of [interpreting] even a solitary [word] out of necessity.
The phrase "even though they exist" was explained previously;

now, in the expression "from this [injunction]," the genitive case is used because of its connection with the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). Thus, we understand that its praise arises from that [remainder], and not inherently by itself—this is the meaning.

Regarding the objection, "But [an injunction] is independent, etc.": if someone were to argue that an injunction lacking an *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) possesses the power to impel action, why would it depend on anything else? Consequently, there would be no regard for other factors even when they are present.
However, the Teacher, speaking with a touch of irony, says: let it be so where that [injunction] is employed alone and is independent; in that case, there is no contradiction.
But here, such independence is not possible, because it is dependent upon other words through its expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*).
For a single sentence is the enjoiner of only one relationship;

in that case, if one were to perform [the rite] only in a pure location, then the section concerning explanatory passages (arthavāda-adhikaraṇa) [would apply]. 651. The section concerning explanatory passages.
If that were the case, there would be a split [in the sentence].
By stating, "This is indeed a merit for those who have been established in a pure place," it shows an inducement (*prarocanā*).
Therefore, because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) exist for the purpose of favoring that injunction.
And the traditional transmission is the same.

The Commentary states: "Now, it might be argued that the injunctive portions prior to the words of praise are independent of anything else because they possess the nature of injunctions, whereas the words of praise are merely a mistaken reading."
In that regard: because the meaning is understood in this way;
moreover, the traditional transmission is equal.

Those dharmas for which there is a traditional transmission (saṃpradāya) and a specific purpose are all equal in regard to both injunctive words (vidhipada) and explanatory words (arthavāda). Regarding the rules for study and non-study, the acquisition [of knowledge] from the mouth of the teacher, and the relationship between student and preceptor—all such matters are treated equally even when the purpose is not directly perceived; and the tradition is firmly remembered.
Therefore, it is not a careless reading.
Or rather—the objection "let there be meaninglessness" was raised for the purpose of explaining the word "or" (vā); that is not so.
Why? Because [the meaning] is understood through an explanatory passage (arthavāda) by means of the reasoning previously stated.

Alternatively, "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the state of being established; thus, because the meaning is understood in this way, it is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) according to the manner described.
Furthermore, the construction is "and it is equal" (*tulyaṃ ca*).
For the sake of favoring the tradition, the collection of dharmas is [established] through recourse to the principles (*tattva*) and through connection with the purpose of heaven.
Nor is there any evidence for its having another purpose, which would justify abandoning the study of what is proximate for the sake of something else;

furthermore, even if the tradition were unknown, it is precisely this [proximate study] that is required. Moreover, because it is remembered as being for that purpose, it cannot have the non-existent as its object.
For nothing else imagined would be consistent with the subsidiary requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*).

If, first of all, heaven were to be imagined [as the result], then it would follow that [the study] is merely for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Alternatively, if it is argued that the accomplishment of the fruit of the sacrifice occurs once the Veda has been recited, even so, it would still be of no assistance [to the sacrifice]. Therefore, for one who accomplishes the grasping of the syllables of the tradition, the collection of restrictive rules (*niyamajāta*) serves as a supportive factor.
Furthermore, there can be no purpose for that which does not exist; it would be better for such a thing to be simply non-existent, so that at least there would be no affliction.
Since they hold the injunctions of the Smṛtis to be equal to those of the Veda, there must necessarily be some other purpose as well.
And because these restrictive rules (niyamas) are rooted in the Veda, this regard for them is indeed established by the Veda itself.

And since that [recollection] would not be possible because it lacks a purpose, one infers a purpose for the general [text]; thus, by implication—according to the principle "or [it is] from the sense, because of the unity of the conception" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.23)—the specific purpose of the *arthavādas* is obtained as being praise (*stuti*).
He states this very point in the words, "and the recollection is firm.
Alternatively, this very recollection of the text consists in its preservation.
Therefore, the possession of a purpose [of the Veda] is established through inference based on the prior intention of the person who studied it for the sake of a specific purpose.
Furthermore, since this understanding can be derived from some [ancillary] statement (*vākya*), there is no lack of authority [in the Veda].
Otherwise, some might discard these [Vedic texts], thinking they are purposeless, and would instead grasp only the injunctions (*vidhi*) while ignoring the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
In that case, there would be no firm recollection of these [words], yet such recollection exists;
therefore, it is not a careless reading.
And thus, regarding the phrase "because they possess meaning":

there is another interpretation of the rule "and the traditional practice is equal. That is to say, the traditional practice (*saṃpradāya*) is the purpose of a statement by which that tradition was initiated—namely, the injunction "therefore, one's own Veda must be studied. Since this applies equally to both injunctions and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) because there is no distinction in their being part of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), it follows by the previously stated reasoning that [the Veda] cannot remain [merely as a ritual act] until the human goal is accomplished. Therefore, according to the capacity [of the words], it is established that the explanatory passages have the purpose of praise.

Furthermore, this inconsistency does not apply; for if there were an application [of the literal sense], there would be a contradiction, since the word, its meaning, existence, and connection are established as such. Therefore, it is consistent. The Commentary states: Moreover, that inconsistency which was stated—beginning with "because of contradiction with the scripture"—does not apply to passages such as "He wept" (so 'rodīt).
Why? Because a contradiction would indeed arise only if acts such as theft were being enjoined through the application [of the literal sense].
The meaning of the word is that it has not been employed [in its primary sense].
Therefore, it is logically consistent to say, "the mind is a thief, the speech of the liar. *Vā*—this concludes the refutation of the aforementioned objection. What follows is further [discussion].

We consider that other "inexplicability" (*anyānupapatti*) mentioned regarding the postulation of an injunction—which was cited as contradicting the scriptures (*śāstravirodha*)—does not apply to our position.

Alternatively, for those who read the text with a short vowel, this explanation of the praise (*stuti*) should be interpreted as meaning that the aforementioned inexplicability does not apply [to our view].

For if one were to postulate [the injunctions] for actual performance (*prayoga*), that is, for practical execution, there would be a contradiction regarding weeping, tearing out hair, hatred, theft, lying, and so forth.

For us, however, that literal meaning of these words is not what is intended to be expressed; nor is there an injunction through ellipsis and the like. Rather, it is mere praise (*stuti*) that is intended, and this does not contradict [the injunction].
Therefore, it is logical.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "of the words," this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) exists for the purpose of supporting the injunctive words; it is not possible for it to be performed according to its own literal meaning.
It is attained through application and does not constitute the state of non-application;
therefore, its occurrence is justified.
There are three readings here: "and the non-occurrence is unattained," where the remainder of the sentence is "we consider this."
Another [teacher] says: "Non-attainment and non-arising"; in that case, the phrase "the explanation of the non-existent" and so forth is supplied.
Another says: "Non-attainment and the impossibility [of arising]"; in that case, they are understood as referring to the position of the non-existent (*asat*).
"But it is figurative praise.

The Commentary states: "As for what was said—that praise is for the purpose of creating interest in that which is to be enjoined—how can that be applicable here, where one thing is to be enjoined and something else is praised?

For example, in the passage, 'He sprinkles the wet ground with reed-shoots and *avakā* plants,' the reeds and *avakā* plants are enjoined, yet the waters are praised in the statement, 'The waters are indeed peaceful.'"
To this it is replied: "But it is a figurative statement. This statement is figurative (gauṇa), in that things which are to be praised are connected with the proximity of what is being praised.
For this is the lineage of the two Vetasa reeds;
from them they were born.
And by virtue of that connection with the lineage, one who is well-born (abhijāta) is praised.
Just as Devadatta, being of our own kin, considers himself praised when the people of Aśmaka are being praised—
so too should it be understood here.
(Aśmakas is the name of a particular region.)
Now, of which injunction is the passage "He wept" (so'rodīt) a supplement? It is of the injunction: "Therefore, silver should not be given on the sacrificial grass" (tasmād barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam).
Why? Because the words are expectant of further connection.

In the phrase "He wept; because he wept, that is the origin of Rudra's name" (so'rodīt yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam), the pronoun "he" (saḥ) refers back to the subject under discussion, for it is dependent upon that context.

Regarding the phrase "that tear of his which fell," the word "of him" (tasya) refers back precisely to the subject previously under discussion. Furthermore, this [statement] serves as the logical justification for the subsequent passage, "If one were to give silver on the sacrificial grass (barhis), there will be weeping in his house before a year has passed," thereby functioning as a substitute for the intended meaning: "Therefore, silver should not be given on the sacrificial grass.
In this manner, all [the statements] are interdependent.
How do they bring about what is to be enjoined? By means of figurative praise (*guṇavāda*).
For one who places silver—which originates from weeping—upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he encounters weeping;
thus, "not weeping" is a figurative statement regarding the prohibition of that [silver].

But how can it be said that he "wept" when he did not weep? Or how can there be the statement that silver is "born from tears" when no tears were produced? Furthermore, since no weeping occurred before this year, how could there be weeping? To this it is replied: it is a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*).
These words are secondary (*gauṇa*).
Because the word *rudra* is seen to have its etymological basis in the act of weeping, it is said, "because he wept."
Because of the similarity in color, he says that even the "tearing out of the eye" (*anaśrubhavana*) originates from tears (*aśruprabhava*).
Furthermore, since one observes suffering when wealth is abandoned, he says, "Before a year has passed, there will be weeping in his house.

Likewise, because of the expectancy of the injunction, "He who desires offspring or cattle should sacrifice this hornless goat to Prajāpati," the following is its supplement: "He drew out the omentum of his own body."
What is the glorification of qualities (*guṇavāda*)? It is this: "She was indeed not non-existent, [but] cattle, when Prajāpati extracted his own omentum.
And this is the efficacy of the ritual act: that when the omentum was first offered, a hornless goat emerged; thus, the meaning is that cattle become abundant.

But how does he say that Prajāpati extracted his own omentum when the omentum had already been performed? It is said in reply: *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from Śabara’s commentary on the Mīmāṃsāsūtra (1.2.10–11), discussing the nature of *arthavāda* as *guṇavāda*.*

The narration of events that lack a corresponding illustrative example is for the purpose of praise, since commendation is what is understood [thereby]. In this context, regarding the narration of events (*vṛttāntākhyāna*), it is established that it is useless because it lacks a purpose; for while a substance is produced through the current narration, and while there may be either an inducement toward something or an aversion, the narration of events itself neither incites action nor causes cessation. Thus, due to the absence of a motive, it is concluded to be purposeless.
One engages through encouragement and desists through aversion; such is the distinction between the two.
Even when the narration of events is being enjoined, the defect of having a beginning is attributed to the Veda.
How, then, is this [Veda] explained as being without a basis? It is said in reply:

There must be some eternal entity, whether it be Prajāpati, Vāyu, Ākāśa, or Āditya; he extracted his own omentum— meaning rain, wind, or a ray— and offered it first into the fire before sunrise, either into the Āhavanīya fire, the domestic fire, or the digestive fire.
