Therefore, regarding the term "aja" (goat), one may either sow or scatter [the seed]. Having seized it and having consumed it, one obtains offspring; thus these are figurative expressions.

The passage "The sun is the *prāṇīya* cup, the sun is the *udayanīya* cup" is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to this injunction, because of the expectancy [of a reason], as in: "The gods, not having determined the sacrificial ground, did not know the directions. This is a praise [of the sun], meaning that the sun is the destroyer of all delusions, including even the delusion regarding the directions.
How is it that there is the term "delusion regarding direction" (*diṅmoha*) when no such delusion exists? It is said:
because a vast collection of non-ordinary tasks is present, the word "delusion" (*moha*) is used figuratively (*gauṇa*).
Its figurative nature is indicated by the taking up of the *avadhāraṇa-vakā* and other implements.

Or rather—where there is a single object for both the injunction (*vidhi*) and the eulogy (*stuti*), let it be granted that this is possible; but how is it so when the objects of the relationship are different?
He says: "Because of a quality" (*guṇāt*).

When something related to an action is praised, another thing related to it may be praised; or, if in the case of an *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirement), that which is related to the base (*prakṛti*) is praised for the sake of enjoining it, then the base itself is praised through its relation to that other thing. Since praise is thus established in both worldly and Vedic usage by means of such indirect methods, there is no fault.
The meaning of this praise will be explained later:
how it is that a transformation connected with peaceful waters, being a cause of peace, brings tranquility (*śamyati*) for the sacrificer.
The explanation of the figurative statement (*guṇavāda*) as being based solely on purity already provides the resolution for the example of weeping (*so 'rodīt*).
The remaining sūtras also serve to substantiate what has been stated here.

Among those, some of the grounds for the figurative application (*gauṇanimitta*) of the examples cited will be explained right here; however, in the *siddhasūtra* (1.4.22), it is stated that because the phrase "he wept" (*so 'rodīt*) is syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣatvena*), it forms a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction, resulting in the abandonment of the suffix [indicating an independent command].
The word "sa" (he/it) refers back to what has been previously mentioned.
Why? Because of the recognition of that;
for it is that which is recognized as being the subject under discussion.
Alternatively, it is well known that the word *tat* (that) refers to what has been previously mentioned.
When "he" is said, because of the cognition produced by the word *tat*, one understands "this is that very same person.
In this way, the possibility arises that "his tears were silver."
All of this is the justification for the subsequent passage of censure; therefore, its mention immediately following that [prohibition] is appropriate.
What is that passage? He shows it: "Whoever should give silver upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), before a year has passed, there shall be weeping in his house.
For what reason does this happen? That is what is justified here.

Because the causes possess the nature of form, and because the effect arises from weeping—that is, the giving of that [gift]—it is called "the origin of weeping" (*rodanopaniṣad*). Therefore, "nothing should be given"; this constitutes the entire logical justification for non-giving.
And the censure (*nindā*) is purposeful as a supplement to that [prohibition].

However, it is a figurative description (*guṇavāda*) based on the word; by the force of the cognition evoked by Rudra’s gift, there is an assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) through the general category of weeping.
Furthermore, because tears are white, if they were indeed solid, they would be like silver; thus there is a harsh censure of their non-existence [as such].
Or, the mention of weeping is introduced because even for one who is extremely magnanimous through the renunciation of wealth, his household members suffer; this is based on that commonality.
Thus, by whatever means a cognition of censure arises, it is helpful for the purpose of prohibition; therefore, there is no fault in the absence of a primary meaning.
Thus is the construction of the passage concerning the cutting out of the omentum (*vapā*) and so forth.

For even by the mention of the owner's lack of repetition [of the act], rituals are performed for the sake of a specific purpose; how much more so, then, by the renunciation of one who is a Brahmin—this is the praise.
Just as in common worldly usage they praise a renouncer, saying, "He gives away even this [body] without regret."

Furthermore, since the Veda culminates in a narrative, it does not attain authority regarding that [narrative] itself; because it is true only in its praise, it is not otherwise [authoritative]. Thus, there is no purpose in the truthfulness of the narrative as such. Alternatively, the explanatory passages (arthavādas) serve the purpose of the verbal productive energy (śābdabhāvanā), and that activity is useful only through cognition, not through the [external] object.
But regarding the objective reality [of the meaning], there is indeed no dispute anywhere; it is already established.
Now, if it should be argued that praise and blame consist in the misrepresentation of what is non-existent, then that is all the more clearly perceived.
Granted, speakers may act according to their own whims, but what praise or blame is there in this?
"This is indeed true.

But regarding the untrue, since one says "he is virtuous" here even though he has been observed elsewhere to be otherwise, one thinks, "Therefore, he surely intends to please me," or likewise, "He is censuring someone who is virtuous in order to turn him away.
And having understood this, one acts accordingly in accordance with that which cannot be transgressed by another.

And it is established that the Veda is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, regarding an object within one's own experience—which is to be engaged with or avoided—the person acquires cognitions of what is commendable and what is not.
In this case, those two [cognitions] are produced by the Veda.
Therefore, one should act in accordance with that [convention].

Even in the world, when people wish to induce someone toward an action that they consider to be connected with another result—such as being caused by intelligence (*medhā*) and so forth—they employ that person by presenting a result such as good fortune (*saubhāgya*), even though it is unreal.
Consequently, the other person also obtains the result based upon that action.

Even though the practitioner knows that this is not the ultimate fruit here, but was presented by these [teachers] in accordance with their own intentions, and that they do not, in any way, urge him toward what is not a human goal—he nevertheless acts, knowing that "this is indeed untrue; I shall obtain something else.

Similarly, in the Veda as well, the fruit is understood through the injunction (*vidhi*), while the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) may indeed incite one through what is untrue. However, the truth or untruth of those [passages] does not detract from the injunction in the least, because the person who is being urged acts on the basis of the superimposition [of desirability].

Since the wise do not fail to act once they have ascertained that whatever exists in another [person's] mind will be realized through the performance of the rite (*vidhi*), the unreality of the narrative (*upākhyāna*) is irrelevant.

For it is not the case that the reality of the perception of mother-of-pearl depends on the silver; rather, if one finds something in that place which serves as a basis (*ālambana*)—just like the mother-of-pearl itself—it is then pursued.
This [interpretation] based on the mere similarity of the Vedic texts (śruti) should be applied everywhere.

Just as here the great elements (mahābhūta) are called "Lords of Creatures" (prajāpati) because they protect their offspring, so too, among the elements such as water and the rest, the essences—rain and so forth—which exist in the middle, are the "omentum" (vapā). That [essence] is sacrificed by that very same sequence: rain is offered into the fire-altar (agnīdh), the wind existing within the body is offered into the wind by means of its nature as moving within, and the ray is offered into the common fire because it nourishes it.
Then, because seeds and the like are generally beginningless, the term "aja" (unborn) is well-established;
by touching—that is, attaining—that [aja], one obtains offspring and cattle.
This is the basis for the ritual, since all progeny originate from the transformation of rice and other grains.
The status of nectar-rain and the like as "vapā" (omentum) is established through their connection with the quality characterized by being the essence situated in the middle.

Since the beginning and end of the rain are occupied by the wind, that which is situated in the middle—as in the passage, "They moisten the [rain] here with the rim"—is the rain; thus, when the wind is praised as the cause of rain, the rain is seen to be its essence.
[This applies to] the space...

In the case of wind (*vāyu*), because its activity exists within it, that which is situated in its midst is its essence; and since the space devoid of wind produces heat and suffering, that [wind] is its essence.
In the case of light (*raśmi*), because it is a constituent part of the sun, it is situated within it; and since the power of illumination depends upon the rays, those [rays] are its essence.
Regarding the lightning (*vaidyuta*), because fire is well known to be a portion of it, there is a specific conceptualization of rain.
Because the *ṛṣītāda* resides in the body and speech, the fire within it is the *āvīśa*.
In the conceptualization of the placement of the wind (*vāyu*) therein, the internal autumnal moon (*antaśśaratsāmānya*) serves as the support.

Based on such scriptural observations as, "The sun, when setting, enters into the fire," since the sun situated in heaven can logically enter the fire on earth in its own form, there is the conceptualization of the entry of its rays.

Since the sprouting of rice and other grains is not observed in the absence of heat, and since that heat possesses the quality of fire (*tejas*), and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "the herbs are fiery," it follows that the [subtle] body is composed of fire. On account of this similarity, the conjunction with rain and water is designated as its cause.

When the essence of food (*annarasa*) has been digested by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), there is a simultaneity [of the subtle body's formation], because it occurs at the same time as the non-seed-like [essence] is rendered non-perishable by the specific wind called *vyāna*.

Thus [it is said]: "Non-eternal (*ākālika*) means quickly perishable; or, that which arises on the previous day at midday or another time and perishes on that very same day in the subsequent day. (Kaumudī)
Or, *akālika* is a corruption (*pāṭha*) [of *akālika*]. In common usage, "time" (*kāla*) refers to distance.
That which exists therein [is called *akālika*]; according to Pāṇini 4.3.11, *kālaṭ ṭhañ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after words denoting time.
[The suffix] *ṭhañ* [is applied] after *māsika* and *sāṃvatsarika*; thus, [from *kāla* with *ṭhañ*] comes *kālika*. That which is not *kālika* is *akālika*.

Praise of Knowledge (vidyā-praśaṃsā). The Commentary states: By the phrase "likewise because of the existence of a result," the statement "his face shines" is cited as a supplement (śeṣa) to the injunction for the Garga-trirātra sacrifice, because it is required [by that injunction].
And for the Vedic consecration formula (vedānumantraṇa), the statement "in his offspring a vigorous one is born" is the supplement.
The beauty of the face and the possession of horses are metaphorical expressions because they denote qualities;
for [the teacher] shines as if with disciples who are being instructed.
It is said that one born into a family where study and hearing have been continuous becomes intelligent, and thus he obtains food through receiving gifts.
Or rather—the injunction for study, being specific, is not an injunction of a fruit, as it merely restates what is already known: that [the Veda] possesses beauty of face and possession of cattle.
Furthermore, there is not only one mode of "beauty of face," namely, its configuration, loveliness, and charm;
for this refers specifically to women.
For the learned, however, the face illuminated by the logic of words and sentences shines with splendor.

Therefore, since it has been established in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) that the *Arthavādas*—such as "The Vāyavya [animal] goes to heaven" (*vāyavyaṃ... gamayati*)—are indeed non-human (authorless) because they lack any indication of an author, whether through injunction (*vidhi*) or prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), the question is now investigated: does that same authority (*prāmāṇya*) exist for them regarding merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), or not?

In that regard, since injunctions and prohibitions—by their own inherent power—convey injunctions and prohibitions whose objects are *bhāvanās* qualified by the end (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it follows by implication that sacrifices and other acts, which are the subjects of those injunctions and prohibitions, possess the nature of being means to the desirable and the undesirable; thus, it is appropriate for them to be authoritative regarding dharma and adharma as being the means to the desirable and the undesirable. However, in the case of *arthavādas*, because they cannot, by their own power, convey established facts (*siddhārtha*) in their true or false forms, there is no possibility of their being authoritative regarding dharma and adharma.

Nor can its expression be achieved through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), textual supplementation (*adhyāhāra*), or other such means, even when there is a connection with that [intended meaning]; for since the purpose is served by the expression of the meaning exactly as heard, there is no ground for impossibility (*anyānupapatti*)—and without that, such [figurative] interpretation is impossible. Nor can it be postulated on the basis of the necessity of the intended purport (*tātparya*), because that too is impossible due to the absence of any indicator of purport (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

Indeed, there is no proof for a restrictive rule that "verbal testimony is only a means of knowledge" or "it has only two purposes," by which that [rule] itself could be established as an indicator of purport.
This is because there is deviation [from the rule] due to the frequent observation of even those things that lack a purpose.

Nor should it be argued that, just like the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*)—which prescribes study for the sake of the knowledge of meaning rather than mere recitation—the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" implies that the subject matter must possess a purpose, since otherwise the study of something purposeless would be untenable;
for study, which produces the knowledge of meaning, is already established as a goal in itself and is therefore not something to be further enjoined.

Because it is of no use for knowing the meaning of that nigama, and because it is impossible to assume its utility as far as the sacrifice (*kratu*) due to the absence of an unerring established relationship, it cannot be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

Therefore, by the injunction of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), study is enjoined solely for the sake of heaven; or, since worldly activity is already admitted as a prerequisite, let the result (*bhāvya*) of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) be the knowledge of the meaning exactly as heard through study itself. Nor does this lead to a lack of engagement due to the absence of a desired result, because engagement is established even by the injunction against non-performance—namely, the statement "those who do not study become [outcastes]," which makes known the sin resulting from its omission.

Therefore, since the statement of two purposes implies the cutting off of its status as Veda, the definition [of Veda] cannot be established by relying upon that [status] in the case of the *arthavādas*. Thus, it is argued that the *arthavādas* are not a means of valid knowledge regarding dharma and adharma. This being the position reached, [the reply is: the injunction for self-study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) does not enjoin the study [of the Veda] for the sake of heaven; for when a visible result is possible, the postulation of an invisible one is improper.

Nor is it for the sake of knowing the meaning exactly as it was heard; for if that were the case, study would be mandatory simply because it makes [the text] audible. Furthermore, for one who has grasped the connection between words and their meanings, knowledge is mandatory—as stated in such passages as: "He who, having studied the Veda, does not know its meaning, is like a pillar carrying a burden" and "He who knows the meaning attains all prosperity and goes to heaven through the injunction for knowledge" (*Nirukta* 1.18). Thus, since knowledge is mandatory, the knowledge of the meaning exactly as it was heard is established as a necessary consequence (*ānuṣaṅgika*) of the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-vidhi*). Therefore, the meaning is not a secondary matter (*prasaṅga*) of that injunction.
By this, the assumption that the study [of the Veda] is for its own sake (*adhyayanabhavya*) is also refuted.

Therefore, in order to avoid futility, the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is enjoined as something to be performed for the sake of knowing the purposeful meaning; or rather, the mere act of study is enjoined by means of the Veda itself—which serves as the instrument for attaining the knowledge of the purposeful meaning and so forth—because of the conviction that the Veda is *dharma* through that very [act of] study.

Consequently, following the method of the *Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa*, once the purposefulness of the Veda’s subject matter is established, the establishment of *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) occurs in the case of *arthavādas* as a means of grasping the intended purport (*tātparya*).

The meaning of that which is to be characterized (lakṣaṇīya) consists of praise or censure, because it depends on the expectation of an adjacent injunction. For instance, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is a human purpose in worldly discourse; however, since such a purpose is absent in the Veda, it must be some property residing solely within the optative suffix itself.

The delimitor of denotability (*vācyatā-avacchedaka*) is common to both [positive and negative injunctions] and consists in being possessed of an operation (*vyāpāravat*), but it does not include being the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), because that is obtainable through other means.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: in the absence of the negative particle (*nañ*), there is the relation of the verbal suffix’s meaning being the cause of engagement; but when it is present, the relation is its being the cause of the non-existence of engagement with that object.

Furthermore, "causality" (*prayojakatva*) here refers to being the cause of engagement, which consists in being the object of the production of a cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā-jñāna*).
Furthermore, it is the cause of non-existence and common to both acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*).
And its reality consists in being that which disrupts the causal complex for activity; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Moreover, that meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is synonymous with "instigation" (*pravartanā*), "impulsion" (*preraṇā*), and "the object [of action]" within an injunctive statement.
In a prohibitive statement (*niṣedhavākya*), the terms *nivartanā*, *nivāraṇa*, *niṣedha*, and *pratiṣedha* are synonyms.

This verbal productive energy (*śābdībhāvanā*) is of two kinds. Its objects to be brought about (*bhāvya*) are, as appropriate, either engagement (*pravṛtti*) or abstention (*nivṛtti*). The knowledge of the verbal productive energy is its instrument (*karaṇa*).
And here, "instrumentality" (*karaṇatva*) consists in being the producer of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
And the "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) consists, as appropriate, in praise and blame.
For it is well-established in the world that the knowledge of praise and blame functions as an auxiliary cause for the instigation of activity and cessation by way of generating desire.

In the case of words expressing praise (*stuti*) or censure (*nindā*), their meanings as "praiseworthiness" (*prāśastya*) and "unpraiseworthiness" (*aprāśastya*) consist respectively in the fitness for being connected with or not being connected to a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*).

These two qualities are conveyed through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of the *arthavāda* passages associated with the respective injunctions or prohibitions, as they are required by those injunctions and prohibitions.

In that regard, in such passages as "To Vāyu [belongs] the most swift [offering]," the secondary indication occurs precisely through the qualities of "most swiftness" and so forth, which are already denotable by the word itself.

It will be explained later that in such cases as "The sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle)," the figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) occurs on account of qualities such as the performance of the same function;
therefore, this is established by the argument found in the section on *arthavādas* (6.4.9).

The authoritative status (*prāmāṇya*) of explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) regarding merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) arises from their capacity to produce valid cognitions concerning praise and blame that are associated with meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
As for the purpose: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the attainment of the result occurs through activity even from a cognition of excellence not presented by the *arthavāda*;

however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since there is a rule—similar to that of mantras—that *arthavādas* must function as indirect indicators (*parokṣaka*), it should be understood that the attainment of the result occurs through activity arising only from a cognition of excellence presented by them.
Maṇḍana: "Praise is the most swift [means] for Vāyu.
Śaṅkara: "The authority of the explanatory passages (arthavāda) and so forth"; and "And utility [is established] from the explanatory passages."

By refuting the meaninglessness of all supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*), the status of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is established precisely within the *Arthavāda* section (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.1–18).

On page 397 of the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, it is elaborated in the *Arthavāda* section that even in the case of human-authored works, the eternity [of the Veda] is established through the eternity of its tradition (*pravāha-nityatā*), thereby justifying the fact that [the Veda] is the subject matter of injunctions (*vidhi*).
In the *Arthavāda* section (Kuṭuka 1.3.10), there is a twofold investigation.

(1) First, because these [Arthavādas] were previously refuted on the grounds that they lack injunctive purpose and are thus useless—since they cannot be enjoined by the injunction to study, according to the portion of the Sūtra stating "But because they form a single sentence with an injunction" (1.2.7)—and also by the Sūtra "And the traditional transmission is the same" (1.2.8); (2) nevertheless, since they are not impossible, they are revived here, and in this section, a specific means for the Arthavādas is considered.

Therefore, by this sūtra, the two prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*) are stated in a combined manner (*tantra*) through their general and specific forms. Because, according to the principle of "the connection [of words] with action for the sake of action" (JS 1.2.9), the status of being for the sake of action is determined; and since that is impossible for the *arthavādas*, they would be purposeless.

Even if one begins to assume some way for them to serve the purpose of action because they are enjoined by the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), nevertheless, due to the impossibility of any such means for the *arthavādas*, their purposelessness remains difficult to overcome.
