*Arthasamavāyāt* (661). Because the object is inherent [in the act], the expiation applies even when only a portion of the object is involved.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, an expiation is prescribed for the breaking of the potsherds, the *sruc* ladles, and so forth, in the rule "He offers when [something] is broken," as well as for the spilling of the sacrificial materials such as clarified butter (*ājya*) in the rule "He offers when [it] is spilled.
This expiation applies whether the breakage or spilling occurs in a single part or in its entirety; that is, whether the whole or even a single part is broken or spilled.

This is because of the inherent connection with the purpose (*arthasamavāya*): since the purpose remains connected to the object—even when only a part is broken—the term "broken" (*bhinna*) is inherently applicable to that object by virtue of the injunction "He offers when broken," due to its being included within the scope of the definition.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that an expiation must be performed even for the breaking of a single part;
however, [the opponent objects] that this is not so because of the resulting deficiency, for [the rite] is for that purpose.
Thus the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises a doubt.
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the established position (*siddhāntapakṣa*).

Expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies only when there is a partial breakage and so forth; it is not possible for expiation to apply when the vessel is entirely broken in its totality, because of the resulting deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), which renders it incapable of performing its intended function.
For this expiation is for the sake of the moment of the oblation (*homakṣaṇa*), intended as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the broken potsherd used for that purpose.
But in the case of total breakage, whose [act] would it be an embellishment? Therefore, the expiation applies only when there is partial breakage, not when there is total breakage.
Alternatively, when the entire potsherd is broken, that expiation does not apply;
because of the deficiency, the expiation would be rendered useless.
For the destruction of the defect is the quality and fruit of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Moreover, not every breach can be remedied by expiation;
because expiation is prescribed for that purpose, namely, for the sake of eliminating the defect of the breach.
But in the case of every distinct [act], it is appropriate;
therefore, there is no expiation for every distinct act.
This is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
The reading in the *Kutūhala* is "aśeṣavaiguṇyāt" (due to the deficiency of all [factors]).
Here, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) expressing the cause (*nimitta*) functions in the sense of the locative (*saptamī*).
The meaning—namely, "due to the deficiency of all [factors] such as the piercing [of the ear]" and so forth—is as explained previously.

"Indeed, [the penance] applies because it is occasioned by the act itself; for it is eternally connected with that purpose, whereas [the act] is non-eternal due to its being for the sake of a subordinate quality.
Having set aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) reached through the Sūtra by means of the word "or" (vā), he states the aforementioned final conclusion (siddhānta) along with its reasoning:
even when there is a total breach, as if there were a partial breach, the expiation (prāyaścitta) should take place.

Because it has the breaking as its occasion (*prātanimittatvāt*): since the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has the breaking as its occasion (*nimitta*), such is its nature. Even when there is a complete breakage, the occasion consisting of the breaking is indeed attained.
And when the occasion has been attained, the contingent rite (*naimittika*) must be performed.
As for the claim that there is an expiation for the purpose of consecrating what has been partially broken, that is not so;
because it is not its property, due to its constant connection [with the whole].
"Its property" refers to the property of that broken fragment, such as a potsherd; "not its property" means *ataddharma*.
The *homa* does not possess the characteristics of the broken potsherd (*bhinnakapāla*).
Why? Because the *homa* is connected with the obligatory *darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual.
For this *homa* belongs to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice dedicated to Agni; it is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the broken potsherd and so forth.
For indeed, since there is a connection of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rite—which is obligatory—with the purpose of the potsherd (*kapāla*), which is an accessory (*guṇa*) of that rite;
or alternatively, there is no connection of that *homa* with the breaking of the potsherd for the sake of the accessory in the form of the potsherd, because the breaking is non-obligatory (*anitya*).
In this regard, there are three intermediate sentences.
Therefore, even when there is every kind of breakage, there must be an expiation.
Furthermore, because qualities are subservient to another purpose, their application [to that purpose] follows from the scriptural statement.
He states another reason for the position that the *bhedana-homa* (the oblation for breaking) is not intended for a broken potsherd (*bhinnakapāla*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction.
Because qualities are for the sake of another, the oblation is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the potsherds (*kapāla*).
In the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), both the potsherd and the oblation are subordinate qualities.
The auxiliary elements (aṅga) serve the purpose of the principal (pradhāna).
Without a scriptural statement, an auxiliary would not have the purpose of another auxiliary.
However, because of the existence of a scriptural statement, even an auxiliary may sometimes be the support (vyapāśraya), that is, the basis (āśraya), for another auxiliary.
And there is no such statement here;
therefore, the oblation following the breaking [of the vessel] is not for the sake of the broken potsherd, but rather for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice itself.
Regarding the word *vyapāśraya*, its meaning is "resort" (*āśraya*), as seen in passages such as *māṃ hi pārtha vyapāśritya* (Bhagavad Gītā 9.32).

Regarding the case of a broken [vessel], it has been stated that because of the injunction, "One offers when it is broken," there would be a recourse to the broken vessel as a means of purification (*saṃskāra*), rather than a non-recourse.
And in the *Subodhinī*, it is stated: "By virtue of the injunction, there is a recourse, which is an application elsewhere.
If it is argued that this is for the purpose of mending the breakage, [the response follows].

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects that the oblation (*homa*) is intended solely for the purpose of consecrating the broken potsherd. He argues that because of the accusative case-ending in the scriptural injunction, "One should join the broken potsherd with the verse, 'With the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables, I join thee,'" the act of joining pertains to the broken potsherd; therefore, even the performance of the oblation must be for the sake of the broken potsherd as its consecration, on account of the specific statement.
Refutation of the Position of Elliptical Completion (Adhyāhāra) 662: Justification of the Position of Elliptical Completion of Meaning;
Refutation of the Position of Elliptical Completion. Now, one might object: "Why complete the sentence by elliptically supplying only the meaning? Why should there be a postulation of words?"
The [meaning] is established as complete by the mere presence of the Lord (nātha).
For it is the word-meanings (*padārtha*), as presented by two words that constitute a single sentence (*ekavākya*), which convey the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), and not otherwise.
Indeed, when only "bring" (*ānaya*) is said, or when "cow" (*gām*) is said—even if the cow is directly perceived—the act of bringing is not construed with the cow [merely on that basis].

And thus, in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *Saurya* and others, since the words "Soma" and so forth—which do not apply there—are excluded, the accomplishment of *ūha* (modification) occurs through the insertion of words such as "Sūrya" to complete the mantra-sentence, which is deficient and requires supplementation.

However, for those who maintain that there is an implicit verbal ellipsis (*arthādhyāhāra*), the *ūha* would not be established, because [in their view] the mantra would merely manifest the offering (*nirvāpa*) as qualified by the implicitly supplied "Sūrya.

Likewise, in cases where only an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is heard in the governing injunction (*adhikāravākya*), such as "Those who perform these nights indeed become firmly established," even there, according to your view, it is the injunctive sense itself that must be supplied, not the explanatory praise (*vidhi-stuti*).
Consequently, neither the assistance provided by the archetypal (prakṛta) elements nor the status of the constituent parts (padārtha) as being for the sake of the *apūrva* would be established.

For even if the constituent parts exist, their connection with those [archetypes] characterized by expectancy, proximity, and compatibility cannot be established without verbal expression (*abhidhāna*).
Furthermore, there is no word here that denotes the *apūrva*, which could express the *apūrva* as connected with the archetypal elements.
Nor do the archetypal words exist in the modification (*vikṛti*) such that they could denote their own meanings as connected with a new *apūrva*.

Furthermore, there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between them and the objects denoted by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), nor with the subordinate *apūrva*; thus, there would be a total lack of connection.

Similarly, in the archetype as well, in the case of "The New and Full Moon sacrifices [are performed] for the sake of all desires," since the injunctive word is neither recited nor supplied, the meaning of the injunction—which is distinct from the *apūrva* pertaining to the qualification of one desiring heaven and from the *āgneya* and other constituent rites—would have to be supplied; consequently, the status of the *samidh* and other offerings as being part of this [central sacrifice] would not be established.

For [the word denoting the material], such as *samid* and so forth, unlike [the word for] threshing and the like, is not capable of expressing heaven as being connected with the *apūrva* of the qualification (*adhikāra*), because it has already been explained as having a different scope. Therefore, in such injunctions of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), only the injunctive word itself is to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*), not the meaning.

Furthermore, since the meaning of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) is entirely beyond the scope of worldly experience, it cannot be brought to mind through either a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or a fallacious one (*tadābhāsa*). Therefore, in the case of sentences concerning eligibility (*adhikāravākya*) where no injunctive word is heard, or in originative sentences (*utpattivākya*) such as "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds [is offered] on the new moon day," how could there be an *adhyāhāra* (supplying) of that intended object simply because it is present in the mind? Thus, even against one's will, the *adhyāhāra* of a word must be admitted. Śābarabhāṣya 11.1.6, pp. 82–83. This is the defense of the position regarding the supplying of the meaning (*arthādhyāhārapakṣa*).
On this point, some maintain that from the heard meaning of the statement, "Devadatta is fat; he does not eat during the day," the very word "he eats at night" is inferred.

For instance, the act of eating inferred from his fatness is prohibited as occurring during the day; thus, the incongruity is resolved by the conceptualization of eating at night through a verbalized, determinate cognition (*savikalpika*).
Therefore, it is inferred based on its primacy and parsimony (*lāghava*), because the incongruity is pacified by the meaning presented by that inferred word.

[Objection: But in this way, even in the case of sensory non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), there would be the undesirable consequence of it being non-sensory (*anaindriyaka*), because by virtue of its primacy and brevity, one might assume that the word itself is the conceptualization.

[Reply: It is not so. Since among animals and others, the capacity of the sense organ is determined to reside only in the object—expressed as "of the sense organ in the object"—it is logical to assume the capacity [of the word] in the word as well.
Furthermore, since the purpose is observed, the capacity is assumed to reside in the object alone.

In this case as well, a word need not be postulated. This is not so; for even there, the postulation of a power (*śakti*) pertains to the meaning that serves as the justification (*upapādaka*), not to the mere object itself.
Here, since the word alone is the justification, it is the word itself that must be postulated in the event of an "implied hearing" (*śrutāpatti*).

For this very reason, in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and similar cases, the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is supplied; in the case of "the door" (*dvāram*) and so forth, the word "be closed" (*saṃtriyatām*) is supplied; and even in the case of modification (*ūha*), it is the word itself—such as "I offer what is pleasing to Sūrya" (*sūryāya juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*)—that is postulated, and the same applies to ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).

Moreover, when the word "he cooks" (*pacati*) is employed, if there is no hearing of a complement such as "rice" (*odana*), the lack of expectancy regarding the perceptible rice would remain unappeased; yet this is not observed. Therefore, because the sentence remains incomplete, one must necessarily postulate a verbal element (*śabda*) to complete it. It is with this very intention that the author of the *Bhāṣya* used the word "heard" (*śruta*) in the phrase "seen or heard.
This, however, is untenable; for even in the case of what is "heard," it is the meaning (*artha*) itself that must be postulated to complete the sense, not a verbal element.

In a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) qualified by a word, it is only the object as qualified by that [word] which is the object of knowledge (*vedya*); the word itself is not an object of knowledge, because it is already present in memory. Therefore, in this case, the conceptual attachment (*abhiniveśa*) to the word-qualified [object] implies that the object alone is what is being conceptualized, not the word. Consequently, the incongruity is not resolved by the conceptualization of the word. If it is argued that the incongruity is resolved because the word in its state of being a signifier (*bodhaka*) is itself what is conceptualized, we say no; for even there, through the discrimination between what is already established and what is yet to be established, it is the object alone that serves to resolve the incongruity, not the word.

Furthermore, if this [word] were to be postulated in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) because one would have to postulate a capacity (*śakti*) both for the object and for the word; therefore, only the ultimate object itself should be postulated.

Moreover, in the case of presumptive testimony based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*), capacity is observed only in that which accounts for the fact; however, in the case of presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), since it brings about the cognition of the accounting factor, there is no postulation of anything in excess of what is perceived—thus a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) is incurred.
Furthermore, elsewhere in determinate perception (*savikalpakajñāna*), a word already ascended to memory is observed; therefore, here too, it must be of that very same kind.

In another sense, "modification" (vikāra) refers to presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), which is a logical consequence of a conceptual construction, not [a modification] of the cognition itself. Thus, even in the case of injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like, because the meaning is incomplete due to the absence of a certain element, that very meaning must be supplied there as well.

As for what was said—that the postulation of a word is observed in examples—that is true, it is indeed observed; however, in those cases, the word itself is the direct means of justification (*upapādaka*), and not the word's capacity to convey the means of justification.

For instance, in the primary ritual (*prakṛti*), the expressive [word] is conceived as the function of the mantras; therefore, even in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), since it is logically established through reasoning, the substitution of the word "sūryām" is appropriate.
The same applies to the case of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).

As for what was stated—that when one says "he cooks," there would be the undesirable consequence of the cessation of the connection with the perceptible rice because of its incompatibility with something else—that is not so; in that case, the lack of connection is due to the absence of a determination of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not due to the absence of the word itself.
Therefore, since there is indeed a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) in the *adhvaryu* [formula], everything is logically consistent.
(Pravibhāga, pp. 55–56).
The application (*viniyoga*) of the *sūktavāka* is according to the sense (*arthānusāreṇa*).
Bhāṣya:
There would be a modification of the meaning because of the distinctness of the deities, due to the co-inherence in a single [form].

In the case of the eleven animals (*aikādaśina*) which constitute a different matter from the *āmīṣomīya* sacrifice, there is a co-inherence (*samavāya*)—that is, the presence—of a single superimposed deityhood in each individual animal; therefore, there would be a distinctness of deities.
These deities are distinct; there is no single group here.

Because the nature of a deity arises from a singular collection, and because they are separate, there would be a modification (*ūha*) of the term *medhapati*—which is associated with the quality of Agni—from its singular form to its dual and even plural forms.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that both [forms] function through optional modification (*vikalpena ūhena*).
What is *arthāpatti*? It consists in the impossibility of accounting for something otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*). (Su.
pṛ. 1401). *Arthāpatti* has cognition as its instrument (*jñānakaraṇikā*).
Maṇi, p. 19. *Arthāpatti* (presumption) is the postulation of a fact because a perceived or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for.
For example, by observing the absence of the living Devadatta from his house, one postulates his presence outside, which was not previously seen.
*Arthāpatti* is that postulation of another fact which occurs after considering the impossibility of a known fact being established without that other fact, for the sake of making it possible.
In this context, only that which is logically possible is to be understood.
For indeed, the existence outside [the house] is not possible without the absence from the house.

For one whose life is perceived through direct observation as being concomitant with presence in the house, when his absence from the house is seen, his life—being rendered doubtful—finds its resolution through the postulation of his existence outside.
Furthermore, prior to the conceptualization of his manifestation [outside], because the person's life is doubtful, it does not possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Indeed, that which is doubtful cannot be a logical mark.

Moreover, the mere absence from the house, being devoid of the certainty of life, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) since it exists even in the case of a dead person; thus, it is not capable of inferring his existence outside.
Therefore, since inference is impossible here, this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And just as in inference that which makes [the object] known is certain, so too in presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that which makes it known is understood to be doubtful,
because of the discrepancy with the form previously perceived based on doubt.

The mutual contradiction between two objects established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when considered as requiring resolution through the postulation of another object, is the cause of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). And the postulation of that other object for the sake of resolving that contradiction is presumptive testimony; it is a distinct means of valid cognition.

(Regarding the opening statement, "An object seen or heard": Although the inclusion of "heard" is already established by the very mention of "seen"—since both are merely objects of cognition—the term "heard" is included specifically to demonstrate that the presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) differs from the presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) in its capacity to apprehend a verbal means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In common worldly usage, for instance, in cases such as "The door! The door!", a word like "be closed" is inferred to complete the expression of the intended meaning, functioning as a syntactic unity with the word actually heard.

Likewise, in the Veda as well, in the case of the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," whether the words "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*) or "for the sake of heaven" (*svargārthe*) are supplied, that very word by which—being syntactically connected with the heard word—the expression of a complete sense is accomplished, is brought to mind and joined with what is heard; thus, from the complete sentence, the meaning of the sentence is understood.

Likewise, in injunctions such as "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," since the words expressing the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are not present and must be supplied, there is a requirement for words that provide that meaning. Because the two parts of the *Āgneya* injunction—which express the objective (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*)—are already established through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the original injunction (*codanā*), they do not need to be supplied. Therefore, the third part, consisting of the ritual details such as the placing of firewood (*agnyanvādhāna*) and so forth, is postulated as the "end of the injunction" (*vidhyanta*). The word that denotes this, namely "like the *Āgneya*," is postulated as the syntactic supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Alternatively, it may be that this very [procedure] belonging to the *Āgneya* sacrifice is assumed—by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—to form a single syntactical unit with the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), even though it is separated [in time], by virtue of being brought to mind through the force of the injunctive indicative (*codanā-liṅga*).

Śābarabhāṣya-saṃkṣepa, p. 76–82. Presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is of two kinds: presumptive testimony based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) and presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*). Among these, presumptive testimony based on what is heard is further divided into two types: worldly (*laukikī*) and Vedic (*vaidikī*).

*Bāla.*, p. 8. *Arthāpatti* (presumption): the postulation of another fact that accounts for a fact already established through perception or verbal testimony. For example, Devadatta’s absence from home during the day and his corpulence are perceived; the presumption (*arthāpatti*) is that he eats at night, which accounts for these two facts.
Presumption (arthāpatti) postulates [the object].

Thus, the instigation (pravartanā) directed toward the efficient-force (bhāvanā) whose instrument is the Viśvajit sacrifice—being established by the injunction—is untenable without having heaven as its objective; therefore, it postulates that heaven is the objective.

In this case, the cognition of fatness qualified by the absence of daytime eating is not the instrument (karaṇa), such that its inclusion within inference might be suspected. Rather, it is the cognition of the impossibility of the relationship—specifically the relation of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—between the absence of eating and fatness. The valid cognition of the connection with nighttime eating is the intermediate operation (avāntaravyāpāra), which serves as the explanatory ground (upapādakatva).

Thus, the postulation of Devadatta’s non-perceived absence from his house based on his being alive while not seen there is what the ancients [mean by] presumption (*arthāpatti*). They maintain that it is not included within inference. In reality, however, it is more logical for this to be a distinct means of knowledge, because of the very experience that "I do not infer, I do not analogize, I do not understand through verbal testimony, but rather I apprehend through presumption."
This very capacity to produce [an effect] is the proof of the *sahaja-brahmatā* (inherent divinity).

For instance, when the capacity of a seed to produce a sprout is apprehended as being delimited by its nature as a seed (*bījatva*), the non-observation of that [capacity] in seeds damaged by mice leads to doubt regarding its causal status; it is then postulated that there is a causal power residing in the rice-grain (*vrīhi*) which is destroyed by the mouse-damage.
In the same way, the capacity to produce heaven (*svarga*) arising from a sacrifice (*yāga*) is postulated; thus say the ancients (*jīrṇāḥ*).
Ma. pṛ. 60–61: Presumption (arthāpatti) is a worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). pṛ. 13: Presumption is capacity (sāmarthya).
When there is a direct statement and when something else is otherwise impossible, presumption occurs through the acceptance of the factual reality.
Or: "Presumption (arthāpatti) subsists by depending upon [the presence of] a perceived inconsistency. (*Rjuvimalā*, p. 34).
Presumption is also the postulation of a fact based on the thought that a perceived or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for. (*Vākyapadīya*, Rāmaśrama commentary, p. 589).

Just as when Devadatta is alive, the existence of him outside [the house] is postulated upon seeing his absence from the house, even though that external existence has not been perceived. Bhāṣya 9.1.5, p. 38.

Vaidyanātha: Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of another fact after observing that a fact established by the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is otherwise inexplicable (*anupapatti*) without that other fact.

Among these, presumption based on what is perceived (*pratyakṣa*) is the postulation of a fact through the inexplicability of what has been perceived; for example, the postulation of the burning power in fire once it has been cognized through perception.

Presumption preceded by inference (*anumāna*) is as follows: having inferred the motion of the sun by means of the inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) of its reaching another location, one postulates the sun’s power of motion because that [motion] would otherwise be inexplicable.

Presumption based on analogy (*upamānapūrvikārthāpatti*) is as follows: from the observation of a *gavaya*, one forms the notion that "the cow is similar to this"; having thus analogized the similarity of the *gavaya* to the cow, one then postulates—on the grounds of the inexplicability of anything else—that the cow, being characterized by such similarity, possesses the capacity to be the object of such a [recognition] in the village.

Presumption based on verbal testimony (*śabdapūrvikā arthāpatti*) is as follows: when one hears the sentence, "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day," the meaning that is cognized—that Devadatta, who does not eat by day, is nonetheless fat—cannot be accounted for otherwise. Having observed this inconsistency, it is logical to resort to the mere postulation of eating at night, namely, "he eats at night," in order to resolve that [inconsistency].

In the case of verbal testimony (*śruta*), it is logical that when there is an inconsistency with the meaning perceived through the sentence, another required meaning is supplied by the very sentence itself in order to resolve that inconsistency, according to the maxim: "That which is conveyed verbally is [understood] by means of words.
An example of presumption based on presumption (*arthāpattipūrvikā arthāpatti*) is as follows: [presumption] based on the primary meaning of a statement.
Presumption (arthāpatti) is that which proceeds to postulate [an object].
Since that object is graspable by conceptual cognition and is perceived as preceded by words, it is the word itself, once understood, that brings forth the object.

[Objection: If this were so, then conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) in perception and the other means of knowledge would likewise not apprehend the object, but would instead terminate solely in the word. [Reply:
This is not the case; for in the cognitions of animals and others, the capacity of the sense organ to produce a cognition is ascertained to reside in the object itself.
Therefore, even conceptual cognition must occur in relation to that very object and not elsewhere, because the postulation of a causal capacity is restricted to its actual locus.
Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), however, never occurs for animals, because it is dependent upon the acquisition of linguistic proficiency.
For one who has not mastered language does not comprehend the meaning of a sentence preceded by [knowledge of] words.

Now, it may be argued that since the capacity of presumption has been established as residing in the object itself in the case of presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*), it ought likewise to reside there alone in this case as well.
True, it is observed that the capacity [of a word] resides only in the object; however, this is by way of being the *upādāna* (the material cause or basis).
For even the object is not cognized in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*), but rather by way of being the *upādāna*.
And that which is the *upādāna* is that upon the cognition of which the apparent inconsistency (*anupapatti*) comes to rest.

Even when the word is directly uttered, the resolution of the inconsistency occurs; thus, the operation of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) pertains to that very word which has first entered the ear.
As the venerable author of the *Vārttika* says: [These verses are not found in either the *Ślokavārttika* or the *Tantravārttika*;
therefore, this Vārttikakāra must be a Prābhākara].
(ke. "Nor is this second object apprehended by us as being the very same as the first object;
for it is concealed because it is graspable by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*).
Fire is not grasped as 'fire' solely through the sense organ or through a logical mark (*liṅga*)."
And thus, by implication, this very object is perceived even by animals;

however, the cognition of presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) never occurs for animals. For this cognition of presumptive testimony based on what is heard is considered to arise from the apprehension of words and so forth.
One does not apprehend these other words by means of the intellect in this very manner;
therefore, for them, the sentence is certainly the primary object of cognition.
Since the sentence itself has already reached the meaning of the sentence, it will cause that meaning to be understood.
The venerable author of the *Ṭīkā* does not accept this;
rather, something is stated here in accordance with the view of our teacher (*gurudarśana*).

In conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*), a word is perceived as having the form of a delimiter of the object (*arthāvacchedakarūpa*), and by virtue of being a designator (*vācakatayā*), the word delimits the object.
Therefore, in the cognition "this is a cow," the meaning grasped is simply that "this is denotable by the word 'cow'";
and the word does not itself express the state of being denotable by a word.
Consequently, in this context, the word is not a communicator of the object.

However, because the denotative capacity (vācakatva) is understood through established linguistic usage (dṛḍhavyavahāra), the denoted object is not [inherently] qualified by it. Therefore, since the meaning (artha) is not what is to be inferred (anupasthāpyatvāt), even its initial presence is not sufficient to dispel the inconsistency; thus, it cannot be considered an object of knowledge through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "heard" (*śruta*) is not even for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction that this [injunction] also has only the object as its domain.

As for those who think that in cases such as the *viśvajit* sacrifice, the word itself is untenable because it is incomplete, and who claim that a word which completes it—serving as its supplement—is therefore to be inferred; since they speak such a conceptual construction based merely on their own imagination, they are to be disregarded even though they are seized by delusion. Thus, something is said here to instruct the ignorant.

What, then, is the "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) of the word here? Is it something distinct from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? If you mean its incompleteness, what constitutes the incompleteness of a word? For it is the meaning itself that becomes incomplete when lacking some portion of its referential content.

If you argue that the word is also incomplete because of the presumptive testimony [required to complete the sense], let it be so. However, one must provide an explanation for that very basis upon which its inexplicability rests.
Otherwise, the very incompleteness of the word would remain in that same state.
Therefore, even when the word is incomplete, it is the meaning alone that must be supplied;
for there is no incompleteness of the word when the meaning is unestablished, because the word and its meaning are related as beggar and alms.
Now it may be argued: "If the object is untenable and the object of cognition (*prameya*) is absent, then the status of the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) is also untenable.
Even so, it would be the status of being a means of valid cognition that is untenable, not the word itself.
Furthermore, it is not the status of being a means of valid cognition that is separately untenable, but rather the object itself that is untenable.
If this is so, let it be that the very impossibility of the foundational [word] itself is what constitutes the means of valid cognition (arthāpatti).

Furthermore, the status of a means of valid cognition is itself untenable due to the suspicion that its object of cognition might not exist in the absence of some referent; it is not untenable due to the absence of the word itself, which would lead one to postulate the word.
Enough of this excessive deliberation.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) occurs necessarily only in that case where there is an injunction by means of a word, and not otherwise.
Bhāṣya 3.1.4.10: But surely, presumption is that which we go to [infer] precisely through the exclusion of the meanings of the words.
And that [cognition] cannot be accounted for without a capacity (śakti),
because in that case the object would have to be the cause of it. There would be a presumption by implication (arthāpatti) only if no other cause could be conceived even in the absence of a capacity.
But the cause is understood:
"What [is the cause]?
(1.1.7.29, p. 96): "The postulation of an object through the contradiction of one means of valid cognition by another means of valid cognition..."
"In this context, they call presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) another name for implication (arthāpatti);
Maṇḍana, 1.1, verse 11. By presumptive testimony, the fallacy of presumptive testimony is sublated;
Bālakrīḍā, p. 131. [This refers to] those two which are directly connected with purchase..."
From presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*), the Veda [is established]; from presumptive testimony and inference,

there is the subsequent connection between the substance (*dravya*) and the quality (*guṇa*)— namely, the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) and the redness (*āruṇya*)— as mutual delimiters (*parasparāvacchedakatva*).

That alone which, without which the connection between the enjoined substance and deity would be impossible, and which is neither seen nor heard [in the text], can be postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); nothing else.
Therefore, nothing more than that is obtained.
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 2.1.21, page 523: "The properties prescribed for rice grains (*vrīhi*) apply to wild rice (*nīvāra*) by implication (*arthāpatti*).
"The capacity of all entities is understood through implication."

For the expressive power (*vācakaśakti*) is absolutely unperceived; it is established solely by the means of proof consisting in the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of the denoted object (*vācyapratyaya*).
[This constitutes] the distinction of Presumption (*arthāpatti*) from Inference (*anumāna*).
Now, the distinction between presumption (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*) is established.
This presumption is the postulation of something such that a fact seen or heard would otherwise be inexplicable;
for example, the postulation of Devadatta’s presence outside—though not seen—upon observing his absence from home while he is alive.
Some maintain that this [perception of external existence] is distinct from inference.

For instance, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is established either through a different object of knowledge (*prameya*) or through a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), as is seen in the case of perception and the others; however, in this case, neither of these two is observed.
That which is the object of knowledge characterized by external existence and so forth can also be understood through inference.

For instance: Devadatta is in conjunction with an external location, because, while being absent from the house, he exists; whatever, while being absent from the house, exists, is in conjunction with an external location, just as I am.

Likewise, the time characterized by Devadatta’s absence from the house while he is alive is characterized by existence somewhere, because it is a time when one who is alive is absent from the house; whatever time is characterized by the absence from the house of one who is alive is characterized by existence somewhere, just as my own time is.
Therefore, since presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is cognizable through inference, no separate object of knowledge remains.
By demonstrating the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), even the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) cannot be established.

Is it then that the inferential nature of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is proven by inference? [The argument would be: "Presumptive testimony under dispute is inference, because it arises through the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), like the cognition of smoke and so forth.
But surely, presumptive testimony is the postulation that "it cannot be explained otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*).
Therefore, it is not unestablished that [the absence from home] is a means of knowledge by virtue of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

If it is asked, "How is it understood that the absence from the house cannot otherwise be accounted for without his being outside?"—if you say, "Because we observe a rule (*niyama*) such that the absence from the house of one who is alive is invariably concomitant with his being outside," then it follows that invariable concomitance itself is what constitutes "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*); thus, there is no lack of establishment. Now, whether in a general or specific sense...
"In that case, where there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is inference; but where both are absent, as in the case of *śakti* and so forth, it is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
This is not correct, because even there the causal conditions for inference in the form of a "pure negative" (*kevalavyatirekin*) exist.

If you argue that it is an inference because of the absence of anything else, then a "pure positive" (*kevalānvayin*) would have to be a separate means of knowledge due to the absence of negative concomitance.

If it is argued that [tactile perception] exists, then since tactile perception lacks color-form (*rūpa*), it would follow that it is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
To this it is replied: *arthāpatti* (presumption) is that which postulates something when doubt has been raised by another fact.

In inference, however, that which is doubtful or which causes doubt is not a means of valid cognition; therefore, the difference [between the two] arises solely from the difference in their causal conditions (*sāmagrī*).
And here, "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) is said to be nothing other than doubt. Even that which is inexplicable is said to be either doubtful or characterized by a doubtful qualification.

What is the cause for doubt here? First, although life is established by means of inference and so forth, it is generally observed as being based in a house; thus, a misconception arises that life is restricted to the house alone. For one who holds this view, when the absence of a house is perceived, life becomes doubtful because the previously determined attribute (the house) is absent.

Furthermore, when life—established through scriptural testimony—is conjoined with the absence of a house, there is a misconception regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that "house-hood" is understood as the absence of the external location, even though the external location is actually the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the absence.
Thus, due to the delusion regarding the state of life common to all people, there arises a doubt concerning the existence or non-existence of that state of life.
Consequently, from this doubt—which constitutes an apparent inconsistency (*anupapatti*)—life itself is postulated as being connected with a location outside [the house].

As for what was said—that a doubtful thing is never observed to be a postulator—if so, where has a pervasive (*vyāpta*) indicator ever been observed? If it is argued that it is observed in the case of smoke and the like, then it is likewise observed in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding life and such.

If it is argued that [the probans] is not seen elsewhere than where [the probandum] is impossible, then in that case as well, it is simply not seen elsewhere than where the mark (*liṅga*) [is present].

If it is further argued that even though it is not seen elsewhere, it is accepted as a prover because it is pervaded by the pervader (*vyāpaka*) through the force of observed cognition, then the same analysis applies here: it is accepted as being pervaded by the producer (*upapādaka*) through the force of observed cognition, despite its impossibility [without it].

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the removal of doubt occurs either through the exclusion of other causes or through the determination of one of the two alternatives—that is indeed present here as well.

For instance, it is not the existence or non-existence of life that is doubted here; rather, having ascertained life itself, there is indeed a definitive determination regarding one of the two alternatives—namely, its being outside.
As for the objection that the very cause of doubt cannot logically be the cause of certainty, that too is incorrect, because the ground [of the person] serves as the cause for [inferring] life.
Here, the absence of the previously established characteristics is the cause of doubt, whereas the postulation of his being outside is the cause of the certain conclusion.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that even in inference the indicator is indeed uncertain because smoke can arise from other causes— [it is not so],
because [the indicator] is connected with the expression of the object and is capable of accomplishing that object.

(Symbol) There should be a state of subsidiarity (*śeṣabhāva*) among those connected with the expression of meaning; therein, that which is obtained without being specifically enjoined [is subsidiary] because it expresses what has been enjoined.

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the offering-mantra (*nirvāpamantra*): "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer you, O Agni, who are dear [to the gods]."

In this regard, there arises an inquiry as to whether the words *savitṛ*, *aśvin*, and *pūṣan* denote meanings inherent in the ritual action (*karma-samaveta-artha*), whereby they would undergo modification (*ūha*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as appropriate; or whether these words do not denote meanings inherent in the ritual action, whereby no modification of them would occur in the modified sacrifice. Regarding this inquiry, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the portion of the sūtra: "In the case of [mantras] connected with the denotation of meaning, there should be the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*)."

In the mantras—specifically in the three mantras containing the words "at the impulse of Savitṛ," "by the arms of the Aśvins," and "by the hands of Pūṣan"—the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*), that is, the state of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) or an auxiliary to the ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*), belongs to the names denoting the deities.

This is because of their connection with the expression of the meaning; that is, because the expressive power (*vācakatā*) is possible through the connection with the manifestation or declaration of the meaning in the form of the deity, which has become an auxiliary to the ritual action.

And thus, because they denote a constituent part of the ritual action and are therefore subsidiary to the action—as seen in the primary rite (*prakṛti*) where it is said, "I offer what is pleasing to Savitṛ," "I offer what is pleasing to the Aśvins," and "I offer what is pleasing to Pūṣan"—these deities also possess the status of recipients of the oblation. There would be an option (*vikalpa*) between these [deities] and Agni and the others; therefore, there is modification (*ūha*).
Thus ends the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Now, with the portion of the sūtra stating, "In that case, what is not enjoined is obtained because of the naming of what is enjoined," he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

"Because of the naming of what is enjoined" means because of the naming by means of the mantra of that very thing which is enjoined—that is, the object prescribed by the injunction, such as Agni, Agni-Soma, Prajāpati, and so forth, who are the deities of the *upāṃśuyāja*.

In that regard, since the forms of the deities Savitṛ, Aśvin, and Pūṣan are not enjoined in the Full Moon rite—and likewise in the New Moon rite—therefore, they would not be included [in the modification].
Consequently, no modification (*ūha*) of the words denoting them should be performed.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa rites, only Agni and the others are prescribed as deities, not Savitṛ and the others.

Therefore, words such as *savitṛ* do not denote meanings inherent to the ritual action; thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is no modification (*ūha*) of words like *savitṛ*, whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*).

This is because, within a single sūtra, two *tu*-words are not recited for the sake of their respective meanings, thereby establishing both the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final position (*uttara-pakṣa*) without repetition, according to the maxim: "The course of the sūtras is manifold.
Consequently, their non-recitation is employed for the sake of the other [meaning].

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, in the mantra "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer what is pleasing to Agni," Savitṛ and the others are manifested precisely by the words "Savitṛ" and so forth which denote them. Thus, how can it be said that they are not intended to be significant in the ritual action? In response to this doubt, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) says:
Therefore, by those words "Savitṛ" and so forth, there is no mention of those [deities] as being inherent in the ritual action; it does not constitute a mention [of them as such].
Those [deities] which are mentioned in the injunction (*vidhi*) are indeed those that are integrated with the ritual action (*karmasamaveta*).

When Agni and others have already been enjoined by the injunction, it is not possible to accept the integration of Savitṛ and the others with the action based solely on the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra.
[Objection: If so, for what purpose is there the recitation of Savitṛ and the others in the *nirvāpa* mantra? [Reply: It is said:
Otherwise, the words "Savitṛ" and so forth are employed in the mantra for the offering (nirvāpa) for the purpose of praising that offering and for the purpose of generating enthusiasm.
Therefore, in the modified rituals (vikṛtis), the words "Savitṛ" and so forth should not be substituted;
nor should there be a displacement (utkarṣa) of Savitṛ and the others to another context.
Ke.

(Symbol). In the section [of the *Tantravārttika*] beginning with "Because of the connection with the expression of meaning" (*arthābhidhānasaṃyogāt*), it will be stated that even for mantras such as "Of the god thee" (*devasya tvā*) and so forth, although their utterance might appear to be for the sake of mere recitation, because they would otherwise fail to form a single syntactical unit with the words "offering" (*nirvāpa*) and "meat" (*āmiṣa*) due to having different purposes, they must—by virtue of that connection—serve to manifest the act of offering as qualified by the meaning of the words "Of the god thee" and so on; thus, they too possess the capacity to express their own meaning.
*Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad*, 12.142, p. 72.
(Symbol) In the comprehension of meaning, the mere fact of being heard (*śrutatva*) is not the sole cause; rather, context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors are also causes.
Śṛju. p. 6.

(Symbol) Since the understanding of meaning occurs at a time subsequent to the study [of the Veda], the injunctions regarding ritual acts do not derive their impelling force through that [understanding] as their medium.

For this very reason, even though the comprehension of meaning is observed, it is not accepted as a qualification for entitlement (*adhikāraviśeṣaṇa*), just like the rule regarding the acquisition of wealth.
This is because the comprehension of meaning is preceded by study; therefore, prior to study, the desire [for such comprehension] is impossible.
Furthermore, since it occurs only at a subsequent time, the comprehension of meaning itself is not accepted as a separate purpose (*prayojana*).
Listen. Page 9.
(Symbol) It has been stated that "only one who is capable [of the task] is entitled [to it]" (Bhāṣya 6.1.15).
(Symbol) The maxim is: "One who is capable of the purpose and is learned is entitled [to perform the rite].

This is found in the *Jaiminīya* [Mīmāṃsā] regarding the assembly (*sadas*). For instance: "Therefore, comprehension attained through capability stands as the end to be accomplished. By the maxim, "One who is capable of the purpose and is learned is entitled," those who observe that comprehension is required even in the case of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices employ the Veda as its own study (*svādhyāya*) for the sake of that comprehension.
And so forth.

[The term] *sāhasī* [is used]. 719. "Because of the unity of purpose, there is a single sentence" (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.46). "Because of the unity of purpose, there is an option" (Jaimini Sūtra 12.3.10).

(Symbol) "A single sentence is that which has a single purpose, provided that if divided, it would remain expectant [of further words]. Now, regarding the *yajus* formulas that are inserted or recited, how is it understood that "this much constitutes one *yajus*"? Since the threefold nature of mantras has been established, and because the measure of *ṛc* and *sāman* verses is determined by a traditional succession of authorities, there arises an expectation as to how much constitutes a single *yajus* among those *yajus* formulas that are inserted or recited; therefore, the definition of their measure is now formulated.

In this regard, the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: First, a sentence is not a single unit simply because its meaning is one; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of every word being a separate sentence due to the difference in meaning of each individual term.

Nor does it consist in "having expectancy when divided" (*vibhajyamānasākāṅkṣatva*); for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the phrase "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; I fashion it well with a stream of ghee" forming a single sentence with the subsequent phrase "sit upon it.
Nor does the definition of a single sentence consist in the words being combined (*milita*); for a single word has a single meaning, yet it does not possess expectancy when divided.

Likewise, with respect to a single or multiple referents, because there is no unity due to the distinction between meanings in each word; as it has been said: "A word would not have a single referent, just as it possesses expectancy;
for that which possesses expectancy, no single referent is found."
Thus [it is said].
(Vākyapadīya, p. 444) The purpose is, as before, precisely for the sake of establishing the understanding. The sūtra itself is indeed easy to understand.
(Symbol) "A single sentence is that which has a single purpose, provided it remains expectant when divided.
Regarding the *yajus* mantras that have been interpolated or recited, how is it determined that "this is one *yajus*"? Therefore, he states the definition of a single sentence:
"Because of the unity of purpose"—that is, because of the oneness of the meaning to be conveyed; a single sentence is that which conveys a single meaning.

A collection of words as large as is necessary to convey a single qualified meaning constitutes one sentence, provided that when it is divided, the resulting parts remain syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*). There may be certain groups of words that have a single meaning, yet do not remain expectant when divided, such as: "Let Bhaga distribute [the inheritance], or let Aryaman distribute it."
This sentence is divided when analyzed;

however, if it is said that "that which is syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) upon division is a single *yajus*," then in such passages as "Ṛtāṣāṭ ṛtadhāmā Agni is the Gandharva, his Apsarases are the plants named Ūrjaḥ; may he protect this priesthood and nobility; may they protect this priesthood and nobility; *svāhā* to him, *svāhā* to them," each individual *yajus* would consist of two *svāhā* utterances throughout the Āprī-hymns.
To prevent the status of being a single *yajus* in such cases despite the syntactic expectancy upon division, it is stated: "because of the unity of purpose (*arthakatvāt*)."
Ke.

(Symbol): In the rule "A sentence is one because of the unity of purpose" (*arthakatvāt*), the word *artha* is accepted as denoting "purpose" (*prayojana*). Su. p. 867: "In the *yajati*s [sacrifices], one performs the *yeyajāmahe*; not in the *anuyāja*s."
"Is it not the case that there is a principle in the rule *arthakatvāt* by which there would be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*)? It is replied:
True, this principle does not apply here; however, the *yeyajāmahe* mantra, which is already present in the mind, is enjoined for the purpose of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)."
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*, page 2059 (symbol 10|8|914).

By the principle stated in *Jaimini Sūtra* 2.1.46, "A sentence is one because of its unity of purpose" (*arthaikatvādekaṃ vākyam*), the extent of the *yajus* mantras that have been interpolated and recited is to be understood.
This very point constitutes the section on "Unity of Sentence" (*ekavākyatādhikaraṇa*).
*Soma*. 9|1|13. (Symbol).

In the section concerning the unity of purpose (*arthakatva-adhikaraṇa*), [it is stated]: "Because of the unity of purpose, there is one sentence" (2|1|46). We have previously explained that the definition of unity of purpose is the state of being a single primary qualifier with respect to a single object of comprehension despite having distinct aspects. *Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya*, 2|1|20, p. 236.
(Symbol) *Arthaikatvād vikalpaḥ syāt katvāt sāmyaṃ tad-arthatvāt*. This is one single sūtra.
Regarding this, the portion *arthaikatvād vikalpaḥ syāt* has been explained by the authors of the Bhāṣya as a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*) distinct from the rest.
Furthermore, this portion of the Sūtra is devoted to the established conclusion (siddhānta).

In the Sāmaveda, under the section concerning the unity of purpose (arthakatva-adhikaraṇa), it is stated: "When there is unity of purpose, [there is a single performance] of the substance and the quality..."
The means of singing are sixfold.
That activity which manifests the specific tones produced by internal effort is called *gīti*;
that very thing is termed *sāman*.

The means for accomplishing that [singing] are the modification of the syllables of the *ṛc*, displacement (*vikṣepa*), drawing out (*vikarṣaṇa*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), pause (*virāma*), insertion (*stobha*), and so forth.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether these are to be combined (*samuccaya*) or used alternatively (*vikalpa*), he states the established conclusion:
since these means have a single purpose—namely, the form of bringing about the melody (*gīti*)—there should be an alternative between them, not a combination.
Ke. § Section on the Unity of Purpose (Arthaikatvādhikaraṇa): "There should be [one performance] for a single purpose, because it is for that purpose. Herein are three expositions (*varṇaka*).
Among them, the first: it is heard in scripture, "They praise with a *ṛc*," and "They praise with a *sāman*."

In this regard, there arises an inquiry as to whether the choice is between using either a *ṛc* (verse) or a *sāman* (chant) for the hymn of praise (*stotra*), or whether there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that it must be performed with a *sāman* alone. Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

because the purpose is one—namely, because they both accomplish the purpose consisting of the act of praise—and because both the *ṛc* and the *sāman* have that as their aim, since they consist of praise; "having that as their aim" means having that as their objective, and because they have that as their aim, the *ṛc* has praise as its fruit.

Regarding the [objections] concerning *ardhanirukta* (674) and *ardhavaiśasa* (655), as well as the application of the *ardhajaratīya-nyāya* (the logic of the "half-old woman"), even that is merely a manifestation of ignorance. For just as when one eats a portion of a gourd or similar object, the prohibition against eating it—established by the scriptural injunction—is not thereby invalidated, so too in the case of relying on the definitive meaning of the words, there is no sublation of the aspect of being an "indriya" (*akṣatva*) and so forth; thus, there is a disparity between the two cases.
Here, the word *jaratī* is taken to mean a bottle-gourd (*alābu*).
In the *Sanāt-pradīpa*, in the section on marriage rites, page 291, it is stated in the *Ardhanirukti*:
"In the case of the moon rising during the *darśa* [new moon sacrifice], the remaining portion is offered silently."
The coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the words *adhi* and *pipīlikāpada*.
Saṃkarṣa.

The statement, "Half [of the altar] is within the sacrificial ground (antarvedi), half is outside the sacrificial ground (bahirvedi)," is spoken for the purpose of defining the location (*deśalakṣaṇārtha*).

Bhāṣya 3.7.6.12. Just as in the case of "half is within the sacrificial ground," even though both [the wife and the sacrificer] are equally intended as objects (*uddeśyatva*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is indeed a restriction (*vyavasthā*) despite both being means to a single transcendental result (*ekāpūrvasādhanatva*), as seen in the passage: "He girds the wife with a yoktra; he girds the sacrificer with a girdle.
Bhaṭṭa 6.1.6, "Half is within the sacrificial ground..."
And the smallness of something [is established] by means of that which is slightly less; and the smallness of something may also exist even when there is much to be measured.
Bhāṣya 4.2.17.47: "The obstruction of the many is obstructed by the obstruction of the few."

*Aprāptabādha* (sublation of what has not yet been established). Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 860. For example, if the *apratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one who does not accept) were intended for the recipient, there would be a multiplicity of sublations: the dative case in *varuṇāya* would have to signify the ablative sense; the word *anyat* (other) would have to refer to the state of being a recipient; and in the phrase *sa svāṃ devatām*, the pronoun *tat* would have to refer to Varuṇa as the primary subject. Furthermore, if Varuṇa were the giver, he would not be the deity (*devatā*), and thus the application of the word "deity" would be inconsistent. However, in the view that the sacrifice belongs to the giver, there is only the abandonment of his own interest by the recipient.
*Bāla.*, p. 140. 🏺 *Alpabhūmivirodhanyāyaḥ* (The Principle of Conflict with the Fewer Levels).

This is the rule that when there is a conflict between fewer levels (*alpānām bhūmīnām*), the sublation (*bādha*) occurs [of the latter]. However, the principle of conflict with the fewer levels does not apply here; for if one were to abandon each individual [instance], it would result in the sublation of many meanings (*bhūyasām tadarthānām*).
Su. Pṛ. 47: A rule with fewer characteristics (*alpalakṣaṇa*) is sublated by one with more characteristics (*bahulakṣaṇa*); this is sublation by what is already established (*prāptabādha*).
Bāla. Pṛ. 143: By the prescription of a single meaning, the prescription of multiple meanings is sublated.

Just as in cases such as "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*) sets aside what is already established by a general injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). (Bālakrīḍā, p. 140). Furthermore, the possibility of enjoining a minor matter cannot be resolved by means of an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*).
Vārttika 3.1.10.21: In the *Agnicayana* sacrifice, the dragging of the altar (*vedivikarṣaṇa*) is performed only once with *avakā* plants and a branch, not repeatedly.
*Avakā* refers to moss (*śaivāla*).

Vi. 9.1.7.26–28: Regarding the term *avakāśa*, a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) to water is not accepted in accordance with the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), "Water indeed is peaceful. This is because, according to the *Guṇavāda* Sūtra in the *Arthavādādhikaraṇa*, the intention is to praise the *avakā* plants themselves by way of praising their origin, thereby avoiding the fault of a lack of syntactic coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the intended meaning and the literal expression.
Valor.

Regarding the *avakāśa* formulas (the *grahavākya*s): by means of the mantras beginning with "The two oceans" and ending with "Who are you? What is your name?", one performs the worship of the cups (*graha-upasthāna*) at both the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) and the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
As for the *avakīrṇin* animal sacrifice: "He who, being a religious student (*brahmacārī*), breaks his vow of chastity, shall immolate a donkey as a sacrificial animal."
This animal sacrifice is to be performed in the common (laukika) fire.
[Vi.
6.8.4] The Avakīrṇi-paśuyāga is indeed in the common fire alone.

However, some maintain that the subsidiary nature of those [rites] belongs only to the Smārta procedure prescribed by Āśvalāyana in the words, "Now follows the ritual for cattle-sacrifice" (AŚS 2.1.1). According to the statement of Āpastamba, they may instead be performed in water.
Bhāṣya 6.8.4: "Those who have fallen from the Kṣatriya order through sexual intercourse with women..."

*Soma* 6.8.4. 🏺 Regarding the *avakaṇīr* animal sacrifice: because the time for the formal installation of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived, the *avakaṇīr* animal sacrifice—referred to in the text, "One should not sacrifice this donkey with its testicles severed"—must be performed in a common fire, not in a fire established through the *ādhāna*. This is like the *sthapati-iṣṭi*. Since the time for the *ādhāna* has not yet arrived—the *ādhāna* not being required during the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*)—the sacrifice must take place in a worldly fire.
The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) occurs after marriage;
if one's *ādhāna* is not performed at the time of morning, that *ādhāna* is considered "out-of-season" (*aprāptakāla*).
Because the *ādhāna* is out-of-season, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *avakaṇīr* animal sacrifice is to be offered in the common fire (*laukikāgni*).

The section concerning the *avakīrṇi-paśu* (the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity). The *avakīrṇi-paśu* is to be performed in a common (secular) fire, because the time for its performance has not yet arrived [at the stage of the Vedic fires].
The Commentary (Bhāṣya): There is an animal sacrifice called the *avakīrṇī-paśu*, [prescribed by the rule]: "One who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇī*) should not sacrifice this donkey.

In that regard, there is a doubt: should the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) be performed for its sake, or should it take place in ordinary (worldly) fires? Furthermore, the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow is mentioned as the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*).
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section is the prima facie argument here; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the established conclusion here.
"Therefore, the installation [of the fires] is for all purposes, and thus [the fires] are installed by those who have already performed the installation"—this is the prima facie argument.
"Because the time for the installation has not yet arrived"—this is the established conclusion.
It has been stated that "this is not the time for the establishment [of the sacred fires].
Therefore, this ritual action also pertains to the worldly [fire]. Soma: The connection [is established] through the extension of the previous [rule].

"Where is the animal [offering] for one who has not performed the fire-laying (*avakṛtāgni*)? Since the fire-laying is possible only through a Brahmin, and because a *brahmacārin* is excluded from performing the fire-laying—whether Vedic or worldly—this section concerning those who have not performed the fire-laying is the principle of the threat (*avagoraṇanyāya*). (Section 677)

**Bhaṭṭa:** As for what was stated in the root text under a different section—that threshing is set aside (*bādha*) in the case of *kṛṣṇalas* because there is no purpose for removing the husk (*vitusībhāva*)—that was said assuming that the *kṛṣṇalas* themselves are the material substance (*prakṛti*) to be offered. This is a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*).

In reality, although there is a scriptural injunction for the *kṛṣṇala* berries to undergo contact with fire based on their being placed in clarified butter (*ghṛta*), since there is no Vaiśya [to perform the sacrifice], there is no evidence for the production of a different substance (caru) having the *kṛṣṇalas* as its material; therefore, those very *kṛṣṇalas* must be the offering. Consequently, even though the properties of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—such as the act of carrying fire around it (*paryagnikaraṇa*)—would apply by virtue of the *kṛṣṇalas* being the material for the offering (as they are the source-substance for the *āgneya* cake), there is no evidence for the application of the properties of the oblation-material (*havis*) itself to them. Thus, the exclusion [of those properties] is not caused by the absence of the process of husking (*vaituṣya*).

Nor is there an inconsistency in the restatement "one should offer" (*nirvapet*) on the grounds that there is no offering-material (*havir-mātra*), because even in the absence of the Vedic vessels prescribed for the archetype, the statement is a restatement intended to indicate the sacrifice by means of the offering itself— which consists of the physical separation [of the material] from its source, whether that be worldly or otherwise. Furthermore, one cannot raise the objection that, although the threshing (*avaghāta*) is not obtained through extension (*atideśa*) based on the indicative mark of the injunction (*codanā-liṅga*), the threshing might still be obtained by accepting that the word *caru* functions as a name-based extension (*nāmātideśa-vidhi*) to extend the properties of the *caru*.

The *caru* (boiled rice offering) is not established as possessing those properties because it is inherently devoid of them; for even though the *caru* is the subject of the injunction, the properties obtained through extension (*atideśa*)—such as threshing (*avaghāta*)—are prescribed for it, yet threshing itself lacks the status of being a property of the *caru*.

Nor can it be argued that the word *caru* here serves to indicate that the *kṛṣṇala* (gold pieces) are the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the *caru*, because when the substance produced from the *kṛṣṇalas* is not actually realized, the status of the *kṛṣṇalas* as its material cause is contradicted.

Therefore, it has been stated [in the *Tantravārttika*] that this word *caru* is a secondary (*gauṇa*) term applied even to what is not rice-porridge, because of its association with the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) consisting of contact with fire; yet, due to its association with hardness, clarity, and the removal of impurities—which establish its nature as having the *āgneya* cake as its archetype—it is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*). For by the statement "he cooks in clarified butter" (*ghṛte śrapayati*), cooking is not being enjoined, since cooking is impossible in the absence of softening (*viklitti*).

The *avaghātanyāya* (the maxim of threshing) refers to the restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) of a means that is capable of producing a result through various methods, which is effected by the injunction of threshing (*avaghātavidhi*) by presenting a specific means. This very [restriction] is expressed by terms such as "limitation" (*niyama*).

For even though threshing is obtained through the implication of the purpose (*arthākṣepa*), its being restricted as the producer of the state of rice-grains (*taṇḍulībhāva*) requires an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) for the restriction between the produced and the producer.

Furthermore, once the state of being rice-grains (*taṇḍulībhāva*) has been produced by threshing, the excellence (*atiśaya*) being brought about in those grains cannot be said to be produced by the act of threshing itself, because it is produced by that [state].

If one were to accept that [the excellence] is produced by the very nature of the act of threshing independently of the production of the rice-grains, then threshing—which is obtained through extension (*atideśa*)—could not be prevented even in the case of *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces.
Therefore, in the fourth section (*adhikaraṇa*, 2.1), it is not accepted that the unseen result of the restriction (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) is produced by the action.

Others, however, considering that an implication of meaning (*arthākṣepa*) independent of the assumption of an injunction is slow because it lacks prior establishment (*aprāptakatva*), and that only that which is in a state of non-establishment and has the nature of an action can be the object of an injunction, maintain that the postulation of a purpose is appropriate, rather than [the postulation of] a mere result for a restriction (*niyama*) that is already established. Thinking thus, they assert that even the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of a restriction is produced by the action itself (Su. p. 539). Therefore, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is the cause for the restriction (*niyama*) of threshing.
This is the "Principle of Threshing" (*avaghātanyāya*).

This is because the acts of threshing are distinct from one another with respect to the state of becoming rice-grains, and it is precisely by way of being an act of threshing that they produce the result. Therefore, due to the multiplicity of those acts of threshing, there is a repetition [of the mantra].
