And that [Sāman], when being refined by the application of mantras and Sāmans, remains that very same thing; there is no difference in its essence.
Furthermore, it possesses purposefulness through the inclusion of the term "Sāman," since it is already encompassed by the inclusion of the terms "mantra" and "saṃskāra.
On this point, they explain: "We do not at all maintain that there is a distinction in the form of the *ūha* (modification)."
But let us determine its subject matter;

why? Because there is a connection between the desired end and the procedure, such that one thinks, "One should perform the sacrifice in this way," or "One should achieve [the result] by means of the sacrifice in this way.
This being the case, we reply as follows.
That which is the effect of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is the primary element;
for it is that which is enjoined as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*). And wherever there is something to be performed, there alone is the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*).

Now, as for what was stated—that there is a connection of the ritual duties (*dharma*) with the word *yajati* (to sacrifice)—that is explained as follows: that refinement (*saṃskāra*) which belongs to one who sacrifices with respect to the materials is connected to that [sacrifice], not to the *apūrva*, because it is for the sake of that [sacrifice].
The connection of the materials with the ritual duties is by virtue of their belonging to that [sacrifice], not by their own nature.
For there exists no mutual expectancy between the meaning of the root *yaj* (the act of sacrificing) and the ritual duties.

For it is with respect to the "object" (pratyaya) that the "manner of performance" (itikartavyatā) is required—namely, "how is it to be done?"—and not with respect to the sacrifice itself, as in "of what nature is the sacrifice?
Therefore, the connection with the manner of performance belongs only to that which is to be performed, and that is the *apūrva*.
Consequently, [the subsidiaries] are connected to the *apūrva*.
Alternatively—*vā*—we shall pursue another line of inquiry.

Since it has been established that the *dharmas* have the *apūrva* as their purpose, in the ninth [chapter], the cause (*nimitta*) is examined: is the cause the *apūrva*, or is it the sacrifice (*yāga*)?
Nor can there be activity without a cause, such that this very inquiry would not even arise.

In this context, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) resulting from the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) does not constitute the occasion (*nimitta*). For this very reason, the result (*phala*) also does not constitute the occasion.
By process of elimination, the sacrifice itself is the occasion, because it possesses a completed form.

Objection: Since the sacrifice is being enjoined as a means toward the fruit, and since it is being presented as the occasion (nimitta), there would be a difference in the intended meaning (vivakṣābheda). Response:
It is said that the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* indicates the occasion, because it is incapable [of functioning otherwise] (due to the absence of any other purpose).
Even though the words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* refer to the original sacrifices, they are indeed enjoined by that [root] *yaj* (to sacrifice).
If this were not understood as being contingent upon specific occasions, the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* would be entirely meaningless.

But surely, an occasion is expressed by a word in the locative case, as in "he offers when [the vessel] is broken" (*bhinne juhoti*), whereas this [term *darśapūrṇamāse*] ends in the instrumental case.
It is said:
"One should observe that all case endings are generally seen [to be used] for the cause (*nimitta*), the fruit (*phala*), and the reason (*hetu*).
Furthermore, because it is intended to be expressed, there is a distinction [of usage], just as in the case of the instrumental case (*karaṇavibhakti*).

Therefore, since the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices lack a specific occasion (*animittatvāt*), there exists a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), but there is no connection with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*; in the absence of that [connection], there is also an absence of the ritual properties (*dharma*). Just as there is no oblation (*homa*) in the absence of a vessel-breakage (*bhedana*), so too in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice, because the *apūrva* is directly present, the *saurya* sacrifice is accomplished through the archetypal mantras by means of extension (*atideśa*) or application (*anuṣaṅga*). However, modification (*ūha*) is not established (i.e., modification does not occur).
To this it is replied:
this fault exists in this interpretation. (He states the fault:)
Regarding the phrase "due to a difference in the mode of expression," it is replied here:
the status of being the prompter (*prayojakatva*) is based on the scriptural statement, whereas the status of being the occasion (*nimittabhāva*) is not enjoined by the statement at all.
Whatever prompts something becomes its occasion.
Just as for a gardener, the garden is both the motivator and the cause for the payment of wages;
when the garden exists, the wages are given, and by means of those wages, one is able to maintain the garden.
Therefore, for dharmas, the *apūrva* alone is both the motivator and the cause.

Or—(now the author of the Vārttika himself states another position)—Alternatively, it is established that *dharma*s have an unseen purpose (*apūrva-artha*); and among these, both the directly contributive (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and the remotely contributive (*ārādupakāraka*) are determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*) as the means of proof.

In that context, the mantra "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) is recited. And by virtue of its being so recited, it must provide assistance to the ritual through that context.
In that regard, a specific expectation arises as to how it will indeed be of assistance: is it by mere utterance, or rather by way of manifestation?
The manifestation of the deity through the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is required;
and this [mantra] is capable of performing that function.
Therefore, it assists by means of manifestation; thus, it is determined that this [mantra] assists through manifestation. Furthermore, there must be a cause for this [mantra];
in that regard, its specific cause is as follows.
And this [mantra] does not exist in the Saurya sacrifice.

In that case, because the causal basis (*nimitta*) is absent, there is an exclusion of the mantra; just as, due to the absence of the act of cutting (*medana*), there is an exclusion of the oblation (*homa*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices. (This is the prima facie view.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the *apūrva* alone is the causal basis, not the similarity of form such as the name "Agni" and so forth.

Since the purpose of the word [the mantra] concludes with the mere fact that "one should effect the *apūrva* by means of the mantra through the revelation of the deity," the *apūrva* is its purpose; and since the performance of that [mantra] becomes the cause for the sake of that [purpose], the revelation of the deity intended for the *apūrva* alone is its cause. Thus, the application of the mantra to the *saurya* sacrifice remains unimpeded.

Soma: Here, because of the absence of words such as "if" (*yad*), neither the sacrifice (*yaj*) nor the *apūrva* is expressed by any word as being the cause (*nimitta*). Rather, since the engagement in dharma is occasional, there is an implied causality; and that too belongs only to the *apūrva*, for it is appropriate for the *apūrva*—as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—to serve as the cause for the performance of the means (*sādhana*). As for the sacrifice, since it is understood as something already established (*siddha*), it cannot function as such a cause; and although the *apūrva* is not yet manifested, it can serve as a cause through its mere presence in the mind, just as in the expression "one kills the leopard for its skin."
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "sacrificial act" (*yajñakarma*) means the effect of the sacrifice, that is, the *apūrva*.

For it is precisely that which is enjoined; therefore, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of substances such as threshing and so forth is connected to that *apūrva*, being prompted by the *apūrva* because its purpose is the *apūrva*.
Thus, according to the position [of the opponent], it is established that [the acts] are prompted by the *apūrva*.
The mention of "substance" (*dravya*) and "preparation" (*saṃskāra*) is for the purpose of indicating all dharmas.
This is likewise the case in the second explanation of the second section.
In the first explanation, the meaning is that [the performance] is prompted by the fact of being a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency), because it is for the sake of that.
In the third explanation, however, it is exactly as it is heard [in the text].
Alternatively, in the final position beginning with "or another," the meaning is that it is "connected with that" (tadyuktaḥ), i.e., caused by that (tannimittaḥ).
Vi—(The third interpretation: "There is no status as a cause for something unprecedented, nor is there such from what has been stated."
There is the status of being the user of words, but the causality is merely implied.
Bhāṭṭa: Thus, since the principle of extension (*atideśa*) has been established, the modification (*ūha*) regarding the ritual elements (*padārtha*) so extended is now considered.
Modification is described as being threefold: modification of mantras (*mantra-ūha*), modification of *sāmans* (*sāma-ūha*), and modification of purificatory acts (*saṃskāra-ūha*).
In this context, modification (*ūha*) is defined as the alteration in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) of that which was perceived differently in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*).

And the principle (*tattva*) is as follows: when a certain thing is heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as having its occurrence delimited by a particular property through a specific relation, then in the ectype (*vikṛti*), that same thing must be distinct from what is delimited by that property through that same relation.
This principle applies to mantras such as "devasya tvā" and to preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) like sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

For, in the case of mantras, their occurrence delimited by the denotation of "Agni" is heard in the archetype through the relation of being a reminder (*smāraka*); and in the ectype, because of the scriptural injunction, they must be distinct from what is delimited by that same property through that very same relation.

In this way, even for acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and threshing (*avaghāta*), their being delimited by the nature of *vrīhi* through a connection with the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*); and in the ectype (*vikṛti*), by that very same connection, there is a requirement for them to be non-different from what is delimited by those properties, because of the force of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other factors. Similarly, regarding the *sāmans* such as the *āgnendra*, the fact that they are delimited by a specific position within a particular chant (*stotra*) through a certain connection is heard in the archetype; and in the ectype, by that very same connection, they are delimited by that same position within the chant.

In this context, "being heard" (*śrutatva*) means being apprehended without regard for the intended meaning (*tātparya*); therefore, there is no defect even if the status of being a *kāru* is not apprehended from the word in the case of what has been stated (*ukte*). Furthermore, by the phrase "by the connection" (*saṃbandha*) and so forth, the mention of the connection with the reminder (*smāraka*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—namely, the perception of the deity of the *agniṣṭoma* through the relationship of the prescribed animal and cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*)—is intended to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the subsidiary benefit (*ṛtūpakārakatva*) of that which is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) due to its connection with the injunction of another deity in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), which is otherwise not required. Thus, the term "connection" (*saṃbandha*) is not intended to be emphasized [in the sense of a specific relation].

Since the threshing and other operations, which are heard [in the Veda] as residing in that which is delimited by the status of being rice (*vrīhitva*) mentioned in the *prakṛti* (archetype), also reside in the *vijaya* and other grains, the terms *prakṛti* and *vikṛti* are introduced in order to exclude those [grains].

Furthermore, because there is a distinction between the *prakṛti*-rice and the *vikṛti*-rice— such as the *saurya* sacrifice, which is distinct from both *prakṛti* and *vikṛti* rice— the qualification "delimited by the nature of *yad*" is added to prevent the application of threshing and other operations to the *ātideśika* (extended) rice and *saurya* grains.

In the *saurya* sacrifice and similar rites, although the absence of the snake is not present as having a counter-correlativity delimited by that specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*), there is nevertheless an absence of it having a counter-correlativity delimited by "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*).
However, in the modified form (*vikṛti*) where barley is the object to be accomplished, there is no fault even if modification (*ūha*) is accepted.

This is because, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), sprinkling and other such acts are intended—by way of their underlying purport—to be characterized by being means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*); therefore, in the modified form as well, they are established as natural through that very same form.

If, however, one intends to express the distinction between the previously unestablished *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and others by means of the phrase "of the two previously unestablished," etc., then one might fear over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *saurya* and similar rites. Anticipating this, the word "stated" (*nirukta*) is used in the sense of "being perceived [by the Veda]. Since the status of being a means to the *apūrva* depends upon the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), it lacks the quality of being "stated in the scripture" (*śrutatva*).

Furthermore, even if the words "Sūrya" and so forth were substituted in place of the word "Agni," because the remainder of the mantra remains archetypal (*prākṛta*), there is no non-applicability of the word "iti" in the definition for that [mantra].

And thus, in that case, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the sequence in the place of the original constituent; it should be understood that the word "modification" (*ūha*) is used here in a figurative sense.

Alternatively, let it be so according to that [figurative sense], and the phrase "of that" (*tasya*) refers to that which has attained the status of the original constituent's function; this is the summary.

That modification would be established only through the extension (*atideśa*) by way of proximity to the object as delimited by that specific form in which it was enjoined in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—not, however, through extension by way of its mere essential nature alone.

If that were the case, by the extension (*atideśa*) of the word "fire" (*agni*) itself, the *saurya* sacrifice would be established; and since the application [of the ritual] would be possible through the assumption of another purpose for that very extension, there would be no occasion for modification (*ūha*).

Therefore, it will be stated in the tenth book that in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is either an extension of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) by way of their contribution (*upakāra*), or an extension of those very elements whose forms have been determined in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

Therefore, as an introduction here, it is considered whether acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and threshing (*avaghāta*), as well as injunctions contained in sentences such as "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), are prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) with respect to that which is delimited by the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*), and consequently, are prompted by rice and the like; or whether they are prescribed with respect to that which is delimited by being a means to the *apūrva* (transcendental result), and consequently, are prompted by the *apūrva*.

If they were prompted by rice and the like, then in the case of the *śyāmāka* grain, the *caru* offering, or the *saurya* sacrifice—since rice and the like are absent—sprinkling and the other acts would indeed be omitted (*lopa*), and not merely modified (*ūha*).

If, however, [the sacrifice] were prompted by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), then even in the case of *śyāmāka* grains and the like, since they too are delimited by that same form, there would be a modification of the established procedure (*siddhayūha*).

In that regard, even where the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*) is not explicitly heard in the text regarding the status of being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), there too, because the injunction for the *prayāja* and other such rites occurs through the cognition of the sacrifice itself—by means of the sequence of expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā’kāṅkṣā*) consisting in the requirement for an agent to grasp the instrument—the very nature of being a sacrifice (*yāgatva*) is the delimiting factor of the objective, and not the state of being a means to the *apūrva*, lest the primary status [of the sacrifice] be lost.
Nor does this entail an over-extension (*pariplava*), because that which is to be restated (*anuvādya*) applies to what is proximate when such is possible.

The injunctions regarding preparatory rites such as threshing (avaghāta) and so forth apply to the *āgneya* sacrifice and others in exactly the same way, because they serve as the delimiters of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

Nor is there a lack of extension (*atideśa*), for just as in the case of being for the sake of a specific *apūrva*, even when being for the sake of the *āgneya* and others, the extension of ritual details to the *saurya* sacrifice— occupying the place of the *āgneya*— is logically established by the extension rule "one should act like that" (*tadvat kuryāt*).

Therefore, these [rites] are indeed employed for the sake of the sacrifice. Under such circumstances, what could possibly be said [to the contrary]? Since sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites are heard of in connection with rice (*vrīhi*) and the like, it follows that "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) and so forth alone must be the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) for the object of reference. Nor can it be argued that there is no unity of the properties (*dharma*) because rice, sacrifices, and so on have different forms; for even those [sacrifices] possess fruitfulness (*phalavattva*), just like the fires (*agni*), and thus lack such diversity. Furthermore, one cannot claim that because there is no evidence for the production of rice and the like apart from the installation of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), they would be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) in its absence—just as sprinkling and the like might be purposeless apart from the production of rice—since rice and the like are produced even without sprinkling and other such rites.

In order to avoid such meaninglessness (*anarthakya*), it is possible to understand that the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) qualified by acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) serve the purpose of the sacrifice, or that they possess *apūrva*-ness, through another assumed sentence. This is because, according to the principle of the "son of a Niṣāda" (*niṣādapati-nyāya*, 6.1.13), there is no evidence for a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *vrīhi*—which would extend it to barley (*yava*) and other grains—to denote the status of being a means to *apūrva*. Or, even if one grants that there is figurative indication in the word *vrīhi*, nevertheless, due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of its immediate presence [in cognition], only the quality of being rice that serves as a means for a specific type of sacrifice (*vijātīya-yāga*) is indicated, and not the status of being a means to *apūrva*.

Nor does it follow that the sacrifice is rendered purposeless because it can arise even without sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other such acts, since it is an efficient means (*niśātōpāya*). For although [the sacrifice] may arise as something delimited by the generic property of "sacrifice" (*yāgatva*) or as something delimited by "unseen potency" (*apūrva*), there is no evidence that it arises as something delimited by a specific type of sacrifice (*vijātīyayāgatva*) without sprinkling and the like. Indeed, there is no established causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of sprinkling and so forth for the sake of that which is delimited by being an *Āgneya* sacrifice, by virtue of which the manifestation of the property of being an *Āgneya* would occur in the individual instance produced by that [complex].

However, by virtue of the force of the injunction, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth constitute the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for that [sacrifice]; since there is no evidence that it could be established apart from them, there is no pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) in sprinkling and the rest being for the sake of the very nature of the sacrifice (*yāgasvarūpa*).
For this very reason, even those factors that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) are not purposeless when they serve the nature of the sacrifice.

This being the position reached: even if the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth were simply the status of being a means to a sacrifice of a different class, nevertheless—just as in the case of being a means to the *apūrva*—the property of being rice (*vrīhitva*) and so on does not enter into it according to the method to be explained. Thus, since that [status] exists even in the case of *śyāmāka* grains, the accomplishment of the modification (*ūha*) is established; such is the reasoning.

In reality, however, being the means for a sacrifice of a specific class (*vijātīya-yāga*) is not the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). This is because the status of being a sacrifice (*yāgatva*), which pervades all individual instances of sacrifices of that class, is already known; and since it is understood from common worldly experience that anything delimited by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is a cause for that [sacrifice], there is no obstacle to the production of individual instances of sacrifices of that class by means of other substances—even in the absence of substances such as *vrīhi* rice—due to the force of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Consequently, the [Vedic injunction] would be rendered purposeless (*ānarthakya*) if it were restricted to those [specific substances].

Nor is there a rule that a general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*) produces its effect only when accompanied by the presence of a specific cause (*viśeṣakāraṇa*); for although such may be the case elsewhere, there is no evidence for such a postulation in the present context, and because the scriptural mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "that very [grain] should be offered, whether it be of such or such a kind"—is not produced.

For this very reason, since the injunctions regarding rice and other materials can be established as restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) in terms of their result after the deficiency of five [grains] has been remedied by means of rice and so forth, they apply even to substitutes (*pratinidhi*).

Therefore, all injunctions regarding substances and preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) are indeed injunctions that serve as means for the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). This is because, according to worldly convention, the causality of substances and the like toward the pervasive *apūrva* delimited [by the sacrifice] is already established; otherwise, they would incur the status of being counter-injunctions (*pratibandhaka*) as defined above. Even for those acts that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), by this same reasoning, their function is to produce a fitness (*yogyatā*) for the generation of the *apūrva*; the substance itself is not for the sake of the sacrifice (*yāga*), for that would result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*). Furthermore, since they produce the fitness for the sacrifice and so forth, there is no risk of these acts becoming primary (*pradhāna*) or of their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) being subverted. These points have been thoroughly discussed in the *Kaustubha*.

As for the claim that the injunction for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth is made with respect to rice grains (*vrīhi*) as delimited by the property of "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*), and that—since metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not admitted in verbal cognition (śābdabodha)—there subsequently arises, according to the *niṣādapatyanyāya*, the postulation of a separate sentence regarding rice grains qualified by sprinkling and the like, and the postulation of their being for the sake of the *apūrva*: that is untenable, because if sprinkling and so forth were the *bhāvyatva* (the end to be achieved) of that which is delimited by rice-ness, the determination of unfitness (*ayogyatā*) would act as an obstacle, resulting in the impossibility of verbal cognition itself; therefore, the admission of metaphorical indication is necessary.

Therefore, since the term *vrīhi* (rice) and others function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote that which is delimited by being a means to the *apūrva*, the injunctions for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth are indeed directed toward that [the *apūrva*]. Thus, it is established that these [rites] are prompted solely by the *apūrva*; consequently, the modification (*ūha*) [of the word] in the case of *śyāmāka* (millet) and other such grains is proven. Nor does this imply that even when the ritual duties (*dharma*) are performed, because rice and the like would still be the occasioning factors (*nimitta*) as performers of those duties, there would be a loss of duties (*dharmalopa*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) due to their absence—just as there is none in the case of the *bhedabhāva* (non-existence of difference)—on the grounds that there is no evidence for rice and the like being the occasioning factors in the absence of the word *yat*.
They threshed [the grain].

There arises this further doubt: because of the scriptural injunction regarding the loss of the portioned oblation (*avatta-havir-nāśe*), and because of the hearing of the mere essential nature of the substance in the text "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*).

The rebuttal—that even in the case of "they thresh the rice" (*vrīhīn avahanti*), its purpose is for the sacrifice because it occurs within that context (*prakaraṇa*) despite the absence of a word denoting the sacrifice—is clear.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is: "Even regarding a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), the scriptural mention (*śruti*) is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), because a primary injunction (*vidhi*) characterized by restriction (*niyama*) is possible.
[Bhāṣya: "Even in the case of threshing, there is a restriction, just as there is with respect to place and so forth; therefore, that [restriction applies]."
It should be employed by the principal [act]; the agreement is prescribed for the preparatory rite.

Just as a restrictive rule (niyama) is prescribed regarding the optional occurrence of place, time, agent, and substance, so too in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*), although it is obtained from common worldly practice for the purpose of producing rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), it is restricted in order to exclude other optional methods such as splitting (*vidalana*) and the like.

In the Bhaṭṭa school, however, this sūtra is included within the ninth section (*adhikaraṇa*). Maṇḍana [states]: "Likewise, the purpose of the injunctions for threshing and so forth is [restriction]."

Śaṅkara says: "And likewise with regard to refinement (saṃskāra), it is the same for us; there is a restriction in that very same way. Just as there is a rule regarding substances and qualities, so too is there a rule regarding refinement.

The word "avaghnan" (striking) serves as the indicator of the time for summoning the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation); [it applies] when the portioned oblation (*avadāna*) or the offered oblation (*havir*) is lost,
[as well as] regarding the portioning and the offering.
Therefore, even in that case, since the contingency of producing another oblation arises, the sacrifice is performed with clarified butter (*ājya*).

Nor does it follow from any school’s view that, if the unfitness of the oblation (as a condition) were delimited by its status as an oblation (*haviṣṭva*), a sacrifice with clarified butter would occur even upon the destruction of the substance's capacity for being an oblation; for a cognition of a condition cannot serve as a means for the conditional rite, and such a destruction—being constant—is unfit to be a condition. However, when there is a destruction of parts exceeding those to be excluded (namely, more than the size of a thumb-joint), the sacrifice with clarified butter indeed takes place.
This indeed is the established position of the Mīmāṃsakas;

however, the ritualists (yājñikas) do not accept it. Their view is as follows: the destruction of a single part does not constitute a cause [for a new sacrifice] in the same way that the burning of a single part does, because even when one part is destroyed, the remaining parts of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)—such as its constituent portions—are still perceived. Since it is precisely those [remaining parts] that define the status of the offering (havis), they continue to define the cake as consisting of the quantity of grains originally measured out; thus, the destruction of that [single part] is unavoidable [and does not necessitate a new rite].
Therefore, even if one part is destroyed, the sacrifice (yāga) proceeds with what remains;
however, the oblation (homa) may be omitted, since it is impossible to perform the ritual cutting (avadāna) in the absence of a middle portion as the locus of extraction.
In reality, however, [the sacrifice should proceed] with whatever remains.
In the *Avadāna* [section], at 694, under the sūtra "From the beginning of the *avadāna* to the end of the offering,

due to the connection with the sequence," it is also easily stated— by means of the presentation of the principle— that what is established for the archetype (*prakṛti*) is to be applied to the modified forms (*vikṛti*).
— *Saṃkarṣa*.

Regarding the *avadāna* (cutting-off) in the five-fold offering, the fifth *avadāna* occurs even before the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). Even if worldly convention depends on human effort and is thus arbitrary, because it is connected to what is to be supported (*apoṣedhya*), and since the observation of the subsequent indicative mark (*liṅga*) does not specify a sequence, one might argue that—according to the principle "accessory elements (*āgantūnām*) are placed at the end" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 5.2.9)—the portion should be cut from the rear half of the oblation (*havis*) after the sprinkling. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [we reply]: because the sprinkling is itself a sanctificatory act (*saṃskāra*), it possesses its own sequential order; thus, for the abundant oblation, the various cuttings-off (*avadāna*) are indeed successive.
*Saṃkarṣa* 2.2.8: Regarding the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvadāna*), the fifth [cutting] belongs to the *aupabhṛta* [ladle] alone.
Since the fourth subsequent [cutting] is established by the very power of the word for those [cuttings], it [the fifth] subordinates the single act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: even if one accepts the mere establishment of the fourth subsequent [cutting] in some way or another, what is intended here is that which has the fourth cutting as its object; thus it is stated.

Regarding the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), including its subsidiaries: since the *pratiprasthātṛ* does not engage in the duties of the *adhvaryu*, he should not be assigned a share in the verses belonging to its subsidiaries.

And restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is the exclusion [of the term] from other referents (*arthāntara*). *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 94. The hearing of a restrictive particle excludes what is similar to that which has been mentioned.

For this very reason, in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, under the view that [the rule] is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), the function of the statement "he performs the two *ājyabhāgas*"—which has the character of a restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*)—is shown in the *Pūrvatantra* (in the section beginning with *sviṣṭakṛt bhakṣapratiṣedhaḥ syāt*, 10.7.21–35) to be the exclusion of other portions belonging to the same class as the *ājyabhāgas*; or else, the function of the indicative term used for the purpose of restriction in the case of the omission of the *sviṣṭakṛt* is shown to be the exclusion of other remaining ritual acts. (Sūtra).

The *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath] takes place in water, whereas in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* it takes place in the *āhavanīya* fire; thus there is a difference in location between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*) rites, because of the scriptural statement: "They perform the *avabhṛtha* in water" (Ke. 11.3.1.9).
Regarding the *avabhṛtha* in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is stated: "This is the *avabhṛtha* of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*s.
This usage is figurative (*aupacārika*), derived from the etymological connection with water (*apām vyutpatti*).

VI. 7|3|4. *Avabhṛtha*: The *avabhṛtha* belonging to the Soma sacrifice is for the purpose of releasing the consecration (*dīkṣā*). (Sūtra 698) One should give [the sacrificial fee] at the *avabhṛtha* as in the case of the *sadhivik* [offering], with the mantra: "In the waters, Soma has spoken to me."

Regarding the statement, "In these two [offerings], these first portions are indeed accompanied by water," this injunction, being devoid of any other quality, must serve as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the other auxiliary parts.

As for the statements, "He performs the *prayāja* offerings with the *apabhṛth* vessel" and "He performs the *prayāja* offerings without the *barhis* grass," these serve to enjoin the *anuyāja* offerings for those *prayāja* offerings that have been excluded.
Therefore, there is an exclusion of only the remaining auxiliary parts.
But because there is a prohibition of only a portion of the *prayāja* offerings, it functions as a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*); therefore, it must be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).
The Commentary: The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that this is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
It has been stated that the enumeration is faultless.
Furthermore, the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa), "He performs the *apāmārjana* after the *prayāja*s," would not be appropriate.
If the injunction were simply "he performs the *prayāja*s," then the *barhis-prayāja* would also be obtained [as required].
In that case, the term "avabhṛtha" (concluding bath) is appropriate. Now, there is the prohibition of the sacrificial grass (barhis), the injunction for the fore-sacrifices (prayāja),
and the use of the dregs of soma (ṛjīṣa) and so forth at the avabhṛtha.
In the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, which is the principal rite, only the vehicle smeared with Soma is prescribed;
this is the meaning of the verbal root.
By this, [the word *avabhṛtha*] functions as an instrument; in the act of relinquishing, it will indicate the location through a concomitance characterized by being the object.
To the place of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
By accepting the third [case ending], they are expressed merely as being in association; thus, as the objects of the action, they should go while taking the *somalipta* (Soma-soiled) implements.
Those [implements] should be [placed] at that location.

Because there is no possibility of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word *avabhṛtha* merely indicates the location; this is the meaning. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever in [the view that it] has a purpose.

Soma: [He states] the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the previously mentioned definition of *pratipatti*. Maṇḍana: [The connection is established] because of the refutation of the objection: "Not having sacrificed with the *avabhṛtha* bathed in Soma. This is the transition (*saṃgati*).
Thus they say.
However, some [hold] the third [view]:
Śaṅkara says— "That which is to be explained is smeared with Soma."
In the case of the verbal substitution (*vyatyaya*), there is the sense of the accusative; for the word *yanti*, there is the sense of the causative (*ṇij-artha*).
Only at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is there a double-portioning (*dviravadāna*) of the single-pot offering (*ekakapāla*), and not elsewhere;
so they determine.
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "In the *avabhṛtha* belonging to the *saumika* [sacrifice], there is disposal (*pratipatti*) by means of that which was smeared with *soma*.
(Bhāṣya 7.1.5.23). In the *avabhṛtha* pertaining to the Jyotiṣṭoma, there should be disposal together with the clarified butter (*ājya*), because that [butter] has already served its purpose.

The two portions belong to Soma alone, and they are accompanied by water, according to the text: "He offers the two water-accompanied portions of clarified butter. As for the carrying away of the Soma-smeared vessel at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), is it a means (*sādhana*) or a disposal (*pratipatti*)? It is a means, because of the Vedic text: "O waters, be united with us; Soma goes into the waters here. Thus, [Soma] goes by means of them.

"Prātassavanam sādhaya" (Complete the morning pressing)— thus [it is said]. Regarding the *avabhṛtha* belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is not so, because its sacrificial oblation consists of a *puroḍāśa*.
Because that [offering] is not separate from the vessel;
that which is the single-pot-sherd offering is a modification (vikāra) of the Vaiśvadeva single-pot-sherd offering.
Thus, the casting [into the fire] is for the purpose of disposal (pratipatti).
The extension of those properties [is as follows]:

Bhāṣya 7.1.10.27. Regarding the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Bhaṭṭas, the fire used for the sweeping (*saṃmārjana*) at the *some* sacrifice itself should be taken for the *avabhṛtha*; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), having enjoined the rite named *avabhṛtha* by the statement, "They go to the waters with a single potsherd offering to Varuṇa," [the fire is not required].
Regarding the passage: "The *saṃmārjanīya* [vessels]—something smeared with Soma; with that they go to the *avabhṛtha* bath"—so it is heard in the Śruti.
In that regard,

there would be a modification of the principal [offering] at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), for the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) indicates that what is smeared with *soma* is the instrument, and that [instrument] is [employed] in the sacrifice.
The connection with that as a cause is mixed, like [the connection] between a substance and a deity;
for even though it would otherwise be impossible, it is appropriate with respect to the *avabhṛtha* bath.
It is not for the sake of the accusative case.
In the *avabhṛtha* rite, whether it be the principal act or merely the principal substance, there is a modification of the fire (*agni-vikāra*).
This modification of the fire is, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a disposal (*pratipatti*). And this is not [impossible] because of the dependence upon such a disposal.
It may be so;
the meaning is that water should be taken in place of fire.
Since the primary purpose is characterized by its intended goal, there is no fault even when it is for that momentary [substitution].
The Niṣādasthapati— meaning that which is to be performed—
is not to be performed on fire in the waters.
For it is not logical [to assume such a thing], because the definition is untenable. Therefore, the cause of that [destruction] is the primary cause: conjunction with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*).
For those who are ignorant, the fire is indeed the instrument for that which is smeared with Soma, as in the case of the *bhṛtha* offering.
Nor is the connection with fire not a cause for the primary act when its performance is prescribed by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).
There is no non-inclusion [of the accessory] because of the presence of substance, deity, and sacrificial pan (*kapāla*), as in the case of another distinct rite named the *avabhṛtha*.

Just as the single sacrificial pan is the substance and Varuṇa is the deity, the inclusion of the accessory is established within the primary act, since it is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As for what has been said by some regarding the distinction of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*):

Because it has been prescribed, it belongs to the Āgneya; likewise, water also, by being accepted as a constituent part of the primary rite, finds its place through combination in that very *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), and not in the previously mentioned subsidiary rites—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). From that perspective, the same principle applies to the *vājina* (curd-milk mixture) as well, since it is desired [to be treated] in the same way.
Therefore:
"Or rather, it [the *avabhṛtha*] is accompanied by its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), because the injunction for performance is a single unit;
for even the *avabhṛtha* is an option, since its function consists in the release from the consecration (*dīkṣā*)."
The word "or" (vā) serves to exclude the prima facie view.
It is not that there is an option only regarding the *pradhāna*; rather, there is also an option regarding the substances that are modifications (*vikāra*) of fire.
For if they serve a single purpose, their performance occurs through a single ritual application (*tantra*).
[The opponent argues: "It is water; however, the *avabhṛtha* is accompanied by its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), that is, it is a collection of waters together with its subsidiaries.
This being the position reached, [the reply is: the word *avabhṛtha* refers to a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
It must be performed, not merely as a primary act.

Because of the unity of the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavacana*), if it were a case of extended application (*atideśa*) by name, there would be the consequence of it being figurative (*gauṇatva*). Furthermore, if it were a direct denotation (*vācakatva*), there would be the undesirable contingency of postulating multiple potencies for the primary act, as in "they proceed with the *avabhṛtha*. Moreover, due to the absence of a deity, there would be the consequence of it lacking a specific form (*arūpatva*). Therefore, [it is] Vāruṇa...
And it is indeed one [and the same].

Therefore, at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), just as with the principal rites, the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) must also be performed in water; since there is no instruction to the contrary and the definition of the location is established, they are not to be performed elsewhere—this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Because it has the nature of a sacrifice, the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the Soma-soiled [vessels] is not enjoined here;
this is also because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
And thus, there is no intention to express the meaning of the verbal root; rather, it is for the purpose of enjoining the *avabhṛtha* rite as a subordinate element (*parapadārtha*).
He states another reason for this conclusion:
the word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the reasons.
Furthermore, the postulation of another ritual action (*karmāntara*) and so forth becomes necessary;
yet by that [postulation],
the form of the *ādhāra* (the pouring) as expressed in the injunction, "Having thrown grass into the water, he pours the *ādhāra*," would not be established.
At the *avabhṛtha*, there is a prohibition of the *bahiḥ* [offerings].
At the *avabhṛtha*, the rule that the *anūyāja* offerings are performed externally in the waters is a sign (*liṅga*) that all the *ājya* offerings are to be performed in the waters.

For the purpose of prescribing the qualities of the form of the mantra as it has been joined, here— by means of this indicative mark (*liṅga*)— the subsidiary parts of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) must be performed in water, because they are subsidiaries, just like the *āghāra* libation. And by virtue of the sequence [of the text], from the observation of these indicative marks, namely "In the waters indeed is your seat" and "Soma is in the waters," the subsidiary parts of the *avabhṛtha* are to be performed in water.
He said: "The two *apsumant* mantras are to be recited at dawn.

Thus, these [rites] must be performed; they are not [omitted]. Because the two *ājyabhāga* offerings prescribed by the primary injunctions possess the quality of being *apśu*, there is a removal of the substance and deity due to the mere division of words, as they are indeed devoid of [other] qualities.
The exclusion of others follows from the specific injunction.
Regarding what was stated by the proponent—that for other unknown [deities] obtained through the *codaka* rule, there is a connection "like that of substance and deity"—to that he says: "And" (*ca*).
From the injunction, there would be the exclusion of the other;

and thus, the purpose of the disparity between the principal [offerings] and the subsidiary offerings is expressed by "the two *ājyabhāga* portions accompanied by water" and "the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath].
The word "principal" refers to the primary rite.
The statement is restrictive (*parisaṃkhyāpaka*).

The word "apabhṛtha" [in the injunction] "he performs the apabhṛtha-prayājas" is the basis for the designation [of those offerings]; because of the division of the term "limb" (*aṅga*), [it indicates] the primary [status].

As for the statement "he performs the apabhṛtha-anuyājas," although there is no removal of the substance and deity from the limbs, [the restriction applies] to the substance and deity [of the other limbs].
It would be for the purpose of prescribing the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings that are distinct from those [performed] outside;
this is not a removal (*apanaya*),
just as in the case of the statement, "with water, by means of the *avabhṛtha*."

And thus, the remaining ritual acts consisting of the *āghāra* libations, the *prayājas*, and the *anuyājas* must indeed be performed; for the connection of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) with the principal (*aṅgin*) denoted by the term *avabhṛtha* is heard in scripture.
This is another prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Likewise, there is the scriptural statement regarding the subsidiary: "Having thrown grass into the water, he performs the *āghāra* libation."

However, because there is a prohibition regarding only a portion of the *prayāja* offerings, it functions as a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). Furthermore, the connection of the *āghāra* offering with the principal rite is heard in scripture: "The two *ājya* [offerings] accompanied by water...
Therefore, it cannot be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
And from the indicative mark (liṅga) "two portions," it follows that the two *ājyabhāgas* are also subsidiary elements (*aṅga*).
The word "but" (*tu*) excludes the view of restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*).
If a connection with water were known for the *ājya* [portions], [then the restriction would apply].

And thus, regarding the exclusion of the ignorant from the status of being a recipient of the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*): if the sentence were a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of other types of ignorance, then even if there were a removal [of the offering] from the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* sacrifices, nevertheless, because it would be a restrictive exclusion, there would be no prohibition against the ignorant performing a portion of the primary sacrifice; for, due to that connection, there would be no removal of them from the ignorant.

And thus, it consists of a single sacrificial cake (*ekakapāla*), precisely because [the other] has not been obtained. The term "apabhṛtha" is formed by negating a part [of the word *prabhṛtha*], and Varuṇa is the deity; the combination of these two constitutes the material and the deity.
Regarding that [phrase], "apabhṛthai":
the analysis of the compound is "the removal of the *ājyabhāga* offerings by means of the partial prohibition."
In the reading *dravyadevatvānapāyaḥ*,
it is understood that the sentence does not function as an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Consequently, although there is no removal of the substance and deity from the primary *ājya* offering, [the result follows].
Why does the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering at the *avabhṛtha* not possess the status of the *hotṛ-pada-veda*? Because it is impossible.
For it is impossible for a single sentence to simultaneously effect both a displacement of the offering (*pradāna-viprakarṣa*) and an extension of ritual properties (*dharma-atideśa*).

Having established the remoteness from the original gift (*pradāna-viprakarṣa*), one cannot effect the extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*) for that which has already fulfilled its purpose.

[In the Śruti, regarding the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture dedicated to Varuṇa, some hold that the meaning is: "with the residue [of the mixture] adhering to the cooking vessel, [one satisfies] the barley-grains which constitute the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the flour-made ram, once they have been satiated."]

Others hold that the flour-based substance is for the purpose of preparing the *āmikṣā* (curdled milk), and since it lacks the status of a primary oblation (*pradhānahavis*), it is not included among the primary oblations characterized as *puroḍāśa* cakes and the like.
Others, however, maintain that because there is no distinction, it belongs to both. [Soma]...
The *āmikṣā* related to Varuṇa is produced.
A portion of it is offered first (at the place of insertion), and a portion is offered later (at the time following the *samid-yajus*).
In that very manner, it is connected with its own deity, Varuṇa.
Just as in the case of the animal sacrifice, where one part is offered at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) and another part at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), so it is here.

If this is indeed the same sacrifice, then how is the term *avabhṛtha* used? To this he says: *avabhṛtha* is an *avamārśa* [a secondary application], based on the well-known meaning of its constituent parts.
Reflection (*avamarśa*):
Indeed, there can be no reflection upon an object that has not been previously apprehended.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 227. The maxim: "The individual parts possess meaning, not the aggregate."
For example: whoever possesses a certain object performs a function with it;
and whoever possesses cows consumes their milk and ghee—this cannot be seen by others.
Thus, even in the absence of a [perceptible] purposeful existence, [the result is achieved].

The *Sāhasrī*. 651. Regarding the members (*avayava*) [in inference for the sake of others], the followers of Akṣapāda maintain that there are five: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).
The Mīmāṃsakas hold that there are only three members, either the first three or the last three.
Maṇi, p. 40: Furthermore, unlike the logicians (*tārkika*), the syllogism for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) does not have five members, but rather only three.

As it has been said: "Those others [the Buddhists] do not accept five members; we [the Mīmāṃsakas] accept three, up to the example (*udāharaṇa*), whereas those who hold the example and so forth [to be necessary]..."
"Thus [it is said].
Bāla., p. 8. Because the whole is not distinct from its parts.
Bhā.
A mark established in a subordinate part necessarily requires [its primary context] (708). Regarding the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*):
the maxim is that between what is necessarily required and what is not required, that which is required must be remembered.
This is clear.

[The term] *sādṛśī* [is used]. 61. *Avasarasaṅgati* (Connection by Occasion): When a discussion that was not to be stated is concluded, that very same [topic] becomes the subject of the intellect. Su. p. 392. For a state (*avasthā*) is indeed a modification (*vikāra*).
Furthermore, a state (*avasthā*) is the cause for the arising of another state;
and a state is not distinct from that which possesses the state (*avasthāvat*).

(Bṛhatī, p. 161). In the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), regarding the rule: "Having filled the mortar made of *udumbara* wood with all kinds of grain, one threshes [them], and then one places this [mortar] down," because the act of threshing serves as the purpose [for the placement], it is performed only once.
"Pounding (ava-hanana) should not be performed in the case of black-gram (kṛṣṇala) coins, because the purpose of removing the husks (tuṣa) is impossible [in their case].
Bhāṣya 10.1.11, Section 2: Pounding, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), pouring out (nirvapaṇa), and so forth, are the properties of the sacrificial materials (aupadhadharmāḥ).
(An *auṣadha* is rice and so forth. 3|1|417. In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the threshing of the grains must be performed before their roasting; after that, the roasting takes place.

10|2|133: Regarding the mantra for threshing, "They thresh with the mantra, 'The Rākṣasa is struck down'" (in one case); "They thresh with [the mantra], 'The Yātudhānas are struck down'" (in another case).

3|1|2131: Regarding threshing and grinding, the rule is an injunction: "One threshes the rice grains" and "One grinds the rice grains"; this is not a mere restatement (anuvāda) in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
4|1|1126: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the mantra for threshing is employed once for the sake of the entire collection of blows.
11|1|12142: In the *rājasūya*, there is a repetition of the mantra for threshing for each individual sacrificer who wins various prizes.
11|1|13143: Actions such as "he threshes" and "he grinds," which have visible purposes, should be performed until the production of rice grains and so forth is achieved.

Bhāṣya 11.1.1527: The act of *avahanti* (threshing) is indeed a single entity, beginning with the downward movement [of the pestle] and ending with the rice grain. The downward movement and so forth constitute the commencement of the root *han* (to strike), and everything up to the husked grain (*phalīkaraṇa*) is its remainder.
This is because the act of striking is for the purpose of producing the rice grain.
Bhāṣya 5.2.719 states: "But *avahanti* (the act of threshing) is neither feminine, nor masculine, nor neuter.
Now, one might object: "Is there not also a feminine word for *avahanti*, namely *kriyā* (action)? To this we reply:

The word *avahanti* is not necessarily feminine; it also exists in the masculine as *avaghātaḥ*, and in the neuter as *karma*. According to Pāṇini 3.1.318, that (*avahanti*) is an auxiliary (*sannipatyopakārī*).

11|1|3143. However, for those who maintain that the term *avahanti* (threshing) applies to the action of raising and lowering the pestle only when the fruit is rice-grains, for them the repetition [of the act] would only occur until the production of the rice-grains. But that is a very weak position, because the usage is observed even without rice-grains, as in "he threshes the *kapāya*" and "he threshes the *kiṇva*."

Nor is this usage figurative, because there is no distinguishing factor [to indicate so]; moreover, by virtue of the established meaning of its constituent parts, it is understood as denoting merely the act of threshing. Furthermore, the word as a whole is not established in any other sense.

However, because the activity regarding rice (*taṇḍula*) occurs predominantly there, its application is frequent. Bhāṣya 11.1.16.28. The intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) is refuted in the section concerning the *videvanā* and so forth belonging to the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice (4.4.12.3–4). Ke. [Commentary]: Regarding the intermediate context: [The opponent] objects, "But if this is so, would it not follow that there is a complete severance of all intermediate contexts? For, since the manner of performance of the primary act (*pradhānakathaṃbhāva*) extends on both sides, no subordinate quality (*aṅgaguṇa*) could possibly exist [in between], and thus a 'sandwich' (*saṃdaṃśa*) would be untenable; consequently, no intermediate context would ever exist. This is the objection raised by the word "but" (*nanu*).

[The author] refutes [the objection] by means of the possibility of *saṃdaṃśa* (sandwiching) when the status of being a subordinate quality (*aṅgaguṇatva*) is understood, having set aside the primary mode of procedure (*pradhānakathaṃbhāva*) by means of a stronger authority (*pramāṇa*). It is said:

"When it is known through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means that [an element] does not belong to a subordinate part within another context (*paraprakaraṇa*), then again, in that very same place, its [status as a subordinate] is desired by way of *saṃdaṃśa*."

The meaning is as follows: because the word "again" (*punaḥ*) signifies posteriority, and because the particle "and" (*ca*) indicates prior existence, when ignorance is recognized as belonging to other contexts both before and after [the central topic] through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) is accepted due to the possibility of a "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśa*).

Regarding all those things considered to be intermediate contexts (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), he says "of all" (*sarveṣām*) to indicate that a doubt might arise before stating their respective definitions via direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.
