A scriptural rule that is stated without qualification (*aviśeṣeṇa*) is doubtful because its application is improper; therefore, it should be set aside by one that is specifically prescribed (*viśeṣaśiṣṭa*).

A scriptural rule that is stated without qualification—that is, a general rule—is doubtful as to whether it applies to all particular cases or only to some particular cases. Consequently, it remains at a distance from the specific rule; having encountered the specific rule, it recedes, meaning it does not operate within the scope of the specific rule.
Therefore, in such a case, that which is specifically enjoined by the specific rule (viśeṣaśāstra) shall prevail.
Because it involves both a general and a specific rule, there is no option (vikalpa);
for an option is improper due to being tainted by the eight defects (aṣṭadoṣa).

For example, in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the specific injunction is: "He offers on the track" (*varman*), meaning he offers on the line produced by the path of the wheel of the *havirdhāna* cart as it moves. The general injunction is: "He offers in the Āhavanīya fire. Consequently, within the scope of the injunction regarding the track, the injunction regarding the Āhavanīya does not apply.
The same should be understood in cases such as, "In the Rājasūya sacrifice, one should offer oblations after taking hold of the ant-hill mound.
Therefore, the conclusion is that, excluding the homas involving the *varman* and other such rites, the Āhavanīya fire should be used for all other homas.
This is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Furthermore, according to the principle of the tenth section (*adhikaraṇa*), that scripture which is without distinction (the general rule) is superseded by the optional (*kāmya*) rite; thus, the optional supersedes the obligatory (*nitya*).
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 488).

"In the absence of a distinction [from what has already been established], it would indeed be purposeless" (2.4.2); this was stated in the section on repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*) by means of the definition of the authority of the Veda. Furthermore, an injunction that lacks another thing to be enjoined and is not directed toward anything else, while enjoining the very nature of the ritual action itself, necessarily effects a different ritual action because the previously enjoined [action] is already established; thus, it relies upon the result of the determination of the injunction. *Vārttika* 3.1.1, p. 649. ("On the other hand, the singularity [of the number] is a restatement [of what is already known]; for otherwise, it would be purposeless.")

The literal meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: in cases such as "He offers the *samidh* oblations," the repetition of the single root *yajati* (to sacrifice) would, like a difference in words (*śabdāntara*), constitute a distinction [between acts], because there is no difference [in the form] and thus no difference in the object.
However, it is stated in the tenth book (10.1.32) that even a sentence which applies without distinction may have a specific intent.
(Bālakrīḍā, p. 101).

And according to the maxim that "what is neither enjoined nor prohibited is permitted," the established doctrine of Audhayaṇa (the doctrine regarding the prohibition of sea-voyage) is indeed accepted by Gautama and others as well, even in the case of the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice where the utterance of *svāhā* is not prescribed.
In the *Sanātanadīpa*, *Pramāṇaprakāśa*, page 295:
"The injunction for the utterance of *svāhā* applies to offerings for which no *svāhā* has been prescribed; such is the meaning of the section [Vi.

It has been stated (7.4.1) that an action for which the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not prescribed takes [its procedure] from an action for which the procedure is prescribed as *dharma*. Bhāṣya 8.4.4.15: The meaning of this section is that in the case of actions such as the *saurya* sacrifice, for which the procedure is not prescribed, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure.
"He gives two barren cows and a ram-bull."

In the absence of co-occurrence with another word, when the word *dhenu* alone is heard, there is everywhere a cognition of qualities such as the milking of cows; therefore, since words like *dhenu* apply to cows in general, their denotative power (*śakti*) resides precisely in qualities such as the act of milking.
Furthermore, the universal (*jāti*) residing in cows in general is well-established through inference from the exclusion of grains and so forth.
And when there is co-occurrence with words such as "cow" (*go*), the word *dhenu* functions by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Bhāṭṭa 10.2.28:
The limbs of the sheep are cooked simultaneously, whereas the limbs of the goat are cooked with delay.
Inspection is a characteristic of the clarified butter (ājya) [Vi.
3.1.4], as well as a specific function of the act of consuming.
In that context, regarding the Soma, there is the mantra beginning with "anṛcakṣasaṃ tvā" and so forth.
3|2|9. The *bhakṣānuvāka* (the liturgical formula for consuming) is to be applied according to its respective indicative marks (*liṅga*) to the acts of looking at, taking up, and proper digestion.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*).

Vārttika 3|1|12|25: In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the purpose of the looking at and the smearing of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is this: that the clarified butter should not come into contact with any other substance.
Bhāṣya 5.2.8.16: The Aveṣṭis are of two kinds in the Rājasūya: the Aveṣṭis of the elements (bhūtānām) and the Aveṣṭis of the quarters (diśām).
The Aveṣṭis of the elements are also of two kinds, beginning with "Svāhā to the Earth," and so forth.
The first six are the Aveṣṭis; those beginning with "To Agni, svāhā! are the subsequent ones.

The *Diśām Aveṣṭi* consists of eleven offerings, as follows: "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee. A cake on eleven potsherds to Indra; a bull is the sacrificial fee. An oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to the Viśvedevas; a cow that has recently calved is the sacrificial fee. A barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa; a heifer is the sacrificial fee. An oblation of cooked rice to Bṛhaspati; a white-backed animal is the sacrificial fee. He immolates a large pregnant ewe to Aditi; a speckled cow to the Maruts; a cow that has recently calved to the Aśvins. He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Pūṣan; an oblation of cooked rice to Satya; a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ of true impulsion; a bow with three arrows and a man with dry teeth is the sacrificial fee" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.9).
VI.
2.3.2. The Aveṣṭi sacrifice.

Since the unity of the sentence is established through its connection with the previously unmentioned desire for food, and since the word expressing the result—"the Kṣatriya desiring food should sacrifice"—is syntactically attached [to the injunction], just as in the cases "the Brāhmaṇa desiring food" and "the Vaiśya desiring food," there is an understanding of a distinction between the performances because the results differ even though the Kṣatriya is mentioned without distinction.
Su. P. 912. The Aveṣṭi sacrifice is twofold: internal to the Rājasūya and external to the Rājasūya.

Regarding that, in the external Aveṣṭi, it is prescribed: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed the offering to Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should offer oblation after oblation and then crush it;
if a Rājanya, [he should crush] the offering to Indra; if a Vaiśya, the offering to the Viśvedevas."

Thus, by this sentence, a different ritual action (*karmāntara*) qualified by specific attributes is enjoined, with Brāhmaṇas and others as its performers. (Vi. 2.3.2) Regarding the *Aveṣṭi*: "If he is a Rājanya, having placed the [cake] for Indra in the middle and offered the oblation, he should cause prosperity. Since this injunction—which is understood through syntactic connection (*anupaṅga*)—prescribes a performance by a Rājanya performer preceded by the naming of the [cake] for Indra, and since this is untenable without a distinct application of the ritual procedure (*tantramayoga*), a difference in the performance (*prayogabheda*) is determined.
SuPṛ 912: The Aveṣṭi sacrifice is performed even outside of the Rājasūya, and there is no difference in the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) therein.

For the arrangement of fees belonging to the Rājasūya is not obtained [here], because the fruit is indicated by the word in the singular number in the statement, "One desiring sovereignty should cause him to sacrifice with this very [rite]"; thus, there is indeed a joint performance.
The Aveṣṭi sacrifice, when performed by Brāhmaṇas and others, possesses a distinct ritual procedure (tantra) from that of the Rājasūya.
And in the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, there should be a single performance (*ekatantrya*), because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The Commentary states: In that very *rājasūya*, there is the *aveṣṭi*: "An *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds, gold is the sacrificial fee... and a *bārhaspatya* chariot with a white-backed bull is the sacrificial fee," and so forth.
Regarding this, it is considered whether there is a difference in the ritual acts (*yajña-bheda*) or whether they constitute a single performance (*tantra-bhāva*).
What is established? And in the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, there should be a single performance (ekatantrya). This is because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga) of such a unified performance.

For an indicative mark is seen that points toward the state of being a single performance: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed the offering to Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should offer each oblation and then sprinkle water; if a Rājanya, [he should place] the offering to Indra; if a Vaiśya, [he should place] the offering to the Viśvedevas."
And placement in the midst of the oblations is appropriate only when there is a totality; and totality exists only in the case of a single ritual procedure (*ekatantrya*).
Therefore, there is a single ritual procedure.
But surely the indicative mark (liṅga) is applicable; from what does its application arise? It arises from the injunction together with it:
"Now these are the Diśām-aveṣṭis...
they indeed descend again to this world."
Regarding the *aveṣṭi*: the *brāhmaṇa* and so forth concerning the *aveṣṭi*.
Regarding the *aveṣṭi*: the *brāhmaṇa* and so forth concerning the *aveṣṭi*.
And because of the singular number in the scriptural statement:
"One should cause this very Vainayaka to sacrifice.
And [in the *Ṭupṭīkā*]: "'Having placed the Bārhaspatya in the middle'—this is the word 'middle' (*madhya*)."

If other oblations as well are performed by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), then the term "middle" becomes appropriate; likewise, the expression "having offered each oblation" is only possible within a single ritual procedure. Furthermore, the singular number is heard in the scriptural injunction: "One should sacrifice with this [offering]."
If there were a separate performance [of each], then in that case the plural number would be heard in the performance.
Therefore, because the singular number is heard in the performance, it is a *tantra* (a single performance for multiple purposes).
This is due to the scriptural statement connected with desire.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, there is no commonality of the ritual procedure (*tantrabhāva*).
Why? Because the principle has already been stated [in Sūtra 1.4.12]: 'Or rather, the connection with the agent is for each separate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
As for what was said regarding the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), we reply to that as follows."
Furthermore, this [rite] is heard of even in connection with desire, as in the statement: "One should cause him who desires cattle to sacrifice with this [offering].
This is the view of that [text].
Moreover, there is no difference in the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in that case.
For the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the Rājasūya is not obtained here [in the Aveṣṭi],
because of its connection with the sacrifice [as a distinct rite].

Since the statement "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," etc., exists, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa and others is understood, according to the logic of the preceding section, as being merely a contingent occasion (nimitta).
Is it not the case that the traditional authorities (smaranti) record that "the act of a king is kingship" (*rājyam*)?

For here, what is understood is that "kingship" is the action of one already established as a "king" (*rājan*), and not that the agent of the act of ruling is a "king. Moreover, such prior establishment is absent in this context.
For the Dramiḍas employ the word "rājan" (king) only with respect to the Kṣatriya caste.
Therefore, according to the principle of the *vahirājyādhikaraṇa*, the fact that a word is well-known in only one part [of its usage] serves as the basis for determination.
As it has been said in that very same work: "Even a single instance where a word is seen to be based on a genus (*jāti*)," [is sufficient for determination].
Because that [nature] is not abandoned, there is no postulation of another cause for it.
Thus [it is said] (Vākyapadīya, p. 343). Furthermore, they also record that "the offspring of a rājan is a rājanya";
moreover, the word *rājanya* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) specifically for the Kṣatriya caste.
If, on the other hand, one were a king simply by virtue of possessing a kingdom, then even a member of another caste would be a *rājanya* for that same reason; but this is not the case.
Therefore, it follows that only a Kṣatriya is a king.
It is replied: for the Draviḍas are indeed Mlecchas.
Furthermore, it has been demonstrated in the very section concerning the *yava* and *varāha* that the usage established among the Āryas is more authoritative than that established among the Mlecchas.
Moreover, from the usage established among the Āryas, the word *rājan* is understood through the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of "one who performs the function of sovereignty.
Thus they record in their tradition: "One should not accept gifts from a king born of the Kṣatriya caste."
Thus it is said; likewise, "One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra.
Furthermore, there exists a contrary conventional understanding regarding items such as sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and clarified butter (*ājya*).
Therefore, because it is strongly established by noble usage (*āryaprasiddhi*), the word *rājan* does not denote a caste (*jāti*).

As for the traditional rule that "the function of a king is kingship" (*rājñaḥ karma rājyam*), that is intended merely to establish the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word *rājan*, which is already conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "protecting the people."

Just as the word "cow" (*go*), which is already conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for a specific form, is shown to have an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*)—namely, "it goes" (*gacchati*)—for the sake of explaining its meaning, so too this term "rājanya" is merely a recourse intended to establish the correctness of the word *rājanya*, which is already conventionally established as denoting the Kṣatriya caste.
Therefore, this word "king" (*rājan*) is based solely on the connection with sovereignty (*rājya*).

Since only those of the three higher castes (traivarṇika) have the entitlement to the Rājasūya sacrifice, and since Brāhmaṇas and others are already included within the Yāma-veṣṭi which is part of that sacrifice, the scriptural statement "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," and so forth, serves merely as a conditional occasion (nimitta).
This being the prima facie view, it is replied:
this would indeed be so if the word *rājan* were etymological (*yaugika*).
What then? This [term] denotes the Kṣatriya caste alone, because it is used by the Draviḍas for the Kṣatriya caste specifically.
But was it not said that the usage of Mlecchas is not authoritative because it contradicts the usage of the Āryas?
Not so; for the denotative power of a word established among Mlecchas can exist through other means as well, provided there is no conscious intention to apply it otherwise.
However, the application of the term to the noble ones (āryas) in another birth is justified only in a secondary sense (gauṇa), by virtue of their performing the duties of a Kṣatriya.
For Manu and others have prescribed for a Kṣatriya the protection of the realm and cities, the extraction of the sacrificial cake (valipiṇḍa), and consecration (abhiṣecana).
Therefore, when this word "rājan" is applied even to one of another caste who performs those duties, it is indeed used in a secondary sense.

This being the case, the two traditional rules—"The king's duty is the kingdom" (*rājñaḥ karma rājyam*) and "This one belongs to the king, thus he is a *rājanya*" (*rājño 'py ayam rājanyaḥ*)—will serve merely to establish the correctness [of the terms] through the conventional usage of words for both established and future meanings. As for the statements, "One should not accept gifts from a *rājanya* born of a royal lineage" and "One should not dwell in the kingdom of a *śūdra*," these should be understood as referring to the secondary (metaphorical) meaning of the word *rājan*. Therefore, since the word *rājan* denotes a Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇas and others are not eligible for the *iṣṭi* sacrifice within the *Rājasūya*, and thus they cannot be the cause [for performing it].

Therefore, by means of the usage [of the term] "Draviḍa" and so forth, another performance of the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice performed by Brāhmaṇas and others is indeed enjoined as a distinct application of that very same previous section. Now, an additional statement regarding the possibility of a specific application of the *aveṣṭi* is heard apart from the injunction for the *rājasūya* performance: "One should cause him who desires food to sacrifice with this [offering]. And since the status of being a caste (varṇa) is already established here, even though it is possible for the Brāhmaṇas and others to be mentioned as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the *rājasūya* performance, their mention as the occasion will apply to the performance of the *anādhyāya* [variant].

It is said: This would indeed be so if the statement regarding the prohibition of study (*anadhyāya*) were intended merely for the performance [of the ritual]; however, because it mentions a result, it serves to assign the ritual action to that result. Fearing the complexity of multiple purposes, and requiring its own application through another context, this word—situated within the procedure of the *Rājasūya*—takes up another [context] and, by the principle "when two [results] are connected to one [action], there is a restriction" (*ekasya tūbhayatve saṃyogapṛthaktvam*, Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.15), assigns it to the result of food (*annādya*). Therefore, its own sovereignty (*svārājya*) is the common result, while food is its specific result.
And since that [sacrifice] has as its agent a Kṣatriya who has destroyed [his enemies], the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others is for the purpose of indicating the occasion (nimitta).
Now, one might object: in the sentence concerning the Rājasūya, the king is understood as the agent of the sacrifice which is specifically qualified by the fruit of sovereignty (svārājya).
This is not so; for the agent is not connected with the fruit, nor with the action as qualified by the fruit, because grammatical factors (kārakas) require only an action (kriyā).
In the phrase "by him [the king]," when there is a requirement for a mere action from the agentive word, it is understood simply that "the Aveṣṭi sacrifice is performed with the king as the agent.

Therefore, there is no contradiction in its connection with a different result in the performance of the *svārājya* (sovereignty). Or, even if the sentence concerning food (*annādya*) is intended to refer to the performance itself, nevertheless, because the term "with this" (*etayā*)—being an instrumental case-ending—refers only to the Aveṣṭi which is proximate according to the understanding [of the context], just as in the case of the skin of the axle (*akṣatvac*), the king is also included as the agent by means of the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) derived from another scriptural authority.
In the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, because of its connection with the *rājasūya*, there is room for the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) regarding the constituent parts.

Therefore, by no means can it be argued that the mention of the Brāhmaṇa and others in the scriptural statement is merely for the purpose of indicating a causal occasion (*nimitta*). Following the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section, it is established that by means of the performance of the *iṣṭi* and so forth, a distinct alternative performance (*prayogāntara*) of the *aveṣṭi* itself, having the Brāhmaṇa and others as its performers, is being enjoined.

Nor should it be asked how, when the ritual act has already been established, the sentence concerning the Brāhmaṇas and others can enjoin multiple meanings; for, just as in the case of enjoining a qualified ritual act (*viśiṣṭa-karma-vidhi*), there is no inconsistency in enjoining a qualified performance (*viśiṣṭa-prayoga-vidhāna*) involving multiple injunctions. This being so, since the performance required as part of the Rājasūya possesses the fruit of sovereignty (*svārājya*) and is thus self-sufficient, the performance associated with the Brāhmaṇas and others—which lacks a fruit—has a need for a result. Consequently, in the passage "One should cause him who desires food to sacrifice with this [offering]," the fruit of food is connected specifically to the performance associated with the Brāhmaṇas and others.
As it has been said: "For the performance in the middle of the season is already fulfilled by [the attainment of] sovereignty itself;
therefore, since it would otherwise remain expectant, there is indeed a connection with the fruit."

Thus (Vārttika, p. 587) is the purpose: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), in the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice included within the *rājasūya*, there is the kindling of the fire by means of the *iṣṭi-havir* and other rites for Brāhmaṇas and others.

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, it is only within the performance of the *rājasūya* that the kindling of the fire by means of the *bārhaspatya* and other rites occurs in the performance of the *aveṣṭi* when performed by Brāhmaṇas and others. As for the Sūtra: "In the *aveṣṭi*, because of the connection with the sacrifice [in the injunction] 'one should sacrifice with the *iṣṭi* joined to the Brāhmaṇa and others,' the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others is made as subordinate to the ritual (*ṛtu*) in order to enjoin a different performance"—this is the meaning.
In the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, because of its connection with the ritual, it is stated that the season is the primary factor.

Having introduced the topic with the injunction, "A king desiring sovereign rule (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," there are prescribed five sacrifices named *diśām aveṣṭayaḥ* (the "conquests of the quarters"), as follows: "An *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds, gold is the sacrificial fee; an *aindra* cake on eleven potsherds, a bull is the sacrificial fee; a *vaiśvadeva* pap, a five-striped animal is the sacrificial fee; an *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa, a barren cow is the sacrificial fee; a *bārhaspatya* pap, a white-spotted animal is the sacrificial fee. Then it continues: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed the *bārhaspatya* in the middle, after each oblation has been offered, he should cause it to be consumed first; if a Rājanya, the *aindra*; if a Vaiśya, the *vaiśvadeva*," and so forth.

Regarding this, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view—reached without a specific sūtra—is that the word *rājanya*, used here in its etymological sense, is heard for the purpose of indicating a condition (*nimitta*), since Brāhmaṇas and others are also entitled to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice. To this, the author states the established conclusion (siddhānta): In the *Aveṣṭi*—that is, in the Aveṣṭi sacrifice—the passage beginning with "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" expresses the primary ritual act itself, not as a conditional occasion.
The meaning is that outside of the Rājasūya, this primary Aveṣṭi sacrifice is prescribed as a distinct ritual (*kratu*) for Brāhmaṇas and others.
The compound *ṛtupradhānam* is analyzed as follows: that ritual action which consists of speech and in which the sacrifice (*kratu*) is the primary element is "sacrifice-centered" (*ṛtupradhāna*).
However, in the case of the *rājasūya*, there is no qualification based on the connection with what is to be given by a Brāhmaṇa.
Since the *rājasūya* sacrifice is connected specifically with a Kṣatriya king, the statement regarding the Brāhmaṇa and others does not function as a conditional cause (*nimitta*).
However, this Aveṣṭi sacrifice is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas and others as being entirely outside of the Rājasūya;

for it is an established conclusion that the Rājasūya belongs only to a Kṣatriya king. Thus, in the Aveṣṭi, there is an injunction for the fruit of the knowledge of the sacrificial oblation (haviḥ) performed outside the Rājasūya.
"But because there is no division when [the sacrifice] is present, the repetition is for the sake of the fruit.
The Commentary states: "The *iṣṭi* of this [sacrifice] begins with the words, 'There is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni,' and so forth.
With reference to that, it is said: 'One desiring food should cause [another] to sacrifice with this [offering].'"

In this regard, there is a doubt: is it a separate ritual distinct from the Aveṣṭi, or is it the Aveṣṭi itself? What is the prima facie view? That it is a separate ritual, according to the reasoning already stated (2.3.12).
This being the position, we reply:
The repetition of the text for the sake of the fruit refers to the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice itself, not to a different ritual action.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
The word "with this" (*etayā*) is not able to denote a sacrifice that is distinct from the *aveṣṭi*.
This word [‘aveṣṭi’] is a designation for the ten substitutes of what is proximate.
Therefore, it is the *aveṣṭi* itself that is enjoined for one desiring food.
What is the purpose? [It is to determine whether] the oblations such as the *āgneya* and others belong to the *aveṣṭi*, or if it is a different sacrifice with its own distinct oblations.

Or rather—the opponents raise this objection: "Since even in another ritual these very same oblations (havīṃṣi) are used due to the similarity produced by this word [jyotiḥ], how can it be a sacrifice involving different oblations?
To this it is replied:
Just as in the case of the Jyotir-Ādi sacrifices, since the primary meaning of the word is possible, a figurative indication based on similarity is untenable.

Therefore, it is a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*) with a different oblation (*anyahaviṣka*). [Objection: If the sentence "with this" (*etayā*) were an injunction for a distinct ritual, then because the rules pertaining to the Soma sacrifice would apply to that ritual by the principle "but in the case of unmanifest [rites], those of the Soma [apply]," a sacrifice with Soma as the oblation (*somahaviṣka*) would have to be performed by one desiring food.
In the Siddhānta, the Aveṣṭi sacrifice consists of oblations dedicated to Agni and the other deities;
this is because of the "division" mentioned in the Sūtra, which means the distribution [of the offerings]. (This very point constitutes the Adhikaraṇa according to the Bhāṣya.)

According to the Vārttika and other authorities, however, although there is a relative strength and weakness regarding non-subordinate factors such as place (*deśa*) and so forth in the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, this is the subject matter of the *Aveṣṭy-adhikaraṇa*.

Section 722–723: The Section on the Aveṣṭi Sacrifice (Bhāṣya). Since the etymological derivation of the word "rājya" as "his work" (*tasya karma*) is possible, it is not appropriate to assume another meaning independent of that. Even without that [etymology], the usage among those residing in Āryāvarta will not be contradicted.

If, however, "rājya" (sovereignty) is first established as a conventional term for "protection," then, since the application of the word "rājan" to its agent is established according to that very capacity [of protection], there will be no contradiction in its usage among the Dravidians for Kṣatriyas who are eligible for sovereignty, even without postulating another primary meaning (*śakya*).
This is what the Commentator stated regarding the common usage of southerners.
Therefore, these two words are neither conventional (*rūḍhi*) nor etymological (*yaugika*); rather, it is appropriate to postulate that for the word "rājan," it is one or the other [of these two].
