The Vedic rite of the sacrifice for receiving a horse is also called the "sacrifice for receiving a horse."
In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, a thousand horses are prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and in the Jyotiṣṭoma, a cow is heard [to be prescribed].
(In the Upahavya, a white horse is the sacrificial fee; Bhāṣya 3.4.10.28).

The former is considered to be for the benefit of man, involving a gift that is not an auxiliary part of the ritual (*akarmāṅgabhūta*); the latter, however, is Vedic, involving a horse given as a gift that is an auxiliary part of the ritual (*karmāṅgabhūta*).
Nor is it asserted that for that [Jaloda], the acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*) is a worldly cause (*laukika-nidāna*).

Bhāṣya 3.4.10.29. Furthermore, in no Vedic collection (*vaiyākasaṃhitā*) is the worldly acceptance of a horse heard as a cause, nor is it apprehended through perception, inference, or other means of knowledge.
Regarding the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for receiving horses): when there is a plurality [of horses received], multiple *vāruṇeṣṭis* must be performed.
On this point, the *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "Therefore, the performances (*prayoga*) of these [sacrifices] are indeed distinct, but their assistance to the ritual (*kratūpakāra*) is one.
If it is argued that there is a collective unity (*sāhitya*) implied by the word 'vāruṇān' (to Varuṇa), in that case, the deity is expressed by the singular suffix."
When heard in the plural, it would effect a distinction in the sacrifice.
In that case, when there is a single acceptance of a horse, many [offerings] to Varuṇa would result;
furthermore, there is no longer any sense of collective unity.
Therefore, in another statement, this [rule] should be seen as indicating simultaneity (*sāhitya*).
In the case of accepting thousands of horses, the performance according to the sequence of sections (*kāṇṇānusamaya*) must be accepted;
however, in the case of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies.
Bhāṣya 5.2.2.3:
In the case of receiving two or three horses, since there is no contradiction regarding the two or three sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the sequence follows the purpose (*yathārthānusamaya*) itself.

However, where there is a contradiction with the primary act (*pradhāna*) in following the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*), there the sequence must follow the sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).
Śā. # The Aśvapratigraheṣṭi (The Sacrifice for Receiving a Horse).

Regarding the reception of a horse, there is a visible defect consisting of the disease of dropsy, as stated in the passage concerning Varuṇa’s seizure: "Varuṇa indeed seizes him who receives a horse.
This description of the defect pertains to a Vedic gift of a horse in relation to a future birth.
Therefore, for those who accept Vedic horses, the Varuṇī sacrifice is the expiation. (Vi. 3.4.14) # The Aśvapratigraheṣṭi belongs to the giver.

The *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice performed upon receiving a horse) is an occasional (*naimittika*) rite; being free from fault, it is an injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*) for the sake of the sacrifice. Bālakrīḍā, p. 14.
# The Aśvapratigraheṣṭi: Regarding the Vedic gift of a horse. The section concerning Varuṇa.
Because of the fault, the sacrifice should pertain to the worldly [gift]; in the Vedic case, there would be no fault, as it is preceded by scriptural injunction.
**Commentary on the Aśvapratigraheṣṭi:** "Varuṇa indeed seizes him who accepts a horse; as many horses as he may accept, so many *cuṣkala* offerings to Varuṇa should he perform.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the sacrifice apply to the acceptance of a horse in a worldly context, or in a Vedic context? Furthermore, what constitutes the worldly acceptance of a horse, and what the Vedic?
In the world, whether one is begging or not begging, if one obtains a horse or clothing, that is a worldly acceptance of a horse (*laukika-aśvapratigraha*).
There is also a Vedic [acceptance]: in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, a thousand horses are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and in the Jyotiṣṭoma, "the cow and the horse.
To this, it is replied:
Since the Vedic [rite] lacks authority, it applies to the worldly [rite].
This being the position reached, it is said:
the expiation for a fault should apply to the worldly [rite].
For a defect is indeed heard [in scripture]: "Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse.
And this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding wherever a defect exists.

That [defect] occurs in the worldly acceptance of a horse when it is given by a Śūdra or others who have committed sinful acts; however, the mention of the defect is not intended as a qualification of the specific scope of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), but rather as indicating its equality with [the expiation for other sins].
It is said:
this would be so only if it were for the purpose of removing a defect.
This ritual is the "Release from Varuṇa" (varuṇamocana); therefore, it ought to pertain to the worldly sphere, because in the world there exists the seizing by Varuṇa.
But in the case of the Vedic acceptance of a horse, that would not be so;
for by the statement of the scripture and other authorities, its performance is understood as a duty.
And if it were to result in sin from that act, its status as a duty would not be understood.
For the fruit of sin is indeed not to be performed.
But surely, even in the case of Vedic acceptance (*pratigraha*), there is sin for one who accepts from someone from whom one ought not to accept? It is said in reply:
This would indeed be so, if the sacrifice were intended for the one who receives the gift;
however, we shall explain in the subsequent section how that [intention] is actually produced by the cause.
Therefore, it is established in this section only that the sacrifice pertains to the acceptance of a horse as enjoined by the Veda.
# In the context of examining the primary relationship between Vedic and worldly matters, those causes for which there is a doubt as to whether they are worldly or Vedic are now investigated.

In this regard, from the statement "as many horses as one might receive" (*yāvato'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt*), which contains the word "as many" (*yāvat*), the receiving of horses is established as the cause [of the rite].
Therein, a doubt arises: does it apply to the mere act of receiving horses, or to the worldly act, or indeed only to the Vedic act?

"But what is the worldly acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*), or what is the Vedic one?"—this question in the *Bhāṣya* is asked by one who considers that there is no acceptance of a horse in either case, because it is prohibited in the world and because in the Veda there is no injunction using the term "acceptance" (*pratigraha*). The other [the author of the *Bhāṣya*] shows the mere essential nature [of each], independent of injunctions or prohibitions: the worldly one is the acceptance of a horse as a gift intended for human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) when not part of a ritual act (*akarmāṅga*), whereas the Vedic one is the horse given as part of a ritual act (*karmāṅga*). What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? Because it is mentioned without distinction, the object being aimed at...
Regarding the Aśvapratigraheṣṭi:
because no qualification [of the recipient] is possible, the mere acceptance of a horse is the occasion for the rite.
This being the case, there is the acceptance of worldly [offerings].

However, the Commentator, without stating the position of non-distinction (*aviśeṣapakṣa*), begins the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the meaningfulness of the word "but" (*tu*) in the Sūtra, stating "in the Vedic [rite]" because of the commonality with the Vedic and because of the absence of the need to postulate a fruit.
For when an occasional (*naimittika*) rite is enjoined, it brings along as its very condition that which is Vedic.
Because it has become self-sufficient through that very [connection], it is not connected with the worldly [result];
furthermore, a result would have to be postulated there.
In the other case, however, the assistance to the sacrifice for which it is connected will be easily postulated.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"It should apply to the worldly [rite].
Why? Because "a fault is heard [in the scripture], and that fault exists in the worldly [rite]."
In the Vedic injunction, because it is subject to a rule, a fault is indeed perceived:
"Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse. Thus, that acceptance of a horse in which there is a seizing by sin is understood as the occasion [for the rite].
And that seizing by sin is stated as something already established.
For if it were enjoined, then perhaps, by the power of this very statement, it might apply even to Vedic acts.
But it is not enjoined, because all fruits [of action] are themselves subject to injunction.
Nor is there an injunction regarding the ritual act itself in that context, because it is impossible for an enjoined ritual act to have sin as its fruit.

And here, the acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*) is not prohibited, because such a prohibition is not heard [in the text], and because [the mention of the horse] serves merely to establish a connection with the occasion (*nimitta*).

Therefore, since there is an absolute connection (*avinābhāva*), the fault lies only where there is a prohibition; and that prohibition applies to the worldly case, as in: "He does not give a maned horse, nor does he accept what has teeth on both sides."

But surely this prohibition is also heard as being general; true, but we say that by that very fact it refers to the worldly [horse-gift], because for the other [Vedic horse-gift], which is connected with a specific injunction, it is impossible to be the object of a prohibition. And therefore, because it is mentioned in conjunction with a fault (*doṣa*), the *iṣṭi* sacrifice must also have the worldly [gift] as its object. But surely, since the acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*) is the objective condition (*nimitta*) being aimed at, it cannot be qualified by a fault; thus, when the mention of the fault is intended merely to praise the enjoined *iṣṭi*, even the Vedic [gift] could be the condition.
It is said:
"I do not conceive this as a fault by way of being a qualifier;
for there is a worldly expectancy due to the capacity desired for the effect of destroying faults."
It is not the case that the acceptance of a horse is faulty because it is performed in this manner; rather, at the time of the occasion [for the rite], it is first grasped in its general form alone.

When, however, there arises an expectancy for a purpose (*prayojana*) regarding the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the sacrifice, then—since there is an absence of any other proximate element such as heaven or an auxiliary to the ritual action, and since this fault [of expectancy] is established within the same sentence and thus possesses proximity; and since it is impossible for it to be understood as a fruit in its own form because it does not depend on the ritual action—the connection with the ritual action occurs through its being removed [as a mere obstacle], while it awaits the destruction of the obstacle for the sake of its connection with the injunction as a means for the person.
And since the absence of further expectancy is established by one [statement], it is not possible to postulate another purpose.
Therefore, where there is a result consisting in the removal of a defect, it is so;
and where there is a defect, there the removal follows from the prohibition.
And that prohibition pertains to the worldly [rite]; thus, even without a specific qualification, by the force of the context, it is the cause for that very [rite] alone.
The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates this: "But this rite is the Varuṇapramocana; therefore, it ought to occur in the worldly [context]."

As for what was stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) while demonstrating the fault: "And that [sin] occurs when a worldly acceptance of a horse is performed by one who gives it to a Śūdra or similar person and is thus a performer of sinful action"; and furthermore, considering this to be the same even in the case of a Vedic [acceptance], he raised an objection—*nanu vaidike 'py apratigrāhyāt pratigṛhṇataḥ pāpagrahaṇam asti*—"surely even in the Vedic case, there is the taking on of sin for one who accepts from one who should not be accepted"—and then offered a rebuttal. (To that, it is said: This would indeed be so, if the sacrifice were for the sake of the recipient; however, it is certainly for the sake of the giver. And that [fact] is no different in the worldly case as well. For instance, regarding the worldly [case]: "But even in the worldly..."

Thus it is prohibited; how much more so, then, the taking [of gifts] from Śūdras and others? As for the fact that he is appointed by the officiating priests (ṛtvij), that may be because of his role as a reciter (mantrī); however, only giving is prescribed for the sacrifice, not receiving.

That is correct; for by the very injunction of giving, prior to the transfer of ownership to another, that [act of] acceptance remains incomplete, as it depends upon that [transfer]. Moreover, it is an established principle that in all cases, an injunction pertains to the completion of an action.

Therefore, since "he should give" is understood through the force of the context as involving a very slight renunciation, how could that which is performed— being accompanied by mantras, joined with observances, and connected as a subsidiary element in the midst of the ritual—
not be understood according to the injunction?
(The mantra "Who gave this to whom? and the rules regarding facing the east, etc., [apply].
If the acceptance (*pratigraha*) were not enjoined, how could its procedure (*itikartavyatā*) be enjoined, or why would there be a deficiency in the ritual (*karmavaiguṇya*) when it is performed?
To this we reply: "One should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests"—thus, the act of giving is enjoined.
It was solely out of greed, and because he did not know better, that he accepted their gifts.
Regarding the statement "one should not give," its counter-positive meaning is "one should accept.

A doubt arises as to whether this prescribes a human purpose (*puruṣārthatā*) when the occasion is a worldly gift of a horse made out of affection and so forth by friends and others, independent of ritual injunctions; or whether it prescribes a duty (*kartavyatā*) when it pertains to a Vedic rite that is an auxiliary part of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma or Pauṇḍarīka; or whether it applies to both.
For that purpose, there is a further doubt: does this [acceptance] serve to destroy the evil [incurred], or not?

In this regard, since there is no distinction [between the two], it might initially appear that [the expiation] applies to both; however, it is stated: "That [expiation] is to be performed where there is the effect of the removal of a fault.
That fault exists in the worldly [act], but not in the Vedic [act], because of its scriptural injunction.
Therefore, on account of the purpose, it should apply here in the worldly case. This is what is said.
If it were intended as an act for the purpose of destroying defects, it would indeed be so; however, it is not thus.
In this case, the fruit understood is liberation from the seizure by Varuṇa.
It is understood that such [liberation] does not exist through the worldly gift of a horse.
In the case of worldly acts, there is the status of being a human goal; in the case of Vedic acts, there is the status of being a subordinate element of a sacrifice.
And it is not possible for a single thing to serve both purposes, because of the resulting inconsistency.
Therefore, it must apply only to Vedic acts.
Soma: This present section proceeds by relying upon the preceding section.

Even the Prābhākara followers, though they are Vaidikas, hold that [the rite] is occasioned by a worldly event (*laukika-nimittaka*), because the study of the ritual context (*prakaraṇa*) is established without needing to assume a Vedic occasion, and because the number of horses specified in the phrase "as many horses as... is possible only in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice; thus, taking it as "it is heard in the Pauṇḍarīka," they state this as a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvā-cintā*).
In that regard, since a Vedic house-burning does not occur at the outset, it is occasioned by a worldly event; however, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is not thereby invalidated.

Since the phrase "as many horses as there are" merely states a quantity equal to the number of horses—and because the specific cause for the oblation is not intended to be restricted—the other numbers, like the plurality itself, must certainly be included; thus, it is based on its occurrence within the context of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Vi [the Vivaraṇa] states: "In the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, the ownership of the horse will be attributed to the giver.
This [sacrifice] should be performed whether the two acts of giving are worldly or Vedic."
When [the rule] applies to both without distinction, the lion [gift] should not be given;
for that would result in a worldly prohibition, and thus it would constitute an expiation.
No, for in some worldly cases, an amount equal to a water-jar has been prescribed as incomparable.
But in the Vedic context, it is heard [in scripture]; therefore, that [offering] is for her.
However, regarding the Vedic gift of a horse, there is a scriptural mention of a fault pertaining to another birth.
Consequently, in the case of a Vedic gift, that *iṣṭi* sacrifice is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Bhāṭṭa: From the beginning, it is heard in scripture: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa; he (Varuṇa) seized his own deity; he was afflicted with dropsy; he saw this four-part offering to Varuṇa; he offered it; thereupon he was indeed released from the noose of Varuṇa. Verily, Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse; as many horses as one might accept, so many four-part offerings to Varuṇa should one offer.
It will be stated in a subsequent section that the word *pratigraha* here refers to giving.

Then, in considering whether this *iṣṭi* pertains to worldly gifts given to friends, heirs, and so forth; or whether it pertains to the gift of a horse alone; or whether it pertains to the gift of a horse that is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *Agnicayana* sacrifice—the conclusion is that, because this *iṣṭi* has the gift as its object in accordance with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and because it is understood from that passage to be for the purpose of expiating a fault, and because that fault—by the statement "he does not give to one who is merely a horse-seller"—pertains to worldly gifts which are not prescribed by Vedic injunction, this *iṣṭi* also pertains to worldly gifts in accordance with that [explanatory passage].

For this is what will be explained: where the gift of a horse (*aśvadāna*) is prescribed generally without specific restriction, there one may proceed according to one's desire; or where it is not prescribed at all, such as in the case of giving to friends, kinsmen, and so forth—that is the intended scope.

Therefore, even though the gift of a horse is mandatory in cases such as the *Viśvajit* sacrifice where the gift of one's entire property (*sarvasvadāna*) is enjoined, and even if it is excluded by another sentence within that very context, this statement from another scripture functions solely as a prohibition regarding the aforementioned subject matter.

Therefore, since the fault is removed there by way of prohibition, even though the *iṣṭi* sacrifice is intended for the purpose of destroying that [fault], its scope remains restricted to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, just as the act of breaking [the vessel] is restricted to it;
thus, the destruction of the fault is the result, and the gift of a horse is the occasion (*nimitta*), rather than being a subordinate element (*śeṣa*).
For if it were so, the stated result would be untenable, and furthermore, because there is no similarity to a sacrifice that has been commenced.

If, however, it is not accepted that this [text] has the purpose of removing a defect, then—since the gift of a horse is understood to be the objective (uddeśya) through its association with the word *yāvat*—the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) associated with the word *tāvat* would necessarily become a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that [gift]; consequently, its status as a causal condition (*nimitta*) would be untenable.
For the word *yāvat* does not denote being a causal condition, but rather denotes totality (*sākalya*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the mere proximity of the action and the substance is understood through the word *yāvat* (as far as), there is no attainment of the meaning of the word *tāvat* (so far) in the case where [the action] is subordinate (*śeṣitva*), which would result in its being a common factor (*tantra*) by way of remote assistance; for in that case, since the meaning of the word *tāvat* has not been attained, it would follow that it must be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). And in the case where it is a condition (*nimitta*), since the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is accepted for every occasion, the meaning of the word *tāvat* is already attained and thus cannot be enjoined. Therefore, the understanding of it as a condition follows from the principle of parsimony in injunction (*vidhilāghava*). This same reasoning is easily available even in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thus it should not be said.

In both cases, since the status of being a *nimitta* (occasioning condition) is not obstructed—whether by following the principal act or by the view of repetition—and since the principle of *tantratva* (common performance) is established through the unity of time, the word "tāvat" necessarily implies a rule of counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).

Therefore, even though the potential suffix (*liṅ*) in "gṛhṇīyāt" may denote causality—which is synonymous with the operation of an instigator—that interpretation is still possible; thus, it is difficult to establish with certainty that [the act] is a *nimitta*.

On the contrary, because it is required, in the final conclusion (siddhānta) there would be only the status of being the subordinate element (śeṣitva). For me, however, since it serves the purpose of destroying defects, its determination [as the primary] occurs; thus there is a disparity.
And therefore, by the force of that, it would apply only to the worldly gift of a horse for one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni); such is the first position (pūrva-pakṣa).

As for the second [position]: since that defect—namely, dropsy, which is a synonym for *varuṇagraha*—is not understood through perception or other means, nor by the *Vaika-saṃhitās*, to be produced by the gift of a horse;

and if it is argued that even in the primary sense of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the term *varuṇagraha* might be used through etymological derivation (*yogavyutpatti*) based on the idea that "it seizes (*vṛṇoti*) sin," then why could the same term *varuṇagraha* not also be applied to Vedic gifts, since they too are somehow seen to result in unhappiness due to the act of relinquishing?

Because [the expiation] is enjoined by the phrase "he indeed [purifies him]" (*sa evainaṃ*) through the pleasure of the gods [attained] by means of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice and so forth, and because there is no evidence that this [expiation] is intended solely for the removal of defects, it cannot be restricted to purely worldly matters; rather, since it would involve an unwarranted restriction of the scriptural statement, it applies to all cases.

Nor can it be argued that only what is prescribed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word "one should take" (*gṛhṇīyāt*) is brought to mind, because a prescription cannot serve as a qualifier for that which is already the subject of the injunction.
Therefore, it applies to all cases.

This being the case, just as in the *Jayādi-naya* (3.4.13) it was established that the postulation of a result applies only to worldly acts and not to Vedic ones, and likewise that even though the fire has been established, its function as the motivator for the *tapaṇayana* and other rites exists only here and not elsewhere—due to the resulting disparity (*vairūpya*), one must accept a self-limitation in accordance with the parsimony of injunctions (*vidhilāghava*), just as in the case of the *kāma*-śruti texts.
Therefore, the object of reference (*uddeśya*) is specifically the gift of a horse connected with the possessor of the fire (*agnimant*).

Moreover, by the principle of the *pratardana* [section] (3.1.12), when there is an inquiry into the purposefulness of the gift of a horse (*aśvadāna*) as a subsidiary (*śeṣitva*), it is inappropriate to assume subsidiariness for a sacrifice that is not otherwise presented.
Therefore, this sacrificial offering (*iṣṭi*) is not a subsidiary of the gift of a horse, but rather its occasion (*nimitta*).
Or, even if that were the case, this offering pertains only to the gift of a horse that is connected with the possession of fire (*agnimattva*).
Maṇḍana: "In the Vedic Aśvamedha, there is the Agniṣṭi.
Śaṅkara: "And also in the Aśvadāna. [Maṇḍana:
"The ritual does not end with this much."
16. In the Aśvapratigraheṣṭi, there is a division of the potsherds into groups of four for each sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
And the potsherds (*kapāla*) are equal in number to the [cakes], like the jars (*kumbhī*).

Commentary: In the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice, it is heard that there are Varuṇa-cakes on potsherds of unspecified number: "As many horses as one might receive, so many Varuṇa-cakes on potsherds should he offer.

In this regard, it is deliberated: should the baking of all [the cakes] be performed upon a single set of potsherds arranged lengthwise, or should there be a separate set of four potsherds for each individual cake?
What is established? That the potsherds are common [to all], just like the cooking-pot (*kumbhī*) in the case of the *prājāpatya* offerings.
The meaning is that, just as the cooking-pot is common to the *prājāpatya* offerings, so too the potsherds are common to the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) which are equal in number.
What is the reason? Because in this way, the simultaneous performance (*sahatva*) will be maintained, and all [the cakes] will be consecrated upon four potsherds each.
Or rather, there is a separate set for each primary offering, as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
Commentary: There is a division of the four potsherds for each sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*);
thus it is performed according to the model sacrifice.

In the archetype of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the potsherds are distinct for each sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); here too, they must be so understood in order to favor the extended injunction (codaka).
Moreover, if the potsherds were to constitute a single common element (tantra), not even a single puroḍāśa would be prepared on four potsherds;
rather, all would be baked upon three sets of potsherds.
In that case, the word "kapāla" would be sublated;
therefore, there is a distinction. And this would be intended by all.
Commentary: And this is heard [in scripture]: "He spreads out the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) made of barley-meal.
That cannot be accomplished if there is a single common performance (tantra);
therefore, there is also a distinction [between the rites].
Soma: In this case, since there is an absence of even the *pakta* (the cooking vessel), it is said that there is no distinction; thus, the connection [of the argument] is established.

Since, by means of the hands as in the *adhvara* sacrifice, the very *kapālas* (potsherds) can serve as the instruments for cooking through their constituent parts, one need only achieve the required length with parsimony (*lāghavena*), and not procure other *kapālas*.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "he spreads out the *yāvaka-kapāla*," because the measurement of a *hasta* (hand) must be specified in terms of circumference (*pariṇāha*) even when the length (*āyāma*) is intended, the requirement for circumference is justified. This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Since, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the potsherds (*kapāla*) are directly the means of accomplishment, here too they must be accepted in that very same way and not through their constituent parts. There is no evidence for restricting the statement, "He spreads the sacrificial cake upon the potsherds" (*yāvakapālaṃ prathayati*), to the mere measurement of its circumference. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [The commentary] says: "Is there a difference in the four parts of the ritual procedure (*tantra*), or rather, is it due to the greatness of that [cake]?"

The state of being a *kumbhī* (pot) is based on the principle of *tantratā* (commonality); thus, there would not be a separate [performance] for each, as in the case of the primary sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

12. Bhāṭṭa: In the passage "as many horses as one might receive," when the *pratigraheṣṭi* (sacrifice upon receiving) is performed by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application) for the gift of two horses, that is not [considered] the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* [performed for each individual horse]. This concludes the section on the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*.
The singularity of the *puroḍāśa* cake is indeed to be enjoined there, because it is expressed by the word itself.

However, regarding the fourfold number of potsherds (*kapāla*), since the specific measure of potsherds was not prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and since length and other such qualities were also mentioned, it is logical that the whole potsherd (*avayavin*)—just as the *arghya* water and so forth are conveyed through the hands—is an instrument (*sādhana*) by way of its parts (*avayava*). Therefore, there is no difference [between the two cases].

This being the position reached: since it is improper to resort to an indirect means (*paraṃparā*) when a direct means (*sākṣāt-sādhanatva*) is possible, and since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) only direct instrumentality was intended—and thus resorting to an indirect means here is untenable—furthermore, because the earthen pot-sherd (*kapāla*) for the barley-meal (*yāvaka*) is already obtained from the archetype, and because there is no evidence to sublate the number already understood by general rule even regarding the potsherds qualified by the phrase "so many Vāruṇas," there is indeed a distinction (*bheda*) among the potsherds.
Consequently, the sacrifice is performed through a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) with as many four-potsherd sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) as there are [Vāruṇas].
Maṇḍana: "There is no commonality (tantratā) among the potsherds. Śaṅkara: "In the horse-sacrifices, there is a single potsherd. This is the distinction between the two.

In the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, the legal determination of the transaction and the authority of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) will be discussed; he will also state that this [act] constitutes the status of being a priest (*ṛtvij*).
Therefore, it is possible to assert that even the act of giving, though belonging to the sacrificer, belongs to the priest.

Alternatively, when there is doubt as to whether [the action] should take place during the master’s ritual or during the reception of guests, the meaning of the sūtra is that it applies where the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—consisting of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*)—is clearly established.

(Regarding this, *Sudhā*, p. 1848: although the words *vā* and *jñā* from the two concluding sūtras of the preceding section are separated [from this context], they are required and thus supplied by *anupaṅga*. Thus, when there is doubt as to whether it pertains to the act of giving—which is an auxiliary of sacrifice—or to the priestly work which is not an auxiliary, [the sūtra says] "or rather, for the master" [*athavā svāmī*] [i.e., *athavā svāmikarmātithyayoḥ*].)

How, then, is it understood through an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that this refers to the activity of the sacrificer? This is explained: "The capacity of the ritual action is one intended indicative mark;
another is the capacity of the sentence, which is discerned by examining the preceding and following [context].
This has been almost established by the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*), namely, that here the fruit belongs to the giver.

For when it is determined that [the horse-sacrifice] is indeed a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the ritual act involving the acceptance of a horse, then— since subsidiaries and primary rites must share the same place, time, and agent (1.2.12)— whoever is the performer of the sacrifice (*kratu*), by that very person this [horse-sacrifice] must also be performed. And whoever is the performer of the sacrifice, he is the giver of this [horse], according to the principle that "the purchase [of priests] is the duty of the master" (3.8.19).
Therefore, there must undoubtedly be the status of a giver here.
For this is the capacity of a subsidiary: that being performed by the same agent as the principal, it is able to provide assistance, not when it has a different agent.
Consequently, just like the principal, the other [subsidiary] must also be performed by the officiating priest (ārṣejya), and not by the sacrificer (yājamāna).

Even though this is established, the subsequent section (adhikaraṇa) is commenced merely for the purpose of dispelling the confusion and doubt caused by the contradiction between the opening and the conclusion of the passage.
And the power of such a concordance between the opening and the conclusion of the passage is precisely this: that it enjoins the giving [of the horse].

For this passage does not consist merely of the words, "As many horses as he may accept, so many horse-keepers he shall offer to Varuṇa"; rather, it has another opening as well, beginning with, "Prajāpati led a horse to Varuṇa," and so forth.
And it has been stated that this [cognition] establishes the giver here.
Now, one might object: "Is this not improper? Since the cognition of the contrary location is stronger, it must be sublated.
This is not so.
Why? Because, "Since it is characterized by direct scriptural statement (śruti), it is set aside by the injunctive portion (vidhyuddeśa) regarding the act [of giving].
In that case, the injunctive portion is not assumed with respect to the recipient.
If the injunctive portion here were indeed concerned with the recipient, then no inquiry would even be undertaken; however, this [injunctive portion] is not of the nature of a definition.
Why? Because: "In the case of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the assumption of an injunction (*vidhi*) occurs after them;
[but] even when there is no relationship between principal and subordinate, another distinction arises based on the prior or posterior utterance of the injunction and the explanatory passage.

In every respect, according to the principle "the primary [is followed] because of the prior injunction, as in the world" (Jaimini 1.2.18), and by the logic of the section on *śruti* and *liṅga*, the prior cognition—being unopposed and not interrupted by a second cognition arising subsequently—establishes itself with authority.

Furthermore, when a subsequent cognition arises regarding an object that contradicts a prior cognition, it is unable to arise in any form other than one that conforms to that contradiction; thus, it also undergoes a change in its nature.

Therefore, in this case, disregarding the distinction created by a mere fragment of injunction (*vidhi*) or explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and because the opening and concluding passages would have contradictory meanings if they were taken as referring respectively to the giver and the recipient—since it is impossible for them to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) in that state, and since if they were separate both would be incomplete in meaning and thus subject to the contingency of pointlessness due to their mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) without any other assumed injunction or eulogy—when a common subject matter is established by force of the resulting single syntactical unit, the latter position, which was previously determined to belong to the giver in a state free from contradiction, is understood through the assumption of a figurative application (*gauṇa-vṛtti*) to refer to the giver, even though the status of the recipient remains unobtainable.
Furthermore: "In this view, the majority will possess a common characteristic;
otherwise, everything previously stated would be inconsistent.
For it would be inconsistent that Prajāpati gave himself—his own deity who had become the object of Varuṇa's worship—to Varuṇa directly. (12.2.7.22)
For my part, however, it must somehow be understood that the prompter's activity itself is what is being enjoined.
As for the claim that an injunction is more powerful than an explanatory passage (arthavāda), that is true; it is the injunction that is stronger.
But only that which is an injunction is strong.

But it is not a rule that [the result accrues] to the recipient. For in every sentence, whatever is not expressed by the preceding words but is required is supplied from the subsequent words, and not anything else, even if it is implied.

For example, in the expression "having returned from the *sattra*," just as in the case of the suffix *-kvā*, many agents who have completed the subsequent action (*udavasāna*) are understood to be mutually independent; because they are intended to be expressed [as such], their association is not yet established. Thus, even though there is an injunction in the passage "they should sacrifice with the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*," the state of having many combined agents will remain unestablished because it was not required by the preceding [text] (10.2.13–14). In the same way, here, by the passage beginning "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa," the liberation of the giver from Varuṇa—[is established].

When a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is understood as being praised by virtue of its being a cause, then it is determined that this very sacrifice alone is enjoined, and nothing more than that is to be said of it. Consequently, the person who is the subject of the injunction—having turned away from the objects of previous injunctions through the inference of the injunction—seeks only that which is being stated, and nothing further. And the capacity of both the injunctive statement (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is equal in making known their respective objects.

As for the fact that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) lacks injunctive power, only that much is indeed accepted from the injunctive source; however, it does not follow that everything contained therein is intended to be enjoined, because it is not required.

Therefore, since the wearing of the mark (*liṅga-dhāraṇa*) cannot occur without a verbal root in the sense of an occasion (*nimitta*), it should be understood that wherever a root is employed, the act of "taking" (*gṛhṇāti*)—which implies the activity of a giver—is included as "he takes [it] having been prompted."
Otherwise, since it was heard thus regarding the giver alone in a former age, the statement "therefore, even today, how should this be performed by the recipients" would be entirely inconsistent.
Therefore, there is no contradiction, as the giver is understood here through the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) that has been set forth.
This has been explained in detail under the sūtra: "On account of the Vedic text, there should be the qualification of the caste" (3.1.1.2).
But surely, since this has already been covered by that [previous discussion], it need not be commenced here.
True; this matter is largely settled.

However, this is undertaken again in order to remove the confusion produced by another commentary—which, due to its misinterpretation of the Sūtra, establishes the conclusion that the recipient [is the owner]—as well as for the sake of further clarification.

Otherwise, indeed, these two sūtras could have been explained even in the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*). Suppose someone, thinking that just as in the case of the *ālambha* (touching) and *nirvapaṇa* (offering), because there is no distinction between the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and the *pratīṣṭi* in the world and the Veda, [the status of] being a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*) is not certain when there is ambiguity, might say: "Even in the sacrificial context, this [status] is not enjoined; for when there is a difference in the ritual acts, there is no cause for a definitive determination. To him, the answer is: "That [act] would belong to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) by virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*)."

That which is the recitation for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should apply there, because optionality itself constitutes a specific indicative mark (*liṅga*), and even that which is employed as a condition (*nimitta*) is indeed an indicative mark.
For it is observed that in Vedic usage, "acceptance" (*pratigraha*) is designated by the term *liṅga*, whereas this is not the case in worldly usage.
Alternatively, since this very point has already been established above without a formal sūtra, the resolution should be described by treating both sūtras as a single unit.
Since that which is not enjoined is worldly, the cognition [of it] does not occur there as a basis (nimitta); this should be applied just as before.

In this regard, one might think: "How is it that this single thing, while being Vedic, becomes a basis, and likewise how could it also be possible for it to be worldly? To this he says: "This is not so. Why? Because of the difference in action (karmabheda).

For indeed, there is a distinction between ritual acts (karma-bheda) arising even from the differentiation of place and so forth, caused by one act being enjoined after another has been enjoined; by means of this, the determination of the occasioning cause (nimitta-vyavasthā) will be possible.
Furthermore, because it is prohibited, the worldly [act] simply does not exist according to the Vedic doctrine.
Therefore, that alone which possesses an undoubted existence serves as the occasioning cause.
Furthermore, its recitation is not necessarily for the sake of the *nimitta* (the occasion), because it culminates in the *saṃgraha-dharma* (the duty of collection).
Therefore, since this procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belongs to this very gift, it will be understood as Vedic by virtue of its purposefulness.
Consequently, there is no connection with that which is not enjoined.
Thus, even though such an interpretation is possible, a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) is established because of its distinct purpose.

Furthermore, since the word "takes" (*gṛhṇāti*) has never before been observed in the sense of the instigating action (*prayojaka-kriyā*), it must be interpreted through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), creating a firm misconception; for the term is applied figuratively to the instigator’s activity just as it is to the one being instigated.
Alternatively, the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) exists even for the causal agent (*hetu-kartṛ*).

In this context, when causality (*hetutva*) is intended to be expressed, the suffix *ṇic* is employed even when the operation of the one possessing the cause (*hetumat*) is what is intended to be expressed.

When there is an intention to express merely the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), it can be said that "he receives" (*pratigṛhṇāti*) even without the suffix *ṇic*, provided he accomplishes the acceptance of the horse in some manner.

For example, in the expression "he plows with six ploughs" (*ṣaḍbhir halaiḥ kṛṣati*), although the verb *kṛṣ* denotes the act of scratching or furrowing, it refers to the operation of the instigator (*yojaka*) because the word "six ploughs" lacks the capacity [to denote the action itself] and because the possibility of a scratcher exists.
Indeed, a single agent cannot clearly execute [the action] alone.

Therefore, he who is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the six executors (*vilekhitr*) through their arrangement is said to be the agent even with respect to that [action of] scratching by means of their activity. Thus, the root *gṛh* (to seize), functioning by the force of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), is made to refer to the activity of the instigator. For verbal roots are shown to have manifold expressive capacities in the section on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*) as expressing both the activity of the one being impelled (*prayojya*) and the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*).
Due to the presence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*), in some cases a certain power (*śakti*) is manifested even apart from what is commonly established.

Therefore, the word "receives" (*pratigṛhṇāti*) is employed in the sense of "giving" (*dadāti*); thus, the root *dā* [is understood] as referring to the giver. This being the case, some raise an objection.

For instance, among the Maitrāyaṇīyas, in the passage "This horse is received," since the beginning and the conclusion are of a single form, it is clearly understood that the sacrifice belongs to the receiver. And regarding that, they say: "In matters of interpretation, we are indeed stronger; if, however, we are defeated by another scriptural statement, what can be done?
But we perceive that [the other statement] is without any valid basis.

How so? "If there were another sentence when the recipient is clearly mentioned, then [the sacrifice] would belong to him as well; however, it is precluded by that [sentence] which serves the desired purpose.
Thus, by the Taittirīya branch passage cited as an example, the sacrifice is established as belonging to the giver.
It cannot be set aside by another principle, nor by another statement.
Even if there were a statement to the contrary, because it would involve both an injunction and a prohibition, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), but not a rejection of the accepted principle.

First of all, that which prescribes the recipient, even without being a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action due to the specific opening statement, follows the meaning of the preceding sentence; therefore, by that [prescription] as well, it would apply to the giver alone. However, if [the prescription] were independent and based on the act of receiving, then it would apply to the recipient; thus, both [the giver and the recipient] would perform it. In that case, since the [act] residing in the recipient lacks the status of being a subordinate part of the ritual action, it would be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and consequently, it would occur even in worldly transactions.

However, for one who, while adhering to this sūtra—"it should belong to the officiating priest"—interprets even the preceding statement as referring only to the recipient, it must be explained: since the acts of acceptance lack the status of being auxiliary to the ritual (*karmāṅga*), they are equal in that they are conceived as serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) for both the priests and others; thus, since they would apply even to worldly transactions, by what authority is it stated that "it is perceived in the case of his horse"?
Therefore, it is established that [the property] belongs to the giver alone.

Śa: Is this sacrifice for the independent agent who receives the gift, or for the causal agent who gives it? To that end, it is considered which is more authoritative when there is a conflict between the introductory statement (*prakrama*), the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*). In this regard, the prima facie view being that it belongs to the recipient, the following is stated: "Because it has not yet encountered a contradiction, the explanatory passage is to be taken according to its literal sense;
whereas, because it would contradict what is established by logic, the term *viśvajit* must be understood through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."

The words *ṛk* and so forth are seen to be used frequently even in the Veda, whereas [the word] *ṛtvij* is nowhere seen in the sense of the act of giving; therefore, it cannot be explained as referring to that [act]. This section (*adhikaraṇa*) is for the purpose of resolving this specific doubt.

Alternatively, other commentators, following the rule "That [rite] would belong to the *ṛtvij* because of the indicative mark" (*sā liṅgād ārtvije syāt*), have relied upon the sacrifice being for the sake of the recipient; to demonstrate that the sacrifice is for the sake of the giver—so that the recipient may not be distinguished [from others]—the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) composed this separate section.

(The meaning of the two sūtras is as follows: Even in the case of a sacrifice (*yajña*), this act of giving (*dāna*) is not enjoined when there is a distinction (*bheda*) for the sake of determination.

Therefore, it should apply to both cases—this is the objection. (In the *Soma* sacrifice and the *Vāruṇī-iṣṭi*, this act of giving is not enjoined even in the context of a sacrifice; that is to say, it does not constitute a cause for [the application of] the rule regarding the gift.
When there is a "distinction," that is, when there is a distinction between worldly and Vedic giving—or, in other words, when there are two types of giving.)
The meaning is that since it is impossible to determine [the rule] even by way of its Vedic character, it would apply to both cases.

The answer to that is: "On account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), because of the commonality of being Vedic, it should apply to the Vedic gift within the context of the *ārvinja* (the priestly assembly)," meaning it belongs to the Vedic gift.

(The meaning of the sūtra *na acoditam* in the section on Soma is as follows: the ritual act consisting of the *vāruṇī* sacrifice is not enjoined for the giver, because there is a distinction between giving and receiving, and this [sacrifice] is connected with receiving.)
This discussion has arisen as a secondary consequence of the primary topic concerning Soma.
(It was stated that rites such as Jaya are auxiliary to Vedic rituals;
by that logic, it follows as a corollary that the Vāruṇī sacrifice is also [required] only for the Vedic gift of a horse.)

Furthermore, it might follow that the sacrifice belongs to the recipient alone; thus, one should understand this as a case of "the relevant and the incidental. In the Maitrāyaṇīya recension, although there is no corresponding passage, in the Taittirīya recension, by the force of the introductory statement (*upakrama*), the conclusion is reached that the sacrifice belongs to the giver. As stated in the Viṣṇu-smṛti: "As many [cows] as he may accept, so many sacrifices must be performed—whether for the recipient or the giver; let the word of the Veda be followed according to the rule."
Because there is no contradiction in the meaning [of the text], the sacrifice (iṣṭi) heard in the scripture belongs to the giver, Prajāpati;
therefore, it leads the injunction back to the giver himself.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: this sacrifice is not for the receiver, but rather for the giver alone.

Since in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of the introductory section, Prajāpati—the primary agent—is referred to by the word "he" (*saḥ*), it is understood from the meaning that Prajāpati himself, having given [himself] to Varuṇa, attained his own deity, Varuṇa, who exists in the form of the recipient, in the form of water; for in that very way, they both arrive at the state of being the agent of the sacrifice for each other's sake. This is because, just as in the case of the term *udait*, the word for the recipient in the concluding section functions as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the giver.

Alternatively, since the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) directly denotes both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) in common, and because a direct application is possible, even though the instigator is not explicitly mentioned, he is implied here in order not to contradict the opening statement. Thus, from the understanding of the meaning "whoever should cause him to do it," the sacrifice belongs to the giver even without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor does this result in redundancy; for in the Maitrāyaṇīya recension, this very [passage] occurs in the sequence of the recipient, as in "this horse is being received.

Since there is a possibility of doubt—namely, that because of ignorance, the figurative indication might apply only to the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) situated at the beginning despite its location there—the sacrifice belongs to the giver.

In the case of those performing the sacrifice in another hall (*śālā*), even though the sacrifice is understood [to belong] to the recipient, there is no sublation of the donor’s sacrifice upon this recitation [of the *Taittirīya*], because there is an absence of evidence for a strong sequence (*prabalakrama*) in this hall, which would otherwise necessitate a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, since the sequence located at a distance is merely restated (*anuvāda*) and does not result in the status of the object being enjoined, this [text] functions as an injunction for a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Moreover, due to the absence of names and other such indicators, the principle applicable to different Vedic branches (*śākhāntara*) does not apply here (2.4.2).

Furthermore, it is possible to explain even the opening statement of the *Maitrāyaṇīya* recension in accordance with the intention of the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) by following the donor's initiative.
Moreover, the position that this sacrifice belongs to the recipient alone— which accords with the ancient commentaries—
is also implied in the *Vārttika* and is approved by the ritualists (*yājñika*).
Likewise,

in the section concerning the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for the acceptance of a horse) at 7.4.1, regarding the *Adhigaveṣṭi* in the Aśvamedha, the Bhāradvāja-sūtra begins with "There is a sacrifice upon acceptance," whereas Ālekhana says, "[It applies] upon the acceptance of a horse," [and further states that] "in the case of acceptance from an officiating priest (*ārvin*), it should belong to the sacrificer alone."

Satyāṣāḍha: "In the case of accepting horses, the priests perform the Vāruṇī sacrifice; for as many horses as one might accept, so many cakes on eleven potsherds dedicated to Varuṇa should he offer. When there is one horse in excess, *imaṃ me varuṇa* and *tattvā yāmi* are the invitatory and offering verses. Maṇḍana: "From the introductory statement, that [sacrifice] belongs to the giver of the horse.
Śaṅkara: "The sacrifice is declared to belong to the giver."

*Although the cessation of the sacrifice is the occasion (*nimitta*) for the *pṛṣadājya* [offering] when it occurs during the *sattra*, nevertheless, according to the principle of the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *sattra* in the prima facie view (Bhaṭṭa 10.2.11).

Regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for touching the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there arises an inquiry as to whether the touching is enjoined or not. In this deliberation, based on the context (*prakaraṇa*) and by means of the principle of the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, the conclusion of the prima facie view is that since the touching is enjoined, this occasional expiation is prescribed as an auxiliary of the ritual act because it is contingent upon that [touching].*

If, however, one should suspect here a distinction from the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for receiving horses) due to the additional prohibition of touching (*sparśaniṣedha*) and the mention of defects (*doṣapādāna*), [we reply]: in the section on the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, the conclusion was stated in accordance with the introduction (*upakrama*). [Objection: Even in the section on the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, the determination is that the sacrifice is not for the giver as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the ritual action established in the preceding section, because that would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

For in the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), having taken for granted the point established in this present section—that the sacrifice belongs to the giver—the determination of its status as a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅgatva*) was made.

If, indeed, the sacrifice were for the recipient (*pratigrahītṛ*), then, in order to establish his entitlement (*adhikāra*), a result directed toward him would have to be postulated; how then could it be a constituent part of a ritual whose fruit accrues to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)?
Therefore, it is shown in the *Bhāṣya* and other works that this present section is commenced precisely because it has been established that the sacrifice belongs to the giver.

1|12. By the principle of the section on the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice (Soma. 2|1|16), it is logical that only a Vedic [rite] may have its purpose fulfilled through a Vedic auxiliary procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Since, according to the method stated in the section on the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, a Vedic procedure is more readily available for application, it is appropriate to adopt it rather than a worldly one.
This is the *aśvabhṛtanyāya*.

Just as there is no determination of the actual fact in the case of "Whose horse is this? He whose is the servant," or "Whose servant is this? He whose is the horse," so it is here as well. [The proponent] is reckless. ※ In the phrase "One should sacrifice the horse" (*aśvam ālabheta*), if one disregards the distinction between the non-agent (*akāraka*) and the object (*karman*), and takes the letter *la* from the word *medhya* (sacrificial), it results in the meaning: "One should sacrifice that which is one's own wealth, namely the poor man."
If, however, the *t* were palatal (*tālavya*), the word would denote a horse;

therefore, because of this doubt, the meaning of that sentence would remain unestablished. [Response: No, for according to grammar, from the root *añj* with the suffix *vap*, by means of an *uṇādi* suffix, the palatal nature of the *t* is determined.
Therefore, the scripture enjoining the seizing of a horse is authoritative. (Vi. 1.3.9, according to the Guru’s view).
The Aśvamedha is well known for its large sacrificial fees.

"His *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice consists of seventeen [stomas]; for its *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, he gives gold weighing twelve *mānas*; twenty-four *mānas* for the *prāyaṇīyā*, and two times twenty-four *mānas* for the *ātithyā*," and so on, ending with "two hundred and eight *mānas* for the omentum (*vapā*) of the barren cow (*vaśā*). By this passage, the giving of abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is described. For therein, starting from twelve *mānas* for the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the *prāyaṇīyā*, the *ātithyā*, the six *upasads*, the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, the three recitations during the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, the *udayanīya*, and the *anubandhya* animal sacrifice, the sacrificial fees are stated to double progressively.
Parimala: 3.4.116. *Vas*. Some who are studying the Aśvamedha bring fodder for the horse; others do not; still others perform other religious duties (*dharma*).
The Aśvamedha and such rites expect assistance from some [regarding the fodder] and do not expect it from others.

*In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, during the *adhiguvaiṣa* rite, for the purpose of not disclosing the horse's purchase price (*aśvavachkīyatva*), when following the alternative view of not employing the specific mantras (*vaiśeṣikamantra*), there is a collective statement regarding the eighty-six [cows] for the sake of the three animals: "This is their large purchase price."*

The mantras for the twenty-four [substitutes] are to be applied as counter-substitutes (*pratidhenu*). Because of the specific statement regarding the horse, there are twenty-four [of them]; this is the distinctive feature.
Commentary: There exists the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
In that context, the Savanīya animal consists of a horse, a hornless goat, and a gayal.
However, in the archetype—the Agniṣomīya sacrifice—there is the scriptural statement: "There are twenty-six ribs of this [animal].
That [statement] is extended here by means of the general rule (codaka).

"One should not say 'twenty-four,' but one should say 'twenty-six'.

Thus, it attains the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). That single syntactical unity would be sublated if it were intended to convey a number; for it is improper to enjoin multiple meanings when the injunction of a single meaning is possible.
For in that case, there would be a greater assumption of what is not perceived (*adṛṣṭa-kalpanā*).
Therefore, the statement should be made according to what is already established.
(According to the opinion of the Vārttikakāra, this constitutes a separate topical section [*adhikaraṇa*] by means of the eighteenth and subsequent sūtras.)

The other replies: "For this is not enjoined" (in the Bhāṣya).

That [quantity] cannot be enjoined because it is already obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), owing to the connection with the particle *eva*.

It applies to whatever else is contextually relevant as a counter-correlative (such as the mantra "twenty-four skins"). Thus, since the other [the mantra] would necessarily be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), the injunction of the prohibition of the *ṛc* verses follows because of its primary status.

"Otherwise, that thunderbolt of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [did] due to an error in the accent" (Pāśupata Śikṣā 52).

And because the *ṛc*s have been enjoined by another injunction, this statement is a specific (*vaiśeṣika*) one.

Since the *ṛc*s themselves are excluded, and that being so, the number twenty-six— which is obtained through the general rule (*codaka*)— is stated as "one should say [twenty-six]."

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: There are twenty-four and six specific [offerings] for the horse; therefore, only the specific [offering] should be performed for the whole, because of the scriptural statement that "in this context, the specific [offering] is prescribed.
Bhāṣya: "Is the prohibition 'not twenty-four' fixed or not?

By the logic of the "instrument" (*karaṇanyāya*), it must be spoken of as a compound consisting of the word "twenty-six" alone.
In that context, however, [the animals are] the hornless goat (*tūpara*) and the gayal (*gomṛga*).

The function of the particle *eva* is to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyāvṛtti*), which constitutes its defining characteristic. Since there are twenty-six paths for each individual [element] and thirty-four for the horse, by taking these together through a compound, one arrives at eighty-six paths; thus it should be understood that "these have three speakers. Alternatively, it is precisely by taking this [compound] that the elision of the object to be restated (*anuvādya*) is established.

(It should be understood that all this concerning the Traidhātavī in the Aśvamedha—namely, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and the *yājyā*—is cited everywhere as an illustration for the purpose of the logical principle (*nyāya-prayojana*). In the Aśvamedha, it is taught: "The Traidhātavīyā [Dīkṣaṇīyā] sacrifice is performed.

If a duty of this kind is prompted solely by the supreme apūrva, then, being bound to a specific benefit for that [apūrva], it will apply to the Traidhātavīyā, which belongs to the same class of effects.

Now, if it were preceded by the *āgneya* and *vaiṣṇava* [offerings], then this would not be the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the *āgneya* and *vaiṣṇava*; thus, in that case, it would not be connected with those properties in the *traidhātavīya* *apūrva*.

Bhāṣya 9.1.2.3, Section 2. [Objection: According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the statement "the *traidhātavīya* becomes the *dīkṣaṇīyā*" means that, having taken over the function of the *āgneya* and *vaiṣṇava*, it is joined with their properties, just as wild rice (*nīvāra*) is joined with the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the ritual properties (*dharma*) are prompted by the *āgneya* and *vaiṣṇava* [offerings], and there is no new transcendental result (*apūrva*) in the *traidhātavīyā* sacrifice. Furthermore, one transcendental result does not take on the properties of another transcendental result. Thus, this proposed purpose is untenable.
"How is it that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] belongs to the three worlds (*traidhātavīyā*)?"—such is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two [terms].
In that case, if both words were taken in their primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*), then coreferentiality would not be possible.
Therefore, one of the two words here must be used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*).

In this context, because of its priority and its lack of conflict, the term *traidhātavī* is primary; whereas the term *dīkṣaṇīyā*, being subsequent and thus subject to conflict, indicates its own auxiliary function (*upakāra*).
Once that [auxiliary function] is indicated, the *traidhātavī* is enjoined [in the sense that "the *traidhātavī* becomes the performer of the function of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*"].
And being so enjoined, because it has taken over that function, it acquires the properties (*dharma*) of that [function].
Even in the Siddhānta, just as the *saṃlavī* being enjoined for the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) obtains its properties (such as *añjana* and so forth),
therefore the acquisition of properties is equal in both positions.
Now, it might be argued that by the statement, "The *traidhātavīyā* becomes the *dīkṣaṇīyā*," [the properties of] the well-known *traidhātavīyā* [are transferred].
That function [of the *nairṛta* offering], having been set aside, is prescribed for the function of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] (and here no new *naidhātavyā* is prescribed).

And that [function of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*] will accomplish its purpose through its own established properties and its own *apūrva* (the *apūrva* resulting from the *naidhātavyā*), and it will not adopt the properties of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if the function of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* were to be performed by the *traidhātavī* exactly as it is already established, then it would accomplish that function through its own specific characteristics (*dharmas*), because those characteristics are well-known. On the other hand, if it does not proceed [in that way], then all the more so do its own characteristics belong to it.

Furthermore, when the external rule is prompted by the primary transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*), the *āgneya* and *vaiṣṇava* offerings served as the specific means (*dvāra*); and that means is absent here.
Therefore, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no external restriction.
[Objection: But by this logic, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) would not apply to wild rice (*nīvāra*). [Reply:
It is said:
It is true that the *viśiṣṭa* (qualified) [grain] is declared to be the means (*dvāra*) for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

However, this is the distinction: rice-grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) do not assist in the visible [result], whereas wild rice (*nīvārāḥ*) are seen to accomplish that [same] function; therefore, in that case, the application of the rule to them is appropriate with respect to that function.
Here, however, the means is invisible (*adṛṣṭa*); there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) that the *traidhātavī* sacrifice functions in that same way toward that result.
Alternatively, this purpose is already discarded from afar (thus the previously stated position is accepted).
How so? The *traidhātavī* sacrifice is enjoined here exactly as it arose [elsewhere]; for by means of the word, that very same [sacrifice] is brought back to mind.
Due to the absence of a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), there is no separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) either.
Therefore, the performance should be exactly as that which was previously understood;

and even if it were a different ritual action (*karmāntara*), one would nevertheless adopt the characteristics (*dharma*) of the *traidhātavīyā* sacrifice by virtue of its name, and not those of the *aṣṭakā* and other rites— this is discussed in the eighth chapter.
The duty [to perform them].

(Vi. 4.1.15) The phrase "eight [portions] in a single drawing" does not enjoin a single drawing characterized by the number eight; rather, it enjoins two drawings, each characterized by the number four.

(Bhāṭṭa 5.1.8). By the statement "He takes eight [spoonfuls] with the *upastṛti*; he offers the *anuyājas* with them," the *ājya* (clarified butter) not otherwise connected is enjoined for the sake of a purpose requiring a substance mentioned in the context; because of its being enjoined for that purpose by the aforementioned text, the *aupabhṛta* (butter in the *upabhṛt* ladle) serves solely the purpose of the *anuyājas*.

As for the statement, “He takes eight [portions] with the *upabhṛt* for the *prayājas* and *anuyājas*,” since it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if both *prayāja-ness* and *anuyāja-ness* were taken as the qualifiers of the object of reference (*uddeśyatā-avacchedaka*), this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fact that the *anuyājas* follow the *prayājas*.

This being the case, since it is necessary to accept it as a restatement in either sense, then by the principle of parity (*samāna-nyāya*) and in accordance with the requirement that the meaning be uninterrupted, the restatement must belong to the mention of the *anuyājas* alone.
