Furthermore, at the *Viśvajit* sacrifice within the *Aṣṭarātra*, there is the giving away of one's entire property (*sarvasva*).
And in the case of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), that same rule should apply, because there is no distinction among all [the days].

Commentary: There is a multi-day sacrifice called the *Aṣṭarātra* (Eight-Night Rite), concerning which it is said: "Now, of this day-and-night [rite], the *Viśvajit* and *Abhijit* are one-day sacrifices; in the middle, between the two *Jyotis* [sacrifices], is a six-day period; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this. In this regard, a doubt arises: should the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the entire multi-day sacrifice be the "all-possessions" (*sarvasva*), or rather, should it be one hundred and twelve [cows] as prescribed for a single day?
What is obtained? One's entire property.
Why? Because there is no distinction among all Viśvajits.
Whatever is the characteristic of the Viśvajit in the archetype, that same will apply to this [variant] by virtue of the extended injunction (codaka).
"Therefore, one's entire property should be given.
[The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: In this section, the refutation of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated in the *Bhāṣya* is being expressed.
For the *Viśvajit* occurring within the *ahargaṇa* does not, either by means of the *codaka* or by its name, take on the ritual details (*dharmas*) of the *Viśvajit* recited in the *Ekāha* section.
For this reason, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a constituent part of the performance (*prayoga*) by way of the agent;
and agents are employed for the sake of that which is intended to be performed.
And if something possesses a fruit, it is that which is intended to be performed.
The *ahargaṇa* (the series of sacrificial days) possesses its own fruit; the *viśvajit* alone does not.

Therefore, separate sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are required for each member of the collective. In the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the ritual procedure for the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) is prescribed by an explicit scriptural injunction.
"Before the four-night [sacrifices], there is a thousand," and so forth.
Because the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*), its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) applies here.
Since the sacrificial fee is intended for a group (*gaṇa*) of priests, and since that group has the twelve-day sacrifice as its archetype, its sacrificial fee applies.
The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that since the Viśvajit sacrifice is included within that [Aṣṭarātra], the same [procedure] is appropriate for it as well;

for the *codakas* (transferred injunctions) apply individually to each ritual action, and in the case of the Viśvajit, there is the giving away of one's entire property (*sarvasva-dāna*) by virtue of its name, even though it is an Aṣṭarātra.
In the Aṣṭarātra Viśvajit... [751] ...in the Aṣṭarātra Viśvajit.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that when the state of being the primary and most excellent is attained, the gift of one's entire property (sarvasva-dakṣiṇā) alone should be given;
or else, twelve hundred [cows] should be given, as in the archetype (prakṛti).
The Commentary (bhāṣya) states: "Or rather, twelve hundred should be given."
It should be performed according to the archetype;
the Jyotiṣṭoma is the archetype.
Therein, the ritual properties (dharmas) have been prescribed in their entirety for the Viśvajit.
[The opponent] concludes: "Therefore, one hundred and twelve should be given. [The author replies:
This would not be so, because it does not possess that quality (*atadguṇatvāt*).
Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. It cannot be thus.
Why? Because this number of one hundred and twelve [cows] is not a subordinate quality (guṇa) of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
For here, the mention of "dharma" is by way of its name;
therefore, one will take [the dharma] from the Viśvajit, not from the Jyotiṣṭoma.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
Commentary: Furthermore, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) also demonstrates this.

What is that indicative mark? It is this: "He indeed is deprived of cattle who does not give away his entire property (*sarvasva*) in the Viśvajit. This shows that the giving of one's entire property is mandatory within the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*).
As for the *Śāstra*: "In the case of the multi-day sacrifices, the rule regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) will be established as the exception."
And one hundred and twelve [cows] more than the Jyotiṣṭoma exist there;
that same sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of a group [of animals] would also apply to the Viśvajit.
However, because the extension by name (nāmātideśa) is stronger, the entire property (sarvasva) alone is indeed the sacrificial fee.

And this is a case of partial application (*prātimātra-adhikaraṇa*). In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, although the rule for giving one's entire property (*sarvasva*) has been established, it must be set aside in favor of the twelve-hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*dvādaśaśata-dakṣiṇā*) prescribed for the other *sattra* sacrifices, because of the greater similarity (*sādhamrya*) with them. Furthermore, since all these sacrifices function within a single performance (*ekaprayoga*), there is only one sacrificial fee according to the principle of ritual unity (*tantra*); it should not be given separately for each. Therefore, for the sake of favoring the majority, only twelve hundred should be given.

Soma: The connection [of this topic] arises from the counter-argument that it is likewise [the case] in the *viśvajit* sacrifice of the *ekāha* type involving the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*), even though it occurs within a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*).
In reality, however, the intent is merely to demonstrate that the gift of all one's possessions is obtained precisely because of the superior force of the name (*nāma*).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: although the *viśvajit* exists within a multi-day session, it is endowed with the ritual characteristics of the gift of all one's possessions, because there is no distinction among all *viśvajit* sacrifices.

Vi—“In the Viśvajit, the Charama-ahaḥ, and so forth, is it one hundred and twelve [cows], or is it the whole? Since the *āśraya* (the model sacrifice) is elevated by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), another [number] applies by name (*nāma*) through extension (*atideśa*).

Regarding this point to be expressed, however, in the Vārtika, with the desire to favor those who know the truth (*sat*), [it is stated]: “...with the intent to show favor toward those who possess [this knowledge].”
The first established doctrine was stated merely as a preliminary position (*prāsaṅgika*).
The Bhaṭṭa [position] is as follows: "There is the *Aṣṭātra* *Ahīna* sacrifice.
Its first day is the *Viśvajit*, then the *Abhiplava* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), and then the *Abhijit*."

From the Vedic scripture, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with a goat," it follows that in the Viśvajit sacrifice, according to the principle of the section on distinct contexts (2.3.11), there is a separate rite; by the transfer of name, the rule of the Viśvajit as recited in the *Ekāha* section—namely, the gift of one's entire property (*sarvasva*)—applies. However, in other cases, because they belong to a group (*gaṇa*), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is that of the Jyotiṣṭoma, following the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

Furthermore, even within the *dvādaśāha*, although there is a distinct transfer for each day, the tenth book will explain that there is a single performance (*prayoga*) due to the unity of the ritual procedure.

In that case, since it is stated that even the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) intended for the fire-altar (*anālarthya*) is to be given either at the beginning or at the end by way of a single performance (*tantra*), the expression “every day he gives twelve hundred” prescribes the time of "every day" as having the result of repetition;
for if the number "twelve hundred" were also prescribed [simultaneously], there would be the fault of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
That [number] is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the original sacrificial fees (*prākṛtadakṣiṇā*).
Alternatively, the meaning of that sentence is: "He gives daily that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which, by virtue of the ritual procedure (tantra), has become incumbent as something to be given.

In this case, although the Viśvajit rules would apply due to the extension (atideśa) based on the name and because it is the first day, it is more logical to favor the majority [of the rules]; thus, since it follows that the one hundred and twelve [coins] alone provide the benefit through the ritual procedure, the Vārtikakāra’s view is that by the phrase "daily" (anvaham), that very amount of one hundred and twelve is to be repeated and given each day.

The venerable author of the Bhāṣya, however, maintains that because of the authority supported by an unestablished otherwise mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "He who does not give away all his possessions in the Viśvajit is indeed deprived of cattle"—the injunction for giving away everything is established by the very injunction [implied] for performing the eight-night rite; thus, in all the days of the first [rite], everything must be given away.
Maṇḍana states: "It should be given even in a group of all [days].
That is, in a group of all days (*ahargaṇa*).
That is the entire property.
Śaṅkara: "And that [is the case] within the Viśvajit sacrifice (according to the Bhāṣya view).
10. Because of its greater frequency, that [property] is set aside (according to the Vārttika view)."
10. In the Viśvajit sacrifice of the eight-night rite (*aṣṭarātra*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *vatsa* and the *vagata* garments.

In the Viśvajit, it is like the *vatsa* [sacrifice] because of its name; otherwise, there would be the repetition of the ritual procedure (*tantra*). Commentary: There is an eight-night *ahīna* sacrifice: "Its [first two days] are the Viśvajit and Abhijit, both being *agniṣṭoma*s; in the middle is a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) with light on both sides; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this."

In the *viśvajit* one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), the use of a garment made of calf-hair (*vatsavat*) for the purpose of wearing is prescribed: "Having risen from the *aśvattha* tree, he puts on the calf-hair garment. In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, however, there is a garment with eight fringes; [this applies] to the *viśvajit* within the eight-night rite (*aṣṭarātra*).

The sense is that even when the suffix denotes the primary meaning, indirect indication (lakṣaṇā) is appropriate because it is subordinate, since there is no contradiction [with the primary sense] and there is no connection with another unrelated object.
(Alaṃkāra, p. 63). It is better to assume indirect indication in the latter member of the compound than to assume it when there is no contradiction [in the primary sense].
Just as in the case of "the first sacrifice" (*prathamo yajaḥ*), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *yajña* toward the performance of the sacrifice (Vi. 3.1.17);

so too, because it is stronger due to its lack of conflict with what has not yet arisen, the *subrahmaṇyā* mantra addressed to Agni should be performed in accordance with the first day of the fifteen-night rite (*pañcadaśarātra*)—this is the prima facie view (Pūrvapakṣa) [1.2.15].

Furthermore, following the opening statement (*upakrama*) which lacks any prior contradiction, even the final injunctive word "he should cause to accept" (*pratigrāhayet*) must be explained as having the sense of "he should cause to give up" (*pratigrāhayet*), with the root *grah* (to take) internally containing the sense of *tyaj* (to abandon).

3|1|15. A great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) is established by non-indication (*asaṃdeśena*), as follows: where something is prescribed in a modified rite (*vikṛti*) by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to an archetypal action (*prākṛtakriyā*), it is grasped by that [archetype] through its performance; for example, "At each *prayāja* offering, one offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain.

In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) known as the *ahīna*, there are twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*) and twelve *upasad* days; thus, the number twelve [is grasped from the archetype]. Bāla. pṛ. 9. A great context arises from non-indication of the archetype, as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and so forth.
Page 9. By that which is non-doubtful, the doubtful is determined.
Vārttika 3.4.12. Page 971. By that which is non-doubtful, the doubtful is sublated.
For example, [the statement] "sugar is an ointment" by anyone is sublated by the praise of ghee.

Non-contradiction of what has not yet been established (*aprāptabādha*). [Bāl. p. 140] It is the sublation of a doubtful scriptural statement by a certain scriptural statement; for example, the sublation of the doubtful scriptural statement—arising from the fourth and fifth case endings in the phrase "at the Āmiṣa sacrifice, [the offering] belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevī*)—by the certain statement "it belongs to Vāyu" (*vājibhyaḥ*). This is stated in the *Guṇādhikaraṇa*.
Non-contradiction of what has not yet been established.
p. 135. Even for one who has not performed the *saṃnayya* sacrifice, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when the moon rises [during the new moon].

Bhāṣya 6.5.6.21–24. [The opponent argues that] non-proximity (*asaṃnidhi*)—when not accompanied by an impermissible factor (*anupādeya*)—is a cause of distinction [between acts], [this being stated as a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*)].
Su. p. 955: "In the case of non-concurrent acts (*asaṃnipātikarman*), since no distinction is perceived and because they are of a single nature, there is a single mention."

(1|4|15–16 Sūtra Concordances) | As for those mantras of non-concurrent rites, such as the invocation of the *subrahmaṇyā* priest on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*) with the words "O gods of Brahman," since they occur at a single time and there is no distinction in their being offered, there should be a single recitation.
Bhāṣya.

X. The Principle of Disconnected Words and Syllables (*asaṃbaddhapadavyayanyāya*). [The principle] continues from [the previous section]: "Now, this is the *go* [sacrifice]. In the word *go*, by the principle of disconnected words and syllables, when the preceding [elements] have vanished, when no further connection arises in the cognition, when a break in the context is recognized, and when the cognition has been eclipsed by another meaning, the [word] falling [into that state], being unable to reach the *Jyotiṣṭoma* because its connection is severed due to the intervention of another name, functions with respect to a different meaning.
For it is said: "A sacrifice separated by a name or a river does not reach back to what precedes."

"And it does not, by force of the context, go to a different meaning such that it reaches the previous [sacrifice]. (The meaning of this is as follows: In the *Tāṇḍya* Śruti—"Now this is the Jyotis, now this is the Viśvajyotis, now this is the Sarvajyotis; one should sacrifice with this [rite] which has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee"—the three names beginning with Jyotis are metaphorically represented as a river of a thousand [streams]. And thus, the root *yaji* ("to sacrifice") in the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), being separated and intervened by the flow of these new names, does not reach the previous Jyotiṣṭoma, nor does that previous Jyotiṣṭoma follow or connect with that *yaji*.)
Therefore, by force, the sacrifice has shifted to a different meaning.
(Ke.
Vārttika 2.1.22, p. 529. X. There would be no connection because of equality; and because qualities are dependent on others, there would be no connection due to their equality.

Having raised the objection—by the principle of *3|1|122*, even if [the word] refers solely to the capacity (*śakti*), why should there not be a connection with another capacity?—it is replied by the maxim "there would be no connection because of equality": because one capacity cannot be connected with another capacity, and because a substance, once brought under the control of a single capacity, cannot be connected with another capacity. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1442). Since the instrumentality of the *ghālya* is understood through the force of the injunction, and because of the lack of connection with that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), [the modification applies] to those things for its sake; due to the lack of connection, the modified (*vaikṛta*) [element applies].
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the collection of words beginning with "medhātither eva" is to be used without modification.
This concludes the first exposition (*varṇaka*).
Alternatively, there is another example.
They recite: "A three-year-old bull, not castrated, is the price for Soma.
However, in the archetype (prakṛti), a one-year-old cow is the price for Soma.

In that context, regarding this one-year-old cow, the following is recited: "This is the cow; for her I purchase [the Soma]; for her the ghee, for her the curd, for her the whey, for her the cream, for her the butter, for her the clarified butter, for her the curdled milk, for her the whey."
This same [formula] is also extended by the force of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) to the purchase of a *sāṇḍa* (castrated) Soma-purchasing animal.
In that case, there is no dispute regarding the modification (*ūha*) of the phrase "This is the cow; with her I buy from you" into "This is the *sāṇḍa*; with him I buy from you.
However, a doubt arises as to whether or not there should be a modification of the remaining words, such as "for her, ghee," and so forth.

Regarding this, the Siddhāntin says: The statement [of substitution] is understood as qualified by that, namely, qualified by the meaning of the word *go* (cow); thus, among those meanings—the referents of words such as *gojanyā* and so forth—the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is *ekahāyanī*, which is not a compound.
[The objection that] it is unestablished because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) [is rejected].
The conjunctions inherent in the threads are [the causes] of the cloth inherent in those threads;

just as the colors of the threads [are the causes] in the production of the cloth inherent in the threads. (Nyāyaratnākara, p. 216). ✱ A syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) consists in the plurality of meanings belonging to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, which is not in a compound (*asamāsa*).
(An example is to be sought; see Bāla. p. 181. "Because [the cause] is not omnipresent, we observe that the effect appears everywhere only successively" (Su.
p. 616). This is the maxim: "But it is not a proof, because it exists for that purpose."

Now, one might object: since that which is without fruit cannot be an object of desire (*kāmya*), and given the presence of the word "desire" (*kāma*), this term "desire for the five" (*pañcakāma*) must refer to a result, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa*—namely, the principle that "that which is not a means [to something else] is [the primary factor], because it exists for that purpose" (*asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt*). In response to this doubt, [it is said]: In the injunction, "A king desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," the one desiring self-sovereignty is the primary factor (*pradhānabhūta*) by virtue of the principle "asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt" (Jaimini Sūtra 6.1.12). This is because the injunction would otherwise be inexplicable (*vidhyanyathānupapatti*), and because the desire is mentioned as a subordinate element (*upanandhya*). (Su. pṛ. 415; Ratna. 6.1.14) *Asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt* (6.1.12) is the sūtra formulating the final position (*siddhānta*). Due to the inexplicability of the injunction otherwise and because the desire is mentioned as a subordinate element, [the desire is understood as the primary factor].
Regarding the *asthiyajña* (760): the *asthiyajña* has been described. This is to be performed by the living participants once the year [of the sacrifice] has passed.
This subsequent ritual act is not merely of the nature of a *sattra* (sacrificial session).
Herein there are two positions: the position that it pertains to the living (*jīvad-adhikāra-pakṣa*) and the position that it pertains to the deceased (*mṛta-adhikāra-pakṣa*).
The second position is presented as a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvā-cintā*), assuming that the bones themselves possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*).
Some [hold that] there is eligibility for the bone-sacrifice even for those who are living.

"The Bone-Sacrifice should belong to others because there is no prohibition; it belongs to the bones because there is a specific prohibition [against living beings]. Commentary: This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "If one who has been consecrated for a sacrificial session (*satra*) should die, they should cremate him, tie his bones upon a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), and having consecrated his nearest relative in his place, they should sacrifice with him. Then, after a year has passed, they should cause the bones to sacrifice. Regarding this sacrifice performed after a year, a doubt arises: does it belong to the bones or to the living? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It belongs to the bones, because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) [with the word "sacrifice"].
What is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? [In the case of the verb] *yājayati*, the bones are the objects (*karman*).
But surely, since bones are insentient, they are not capable of acting as the instigators (*tantrayitum*) themselves; how then can they be agents (*kartṛ*) in the action? It is said in reply:
Their status as instigators is heard [in scripture]: "Others are the instigators; they will cause these people to perform these actions.
He says: "It is not the case that one causes another to act when the other does not act."
The prompter (*prayojaka*) is the cause (*hetu*). And these [factors] are not able to bring about the action in its entirety. It is said in reply:
Because of the authority of the scriptural statement:

as long as they are capable of performing the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), so long shall they cause them to be performed—such as the touching of the *audumbarī* post and the taking hold of the parrots, and so forth.
[The opponent] says: "They are unable to perform even the primary acts; they do not perform the subsidiary acts that belong to the sacrificer."
To this it is replied:
by the force of the scriptural statement, those two words refer to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); they indicate them because [the priests] are consecrated and purified by that [act].
Thus, such a relinquishment of the substance will be established as being based on the scriptural injunction.
He says: "If it is described in this way, then agency is taught as belonging only to those who cause the sacrifice to be performed, not to the person [who performs the act].
It is replied: "In this manner, agency itself is indeed taught;
for one does not say 'he causes one who is not an agent to act'."
Furthermore, when a sacrifice exists, the status of being the cause for those [desiring a result] is already established and is merely restated;
just as in the case of "one desiring a village should cause [another] to sacrifice," it is enjoined that "one desiring a village should sacrifice.
And the status of being the cause is a mere restatement of what is already established.
And he demonstrates this: "He places the bone-pitcher with hymns," whereby the bones themselves are seen to possess the status of the sacrificer.
Therefore, the sacrifice belongs to the bones, not to those who are living.
This being the position reached, we reply:
The bone-sacrifice (asthiyajña) would belong to those [bones] while they are still living;
for them, the sacrifice is not prohibited.
However, [the sacrifice] is prohibited with respect to the bones themselves.
Renunciation is performed by means of the mind, and bones do not possess a mind.

As it has been said: "The officiating priests, having received the sacrificial fee, perform the renunciation after being consecrated by that [fee]; such is the renunciation prescribed by the sacred word."
This is not so.
For when it is said, "one should sacrifice," another sacrifice does not come into being for those who are unable [to perform it] merely by virtue of the authority of the statement.
Indeed, that statement means "they perform the sacrifice," not that there are other things for the sake of the sacrifice.
Nor does this follow from the authority of the statement that "whatever consists of two words is taken";
for it is not the case that [the substance] is given by means of bones,
nor is there a purchase in the absence of a gift.
Furthermore, a figurative meaning is not understood from the injunctive word itself;

for a figurative sense is determined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas the word is connected [directly] as it is. For example, in the injunction "A cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*), it is an animal characterized by the genus "cow" that is denoted, and not a *vāhīka*.
In the common usage "This Vāhīka is a cow," the term "cow" is applied figuratively to the Vāhīka;
therefore, when there is an injunction for the relinquishment [of the animal], there would be no other purpose for the sacrifice.
Furthermore, the bones do not possess their own substance such that the officiating priests, having taken them up, might think, "We have been consecrated by these.
Therefore, the bones cannot in any way constitute the sacrifice.
Consequently, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not intended to be significant.
He says: "In that case, this statement is meaningless because it consists of incoherent words.
We reply: "No;
for a statement is not meaningless when its meaning is understood."
From the sentence "Then, after a year, they should perform the sacrifice," whoever is understood as the "bones" (asthi) is the one intended here.
The connection "they should cause the bones to perform the sacrifice" is not what is being enjoined. [The opponent] asks: Is the word "bones" a mistake? We reply: No, it is not a mistaken reading.
For not every non-erroneous recitation (*apramādapāṭha*) is one that serves as an injunction (*vidhāna*) with its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*).

Even when restating (*anuvāda*), a word may enter into syntactic connection within a sentence by expressing its meaning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and yet it does not become an erroneous recitation.
In this context, the word "bones" (*asthīni*), while enjoining its own object by expressing it through its primary function, does not fit coherently within the sentence.

The subsequent statement, however, will apply by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*): "Then, after a year, they should cause them to sacrifice. This will refer to those who were previously mentioned as being alive; therein, the word "bones" (*asthi*) will function by way of secondary indication, [meaning] "Then, after a year, they should cause those possessing bones to sacrifice.
Who are those "possessing bones"? They are those who went with him [to the sacrifice], [namely] those of the Bone-Sacrifice (*asthiyajña*). (2) Of the Bone-Sacrifice.
[The bones] have been carried away.
Therefore, he whose bones these are can be identified by those very bones;
for this reason, the sacrifice belongs to those who are living.

If the *pyaudha* were being enjoined, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated, namely that something accrues to the officiating priest from causing one who is already sacrificing to sacrifice;
yet no one would desire to sacrifice for their own sake.
Therefore, the *pyaudha* is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
The application [of the bone-urn] should be as far as its utility extends.

The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that it shows the rite pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) when it says, "He places the bone-urn upon the *stotra*"—this does not pertain to the sacrificer.
It has been stated that bones do not perform sacrifices;

therefore, by virtue of the authority of this scriptural statement, this ritual action possesses the essential nature of being performed by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). To the extent that there is a scriptural injunction, to that same extent the ritual action deserves to be considered as such; however, it is not possible to characterize the entirety of it as belonging to the sacrificer.

Therefore, the sacrifice belongs only to those who are living. [Objection: In the previous case, because there was a mention of an enemy, it was meaningful [to speak of] bones; here, however, since there is no mention of bones and so forth, it is said that the qualification for the rite pertains to the dead. This is the resolution of the doubt.
It is stated in the *Tantraratna* that because [the sacrifice] is performed by means of bones (*satrānna*), no result need be postulated in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: regarding the injunction "one should cause the bones to sacrifice," this sacrifice belongs to the others who are living, because there is no contradiction;
whereas for the bones—that is, for the deceased who possessed the bones—there is a prohibition, since the possibility of qualification [for the rite] is precluded.

In the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, however, the word *asthi* (bone) is taken according to its literal sense. [The question is: "Is the *asthi-yāga* (bone-sacrifice) to be performed by those who possess bones, i.e., the living, or by the bones themselves? [The answer is:
Not so; because at the beginning and end of the journey, the living person remains with the bones.
From the word *asthitaḥ*, meaning "from the bones.
Bhaṭṭa says: "It is heard in the scripture: 'If they should cause [the bones] to sacrifice for the sacrificial session (*satra*).

In that regard, concerning this bone-sacrifice performed after a year, there arises the inquiry: does it have the deceased as its qualified performer (*adhikārin*), or does it have the living as its qualified performer? Upon reflection, because the qualification is perceived to belong to the bones themselves—just as in the case of the injunction, 'One should cause the Niṣāda-chief to sacrifice with this [offering]'—"
And although that [agency] is impossible for them in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is eligibility for the deceased as indicated by that [nature].
Nor is agency impossible for him, because the bones themselves would attain the status of the indirect agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) in the undertaking of the *śulka* and other rites.

Furthermore, in the case of the offering of materials and so forth, just as in the chapter on the living, all others grant their consent through the mental representation of death; thus, agency is established by way of such consent.

Otherwise, even if there were a performance of the *sattra* sacrifice together with one who has been brought to the place of death, the latter would have no authorization (*anumati*) due to the absence of consent; consequently, the acquisition of his mixed property would be impossible.
Therefore, the entitlement belongs only to the deceased.

As for officiating as a priest (*yājana*), however, it must be performed by those very individuals who were initiated for the performance of the *sattra*, because the passage beginning with "Then, after a year" indicates that the performers of the ritual and the officiating priests share a common agent.
If, however, it is distinguished that from that word there is the cognition of immediate succession alone and not of common agency as well, then there is a different rule.

And this [rule], although occasioned (*naimittika*), does not pertain to one who has already commenced the *satra* sacrifice, because their qualification (*adhikāra*) is distinct; rather, it is for the sake of an independent fruit for one who is merely striving (*yatamāna*).
Therefore, it should be noted that according to the method of the sixth [chapter], even if the fruit of the *satra* is impossible upon death, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding this fruit.
This being the case, the bones themselves cannot be the agents, because the status of being the locus of the volitional effort conducive to the sacrifice is impossible for them.
Therefore, since that [volition] must be characterized by its connection to the living state, the entitlement (adhikāra) of the deceased must be asserted.

Consequently, rather than assuming a consent (*anumati*) or a fruit (*phala*) when there is an absence of the causal condition (the living state) in the case of the bones—which would entail many faults such as these—it is better to take the word "bones" as indicating the living persons themselves who are connected to those bones, and to base the entitlement upon them.

Furthermore, regarding the state while still alive, is it said that even with consent (*anumati*), [the ritual] is completed immediately thereafter for a very short duration, or is it after death? It cannot be the former, because renunciation (*tyāga*) would not be possible during the state of being alive. Nor can it be the latter, because since consent is momentary, it is illogical for it to produce [the result] after death. Therefore, even when the performance of the *sattra* sacrifice is concluded after death, one must—according to the method of the sixth [chapter]—separate the deceased's property from the belongings of those still living and complete the performance with their own wealth; this is how it should be understood.

And for this reason, since even the assumption of an implied injunction (*anumatikalpanā*) is untenable, and because it is impossible for a deceased person to have any qualification [for the rite], the word "bones" (*asthi*) must be taken as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) referring only to those who are living. Furthermore, the act of wrapping the bones (*asthyupanahana*) and so forth constitutes a possible relationship [with the living]. Moreover, this refers to one who is currently engaged in a *sattra* sacrifice. And this "bone-sacrifice" (*asthiyāga*) is not of the nature of a *sattra* itself; for even though there is recognition [of the ritual form], the difference between the acts is understood by the force of the causative suffix (*ṇijanta*) in the expression "they should cause [them] to sacrifice" (*yājayeyuḥ*).
For if it were of the nature of a *sattra*, the distinction between the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) would indeed be established there;

however, the performance [of the ritual] by others would be untenable, or else there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in the injunction, because it is enjoined as being like the *yaji* (the act of sacrificing).
Therefore, on account of that [distinction], this is indeed a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
And in that case, since the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the *abhyakta* sacrifice, [the present text] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, because this discussion is taken up in the subsequent section, it maintains its connection to the chapter. (Mīmāṃsākośa 15.2)
Regarding the bone-sacrifice (*asthiyajña*),
because it is logically established that the bone-sacrifice has a performer,

Because it is not desired [to perform them], they are absent in the other case.

This principle applies where, for the sake of establishing an extremely subtle object, one describes an object that is proximate to it, or more proximate, or even most proximate. For example, when there is an instruction such as, "When the sun has set, show the Pole Star (Dhruva) and Arundhatī," and the task of showing them arises, since the extremely subtle Arundhatī cannot be pointed out instantaneously, one points out the Seven Sages (Saptarṣi), who are more proximate, and then that which is most proximate to them, thereby causing the student to recognize that very [Arundhatī] through them.

Likewise, ordinary people, regarding planets and so forth as their very self, are seen crying out, "We are lost when the house is destroyed," when [their property] perishes. To ward them off, the Śruti—beginning with "The son is indeed born as one's own self" (*ātmā vai jāyate putraḥ*), and continuing with "This person consists of food" (*sa eṣa puruṣo 'nnarasamayaḥ*), "Another inner self consists of breath" (*anyo 'ntara ātmā prāṇamayaḥ*), "Another inner self consists of mind" (*anyo 'ntara ātmā manomayaḥ*), "Another inner self consists of consciousness" (*anyo 'ntara ātmā vijñānamayaḥ*), and "Another inner self consists of bliss" (*anyo 'ntara ātmā ānandamayaḥ*)—shows that everything from the son down to bliss is not the Self.

The sense is that [the text] leads [the mind] to the state of non-distinction from the Self itself by showing it as the Self. Furthermore, the nature of the method (*nyāya*) has been stated without the letter "a" in the phrase "this is the gross Arundhatī.
