Repetition must be performed; thus, in the explanation of specific [details], it applies to the original rite (prakṛti) over two days.

Maṇḍana [states]: "One should throw away the horn on another day"—the intent of such statements is merely to indicate the time of the Soma-pressing (sutyā), and not [to prescribe] the state of being two-day [rites] and so forth.

Śaṅkara says: "In the case of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), there is a state of being a single ritual procedure (*tantratva*). This follows from the fact that even the term "in the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhe*) serves merely as an indicator for the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*).
It proceeds.
Because there is no intention [to specify] any particular one, since all [the days] are without distinction as being of the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*),
when the *Aṣṭarātra* sacrifice within the *Ahargaṇa* is taking place, at the *Viśvajit*, [there is the giving away of] one's entire property (*sarvasva*).
This is for the purpose of explaining the term *pāta-tantra*, and not for the sake of its mere literal meaning. [The sūtras] on giving:
Bhāṣya 6.7.8.14–17. § In the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, [there is the rule concerning] the *udgātṛ*...
If this is argued, [the answer is] that [expressions] such as "on the ninth day" or "on the second day" serve as indicators for the time of the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing).
It is only the repeated day that possesses the [required] cutting, not the entire group of days (*ahargaṇa*),
because this point is already established by what will be stated later in the section on the *agrima* (11.4.9).
Vi— "Is the Subrahmaṇyā formula to be repeated at each Upasad, or not?
It would be repeated because of the difference in the primary acts; it is differentiated by the difference in time.
And that characteristic applies to the multi-day sacrifice (ahargaṇa)."

In the case of the *ahargaṇa* [multi-day sacrifice] consisting of twelve days (*dvādaśāha*), according to the Bhaṭṭa school: at the time of the *upavasatha*, the *subrahmaṇyā* invocation is performed;
and in the *viśvajit* which occurs within the eight-night sacrifice (*aṣṭarātra*), one hundred and twelve [cows] are to be given.
Because it is the archetype (*prakṛti*).
This is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), wherein the *tantra*— delimited by the time, place, and other factors coinciding with the Soma-pressing day—
is as it is in the archetype, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma.
It is not indeed beneficial to all, because there is no apprehension of any distinction;
nor is it so,
because it does not possess those qualities.
Having been directed with the words, "Stay! Come to the Soma-pressing," there is a repetition [of the rite] due to the observation of the [sacrificer's] arrival.

In that regard, for the Viśvajit sacrifice within the *ahargaṇa* (multi-day sacrificial session), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one hundred and twelve, following the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Because it will be stated that [the existence of the self] is established even through the nature of the body (*tantratayā*),
this [objection] is refuted by the Sūtra, which sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "this would be [the case] for one who is in agreement."
In cases such as the *subrahmaṇyā* addressed to the deities mentioned in the *pūrvapakṣa*, as in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice and others; however,
in certain instances where—

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of indicating a distinction: it would not be thus; because [the sacrifice] is like the archetype (*prakṛti*), there would be the *subrahmaṇyā* liturgy addressed to Agni during the twelve days, and in some cases there would be no hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*śata-dakṣiṇā*) consisting of various fires.
Because the group of twelve hundred does not possess those qualities.
Its status as having a deity will be stated later, namely that there is indeed a distinction in that regard.
The quality of the Viśvajit is *tadguṇa*; that which is not *tadguṇa* is *atadguṇa*.
Maṇḍana [states]: "In the *ahargaṇa*, the Subrahmaṇyā is common (*tantra*) at the beginning."
The quality of the *viśvajit* sacrifice does not belong to that which has a hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*śatadakṣiṇā*), because it lacks that quality.
Śaṅkara says: "Even when there is a single *upasad* among the group..."
Therefore, it would not be so;
rather, the giving away of one's entire property (*sarvasva*) alone is the specific quality (*guṇa*) of the Viśvajit sacrifice,
and that rule would apply to the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*) as well, because there is no distinction among all [the days].

In the Viśvajit one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvasva*) is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); this is the characteristic feature (*dharma*) of the Viśvajit. Furthermore, the Viśvajit occurring within the eight-night rite (*aṣṭarātra*) is a modification (*vikṛti*) of this very same one-day sacrifice.
Regarding this, the reading "taddharmaḥ" (his duty) is found in the Vṛddha-laghv-aśvalāyanasmṛti as written in the commentary of Trivalakara;

thus, for him too, the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*) alone is the duty, not the [giving of] twelve hundred. However, in other places, such as in the manuscript from the *Yajurveda* collection and elsewhere, the reading is simply "taddharmāḥ" (his duties).
Because of the observation of an indicative mark:
"Whatever is the ritual property of the Viśvajit in its original form, that same [property] applies to this [variant] as well.
In the case of the Viśvajit occurring within a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one's entire possession.
The commentary, "By what will it come to be? demonstrates the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), which indeed excludes the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
"He who [does this] is deprived of cattle."
Yayāti [says]: On the contrary, there are the words, "The rule of the Viśvajit applies to the archetype";
and in the context of the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), there is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) stating, "In the Viśvajit, one does not give away all one's possessions."

These [words] are naturally appropriate only in the sense of a *tatpuruṣa* compound; moreover, because of the observation of this gender in the *bahuvrīhi*, in the *viśvajit* sacrifice, "all one's possessions" (*sarvasva*) alone constitutes the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

"Laghīyān" (lighter/more concise)—this is its property; "syāt" (it would be) is the very reading [of the text]. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the reasons previously stated. Who? [The opponent.]
It is accepted.
Now, the explanation of the sūtra: in the *ahargaṇa* [sacrifice], specifically in the eight-night rite (*aṣṭarātra*).
In the case of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), [the ritual details] apply precisely at the time of the concluding *soma* extraction for each respective day.
When the *Viśvajit* is being performed, its specific characteristics belong to that [sacrifice] as recited in the section on one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*).
Alternatively, separate clothing must be produced.
The duty of the Viśvajit sacrifice should consist precisely of the giving away of one's entire property and so forth;
[this applies] to all [performers] at the Viśvajit.

In the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, specifically in the *dvādaśāha*, with the exception of the final day, the wives [participate] because there is no distinction, because they are identical, and because their duties are equal. Therefore, eight...
The conclusion at the *saṃyāja* offerings.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice occurring within the *rātri-satra*, one's entire property must be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
"The fee for all [the priests]..."
The conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* applies to all [offerings] because there is no distinction;
that is, because there is no distinction among the ritual properties (*dharma*) such as the introductory mantras (*praiṣa*), according to the *Kutūhala*.
For all [of them].
"But regarding the *viśvajit*s, there is the Bhāṣya.
"Their properties" [are mentioned] in several places.
The Bhāṣya states: "This is a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*): 'One desiring progeny [should sacrifice] with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*')."
The reading is:
"Therefore, when the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice is being performed, the *viśvajit* should possess those same characteristics;
one should cause it to be sacrificed."
In this regard, it is heard: "The days end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
This refers to one whose characteristic is precisely the rule of the *viśvajit* sacrifice as recited in the section on the *ekāha* sacrifices;
thus [the days] conclude.

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: since it belongs to all [the stages], the compound *taddharmāḥ* should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi*. In that case, the suffix *ini* is applied to form the word *sāṃsthika*.
Is the conclusion at the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, or prior to the last [offering],
excluding the tenth? It concludes with the end.
On the other hand, according to the alternative view, because it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is no *anit* suffix;
thus a doubt is raised,
for its ending in *mānasa* has been stated by the authoritative word.
What [is meant]?

The word "but" (tu), however, serves as an illustration for that which is recited in the section on the one-day sacrifice (ekāha). Is it then established that [it applies] to all days? No, it applies to all days.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
Or rather, it is one hundred and twelve, because it is the archetype.
No distinction is stated [elsewhere] regarding the rule: "The days conclude with the Patnīsaṃyājas."
"When eight nights have passed in the Viśvajit sacrifice, one's entire property must be given away.
Thus it is said;
and no specific qualification is resorted to.
Therefore, refuting the conclusion of all [the preceding views] by means of the word "or" (*vā*) in the Sūtra, the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "Of all... and so forth.
Mīmāṃsākośa 16: Regarding the multi-day sacrificial session (ahargaṇa), specifically the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha).
Regarding the multi-day sacrificial session, specifically the twelve-day sacrifice.
Regarding the statement, "The days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings," because this is heard as a general rule (*aviśeṣaśravaṇāt*), all [the days] conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja*.

But is it not understood that there is a distinction, namely: "For then the sacrifice is not yet completed"? [This implies that] where there is no specific number [of days], there they conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, while on other [days] they conclude [differently].
To this we say: it is not so, because of the force of the reason [provided in the text].

No; since [the rule that the sacrifice ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings] applies to all [sacrifices] by virtue of the scriptural statement, how could it be restricted to a specific case without another scriptural statement?
As for what was said—that on the basis of the force of the reason (*hetu*), wherever there is no suspension (*asaṃsthā*), there the sacrifice ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings—it is replied:
The statement regarding the reason will serve the same purpose as [the rule] that the Patnīsaṃyājas are the conclusion; it is because of the long duration that the number is mentioned.
For that which concludes after a long time is, as it were, not yet concluded. It is for this very reason that this sacrifice concludes after a long time, due to its length.
Therefore, for the sake of brevity, having performed the Patnīsaṃyājas at the end [of the sacrifice], the remainder should be omitted.

Consequently, having performed the Patnīsaṃyājas at the end of the final day, only the Avabhṛtha and subsequent rites should be performed; the remainder of the day need not be completed up to the Hāriyojana offering. (Ratna)
And because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), [the rite] should end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* before the last day.
Commentary: The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the previous position.
Before the last day, it should conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja*.

Why? Because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). There is an indicative mark: "The days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; one does not throw away the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) or the cups (*graha*), for at that time the sacrifice is not yet completed. This shows that on whichever day the sacrifice is not yet completed, it concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. How so? The non-completion is indicated by means of a causal particle (*ha*).
Since these days are characterized by non-termination (*asaṃsthiti*), therefore the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings occurs on them.
Termination (*saṃsthiti*) occurs on the final day. Furthermore, in those days where the rites conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, a state of non-termination is observed as being scattered about.
Therefore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "non-completion" (*asaṃsthā*) and "ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Having observed non-completion prior to the final [offering], it is understood that [the sacrifice] ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings precisely before the final one.
Or rather, the mention of the consecration (*dīkṣā*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), just as in the case of not performing the concluding rite (*naṛtusaṃsthāpana*).
Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
This is not so;
[the view] that it should end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings before the final [offering].
What then? [It applies] to all, because there is no distinction.

As for what was said—"In those cases where the Patnīsaṃyājas are the end, an incomplete conclusion (asaṃsthā) is observed; therefore, we conclude that before the final burning, they end with the Patnīsaṃyājas"—this is not so.
For this observation is not rooted in an injunction, nor is it based on any other means of valid knowledge.
Therefore, this perception is of the nature of a mirage.
As for the claim that "the cause is non-existent," that too would not be the case;
for it has been stated: "But the scripture [is authoritative], because sound is preceded by [another] word" (JS 1.1.27).

Furthermore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s" and "not concluding" (*asaṃsthā*). By the word, it is understood that all the cremation fires end with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s; however, "not concluding" (*asaṃsthā*) refers, by way of an improper application, to [the fires] prior to the final fire.
As for this statement, "For then the sacrifice is not yet concluded," it is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to extol the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
For it is considered thus: "The sacrifice is not yet concluded; it will be concluded after a long time.
Because it will be concluded after a long time, therefore [the ritual] should be kept low; thus, the days end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
While the days are indeed being concluded, the mention of "conclusion" (saṃsthā) is for the purpose of praising the point at which they end with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings;
for those days do indeed have conclusions.
The Avabhṛtha bath and other such constituent elements will be performed as the remaining rites for them.
Just as the statement regarding the release from initiation (*dīkṣā*) is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) for the non-consummation of the sacrifice, so too should this be understood:
"He who is initiated is indeed bound by the two nooses of Varuṇa;
day and night are the two nooses of Varuṇa."
Or rather, if one were to conclude [the rite] at this point, he would be released from the two nooses of Varuṇa;
for it is said: "Having concluded it at night, he is indeed released from the two nooses of Varuṇa, so as not to harm himself.
But if he is not released from the two nooses of Varuṇa, he is not liberated from them until then.
For the *avabhṛtha* is for the purpose of releasing one from the initiatory vows (*dīkṣā*). Since it is not otherwise [than this], one is released from the bonds of Varuṇa.
At that time, many observances (*niyama*) are relinquished; having taken these into account, this statement is made.
Likewise here too, having observed that it takes a long time to reach completion, the statement "it is not yet completed" occurs.
Or rather, because it is prescribed as an independent injunction (*anārabhyavidhāna*), there would be a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) at the end.
Bhāṣya: By the word "or" (*vā*), the position is reversed.
Or rather, [the ritual] would end with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings before the final day;
for this rule is not prescribed having begun from the final day.
How then? It is prescribed generally: that the days end with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.

In that case, there would be a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*). What, then, is the application by means of the method of logical sequence (*yāya*)? It is the rule: "The *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings conclude on the final days.
This is not so, for what remains will be explained.

"It concludes" means it is not performed; this refers to the completion of the ritual activity. When those days are being performed together, regarding some particular rite (*padārtha*), the rites of another day must necessarily be performed.
Since there would otherwise be no fixed rule (*aniyama*) in that regard, it is prescribed that the sacrifice should be concluded at the end of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
The purpose of this suspension is so that the simultaneous performance of the ritual elements of another day may be experienced;
for this is the visible effect of the suspension in the case of a group of days, such as the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
In a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) such as the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*),
where this [concluding rule] is not observed, it cannot be assumed; therefore, in that case,
there is no conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
And that purpose does not exist for anything else.

Therefore, since it is established by the principle that "until the end [of the sacrifice], the conclusion is at the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings," there is the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "For then the sacrifice is not yet completed. [Durga says:
One should cause progeny to flourish.

By what? By that [sacrifice] known as the *dvādaśāha*. In this regard, according to the rule "Number [expresses] the object of the action" (*saṃkhyayā karmādau*, Pāṇini 2.1.7), these are twelve sacrifices.
Because of its grammatical coreferentiality with the word "sacrifice" (in the injunction *yājayet*), the word *ahaḥ* (day) denotes the sacrifice itself, since it is designated by the term "day."
In the archetype (the Jyotiṣṭoma), the sacrifice beginning with the Upāṃśu and ending with the Hāriyojana is delimited by the word "day" (ahaḥ).
Here too (in the Dvādaśāha and similar rites), it should be understood in this same way.
(In that case,) since twelve sacrifices are enjoined together for a single result, they must be performed on the very same day.

Whatever procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belongs to these [sacrifices] up to the *āgnīṣomīya*— that is, the procedure previously mentioned extending up to the *āgnīṣomīya*— must be performed by way of a single performance (*tantra*), because there is no distinction in the days. The subsequent members (*aṅga*), such as the *avabhṛtha* bath and so forth, must likewise be performed by way of a single performance.

However, those auxiliary elements that provide assistance through conjunction (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), such as the *adya-yajya* and others, as well as those that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) falling within that interval, such as the *savanīya* offerings and others, are to be repeated.

Because of their simultaneous performance, based on the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), one must remain established in a certain [day] and proceed from the second day onwards. In that context, when the sequence of days has been established, it is restricted that the rites end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* on each day.
In that regard, because there is no subsequent sacrifice to be performed, there is simply no persistence [of the rule] by way of non-restriction.

Since there is an absence of non-restriction, there can likewise be no restriction dependent upon it (namely, that the rites end with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s). Furthermore, this very sentence (*patnīsaṃyājāntāni*, etc. cannot be both a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) in one instance and an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) in another, due to the difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābhedāt*).
Moreover, for one for whom [this] statement serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), its purpose is clearly perceived;
therefore, [the sacrifice] is restricted to ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings before the final one.
Śabara says: "In that case, since there is no distinction, the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* applies to all."
The statement regarding the "non-consummation" of the sacrifice is figurative, referring to its long duration.
This being the position, we reply: "This injunction prior to the last one is for the purpose of enjoining what is required;
since its primary sense is possible, there is no secondary (metaphorical) meaning for the remainder of the sentence."

Having performed all the days ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the remainder of the day beginning with the *hāriyojana* offering is to be performed collectively (*tantra*) at the conclusion of all [the days].
The purpose [of this rule] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no modification (*ūha*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), in the case of the *dvirātra* and other such sacrifices which are modifications of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), whatever other day—whether the second or the third—is performed, it is performed in its entirety after having modified even that portion which, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja*.

*Soma*—Because of the context of the collective whole (*samudāya*), the discussion concerns the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* rites belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which consists of a collection of days; this is the connection (*saṃgati*).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), on the final day, one should perform only the concluding rites such as the *avabhṛtha*, omitting the remainder of the day starting from the *hāriyojana* offering; however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the remainder of the day must also be performed—this is the distinction.
It is enjoined that the principal rites, along with their auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), are to be performed together.

In that context, the preceding subsidiary rites ending with the Agniṣomīya and the subsequent subsidiary rites beginning with the Avabhṛtha are performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Regarding the conclusion at the Patnīsaṃyāja: "Is the conclusion at the Patnīsaṃyāja for all these [sacrifices] or only for some?
Because there is no distinction, the first [view] holds; the other [view] follows from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the statement regarding the non-conclusion."
Bhaṭṭa: It is heard in scripture: "In the Dvādaśāha sacrifice, the days conclude with the Patnīsaṃyājas, for at that time the sacrifice is not yet concluded.

Regarding this, there arises the inquiry: is it enjoined that all twelve days conclude with the Patnīsaṃyājas, or only the last day? Since there is no distinction among the days as being "days," [the injunction applies] to all.

Nor can it be argued that because the non-conclusion of the sacrifice is the reason for concluding with the Patnīsaṃyājas, and since that non-conclusion exists only on the last day, the conclusion with the Patnīsaṃyājas must therefore apply only to that day.
This [statement] cannot serve as a reason, because—like the statement "it is performed on that day"—it is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) and lacks the nature of a logical cause.

Nor can a definitive conclusion be reached by that alone, as in the case of "the pebbles are gravel," because here too there is doubt and thus it lacks the power of determination; furthermore, since the quality [of long duration] must necessarily be supplied, it is impossible for a general injunction to be restricted by an explanatory praise.

Therefore, even as an explanatory praise, it should be interpreted through a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) with the intention of referring to a long-standing state, since it takes many days to accomplish.
But surely—the injunction itself is understood to have the newly initiated [sacrificer] as its object, in accordance with the principle of parsimony regarding restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*).

To explain: since all twelve days are means to a single result, their performance (*prayoga*) is understood to be one; for this very reason, the constituent elements ending with the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice are performed collectively (*tantra*), as are those beginning with the *avabhṛtha* bath and ending with the gratification of the Brahmins.
However, there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the elements denoted by the word "day," in order to maintain the number twelve.

For the word *ahar* (day) is well known among ritualists as referring by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the entire performance of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), which consists of a series of days, beginning from the repetition of the *upāṃśu-graha* and ending with the repetition of the *hāriyojana* sacrifice.

For this very reason, it will be stated that the subsidiaries—both those that provide immediate assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and those that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*)—are repeated equally for each [day] situated within that [period].

And thus, having completed each individual day at whichever point one chooses, another day should be commenced. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the following is established]: the injunction regarding the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* rites becomes a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) for the first eleven days; however, since the entire sacrifice must be concluded on the final day, the injunction regarding the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* rites would result in being an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

And therefore, if it is argued that—since [the injunction] would otherwise result in the anomaly of being both an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) and a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding all purposes—this injunction applies to everyone except the highest caste in accordance with the parsimony of the restrictive injunction; [we reply: because the twelve-fold number requires that the practical application of the term "day" (*ahaḥśabda*) must be repeated until its conclusion, it follows that the completion must occur within whichever subsidiary part belongs to that [repetition], and thus it applies everywhere, as it is indeed an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

Since the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are to be performed by all the *adhvaryu* priests according to the measurement [of the altar] immediately after the *hāriyojana* offering, and because they are to be performed collectively (*tantra*)— like the *avamṛtha* and other rites— they are [included] in the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*). Regarding the disposal of the horns (*viśāṇāprāsana*) during the time of the Soma pressing (*sutyākālīna*) in the multi-day sacrifice, there is a conflict of ritual rules (*dharmavipratiṣedha*).
Because it is stated, "He throws the *ṛjīṣa* into the waters;
he throws [it] into the waters," there would be an option regarding the first day of the ten-day period (*daśarātra*).

Om. In a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), the invocation of the *Subrahmaṇyā* at the time of the Soma-pressing is as follows: in the *agniṣṭoma*, "he scratches with the black antelope horn"—this is the direction [of the rule].
The repetition is performed every day.
His vow,
and that of the black-antelope-horned [girdle]:
it is made from the horn of a black antelope.
However, it should be performed at that specific time, because of its connection with a particular application [in the ritual procedure].
For, according to the scriptural injunction, "When the sacrificial fees have been led forward, he throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit," the throwing is performed.
Regarding the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, however, there is the twelfth [day].

The commentary states: "In that very *dvādaśāha*, at that time, the *subrahmaṇyā* [is performed]; on that day, the throwing away (*prāsana*)—that is, the abandonment—of the *viśāṇā* [horn] occurs. Others say it occurs on the first day."
It would have to be repeated;

it would exist separately. Why? Because with respect to the performance, there would be an option as to whether it is to be performed on that day or not, due to the contradiction of the ritual requirements (dharma).
There would be a connection with a specific [time], namely, "Then come to the Sutyā day.
This is because, on the first day, there would arise the contingency of a contradiction regarding ritual duties (dharma),
if it were restricted by rule to the very first day alone.
It is not stated as "on the joined [day]," "tomorrow," or "the day after.

Even in that case, one should abandon it; then, because of the extension of the archetypal rule (*prakṛtyatideśa*), one must proceed on the second and subsequent days until the sun begins its southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
Therefore, one should repeat it.
Scratching with the horn refers to those ritual acts which are performed facing the east.
If it is argued that this constitutes a repetition of the performance:
The rule is contradicted.
Now, if you think that one must necessarily abandon [the practice] on another day—

[as stated in] the Bhāṣya— "if you see the specification 'today'"— then those items which follow the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) and precede the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) would fall under the former [category].
"That it arises from conjunction" is not tenable. Why? Because the property known as scratching would be contradicted.
Thus, in both ways, there is a contradiction;
this statement "today" is not an injunction,
for it is indeed a prohibition.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the eleventh day is not intended to be expressed, as it is established by the very nature of the matter. It would apply to the horn because it is directly heard in the text regarding the animal's own parts.
Furthermore, because it is not formally accepted, it is not obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
It would apply only as far as stated, because it is intended [to occur] due to being in the middle of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*),
as in "Come to the *sutyā*," so too [is it limited] by "today."
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta) regarding the nature of the Soma-pressing: because this [act] is explicitly stated in scripture (śruti), it is the pressing.
Pāṇi.
It is common to all days;
therefore, it is a *tantra*.
It does not become something that is heard [in the text] or prescribed by the *śruti*.
One should scratch with the hand;
this follows from the instruction regarding the application [of the rule], just as there is a distinction between different agents.
There is no injunction stating that it must be done after the southern solstice.
And therefore it exists.
The Commentary says: "It might be so. Why? Because of the indication in the application [of the rule].
There would be the consequence of contradiction.
Therefore, it should apply to the *viśāṇā* [horn] throughout the entire [series].

Even if the meaning of the word "today" (*adya*) is not intended to be emphasized, nevertheless, on whichever day within the series of days (*ahargaṇa*) the scratching with the *viśāṇā* is prescribed, [that rule would apply].
Therefore, it is employed; it assists the principal rite at that specific time, not one at another time.
On another day, there would be the throwing away.
Because it has the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) in its middle, it is [called] *prātaḥ*—just like the difference in performers.
For example: "In the northern sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*), there are eight oblations; that which has many pressings in its middle is the *prātaḥsavanamadhya* day."
He deposits [the vessels]; let not the Pratiprasthātṛ act thus in the southern group.
Since the morning pressing belongs to the middle, it should be at the tip of the horn.

Thus, because of the difference in location by the Adhvaryu who performs the northern rites, the Marut-vessels are not left over; and even during the time following the southern course, when they remain, they are in the two northern [vessels].
They perform [the acts].
Just as those [acts] assist by virtue of the difference in location, so too this [act of scratching] should belong to the *viśāṇā* alone during the two pressings (*savana*),
because it is intended for that purpose.
Because of the difference in time, that which belongs to another time will not provide assistance;
therefore, it must be repeated.
According to the scripture, the scratching with the horn [is prescribed] until the end of the first day.

If it is argued that [the word] denotes [the object] because it is situated in that [object], we reply: no, because it functions for the sake of that [object] through its exclusion (apavāda) of others;
thus, the intended purport of the scripture is understood. This may be so.
[This is] the state of being.
Therefore, in the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, [the offering] of the horn occurs on a different day.
The Commentary says: "Now, it might be argued:"
The established conclusion is that on a single day, the invocation is performed for the sake of the seat (prāsana).
Why? Because the deity becomes consecrated by the act of invocation.
And it is singular;
in the case of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), the *ṛjīṣa* of all the days is offered in the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
A subsequent invocation would be purposeless.
It is as follows:
just as the Āgneya offerings are not maintained for their purpose by a single kindling, so too [it is] not [the case here].

11|13|134. In a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), there is no further consecration (*saṃskāra*) for a rite that has already been consecrated; rather, it is performed only once. Whatever [consecration] belongs to those days, all of that—without distinction—is performed in the waters at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
And that is incorrect;
for the reason is that there is a cessation of each respective cognition.
In which...
If it is argued that the invocation is performed for the sake of that [deity] which possesses [the quality], because it is enjoined at the end of the ritual action;
[Response:
No, because it is connected with the injunction.
The *pavarga* [group of consonants].
For example, regarding the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of other [sacrificial] days at the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), the commentary states:
"Now, someone might say that here, in the case of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), [the rites such as] the sweeping (*saṃmārjana*) and so forth..."
Therefore, there is repetition. Since the sequence of injunctions is observed, it extends as far as the *vastutīvarī* waters, beginning with the *āsvabhyāditha*.
If it is argued that this [case] is also like the fire-altar (*agni*).
And there is the twelve-day rite.
Therefore, it must be explained that even by giving today [the result] will be so; as it has been said: "Just as the *agredādhāna* [is required] for every ritual act."
The tantra [of the ritual] applies; so it is with this as well.
What is the rebuttal to this?
No, because there is a repetition of the entire procedure, just like the primary act.
The Sūtra says: "It extends up to the word 'āmāpā'.
The Bhāṣya states: "That is not so. Why? Because the entire [mantra] is used again."
No, because it is the substratum for the performance (*prayoga*).

The entire other injunction (*vidhi*) is performed again; this is the commentary on the drawing of the vessels while being pressed: "This is not equal to the act of kindling (*ādhāna*)," because the kindling has its own specific time.
The *camasastotra* and so forth are like the principal [offerings],
because they are principal. Just as, for example, the principal [offerings] are.
For that is performed at its own proper time; no distinction is perceived therein.
Likewise, they are performed every day.
In that case, it might be done once, as in the instance of the *vasatīvarī* waters; however, this is an invocation [performed] at the time of the ritual action.
That [act] is performed at the time of that ritual action;

it may be performed many times, like a *stotra* or other such rites. In that case, because it is characterized by being performed many times for the sake of that purpose, it is not equal to the *ādhāna* (the fire-consecration).
This is the logical principle:
"It benefits all;
for what is done once [benefits all], and because of the observation of indicative marks."
Wherever it is performed, there alone it should provide assistance due to the difference in time;
therefore, there must be repetition.
The Bhāṣya states: "And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) shows this meaning: [the Subrahmaṇyā formula is recited] every day."

Regarding Soma: as before, it is stated that the invitation at the time of the *sutyā* sacrifice is also performed once for all (*tantra*). Thus, he says: "The invitation [is made] at every completion."
[This refers to] the conjunction.

Nor should it be said that for the subsidiary elements performed at the time of the Agniṣṭomīya [sacrifice], there would be a completion [of their effect] upon the completion of that [main sacrifice], such as when one enters the Āgnīdhra shed and issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā!
For even in the case of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), its completion would indeed occur upon the completion of that [main sacrifice].
Thus,
it is for the purpose of the acts of sending and summoning;
therefore, [it should be performed] every day.
It is not because of ignorance and so forth, nor because of being located in the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), but rather it is the very nature of the post itself.
If it is argued that, since the injunction regarding the joints of the post applies there, even for three animals there is but one [post], and therefore it is indeed so; [we reply: no.
In the exclusion of the three types of sacrificial animals, there is the exclusion of ignorance and so forth.
Here, however, the commentary provides the gateway for the invocation: by the word "that" (tat), he refers back to the extraction of the sacrificial post (yūpa).
Because it pertains to the deity, that [post] is one and the same for all the days.

In this regard, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that ritual of bringing the sacrificial post (*yūpāharaṇa-karman*)—just as it serves as a *tantra* (common procedure) in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*)—will likewise serve as such for each day on which it is performed, until its completion.
What, then, is the similarity between that [eleven-post rite] and this [single-post rite]? That [is the similarity].
Because it is logical that liberation (apavarga) occurs through the cleansing of the fire and so forth;

for the rite being performed takes place in the vicinity of some sacrificial post (yūpa), and since proximity to all [posts] simultaneously is difficult to obtain, the invocation at the time of the Soma-pressing (sutyā) should be a single common performance (tantra), as it would otherwise be divided.

Just as for a certain individual, there is either a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or else, due to the bringing of the posts, there is a common procedure (*tantra*); yet, due to the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), there is a distinction.
Just as [an act] performed in the proximity of one person is for the sake of all, so too is this [case].

Bhaṭṭa: However, the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā at the time of the Soma-pressing (sutyā) in a multi-day sacrifice (ahargaṇa), though performed in the proximity of a particular ritual action of a certain Soma-offering, is for the sake of all;
because it is a specific [ritual] element, it must be repeated at each pressing.
The *savaniya* and other offerings will take place at the time of the *sutyā*;
it is not as in the case of the *antarvat*.
Furthermore, even when words such as "today" (*adya*) and so forth are employed, there is no lack of refinement, because [the usage] follows the logic of the other [standard rules].
This point is now determined.
Nor is it the case that the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing) has a single scriptural mention in the archetype; this is not comparable to that.
Why? Because of its distinctness.

Because of this, the meaning of "today" (*adya*) is not intended to be expressed; [the injunction] is "come to the *sutyā*," and here there is no oblation near the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Proximity is not intended, because by that very [injunction], the manner of arrival at the time of the *sutyā* is appropriately revealed. Thus, it is argued that "today" is for the purpose of prohibiting [arrival] at the *āhvayanīya* [fire], or else it is a prohibition of the other [times].

The word *padasya* is redundant because [the meaning] has already been stated by the phrase "sutyādīti" through this repetition (11|12|27). Furthermore, because the regions (*deśānām*) are not prescribed by scripture (*aśāstratvāt*), one must assume that they possess a head [of the sacrifice].
And for this reason, there is a distinction of days according to the difference in the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing) (21|29).
Because of the logic of "the other" (*itaranyāyatvāt*).

Here, the logic is from the other side. Due to the difference [in the deities], because they must necessarily be recited, and because of the difference in time for the manifestation of the days following the *sutyā*, there must be an oblation for that specific distinction being grasped.
Repetition is indeed necessary because of the impossibility [of otherwise];
and it is precisely for the purpose of explaining this statement that these aphorisms (*sūtra*) have been presented.

Otherwise, since the bringing down of the Soma (*somopāvaharaṇa*) in a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*) would already be established by the principle of the *savaniya* and others to be described later— according to the maxim of the path of those who do not cause injury (*ahiṃsukair vartanyāya*)—
and since the repetition of the number of the threads (*sūtrasaṃkhyā*) is thereby accomplished, this would have been treated as a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that, since the *apūrva*s of the *savanīya* and other offerings require the application of their respective *apūrva*s, and since this requirement cannot be fulfilled through *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) when those [offerings] arise independently, there must be repetition even if such repetition is otherwise possible; for in the present case, because the deity is one, it is logical that all assistance is provided by *prasaṅga* through the single invocation and consecration performed once. Thus, how can there be repetition? This is what must be addressed.

Since the invocation (āvāhana) does not exist in its own form [as a physical act], it consists merely of the recollection of the deity; and because this visible benefit perishes at that very moment, the impression (saṃskāra) produced by it is also destroyed by the recollection of the deity occurring at the time of the primary sacrifice. Consequently, the principle of "extended application" (prasaṅga) would be untenable. For this very reason, in cases where the impression produced by the recollection of the deity of the animal sacrifice has not yet perished—because the recollection of the deities of the subsequent sacrifices, such as those of the heart and other parts, is yet to occur—there indeed exists the principle of extended application in the case of the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa).

Nor should it be argued that since it is established in common worldly experience (*loka*) that the very recollection of a subsequent [deity] destroys the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding cognition, and since that [impression] is destroyed by the recollection of the deity of the *vapā*-sacrifice itself, how could there be a case of "extended application" (*prasaṅga*)?

For if that were the case, then because that [impression] would be destroyed by the recollection of the deity of the final *prayāja* itself, the invocation (*āhvāna*) could not logically function as an auxiliary to the primary sacrifice.

Therefore, what is to be abandoned is the following: the recollection of the deity belonging to the primary sacrifice is the destroyer of that which is delimited by the nature of the latent impression produced by it.

And since this delimitedness [of the function] occurs through the relation of *paryāpti* (inherence), it is logical that there is no destruction of that [delimitedness] by the recollection of the deity associated with the offering of the omentum (*vapā*); thus, the principle of *prasaṅga* (extension) applies.
Regarding this, the *Prakṛtabhāṣya* states, concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: "There are three [sets of] seventeen [verses] for the *sadas*; twelve for the *ahīna*."
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the state of having twelve attendants (upasads) belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma, or to the Ahīna?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Why? Because of the context.
In this way, the context is upheld;
nor is it contradicted by the sentence.
It is not contradicted.
By the word *ahīna*, we shall refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma. Why? Because it is not deficient (*na hīyate*), thus it is *ahīna*.
It is not deficient in terms of sacrificial fees, ritual procedures, or its fruit.
By that, the Jyotiṣṭoma is an Ahīna sacrifice.
The word "or" (vā) removes doubt.
Or—whatever matter was promised at the beginning of the chapter, all of that has been established.

Why is there no distinction now, such that the fourth characteristic is not commenced? To this it is said: "Henceforth, the subject matter is being refined by showing that there is no conflict between the rules regarding relative strength and the means of knowledge, such as direct audition (śruti) and the rest."

In this regard, first the conflict and non-conflict of *prakaraṇa* (context) with *śruti* (direct statement), *liṅga* (indicative mark), and *vākya* (syntactical connection) are deliberated upon (by means of the text ending with the section 3.6.6).
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard: "Only three [sessions] are to be performed for the *sadas*; twelve for the *ahīna*.

In that context, by the word *sāhasra*, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is understood because it is completed in a single day (*aha*), as in the expression "they conclude it together with the day"; thus, its status as a *nyūpasat* (one with fewer sessions) is established.
Regarding the phrase "of the *ahīna*," a doubt arises as to whether the state of having twelve [upasad days] belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma or to the *ahīna*, such as the Dvādaśāha and others.
If the word *ahīna* can somehow be applied to the Jyotiṣṭoma as well, then, because there is no contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would be placed within that very [sacrifice].

However, if *ahīna* is the name for a group of sacrificial days (*ahargaṇa*), then, because it is already occupied by direct statement (*śruti*), it is not included in the context, since the nature of the context is to take up what is not already connected [by another means of proof].

For at that time, there is indeed a conflict between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*). What is the prima facie view? We maintain, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), that the context—set aside by the word "or" (*vā*) from the opening—is for the sake of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Nor is there a conflict with the direct statement; for precisely because of the context, the term "Ahīna" also pertains to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Furthermore, there is the capacity for denoting that [meaning] through the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*).

Therefore, although the Vārttika "In the case of a sacrifice, *kha* follows *ahan*" was cited under Pāṇini 4.2.43— "The suffix *kha* follows *ahan* when referring to a collection of seasons" (the Siṃhakaumudī,
however, cites the Vārttika as "In the case of a sacrifice, *kha* follows *ahan*")— [it is nevertheless established].

Although the word *ahīna*— derived from the rule "a collection thereof" (*tasya samūhaḥ*) under the heading of "collections"— is thus established as denoting a group of sacrificial days (*ahargaṇa*), nevertheless, for the sake of resolving the contradiction, its application to the Jyotiṣṭoma must be justified on the basis of its connection with the quality of being "non-deficient" (*ahīna*).
For that [Jyotiṣṭoma], because it is fully prescribed and because it is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of all [sacrifices], is not deficient in any respect whatsoever.
Furthermore, no seasons whatsoever abandon it as their material cause (*prakṛti*).

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that "it is not deprived [of its nature] by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or by the performance of the ritual acts (*kratukaraṇa*)"—that is irrelevant; for the sacrificial fee and the performance of the ritual acts are not adopted as the causes for the realization (*pratipatti*) [of that nature].
Or, because there would be the consequence of an unstable meaning for the compound if one were to conceptualize it according to one's own whim;

and because even that which is performed with a thousand sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) would not be deficient, since the number of verses such as the *ṛk* and others is stated to be subject to modification even when the sacrifice is being performed,
due to the deficiency of the *agniṣṭoma* configuration.
Therefore, because it is not abandoned by this [defect] nor deprived of anything by it, it is called *ahīna* (unabandoned).

It is called *gauṇa* (secondary) because it is so designated through its connection with these qualities by virtue of the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*), and not because it relies upon being secondary.
Since there is no connection with the primary [meaning], it is therefore extracted [from the context].
Commentary: It is set aside from that which has twelve *upasads*. Why? Because of the lack of connection with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
How is there no connection? Because the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the *Ahīna* sacrifice is directly perceived.
Is it not the case that the Jyotiṣṭoma itself is the secondary (gauṇa) Ahīna?
No, it is replied;
for when the primary sense is possible, one ought not to accept a secondary sense.
[Objection: But surely it will be a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*).
[Response: No, we say;
for if that were the case, the word *ahīna* would have its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).
The accent of the word *ahīna* itself is udātta on the middle syllable;
therefore, setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*), this is a property of the *ahīna*.
Furthermore, there is a specific designation: "There are indeed three [sets of] seventeen [verses] for the *sāhnas*, but twelve for the *ahīna*."
If the *sāh* were one thing and the *ahīna* another, then such a designation would be possible;
and indeed, there exists a statement of such a designation. Therefore, it belongs to the *ahīna*.
Or rather: "The *mukhya* [sacrifice] is designated as such in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* because it is the primary performance;
however, this designation does not apply to it in any way when there is a connection with the term *ahīna*.
And since it is not connected with that [term], whatever number is associated with it [the *mukhya*] remains linked to that [number]."
That [number] is not removed from him by that [context],
because it is connected to the *ahīna* by the direct statement of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-śruti*) as being twelvefold;
for the collection of days belonging to the *ahīna* is indeed included within the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
As for the claim that "the qualities apply there," he refutes it by means of an analysis:
if, first of all, it is said to be "secondary" (gauṇa) because it functions through metaphorical application (*upacāra*), then it is not proper to conclude its meaning in accordance with the context.

Nor is this for the purpose of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), whereby it might be metaphorically applied as being praiseworthy even in a single-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), just like a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no other word for this [term] by which it could be explained through etymological difficulty, as is the case with the collection of qualities belonging to a lion.
Therefore, its status as a metaphorical usage (apacārika) is first of all untenable.
Nor can there be an etymological derivation of the parts via a negative compound (nañ-samāsa), because that is precluded by the established conventional meaning of the whole.
Furthermore, a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) would not have its final syllable unaccented according to the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* (Pāṇini 6.2.2);
however, this word is recited as having an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Therefore, it ends in the suffix *kh*.

For if that were the case, when the substitution of *ī* is applied according to the rule "in *āyana* and so forth, *ī* is substituted for the sake of establishing the correct accent," the accent on the vowel *ī* would be established by virtue of the acute accent (*udātta*) belonging to the suffix.
Therefore, this is the name of a *ahargaṇa* (a multi-day sacrifice).
Furthermore, even if a connection with the number twelve were not assumed through the word *sāhasra*, the mention of the term *ahīna* makes it known that this treatise refers to a different meaning.
Since the connection between the *sāha* and the *dvādaśāha* is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), both terms—*sāha* and *ahīna*—could apply.
However, if they have different meanings, then the term *ahīna* must necessarily be adopted [for the twelve-day sacrifice].

Consequently, because of its endlessness (*ānantya*), the connection of the number three with that [twelve-day sacrifice] would also inevitably follow; thus, the mention of the *sāha* is meaningful for the sake of establishing a restriction.
"Therefore, it is a displacement" (tasmād apakarṣaḥ).
(Having thus explained the section [adhikaraṇa] according to the Bhāṣya, he states his own view: "But indeed, this is not logical.

For the injunction of another attribute within the context of something else serves a different purpose; or rather, because of the difficulty of reconnecting a context that has been interrupted by two unrelated words; and furthermore, because 'twelve upasads' is enjoined in the context of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha), it applies to all *ahīna* sacrifices by virtue of being their archetype (*prakṛti*)."

Therefore, it is precisely the state of being three that is enjoined in this sentence, because it is free from all defects; whereas the state of being twelve, already established by another sentence concerning the *ahīna* sacrifice, is merely restated here in the form of a contextual propriety for the purpose of praise, like the *nivīta* and other such examples. How, then, should this section (*adhikaraṇa*) be interpreted? It is said: "Just as the *jyotiṣṭoma* possesses the character of an *ahīna*, so this must be an injunction [of the number three]."
In the case of the *ahargaṇa*, however, this [mention] is stated for the purpose of praising it.

What is meant is this: Is this [rite] enjoined by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) as belonging to the *jyotiṣṭoma*—which is an *ahīna* sacrifice—or rather to the *ahargaṇa*; and in the latter case, is it merely restated because it is already established for another purpose?

Now, if this were so, then even the connection with the *ahargaṇa* would be employed for the purpose of praising the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and consequently, since there would be no conflict regarding the context, the aforementioned inquiry would not arise.
This is not a fault.
For in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) is accepted as the enabler (*grāhaka*) of the twelvefold nature being enjoined;
however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the context is not desired for that which is connected with the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), it is set aside (*bādhyate*).
Now, as for the objection that even though this is so, it might be applicable to the context in another manner:

if, by the principle of duality and plurality (3.1.9), one were somehow to resort to "extraction" (*utkarṣa*), and if, despite there being an injunction for another ritual manual (*śālā*), the status of that other manual as an injunction could be justified as lacking any other purpose, then it would be possible to justify [the position] exactly as stated in the Bhāṣya.
In any case, it is established that the phrase "of the twelve-day [sacrifice] which is an *ahīna*" is extracted from the context because its scope is restricted to groups of days (*ahargaṇa*).
Śā—In that case, its status as a subsidiary to the Jyotiṣṭoma is understood from the context;
moreover, the word *ahīna* itself occurs there in the sense of "not deficient" (*na hīna*).
This being the position reached, we reply:

First, it is understood that *ahīna* has a distinct meaning from "day" (*aha*). If it is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), then it applies to the *dvirātra* and other sacrifices; moreover, conventional usage is stronger than etymological derivation (*yoga*).
Even if it were etymological there too, it would apply specifically to the *satra* because of its connection with that alone.
This word *mayodāttaṃ* ends with the suffix *kh*.

Soma: "The definition of the final [element] regarding the matter promised in the first sūtra of this chapter is now the occasion for discussion; thus, there is a connection by way of occasion (*avasara-saṅgati*).

By the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthatṛtīyāsaptamyupamānāvyayadvitīyākṛtyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.2), it is prescribed that in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) is maintained for those words beginning with indeclinables (*avyaya*) when they function as the prior member (*pūrvapada*).
The term "original accent" (*prakṛtisvaratva*) refers to that accent which belongs to words in their state prior to compounding; even when they are in a compound, they retain that same accent.

Consequently, in this case, if the negative particle *nañ*, as the first member of the compound, were to have its original accent—being acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the rules "particles are acute on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*) and "prepositions, with the exception of *ā*, [are acute on the first]" (*upasargāścāmivarja*)—then the same fault would apply to the compound. However, since the entire word *itaratva* would be grave (*anudātta*), except for one syllable, according to the rule "a word is grave except for one [acute] syllable" (*anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam*, Pāṇini 6.1.158), the word *ahīna* would instead be acute on the first syllable.

[Objection: But surely, by the rule *ādyudāttaśca*, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) prescribed in connection with the suffixal portion occurs precisely before the substitution of *īn* because it is an internal element (*antaḥstha*); consequently, in a form ending in the suffix *kha*, there would be only a final acute accent (*antodāttatva*), not an acute accent on the *mā* [portion]. [Response: This is not so; for in the case of those substitutes such as *āyan* and others prescribed by the rule *āyaneyīnīyaḥ* etc., [the acute accent is established] by the principle that "in the case of substitutes beginning with *āyan* etc., the accent is established from the original instruction (*upadeśa*). Here, "instruction" (*upadeśa*) refers to the original formative process.
It is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
For all other sacrifices are taught as having a specific injunction (*pratyayopadeśa*).

That which possesses such an injunction is "possessing an injunction" (*upadeśī*); because they are modifications (*vikṛti*), they do not abandon their dependence on it, being equal to that which possesses the injunction.
Now, [the term] "upadeśivat" (like the instructor) is used in the sense that "this [person] does not act [in that way].

Therefore, the expression "upadeśivat" is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). Since it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in that case, for the sake of establishing the correct accent, the substitution of *īn* [for the suffix *vat*] must be applied according to the rule: "In a *tatpuruṣa*, [the substitute] should be applied after words meaning 'equal' (*tulyārtha*), after the third and seventh cases, after words denoting the object of comparison (*upamāna*), and after the second case. Thus, [the form is derived].

Thus, by the traditional rule (*smṛti*)—or rather, by the instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding the teaching of suffixes (*pratyaya*)—and because the substitution of *ī* occurs precisely at the stage when the technical name "suffix" (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*) has been applied to the item following the rule "the preceding member [is treated] as a stem" (*prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*), which includes the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) [of that rule], the accentuation of the acute (*udātta*) is prescribed for the compound whose prior member is negated (*nañ-pūrvapada*) based on its designation as a "stem" (*prakṛti-svara*). Consequently, although the acuteness is ordained in conjunction with the initial acuteness (*ādyudātta-saṃniyoga*), it would result in the vowel *ī* being acute. However, since [the word] *ahīna* is actually acutely accented in the middle (*madhyodātta*), it is correct that the middle-accented nature of the word *ahīna* follows from the rule "in the sense of a sacrifice (*kratu*), [the word] *ahaḥ* becomes *ah-*" (*ahaḥ svaḥ kratau*). Thus, the middle-accented status of the word *ahīna* is justified.
Regarding the ritual acts:

in the case of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, since the days are indicated by the collective term "Pauṇḍarīka," the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), being enjoined as a subordinate quality (guṇa), would have to be repeated for each primary element (pratipradhānam).
This is the prima facie (pūrva) position.
Because the whole [sacrifice] constitutes a single unit.
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—ten thousand cows and one thousand horses—should belong to the entire Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice consisting of eleven nights, not to each individual day.
This is because the Pauṇḍarīka is a single unit; it is a single unit.
It is "one action" (*ekakarma*) because it is a single action due to its being of such a nature;
or else, it is "due to the unity of action" (*aikakarmyāt*) because the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) perform a single function in the form of hiring the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

It is called "action" (*karma*) because it is performed (*kriyate*); those sacrificial fees which have a single action—a single task in the form of hiring the priests—are "those having one action" (*ekakarmāṇaḥ*); the state of having one action is "unity of action" (*aikakarmyam*), and [the rule applies] because of that—such is the analysis of the compound.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are intended for a single purpose, there is only one fee for the whole.
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Alternatively, it may be said that the recitation of the *guṇa-śastra* is like that of the *pṛṣṭhya* and other [stotras].
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies again:

"In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, there is the scriptural injunction regarding the subsidiary element of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), namely 'one thousand horses and ten thousand cows'; this [injunction] should apply to the eleven [days], since there is a requirement for each day."
In this context of expectancy, immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is not the cause.
For the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is established only when the meanings of the individual words have been understood everywhere, and not otherwise.
A word functions with reference to a general sense (*sāmānyavṛtti*), whereas a sentence functions with reference to a specific sense (*viśeṣavṛtti*).
The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is that which consists in the particularization of word-meanings (*padārtha*) that have been presented in a general manner.

This has been stated [in the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "The collection of those [word-meanings] already existing [as generalities] with an action-meaning is for the sake of the [sentence] meaning, because that [meaning] is caused by them" (1.1.25).
In this regard, the word-meaning is perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the sentence-meaning, moreover, is inferential (*anumānika*).

Therefore, let this be understood: a word by itself does not convey the meaning; rather, it must be accepted as forming a single syntactical unit with another proximate word, and not otherwise. (Bhāṣya 3.1.12, pp. 688–89). When expectancy exists, mere proximity is not the cause [of syntactic connection], as in the example: "The king’s wife, Devadatta’s man."
In a single sentence, there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for that which constitutes a part of it;
for example, in the phrase "He goes on horseback with a white cloth, [like] a falcon. A horse that is not required [by the context] cannot serve as a qualifier for the falcon.

Bhāṣya 6.4.123, p. 1443: When there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), a word known to be in proximity and capable of fulfilling that expectancy becomes a qualifier of a specific part [of the whole]. Ṛjuvimalā, p. 71: When there is expectancy—as in the case of the injunction "one should cleanse the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*)—it would be intended [to be expressed]. And that expectancy arises with respect to things being enjoined (*upādīyamāna*), not with respect to things being merely referred to (*uddiśyamāna*).

For when [a word] is being taught, there is no expectancy for number because it depends merely on its connection with the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and so forth, since its existence is already known from other means of knowledge. (Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 723). Context (*prakaraṇa*) consists in expectancy.
(Sūtra 3.1.7–14, p. 829). This is because connection is based upon expectancy.

Su. Pṛ. 525: In every case, a relationship occurs preceded by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Vā. 2.1.13, p. 409: In the absence of expectancy, it is improper to restrict the meaning of a word according to the [literal] sequence of the mantra. For a mantra is subordinate to the ritual act (*padārtha*) insofar as it reveals that act at the time of its performance.
*Parākrama*, p. 43. "The state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) has expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as its root" (*Vārttika* 3.1.14, p. 829).

Expectancy, semantic competency (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) are the factors that cause the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) in what is called the "theory of expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣāmūlavākya*); the fact of being expressed by a word (*śabdopāttatva*) is not [a requirement].

For if it were so, there would follow the undesirable consequence that an archetypal auxiliary (*prākṛtopakāraka*) not denoted by a word could not be denoted as related by a modified injunction (*vaikṛtavidhi*) (this is according to the Prābhākara method).

Soma. 5.1.1, Section 3: Because of the presence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), semantic competency (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhi*), a sentence (*vākya*)—being capable of fulfilling its own expectancy—is a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*).
And that which has been previously perceived requires a subsequent [element] that is either concordant with itself or additional.

(Vākyapadīya 3.1.12, p. 806). For when there is a connection of meaning, the cause of the requirement for meaning is neither subordination nor non-subordination, as seen in such examples as "whose teacher's family?
(Bṛhatī, p. 71).

When there arises the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to whose teacher’s family [is meant], the relation is seen through the qualifiers of the teacher’s family, such as Devadatta and others, [resulting in the understanding]: "Devadatta’s.
Regarding "expectation": for once one [word] has satisfied the expectation, another will not expect it;
rather, it expects because of its own lack of meaning [if left alone].
And because it is augmented by one [element] and not otherwise, therefore the other does not require it.
Bhāṣya 2.1.16–18, p. 457. "Context" (prakaraṇa) is the statement of that which requires a manner of performance (kartavyatā).

"How" (*katham*) is explained as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhanta*), meaning "the desire for the manner of the means of favor" (*anugrahopāyākāṅkṣaṇa*). Alternatively, it is explained as "that which desires the procedure" (*itikartavyatām ākāṅkṣati*), thus forming the compound *itikartavyatākāṅkṣa*; this refers to one [aspect] of the two, namely the efficient force (*bhāva*) and the apūrva. The word "its" (*tasya*) is construed in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇe*) with that.
"Speech" (*vacana*) means communication by means of words.
What is meant is this: even though expectancy exists as a property of the thing itself (*vasturūpa*), it is not designated as "context" (*prakaraṇa*); rather, it is that which is being cognized.
And even that [expectancy] is grasped as something to be accomplished (*kartavyatā*) because it is non-human in origin, not through its own independence.

Therefore, when expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is being expressed, it should be understood that either the context possesses expectancy, or the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) possesses expectancy. (Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 892). Furthermore, connection is preceded by expectancy;
and this [expectancy] is seen to extend forth from words denoting action (*bhāva*), not from words denoting substance (*dravya*) or quality (*guṇa*).

2|1|12, p. 376: "When something is heard in proximity to that which has expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and it is capable of fulfilling [that expectancy] either from above or below, it becomes a syntactical supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*).
(Bhāṣya 2|1|16–18, p. 454). "And that which is capable of fulfilling an expectancy enters into a state of relationship.
(Bṛhatī, p. 71). This is the principle known as *ākāṅkṣitavidhāna-nyāya*.
The meaning of the logical principle is that only what is required (*ākāṅkṣita*) is supplied, not what is unrequired (*anākāṅkṣita*).

As for the statement by the Mīmāṃsakas—that the grammatical rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) is the indicator of the expressive power (*śaktigrāhaka*) [of the suffixes]—that too is merely superficial.

This is a supplementary rule (*kudākyaśeṣaḥ*) that applies to [suffixes] such as the masculine endings whose referents are not explicitly specified, but it does not apply to [suffixes] such as *śatṛ*, because—as will be stated in the Mīmāṃsākoṣa (p. 98)—they are already satisfied by their own original forms (*sthānin*).

The principle that "the rule applies to what is required" (ākāṅkṣitavidhānaṃ nyāyaḥ) is established by the maxim [stated] in the *Vyākaraṇakaustubha*, in the section on *sphoṭa*: "The maxim of the prescription of what is required."

It should not be argued that, "Just as one brings [the fee] like the *bhṛti* (wages) for the initiated (*dīkṣita*), this [act] is a refinement of the substance (*dravyasaṃskāra*) by way of obtaining the substance; and since the substance exists, the mention of it as a condition (*nimitta*) would be purposeless, so by the logic of supplying what is required (*ākāṅkṣitavidhi*), it is appropriate to treat it as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) due to the necessity of the purpose. This is because prescribing what is not required is a fault, as it necessitates the postulation of a result (*phalakalpanā*). (Bhaṭṭa 6.1.16). Furthermore, since shape (*ākāra*)—which is synonymous with the arrangement of constituent parts and configuration—is essentially a particular dimension (*parimāṇaviśeṣa*), it is an attribute (*guṇa*) and, being incorporeal (*amūrta*), is equal to a genus (*jāti*).
Su. pṛ. 1029. Space, though eternal and existent, is likewise covered by earth and water;
it is manifested through their removal by means of digging, draining, and so forth.
Consequently, even in that case, cognition following upon effort is observed.
Now, even though this [space] is covered, it is inferred to belong to that very same [space].

Bhāṣya 1.1.15, p. 82: "The auditory organ (*śrotra*) is simply the single space (*ākāśa*) delimited by the ear-canal. It may be so. Straightforwardly (Ṛju-pṛ., p. 76): because space is one, that which is the auditory space here is the very same in another location as well.
