Even so, for one who is unable to refute the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), there is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in refuting something else established by that [opponent], because it does not prove [one's own position]. For he will say: "Let it be refuted; if it is refuted, what of it? Whether it is refuted or not refuted, your subject has been proven by you. Does my own thesis become refuted? No—it is neither."

And since no forest is perceived apart from the trees, it is understood that the forest does not exist. If, even when the forest has arisen due to some other cause, the cognition [of it] arises, then we understand that the cognition of a "forest" is indeed false, and consequently that the forest does not exist.
Furthermore, the cognition regarding cows and so forth does not undergo reversal; therefore, there is no error.

Furthermore, it is not the case that [the universal] does not exist at all in forests and so forth, nor is it that they do not exist there. Therefore, the objection regarding the mention of a "row" is irrelevant. Consequently, Jaimini’s statement that "the word-meaning is the form (ākṛti)" is established.
"And as to how the form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of a word, we shall demonstrate that more precisely later on (1.3.9.33).
(Bṛhatī on 1.1.5, pp. 49–52): "'Now, what is the meaning of this word "cow"?'—this question [in the Bhāṣya] is not tenable."
Then, the question "What is this word *gauh*? is appropriate;
for even on the view that the word consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), denotative capacity is not established, and so on, in order to refute what was previously stated.

But regarding the denoted object, there is no distinction whether it be the form (*ākṛti*), the individual (*vyakti*), or a quality (*guṇa*); for there is no contradiction whatsoever in its being innate (*autpattika*).

And this position—that the denotata of words consist of the configuration (*ākṛti*), the quality (*guṇa*), and the individual (*vyakti*)—is not the established doctrine (*rāddhānta*) of the Mīmāṃsakas. For they maintain that all words denote only the configuration;
furthermore, the denotation of a quality is observed in cases such as "red" (*aruṇā*).

(Ṛju—Objection: Since there is a distinction among the various qualities such as redness (*aruṇa*) and so forth, it is appropriate to admit a single universal (*sāmānya*); otherwise, the application of words would be untenable. To this, it is replied:)
Whether a thing is different or non-different is bound up with the establishment of its appearance as different or non-different.
In that regard, first of all, there is no cognition of difference in the case of [colors such as] red and so forth.

Furthermore, even that cognition qualified by distinctions such as intensity or dullness does not bring about a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*), because it pertains merely to the distinction itself.
[Objection: Surely, redness and the like are produced by heating (*pākaja*) among earth-atoms, and in all effect-substances they are preceded by the qualities of their causes;
thus, it is determined that this is merely a case of production (*utpatti*).
[Reply: It is not so.
Regarding the question of "in what does inherence reside?", [the opponent] says: "Just like a universal (ākṛti), a quality inheres in a substance.
We, however, maintain that this inherence of qualities arises and passes away for something in some manner;
nor do we accept that even inherence is eternal and unitary.

Therefore, since [the word] *go* applies to all individual substances (*dravya*), and since it is to be understood by us and others as referring to individuals such as the reddish-brown cow (*aruṇā*) and so forth—just as in the case of "the one pointed out" (*uddiṣṭa*) and other examples—the claim that it denotes the individual (*vyaktivacanatā*) has been established.
Consequently, the question is useless with respect to the true nature of the matter;
furthermore, the answer—that "the form (*ākṛti*) qualified by the dewlap and so forth [is denoted]"—contradicts the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).
But it should rather be stated as "due to form and so forth. Now, if the intention is that the example itself constitutes the intended meaning,
then in this case too, both the question and the answer regarding the true nature [of the matter] are entirely purposeless.

If [the universal] is distinct from the word, or even if it is the universal itself, is the relation a particular? And if there is an intention to express a particular, the purpose must be stated. Now, if it is also argued that under the theory of individuals (vyaktipakṣa) the relation would necessarily involve dependence on something else, what need is there to mention the theory of forms (ākṛtivāda)?
The theory of form applies to cases such as "cook" and the like.
If it is argued that in those cases the action is perceived, then here too there will be a form.

If it is argued that in that case [the verb], the action is expressed by the verbal root portion, whereas here [in words such as *go*], the genus (*jāti*) is not expressed and is therefore incapable of serving as a qualifier—let it be granted that there is expression; however, we do not see its utility either in an expression that is dependent or in one that is independent. Therefore, the question and answer are of little purpose. To this, it is replied:

Thinking that comprehension arises from the denotative capacity itself in all sentences, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) asked, "The non-difference between word and meaning is not tenable.

[The opponent] replied: "Previously, it was concluded that the letters alone, beginning with 'ga' and ending with the visarga, constitute the word. Disregarding that, the proponent of the prima facie view asks: 'Now, what is the meaning of this word "gauḥ" (cow)?'"
The word "forest" (*vana*), ending in the singular number, is not appropriate when it refers to many trees;
it is appropriate when its denoted object is the form of the word itself.
Therefore, in all sentences, comprehension consists solely of the expressive form.
In this regard, if the word (*pada*) were of the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*), then there would necessarily follow the absence of a clear distinction [between words].
Therefore, this reality of speech (*śabdatattva*) is something entirely different.
Consequently, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya: "What is the object intended by you for the word 'cow' (*gaur*); is it distinct from the sound, such that you say it is merely the phonemes?"

And here, no denial of external objects is being made, as that has already been established. Rather, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that what is denoted by a word is not distinct from the word itself.

However, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*)—noting that in this context there is a single [entity] both in its application and its denotation, and that the conceptual cognition arising from application determines the object of denotation—stated that "it is the form (*ākṛti*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth" in order to refute that [prima facie view].
This is stated merely for the sake of illustration, like the term *abhidhāna*.

For this grammarian who holds the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), there is a lack of discrimination regarding what is correct in terms of usage (*prayoga-sādhū*) and what is correct in terms of meaning (*artha-sādhū*).
He does not distinguish in this way: "That which is correct in terms of usage is employed only when it is correct in terms of meaning."
"Usage is correct even when used without the object [intended].
Therefore, the conventional usage (*prāyogikī*) determines the innate understanding (*bhāvikā buddhiḥ*) regarding correctness within the usage with respect to the denotable object.
Let it be so; indeed, the thing to be designated (*anyapadārtha*) is certainly distinct from the word itself.

Regarding the denotable object (*abhidheya*), however, the other proponent—the Siddhāntin—speaks of "the form (*ākṛti*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth" in order to demonstrate another denotable object consisting of sound, while taking into account a distinction within that which consists of sound.
This is for the sake of illustration, just like the term "form.

Just as in the case of the word "cow," where "denotation" (*abhidhāna*) is used as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) to include other words as well, so too "form" is an indicative mark, and individual instances (*vyakti*) and the rest should also be understood as included.

[The opponent] stated that [the universal] does not abandon its nature as a word by virtue of being denotable, [in response to the question]: "Is the universal something to be established, or is it not? [That is to say: "It is not said that the universal does not exist in its own form; rather, it is said that it does not exist as a word-form by virtue of being denotable.

[Objection: But what is the purpose of stating its non-existence in terms of that [word-]form? [For] according to the Bhāṣya, the non-existence of the universal is indeed propounded by the passage "Does it exist or not? and that is not logical. It should rather be stated thus: "The universal is nothing other than the very form of the word."
[The author] refutes [this]: this "non-existence" (abhāva) mentioned was stated with reference to the denotable object (*abhidheya*), not with reference to its own nature (*svarūpa*).

For it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* whether the genus (*jāti*) of the denotable object exists as something distinct from the word or not; it is not, however, stated whether it exists or not by way of its own nature.
[As the *Bhāṣya* says: "Being perceptible, it cannot be something to be proven (*sādhya*)."
If, on the other hand, non-existence itself were established by its own nature, then only would there be inexpressibility (of the external form;
for when it exists, that very thing must be expressible).
And non-existence cannot be spoken of, because it is accessible through direct perception.
"If it is argued that this is a misconception," [the opponent asks].

"By whom was it said that its absence exists in its own nature? (The proponent replies: "It was not by me that the absence of the universal is stated in terms of its own nature; rather, it is stated precisely in terms of its own nature.
That very [absence] is what is being denoted—thus, [your objection] is indeed a misconception."

The other (the proponent of the final view), however, keeping that very intention (previously stated: "it is not logical to deny the denoted object without denying its essential nature") in mind, says: "If there were no subversion of cognition regarding this denoted object 'forest,' then a single cognition would not be possible. Can it be said that even the trees, which are objects of perception, do not exist?

What is the intended meaning? (It is replied: It is the trees themselves that are perceived here as a unity; they are not, however, perceived in the form of the word 'forest' (for when the word 'forest' is uttered, it is the trees themselves that are perceived)."
In this regard, the Bhavanas argue as follows: "There is no object distinct from the word. If that were so, it would follow that [objects] do not even exist in perception itself;

yet this is not tenable, because those things which exceed the word are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Alternatively, if the intention is that "even trees do not exist at all," then that Mahāyāna position is refuted by the fact that the very nature of the tree is nothing other than the word.
For it has been stated that perceptual consciousness has external objects as its domain, not the intellect (*buddhi*) as its domain.

Or, if consciousness were to have the intellect as its object, what would be established regarding the superimposition of sound and so forth? (For if one wishes to refute the superimposition of sound and so forth, one must refute that consciousness has the intellect as its object. The consciousness of a tree is one thing, and the consciousness of a forest is another. (If the consciousness of a tree and the consciousness of a forest were one and the same, then this consciousness would not [be distinct] when it has the intellect as its object.)

If even a universal (*sāmānya*) were to be a real entity (*vastu*), then it too would necessarily be either distinct or denotable by a distinct name; yet neither of these two possibilities is feasible. Therefore, [it follows that] it is not a real entity. By speaking in this manner, one must admit that "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) is itself a universal.

Otherwise, how could it be possible to state that "because the property of being a real entity (*vastutva*) is pervaded by both difference and non-difference, the reality of a universal is not possible due to the non-perception of its pervader"? [Objection: But the word "real entity" is based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), not caused by a genus (*jāti*); so how can this [universal] be subject to the application of that genus?
[Reply: It is said:
Whether it be a genus (*jāti*) or something adventitious (*aupādhika*), in any case, a common form must necessarily be admitted;
for even among adventitious properties, there can be no manifestation of their own nature without a single underlying basis that characterizes them.

Furthermore, for the Buddhist who maintains that the entire collection of things is exclusively differentiated (*vyāvṛtta*), no persisting form whatsoever is possible anywhere; thus, conventional usage based on adventitious factors is simply untenable.
Therefore, the universal, which is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be denied. What, then, is the refutation of this conceptual construction?
It is not that those [particulars], even if not refuted, are able to deny the universal; for it has already been stated that they too are dependent upon it.
Nevertheless, a rebuttal is stated:
regarding the dilemma of difference and non-difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), some say that the universal is indeed distinct from the individuals.

Nor does it follow that there would be a perception [of the universal] as separate [from the individual], because it resides in the individual. What, then, is this residence? It is inherence (*samavāya*).
And what is this? Some say that residence is the cause of the cognition "it is here" with respect to things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*).
That is incorrect, because the cognition of "here" is established [in this case].
For everyone always has the cognition, "This is a cow," and not, "Here is cowness.
And what is this non-separateness (*ayutasiddhi*)? It is the absence of separateness (*yutasiddhyabhāva*).

What, then, is *yutasiddhi* (separate existence)? It is either the state of having separate motion or the state of depending on separate substrata; the absence of that is *ayutasiddhi*. If this were so, the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between part and whole would not exist.
For even without the motion of the whole, there is motion of the parts, and both the whole and the parts depend upon their own respective substrata.
Likewise, since a universal depends upon an individual and the individual depends upon its own parts, there is a dependence on separate substrata; thus, inherence is untenable.

Therefore, it must be stated as follows: that relation by which the substratum (ādhāra), through its own support (saṃśraya), produces in the intellect a cognition corresponding to itself—that is, makes [the object] known through its own form—is inherence (samavāya).

If, however, the individual (vyakti) is perceived in the form of the universal (jāti), then because the non-difference of the universal and the individual would be what is perceived, how can their difference be admitted?
It is said:

In both cases—“This cow is a *śābaleya* (the offspring of Śabalā)” and “This cow is a *bāhuleya* (the offspring of Bahulā)—the form of ‘cow’ (*gavākāra*) is observed to persist, whereas the forms of *śābaleya* and *bāhuleya* are excluded.
Therefore, if there were no difference between those two forms of *śābaleya* and *bāhuleya*, the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of one would also persist in the other.
Or rather, [if one were to argue that] even the form of the cow (gavākāra) is excluded from those two;

furthermore, even when that very individual is perceived as having the nature of a cow in the cognition "this is a cow," the synonymy of the two cognitions—of "cow" and "cow"—is not perceived in the way it is for the word "cow" repeated twice.
Therefore, there is non-difference.

How, then, is that identity (tādrūpya) perceived in the individual? This very identity of the individual is indeed its inherence (samavāya) as a relation. It is the power of this [inherence] itself by which the substrate (ādhāra) colors the superstratum (ādheya) with its own cognition.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Alternatively, since there is a cognition of identity (*tādātmya*), let there be non-difference; yet by the logic previously stated, there is also difference.
Therefore, on the strength of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that [the object] is indeed both different and non-different.
But how can the contradictory [pair of] difference and non-difference exist in one and the same place?
There is no contradiction, because they are perceived together.

For if difference and non-difference were perceived through their respective terms as in "this is silver" and "this is not silver," then they would indeed be contradictory. But there is no such perception of them through their respective terms.
And the cognition "this is a cow" establishes a single appearing object as having a dual nature.

For grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) brings about non-difference, while non-synonymy brings about difference; therefore, there is no contradiction within the cognition itself, due to the difference in perspective.

For instance, when an individual is examined through its universal (jāti) as "cow," it is perceived as non-different [from that universal], as in: "This spotted one is a cow. But when the universal is examined by way of another individual, then this individual is determined to have a form distinct from that [other], as in: "That which is a spotted cow, this [particular] spotted one is not that.

In this same manner, for a substance (dravya) as the substratum (dharmin), there is difference from color and other qualities (rūpa-ādi) by way of its other attributes such as taste, while there is non-difference by way of its nature as a substance.
Likewise, there is non-difference of the whole from its parts in terms of the form of the whole, but there is difference from other parts in terms of the form of those other parts.

In this regard, just as the coexistence of contradictory natures such as long and short is accepted—even in a single locus—because they are perceived without contradiction due to a difference in perspective, so too are difference and non-difference accepted for a substance based on specific modes of perception.
However, some (the Prābhākara) further asserts that "a perception itself that manifests both difference and non-difference is impossible."
Cognition of a distinct form is the appearance of difference, and cognition of a non-distinct form is the appearance of non-difference.

Therefore, by that same person who perceives both the universal form and the individual form at the time of the manifestation of difference, one or the other of those two must be perceived at the time of the perception of non-difference.
In that case, there would be a double appearance of a single thing, but it does not follow that non-difference is thereby perceived as intended.
Therefore, there is no perception of both difference and non-difference in one and the same place.
Let this [objection] rest.
For there is no cognition of difference apart from two distinct entities, since even in that case [of your own view], there is non-difference.
Indeed, even when an individual is first perceived, there is a cognition of both the universal and the individual.

At that time, their difference is not cognized; rather, it is through the observation of another individual that the persistence (*anvaya*) of the universal and the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the previous individual are perceived, and thus, according to your own established doctrine, the difference between the universal and the individual is determined by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Likewise, having perceived Devadatta at one time and subsequently seeing someone similar to him, while also remembering the previously perceived Devadatta, one understands that in reality these two persons are characterized by difference; nevertheless, one does not ascertain their distinctness, for one hesitates, thinking, "Is this the very same Devadatta, or is it another?
Therefore, it has been stated that the cognition of difference is indeed the apprehension of two distinct entities.

Likewise, when one sees that very same Devadatta from a distance at another time, one feels doubt, thinking, "Is this the same person, or is it another? Even though, in reality, there is only a single object, one is not able to ascertain its identity. Therefore, the cognition of difference is not simply the cognition of two distinct objects, nor is the cognition of non-difference simply the cognition of a single object.
However, the cognition "this is other" is an appearance of difference, while the cognition "this is that" is an appearance of non-difference.

Furthermore, for one perceiving a *śāvaleyā* (a spotted cow) and a *bāhuleya* (a black cow), there is an appearance of non-difference in the form "this is a cow, and this too is a cow," as well as an appearance of difference in the form "the *bāhuleya* is other than the *śāvaleyā*. Therefore, both difference and non-difference are established.

Now, it may be objected: the universal (*jāti*) is inclusive, eternal, and possesses the property of not perishing even when its instances perish; the individual (*vyakti*), however, has a contrary nature. How can these two be one?

For it is impossible for a single entity to be both inclusive and exclusive, eternal and non-eternal, subject to appearance and destruction, and yet non-differentiating from that which it is not; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a total confusion of the three worlds.
Consequently, the universal would likewise possess properties such as non-eternality, and the individual would likewise possess properties such as eternality.
This is not a fault.
For that entity possesses various forms; it is not contradictory for it to bear such qualities as permanence through one form and impermanence through another.

Even a universal (jāti) is impermanent in the form of its manifestation (vyakti), and even a manifestation is permanent in the nature of the universal; thus, there is no logical inconsistency whatsoever.

(Whether the universal is omnipresent or not): As for the elaboration regarding whether the universal is omnipresent or resides in the individual, that too is refuted simply by the assertion that it has the individual as its very nature (*vyaktyātmatva*).
For how could the individual, being its own self, exist elsewhere?
[Objection: But if this is so, since the universal does not exist at the location of the individual prior to the production of that individual, how can it come to be there afterwards?
There is no fault in this, for an individual being produced from its own causes arises already connected with the nature of a specific universal (*jāti*).

To this it is asked: how can a universal that does not yet exist become connected with the individual? For it cannot arise there at that very moment, because it is eternal; nor can it come from elsewhere, because it is immaterial.
It is replied:

Even one who comes from another country and becomes joined with this country—how could he experience conjunction with this country if he was previously non-existent in it? It must be said that it is "by virtue of a cause.
(It must be said:
In the same way, a universal (*jāti*) also experiences connection with individuals solely by virtue of a cause.
However, there is a distinction regarding conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

An object already situated in a prior location first conjoins with the immediately adjacent space, and thereafter with the space immediately following that; thus, it proceeds to conjunction with successive locations in a sequential manner. In the case of identity (*tādātmya*) or inherence (*samavāya*), however, its production from its own causes occurs precisely in dependence upon the immediately adjacent space. Indeed, the very nature of conjunction cannot be accepted as being identical to the nature of identity or inherence.
Because there is a lack of valid evidence, or because their intrinsic natures are distinct;
therefore, there is no fault.
Let it be that the universal is omnipresent.
Nor does it follow that everything would be perceived, because individuals are not manifested [to the senses].
Although the universal is omnipresent, its essence is that of the individual itself, or it is conjoined with it.

Furthermore, the perception of the universal occurs through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*); thus, since this contact is possible only in the location of the individual and not elsewhere, there is no perception of everything.

Furthermore, there is no non-difference between the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), because their difference is also present; thus, like those who argue for both permanence and impermanence, the [notions of] omnipresence and non-omnipresence are likewise untenable.
As for the dilemma posed—whether existence occurs in its entirety or by way of parts—that too is incorrect, for "in its entirety" presupposes a distinction [between the whole and its parts].
Furthermore, there is no division of the universal either by way of its own nature or by way of parts, because it is unitary and partless.
Precisely because it is partless, a subsistence in parts is impossible.
Therefore, one can only say that the genus exists in the individuals, as this is what is understood through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
There is no whole-to-part relationship because there is a lack of evidence and because it is impossible.

Likewise, for a whole (avayavin) as well, existence in its parts cannot occur in its entirety, because there is an absence of multiplicity; this is the argument regarding form (ākṛti) based on that [absence]. This concludes the section on form (ākṛtyadhikaraṇa).
And because the conventional usage of "wholeness" (*kṛtsnatva*) would follow from its own nature;
furthermore, subsistence by way of parts is also untenable due to the absence of further constituent parts.
Is it then the case that the manifestation of a universal is of a single form, and the subsistence of a whole in its parts is likewise? No, it is said in reply.
The distinction is this: a universal (sāmānya) exists in each [individual] separately, whereas a whole (avayavin) exists pervasively (vyāsajya).

A genus (jāti), which produces a cognition corresponding to itself by existing in one individual only in dependence upon another individual, is said to "exist in each," but not by way of a complete (kārtsnyena) presence.

The whole (*avayavin*), however, exists in its parts by subsisting in one part while [simultaneously] subsisting in other parts, thereby generating a cognition of its own form; thus it is designated as "subsisting in the parts.

For a cognition of a cloth does not arise with respect to a single thread alone, in the same way that the cognition of a cow arises with respect to a single individual cow. Therefore, even the universal (*jāti*) cannot be said to possess two prongs or the like.
As for the claim that because the universal (*jāti*) is eternal and possesses the capacity to produce a cognition of its own object, it cannot be the apprehended (*grāhya*),
that is incorrect.
We shall demonstrate in the refutation of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) that even eternal things possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, being an object of cognition (*grāhyatva*) is not the defining characteristic of a cause; for that [characteristic] has been described in the *Śūnyavāda* as consisting in the possession of the characteristic of being produced by a cognition. Therefore, this too is not a fault. As for the claim that the postulation of a universal (*jāti*) is without basis in authority, since the arising of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) such as "cow" and so forth is possible through the particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves by means of one's own experience—[we reply: [The argument continues: ...because the arising of conceptual cognitions such as "cow" and so forth occurs through the particulars themselves by way of one's own experience, the postulation of a universal is without basis in authority. [Response: This is not so. For it is observed that when a person who has previously experienced a cow sees another cow, there arises a conceptual cognition characterized by the form "this is a cow," which is distinct from the cognition of the particular. And this [cognition] cannot have the particular as its object, because the particular is not present at that time. Nor can it have the non-existent as its object, because it appears clearly. Therefore, it must have a real entity as its object. And that [object] is the universal. Furthermore, if the universal did not exist, then even upon seeing a different individual, the same conceptual cognition would not arise, because the particulars are mutually distinct. Moreover, if the universal were not real, then the application of a single word and a single conceptual cognition to many individuals would be impossible. Therefore, the universal exists. And it is eternal, because it is not perceived as having a beginning in time. Thus, the universal is established. And it is not the case that the universal is merely a mental construction (*kalpanā*), for it is perceived by the senses. Nor is it a mere exclusion (*apoha*), for it is affirmative in nature. Therefore, the universal is a real entity. And it is not the case that the universal is unperceived, for it is perceived as residing in the individuals. Nor is it the case that the universal is not perceived apart from the individuals, for it is perceived as distinct from them. Therefore, the universal is a real entity. And it is not the case that the universal is not perceived because it is subtle, for it is perceived by all people. Nor is it the case that the universal is not perceived because it is obstructed, for it is not material. Therefore, the universal is a real entity. And it is not the case that the universal is not perceived because it is dependent on something else, for it is independent. Therefore, the universal is a real entity. And it is not the case that the universal is not perceived because it is a property of another, for it is a property of itself. Therefore, the universal is a real entity. And it is not the case that the universal is not perceived because it is a relation of coexistence, for it is not a relation of coexistence. Therefore, the universal is a real entity. And it is not the case that the universal is not perceived because it is a relation of memory, for it is not
That too is without substance;

for it is not the case that the universal (*jāti*) is not perceived, such that this kind of censure would be appropriate. Rather, a cognition as it arises brings to mind the universal which constitutes its own object; therefore, there is no occasion for such idle chatter.

And how do particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are absolutely distinct from one another, produce a single-formed cognition, given the established principle that "entities possessing such-and-such forms or not possessing them arise from causes that possess those same forms or not"?
If you ask, "How then, according to you, can distinct particulars be the cause of a single-formed universal (*sāmānya*)?", we reply: it is by virtue of their own nature.
Certain particular characteristics, arising from their own causes, partake in identity (*tādātmya*) or inherence (*samavāya*) with some one or another universal.
But surely, how can causes that are dissimilar produce *svalakṣaṇas* endowed with a single type of capacity?
They would not produce them if they were indeed dissimilar; however, they too are of one and the same kind.
[Objection: But in this way, if there is a requirement for further and further universals (*jāti*) in order to establish their relationship, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
This is not a fault.

Just as a single *tāla* seed, through a succession of transformations, brings about an individual tree belonging to the *tāla* species, and that tree likewise produces another seed of the same species as its own causal seed, so too from a single individual cow of a certain species arises an individual cow of that same species, and from that [individual] arises another of that same species; thus, there is no absolute identity [of cause and effect].

Therefore, there exists a single entity—an *ākṛti*, a genus (*jāti*), or a universal (*sāmānya*)—which is denoted by words and which persists through individual instances such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others.
Nor is similarity itself the universal, because there is no cognition of it;
the cognition is "this is that very same [thing]," not "this is similar to that."

Furthermore, for one who denies all universals (*sāmānya*), even similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not possible, because it consists of a multiplicity of common parts. Nor can a universal consisting of the exclusion of others (*atadvyāvṛtti*) be apprehended by someone who does not accept a universal in a positive form (*vidhirūpa*). For when the exclusion of the non-cow is cognized, the cow must necessarily be cognized first, and that [must be] in a positive form.

For it is not possible to determine the nature of non-cows through their exclusion from a cow that has not itself been apprehended; thus, the cow must first necessarily be cognized in its positive form. Indeed, it is impossible to grasp individual instances such as Śābaleya and others in their specific forms by way of their exclusion from those [non-cows], because those infinite individuals cannot ascend into the mind, and as long as they have not ascended, it is impossible to cognize the cow in the form of their exclusion.
Furthermore, how can a universal understood in a positive form, such as "cow, cow," be accepted as being of a negative nature?
Therefore, this view is extremely feeble.
Consequently, the universal exists.

Śābarabhāṣya, pp. 97–104: Since it would follow that the Veda lacks authority if individual entities were the meaning of words, the eternal *ākṛti* (form/structure) is established as the referent of a word through the theory of *ākṛti*, with the aim of establishing its authority. Bālamanoramā, pp. 6–7: Because there is no absolute difference between *ākṛti* and the individual (*vyakti*), a substance is sometimes cognized in the form of an individual and sometimes in the form of a universal, according to the speaker's intention.

... because there is no absolute difference between the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), properties applied to the individual are indeed applied to the genus. Vārttika 2.3.9.35; "In the case of words denoting form (*ākṛtiśabda*), the capacity [to denote] the individual is understood.
(3.4.4.13, p. 913); "Words denoting form do not apply to the form itself, but serve to indicate the individual."
These [individuals] become weak because they are imperceptible (*parokṣatva*) in relation to the individuals;
3.4.14.41, p. 978. Section on Form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*): Form is the meaning of the word.
Because there is no injunction for practical application [in the case of universals], just as in the case of oneness and division.

The Bhāṣya states: "If those very things which are worldly are also the meanings [of words] in the Veda, then a doubt arises: is the word-meaning the universal (ākṛti), or is it the individual (vyakti)? What, then, is the universal, and what is the individual?"
The universal alone is the form (*ākṛti*) of substances, qualities, and actions;
the unique particularity is the individual (*vyakti*).
Why is there doubt? Because when "cow" is uttered, there is a cognition of the universal, yet action is possible only in the individual.
Therefore, it is said that the individual (vyakti) is the meaning of the word.
Why? Because there would be an absence of injunctions for ritual application.
Injunctions for the performance of acts such as touching, sprinkling, and immolation would not be possible if the meaning were the class-form (ākṛti).

If it is argued that "where there is a purpose for pronunciation, there the meaning is the individual (vyakti); therefore, in this case, the word denotes the form (ākṛti)," [the reply is] as stated: "And it is improper to have multiple meanings.
If it is asked, "How is there a cognition of the universal (sāmānya)? [the answer is: "Because it is based on the individuals (vyakti).
If it is asked, "How is there usage with another individual?"—it has been stated in the *Sudhā* that these two portions of the *Bhāṣya* have been omitted here.
356–57) The individual entity will have its form as its substrate, such that "that which has such a form is a cow," just as "one who possesses a staff is a staff-bearer."
Furthermore, the word *daṇḍa* does not denote the stick itself;
it is the same here as well.

Or rather: since it is established that in both common usage (*loka*) and the Veda the word *agni* denotes the referent, it is now deliberated whether the word-meaning is the generic form (*ākṛti*) or the individual instance (*vyakti*).
"Although the author of the Bhāṣya has presented only these two positions and explained them,
the commentators here have also [discussed] other alternative positions."
The relation [of a word] is either by necessity (niyoga), or optionally (vikalpa), or both together as a combination (samuccita);
or it is a connection with a collection (samudāya), or a qualified [relation] where one is distinct from the other.
Furthermore, these positions (pakṣas) are to be applied to one another in a crosswise manner,
through the combinations— both joined and unjoined— of gender, case-role (kāraka), and number. Again, the application of the categories such as genus (jāti) and so forth here is exactly like that.
First, having thus presented the "eightfold alternative" (*aṣṭapakṣī*):

Is the referent of the word "cow" and so forth the *ākṛti* (form/structure) or the *vyakti* (individual)? (4) Or both the *ākṛti* and the *vyakti*? (5) Is there a synthesis of both? (6) Or a collection (*samudāya*)? (7) Is it the individual qualified by the form? (8) Or the form qualified by the individual? (The objects of knowledge are also eightfold; several further *aṣṭapakṣīs* are shown in the Vārttika hereafter, and their explanation is also provided in the *Sudhā*.)
And previously, after stating, "There are two thousand and four hundred [verses]," it was said: "Due to their mutual intermingling, many others also exist;
however, they are not mentioned here for fear of making the book too voluminous."
However, because they do not yield much fruit, even each individual *saṃhitā* is not an excessive expansion.
In this regard, the firm position is that "it is only the form [of the word]," while others hold the opposite view.

All [theories] follow the side of the manifest (vyakti). And once the manifest has been refuted, the refutation of all [other theories] is easily achieved; therefore, not all of these have been demonstrated by the Commentator.
This is not merely for the sake of their occurrence, nor are they purposeless;
for conceptual inquiries are capable of expanding wisdom.
Even though all [topics] have been shown, investigation is undertaken regarding two [of them].
Which [of the two] is denoted by the word, and which is understood through it?

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the primary subject of investigation, the essential nature of these two is first set forth by means of questions and then defined according to their true character.
[Objection: Since the universal (ākṛti) has already been defined in the very first chapter (pāda), the present question and answer serve no purpose.
[Reply: It is said:
"It is true that the universal was previously defined through perception."
(Ślokavārttika, Ākṛtivāda): "But you define the aspect of configuration (*saṃsthāna*) as being of the nature of a universal (*sāmānyātmā*).
[As stated in the Bhāṣya: "Configuration is the mere universal of substances, qualities, and actions.
And, "The universal of substances and so forth is divided into higher and lower [universals]."
In that regard, "substantiality" (vastutva) is the first; likewise, "substanceness" (dravyatva) and so forth are the subsequent.
Furthermore, there is the differentiation of airness, fireness, waterness, and selfhood;
from earthness comes potness, and that [potness] is obtained even in a single individual instance.
From the state of being a tree and from its lordship over others, [the existence of] things such as *śipā* (a type of tree) is inferred;
and from the state of being a body, [the existence of] cows and so forth, as well as the destruction of virility and the like, is understood.
From the state of being a stallion and so forth, the state of being a horse is inferred, while the white color (*karka*) and other qualities are considered mere attributes.

According to the commentary on the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (1.1.2), which states, "Having become a *haya*, he carried the gods; a *vājī*, the Gandharvas; an *arvan*, the Asuras; and a *aśva*, human beings," there is another level of generality: *haya*-ness, *vājī*-ness, *arvan*-ness, and *aśva*-ness.

What are these? Regarding "among the *karka*s and so forth"—the meaning is that *karka*-ness is a further generality inherent in the whiteness that is co-inherent in the effect of *aśva*-ness, while *śoṇa*-ness is a further generality inherent in its redness.
(Su. Pṛ. 342) "From the state of being an elephant (*hastitva*), there are the lineages born from the two families of elephants, namely the *bhadra* and *madra*, etc.
(The phrase "from the state of being an elephant" refers to those [elephants] who are superior;
the word "etc. includes the inclusion of the *mṛga* lineage).
And those [elephants], born from the lineage of the elephants of the quarters, exist here indeed as elephants;
see Su. p. 342.
Furthermore, the various breeds such as Bhadra, Bhadrapada, and others are described elsewhere according to their distinctions by mountain.
Not only those born of the species of world-elephants [are thus]; who [are they]?
(From manhood, it culminates in the state of being a Brahmin, like the *auṇḍraka*.)

In this way, the nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*), the nature of being an action (*karmatva*), and so forth, as well as "arising" (*janmatā*) and the like, are established. [Regarding these: "Arising" (*janmatva*) is the general activity of an agent who is not yet established, which has the attainment of its own self as its fruit; [whereas for one who is already established...]
The section on *ākṛti* (form);

the agent of the section on *ākṛti*: by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the general category of activity whose fruit is the non-acquisition of a self (*anātmalābha*), such as sacrifice (*yāga*), is expressed.

"Then [consciousness] becomes established in the qualities (guṇa) such as whiteness and so forth, and in actions (karman) through their divisions into sacrifice (yāga), oblation (homa), and the like. (Su. Pṛ. 343)

It is stated that [the meaning] is understood through elements (*dhātu*) situated in non-synonymous forms; furthermore, it is expressed through various other sections concerning prescriptions, formations, designations, qualities, and so forth.
However, other teachers maintain that there is a distinction solely among the verbal roots (*karman*).

(The meaning is as follows: "Just as there is a distinction between subordinate acts (*karmāvāntarabheda*) through differences in form, word, and other factors such as *yajati*, *juhoti*, and *dāti*, so too [distinctions] arising from repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), name (*ākhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*)—these also constitute distinctions between acts; thus some teachers maintain that these are indeed subordinate universals of action (*karmatvāvāntarasāmānya*).
"But rather, because there is no difference, there would be a single nature for the place and so forth;
and because of the division of form, word, and so on, Jaimini will state this."
Thus, everything elaborated above is the universal (sāmānya) of objects, which is the generic form (ākṛti).
It is not a configuration (saṃsthāna); for how could that [be so] in the case of the self and other [entities], or in the case of qualities and actions?
For among all things composed of earth, there would indeed be configurations such as "cow" and so forth, or "pot" and so forth.
However, in the case of atoms, space, and so forth, the conformity to shape would have to be postulated due to their being occupied by earthly substances, and not independently [of them].
(In earthly substances, shape is intrinsic.)

First: because this [space] is seen to possess a configuration that conforms to the configuration of the fuel; because a difference in configuration is seen in the third [air], which conforms to the configuration of its substratum such as a vessel; because a difference in configuration is seen in space, which conforms to the configuration of limiting adjuncts such as a jar; and because air moving through space delimited by a jar or similar object possesses a configuration conforming to that jar—this [configuration] is adventitious (aupādhika). Furthermore, no configuration whatsoever is possible for actions.
(Su. Pṛ. 344) However, for space, time, self, and mind, as well as for qualities and actions, no configuration whatsoever is possible.
Only the universal (*sāmānya*), which consists in the persistence through all its own particulars, is conceivable.

Even in the absence of a form called "configuration," that which is cognized by a uniform cognition, which is inherent in all its individual instances, which is excluded from heterogeneous things, and which is apprehended by a non-objective cognition—just as the notion of "Brahmin" cannot be denied—is not capable of being rejected.
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose very form (*rūpa*) consists in the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) through all its own particulars.

(Su. p. 344). Therefore, this alone is the definition of the *ākṛti* as the denotable object; it is not tenable that *ākṛti* is the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the arrangement of parts (*avayava-caraṇa*).
"Because configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is perishable and because it differs with each individual instance,
the application of the term 'universal' (*sāmānya*) is not possible for configuration.
Now, if it is argued that configuration is understood as the universal of configurations (*saṃsthānasāmānya*),"
Because it would be the same in the case of horses and so forth, there would be a confusion of generic forms (*ākṛti*).
Nor is there any intermediate configuration that resides in every individual cow.
Furthermore, the referent of the word "cow" would have to be excluded from horses and the like;
for when that [referent] is perceived and examined, nothing other than the universal (jāti) is apprehended.
Consequently, it follows by logical necessity that the universal alone is the commonality (sāmānya).

By this, [the objection] is excluded by means of these two questions and answers (from the Bhāṣya)—namely, the mention of the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and form (*ākṛti*) through the examples of *rocaka*, *svastika*, and *vardhamāna* in the first quarter [of the verse], and the statement "it was" (*āsīt*) which serves as an illustration of the name (*ākhyā*). (The grammatical connection is: *tena vyāvartyate*; cf. Su., p. 245).

And therefore, intending that whatever generality (*sāmānya*) exists in substances, qualities, and actions prior to their individual manifestations (*vyakti*), all of that is indeed the configuration (*ākṛti*), the word "only" (*mātra*) is employed in the Bhāṣya.
[The Bhāṣya states: "The individual manifestation (*vyakti*) is the unique particular (*asādhāraṇaviśeṣa*)."
Some say: "The individual is nothing other than the unique particulars (*asādhāraṇaviśeṣa*), because there is no individual apart from the particulars. That is not so;
for it is precisely this individual that is intended [to be distinct] from the various particularities.
All such [individuals] as Khaṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others are accepted as being specific instances (*viśeṣa*); they are observed elsewhere as well, even among other species,
and even among the various offspring of a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are indeed other individuals as well, such as those with mottled or hornless bodies, including the *gavaya* and the buffalo.
Just as one is a *śābaleya*, so too is any other understood to be a *śābaleya* by virtue of being the offspring of Śabalā;
this name, whether based on both colors or occurring by chance, is applied here alone due to its specific application elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, regarding its offspring, the designation "Śābaleya" would be untenable as a non-common [term]. There would also be the fault of a discrepancy between the number of words and their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—namely, using a plural form for a word denoting a particular and a singular form for a word denoting the individual (as in *vṛkṣāḥ* [trees] and *vanaṃ* [forest]).
Therefore, it should be explained thus: "the individual (*vyakti*) is that in which the particulars (*viśeṣa*) are non-common."

[Objection: But surely, by the logic previously stated, since even [words like] *khaṇḍa* and so forth are common to a plurality of instances, and since other qualifiers—distinct from the individual—which reside in only a single individual are impossible, even the *bahuvrīhi* compound is untenable.
[Reply: It is said: We do not maintain that the individuals are qualified by assuming that the qualifiers are each individually unique (*asādhāraṇya*).

How, then, is this so? Even for those things whose forms are common [to many], because they are perceived in certain instances through distinctions of one, two, three, and so forth, their status as "uncommon particulars" is designated with reference to that grasping of them when they are gathered together in a single mass. For it is said: "Those things which were seen separately are seen again when conjoined; by virtue of being common to the mass, they are characterized by a single form."
Furthermore, those very qualities which are observed to be present in this individual in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* are seen in other individuals as well, neither less nor more.
That very thing which was previously unperceived and is now seen in that collection brings about its unique character (*asādhāraṇatā*).

Even though individual instances (*vyakti*) possess infinite differences, there is no requirement to apprehend an absolutely unprecedented particularity; for everywhere, uniqueness is apprehended merely through some degree of excellence or deficiency.
Furthermore, in relation to a higher generality (*parasāmānya*), all intermediate generalities (*avāntarasāmānya*) attain the status of being particulars (*viśeṣa*).
And because they serve as qualifiers of the individual (*vyakti*) during the state of integration (*saṃdhāna*), the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is applied to them.
Furthermore, the author of the *Bhāṣya* will indeed state later on that this distinctness (*anyatva*) of the qualifiers of the individual is established by the statement:
"That which is the constituent part (*avayava*) of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particulars (*viśeṣa*) is the individual" (p. 303).

In order to refute the interpretation of those who hold that "the universal *sattā* (existence) inhering in substances is itself the *ākṛti* (form), and not subordinate universals such as *gotva* (cowness)," he introduces their view with the words "by him" (*tena*). This is intended to invalidate the understanding of those who maintain that [the term] is denotative of *sattā* and so forth.

(Su. Pr. 346) In this regard, some—having accepted that [universals] such as "cowness" (*gotva*) are particulars (*viśeṣa*) because they cannot be denoted by words expressing generalities (*sāmānya*)—maintain that it is precisely that Great Generality (*mahāsāmānya*), which is the reality (*vastu*) or existence (*bhāva*) denotable by the word "Being" (*sattā*), that is the denotation of the word when it is distinguished from the nature of the word itself or distinguished from particulars such as "cowness. This is what is called "the Being of the cow" (*gosattā*), or the denotation of the term expressing the form (*ākṛti*). As they say:
"The definition of the object of cognition for all words is simply that 'it exists' (*asti*)."
In [the passage] beginning with "They say that it is like the unprecedented deity, heaven,
and so forth," they state that the definition of the denoted object (*vācya*) of the cognition of the word "this" (*idam*)— which consists of all words in the form "it exists"—
is as follows: in words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*), and in words such as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*).

The meaning is: "because of their equality" (saha-tulyatvāt). (Su. pṛ. 347) "Because universals are defined through their non-distinction from the threads [of the word], it is incorrect; for words such as 'cow' do not possess the power of denotation with respect to those [universals]."
For the denotative power (*vācakaśakti*) of words is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) to have as its object a specifically determined meaning.

In that regard, since words for substances, qualities, and actions—which denote infinite internal universals (*sāmānya*)—do not have their meanings conflated, it is already untenable for them to have "Being" (*sattā*) as their meaning; how much more so for words such as "cow," whose objects are even more remote?
[The word *kaśya* means "a word"; it is a synonym for *koṣa* (treasure/lexicon).]
Because they possess the property of being substances, qualities, and actions, they reside within the lower generality (avāntara-sāmānya) of "existence" (sattā).

Earth, water, and so forth reside within the lower generality of "substance-ness" (dravyatva); color-ness, taste-ness, and so forth reside within the lower generality of "quality-ness" (guṇatva); such is the classification within these categories.

In this regard, by the word "substance," there is a certain cognition of substance-ness; regarding earth-ness and the like, the cognition is doubtful; but regarding quality-ness and the like, there is no cognition at all.

And likewise (it has been stated): Just as words such as "substance" (*dravya*), which have existence (*sattā*) as their intermediate universal (*avāntara-sāmānya*) as their object, are said to denote existence itself;
so too, this being the case, words such as "cow" (*go*), whose objects are separated by a great distance [from existence], certainly lack the capacity to denote existence directly.
As it is said: "And those who speak of these [entities] as existence do not [denote] pure existence, but rather existence with qualifications. (Su. p. 347)
Indeed, it is impossible to maintain that they "express" [the object] in either of two ways.
First, if they were pure denotations, since all of them would result from an effort toward a single meaning, they would necessarily be synonyms.
Furthermore, because of this tautology, the employment of the word "existence" (astitva) would be untenable.
"Furthermore, the formulation 'the cow does not exist' is not tenable due to contradiction;
for how can it ever be understood that existence itself does not exist?
Even with reference to [specific] place, time, and so forth, it is not proper to predicate non-existence of existence."
Because it pervades all places and times by virtue of its omnipresence and eternity;
furthermore, this term is not recognized as a conventional designation (*rūḍhiśabda*) through worldly perception.
Therefore, it is not tenable that *sattā* (existence) is a universal (*sāmānya*) of substance (*dravya*) and so forth.

For that which is expressed by the word "exists" (*asti*) is indeed the second transformation of being (*bhāvavikāra*). As stated in the Nirukta (1.2): "There are six transformations of being: it is born, it exists, it changes, it grows, it declines, and it perishes. Thus, in all things—from those being born through those undergoing change, accumulation, and decline, up to those perishing—the cognition of the essential nature of the thing (*vastvakṛti*) is observed.

Therefore, even if it is asserted that the denotable object is the "Great Universal" (mahāsāmānya), then the definition of a word's meaning would be: "the meaning of all words is a non-entity. This may well be said, but not that "it has existence as its meaning."
Furthermore, the words *sat* and *sattā* do not function by abandoning their etymological meaning; rather, the existence (*sadbhāva*) of "being" (*bhavat*) is *sattā*.

One should not understand this as a universal (*jāti*) defined according to the Vaiśeṣika technical terminology as: "That from which the cognition 'it exists' arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions is *sattā*" (VS 1.2.7).
(Note: The reading of the Sūtra is *saditi yato dravyaguṇakarmasu sā sattā*).

The meaning is that *sattā* (existence) is that from which the cognition "it exists" arises with respect to substances and so forth, because they are real entities (*vastu*) and because they possess the nature of the great universal (*mahāsāmānya*). (Su. p.

348) This very [existence] has been established as a well-known term by means of an indeclinable word (*avyayaśabda*) that expresses a synonym for "real entity" (*vastu*) and signifies the common property of "being" (*bhava*).
Since this cognition "existence" (astitva) is observed [to arise],
that word expressing the object is a nominal derivative (ākhyāta-pratirūpaka).
Because it is not a nominal stem (apratipadikatvāt), verbal forms (ākhyāta) are not recorded as such in the grammatical tradition.
And for that reason, [the compound] *astikṣīrā* is accepted by him as a *saddhita* (compound with a finite verb).

Since there is no supplementary rule (*anupasaṃkhyāna*) for treating *astikṣīrā gauḥ* as a compound containing a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), it necessarily follows from the section on *ākṛti* (the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*).
In the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*,

it is accepted that the word *kṣīra* forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the indeclinable (*avyaya*) "asti"— an indeclinable that is a substitute for a case-ending— to denote another referent (*anyapadārtha*), because the cognition "a cow with milk" (*sakṣīrā gauḥ*) arises [thereby]. In this context, the term *sārtha* signifies "possessing meaning."

Furthermore, when the word *asti* is employed with reference to an existing entity (*vastu*), the word *sat*—which is etymologically rooted in *asti* and closely approximates its meaning—is understood. Just as in the rule *devāt-tal* (Pāṇini 5.4.27), where the suffix *tal* forms *devatā* as a *svārthika* (taddhita) derivative, here too, the logicians have imagined that the words *sat* and *sattā* denote only the pure meaning of "being" (*dyotya-artha-mātra*), without admitting a cognition of an agent (*kartṛ*) qualified by the meaning expressed by *astitā*. Thus they maintain: "That which is denoted by the word *sat* is *sattā*, the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*)."

Because it has been rejected by logicians upon reaching its conclusion, and because it has been disregarded even by those learned in words and sentences, this [universal] has reached a state as if it were well-established—having reached a state where it is subjected to the investigation of what is logical and illogical—and it is even conceivable that it is denotable by words such as "cow" and so forth.
However, there is no denotability for the "thingness" (*vastutva*) that is understood through implication;
how much less could there be such denotability for "existence" (*sattā*), which is merely one among various attributes?
For the word *vastu*, because it is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*),
is understood by proponents of [the theory of] meaning to denote that universal which resides in a multitude of individual instances;
this is sought by them because the position of pure denotation is flawed.
If it is claimed that the "great universal" (*mahāsāmānya*) is the intended denotatum, that too is difficult to establish.

Whatever reason was given for rejecting the position that the word denotes an individual qualified by its form, or the cognition of an individual qualified [by a universal], those same reasons apply here as well, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that the qualifier must be denoted prior [to the qualified]. Even if this word "cow" were to express the existence of a cow (*gosattva*), [it would still face the aforementioned difficulties].

Or one might say that it is qualified by the universal "cowness," or perhaps by the individuals themselves. In that case, it would be "existence (sattā) as qualified by the universal cowness" that is denoted by this [word].
Since that [existence] is already established by the aforementioned qualifier alone, why is it mentioned?

Since it is impossible to perform the act of placing (abhyādhāna) upon that which is qualified without first denoting the qualifier, and since the qualifier is invariably connected with the qualified, the comprehension of "Being" (sattā) is already established simply by the existence of "cowness" (gotva), which is the previously denoted qualifier; therefore, even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) does not operate toward the postulation of a denotative power for that [Being], being obstructed by the fact that the result can be accounted for otherwise.
This same reason for refutation applies even to the theory that the word denotes "Being" as qualified by the individual (*vyakti*).

In the hypothesis that a single *sattā* (Being) is denoted after first denoting the infinite individual manifestations (*vyakti*) of word-powers based on impermanent substrates, there is an untenability similar to the position that only the individual is denoted.
As for the point made in the verse regarding the view held by some—that [the theory of *sattā*] is equal to [the theories concerning] the *apūrva*, the deity, and heaven—it is replied:
"It is not at all established that Being (*sattā*) is the denotable meaning of words such as *apūrva*."

Regarding the qualifiers, they also say that these are postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and other means. Some [qualifiers] exist as being presented by presumptive testimony based on what has been heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), while others exist as being presented by the remainder of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) or another sentence. Being such, they indicate existence (*sattā*) by way of a well-established object that is absolutely non-deviant; thus, they are determined to be non-denotative. Since the category of existence (*sattā*) does not deviate from its referent, the cognition of existence arises from them solely through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
[The result is] the capacity for action and the connection with the bliss produced by Indra and the other [deities].
Even in a general sense, something other than mere existence (sattā), such as the "unprecedented" (apūrva) and so forth, is obtained.
For all things indeed possess capacities that are to be understood through the presumption based on their effects (kāryārthāpatti).

Furthermore, the capacity of persons to attain a fruit produced by sacrifices and the like—which is denoted by the term *apūrva*—did not exist prior to the performance of the sacrifice, and it arises after the performance; thus, because of its etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*), the designation *apūrva* is applicable in all instances.

Likewise, they are called *devas* because they "play" (*divyanti*) or "shine" (*dyotante*) in the form of the moon, sun, fire, stars, and so forth; and because the winds are praised by all mantras as being in constant motion, they are associated with the word *sujñāna* (good knowledge). Thus, they are understood through their specific forms alone, and do not fall within the scope of [pure] existence (*sattā*).

Similarly, the word *svarga* (heaven) is said to refer to the region of the stars, as seen in Vedic tradition, Purāṇas, and other texts; for instance, in the Veda: "Those people who perform meritorious deeds go to the heavenly world (*svarge loke*); these stars and constellations belong to them."
And thus it is said: "He conquers the luminous world of merit.

Alternatively, it may be the summit of Mount Meru as established by the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*; or else, it is that which is easily accessible through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), to be experienced in another region proven by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—a place entirely free from the means of suffering such as cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and fatigue, which are experienced during the year and other such cycles.

And although that [universal] is of such a nature as to have never been perceived before, nevertheless, having been extracted through discrimination from the very experience of the mixture, it is known as the meaning of the word "heaven" and thus brings about the cognition of its existence; therefore, it does not depend upon a specific denotation for itself. Thus: "It is true that words such as 'cow' denote existents; however, words such as 'the unprecedented' (apūrva) are capable of indicating existence only when they themselves are denoted by their own words."
And for this reason, the word "cow" will certainly not denote the existence of the cow;
rather, it is investigated because of the doubt as to whether it denotes the class-character (*jāti*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*).
Why is there this doubt? It is because of the determination that its object is capable of purposeful action (*kāryayogya*).
One who considers the individual alone to be the meaning of a word raises an objection;
it is replied [in the section] on the "Class" (ākṛtyadhikaraṇa).
In the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, it is understood that the individual (*vyakti*) is the denotation because of its connection with action; however,
due to the constraints of the word's expressive power (*śabda-śakti*), the form (*ākṛti*) is not distinct from the meaning.

"Because there is no discrepancy between the word's capacity and its effect regarding the object denoted by the word, why should one not simply accept [the conventional view] without investigating whether it is logically consistent? (In the *Lokavedādhikaraṇa* established in the sūtra "Because of the absence of injunctions for usage," it is stated that [the word] is to be applied to something else; furthermore, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, it is said that it is applied to the form [*ākṛti*]. As for the question "What, then, is the conclusion?": What is the prima facie position? Because there is an absence of injunctions for usage, the individual (*vyakti*) is what is denoted, and not both [the individual and the form].
Since the unity of meaning is logical because the two [word and object] are inseparable, there is always a single cognition of them, just as in the case of words and their meanings;
for they exist for the purpose of producing the cognition of meaning, and this observation is not contradicted.
Thus, for all word-meanings, there is no impairment of the cognition of the sentence-meaning;
for their forms are to be determined in accordance with how they are to be employed.
If the generic form (*ākṛti*) were the meaning of the word, to what would acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) apply?
And by that [word], it is intended; however, the renunciation of a generic form (*ākṛti*) is not possible.
For the generic form is incorporeal and is the locus of such qualities as being inexpressible;
therefore, neither its injunction nor its prohibition can be conceived with respect to it.

"One threshes the rice, one sprinkles the animal, one purifies it; one sacrifices with Soma, with the animal, and with the rice"—all such preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) as these, which consist of perishable, corporeal objects, are either for the sake of accomplishing a purpose or for the sake of the injunction of performance. Since these do not apply to the generic form (*ākṛti*) but do apply to the individual (*vyakti*), and since the comprehension of word-meanings is primarily concerned with the action to be performed (*kārya*), and because all human endeavors are dependent upon injunctions, one must necessarily admit the postulation of word-meanings that are capable of being the object of an injunction and are preceded by a sentence.

Likewise, even regarding the injunctions of prohibition such as "A Brahmin must not be killed" and "Kalañja must not be eaten," since these too presuppose a prior possibility of occurrence and depend upon that, and since such possibility exists only in the case of the individual (vyakti), while the generic form (ākṛti) lacks the capacity for such engagement, they would be entirely meaningless if no such possibility existed.
Therefore, it is logical to accept only that meaning of the word by which the application of the injunctions becomes effective.
It is not proper to postulate a word-meaning merely for the sake of establishing a knowledge of ultimate reality.
It might be argued:
"In injunctions concerning the production of an individual, the meaning is the individual; therefore, in other cases, it will apply by means of the form (ākṛti) alone.
That is incorrect.

For this is the established logical position regarding the meaning of a word: because the relationship [between word and object] is not fixed, there would follow the undesirable consequence of having to postulate various capacities for denotation that have never been observed.
(He states the logic as expressed by Yajñavarāha in the *Abhikaraṇa*: "Because when objects are related, the comprehension of one is established simply through the denotation of the other.
If it is asked, "How then is there a cognition of the universal (*ākṛti*)?", he says in response: "Because of non-distinction."
Since there is always an inseparable connection between the individual (vyakti) and the form (ākṛti), the form, while being distinct [from the individual], can convey the capacity for denotation.

This has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*: "When a certain meaning is accepted as the primary denotable sense of a word, since it is impossible to abandon that [primary sense], one must necessarily accept another meaning residing therein as being indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). (This is the essential point of the Bhāṣya, though not the literal wording of the Bhāṣya itself.)

And so, the *Sudhā* states: "This has been stated because it follows the same logic as the commentary on the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* [pp. 96–97], which says: 'For when a quality such as "white" or "black" is perceived, it indeed serves to produce cognitions regarding that which possesses the quality. Therefore, one might ask: how is that so? (p. 367).

Furthermore, if the generic form (*ākṛti*) were the meaning of a word, there would be no definitive determination [of the specific object], because the generic form is common to many individuals and thus lacks exclusivity (*anekāntikatva*).

Furthermore, since the determination of the individual (*vyakti*) as the referent of a word is established through its being entirely subsumed within the action (*kriyā*), there is no need to postulate the operation of the word upon the form (*ākṛti*). Therefore, the individual alone is the meaning of the word, not the form.

Nor is the position tenable that the word denotes something qualified by any one of the following: alternative, conjunction, doubt, or aggregate; for all these cognitions are established precisely because there is no differentiation [in the object].
Because it is not a word denoting a substance (*adravyaśabdatvāt*).
The Commentary states: A "substance-word" (*dravyaśabda*) is a word that denotes that which has a substance as its substratum.
In that case, there would be no word expressing a substance as its substratum if the form (*ākṛti*) were the meaning of the word.
"One animal is to be given, twelve are to be given, twenty-four are to be given"—thus [it is said].
For a generic form (ākṛti) cannot be connected with a number;
therefore, it is a word denoting the generic form.
Or rather: "Furthermore, because they are not words denoting a substance (*adravyaśabdatvāt*), the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the denotation.
For co-referentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) does not exist between that which has the form (*ākṛti*) as its meaning and that which has a quality (*guṇa*) as its meaning.

If words such as 'cow' (*gośabda*) were to denote only the form, then in cases such as 'the cow is white,' 'one buys [the Soma] with a red, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow,' 'six cows are to be given,' or 'one should give a single cow as the sacrificial fee,' co-referentiality would not be possible, since all [of these words] would be denoting only the genus (*jāti*) or the quality (*guṇa*)."

For there is no connection between the universal "cowness" (gotva) and qualities such as white or red, by virtue of which even a genitive case could exist; how much less, then, could there be the relation of subsisting in the same effect? Indeed, the form of cowness is neither white, nor red, nor possessed of many qualities.
In this way, the individual [is the referent], and the qualities [are subordinate]; [this is established] in the section concerning the generic form (ākṛtyadhikaraṇa).
Therefore, only the individual (vyakti) is the denotable object.
For me, since it is established that [the word] is a term for the individual, its application is to the meaning;
therein, because it is a term for that [individual], the individual is also [denoted], just like the universal *g*-ness (*gatva*).
Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs in perception either through words denoting individuals qualified by genus and qualities, or through words denoting pure individuals;

in each such case, there is a substance. He demonstrates the undesirable consequence of the absence of that [co-referentiality] by means of the negative particle (*nañ*), showing that even such a state of having words for the same substance would not exist in your position.

As for the fact that the author of the *Bhāṣya*, by means of the word "substance" (*dravya*) taken in its opposite sense, employing a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the qualities residing in that [substance], and treating the negative particle (*nañ*) as forming an "incompatible compound" (*asamartha-samāsa*), states: "For the proponent of the theory of form (*ākṛti-vādin*), there would be no word denoting that which resides in a substance"—this is excessively strained and involves an improper use of a non-co-referential construction (*vyadhikaraṇa-nirdeśa*); thus, it should be disregarded.

Even in that case, it is merely a mechanical combination of syllables: the word "substance-word" (*dravya-śabda*) refers to a word for a quality that resides in a substance; such a word does not convey co-residence with the form because the form is devoid of qualities, unlike cases such as "cow-ness" or "white," where [the quality and the universal] reside in a single locus.
Furthermore, since common substratum (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) is no different even in our own position, it remains untenable at that time as well; thus, the previous explanation must be applied here.

(In the view that [the word] denotes the individual, there are faults such as the postulation of a substance qualified by a quality. *Anvākhyāna* means explanation or statement; the absence of that is *ananvākhyāna*. )

When it is possible for a word to function by means of a common form (*sādhāraṇarūpa*), the individual (*vyakti*) as delimited by a particular (*viśeṣāvacchinnarūpa*) would be the denoted (*vācya*). In that position, there would be the following faults arising from the absence of a statement regarding the relationship [between word and meaning]:

the loss of the restriction between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakatvaniyamahāni*); the contingency of the relationship being non-eternal (*saṃbandhānityatvāpatti*); the occurrence of an undesirable alternative (*vikalpaprasaṅga*); the contingency of having to bring forward every single individual (*aśeṣavyaktyākhyānayanāpatti*); the contingency of having to state [the relationship] eternally (*nityatvābhidhānaprasaṅga*); and the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "white" (*śukla*). These are the ones included by the word "etc. (*ādi*).
(Su. Pr. 163) Furthermore, that which is subject to doubt cannot be the object of cognition; thus, the charge that the word lacks a referent is refuted.
By this, the theory of the independent denotation of both [the individual and the form] is also answered.

Moreover, because of the principle that "a qualified entity is not perceived when its qualifier has not been grasped," there would be the undesirable consequence of the individual being apprehended first [if the form were not primary]. (It is refuted.)

Since the relationship and the collection themselves lack any intrinsic nature that could serve as a referent, one must necessarily admit that they function as qualifiers for the aggregate, the collection, and so forth, in all cases without distinction.
In that case as well, there would be the postulation of three powers (*śakti*). Furthermore, regarding the individual aspect, the aforementioned defects would follow as a consequence.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the individual (vyakti) and the form (ākṛti)—which have distinct functions and are related as subordinate and primary—to be understood as a collective whole.
Moreover, because they are not different from one another, a collective relationship consisting of distinct properties is not tenable.
Even when qualified by the form, a specific individual is never actually perceived.
If it is argued that [the word denotes] "mere individual" because there is no specific individual, we say no; for at that time, it cannot be defined as something other than the *ākṛti* (form).
Indeed, since the word "mere" (*mātra*) expresses a universal, it refers to the *ākṛti* itself.
