Furthermore, because capacities (*śakti*) in objects follow their respective distinctions, it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the capacity for being denoted by the word "cow" is based solely on the form of "cowness" (*gotva*).
The cognition of another universal that shares the same substratum, or the desire for a particular, occurs because [the universal] is pervaded by the object;
and since the form (*ākṛti*) is not absolutely distinct [from the individual], there is no possibility of defects pertaining to its substratum, because it is incorporeal (*amūrta*).

For that [form] is indeed perceived in its abstracted nature, yet when connected with action, it necessarily exists apart from the individual. However, [rites such as] sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) or inspection (*avekṣaṇa*) cannot possibly apply [to the form alone].
Furthermore, although the particular (*viśeṣa*) is beginningless, it is indeed possible [to speak of its priority] in relation to its non-distinction from the individual (*vyakti*).

For instance, in the case of animals and the like from which the head and other parts have been removed, since there is an absence of cognition of particulars, a cognition characterized by dismemberment and so forth is observed in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*).
Now, one might object that in this way the generic form (*ākṛti*) would be immeasurable; however, it is precisely intended in that respect.
Since there is no destruction of another substratum, its non-destruction must be accepted by all as being merely a matter of parts.
Therefore, its destruction occurs only to that extent [of the parts], while in other locations there would be no destruction whatsoever;
thus, the conventional usage is twofold.
If there were absolute exclusion [of the universal from the individual], however, the object of the injunction regarding the property (*dharma*) would not be established at all.
Nor can "cowness" (*paśutva*) be the object of the injunction, because it is formless (*amūrta*).

As for the substance indicated by that [cowness], since it is a substance, it cannot be understood in its specific form apart from [the universal] "substanceness" (*dravyatva*); therefore, due to its inherence in the same substrate and its pervasiveness, the substance must be inferred. Yet even in that case, the lack of form remains a defect.
Furthermore, because it would merely characterize the substratum, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a mere substance (*dravya*).
Moreover, whether it is the particularity of the animal or of the nature of a substance, it cannot be understood because it is not taught;
and that which is not cognized cannot be connected with an injunction (*vidhi*).
And that which is subject to doubt is not something already known. Furthermore, since a property stated in one way cannot possibly exist there, it must apply elsewhere.
Therefore, what is established in a general sense is appropriately applied to specific instances.
Even a particular, because it is designated [as such], is in fact a universal and is thus formless;
however, there is no linguistic usage based on its uniqueness.
Therefore, the object of the injunction regarding dharma is indefinable.
The universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, as well as silver and the like, should not be postulated as the definition [of a thing] if they are contrary to what is established by common experience.
However, the Commentator, by accepting their distinction [from the individual], has merely defined the substratum (*āśraya*). An individual is never perceived in its specific form alone.
Even that relationship of substratum and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva) is merely figurative (aupacārika).
Furthermore, the definition of the particular (viśeṣalakṣaṇa) should not be relied upon there, because it is merely implied (ākṣepamātratvāt).
Alternatively, this too is an elaboration (prapañca) of the same point: whether [the word denotes] by means of the individual form (kiṃ śabdena) or by means of the class-character (ākṛtyā).
And through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), the determination is that [the word denotes] the form (*ākṛti*).
For that which, by virtue of its permanence, attains the status of being the primary [referent], its expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) with respect to those [individuals] is established.
"Because of the absence of mental exhaustion" (Bhāṣya).

For one who, out of dullness, abandons the denotation of the universal and considers only some particular in which a connection has been experienced to be the denotable object—for such a person, once the universal is cognized, there is no further dependence on other particulars. Or rather, just as one understands the form (*ākṛti*) from the word as independent, one never understands the individual (*vyakti*) without first understanding the form.

What, then, is the difference between the word "cow" and the universal "cowness"? It is that in one case (the word) there is an intention to express the aspect of distinction (*vyatirekāṃśa*), whereas in the cognition "one possessing cowness," the expression of the distinctness of the class is clear due to the manifestation of differentiation.

Alternatively, because the universal serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the fault regarding the position of particularity does not arise; it is the denoter of all particulars, whether taken individually or collectively. As for the doubt that arises when [the word] is being employed, that concerns the number and the substratum.
When [the words] are being pointed out, this is indeed the definitive conclusion.
The mention of words such as "cow" (*go*) is for the purpose of including all nouns, pronouns, and verbs within it.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, because general and particular terms share the same object, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), that which is enjoined by a general term is not sublated by that enjoined by a particular term; whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is sublation (*bādha*).

(Regarding this, the *Sudhā* states: "Even though there is no difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), because the previous method of explanation might cause confusion for some and lead to distress for the students due to its lack of clarity, he begins another method for the sake of easy comprehension, saying: 'Or thus' (*evaṃ vā*).
"Or thus:
Words such as 'cow' (*gauḥ*) are determined to be correct."
It is now considered: what is the function (*vyāpāra*) of these very [words] with respect to the meaning expressed?
Here, in the case of the four types of words, the determination of the two-fold meaning is carried out;
however, this is not done for prefixes (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*), because doubt arises [regarding them].
For those two possess no function whatsoever in the expression of an object;
rather, that which illuminates the object is considered to be the denoter (*vācaka*).
Even when there is denotative power, as in cases such as "pāścātya" (westerner) and "mayūta" (a specific measure),
that specific distinction which is perceived is not obtained through doubt.
For if the intellect were to apprehend two meanings through the proximity of a particle, then a deliberation would arise; but that cannot occur without a cognition of commonality.

(One might object that, because it would result in redundancy, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) should not be investigated: "But surely, an investigation into the meaning of the verbal suffix is not appropriate here, since this will be done at length starting from the second [chapter]."

In the Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 2.1.1, beginning with the words "What, moreover, is *bhāva*?", the determination of the meaning is made through analytical distinction (*viveka*). Since that [determination] pertains to the *kṛt* suffixes, the investigation of the *ākhyāta* (verbal) suffix does not apply there.

(He offers a rebuttal by suggesting that the inquiry into the meaning of the suffix is itself an inquiry into the meaning of the stem—) It has been established that the meaning of the suffix is "being" (*bhāva*) as its denotation.

(He offers a rebuttal according to his own view—) Now, an investigation is being conducted for the purpose of distinguishing the meaning of the stem; or rather, once it has been determined that even the suffix has "being" as its meaning therein.
It is considered whether the universal or the particular is that which is denoted.

And as for that denotability of sacrifice and so forth which was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, it is established here for the sake of distinction; there, however, it was spoken of in terms of the "bhāva" (the action).

(Out of dissatisfaction, he offers another rebuttal: "Or rather, regarding whatever object is to be expressed, why should the consideration of whether it is the universal or the particular as the denotable apply to the verb?"
What is desired from words denoting substances and the like that signify an *apūrva*? In that regard, this specific inquiry has been stated; the rest is incidental discussion.
Since a word is said to be the designator of its meaning,
a deliberation arises as to whether it denotes the form (ākṛti) or the individual (vyakti).
Because the application and the cognition are equal in both cases regarding the definition of a word,
and because there is expression [of the universal] even in the view that the individual is denoted, a doubt appears to us.

(However, the doubt stated in the Bhāṣya is not appropriate. How [is this so]? For it must be stated from the very beginning that this inquiry into the connection with the definition [of Dharma] is either related to the subject at hand or to the investigation into the basis of Smṛti.
This incidental reflection has been completed once the correct word has been analyzed; now, the determination of the meaning of the example cited is likewise carried out.
(Objection: The meaning must be stated first, prior to the determination of the form of the word;
for one cannot ascertain the correctness [of a word] without knowing its denoted object.

(It is said: Even if the status of being denotable is not definitively established, correctness can be known through the distinction between the individual and the form; therefore, it is here stated that [the word] must have a denotation.
For grammatical correctness is not obtained when the mere object of expression is unknown;
nor is it possible there [to establish correctness] without either the form (ākṛti) or the individual instance (vyakti).
Alternatively, since it has been established that the entire traditional corpus of grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is authoritative according to the path already stated, something is now considered here.
The cognition that "the individual is the denotable meaning" is not well-founded because it is impossible;
therefore, even in grammar, traditional authority (smṛti) is not considered a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Therefore, this exception to memory and its validity has been established by means of the two chapters on definitions and also by the preceding inquiry.

(He raises a doubt regarding the commencement of the inquiry on the grounds that there is no purpose: But surely, even in the view that the word denotes the form (*ākṛti*), agency and non-agency reside only in the individual (*vyakti*), since these are possible in the meaning of the word; therefore, what is the purpose of this investigation?

(He first offers this rebuttal: "Even if there is no purpose in the Veda, there will be a purpose in the world"—even though [this may be so]: "Even if such a distinction does not exist regarding the composition of the meaning of the Vedas, [sentences] such as 'Curd for the Brahmins' will have their fruit in the world."

In the view that [the word] denotes an individual, there would be an option regarding Kauṇḍinya with respect to the two [prohibitions] "dadhi" and "ta," because the general statement is weaker; however, it is the opposite in the other case.
(He states the purpose according to his own view: "In the Veda as well, there is a distinction in the injunction for the sprinkling of rice grains;
and a difference arises in the injunction for the oblation regarding [the words] 'seen' and so forth."
The sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) must be performed even on the prior day (pūrvapakṣa), and even upon ordinary rice;
for, by the force of the direct scriptural statement (śruti), it overrides both proximity (sannidhi) and the order of sequence (krama).
In the established conclusion regarding the subject at hand, due to the favor of both direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*),
it is indeed the *kula* [grain] that possesses the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*), as declared by scripture.
The same applies to the oblation (*homa*) as well, whether it is the primary or the non-primary [element] in substances such as curd;
for in the case of the primary, the status of being an oblation (*homatva*), which is denoted by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), is also possible.
And other things with their logical justifications should be stated in this same manner;
by him [the practitioner], it should be reflected upon with diligent effort.
Because it is not divided, it is therefore not a tautology;
and when the meaning is non-different, there is a [grammatical] construction. But when the word-forms are identical, even though they exist, it must be considered [as a case of repetition].
It is appropriate [to ask]: "To what [does this apply]? Indeed, all of this has been examined in the context of the word "cow" (*gauḥ*) and so forth:
that denotability (*vācyatva*) belongs to both the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*).
(He states the cause for doubt: "In that which begins with the word 'cow'—that is, in the case of the word 'cow' (*gauḥ*)."
And there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the word despite differences such as its designation;
[as stated] in the *Bhāṣya* (p. 49, line 1115): "What is the meaning of the difference of the word?
Doubt arises from both the perception of difference and the negation of difference.
(Having reflected on this: Since the matter has already been understood by that [previous reasoning], further deliberation is not appropriate.

(He states the prima facie view: What is the conclusion? That word and meaning are distinct. (He refutes it: The proposition that the generic form (*ākṛti*) alone is the denotable object applies equally to both common usage and the Veda.
Because the designation [of the action] is distinct from the name [of the agent],
the author of the *Lakṣaṇa* has now stated the reason for that very [distinction] regarding the verb (*ākhyāta*).
This is because of the difference in the pronunciation of the vowels, the observation of elision and suffixes,
and as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya in the passage beginning with "yathā cākṛtiḥ."
This is untenable, because since the individual (vyakti) is also perceived, how can it be maintained that only the universal (jāti) is perceived?
Furthermore, if the individual were not perceived at all, there could be no doubt as to "what is being denoted by this [word].
Nor is the possibility of action a ground for being denotable, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of other individuals also being denoted.

Therefore, one should consider the cause of doubt to be exactly what was stated previously: because [the word] is common to both the usage (*prayoga*) and the cognition (*pratīti*); because in another treatise (the *Nyāyaśāstra*), the position of the individual (*vyakti-pakṣa*) is accepted; or because when a word is uttered, there arises from it a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*)—since both the individual and the configuration (*ākṛti*) are universals—and because, while the cognition of the individual arises from the word, the possibility of actions such as taking hold (*ālambana*), touching, or uttering words similar to "hawk" (*śyena*) occurs with respect to the configuration, and the possibility of action occurs with respect to both the universal and the individual. (By this, the *Bhāṣya* is justified.)

"But what is the *ākṛti* (form), and what is the *vyakti* (individual)? (Bhāṣya). How, then, can this question arise, when the universal (*jāti*) has already been defined in the section on the theory of form (*ākṛtivāda*) under the statement: "What is the meaning of this word 'cow'? (1.1.9)? This is not a fault;
for one who has not understood this asks: "But what is the *ākṛti*, and what is the *vyakti*?"
Or, because of doubt, when both [the individual and the universal] are perceived here, one might ask: "What is the genus, and how much of it is there?

Or, conversely, someone might ask: "When no distinct, separate entity is perceived from the mass of written scriptures and so forth, then from what source does this discrimination arise that 'this is the individual' and 'this is the genus'?
Alternatively, such reflection is undertaken everywhere for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*).
Even though the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning of the word, since the individual (*vyakti*) is capable of performing actions, this inquiry would be purposeless.

The fact that he examines this with such effort implies that he intends a novel kind of universal, which is entirely distinct from the physical object (*piṇḍa*) and fit for a separate linguistic usage. To this, he replies: "The form (*ākṛti*) is the mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*) of substances, qualities, and actions.
As for those two who maintain the positions of ignorance and doubt, their refutation must be stated by means of a description of the true nature [of the universal].
However, the refutation is stated specifically for one who holds the contrary view.

Even though a universal (*jāti*) is not perceived as being absolutely distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), nevertheless, when that [individual] is perceived by the author of the treatise, the basis for the cognition of the commonality is the configuration (*ākṛti*) according to the logic stated in the first quarter [of the verse], while the other is the individual.
Nor is the existence or the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of the universal established by this passage; rather, only the distinction from the individual is stated.

The word *mātra* (mere) is used with that very intention; otherwise, its meaning would be redundant. Although it was stated that no genus (*jāti*) intended here is absolutely distinct [from substance, quality, and action], the response to that is as follows: what is intended by "form" (*ākṛti*) is the mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*) of substances, qualities, and actions, not something entirely separate from them.

And that which is the generality common to all of these—substances and so forth—which consists of the nature of existence (*sattā*), is what is indicated by this term; by the indication of that, the indication of intermediate generalities is also established.

When the word *sāmānya* is heard in connection with each [of the categories], it indicates the three generalities beginning with substantiality (*dravyatva*), because existence (*sattā*) is excluded from conventional usage.
Alternatively, due to the employment of the word *mātra*, everything included among the intermediate generalities and the great generalities within substance and the other categories is denoted.
"The individual (*vyakti*) is that which possesses uncommon particularities" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

The term *asādhāraṇaviśeṯāḥ* refers to those specific qualities (*viśeṣāḥ*) which belong to a particular individual (*vyakti*). It is not a case of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) where "asādhāraṇa" and "viśeṣa" are taken separately as "those which are both uncommon and specific," because—as will be stated later—the individual is designated as the substratum of the specific qualities; furthermore, this is supported by the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) in the Vaiśeṣika system that substances, qualities, and actions are the substrata of generalities and specificities (Sudhā, p. 379). Therefore, it has been correctly stated: "Is it the form (*ākṛti*) or the individual (*vyakti*)?"

What is established? (The sūtra *prayogacodanābhāvāt* [due to the absence of injunctions for performance] applies this preliminary argument for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the universal as well—) because injunctions for performance such as grasping, sprinkling, and immolation exist only in the case of the individual (*vyakti*) and not in the case of the universal (*ākṛti*), and because prohibitory injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" and "Liquor must not be drunk" are possible only in the case of the individual, and because worldly transactions and injunctions such as "Devadatta, bring the cow" are likewise consistent [only with the individual], it is determined that the individual is the meaning of the word.
(With this very portion of the Sūtra, he states other reasons that have been implied: "And because of the occurrence of number and grammatical case-role (*kāraka*).

For if the individual (*vyakti*) were the meaning of a word, then in cases such as *vṛkṣau* (two trees) and *vṛkṣābhyām* (by two trees), both would be possible: the number—duality and so forth—denoted by the suffixes applied to the individuals expressed by the nominal stem, and the grammatical case-role, such as the instrument (*karaṇa*). In the alternative view, however, since the universal (*jāti*) is neither enumerable nor possesses a case-role, both would be impossible; moreover, resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be unacceptable. And thus, all Vedic sentence-meanings would become merely figurative.

On the view that the individual is the meaning of the word, however, there arises the possibility of primary grammatical coreferentiality (*mukhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such cases as "The person is Devadatta.

On the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning, one would have to assume a figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) coreferentiality; yet even by that, it is understood that the individual is the word-meaning.

Furthermore, from the Vedic injunction "One should sacrifice the animal," the cognition of the individual is derived through the [details of] the two-fold sprinkling and so forth; subsequently, we observe linguistic usage directed toward the individual, not toward the universal.
This is because a substance mixed with action is required [as the referent].
In the view that the individual (vyakti) is the denotatum, there is the expression of what is required, but not in the other case.
Furthermore, it is logical that an individual whose nature is established should be the denotatum, and not a genus (jāti) which is unestablished.
Therefore, the individual (*vyakti*) is the meaning of the word.

(To introduce the portion of the sūtra beginning with *ayam kathyaḥ*, one might ask: Why is it not accepted that both [the universal and the individual] are denoted, since the application [of the word] and the act of cognition are both possible?

(He refutes this with the portion of the sūtra: No, because it would entail the assumption of multiple powers; since the connection is established through the expression of only one [of them], and since the cognition of the other is logically accounted for [as being secondary], the individual alone is the denotable object.

(To introduce the portion of the sūtra beginning with "avibhāgāt," one might object: "How can there be a cognition of a universal? (The author refutes this with a portion of the sūtra: Because it is possible [only] through its connection with individuals. If it is argued that "wherever the application of an action is impossible, it is only there that denoting an individual is appropriate by way of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), whereas elsewhere, because it is previously perceived, it denotes only the universal"—this is not so; for by the path already stated, there would follow the fault of postulating multiple powers [for a single word], the contingency of an unstable relationship between word and meaning, and the occurrence of doubt.

If it is asked how there can be a lack of cause for those who maintain that the word denotes the individual—namely, how the word can apply to another individual—the answer is that there is no contradiction in its application to another individual because its cause is the mark provided by the form (*ākṛti*). However, when the author of the *Bhāṣya* introduces the question, "How is there the comprehension of the universal? and provides the reply, "For the form is what will exist as the basis," that is irrelevant; for when the cause of the cognition of the universal has been questioned, one should instead postulate the cause for the application to another individual.
This should be explained by supplying that [missing word].

If it is asked, "How is there the non-attainment of the universal? [the answer is: because it is connected with the individual. If it is asked, "How is there the application [of the word] to another individual? [the answer is: because the configuration (*ākṛti*) serves as the mark; thus it is.

Alternatively, when the question "How is there no comprehension of the universal? is posed, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), unable to withstand this objection, adopts the position that the individual qualified by the form (ākṛti) is what is intended. For the form, having previously been non-existent [as a denotable], will become a denotable qualifier; therefore, the objection regarding the cognition of that [form] is raised.
Consequently, the word-meaning is either the individual alone or the individual as qualified [by the form].

(Regarding the sūtra *adṛśyaśabdatvāt* [31], the reasoning is stated in brief: Likewise, in cases such as "six [cows] are to be given," the number six and so forth is logically possible [only if the word refers to the individual]. (Regarding the sūtra *anyadarśanācca* [32], which is explained by way of another perspective: Furthermore, in the case of "this is that same wool," the application of the same word to a different individual and its persistence as a property of that [individual] will be possible. (The author follows the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra by way of a negative argument: Otherwise, because the universal would be distinct even from other individuals and because it would lack qualities, both [the aforementioned facts] would be untenable.
Therefore, the individual object is the meaning of the word.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
this is not so; the individual is not what is expressed by the word, but rather the class-form (ākṛti) is understood to be the meaning of the word.

Because of the scriptural statement, "He piles the *śyena-cit*," the meaning of the sentence here would have to be either that one should perform the piling of an individual *śyena* bird or that one should perform the piling of its form (*ākṛti*).

However, since it is impossible to construct an individual *śyena* bird according to one's desires, and because even things such as bathing are not specified [as the object], and because the individual *śyena* bird is made of bricks, and because the purpose of the individual *śyena* bird must be postulated, and because the root *ci* (to pile) primarily denotes the act of piling, and because there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the traditional grammatical rule (Pāṇini 3.1.92), "In the case of the word *agni*, when it is a name for the fire-altar," it is first of all not tenable that one should produce an individual *śyena* bird by means of piling.

Likewise, because it is impossible to create even the *ākṛti* (form) by mere desire, because it is created by the gods (*deva-nirmitatva*), because of the postulation of a purpose, because the root *ci* (to pile/build) does not have that as its primary meaning, and because it would contradict traditional scripture (*smṛti-bādha*), the statement "one should make the *ākṛti*" is also untenable.
By process of elimination, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should accomplish the construction by means of piling [bricks] so as to resemble a hawk."

Furthermore, because fire is similar to a particular hawk (*śyena*) in its mode of being a substrate, because it possesses all individual forms, because it appears as a thousandfold due to its nature as past and future individuals, and because it attains a thousandfold state, it is established that the word's meaning is the *ākṛti* (form/generic class), which consists in the attainment of similarity to the act of making a hawk.

Now, why is this injunction for piling not accepted as referring to the individual hawks—as in the statement, "He piles the hawk-pile" (*śyenacitaṃ cinoti*)? To this, the author of the Bhāṣya has given the answer: "For that which is most desired to be attained is indicated by the word 'hawk'.
That, however, is incorrect.

In the case of the word *śyena* [in the compound *śyenacita*], its own primary meaning is not [the bird] because it is heard after the exclusion of all [other] hawks; furthermore, since the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) follows that [word], the word *śyena* ends in the second case (*dvitīyānta*), whereby it would express that which is most desired to be attained (*īpsitatama*).

Therefore, by the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "when the name *agni* [is to be formed], [the suffix *kvip* is used] after a word denoting the object (*karman*)," the status of being the object (*karmatva*) must be attributed to the meaning of the word *śyena*. For it is taught that the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ci* [meaning "to pile"] when it denotes the object, provided that it refers to the name *agni*.

Furthermore, the designation "fire" (agni) cannot apply to the root *ci* alone. Therefore, from the scriptural mention of *cinoti*, it is determined that the entire term *śyenacit* denotes the act of piling the fire-altar; the word *śyena* does not have a separate meaning.
Consequently, the meaning of the word *śyena* is not understood as being the instrument [of the action].

If this [the act of building] were the instrument (*karaṇa*), then, due to the mere indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the instrumental case, there would be the impossibility of the proximity [of the word "brick"] to the third case-ending; furthermore, the unexpressed third case-ending would have to be postulated.
If one were to postulate what is not heard in the text (*aśruta-kalpanā*), there would be the abandonment of the bricks.
Moreover, when an alternative is available, the performance of various prohibited forms of the Śyena sacrifice results in the act of violence (*hiṃsā*).
Because it is impossible for that [the *śyena*] to function as an instrument, the meaning of the sentence is: "One piles the fire-altar built like a *śyena*.
And therefore, by the aforementioned *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*...
"By logic, since this statement is possible under the view that the word-meaning is the *ākṛti* (form), the *ākṛti* is the word-meaning.

This is not so; for the *ākṛti* does not acquire the status of being the expressed meaning merely because the act of leading [the animal] is possible [with respect to it]. Even under the view that the word-meaning is the individual (*vyakti*), acts such as immolation (*ālambhana*) and so forth are possible [with respect to the individual]; moreover, because there are many statements regarding immolation and the like, the fact that the word-meaning is the individual itself is determined by the impossibility of those statements otherwise. If it is argued that even under the view that the word-meaning is the *ākṛti*, those [acts] are possible through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the individual, then one can equally say that in the statement concerning the *śyena* sacrifice, the individual is indicated by the *ākṛti*.
Furthermore, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is appropriate in one instance [the word "hawk"] and not in the many others;
and by means of comprehension, the recourse to a third-case compound will be made in the sentence concerning the hawk-sacrifice (śyenavākya).
Moreover, the logical consistency of number, case-role (kāraka), and so forth is established under the theory of the individual (vyaktipakṣa).
Therefore, the individual is the meaning of the word;
likewise, it is stated that the universal is the denoted object.

Why? Because the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) precedes [the cognition of] the individual, as it is admitted by both the mind and the intellect; and because of the statement "the universal," since one adopts [the object] according to one's inclination. For when the word "cow" is uttered, first of all, through comprehension, the names and meanings are understood in those individuals, and only after the arising of the cognition having that form (*tadākāra*) are the individuals perceived. Therefore, for the cognition of the configuration (*ākṛti*), there is no other cause.

The Section on Form (Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa): [Objection] "If [the word denoted] were the form (ākṛti), then its application to another individual would not be possible, because the qualifier [the form] is different [in each case]."
Therefore, the universal (*jāti*) alone is the meaning of the word.
[Objection: But since it is perceived as subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), there must be something else that is the primary denotatum (*abhidheya*).
[Reply: Not so; for by the word, that very [universal] is what is denoted.
If, by virtue of the context, it acquires the status of a quality (*guṇatva*) or predominance (*prādhānya*), let it be so; however, its status as the denotation of a word is not thereby contradicted.
And when it is denoted by a word, its status as a quality is not perceived at all; therefore, there is no fault regarding the perception of its quality through the context.
[Objection: But surely, for the reasons stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is logical that the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the meaning of a word.
If it is argued that the application [of a word] to another individual would not be possible, [we reply: the generic form (*ākṛti*) will serve as the sign (*cihna*).

Just as, for example, even when not explicitly denoted, the "crow's nest" (as a mark) is understood to be the sign for the house of Devadatta—which is similar to other houses—so too the generic form will serve as the sign in the denotation of the individual.

The author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, has cited the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) as an illustration: just as by that word the staff is indeed not named, yet a person qualified by a staff is conveyed, so it is with the generic form as well.

[Objection: But surely in the word *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer), the staff is indeed denoted by the base (*prakṛti*); how then can it be said that "the staff is not denoted"? And how is it that when the generic form (*ākṛti*) is presented as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the qualified object is conveyed?
[Response: This is not a fault, because the statement that "the staff is not denoted" intends the suffix (*pratyaya*) which denotes the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Just as a staff is not denoted by the word [denoting the person] through its causal condition, yet a person qualified by that [staff] is nevertheless conveyed, so too will it be in this case—this is the intended meaning.

As for the objection that it is improper to cite a qualifier as an example when presenting a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), that is not a valid challenge, because even a secondary indicator functions as a qualifier.
Furthermore, it has been stated that there will be an analogy based on some commonality, namely, by way of being non-denotable and by way of being a qualifier.
And thus it has been correctly stated that, just as in the word *daṇḍin*, so too will it be in this case;
and in this way, neither the [unwanted] consequence (*aprasaṅga*) nor the excessive consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) will occur.
This, however, is not tenable.

It is appropriate to denote Devadatta’s house and the person alone, even when there is a cognition of a qualified object, just as in the case of the words "crow's nest" and "staff," because their status as qualifiers is established. However, it is not tenable for "cowness," which is not present here, to function as a mere secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa).
For when a qualifier is not previously cognized, there is no cognition of the qualified object;
nor do we perceive the denotation of "cowness" as being subordinate to the word "staff," in which case the individual would be denoted by virtue of being a second [element].
And therefore, if the universal "cowness" (gotva) were denoted first, then by the logic already stated, that alone would have to be the expressed meaning;
for that which is not yet cognized cannot function as a qualifier, and because it would be impossible [to apply a qualifier to what is unknown],
there would result the aforementioned over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the employment of words.

Furthermore, just as the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is not used for the staff alone and is therefore determined to denote a qualified entity, so too [the word "cow"] cannot be determined to denote a qualified entity because it is not used for the form (*ākṛti*) alone. Rather, since its usage is observed for the form in cases such as "one should sacrifice with a cow" (*gavā yajeta*), and because through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) it is determined that the genus (*jāti*) alone is the denoted meaning—given that it is used for the form alone in "one should sacrifice with a cow," and because its usage is never observed for the individual (*vyakti*) alone apart from the form—it is concluded that the genus is indeed the denoted meaning.
In this way, those prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣas) such as [the denotation of] relation, collection, and so forth, are also refuted by the reasoning already stated.
Therefore, it is the form (ākṛti) alone that is the meaning of a word. [Objection:

If it is argued that there would be no action [if the form were the meaning], or that there would be an injunction regarding a different object, or that there would be no substance—[we reply: [this is not so].
The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that the action [expressed by] "he sprinkles the rice grains" would not be possible;
that there would be no word denoting a substance [as in] "the jars should be given";
and that there would be no statement regarding the observation of another [object], such as "another of that same form."
That must be refuted.
Because the application [of the word] is for that purpose, there is no distinction.
The Bhāṣya says: "If the word has the class (*ākṛti*) as its meaning, then just as the individual (*vyakti*) is related to the class, so too is the application [of the word] therein."
For it is heard in the scripture that the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) must be performed upon a substance.

Which [substance]? That which is the means of sacrifice, because it is prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and not the generic form (*ākṛti*), because the latter lacks causal capacity.
In this context, the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) is employed as a designation for the generic form in order to specify the substratum of the sprinkling.
For that [the word "cow"] will cause the form (ākṛti) to be understood; once the form is understood, it will specify the substrate for the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement regarding the form.

Likewise, in the case of the statement, "Cows are to be given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)," since the substance of the fee is what must be expressed, the mention of the form "cows" serves as the specifier.
Likewise, the term "another" implies a substitute for what has perished, which is the possibility of otherness.
In that context, the word "animal" (paśu) denotes the generic form (ākṛti), as it qualifies [the individual] by means of the form.
Therefore, it is established that words such as "cow" and "horse" denote the generic form.

Bhā: As for those reasons stated in the prima facie argument—such as the absence of injunctions regarding the touching (*ālambhana*) and so forth, which were brought forward by the commentary on the sūtra "There would be no action" (*na kriyā syāt*)—the refutation of all of them is stated by this sūtra:
"Because it is for that purpose, there is no division of the performance" (*tadarthatvāt prayogasyāvibhāgaḥ*).
Because it is for that purpose—that is, because it is for the sake of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).
The Section on Form (Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa):
However, because of the section on form, sacrificial acts such as immolation and sprinkling must be applied toward that which accomplishes the *apūrva*.

And the substance (*dravya*) is the means for accomplishing the *apūrva*, because it is resorted to by the sacrifice for the sake of its own realization; the form (*ākṛti*), however, is not, because it lacks efficacy.

The denotation of that [form], moreover, should be understood as being for the purpose of restricting the substance, and not for its own sake, because the universal (*jāti*) is not required [as a means] and because it would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). It is simply the attainment of the means [of accomplishment].

As for the fact that the instrumentality of the universal, expressed by the nominal stem, is perceived, that too is only through its function of restricting the substance, and not directly, because it is incapable [of such a role].

Because the denotation of the form (ākṛti) serves the purpose of restricting [the application] to the substance, and since in the case of the substance there is the possibility of [performing] acts such as immolation (ālambhana), sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), number, and grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the agent, there is no transcendental result (adṛṣṭatā). Thus he says: "The non-distinction of the performance" (prayogasyāvibhāgaḥ); that is, even in the view that the form is denoted, the performance of acts such as immolation is inseparable from the substance.
Alternatively, because the denotation of the form serves the purpose of restricting [the application] to the substance, there is a distinction of the performance as previously stated.

Or rather, because there is no absolute difference between the form (ākṛti) and the individual (vyakti), sometimes a substance is denoted in the form of the individual and sometimes in the form of the universal, according to what is intended. Thus, since the word possesses both forms, even when it denotes the individual, there is no distinction in its usage nor a multiplicity of forms. Or else, because there is no absolute difference between the genus (jāti) and the individual, the properties established in the individual are indeed established in the genus; therefore, there is no need for a distinction in usage.

Alternatively, since both the form (*ākṛti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) serve the purpose of sacrifice, and since ritual duties (*dharma*) performed in any means that accomplishes the sacrifice possess utility—just as in the case of substances and their divisions—it is established that even according to the view that the form is the meaning of the word, the form alone is the word-meaning, because acts such as "touching for slaughter" (*ālambhana*) are possible therein. Now, having understood the expressive [word], one seeks to know the specific object expressed: is it the form, or is it the individual?

In this regard, if there were a difference between words and their meanings in common usage (*loka*) and in the Veda (*veda*), then this [treatise] would not need to be commenced. Therefore, as an introduction to the section concerning the generic form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*), the difference or non-difference between words and their meanings in common usage and in the Veda is investigated.
When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are different, it is stated in reply: "The identity of the phonemes is established because of direct perceptual recognition."
The word is the property of denoting color, and it is differentiated by its non-difference from that [color].

Thus, once this is established, it is investigated: is the meaning of a word the *ākṛti* (form), or the *vyakti* (individual), or the individual qualified by the *ākṛti*? These three positions are primarily considered. ... In that regard, because there would be an absence of injunctions for usage, the denotability belongs to the individuals alone.
Since the form (ākṛti) is not a substance, it cannot be employed for the application of a substance; therefore,
its connection with gender, case-role (kāraka), and number is not possible.

Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not occur between words denoting a genus and words denoting a quality; however, under the view that words denote the individual (*vyakti*), all of this is consistent. Therefore, the object of a word is either the pure individual or the qualified individual.
"This is not tenable.
Why? Because of infinity, because of deviation, and because of the fault of manifold powers;
since the form (ākṛti) is known first, it alone must be the denotatum."
Furthermore, because there is no difference between the individual (vyakti) and the form (ākṛti), their utility for linguistic usage—
including the connection with gender, number, and so forth, as well as the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—
is all perfectly consistent for one who maintains the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) regarding reality.

Alternatively, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must be accepted, because by that means the genus (*jāti*) becomes the denoted meaning. [The connection between this section and the previous one is as follows:
Since the section concerning "Soma" in the *Loka-Veda* treatise serves as the introduction to the section on "Form" (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*), there is a logical connection (*saṃgati*).
[Second Exposition (*varṇaka* 2): Is the referent of words such as "cow" the individual (*vyakti*), or is it the form (*ākṛti*), since action is impossible otherwise?

Alternatively, the individual (vyakti) is indicated by the form (ākṛti), according to the view of Āpiśali; or, based on the reasoning of the Śaktimad-vāda and others, it is appropriate that the form itself be the indicator. Or rather, let the individual be indicated for the sake of accomplishing the action.

In this very context, the teacher’s (Guru) opinion is stated: "Let there be no determination between the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) regarding [the denotation of] words such as *go* (cow).
Because of infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is determined that the individual is not [denoted].

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains: Since actions such as threshing (*avaghāta*), as well as gender, case-role (*kāraka*), number, and so forth, are incompatible with the genus, and because of the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as *gauḥ śuklaḥ* ("a white cow"), it is the individual alone that is the denotatum.
Nor does this entail the fallacy of infinite regress (*jāty-anavasthā*), because that [cognition] is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth.

Alternatively, the delimiting factor of the causal efficacy (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) with respect to the individual (*vyakti*) is simply the cognition qualified by the universal (*jāti*).
Therefore, there is no fault.

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), because parsimony (*lāghava*) itself serves as the regulator. To explain: the apprehension of the word-meaning relation (*śaktigraha*) is not a cause in its own right, but rather, by virtue of parsimony, it is the cognition of the word "pot" (*ghaṭapada*) as possessing the property of being the denotatum (*śakyatva*)—that is, as having the nature of "potness" (*ghaṭatva*). Therefore, it is accepted that the cognition of the word "pot" as the denoter, taking "potness" as the delimitor of the subject-property (*dharmitā'vacchedaka*) and related to it through the relation of being the denotatum (*śakyatvasambandha*), is the cause of a qualified verbal cognition delimited by the nature of such a cognition, namely, the cognition "the pot possesses the word 'pot'," which occurs through the relation of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāsambandha*).
In your view, however, that [denotability] must be predicated with respect to the property "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) as the delimiting factor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*).

Consequently, because the entry of "pot-ness"—which consists of the delimitation of pot-hood and so forth and is composed of multiple entities—occurs in that causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), there is prolixity (*gaurava*).
Nor is there the fault of an infinite number of powers (*śakti*) and so on, because such a fault is "consequential" (*phalamukhatva*).

And for this reason, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), the expressive power (*śakti*) resides either in the individual alone, or in the individual qualified by the class (*jāti*), as established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, but not in the class alone.

This being the position [of the opponent], [we reply: taking *ghaṭatva* (potness) as the delimiting factor of the subject (*dharmitā'vacchedaka*), there would be no reason for determining [the direction of causality] (*vinigamanā-viraha*) because it would lead to an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations (*ananta-kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva-prasaṅga*) regarding the denotability of the word "pot" through the relation of being denotable (*śakyatva-sambandha*). However, in our view, by taking the word "pot" (*ghaṭapada*) as the delimiting factor of the subject, one postulates a causal relation consisting of the ascertainment that the word "pot" possesses potness (*ghaṭatvavattā-niścaya*)—in the form "the word 'pot' possesses potness"—through the relation of being denotable; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*).

Nor can I establish a contrary position; for if that were the case, since "potness" (ghaṭatva) would be the subject (dharmin), it could not be the subject in its own form (svarūpeṇa). If it were introduced as "potness-ness" (ghaṭatvatva), the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) would have to be accepted. Therefore, it is not "potness" as delimited by "potness-ness" that is the cause of the knowledge of the object denoted by the word "pot" through the relation of denotability (śakyatva); rather, it is simply the cognition "the word 'pot' [denotes] potness" through the relation of denotability. This is because a universal (jāti) is a qualifier (prakāra) in its own form, and thus "potness-ness" does not enter into the picture.

Furthermore, there is no evidence for the claim that a universal (jāti) is a qualifier by its own nature only when it exists through inherence (samavāya), and not through any other relation; for even our opponents do not accept this.

Consequently, even regarding the causal relationship, on the grounds of parsimony (lāghava), the potency resides in the "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) itself. And there is no disagreement among us that the potency is non-different from the thing itself.
Therefore, because it is established first, the expressive power (śakti) resides in the genus (jāti) alone.

Likewise, in the case of words such as "aruṇā" (red), the power resides either in the quality (guṇa) or in the state of being a quality (guṇatva), but not in the substance qualified by that [quality].
How, then, is there the cognition of the individual (vyakti)? Through non-difference (abheda).

Alternatively, this is because the aforementioned cause is accepted as having the property of being the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatvāvacchedaka*) only when the individual (*vyakti*) is denoted by the word as qualified by the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*).

In reality, however, the state of being denoted by the word as genus and quality (*jātiguṇa-śābdatva*) alone is the delimitor of the effect due to parsimony (*lāghava*). As for the individual, it does not appear from the word at all in cases such as "one should sacrifice with a non-blind cow" (*apaṅkhyā yajeta*) or "one buys [the Soma] with a red, yellow-eyed [cow]" (*aruṇayā piṅgākṣyā krīṇāti*), since it is established that the genus and the quality themselves serve as the cause by means of delimiting the individual.

Even regarding gender and number, according to the logic of the *pāśādhikaraṇa* (PMS 9.1.4–6), there is a relationship of genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) with the [substantive] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Therefore, in that case, the cognition of the individual occurs as qualified by the genus and the quality. However, in the second and subsequent instances, just as the genus and the quality are unfit for connection with the status of being the object (*karmatva*), the individual is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The connection with its very [abstract] actionhood (*karmatva*) [is established];
gender and number, however, are connected directly.
And grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is mediated through the individual (*vyakti*); thus, everything is well-established.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since words such as *rathaṃtara* denote *ṛks*, in passages such as "one should chant the *rathaṃtara* on the *uttarā*," the injunction would apply to the *ṛk* indicated by the word *uttarā* and to the action performed upon it.
However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it will be stated that the location of the song is the *uttarā*.
Maṇḍana [says]: "The word *go* and others denote a genus (*jāti*)."
Śaṅkara says: "The denotability [of words] belongs to the *ākṛti* (form/class) alone.
If there were no connection between worldly and Vedic words, this *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* would not even need to be commenced.

However, since they are distinct from analogy (*upamāna*), the determination of word-meanings established in the world will be useful in the Veda even if it is not useful there [directly]. Thus, as an introduction to the *adhikaraṇa*, the connection or lack of connection between words and their meanings in the world and the Veda is investigated."

*Kau.* 3.1.6.12, p. 166: Since the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the verbal suffix is untenable without an agent, it implies the agent. Since the agent is understood through this very implication (*ākṣepa*), why should the verbal suffix itself be postulated as having the nature of the agent?

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha), for the agent is indeed the possessor of volitional effort (kṛtimān). Thus, since it is possible for the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) to denote the agent through the very act of volitional effort (*kṛti*) via a succession of productive operations (*bhāvanā*), according to the logic of the section on generic form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇanyāya*), one need not postulate the status of being an agent as something distinct from that [volition]; for that would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). This has already been stated.

Elsewhere it is also stated: Even in the view of those who maintain that the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the sentence "Devadatta cooks" is possible according to their theory; for in their view, since the verbal suffix expresses only the isolated power (*śakti*)—that is, the single *kāraka* under discussion—the substance possessing that power (*śaktimat-dravya*) is not expressed, following the logic of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

6.1.1042: "The efficient force (bhāvanā) is expressed by the verbal suffix; since that is not possible without an agent, it implies (ākṣipati) him.

Now, why is it described in this way—that "the agent is implied"—and why could it not be directly denoted (vācya) by the verbal suffix itself? For upon hearing the verbal suffix, there is a cognition of the agent just as there is of the efficient force.
Nor is it correct to argue that since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) can be implied [by other means], there is no need to postulate its identity [with the verb root];

for if that were the case, then even though the *bhāvanā* is implied by what is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), its identity with that [suffix] would not exist either. Furthermore, the agent is not the only relation of the *bhāvanā*, as it is related to other *kārakas* (factors of action) as well.

Therefore, that [the *bhāvanā*] would not immediately imply the agent alone, as there is no specific reason for such a restriction. Rather, the agent is connected only with the *bhāvanā*, and not with any other *kāraka*, according to the principle: "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, their connection would be based on equality" (PMS 3.1.12.22).
Consequently, since the agent would immediately imply it [the *bhāvanā*], that [agent] alone is what is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
But why should the *bhāvanā* not be the very thing implied?

For the proponent accepts that in the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, such as "cook" (*paktā*), the agent is the denotable meaning (*śakyatva*) while the *bhāvanā* is merely implied; likewise, it is appropriate to accept the same for verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*).
Alternatively, just as in the case of verbal suffixes, it is more appropriate to say that even in words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, the *bhāvanā* itself is the denotable meaning.

Now, if it is admitted that the agent possesses the capacity for the connection with gender and number in that case [the past passive participle], then let it be admitted that the same applies to verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) for the sake of their connection with number.

Alternatively, if it is argued that in the case of verbal suffixes, the agent is implied because the denotation of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is necessary for the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*), then it would follow that the denotation of the productive operation must also occur in primary derivative forms (*kṛdanta*) such as "cooked by wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pakvaḥ*), in order to connect them with the factors of action.

If it is replied that the agent and so forth are the expressed meanings in primary derivatives, whereas the productive operation is the expressed meaning in verbal suffixes because its predominance is perceived there; [we respond:]
That is not so;
for even in cognitions where the genus, quality, and so forth are subordinate, there is an experience of the individuals as being primary.
Furthermore, if this were the case, the third and other case-endings would also not denote the instrument and so forth, since those too could be obtained through the implication of agency.

Furthermore, if the agent were not to be expressed [by the suffix], how could there be such a syntactic connection (*anvaya*)? For it is not logical that what is verbal should be connected with what is non-verbal; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the rule] applying even to cases such as *udbhid* [where the word is used as a name]. [As stated in the *Mīmāṃsākośa*: "At the time of grinding the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the meat-grinding stone is present before one's eyes... (MīmS 10.2).

Because the accomplishment of the ordinary task is achieved by the mantra through the manifestation of its own function, there would be no modification (ūha) such as "māṃsam" [instead of "medhaḥ"]. Furthermore, since the injunction of the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), which prescribes a productive activity (bhāvanā) characterized by the assistance of the archetypal subsidiaries indicated by the archetypal injunction through comparison, can achieve self-sufficiency, there would be no assumption of an extended application (atideśa).
Moreover, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the expression "Devadatta cooks."
For it is not possible for the verb, which denotes the mere action (*bhāvanā*), to have coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Devadatta," because they do not reside in a single object;
however, this is indeed possible if [the verb] denotes the agent (*kartṛ*).

Furthermore, the contradiction with the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*)—specifically the rule "laḥ karmaṇi"—is evident if the agent (*kartṛ*) is not denoted [by the suffix]. For, in the rule "kartari kṛt," the word *kartari* indisputably conveys that the agent is denoted by the *kṛt*-suffixes; and because the term "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) from that rule into the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ," it establishes that the *l*-suffixes in the rule "laḥ kartari" denote the agent. If they did not so denote, then since there is no difference in their being substitutes for *l* (*lādeśatva*)—just as in the case of the *tiṅ*-suffixes—it would follow that even the *śnā* and *nac* suffixes would fail to denote the object (*karman*).

Furthermore, [if the agent were not denoted], the recitation (*japa*) enjoined by the rule "one who is about to sacrifice should recite" would not be a duty of the person connected with the ritual (*ṛtu-yukta-puruṣadharma*).
Moreover, if the agent were not denoted, the usage "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattena pacati*) would result;
for the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) would certainly apply to express the agent when it is not already denoted by another word.

However, when the agent (*kartṛ*) is already expressed, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) does not apply simply because it has already been expressed; for that [third case] applies only when [the agent] is unexpressed (*anabhihita*), whereas the first case (*prathamā*) is a case-ending whose function is to express an already-expressed grammatical participant (*kāraka*). Consequently, the state of being unexpressed (*anabhihitatva*), which is obtained through the governing context (*adhikāra*), is construed with the number as its qualifier, since a qualifier must attach to the principal element.
