Therefore, although the agent is not denoted by the word *pacati*, since the number of the agent is denoted, there is no contingency of applying the term "agent" (to the agent) as a secondary metaphorical designation (*bhakti*), because [the agent] is identical with that [number].
That is not correct;

for since the *lakāra* suffixes are not designated by the terms "singular" and so on, while the rule *laḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.77] is designated by the terms "dual" and "plural," they stand in a relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) according to the established principle.

By accepting that the rule *itsaṃjñāntena laḥ* (P. 1.3.7) refers to the general category of the letter *l* regardless of its specific diacritical marks (*anubandha*), [it follows that] the verbal suffix (*la*) prescribed by rules such as *vartamāne laṭ* (P. 3.2.123) undergoes substitution;
and by means of the verb (*ākhyāta*), the *bhāvanā* is expressed. By means of the verb, the *bhāvanā* is expressed.

It is argued that *bhāvanā* is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). [Objection: If this were so, then even in cases such as *pacyate* ("is cooked"), there would be the undesirable consequence of number being associated with the agent (*kartṛ*) who is dependent on the *bhāvanā*; furthermore, if the action is established as residing in the object (*karman*), it would contradict your own tenets; and the instrumental case in *devadattena* would not occur, since the rule for the object would apply. [Reply: This is not so.

For just as you, by the power of the diversity of linguistic capacity (*śabdaśakti*), maintain the distinction between the expression of the agent and the object despite their equal status as verbal suffixes, so too can we maintain the distinction of the definitions of agent and object through the very same meaning of those suffixes.
And the determination of specific capacities is equal regardless of the difference in the explanations [of the grammarians].

Furthermore, even though there is a distinction between the quality (*guṇa*) and the excellence (*atiśaya*) in the case of the words *śukla* (white) and *rūpa* (form), the designation of a substance (*dravya-lakṣaṇā*) and so forth is established solely by virtue of their expressive power (*śakti*).
As they have said: "Certain secondary designations (*lakṣaṇā*) are conventionalized (*nirūḍhā*) through capacity, just like primary denotations (*abhidhāna*)."
At present, some of his intentions are being carried out, while others are not at all.

(He states a verse: "In this world, with respect to certain meanings, the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is as firmly established (*nirūḍhā*) through its operation from time immemorial as the power of primary denotation (*abhidhāna*), as in the case of words such as *śukla* ('white').
In some cases, it is brought about [by convention], as in the expression 'the rathāṅga-named one is the cakravāka bird.
In other cases, however, it cannot even be produced, as in the case of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell."
But how is it that, when the connection (*saṃdhi*) here is indistinct, there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? To this, the answer is: "like denotation" (*abhidhānavat*).

Just as for you, despite the word being equally a quality-term (*guṇaśabda*), words such as "white" denote a substance with the quality as a subordinate factor (*guṇopasarjana-dravyavacanatva*), whereas words such as "color" do not; so too, for me, it is indicated. (Vākyapadīya 3.14.6–12, p. 683). [Objection: But if this is so, then since one must admit a separate power (*śakti*), there is no distinction here from the view of the opponent.

It is accepted by Bhavadeva that the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) between the denotatum and the word is established by the very power of denotation (*abhidhānaśakti*) itself—specifically, through the power of indication (*lakṣaṇāśakti*) consisting of the intended meaning and purpose (*tātparya*), since this is the meaning of the word. Furthermore, the determination of indication establishes the determination of the application of number (*saṃkhyā*).
As they have said: "Just as someone, having spoken of an action in one place, will not speak of it elsewhere..."
In the same way, even its number is established solely through the power of the word.

(He explains the verse: For one who thinks that in some instances the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) denotes the agent, and therefore there must be something else [denoted] as well—for such a person, because the non-denotability [of the agent] is observed in some cases, it would follow that it is denotable everywhere. Or, if that [agent] is restricted to certain specific cases, then the number would likewise be restricted in exactly the same way; thus, these two [the agent and the number] are mutually dependent. (Vārttika 314, 4.1.3, p. 915).

Alternatively, according to the logic already stated, since it is accepted that number is restricted to other [grammatical] factors when there is an exclusion from the specific cognition produced by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), its cognition is established.

Some, however, maintain that just as the words *gauḥ* and *aśvaḥ* do not denote the cow and horse themselves but rather denote their specific forms as qualified by those [entities], so too they accept the denotation of the respective numbers for the purpose of conveying the agent and the object; and they claim that the determination of the status of agent and object arises solely through the power of that [number-denotation].
That is not correct.

For it is indeed experienced through perception that a cow and a horse possess internal subdivisions such as "calfness" and "horseness," and thus they can be denoted by those terms; however, no such internal subdivision of number is experienced in the case of the agent and the object.

As it has been said: "Number is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in the same way that 'redness' and other qualities are [expressed] as distinctions within a genus, nor is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) so expressed."
Regarding a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) that expresses number, its very nature as a verbal suffix is what is perceived; thus, there is no dependence on anything else therein.
As they have said: "The cognition of either number or grammatical relation (*kāraka*) proceeds indeed by means of the case-ending (*vibhakti*)."
In this context, both of these are established: the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*).
In the sentence "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadattaḥ*), agency (*kartṛtva*) is understood as being nothing other than the efficient force itself;
and as for the number (*saṃkhyā*) as well, that too is expressed by the verbal suffix.

However, where that number is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the third case ending indeed occurs there, as in "odanaḥ pacyate devadattena" ("the rice is being cooked by Devadatta"). Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in the expression of the agent.

Furthermore, if the agent were denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), then in the case of the *samid* and other such offerings, there would be the consequence that they are directly connected (*saṃnipātin*), and thus the injunction would pertain to them as agents.

If you say, "Let it be so," [we reply: the oblation prescribed in the text, "He offers the *sthāṇu*-oblation upon the sacrificial post (*sthāṇu*)," would serve only to purify the agent, and not the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
For this is exactly what was stated on the basis of the strength of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the tenth book (10.1.6.10).
Nor is it stated out of a desire for a visible purpose, but rather out of a desire for a direct application (saṃnipātitva);
and this will be explained later.
Furthermore, the quality of being directly applied is equal in both the case of the sacrificial post (yūpa) and the status of being the agent (kartṛtva).
However, this [case] regarding the agent is designated as the *yūpa* (sacrificial post), even though the act of "offering" (*juhoti*) has been mentioned and the action is directly connected [to it].
Nor can it be argued that there would be no subversion of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the *yūpa* being for the sake of the sacrifice;

for in the mantra of the oblation, "Therefore, O divine Lord of the Forest, sprout forth with a hundred branches," it would be impossible to manifest the excellence of the *yūpa*-nature denoted by the words "divine" and so forth.

Furthermore, in that case, the status of being for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is not established solely by that purpose, because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a mantra contradicted by logic is ineffective.

Moreover, since the *upāṃśuyāja*—established by another sentence as being common to other sacrifices—is connected with a result, its connection with the agent situated within its own context via the phrase "he sacrifices between" occurs more rapidly; thus, the *samit* and others would indeed have that [agent] as their purpose. And it is understood from the statement "the sacrificer gazes at the clarified butter" that the agent possesses a purpose.

In the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings, however, because they have as their object of accomplishment (bhāvya) agents who are fit for refinement (*saṃskāra*), they are connected with the fruit by the principal sentence.

If it is argued that this may be so, [we reply that] it is not the case, because if the Upāṃśuyāja were extended to the Vaiśvadeva section like the Samid-yāgas and others, the scriptural statement of "thirty oblations" would be untenable;
furthermore, the inclusion of the Upāṃśuyāja in the primary group [of offerings] as expressed in the phrase "the Upāṃśuyāja is the heart" would be untenable.

Furthermore, if the *stotra*s, *śastra*s, and so forth were also purificatory rites (*saṃskāraka*) for the sacrificer, it would follow that they must be performed by the sacrificer himself; in that case, there would be a contradiction with the designation (*samākhyā*) as belonging to the *udgātṛ* priest.

Moreover, since these [stotras and śastras] are being established as such, there is no occasion for their sublation by the first two [classes of rites]; thus, there would be a sublation of that [designation].

Nor is there any room for the objection that, even in the Siddhānta view, because the agent must necessarily be present through implication (*ākṣepa*) by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the aforementioned defect would persist due to the consequence of [the stotras and śastras] becoming "subsidiary" (*saṃnipātin*) acts like the *prayāja* offerings.

In this regard, since the requirement for further specification is satisfied by the agent of the principal action alone, and because the number of that very principal agent connects with the subordinate sentence (*aṅgavākya*), one should understand—according to the wise—that the other two [theories] are accepted there as being characterized by the implication of agency (*kartṛtva*). Enough of this elaboration.
[Mīmāṃsābhāṭṭālaṃkāra, p. ...]
With a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), there is no production of a causal suffix (*nimitta-pratyaya*) when used in its pure form.
For, regarding the meaning expressed by a finite verb as "that which is to be done," this [principle] is applied therein: "in such a way as it is possible."

Bhāṣya 6.5.19.54: "The grammarians state in the Nirukta (1.1): 'One expresses an action that has become a sequence of prior and posterior stages by means of a verb; for example, *vrajati* (he goes) or *pacati* (he cooks), [denoting] everything from the commencement until the final completion.'"
Page 47, 1.1.15.5: From the verb alone, merely a person (the agent) is understood. Page 2099, 1.1.14.1: From the verb itself, the unique productive operation (*apūrvabhāvanā*) is understood;
and therein, the meaning of the verbal root is apprehended as the instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its proximity.

"...when there is a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) expressing an action whose agent is unestablished (*asiddha*), [the meaning] extends up to the sense of 'doing' (*karoti*) by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). ... Verbs (*ākhyātāni*) denote the operation of an agent who has attained its own nature, and thus possess the sense of 'doing' (*karotyarthavat*)."

... when this [verb *karoti*] denotes production (*utpādana*), it is precisely then that its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a specific finite verb form (*ākhyāta*) is observed. Vākyapadīya 2.1.1.1, pp. 376–377: Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the finite verb has *bhāvanā* as its primary meaning... "In the performance of sacrifice, giving, and so forth, the nature of *bhāvanā* is understood.
Therefore, from finite verbal forms, that [bhāvanā] is always expressed as the meaning of the action."
"For whatever meaning, being non-different [from the word], is understood from a word, all that is the meaning of the word.
And in every case within the verb (*ākhyāta*), both the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) colored by it are cognized.
(Śābarabhāṣya on PMS 2.1.1, pp. 374–375). He teaches the meaning of the verb as follows: "It expresses [the action] from its commencement until its completion."

The meaning of that [verb] is this specific activity extending from its commencement until its completion; it is not like "cooking" or "giving," for in those cases, only the mere existence of the cooking or giving is indicated, without the implication that it must begin and be brought to completion. Furthermore, even ordinary people understand the meaning of a verb in this way.

Bhāṣya 6.2.1.13: Since the verb *kalpa* [in the sense of "one who fashions"] is dependent upon the agent who fashions (*kalpaka*), difference and non-difference are not obtainable through implication (*ākṣepa*) in all verbs.

Because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), as heard in such passages as "One should sacrifice with this [rite] involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee" (*etena sahasradakṣiṇayena yajeta*)—which functions through the connection with qualities—and "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with this" (*etena ṛddhikāmo yajeta*)—which functions through the connection with results—is incapable of effecting either difference or non-difference, it is not contradictory that even the noun (*nāman*) connected to it may effect a distinction.

(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 712). The verbal suffix has no denotative power (*śakti*) regarding the agency and so forth obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*); rather, its power lies solely in the act of implying them.
Maṇi, p. 1184:
Because it cannot be determined that a noun expresses a prior action unless the verb has as its object a prior action.

The verb possesses the capacity to enjoin the primary object, the capacity to enjoin a subordinate factor, and the capacity for denotation; this is because the verb has the state of being (bhāva) as its primary meaning.
(Vi.
2.1.6) This is because the verb has the state of being (bhāva) as its primary meaning.
Or: Vārttika 2.1.1.4, p. 463;
Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 712: "Since the verb is the differentiator, the quality cannot be the differentiator because it is dependent upon it."

The Naiyāyikas maintain that effort (*yatna*) is the meaning expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), because the verb *pacati* is analyzed as *pākaṃ karoti* (he performs cooking), wherein the sense of effort is conveyed by the verb *karoti*. (Maṇi, p. 106). Furthermore, regarding the verbal suffix as being subordinate to other words in a sentence, it is said: "He who considers the verbal suffix to be for the sake of another word [is also refuted]. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 347).
"The sentence [is the means] for the sentence-meaning, and the efficient force (bhāvanā) is also [the means] for that.
(Sūtra-pṛ. 1184).

Since the finite verb can be employed through its primary meaning, namely the efficient force (bhāvanā), there is no need for the semantic intention (tātparya) to rely on a secondary (lakṣaṇika) sense.

On page 1384, it is stated that since the agent is established through the very implication of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) by virtue of the verbal suffix expressing that force, the view that the verbal suffix denotes the agent is refuted in the section on the Agent (Kartṛ-adhikaraṇa) [on page 547]. For two verbal suffixes cannot constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) without some form of connection between them.

Vārttika 3.1.14.4, p. 741: The syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) of multiple finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) is not possible without [factors such as] being the cause (*nimitta*) and so forth. Vārttika 3.5.20, p. 1023: The principle is that when finite verbs express their meaning, their inherent capacity (*śakti*) acts as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*).
This principle has been explained in the Mīmāṃsā system.

Regarding the expressions "he eats on a mat" (*kaṭe bhuṅkte*) and "he eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyapātryāṃ bhuṅkte*), worldly people establish the meaning according to observed reality: [in the first case] he is sitting on the mat, and [in the second] the rice is placed within the bronze vessel.

Similarly, in the Veda, regarding the injunction "one should offer once with the *añjali*," although the *añjali* is indeed the joining of two hands, it does not refer to the well-known joining of hands used for propitiating gurus, deities, and so forth; for such a gesture lacks the specific designation of being "once" (*sakṛt*).

Therefore, by implication, the *añjali* (joined palms) consists of two joined handfuls and includes the intervening space; likewise here, the *sruva* ladle is appropriate for the clarified butter (*ājya*), which is a liquid substance; the *svadhiti* (dagger) is a specific type of blade for the meat that is to be cut; and the hand is for the *puroḍāśa*, which is a solid mass—in this manner, the distribution [of implements] is established by the capacity [of the substances].
Capacity (*śakti*) refers to human capability. Sādṛkṣī. 232.

The nature of the principle of the section *arthād vā kalpanaikadeśatvāt* (JS 1.4.20–30) is that when verbal roots express their meaning, their inherent power (*śakti*) acts as a cooperative factor. [Objection:

In the case of the sacrificial oblations consisting of the *jyāmā* cakes along with the *puroḍāśa*, the reasons for the portions (*avadāna-hetu*)—such as the status of being the first or subsequent—are confused because there is no word to establish a distinction.
If this is argued, it is not so.
Because of the determination [of meaning] by capacity, according to the maxim "of verbs" (Pāṇini 3.4.69):
Verbs express the number of the agent, but not the number of the substance that is the substratum of the agent.

Soma. 6|2|1. When the verb is the primary element, its qualification is intended [to be significant]; when it is subordinate, it is not intended. That which is enjoined by the verbal operation is said to be for the sake of another. Therefore, this is the meaning: where the meaning of the verb is stated for the purpose of enjoining itself, there the qualification is intended; where it is stated for the sake of an injunction—as in "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where the oblation is mentioned for the purpose of enjoining the connection with curd—there there is no connection with a second word, because that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

If it is argued that in verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), the delimitors of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) are *la* and so forth, because they reside in the cognition [of the suffix] such as *jñāni* (the suffix *-ni* in *jñānin*), since the meaning is understood through the recollection of the substitute (*ādeśin*), others say: even for one who does not know *jñāni*, *bhūtala*, and so on, the meaning is understood; and since [suffixes like] *śap* and so forth are postulated merely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and differ according to each grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), it is impossible to grasp their expressive power (*śaktigraha*) therein. Therefore, only the status of residing in the substitute (*ādeśavṛttitva*) and so forth is the delimitor of expressive power; thus, in cases such as *gaccha*, it resides in the suffix *śap* and so forth. (Maṇi, p. 110)
In verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), because the emphasis is on the action (*bhāva*), there is never a fixed determination of the root-meaning as being the instrument (*karaṇa*).
(In the *Bhāvādhikaraṇa*, Vārttika 3.4.14.2, p. 903): In all verbal forms, the sense of "causing to come into being" (*bhāvayati*) is established by way of the sense of "doing" (*karoti*).
In all verbal forms (ākhyāta), the performance of an action (kriyā) is heard, not any factor of action (kāraka).
How is this understood? From the suffix (pratyaya).

For it is from this that the action (*kriyā*) is understood as something to be performed. [Objection: But do they not also understand the agent (*kartṛ*)? [Response: True, they do understand him, but not from the word itself.
From what, then? From the sense (*arthāt*). When the action is enjoined as something to be performed, then, by implication, the factor of agency—
In all verbal forms,
the operation of the agent and so forth residing in the verb is understood.
That which is understood from the literal sense is not directly stated by the words (*śrauta*);
and that which is not directly stated by the words cannot be understood from the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
How, then, could it set aside the context (*prakaraṇa*)?
He said: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together.
From this instruction of the Teacher, it is understood that the agent is the meaning of the word, as is the object;
for in the rules "śap [is used] in the sense of the agent" and "yak [is used] in the sense of the object," the Teachers indicate that the agent and the object are the meanings of the suffixes.
Therefore, it is said that the word-meaning is both the agent and the object.
It is replied: the meaning does not arise from the word merely by virtue of the teacher’s statement or the author of the aphorisms’ statement;
rather, it is understood through the suffix (pratyaya).
It is understood that an action (*kriyā*) which is to be performed, once manifested, brings about the factors of action (*kāraka*s).
Furthermore, the Teacher has stated that neither the agent nor the object is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*).
But surely, the suffix is heard in the sense of both the agent and the object?
This [suffix] is not heard to denote either the agent or the object; rather, there is another statement therein: "the singular number is used for one, the dual for two, and the plural for many.
In that context, the connection is made thus: "when there is one agent," "when there are two agents," or "when there are many agents.
This is the theory of the verb (*ākhyātavāda*).

The theory of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātavāda*): It must be stated that even in the case of roots such as *pac* (to cook), the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the result (*phala*), not in the operation (*vyāpāra*).

In that regard as well, even in the Bhāṣya which states "there is [the suffix] even when there is an agent," there is indeed either *latva* (the property of being a *la*-suffix) or *tiptvādi* (the property of being *tip*,
etc.), because that is the meaning of the affix, not the meaning of the verbal root.
In that regard, [it occurs] in the state of being produced by [the notions] "he knows," "he desires," and so forth;
according to the method stated in the *Vākyapadīya* regarding "bhāvanā" and so on, and according to the method stated in the *Vārttika*: "The pot, like the potsherd, brings itself into being."
The status of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) has been established based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) indicating that the meaning of the suffix is primary.
The use of the verb (*ākhyāta*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), or rather, it is metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) because it denotes merely the state of being conducive (*anukūlatvamātra*).
Nor does that [root] have its power residing in the result alone;

for it is possible [to say], "The cooking has ceased, yet the cooked [food] remains," based on such a cognition. Furthermore, the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) [is construed] with the qualificand of the meaning of the verbal suffix.

It is proper to assume the status of being a *niketa* (abode) for the word "brāhmaṇa," just as the term "śrotriya" [is used] for a learned Brahmin; likewise, it would otherwise result in the improper usage of the expression "the village possesses going."
In the hypothesis that the activity (*vyāpāra*) of the abiding (*vihāra*) produced by Indra and others is what is excluded, it either connects with the result, the cognition,
or the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) which is the intended object of the speaker's intention.
Furthermore,
if one assumes that the first-person ending is restricted to the second and third persons (*yuṣmad* and *asmad*) when they denote consciousness,
or that it is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); for instance, [such a restriction] would preclude the usage "you two cook" (*pacyathaḥ*).

And there is the suffix *kvin*. However, the assumption that [the suffix] *ghañ* and others denote the operation (*vyāpāra*) applies to all nominal suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*); what is presented [by them] is the operation.

Because [otherwise] there would be the consequence that "Caitra cooks" would imply that Caitra is the object, and "rice" would be the agent, there is an inconsistency regarding the meaning of the root.
Therefore, the meaning is the activity (*vyāpāra*); by means of that...
By the very fact that there is no denotable object exceeding the verbal root (dhātu), [the view that the result alone is the meaning of the root] is refuted;
therefore, the meaning of the verbal root is not merely the result.

Nor is it merely the activity (*vyāpāra*), for [otherwise] *tyaji* and *gami* would be synonyms. Furthermore, in the case of verbal suffixes expressing the object—as in "the rice is cooked by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*)—the capacity of those verbal suffixes resides precisely there [in the object]. This is the explanation.
This being the case, that consequence would follow.
Therefore, the meaning of a verbal root consists of both the result and the operation.

In verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook), there is not a separate power (*śakti*) for each of the result, such as softening (*viklitti*), and the operation conducive to it; rather, [there is a single power].
Thus, in the case of active and passive verbal endings (*ākhyāta*), there is a verbal cognition in which the nominative-ending subject is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Even though the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists of an activity conducive to the result, effort (*yatna*) is not its meaning. For if [effort were included], the activity would become a mere part of the qualified whole, resulting in the loss of its status as a *kāraka* (participant in action). Furthermore, "activity" refers to an exertion residing in the self (*ātmaniṣṭha*), such as the movement of the hands and so forth.
Residing in the body;
from existence;
it is stated that, through inherence, there is [the quality] in Caitra produced by itself.
In expressions such as ‘pāke yatate’ (he strives for cooking), ‘pākaṃ karoti’ (he does cooking), and ‘pākaṃ bhāvayati’ (he brings about cooking), there is effort (ceṣṭā).
Since the property of being conducive [to the result] is obtained through the constraints of the relation [of verbal suffixes], it is not [explicitly] present there.
The capacity [of the verb] is such that, as long as there is the usage "he cooks" (*pacati*) with respect to the operations,
the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), which are presented by the word ending in the nominative case, possess the fruit produced by those operations through the relation of being the locus of that fruit.
In cases such as "yati" (he exerts), since effort (*yatna*) is manifested through its distinction from cooking (*pāka*),
there is a separate expressive power (*śakti*) for each of those [meanings]. And the delimitors of that expressibility (*śakyatā'vacchedaka*) are as many as those [meanings].
It is either uniqueness, conformity with the result, or reality;
by this [it is shown that] it is not so because [the object] is a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the effort or of the letter *l* and so forth.
By this, the fault of [the rule] falling under the jurisdiction of *anabhihita* (not being expressed) does not arise;
therefore, at the time of exposition, [it refers to] that which appears [as such].

The objection that [the definition] would over-extend to include even remote agents such as those who perform the act of plowing, because the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is not the cause [of the action] due to being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*),
is refuted.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usages as "the rice is being cooked" (taṇḍulaṃ pacyate),
because it is impossible for the effort (*yatna*)— which is the operation producing the result— to be denoted by the verbal root.
Nor can all the factors of action (*kārakas*) be designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) on the basis of being the substratum of the operation expressed by the root.
It should not be said that there would be the occurrence of the third case ending due to the attainment of agency;
for [the agent] is non-distinct [from the action].

Because it is precisely the non-expression of the number associated with the agent or the object that serves as the restrictive factor; or else, according to the aforementioned reasoning, being expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) consists simply in being the meaning of the verbal root.

Therefore, when the operation of the real factors of action (*tattvakāraka*) is intended to be expressed as the meaning of the root *pac*, one says "the wood cooks" (*kāṣṭhaṃ pacati*) or "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*),
because [the root] has the purpose of designating that which is beneficial (*hita*).
Nor is the verbal root-meaning itself the meaning of the suffix;
nor is there synonymy between the roots *tyaj* (to abandon) and *gam* (to go) at the end [of the compound], for otherwise the usage of such expressions as *tattva* would be untenable.

Nor should it be argued that the cause and the effect are not thus [related], because the status of being the substratum of an operation whose fruit is inherent in its nature belongs either to the verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) or to the *tiP* suffix and so forth, even in the absence of the [verbal root].

Since the universal *yatnatva* (effortness) is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the nature of activity (*vyāpāratva*), it is like the movement possible for a verbal root; and just as the accusative case itself [denotes] a result such as conjunction,
so too, without the singular number and so forth, there is no [denotation of] numbers such as unity, nor without the property of being a present-tense suffix (*laṭ*) and so forth.
And because the state of being present and so forth has that [the action] as its object;
even there, by parsimony, the denotability of the substratum is preferable due to its being the delimitor.
For this very reason, it is not the agent,
because it is accepted as expressing a specific [quality].
In all cases, the accusative case has the sense of the result (*phala*).

The status of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for this very [action] belongs to [the root *sthā*] because it is the relation (*saṃsargatva*) characterized by effort (*yatna*), and so forth.
For this very reason, since the locus of the result and the operation constitutes the meaning of the root *sthā*, [it follows that...]
It should be stated [that it is not so], because it is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*).

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of its being intransitive (*akarmaka*), since it would denote an activity that resides in the same locus as its fruit (*phala-samānādhikaraṇa-vyāpāra-vācitva*).

Thus it is established that *bhāvanā* is effort (*yatna*), denoted by the suffix either as an operation (*vyāpāra*) or as effort itself. And it is invariably transitive, because it is explained by means of [the verb] *kṛ*, which is always transitive, and by the causative form of *bhū*. In this way, even for intransitive verbal roots such as ‘one desiring health should sleep,’ the possibility of postulating health and so forth as the object of accomplishment (*bhāvya*) is justified, since that [health] is construed as the object within the *bhāvanā*.
And its connection occurs precisely as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*).

It should not be argued that its status as the primary qualificand is impossible because, in sentences such as "Caitra cooks," it is accepted that it connects as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) with respect to Caitra and others presented by the word ending in the nominative case.

In instances such as "He cooks in a pot," "He cooks with wood," and "For one desiring virility, one should make the sacrificial post of khadira wood," since we experience verbal cognition even in the absence of a word ending in the nominative case, it is impossible to assert that the presence of a word ending in the nominative case is a cause for the cognition of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force). This is because the *bhāvanā* is understood from the verbal root itself.

Nor is there, in that case, the status of being the subject (the ending of the first case) or the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of various such [verbal] forms; for since the number denoted by the suffix can occur as being presented by the same word [as the verb], and since *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is simpler than *adhyāhāra*, it is more appropriate to assume *lakṣaṇā* for the agent in the verbal form itself.

By this, the following views are refuted: "Number is construed with the qualificand of the meaning of the verb, or with the qualificand of the object of the verb, or with what is presented by a word ending in the first case"; and [the objection that] "in the sentence *gaganena sthīyate* ('it is stayed by the sky'), because of the absence of a word ending in the first case, the number remains unconnected."

Otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of [the relation] applying even in the case of "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*); for if one accepts that the particular effort (*kṛti*) is the qualificand in "he cooks," there would be a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*). Furthermore, being the qualifier of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) and so forth as the cause [of the cognition] is more cumbersome than taking the cognition produced by the verbal suffix itself as the cause. And thus they say that in such cases, even in the absence of a word ending in the nominative case, effort alone is the delimitor of what is expressed (*vācyatāvacchedaka*). In expressions such as "he knows," "he desires," "he exerts effort," "he does," "he comes into being," and "he perishes," [the meanings] are the locus (*āśrayatva*), the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), and so on, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Nor should it be said that "being the locus" (*āśrayatva*) constitutes the relation;
for it is accepted that the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root are construed through a relation other than identity (*abhedātirikta*).
Otherwise, there would result the absurdity of construing [the relation] in such cases as "the rice is being cooked" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacyate*) and "Caitra is cooking the rice" (*caitraḥ pacati taṇḍulam*).
The delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) are *kh* and so forth, [as in] "knowing" (*jñāni*).
Regarding this, some hold that because of the suffix *ādi*, there is a recollection of the meaning through the recollection of the substituends (*ādeśin*).

Others, however, maintain that since the meaning is understood even by one who does not know the *kh*-type elements such as *l* and so forth, and since it is impossible to determine the specific denotative power (*śakti*) for each individual grammatical system—given that forms like *śatṛ* are mentioned merely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and are mixed across various systems—the delimitors of denotability must be the status of being a function of the substituend (*ādeśavṛttitva*) and so on.
Regarding the words "Go" and so forth, they say that this is the function of the modification (*vikaraṇa*) such as the suffix *śap* (the verbal suffix).
It must be stated that [this is] possible,
because the status of being the object of knowledge (*jñānakarmatva*) is possible, and because its status as the locus of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is also possible.
Therefore, even though syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is not established [between the two verbs], the [first verb] possesses the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*).

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the expression "he cooks, [it] comes into being" (*pacati bhavati*) would apply in the sense "the efficient force of cooking (*pākabhāvanā*) arises"; for such an outcome is accepted. Furthermore, the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "a verbal suffix has the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) as its primary meaning" (Nirukta 1.1) gains its purpose through the predominance of the efficient force; otherwise, it would result in its being rendered meaningless.

Nor should it be argued that this [passage] does not intend to indicate the primacy of *bhāvanā*, but rather intends to indicate the primacy of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) as defined by the grammarians in the maxim "the root-meaning alone, pure, is *bhāvanā*.

For such an interpretation would result in the impossibility of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the verbal suffix (*liṅ*), which expresses [the *bhāvanā*], and the word "verb" (*ākhyāta*).
Nor should it be argued that, based on the traditional rule "every noun is born from a verb," the word "verb" (*ākhyāta*) refers here specifically to the root-meaning.
In cases such as "pākaḥ" (the act of cooking), because there is no use of a verbal form (*ākhyātapada*),
the verbal form used in the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) refers metaphorically (*lakṣaṇika*) to the respective action (*kṛti*).

Consequently, since the word "verbal form" (*ākhyātaśabda*) does not denote the verbal root (*dhātu*), its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verbal form denoting the suffix (*pratyaya*) is untenable.

Therefore, in this context—as in the case of "The sixth [pressing] is the midday pressing"—there is an injunction whose primary focus is the *bhāvanā* (productive activity) by means of indicating multiple meanings of the verbal suffixes.

Consequently, the primacy of the *bhāvanā* exists with respect to time, number, measure, agent, and object, which are denoted or indicated by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). This is based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the verbal suffix has the *bhāva* (productive activity) as its primary meaning. Otherwise, if the primacy were attributed to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then because of the applicability of the traditional rule "the base and the suffix [together express a single meaning]," there would result the fallacy of redundancy (*ānarthakya*) in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

The grammatical technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), however, such as "the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) when neuter" (Pāṇini 3.3.14), is intended to indicate that in such cases only the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be understood, and not meanings such as gender (*liṅga*) and so forth; it does not, however, establish the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *bhāva*. Similarly, in the statement "nouns (*nāman*) have substance (*sattva*) as their primary meaning" (Nirukta 1.1), there is the communication of primacy regarding those nouns with multiple meanings—such as *pāvakaḥ* (purifier) or *lāvakaḥ* (cutter)—which are capable of being construed with gender and number.
Even in words like *ghaṭa* (pot), both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) possess primacy.

For this very reason, in the section on verbal suffixes (*ākhyātādhikaraṇa*, PMS 1.3.15–35), they state that there is a twofold cognition regarding both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, among verbal suffixes that convey multiple meanings, the rule of the predominance of *bhāvanā* is established by the traditional authority (*smṛti*) stating, "The verbal suffix has the *bhāva* as its primary meaning. By the traditional authority stating, "Nouns have substance (*sattva*) as their primary meaning," since nouns that convey multiple meanings do not produce a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) without a verb, and since the status of being a *kāraka* is contradicted without a connection to an action, there is a rule of predominance for the agent (*kartṛtva*) and other factors through their connection with the predominant action.

The primary status belongs to the *kāraka* (the factor of action), while number and other properties—though they are also meanings of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—are subordinate because the primary status of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) requires that the *kāraka* be connected [to the verbal root].

However, number and the like are connected specifically to the *kāraka* by means of their delimitation [of it], through the force of the direct statement of co-occurrence (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*); this is made clear in the fourth [chapter] (PMS 4.1.11–16).
Therefore, since all *kārakas* are connected to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), it is established that the *bhāvanā* possesses the status of the principal qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*).

And since a direct connection of the factors of action (*kāraka*) with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is impossible, they connect with it through the mediation of delimiting the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

In that regard, according to the view that "the nominative case expresses the agent or the object already denoted," the connection of the productive urge is with the agency and so forth that constitute the meaning of the nominative.
According to the view that "the nominative case expresses the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," agency and so forth connect in exactly the same way.
Some maintain that in that case, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) belongs to Caitra and others alone.

In reality, however, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone is appropriate, because a relation of difference (*bheda-anvaya*) between two things is impossible if they are both the meanings of nouns other than particles (*nipāta*).
And in that context, there is a relation with the governing case-ending (*adhikāra-vibhakti*).

Thus say some. In this way, since even the meaning of the gerundive suffix (*saṃśoṣanavibhakti*) has as its referent the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamāntārtha*), that meaning also connects with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Likewise, the meanings of the suffixes *kyap*, *apamul*, *kṛsuc*, *nañ*, *ghañ*, and so forth—such as the state (*bhāva*) arising from time and the like—also connect with the productive urge.

Similarly, although a causal factor (*nimitta*) lacks the status of a *kāraka* (participant in action), it connects with the productive urge because it possesses the quality of being an indicator (*anujñāpakatva*).

However, according to the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*), since the genitive case lacks the status of a *kāraka* (case-role), its meaning is construed with the meaning of the *upapada* (governing word) and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that it is more logical for [the meaning of the genitive] to be construed primarily with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) itself, through either a direct or indirect relationship.
In this same way, [grammatical markers such as] the present tense and so forth are also [construed] with the *bhāvanā*.
Even the meaning of the root (*vidhartha*) is connected to *bhāvanā* through the relation of being its producer (*janakatva*).

As for number (*saṃkhyā*), however, its connection is with the agent or the object as denoters of an indivisible [action] implied by *bhāvanā*; it is not, however, a relation of being supported by that [action] or having that as its substratum.
And thus, in cases such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the use of the singular number is justified even when there is a difference in the substrata.
In passages such as "vasānaḥ" (clothed), the connection [of number] occurs with the substratum (*āśraya*) characterized by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), namely the couple (*daṃpatyoḥ*).

Regarding that, the established tradition (*saṃpradāya*) holds that when there is the suffix *-śānac* (present middle participle), the connection is with the agent (*kartṛtva*), whereas in the case of the suffixes of sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, the connection is with the object (*karmatva*).

However, some maintain that in cases such as "sthīyate" (it is stayed) and "supyatām" (let it be slept), the connection of number is with the productive operation itself (*bhāvanā*), because its status as the primary element is more appropriate.

Nor does the number, when connected with that [bhāvanā] thus produced, result in its being a substance; for that reason, even there, there is no cognition of memory, nor does the dual number apply to the bhāvanā and so forth, since the singular alone is grammatically correct.
Therefore, connection with the bhāvanā through a mediated sequence is logical.

Regarding such instances as "it remains in the sky" (*gagane sthīyate*), some say that number either co-referentially relates to the locushood expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātastha-āśrayatva*) or does not relate to it at all. Furthermore, agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) also relate to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

In that regard, in the case of an agent-verb, the agency residing in the verbal suffix relates [to the object] through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); in the case of a patient-verb, the result—indicated by the effort denoted by that [suffix] through its being the motive for that effort—relates [to the object] through coreferentiality.
In that case, by virtue of the non-difference of the substratum implied by that [action], another [agent] is also understood as the subject of the nominative case-ending.

And thus, in the case of a verb in the passive voice (*karmākhyāta*), there arises the cognition: "An operation which is the instigator of a result that is co-located with the state of being the object (karmatva) residing in something distinct from the rice. In the case of a verb in the active voice (*kartākhyāta*), there arises the cognition: "An effort conducive to cooking, which is co-located with the state of being an agent (kartṛtva) residing in Devadatta.
Furthermore, the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is the meaning of the instrumental case.

Thus, in the case of the verbal forms expressing agent and object, such as "the rice cooks by itself" (*odanaḥ pacyate svayameva*), the cognition is as follows: there is a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) conducive to the act of cooking, which has as its locus the rice, possesses agency residing in the rice, and is the motivator of a result that is co-locative with the objectness residing in the rice.
In this context, there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the effort (*kṛti*) within the operation of the verbal root.
Nor does it follow from this that the usage "the rice cooks by itself" (*odanaḥ svayaṃ pacati*) would be possible [as a subject-agent construction].

Because such [usage] is ungrammatical due to the rule for the introduction of *yaṅ* and other affixes, namely *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), it follows that in that case there is neither a nominative nor an instrumental for Caitra, but rather a genitive; this is the established tradition (*saṃpradāya*). Therefore, it is proven that the traditional teaching that "the verb has the action as its primary meaning" indeed establishes the primacy of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as determined by the agency and other roles of all the *kārakas*.

Furthermore, since this very Smṛti (the grammatical tradition) indicates that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is primary, it is logical that the *bhāvanā* alone—by the rule that the principal implies its subordinate elements—implies both agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*), and not the reverse.

Moreover, because the meaning of a word must be what is not obtainable through other means (*ananyalabhya*), there is no expressive power (*śakti*) for agency and so forth which are obtainable through implication; rather, the power resides only in that which performs the implication.
For this very reason, where there is no implication, there is no power at all, as is the case with number (*saṃkhyā*) and the like.
Nor should it be argued that this is not the case,

and that even [terms such as] *paktā* (the cooker), *pacamānaḥ* (cooking), and *pacaḥ* (the act of cooking)— which denote the agent, the object, and the action respectively— must be understood as expressing *bhāvanā* due to parsimony (*lāghava*). For [otherwise], there would follow the undesirable consequence of the syntactic relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*) between the meanings of two nouns.

Therefore, in that case, the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the substratum, according to the grammatical rule "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67). Nor can there be a cognition of that [substratum] through implication (*ākṣepa*), nor through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), nor even through denotation (*śakti*); for indication is not established unless there is a cognition of the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) when the word is not used in its primary sense.
Therefore, in that context, [the word functions] as a noun (*nāman*).

By the traditional rule (smṛti) stating that the primary element [the agent] is predominant, there is the cognition of the action (kṛti) as implied by the verbal suffix, which is capable of being construed with gender and number and is the principal factor.

Nor is there a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the action, nor is there a primary denotative power (śakti) residing in the agent; for even the principle of parsimony (lāghava) is not a decisive factor when it contradicts predominance.
Thus it is established that agentive and objective participial suffixes (kṛt) possess the power to convey the action.

However, in cases such as *apākaḥ* ("non-cooking") or *yāmaḥ* ("going"), where [the suffix] is produced by a state (*bhāva*), the understanding occurs through the mediation of the meaning of a verbal root that expresses an action, such as "is born" (*jāyate*) or "is done" (*kriyate*). Otherwise, since there would be the cognition of the mere meaning of the verbal root,
the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) would be untenable in those instances.

Therefore, it is established that the verbal root has denotative power (*śakti*) only with respect to the meaning of the root itself, while the performance of action (*kṛti*) is merely implied (*ākṣepa*).
Consequently, the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) in the form of *kṛti*, which is distinct from the meaning of the root;
its substratum (*āśraya*), however, is obtained through implication.
Precisely because [the agent and object] are obtainable through implication (*ākṣepa*), the view stated by the Grammarians—that the agent and object are denoted by the suffixes—is rejected.

Even the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "The *l*-suffixes are used for the object and for the state [of the action] after intransitive roots" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), when considered in light of the observation "the *l*-suffixes," must be explained as being intended to prescribe the singular and other numbers for the agent and object—by way of the number of the time-periods (*kāla*) associated with them—on account of the grammatical injunctions: "Singular and dual for two" (Pāṇini 1.4.22) and "Plural for many" (Pāṇini 1.4.21). Thus, it is the proponent of the *l*-substitutes (*lādeśavādin*) who provides this interpretation.

The grammatical rule (*smṛti*) concerning the topic of what has not been expressed (*anabhihitādhikāra*, Pāṇini 2.3.1) is intended to prescribe the second case (*dvitīyā*), third case (*tṛtīyā*), and so forth, for the expression of number residing in the object (*karman*) and other factors.

However, the rule "the *kṛt*-suffixes [denote] the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67) does not intend to express the action (*kriyā*), because the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the action is untenable; rather, it intends to express the agent alone.
This is the general direction of the argument.
It is not an absolute rule that the injunctive power of specific verbal forms is obscured by their being mantras;
for injunctive elements are indeed observed even within mantras, such as "In spring, one should sacrifice kapiñjala birds," and so forth.
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 2.1.6.30, page 431:

Those verbal expressions (*ākhyāta-śabda*) which are capable of enjoining both a quality and an action when accompanied by a word expressing a quality, are not capable of enjoining that quality alone. For example: "He who eats the food of the wicked—his *mudga* beans and *śaṅku* porridge become like those of one who performs meritorious deeds."

The agent, being obtained through the very inseparable connection with the *bhāvanā* denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), cannot be the object of direct denotation (*abhidheya*).

The meaning of the verb root (*ākhyātārtha*): According to the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*, it is the general activity conducive to cooking (*pākānukūla-vyāpārasāmānya*) alone that constitutes the meaning of the verbal suffix. This is because [the verb] is explained by the causative form (*ṇijanta*), namely *pākaṃ bhāvayati*, which expresses general activity.
As for the explanation *pākaṃ karoti* ("he performs cooking"), that too is simply conducive [to the result] through the root *karoti*, which denotes general activity.
For the meaning of *karoti* is not "bringing into being" (*janana*); if it were so, then since *karoti* would have only that [single] meaning, it would follow that it is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
For a verbal root (*dhātu*) is transitive (*sakarmaka*) when it denotes an operation (*vyāpāra*) that has a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) from its result (*phala*);

it is intransitive (*akarmaka*) when it denotes an operation that has the same locus as its result. In the case of the root *pac* ("to cook"), the result is softening (*viklitti*), which resides in the rice (*odana*); the operation resides in Caitra. Because these reside in different loci, the root is transitive.

The fruit of sleeping is pleasure (*sukha*), and since that [pleasure] belongs to Caitra alone, there is coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) between the two; thus, [the verb] "he sleeps" (*svapiti*) is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

If both "to do" (*karoti*) and "to strive" (*yatati*) possess the nature of a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*), then it would be contradictory for a single meaning to have its fruit in a different locus (*phalavyadhikaraṇatva*) and its fruit in the same locus (*phalasamānādhikaraṇya*).
Therefore, even "to do" (*karoti*) expresses only the general notion of activity (*vyāpārasāmānya*).

For this very reason, even the analysis "the chariot performs going" (*ratho gamanaṃ karoti*) in the case of "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*) is consistent. Therefore, since the verb root *karoti* (to do) serves as the explanatory gloss (*vivaraṇa*), the meaning denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must also be something distinct from the meaning of the base root (*prakṛtadhātu*), namely, a general activity (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*). And whether that result (*phala*) is the meaning of the root itself in some cases, or heaven (*svarga*) and so forth in others, is another matter.

Pārthasārathi [Miśra] maintains that since a general activity (*vyāpāra*) requires a specific instance, there is an expectation for such specificity, which is supplied by sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. However, in reality, because there is no single, light, and inclusive property (*anugata-laghubhūta-śakyatāvacchedaka*) that could serve as the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) across various activities distinguished by their respective fruits, the analysis of expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), "he exerts effort toward cooking" (*pāke yatate*), and "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) shows that the delimitor of the denotatum for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is simply "effort" (*yatna*).
Nor is it the case that the denotation is the activity conducive to that effort.

When Caitra moves due to a disease such as rheumatism (*vātaroga*), even though the movement is an action (*vyāpāra*) of a nature distinct from [volitional] effort (*prayatna*), there arises the cognition "I am not performing this movement; rather, my body is moving due to a rheumatic disease. This shows that the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/perform) consists in the notion of effort (*yatna*), because effort is the most parsimonious (*laghu*) determinant of its denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Thus, in expressions such as "the chariot performs going" (*ratho gamanaṃ karoti*), it should be understood that the term *karoti* indicates the favorable operation (*anukūlavyāpāra*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nor does the root *kṛ* (to do) become a synonym for *bhāvayati* (he causes to be) simply because there is no difference in their having the same agent and object as the meaning of the suffix *-ti*; for even in the absence of synonymy, it is possible for *kṛ* to have the same agent and object as the meaning of *bhū* (to be), since its own denotable property (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is not delimited by "effort" (*yatnatva*), which is the delimitor of the denotable property of *bhāvayati*. Furthermore, there is no consequence that *kṛ* would be intransitive if its meaning were identical to the meaning of *yat* (to strive), just as *yat* is intransitive; for even when the [essential] nature of effort is the same, the distinction between transitivity and intransitivity is established through the difference in the delimitors of the verbal root's denotation (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*).
For in the case of *yatate* ("exerts effort"), the result—which is co-located with the effort—is indeed the action itself residing in Caitra.

But in the case of *karoti* ("does"), the result—namely, that which is called "origination" (*utpatti*) and serves as the delimitor of the verbal root's meaning—is located in something other [than the agent].

Consequently, just as in the cases of *pacati* ("cooks") and *gacchati* ("goes"), the distinction between actions consisting of operations is established by a difference in their results, so too here, even though the effort consisting of the operation is one and the same, the establishment of the distinction between transitive and intransitive status is possible solely through a difference in their results.

Furthermore, as for that result (*phala*), whether it is understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and merely indicated by the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), or whether it is actually denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*)—this is another matter. In reality, however, since the definition stated in the *Kaustubha* is marred by defects such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and the like, the state of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) is simply the capacity for expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) characterized by the absence of non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding the object; and the absence of that [capacity] is the state of being intransitive (*akarmakatva*). Thus, the definition stated in the *Kaustubha* is indeed correct. In this context, expectancy is a property of the word consisting in its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*).

Therefore, even though there is a unity of meaning, just as in expressions such as "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), where the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is independent (*anākāṅkṣatva*) while the nominal stem "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth are dependent (*sākāṅkṣatva*), in the same way, the independence of the root *yat* with respect to an object and the dependence of the root *kṛ* for an object remain unobstructed.

Although the five [roots] are inherently expectant of an object (*karmasākāṅkṣa*) by their very nature, they are considered intransitive (*akarmaka*) during states where such expectation is not intended to be expressed; thus, there is no interruption of that non-intention.

For this very reason, the usage "odanasya pacyate" (the rice is being cooked) occurs even in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, since roots such as *ās* (to sit), though intransitive by nature, become transitive when expressing a duration of time such as a month, the usage "caitreṇa āsyate māsaḥ" (Caitra sits for a month) is logically established.

Thus, it should be understood that for the very same verbal root *granth* (to tie), there is transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) because it requires an object when considered under the property of denoting an operation residing in Caitra; and there is intransitivity (*akarmakatva*) because it does not require an object when considered as denoting an operation residing in the flower.
Therefore, although *karoti* has the meaning of *yāti*, it possesses transitivity; likewise, although the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) are distinct, they still possess the meaning of *yāti*.

And thus, in cases such as "the chariot goes," "he knows," "he desires," or "he exerts effort," where effort (*yatna*) is precluded, it should be understood that there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of either a favorable operation (*anukūla-vyāpāra*) or the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*).

In the usage of verbs such as "perishes" (*naśyati*), there is likewise metaphorical indication. Therefore, it is established that, whether taken in a figurative or primary sense, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) everywhere is *bhāvanā* (productive activity) as something distinct from the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*).

Thus, the delimitor of its capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is a distinct verbal suffixhood (*ākhyātatva*) consisting of the element *karoti*. Consequently, in cases such as *bhavati* ("it exists"), because there is no analysis (*vivaraṇa*) by means of *karoti*, there is an absence of productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, the ancients hold that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself is distinct from the case-role (*kāraka*), and that the singular number (*ekatva*) is construed with it through a mediated connection (*paraṃparayā anvaya*).
In reality, however, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the property of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) alone is the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

In cases such as *bhavati* ("it exists"), there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the substratum (*āśrayatva*). And thus, in the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*), there is no need to postulate a separate linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).
Furthermore, the delimitor of the capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) [of the verbal suffix] is not the property of being a *la*-suffix (*latva*).
For otherwise, it would follow that the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) could be understood even from a *lakāra* that is presented in some arbitrary manner.

Nor is it the state of being conveyed by a substitute (*ādeśīyapratipāditatva*), because it would then follow that the productive urge could be cognized through its denotative power (*śakti*) even from a *lakāra* presented as a substitute for *jñāna* and so forth.

Nor is it the property of being a *la*-suffix as presented by the substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *tiṅ* and so on; for if that were the case, since only some [of these], namely *tiṅ* and others, would enter [into the definition], one would have to assume that the denotability (*śakyatva*) follows from the inclusion of the delimiters of denotability (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). It is better, therefore, to assume a power (*śakti*) residing in each of *tiṅ* and the others individually.

For this very reason, there is verbal cognition even when the *la*-suffixes are not presented by *tiṅ* and the others; otherwise, there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of assuming the causality of so many instances of erroneous cognition of power with respect to the numerous *tiṅ* and other suffixes.

By this, the following view is also refuted: "The property of being a verb (*ākhyātatva*) alone is the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*); and that [property] consists in possessing the word 'verb' through the relation of being denotable (*śakyatva*). And since that possession exists in *tiṅ*-suffixes and the like, they are the possessors of the power.

For even when there is knowledge that *tiṅ*-suffixes and the like are denotable by the word 'verb', and even when there is knowledge of them as *tiṅ*-suffixes in cases such as *pacanti*, the cognition of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) still arises.
Therefore, it is established that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is *bhāvanā*.

✱ Where the meaning of the verbal suffix is stated for its own prescription, there a qualification is intended; however, where it is stated for the sake of prescribing something else—as in "He offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where the oblation (*homa*) is mentioned for the purpose of prescribing the connection with curds—there no second connection with curds exists, because that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

The grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) is that the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*) is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*). See *Rahasya*, p. 24. ✱ When the meaning of the verb is the principal element, it serves as a qualifier for the temporal connection (*saṃdhi*); however, when it is for the sake of another [element], it is separated.
It is said:

when either the form (*ākṛti*) or the quality (*guṇa*) is the primary element, it is mentioned for the sake of its connection [to that primary]; therein, a single object qualified by both qualifiers is understood from a single sentence. And having performed [the action] as qualified by that [primary], one fulfills the requirement. If one were to perform it as qualified by only one of them, one would fail to fulfill the requirement.

Furthermore, where the meaning of the verb pertains to an object characterized by its form (ākṛti), there the action is declared for every member of that class. One should not think that it is performed only when one such instance has been manifested; for even in another instance characterized by that same form, it is indeed declared to be performed.
It has been stated therein: "Why should that which is not prohibited not be performed?"

Furthermore, when the meaning of the verb is the primary element, it has no connection with that which is characterized by the generic form (ākṛti). Thus, even if another instance possessing that same form is not brought forward, the primary element remains accomplished; and the primary element is accompanied by its qualities.
