Where a rule regarding a substance is recorded in the *Kalpa-sūtras*, and not merely its arrival at a specific location, even there the performance occurs at the very end, according to the maxim: "The insertion of adventitious elements is at the end" (*āgantukānām ante niveśaḥ*).

(Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya 1.2.13, p. 35). And by this same maxim—"the insertion of adventitious elements is at the end"—it is appropriate that Varuṇa and the others, who are not dependent on anything common [to other rites], should be enjoined for that purpose at the conclusion.

*Nyāyanirṇaya* 4.3.13 (Brahmasūtra): When certain people have already taken their seats in assemblies, others who do not find space do not sit down; in such a case, the principle of the newcomer (*āgantunyāya*) applies.
Where the placement of the primary constituent elements is fixed, there is the omission of other [elements] according to the principle of the newcomer.
In assemblies and gatherings, those who arrive later settle down without displacing those already seated.
In assemblies and compounds, a newcomer settles by displacing the original inhabitants;

however, when the location is already occupied by the original inhabitants, the newcomer, having no other possibility, settles at the edge. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the world is full, the placement of bricks—which occupy a single central space—attained through the principle applicable to newcomers cannot be obstructed.
Ratna. 5|3|8:
Insertion at the end of adventitious elements.

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, in the injunction “One who desires preeminence should recite twenty-one [verses],” the six additional verses among the *sāmidhenī* verses are to be inserted at the end.
Regarding the additional *stomas* (hymns), their placement occurs after the *paryāsa* verses in the *bahiṣpavamāna*.
Bhāṣya 5.3.13–12: Let there be the insertion of the *sāmans* into the *gāyatrī* and other meters in the *pavamāna* chants of the *mādhyaṃdina* and *ārbhava* days.

5|1|15|13-14. ✱ Even though worldly practice (*lokavyavahāra*) is based on desire due to the effort of filling [the vessel], it is not so in the case of the *Veda*, which is beyond human form (*apauruṣeya*). Therefore, according to the principle that "new elements (*āgantavaḥ*) are placed at the end," the portion to be cut from the rear half [of the cake] after the sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) should be taken last; thus, for those who perform the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*), the first portion is the last—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Saṃkarṣa. 2|2|8.
✱ There is the introduction (*āgama*) of other *Sāmans* when the number [of chants] heard in the *kratu* characterized by a defective *Stoma* is to be completed.

Bhāṣya 10.5.16.25–26: When the required number is completed by means of *āgama* (addition), one should recite the first and last *sāmidhenī* verses three times; the remaining ones are the *vidyudau*. 10.5.1.27–33: When the number is to be completed by *āgama*, the verses to be added must follow the order of their general recitation (*sāmānyāpāṭhakrama*): this applies to the twenty-first, the twenty-ninth, and the twenty-third *atirātra* sacrifices. 5.1.16.13: Because there would be an endlessness of *āgama*, the specific instruction [regarding the order] is purposeful.

*Bṛhatī*, p. 270: [Objection: "Since the scripture (*āgama*) has no purport (*tātparya*) regarding the matter of logic (*nyāya*), even in the absence of its contradiction [by perception], it will have the power to subvert [logical reasoning] because it expresses a meaning contrary to logic. [Reply: No, because without purport, the scripture lacks authority (*prāmāṇya*); and since it lacks authority, it cannot function as a subverter. Furthermore, even if the scripture were present and imminent, [it would not subvert logic]. This is the *āgnāvaiṣṇava-nyāya*. (Mīmāṃsākośa, 104; 826).

Su. Pṛ. 1418: In that case, it is indeed appropriate to raise an objection regarding contradiction with scripture (*āgama-virodha*), where both logic (*nyāya*) and scripture have the same object. Vā. 5/4/413, p. 122; 3/4/4/13, p. 138: When there is a contradiction with scripture, logic is not capable of performing its function.

The reference by means of this word [etad] is possible even for that which is yet to come and is proximate, just as it is for that which has passed away and is proximate, by virtue of its being connected [to the context],
as in: "Now this is the Jyotis," "Now this is the Viśvajyotis," and "Now this is the Sarvajyotis" (Vedāntasūtra 2.2.8).
In the *Āgneya* section (*Saṃkalpa*), there is the *Satra*; for one who has not [previously] engaged [in such rites], there is the injunction for the *Viśvajit*.
In the *Rājasūya*, when [the sacrifice] is first connected with the three [days], the cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni-Viṣṇu is the first oblation.

Bhāṣya 11.4.12: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu as the first oblation at the morning pressing, the midday pressing, and the third pressing, according to the *Adhvarakalpa*.
Regarding the statement "a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu," the *Āgnāvaiṣṇava* [offering] in the *Adhvarakalpa* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *Āgnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake.

Bhāṭṭa 8.1.19: Based on the Vedic injunction, “One should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Viṣṇu; one should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with clarified butter,” the primary offering to Agni-Viṣṇu—being an optional modification of the Agniṣomīya—is satisfied by the very *tantra* (ritual procedure) of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) because it is independent. Consequently, the application of the Full Moon *tantra*-rules—which are based on the offering to Sarasvatī being a modification of the Upāṃśuyāja—does not occur for the subsequent offering to Sarasvatī; this will be explained in the twelfth section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Su. P. 1171: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; one should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with clarified butter.
In this case, the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the offering to Indra and Agni.
(This was stated while remaining in the position of the prima facie view.)

VI. 11|2|8. In the *adhvarakalpa*, the first pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is that of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* [offering], followed by the pouring out of the *havirpati-varaṇa*, in accordance with the modified primary order (*vaikṛtamukhyakrama*).
Bhāṭṭa 5|1|10:

In the *adhvarakalpa*, since the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *aindrāgna*, the two *anuvākyās* for the *ājyabhāgas* are the *vṛdhanvatī* verses: "agnim īḷe purohitam" and "somam gīrbhir havāmahe".
But if it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agnīṣomīya* [offering], then the two *vārtraghnī* verses are "Agni, the slayers... and "O Soma, you are...";
and the twelve-potherd offering to Agni-Viṣṇu is a modification of the *aindrāgna* [offering] in the *adhvarakalpa*.
The *Āgnāvaiṣṇava* principle:
when there is a conflict between ritual properties (*dharma*) among primary acts that are equal in number, only the property mentioned first is to be favored.
Or rather, [the rule of] the primary applies, because of the prior injunction, as in common worldly practice.

The Commentary states: Where there is a conflict of ritual properties (*dharma-vipratipatti*) among principal acts (*pradhāna*) that are equal in number, there the property of the primary must be followed.
For example: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu in the afternoon; one should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with clarified butter."
In that context, the ritual procedure (kalpa) for the primary offering to Agni and Viṣṇu occurs.
Why? Because of the prior injunction; that is, because it was enjoined first.
According to the order of the text, the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu must be performed first.
Its factors become non-opposing;
however, for the subsequent [moment], they are opposed by the preceding one,
for its acquisition and that of its factors occur at a time subsequent to that.
Since the purpose of the latter is accomplished by the former alone, its own procedure ceases.
However, some maintain that they share a single substratum;
according to them, even in the case of the *pañcadaśarātra*, it is indeed the primary ritual rule (*mukhyadharma*) that prevails.

"Or rather, the primary [element] [prevails], because of the prior injunction, as in common worldly practice"—by this sūtra, it is stated that when there is a conflict between the properties of two principal elements of equal number, the property of the primary element prevails.

In a conflict between the few and the many, there is conformity with the majority; however, the few incidentally derive benefit from the qualities produced by that [majority]. In a conflict between equals in number, however, there is conformity with the primary one alone, while the others incidentally derive benefit. Since there is such a variety of distinctions between these two principles, these two *adhikaraṇas* (sections) are indeed distinct; it is not correct, as done by another commentator, to treat them as a single *adhikaraṇa* merely because of the hearing of the word "or" (*vā*). And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose. The Bhāṣya states: "Even for another purpose, it demonstrates the superior strength of what was previously established."

"Just as in the case of the *adhvara*, first [the fire] belonging to Agni is established; for this ritual act (*karma*) is indeed like the *agnikarman*," so it is said. (In the Vīvalakarīya, however, the reading is: "In the *adhvara*, first [the fire] belonging to Agni is approached; for this ritual act is indeed the *agnikarman*"). And this is also like this: just as those who have already performed their morning worship do not lead (*nenīyante*; in the Vīvalakarīya, "they do not cause to lead") one who speaks later, nor do they clothe him, even so is this.
(Here, the portion from “adhvarasyeva” up to “mikarma” constitutes the Vedic statement (*śrutivākya*).
The words “iti” and “idaṃ cāpi” are the words of the *bhāṣya*.)
The portion beginning with “*yathā*” and ending with “*mevaitat*” is a scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*); the word “*iti*” is a term from the commentary (*bhāṣyapada*).

In this [passage], Sūtra-Bhāṣya 5.1.9.20, having printed [the text]: “This ritual act, which is the *agnikarma*, belongs first to the *adhvara* and then to the *āgneya*,” [it continues]: “The performance of that which is recited later occurs later;
this is the *āgnāvaiṣṇava-nyāya*, following the *āgnimāruta*.”
The printed commentary (*bhāṣya*) reads “darśayati.

However, in the *sūtra-bhāṣya* on [Jaimini Sūtra] 10.1.4.129, the sentence is printed as: “adhvarasya pūrvamathāgneḥ, upāyi hyetat karma yadamikarma,” and the commentary thereon is printed as: “pūrvamadharasya, athāgneḥ” iti vyapadeśaḥ samuccaye avakalpate nāsati viśeṣe.
In any case, this reading of the scriptural passage (*śrutivākya*) is correct, though it appears difficult to pronounce.

[Question: Where there is a prohibition of the properties of [elements] of equal number, in the consideration of which one obtains its own property (*svadharma*) and which one subsists upon the property of another, since no fixed rule is established, the primary element’s own property is desired.

For its property is understood without confusion because opposition has not yet arisen; however, the property of the subordinate element cannot be grasped because it is opposed to that [primary property].

In the case of the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *sūktavāka*, there is no displacement of the deities of the *savanīya* offerings; because they are fivefold, just as in the case of the extraction (*niṣkarṣa*), there is no connection [of those deities with the displaced formula].
Commentary: When the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are displaced, they also displace the *sūktavāka*.

In that context, the deities of the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are recited, beginning with: "O *Bhṛjjabhr̥t*, for Indra accompanied by the *Haris*, the parched grains (*dhānā*); for you, O Pūṣan, the groats (*karambha*)," and so forth.

There is a doubt as to whether there is an extension (*utkarṣa*) of these [deities] or not. What is the prima facie view? There is an extension of the *sūktavākya*, but not an extension of the deities of the *savanīya* offerings.
Why? Because of the mention of five constellations (*pañcanakṣatva*).

Having stated that the five *anuyāja* offerings are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is only these five that are postponed (*utkṛṣyante*), not the members of the Soma sacrifice.
And the members of the Soma sacrifice are the deities of the *savanīya* offering;
therefore, there is no postponement of them.
Just as there is no connection [of one deity] when another is extracted:

for example, in the performance on the full moon day, when the deities of the full moon sacrifice are extracted, the deities of the new moon sacrifice have no connection, and vice versa in the other case.
For what reason? Because each is not a constituent part of the other.
Similarly, here too, there is no displacement.

(The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: Those deities who belong to the *savanīya* offerings are not displaced even when the *sūktavāka* is displaced, because the *savanīya* offerings possess five characteristics (*pañcanakṣatva*).

Just as the *sūktavāka* employed at the full moon sacrifice does not displace the deities of the new moon sacrifice, so it is here as well. There is no displacement due to the syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*); rather, there is no application because of the common ritual procedure (*samāna-tantra*) and the loss of purpose (*artha-lopa*).
Commentary: Displacement according to the [specific] course (*ayana*) alone is logical.
Why? Because of the connection with the sentence.

The mentions of the deities of the Soma sacrifice, which constitute parts of the *sūktavāka*, are connected as follows: "For Indra Harivat, the parched grains (*dhānā*); for Pūṣan, the groats (*karambha*); for Sarasvatīvat, the scattered grains (*parivāpa*)—this sacrificer [has offered].
Likewise, it is connected thus: "With the parched grains for Indra Harivat, with the groats for Pūṣan, with the scattered grains for Sarasvatīvat, this divine Vanaspati has become well-winged."

These very [formulas] being recited in the midst of the *sūktavāka* are meaningful; they do not exist as separate, isolated units. Furthermore, there is no *sūktavāka* belonging to the *savanīya* offerings by which [the *sūktavāka* of the animal sacrifice] could be imitated.
The *sūktavāka* is indeed fivefold, as established by its original form;
therefore, the mention of these deities therein is appropriate,
and it is heard [in the scripture] as having been so stated.
Therefore, there is also an excellence (utkarṣa) of those [verses].
And this will be supported by the *ārṣa* [tradition].

As for the statement, "Just as in extraction (*niṣkarṣa*), there is no connection (*anvaya*)," because they share the same ritual framework (*samānatantra*), there is no connection due to the disappearance of the purpose (*arthalopa*).
The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices constitute a common ritual system (*samānatantra*).
For these two, there is a common *sūktavāka* formula. It is applied according to its specific purpose.
Furthermore, there is the mention of the deities of the New Moon sacrifice at the Full Moon sacrifice, and likewise for the others there.
For this reason, whatever deities are mentioned here and thus observed, none of them is excluded from this [Full Moon sacrifice] either.
Therefore, just as in the case of "exclusion" (*niṣkarṣa*), there is no connection (*ananvaya*); such is the illustration.
The *Ṭup-ṭīkā* states: First, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) to these *savanīya* offerings.

And for whatever purpose the *prastara* exists, for that very purpose is the throwing (*praharaṇa*), which consists of its consecration (*saṃskāra*). And the *sūktavāka* is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to that act of throwing.
Therefore, the *sūktavāka* also serves the purpose of another [the sacrifice] (*parārtha*).
Since the deities of the *savanīya* offerings are recited within the *sūktavāka*, it is understood that they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with it.
If [the *sūktavāka*] were to be displaced [from its context], this syntactical unity would be sublated.
Furthermore, if [the *sūktavāka*] were to be drawn down [from its original context], the meanings would remain expectant [of completion].

Moreover, no drawing down of the *tantra* words (such as "he has kindled Agni, the Hotṛ"—etc. is possible, by which they might become free of expectancy; for the *sūktavāka* exists for the sake of another.

Since the *sūktavāka* is enjoined by way of the *tantra* (i.e., as common) to both the full moon and the new moon sacrifices due to the lack of distinction in the context, a drawing down [of it from that context] would be appropriate [only in those cases].

But here, because of the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *sūktavāka*—that is, the displacement of its constituent *tantra*-words—the deities of the *savanīya* offerings will indeed be manifested as displaced. Śā: Having previously stated the displacement of the performance dedicated to Prajāpati, the connection (*saṃgati*) is that, by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), the displacement of the deities of the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) is now being established.

In the *Toma-sūtra*, regarding the statement "as in the extraction there is no connection," the meaning is: "as in the case of the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices"; and this means that when there is an extraction of the [principal] offerings, there is a connection with the offering of the other deities, just like that. *Vi*: "Is there no displacement of the deity for the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*?
Or is there? Because of its fivefold nature, and because there is no [contrary] principle, there is such displacement."
Therefore, there is displacement (utkarṣa).
Bhaṭṭa: In the Savanīya animal sacrifice, a modified recitation of the archetypal *sūktavāka* is prescribed.
And it has been established that this [recitation] is displaced from the Āgnimāruta [offering] due to the displacement of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*).

In that context, the deities of the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes are proclaimed by such [formulas] as "O Agni, for Indra accompanied by the Bhr̥gus, for Indra accompanied by the Haris, the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*)," and so forth; and by means of the words "accompanied by the Haris" (*harivat*) and the rest, Indra— the deity of the aforementioned [deities]— is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as the recipient of the *āgneya* cake from the *āgnimārutī* sacrifice.

Although, according to the method stated by Āpastamba, the mention of Harivat and others is understood during the *nirvāpa* (offering), nevertheless, at the time of the formal renunciation (*tyāga*), it is not improper that Indra alone is indicated in the *sūktavāka*, since that [mention of others] is established there through the force of the primary expression and its secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
It will be stated later that the fivefold ritual procedure (*pāṅkta tantra*) is extended to the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) offered at the *savana*.

In this regard, when the *sūktavāka* is being postponed, there arises the inquiry as to whether the mention of the deities of the *puroḍāśa* (cake-offering) is also postponed or not. Upon consideration, since the mention of the *puroḍāśa* deities possesses fivefold character (*pañcanakṣatā*) and thus lacks the sequential order associated with the fivefold *anuyāja* offerings, they do not undergo postponement—just as the oblations in the southern fire (*dākṣiṇāgnika-homa*) do not. Consequently, those [verses] are to be recited at a time subsequent to the consumption of the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*.

Therefore, because the *tantra*-words (common elements) that have attained syntactic unity with them possess that same quality, their recitation is necessarily required there. And so, when they reach the words for the deity of the animal sacrifice (*paśu-devatā*), they must be repeated due to that subordinate quality (*guṇatva*).
This being the position reached, since these [mantras] depend upon the *tantra* (common) words, there is no possibility of their employment independently.

Furthermore, the assumption of *tantra*-words and the like in accordance with them is improper; for, in the case of the portion of the *tantra*-words belonging to the specific *puroḍāśa*, it would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) in assuming a motivating factor (*prayojaka*), as they would obtain their benefit from those very words employed for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).
Indeed, there is no merit whatsoever in employing the deities of the *puroḍāśa*—which are the primary elements—at a time subsequent to the *anuyāja* offerings.
Because the property of occurring after the consumption of the *iḍā* portion, which is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), is present here as well;
and because even in the archetype, there is no immediate sequence [of that specific act] following it.
Furthermore, although the effort toward the primary action is being sublated, the resulting complexity in the conceptualization of the causal agent (*prayojaka*) does not constitute a fault.
Therefore, there is also an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) of those [deities]. Maṇḍana states: "The deities are displaced upward in the *sūktavāka*.
Śaṅkara states: "There is an upward displacement of Indra in the *sūktavāka*."

In the case of Indra, there is postponement (*utkarṣa*), indeed postponement. However, from the *āgnimāruta* [section] onwards, there is no postponement for the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*, the flour-smearing (*piṣṭalepa*), and the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation, together with the five after-offerings (*anuyāja*).
When the sequence of the Āgnimārutī sacrifice has passed and the Soma-Raudra sacrifices have not yet arrived, the Manu-deva [hymns] are mentioned as being among the *sāmidhenī* verses, and so forth.
Likewise, two *dhāyyā* verses, "pṛthupājāḥ" and "saṃ satrā-dhaḥ," are prescribed. Bhāṣya 3.2.120.
The Āgnīdhra (priest) recites "For the bull-eater, for the cow-eater" and performs the second oblation.
Bhāṣya 3.2.12–130, Āgnīdhra; generally; the Adhvaryu's direction.

3.8.12–124, because the excellence (of the response) is common, the Āgnīdhra, remaining stationed right there (even at the northern altar during the Vaṣaṭ-prayers), assists both performers (the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ) in the response.
Therefore, this [mantra] is not used [there].
11.2.10.14. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, one worships the Āgnīdhra (the shed) with the [mantra] belonging to the archetype, and not with one situated in the Daśataya [Saṃhitā].
3.8.12.1–24. From the Āgnīdhra (the fire), they distribute the Dhiṣṇya hearths (in the Soma sacrifice).

*Saṃkarṣa* 3.2.15: Regarding the connection with the *Āgnīdhra* shed, the followers of Hiraṇyakeśin perform it with the verse "This is our Agni" (*ayaṃ no agniḥ*), while the Baudhāyanas do so with "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*). According to Mīmāṃsā, the worship of the *Āgnīdhra* shed must be performed with the very verse belonging to the archetype, namely "Come here for the feast" (*agna ā yāhi vītaye*), and not with any verse from the *Dāśatayī*.

VI. 3.4.8. The Āgnīdhra-hall rule. (The designation of the location by the name of its occupant. But surely, according to the Āgnīdhra-hall rule, just as the word "Āgnīdhra" applies to the priests and others situated in the hall, so too is the use of the word "Self" (ātman) observed even for the primary [Brahman] when it resides therein.
Śrīkara. 11.7 Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya: The fire named Āgnīdhrīya is used in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
And that [fire] is located in the Āgnīdhra shed.

Ke.: One should carry forth the fire situated in the Prācīnavaṃśa hall from the Āgnīdhra shed (in the shed) for the sake of the Vaisarjana-homa up to the Āgnimāruta offering. Vi. 5.1.144. And the carrying forth of the Āgnīdhra fire occurs after the carrying forth of the fire to the Uttaravedi.

(Some) | Saṃkarṣa. 3.2.14: The section concerning the oblations at the beginning of the sacrificial procedure with the fires of the Āgnīdhra; 3.2.14: Even the fire of the Āgnīdhra is indeed a portion of the Āhavanīya fire.

3|2|14. The carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the Āgnīdhra fire is from the Śālāmukhīya fire alone, because it is not located on the Uttaravedi. 3|6|7|18. The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice belongs to Agni (*āgneya*). Bhāṣya: That which has Agni as its deity independently is designated as *āgneya*.
Furthermore, in a rite dedicated to two deities, the deity Āgni is not independent.

Therefore, this secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix does not arise from the grace of Agni alone as found in the case of Agnīṣoma and others; thus, it does not declare that the object [of the sacrifice] has Agni as its deity. However, where that [deity] is independent, it can be called "Āgneya" (belonging to Agni).
Vārttika 3.1.15.127: "The black-necked [goat] is for Agni" is the first animal among the eleven (ekādaśinaḥ). Vi. 8.1.17:

Since there are multiple deities for the eleven animals—as in "the black-necked for Agni, the ewe for Sarasvatī, the tawny for Soma, the dark-grey for Pūṣan"—there is an adaptation (*ūha*) of the mantra ending in the singular, "medha to the lords of the sacrifice" (*meghapatibhyo medha*).
9.1.14: The animal for Agni (*āgneyaḥ paśuḥ*) is to be sacrificed at the *agniṣṭoma* as the *savanīya*.
Bhāṣya 3.6.7.18: "The cake (puroḍāśa) belongs to Agni;

for the Brāhmaṇa indeed belongs to Agni" (830). [The offering] of the hymns dedicated to Agni is prescribed for both occasions, as it is stated: "That cake for Agni on eight potsherds which is never omitted at the New Moon and the Full Moon sacrifices."

Regarding the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there arises a doubt: should the entire cake be offered to Agni, or should some portion be reserved? The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a portion must be reserved.
In the statement, "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed *āgneya*," the word *āgneya* is intended as a praise of the Brāhmaṇa;
for the quality of being born from the mouth of Prajāpati—which characterizes Agni—is found in the Brāhmaṇa.

VI. 1.4.14: In passages such as "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed related to Agni," words like "related to Agni" (*āgneya*) are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), not injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that by the statement, "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed related to Agni as his deity," the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the entire Black [Yajurvedic] ritual for the Brāhmaṇa is enjoined, and thus for him, the Soma sacrifice must necessarily come first.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that by that statement, either the postponement of the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa is enjoined, or else the postponement of only a single part of it—the Agnīṣomīya—is enjoined.
In either case, there is an option (*vikalpa*) for the Brāhmaṇa between having the Iṣṭi sacrifice come first or the Soma sacrifice come first.
Thus is the position of one part of the Siddhāntin.

This is indeed a separate ritual (*karmāntara*) enjoined for the Brāhmaṇa after the Soma sacrifice; consequently, there is only an option (*vikalpa*) for the Brāhmaṇa—this is the subsequent position of another part of the Siddhāntin.
Only the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of a single oblation is enjoined, and there is an option even for the Brāhmaṇa.
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta):
This injunction, "An eight-potherd [cake] for Agni," is applicable even when the sacrifice is accomplished with wild rice (*nīvāra*).

Or [it may be understood as follows]: Pāṇini 6.4.15 states, "The term *āgneya* [is formed] when there is a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*). Thus, in the case of the cake on eight potsherds, the substance is present; therein, rice (*vrīhayaḥ*) is prescribed as the specific material.

2070] In passages such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," having established an injunction, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"Agni was indeed the first to go from here to the heavenly world"—is connected as a supplement to that injunction.

Regarding the statement "the milk belongs to Agni," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *Sāṃnāyya* offering, because the similarity of the sacrificial substance (*havis*) is stronger than the similarity of the deity.
Having cut off and offered the portion belonging to Agni (the accusative case), one should cut off and offer the portion belonging to Agni-Soma.

"‘He divides the *āgneya* into four parts’ and ‘He divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts’—this is a rule of subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*). (Bālakrīḍā, p. 17). In cases such as “He divides the *āgneya* into four parts” and “He divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts,” even though they reside in different sentences, there is a syntactic connection of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) between the two primary terms through the subordination of the subordinate term. [That is to say, the subsumption here is: "That which one divides into four parts, being the *puroḍāśa*, is the *āgneya* one divides into four parts. Therefore, there is a connection by way of non-difference between the word *āgneyam* and the word *puroḍāśam*.]

(Bhāṭṭa 3.1.7) In this sacrifice—[namely], "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu"—the *āgneya* rites belong to the deity whose name is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇābhidevatva*), whereas the *ājyā* verse, "O Agni, [come] with life, enjoying the oblation," is applied to the deity whose name includes attributes (*saguṇābhidevatva*).

"One should offer an eight-potherd oblation to Agni; [the result is] gold. This is a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), and not an injunction regarding a fruit for the *Āgneya* sacrifice belonging to the New and Full Moon rites (*dāśapaurṇamāsika*). (Bhāṣya 2.3.12.25).

and this is to be understood as the "principle of the concluding summary" (*upasaṃhāranyāya*).

The Principle of the Āgneya-Sacrifice for Purification. It has been explained that simultaneous performance applies to equal rites when no distinction is perceived.

Now, the following is considered in the Bhāṣya: "One should sacrifice a black-necked animal to Agni; a brown one to Soma; [and] a black-necked animal to Agni when competing in a sacrificial cake-offering."

In this regard, it is deliberated: should the offering of the black-necked [animal] and the third [animal] be performed together, or separately? What is the prima facie view? It has been explained that there is simultaneity for equal things when no distinction is perceived;
it has been explained that there is simultaneity in the performance.
"But for those that are equal, simultaneity [is established] because of the instruction by a single word" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 11.1.10.16).
In this case, however, since the two black-necked [animals] have a single deity, no distinction is perceived when their performance is carried out together;
and their simultaneous performance is established because they share a single result.
Therefore, there is a simultaneous offering.

However, there is a distinction due to the difference in time, because of the connection with the injunction; there would be an injunction for the qualified [offerings] since they share the time of the principal act. Commentary: But a distinction in the offering is logical, not a single performance (tantratā).
Why? Because of the difference in time.
How is there a difference in time? Because of the connection with the injunctions:
the injunction regarding the black-necked [animal] is separated by the injunction regarding the Soma-related [animal].
In that regard, according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the performance of the Āgneya [offering] occurs first and that of the Saumya later;
however, these two are offered together, so that the sequence of one or the other might be perceived. If the action were performed first for the latter, the former would follow after it.
Therefore, the application is by way of distinction.
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose.
The Bhāṣya states: "The Soma and Āgneya [offerings] are on both sides."
If it be argued that this is an injunction (*vidhi*), we say no, because it is a statement of an existing fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*).
Commentary: If an injunction were to be postulated here, then, having abandoned the direct meaning of the Vedic text (*śruti*), one would be resorting to a figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, there is a distinction between the offerings (*pradāna-bheda*).
Regarding *soma*: "The connection [of the rites] is as previously stated for those [deities] whose *tantra* has been mentioned.
As for *vi*: 'The two black-necked [goats] may share a *tantra* or be separate; such is the deity.
There is a *tantra*, but due to the difference in time according to the rule for the *saumya* [offering], they should be separate.'"

Bhaṭṭa: It is heard in the scripture: "One desiring to excel in the offering of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) should sacrifice a black-necked animal to Agni, a brown one to Soma, and a black-necked one to Agni.

Here, by favoring the word *ālabheta* (should sacrifice), three distinct sacrifices are enjoined through three sentences. Then, by supplying the word *tān* (them) and *ālabheta*, all of them are connected to the result collectively; it is not the case that only the three sentences are accepted as having a connection to the result individually, each with the person desiring excellence.
For if that were so, the second sentence concerning the sacrifice to Agni would result in being redundant.

Therefore, since the unity of performance (*ekaprayogatā*) is established for the *Śravaṇa* and *Paśu* sacrifices, there arises the following inquiry: is the principal rite performed by way of a single procedure (*tantra*)—as in the case of the *Sāṃnāyya* offering—because they share a common deity, or rather, is it according to the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)? In this deliberation, when the simultaneous performance of the principal rites along with their subsidiaries is understood through a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*), then even where there is a connection with different deities and a sequence is determined by the order of recitation and so forth, there is still no requirement for sequence where simultaneity is possible because they share a common deity. In such a case, since there is no need for sequence, the restriction [of order] by means of the order of recitation and so forth does not apply; thus, the performance is by way of a single procedure (*tantra*), just like the *Sāṃnāyya*.

Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for simultaneity—in the form of occurring in a single moment—even when multiple factors are taken up by a single word in an injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), as in the case of the staff and the wheel [in producing a jar]. This is because, in common worldly usage—as in the expression "the fruits exist"—it is an empirical fact that the production of a single performance is generally understood to involve occurrence in the same place and time.
For this very reason, authoritative scholars maintain that when [an action] occurs in a place, time is the delimiting factor, and when it occurs in time, place is the delimiting factor.

(The Naiyāyikas—those intent on establishing the means of valid cognition [pramāṇa]—state: Therefore, even by way of simultaneity (*yogapadya*) consisting in occurrence at a single moment through the rule of performance (*prayogavidhi*), the principle of the two *āgneya* animal sacrifices applies. Although there is the possibility of a common procedure (*tantratva*) based on the section concerning equal status (*tulyardhatādhikaraṇa*), it must be said that because of the sequence of those two with the *saumya* sacrifice, the first has already been reached by the *saumya*, and thus the subsequent timing of the other would be sublated if performed according to a common procedure.
There is no evidence that the meaning of the prior member serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) existing at a time preceding the meaning of the subsequent member.

As for the fact that the *āgneya* sacrifice is a subordinate element following the *saumya* sacrifice—despite the commonality (*tantratva*) of the subsequent [element] with the *āgneya*—this is not contradictory, because the *saumya* sacrifice lacks the status of being posterior to the *āgneya*.

Furthermore, the status of the *saumya* sacrifice being posterior to the *āgneya* in the case of the subsequent *āgneya* is by no means authoritative, just as the *dadhi* sacrifice is not posterior to the *payas* sacrifice.

Nor does it follow that the *tantratā* (commonality) of the principal [offering] would thus apply even to the *Āgneya-ājyabhāga* (the butter-portions for Agni), because in that case, difference is admitted due to the distinction between the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. This being the position reached, since the sequence of the second *Saumya* following the first *Āgneya* would result in the sequence of the second *Āgneya* following the second *Saumya*, and rather than resorting to the sublation of what is established by authoritative means, it is more appropriate to abandon the simultaneity understood from the performance injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*)—which is a single factor—rather than the *tantratā* of the *Āgneya*. Thus, there is no *tantratā* for the *Āgneya*.

The distinction is this: although the milk-offering (*payoyāga*) is performed simultaneously with the curd-offering (*dadhiyāga*), its status as occurring after the milk-offering is not contradicted in the case of the *triṣṭut* and other [stomas] that follow it.

Nor should it be argued: "In the present case as well, since the milk-offering is understood through the textual sequence (*pāṭha*) to occur after both the curd-offering and the Soma-offering—in accordance with the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) for the second *āgneya* sacrifice—how can there be a sublation of simultaneity, given that the *triṣṭut* and other subsequent parvans are not recited together with the second *āgneya*? This objection cannot stand.

Even though simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is expressed by the rule of performance (*prayogavidhi*), because the textual recitation (*pāṭha*) of the Soma-offering and the second Agneya-offering cannot be explained otherwise (*ananyathāsiddhatayā*) and constitutes a unique ritual act (*apūrvakarman*), the simultaneity is not sublated. For it is only through the distinction between the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses that the sublation of simultaneity is logically possible; thus, no particular textual recitation of the curd-offering and the milk-offering is set aside as being otherwise explainable, and so it does not sublate simultaneity. In the present case, however, if "commonality" (*tantratva*) were intended, there would have been a single recitation for both Agneyas together with the threshing (*avaghāta*).

However, because of the recitation in the order of the gentle [deity] first, the recitation is established otherwise; it even postulates a sequence not previously known. Therefore, it is logical that simultaneity is sublated by that.
Consequently, there is no *tantra* (common performance) for the two *āgneya* offerings. Maṇḍana says: "And in the *āgneya* sacrifice, there is a separate offering."
Śaṅkara says: "This is not [the case] because it is inwardly gentle and immeasurable.
That is the *tantra*.
It belongs to those two who are inwardly gentle (*antaḥ-saumya*).

The repeated scriptural mention regarding the Āgneya sacrifice states: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is offered at the new moon. The Aindrāgna sacrifice has an equal status [in this regard]. VI. 8|1|12. Regarding the *āgneya* injunction (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*), when another state is conceived, there is modification;

The scriptural text regarding the *darśa* sacrifice states: "The offering to Agni is equal in its share; the offering to Indra-Agni is equal in its share.
Because the offering to Agni possesses an identical cause, it is understood through inference.
The *Bhāṣya* states: Having prescribed for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices that "the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is offered on the new moon day and on the full moon day,"...
Furthermore, it is stated: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is offered on the new moon day.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should one sacrifice with the offering to Agni twice on the new moon day, or only once? What is the prima facie view? Because the *sūkta* (hymn) concerning Agni is the cause [of the connection], it is understood that the sacrifice is performed by means of the new moon; for the repeated mention of the same [offering] would be purposeless unless it were for the sake of a specific distinction. (2.3.12)

It is heard in scripture: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is offered at the new moon. A doubt arises: is this very same rite constant in both [the full and new moon sacrifices], and this repetition of its mention is for some specific purpose, or is it a different rite? In this regard, although the new moon is an unenjoinable factor (*anupādeya*) with respect to the act of taking up [the materials], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—based on the principle "But because of non-separation in proximity" (2.3.13)—is that it is the same rite. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: "A repetition of a scriptural statement, when not for another purpose, is determined to be a cause of difference."
And since this [offering] is of such a nature, let the Āgneya be performed twice;
for by means of the double performance, this is indeed the declaration of the duality of the ritual act.
Because the ritual act is undivided, it is enjoined by the doubled statement.
The Commentary states: This is not so; [the word] "again" (punar) does not signify "for Agni.
Why? Because there is no word expressive of that [repetition]. [Objection:
But surely the repetition [of the verb], being uttered again, will enjoin a further action.
This is not a delusion;
for a word, once uttered, cannot say, "The meaning should be made different again.
Whatever was the meaning of this word when it was first uttered, that same meaning shall remain even if it is uttered a hundred times, and no other.
But surely, by enjoining something already enjoined again with a qualification, [the injunction] becomes purposeless.
Let it be purposeless if you wish; however, it cannot be said to express anything else.
Purposelessness may indeed result, but not the expression of a different meaning.
Therefore, one should repeat it twice;
or rather, he states another position there: "Because the action is undivided, it is prescribed by the double utterance.
It is appropriate that in the case of the *samid* and other offerings, the repetition of the direct statement constitutes a differentiator [of the act].
In this case, however, because of the presence of both substance (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*), eight [offerings] are to be inferred.
And that substance-and-deity complex, due to its prior connection with the experience of the mental recitation (*abhimarśana*), unilaterally indicates that very same sacrifice.
If it is argued that the substance-and-deity complex is different [in each instance], we reply: no, because an awareness of non-differentiation is perceived.
If, however, a distinction based on individual instances is resorted to, that too would entail a further distinction in another application.
Therefore, by means of two optional statements, there is the prescription of the Āgneya sacrifice on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Alternatively, because they proceed simultaneously, according to the principle "so that the existence [of the rite] may be seen" (6.1.12), that very same action is established by one [statement] and by the other as well.
Nor is a distinction perceived as to which [of the two] conveys the meaning and which is redundant and purposeless.

Granted that it may be purposeless, for it is precisely by virtue of its lack of purpose that its repetition is logically established here; it does not possess a different meaning, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the eternity of word-meanings.

Therefore, the application [of the mantra] occurs only once. Although all of this has already been refuted in the section concerning other purposes (2.3.21), it is studied here out of pride regarding the subsequent sūtra; however, in reality, the Veda cannot tolerate the admission that its own words are purposeless. Or rather, the repetition serves another purpose.
The Commentary says: Or rather, the repetition is not purposeless;
it will serve as an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
This is stated.

What is the purpose of this [praise], since the *āgneya* has already been enjoined by the preceding sentence together with its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)? Why would the praise be employed to enjoin some other matter?

Where praise is used for the sake of enjoining something, it is said to have that as its purpose, according to the principle: "Because the *āgneya* is for the sake of action, there is purposefulness in the meanings [of the words]" (JS 1.2.1).
However, in the case of praise and injunction (*stutaśāstra*), the meaning is exactly that much [the praise itself].

Just as a deity, whether praised or not praised, accomplishes its status as a constituent part [of the sacrifice], so it is with this. To this it is replied: "Or rather, the repetition is purposeless; this is not for the sake of enjoining [the Indra-Agni offering].
It is for the sake of enjoining the Indra-Agni [offering]."
The offering to Agni on eight potsherds indeed takes place at the new moon; it does not become properly effective through Agni alone, for Agni accompanied by Indra is more appropriate.
Therefore, the offering to Indra and Agni (Aindrāgna) must be performed.

Alternatively, since no additional quality (*guṇa*) is heard when searching for one among those [passages] arising from repeated hearing (*punaḥśruti*), and since a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) involves three defects (*tridoṣa*), it is clear that they cannot function as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, having analyzed the matter, since there is no specific mention of which [passage] serves as the *arthavāda*, one concludes that it must belong to the *Āgneya* sacrifice itself; thus he says: "What is the use of an *arthavāda* located in another section, which does not achieve syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with what is enjoined by the injunctive passage?
It is established that the *arthavādas* are indeed subordinate to the injunction. The objection (*paricodanā*), however, was raised merely for the sake of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In this regard, when it is understood by those who are not indifferent that "whether praised or not praised, she is indeed the deity," one asks: "Of what subject is this [statement]? This point is seen to be referred to as having been stated previously in the *Mahendra-adhikaraṇa* (the section concerning Mahendra), specifically in the sūtra: "The mention of a quality would be purposeless" (2.3.15.18). Therefore, its purpose is indeed visible;
it is not possible to postulate an invisible (transcendental) result.
Consequently, the utterance of "svāhā" is for the purpose of consecration.
But does not the Ājyabhāga also obtain such a purpose?
True;
however, because of its specific injunction, it has precisely that [purpose].
In the *Likhita* it says "iva," while in the *Tantraratna* it says "eva"; however, in the *Ānandāśramīya*, nothing at all appears. It is not required by the *apūrva*.

For many other elements pertaining to the nature of the deity have been prescribed: the invocation (*āvāhana*), the utterance of *svāhā* (*svāhākāra*), the *sviṣṭakṛt* formula (*sviṣṭakṛnnigada*), and the *sūktavāka*.

Thus, while those [other factors] exist, it is that very performance of the same function which requires another. And that [connection] proceeds by virtue of some common attribute (*samāna-dharma-yoga*); therefore, the primary status or the subordinate status must be attributed to both. In this regard, Soma as the deity is certainly an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), of which there is no doubt; if Agni were also an indirect auxiliary, then the number two would be appropriate, and not otherwise.
(Therefore, because of the equality of the two, the *āgneya* [offering] is also an indirect auxiliary.
The connection with "Soma" arises from the same [context] as before.
If it is argued that "the Ājyabhāga fire also is to be consecrated"—this is the meaning of the first sūtra. [The response is:

It does not cease in the case of the Saurya and other such rites.
"The sublation of an exception is the fruit of the investigation.
According to the Bhaṭṭa view: in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One performs the two Ājyabhāga offerings to Agni and Soma."

In that regard, although there is a distinction in the ritual acts by number, the status of Agni and Soma as deities (*devatātva*) is fixed within each individual sacrifice; for, by the dative case heard at the end of a *dvandva* compound, the status of deity is understood to belong to them only when they are joined together with one another.
This is stated with reference to their supreme substratum (*paramadhiṣṭhāna*).
In this very context, both [Agni and Soma] serve to consecrate the deity Agni-Soma; furthermore, the mantras, through this [recitation], indicate both of them.

The additional refinement resulting from the double utterance does not entail the performance of rites such as invocation (*āvāhana*) or the offering of *svāhā* as would be the case with different deities.

Alternatively, based on the statement in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), "Then he proceeds with the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) for Agni and Soma," it follows that even in this branch each [deity] possesses the status of a deity individually; for while it is possible for the dual form to denote a single substratum through the synonymy of deity-status, there is no evidence for postulating a different relationship intended to refer to a shared substratum.
Consequently, one is dedicated to Agni and the other to Soma.
In that regard, although it is possible for the *soma* to be a purifier (*saṃskāraka*) of the deity, the *āgneya* [oblation] serves as a purifier of the deity Agni;
this applies to the various primary rites such as the *āgneya*,
as previously stated.

Nor does there arise a defect of dissimilarity (vairūpya) such that one part of a single injunction would be an indirect auxiliary (ārādupakāraka) while another part would be a direct auxiliary (saṃnipatyopakāraka); for this is resolved by the assumption of an implied secondary injunction (ārthika-vidhyantara), as is the case with other acts that have a substratum (āśrayika-karma). Therefore, since there is no dissimilarity even when the connection [of the material] occurs through the very form of the Agni-Soma sacrifice within the heard injunction itself, it follows that here too the act is a purificatory rite (saṃskārakarma).

This being the position reached, it is understood through an examination of the sequence that the fire mentioned in the *āvāhana* and other mantras—read twice, once before and once after Soma—is distinct from the deity Agni; for even in the *abhimarśana*, that [fire] is merely subordinate with respect to the portion of the object of reference (*uddeśāṃśa*), just like [the offering] to Agni and others. Otherwise, the explicit prohibition of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings in the animal sacrifice would be untenable.

Furthermore, in the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, because the *ājyabhāga* offering to Agni lacks a pre-established auxiliary benefit (*klṛptopakārakatva*), it does not necessitate the production of a new transcendental result (*apūrva*). Consequently, the re-enunciation of the offering to Soma (*saumya*) would otherwise be rendered purposeless. Moreover, if one were to assume a new *apūrva* by enjoining the Soma-offering alone, there would arise a structural inconsistency (*dairūpya*) in the injunction: the portion dedicated to Agni would be enjoined as an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), while the other portion would be enjoined differently. Therefore, since that [offering] functions as an indirect auxiliary even in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), it follows that in the *saurya* and similar sacrifices, the deity remains Agni himself; there is neither a sublation (*bādha*) of the deity Agni nor a modification (*ūha*) to the deity Sūrya. Thus it is established. Maṇḍana: "The sacrifice is not for the sake of purifying the deity."
Śaṅkara says: "The Ājyabhāga is not dedicated to Agni as its deity; it is not a subsidiary performed in close conjunction (saṃnipātī).

When there is suitability for performance, then there is the nature of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Why? Because of the instruction by a single word.
From the instruction by the single word, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," there is a single result.
Because they have a single result, there is a joint performance (*sahaprayoga*).
In that case, no distinction is perceived among the place and other factors with respect to this purpose.

Herein is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): the *āgneya* and other sacrifices (characterized by such injunctions as "The *āgneya* is an eight-potherd cake," etc. are already established.

Having referred to those [sacrifices] that are not previously known, others such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are enjoined by injunctions such as "one should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*" (*same darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*). For those [sacrifices] being enjoined, there is a connection with the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), but not for those being merely mentioned.

And in that connection, although those sacrifices are not explicitly denoted [by the name of the ritual], nevertheless the *āgneya* sacrifice is connected with the *itikartavyatā* independently of the *agnīṣomīya* and other sacrifices.

Therefore, since place, time, and agent—being enjoined by a location that does not intend their mutual association—and the various fire-installations (*anyādhāna*) are established as such, it is logical that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belongs to the *Āgneya* sacrifice independently of the *Agnīṣomīya* and others; thus, there is a repetition of the procedure.

Here an objection is raised: if the *Agnīṣomīya* is commenced only after completing the *Āgneya* from the fire-installation up to its primary conclusion, then the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) intended for the attainment of the result would be completely subverted (due to the interruption of the primary acts).
Just as there is no suspicion of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) between the *saurya* rite and the *āgneya* rite, so too would it follow here [in this case].
Therefore, if the performance of the ritual procedure (*kartavyatā*) is carried out by way of a single application (*tantra*), then mutual conjunction is established; not otherwise.
(Therefore, the *tantra* status of the place and other subsidiaries is established precisely through the concomitance (*sāhitya*) understood from the sentence regarding the fruit.)
It is said: this mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is obtained; even when a sacrifice is performed by only one [of the two], the fruit is not attained.
Therefore, the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*) being performed for each individual does not sublate the mutual conjunction.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: although this time is heard in connection with a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka*), nevertheless, by its very nature, it is not something to be adopted as a primary objective (*anupādeya*).
Furthermore, a necessary connection must be made between it and the action (*kriyā*).

And in that connection, since there is no mutual relationship between two visible objects or two things to be adopted, when one of them is to be adopted by means of the other, the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and so forth is intended with respect to what is not to be adopted (*anupādeya*). (By the word "and so forth," the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*), which is mentioned as the third [factor], is included. Furthermore, neither the instrumental case-ending nor the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) would be applicable.
Therefore, three sacrifices conjoined with one another, together with their *itikartavyatā*, are enjoined for the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*);
likewise for the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) as well.
And thus, because the time is prescribed [as the object of the injunction], the meaning of the verbal root is enjoined elsewhere; in that case, the Vedic revelation (śruti) would be upheld.
Otherwise, however, the verbal root would be uttered for the sake of another [purpose], namely, for the purpose of prescribing the time.
The same should be understood regarding place as well, since its non-prescriptibility (anupādeyatva) is equal.

When the performers are known through the statement of the result (*phalavākya*) in a ritual procedure where the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is prescribed—namely, at the stage of considering how the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) will perform it (whether with assistants or without)—the rule "it would be [performed] by oneself" (*svayaṃ prayoge syāt*) would imply that the sacrificer alone is obtained; however, by virtue of the scriptural injunction (*vacana*), the Adhvaryu and others are ordained.
(He concludes: Therefore, if each one were to act independently of the others, then the mutual association (*itaretarayoga*) enjoined regarding the location would be sublated.

Likewise, even with respect to time, if the limbs were absent, the instrumental case-ending would be contradicted. Therefore, by virtue of this statement, there is a common application (*tantratā*) of place and the other factors toward the principal rites together with their limbs. (In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited the injunction of time, "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī [offering] on the full moon day," and therein he raises an objection: But surely, the injunction of time is not being made by the statement "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day," because the time is already established by the originative injunctions such as "That which belongs to Agni" (*yad āgneyaḥ*); this [statement] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

[Objection: But surely, since it is for the sake of a result, how can it be a mere restatement? [Reply: He says—it is not even a connection with a result that is being made, because that has already been established by the sentence concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Moreover, there is no suspicion at all here of a connection with a result, because the result is explicitly heard [in that context]. Therefore, this [present statement] is indeed purposeless. It is said in reply:

Without this sentence—since the time of performance is heard for each [rite] individually in the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), and that [time] pertains to the primary rite together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅgapradhāna*)—the entire section on procedure (*itikartavyatākāṇḍa*) would have to be repeated for each individual [rite], such as the *Āgneya* sacrifice and others.
However, when this sentence exists, all those sacrifices produced at the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) are enjoined toward the fruit because they possess the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇavibhakti*).
And an instrumental case-ending is not possible without a corresponding procedure.
Because they are being taken up [as a group], there is an intention to express their conjunction (*sāhitya*).

Therefore, if each one were performed as possessing the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*), that conjunction which has been understood would be sublated. Consequently, in order not to sublate that [conjunction], conjunction is established with respect to the procedure.

Therefore, by this statement, the procedure (*itikkartavyatā*) applies *tantra*-wise to the three sacrifices; this is the meaning (*artha*) being established. [An objection is raised here: "This is the intended purpose (*prayojana*) of this statement.
And this is indeed already accomplished (or obtained) by another statement"—this is the reading of the *Rūpa* commentary.

For instance, by the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa at the [proper] time," the sacrifices—conjoined with one another and accompanied by their respective procedures—are enjoined with respect to the location; and for those being enjoined, their simultaneity is intended.
If the procedure were to repeat itself, then that simultaneity which has been understood would be sublated.

Therefore, since this statement exists, the fact that the *ājyabhāgas* are subsidiary (*tantra*) is established; thus, the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī [offering] on the full moon day" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
On this point, some explain as follows:

the time for the principal [sacrifice] alone is understood from its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), whereas the time for the *ājyabhāgas* is not understood. Consequently, their performance would also occur on the fifth day; therefore, by this [injunction], a restriction of time is made for them.
That is incorrect.

How so? It has been stated that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), by favoring the instrument (*karaṇa*), renders assistance. Furthermore, it has been stated that at whatever time the instrument [is employed], at that very same time the procedure [is to be performed].

Both that which is the proximate auxiliary procedure (*saṃnipatyopakārikā itikartavyatā*) and that which is the remote auxiliary (*ārādupakārikā*) are connected by this [primary] manner-of-performance (*kathaṃbhāva*).

In that regard, one performing the primary rite on the full moon day must necessarily perform the proximate auxiliaries (otherwise the primary rite itself would not be accomplished); by whatever means one performs the proximate auxiliaries, by that very same means one should also perform the remote auxiliaries.
Nor is there any such principle by which only the primary act (*pradhāna*) itself would have to be performed.
[Rather,] with respect to the place, it is precisely those acts that have become the instruments (*karaṇa*), together with their procedural details (*itikartavyatā*), that are to be performed.
And since that [performance] is accomplished when there is identity of time, and not otherwise, it is established that even the subordinate acts (*aṅga*) possess that same time.
Therefore, this [statement] is inexpressible (i.e., meaningless). [Objection: It is not the case that fire is being denoted [here]. [Response: This is not so.

By the injunction, "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground," all six sacrifices, together with their constituent procedures and mutually connected, are enjoined with respect to the location.
In that case, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for all six sacrifices is obtained through a single performance (*tantra*), because their conjunction (*sāhitya*) is intended.

(But the performance-procedure itself is not different). Therefore, those sacrifices designated as "Full-moon" (*paurṇamāsī*), being performed on the full moon day, will have their archetypal subsidiaries up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings performed according to the order of the recited text (*pāṭhakrama*). Likewise, for those connected with the New-moon day (*amāvāsyā*)—namely the *sāṃnāyya* and other sacrifices—their subsequent subsidiaries, such as the *anūyāja* offerings, will be performed [in that same manner].

Thus, when the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous performance) regarding the application of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) would otherwise apply, the repetition of those parts is established by the injunction: "One should sacrifice with the Full-moon [offering] on the full moon day.

Furthermore, because mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is intended by the injunction "One should sacrifice with the New and Full-moon sacrifices on level ground," the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained through *tantra*.
In that case, the primary rite (*pradhāna*) commenced on the full moon day is completed on the new moon day.

Just as the *savanīya* [offering] commenced at the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*) [is completed] at the third extraction (*tṛtīyasavana*), so too the entire time for the principal rites [is covered]. Therefore, performing the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) anywhere within the interval between the full moon and new moon sacrifices does not contradict the injunction "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on level ground," nor does it contradict the statement regarding the fruit [of the sacrifice], since even there [the two sacrifices] are understood to be conjoined (*itaretarayoga*).

Therefore, by this sentence (*paurṇamāsyāṃ paurṇamāsyā yajeta*), a restriction of time (*kāla-niyama*) is prescribed for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) that might otherwise be performed at any intermediate time due to ignorance; and because they were previously unregulated in time—namely, those ending with the *ājyabhāgas* [being restricted] from the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), and the *anuyājas* and so forth [being restricted] from the time of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)—this [sentence] sets aside that lack of regulation. Consequently, by this [sentence], an injunction regarding the time for the subsidiaries is established.

(For by this, because the sacrifice—which serves as the instrument—is taken up with respect to time, it follows that the sacrifice along with its subsidiaries must be performed on the full moon day, and likewise on the new moon day; thus, two performances of each triad [of sacrifices], complete with all their subsidiaries, are established for their respective times.

There is no perception of a connection between the actions and the fact of not being subsidiary to an injunction, because of their connection with a secondary indicative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) and because these are injunctive commands (*codanāvidhi*); therefore, there should be a distinct manifestation (*bhāva*) for each primary action.

Commentary: If it were not a supplement to the injunction (*codanāvidhi*), that is, if the injunction regarding the place and so forth were not a supplement to the injunction, then the connection of the rites—such as the *Āgneya* and others—with specific locations and so forth through their distinctions would not be understood.
[Therefore,] it is a supplement to the injunction.

What is the reason? Because in this context, locations and so forth are enjoined by such sentences as "In a level [place], one should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," since they are not otherwise established.

If they were indeed enjoined, then a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *Āgneya* and other offerings by means of the term "New and Full Moon Sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) would have to be sought; otherwise, there would be the enjoining of multiple purposes within a single sentence. Furthermore, in the case of a reference, their simultaneity is not established. If it were intended to be expressed [as a simultaneous injunction], a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would occur.
[This refers to] the location and so forth for the Āgneya and other [sacrifices], as well as for them when performed together.

But how can the location and so forth be enjoined in sentences such as "One should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices on level ground"? It is because of the connection with an indication (lakṣaṇā).
The connection is understood to be for the purpose of indication.
The term *darśapūrṇamāsa* has a collective meaning. And a collection is able to indicate its constituent parts through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by virtue of their association.
[Objection: Even so, secondary indication is still resorted to.
By means of the words "Āgneya" and so forth, [the rites] whose primary offerings are the Āgneya and others [are designated].
For everything belonging to this [ritual], each individual element possesses the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to every primary element (*pradhāna*).

Because those elements connected with their specific application (*viniyoga*) function through association (*sāhitya*), they possess the status of being subordinate members to all primaries; for it has been established that even the connection with subordinate members is subject to the injunction of the performance of the primary.

In that case, there is a single sentence—whether devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) or endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*)—wherein origination (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), and performance (*prayoga*) are enjoined by a single injunction, while accepting that each preceding stage is qualified by each subsequent one. Furthermore, the attributes (*guṇas*) are connected to their respective places according to the suitability of the ritual action itself.

However, where two or three sentences are heard, there—in order to avoid the inconsistency of the sentences and to establish their status as injunctions—one sentence contains one injunction and the others contain the rest; and in that case, the connection with this or that specific quality is precisely what serves as the regulator.
Thus it should be understood.

Thus, here in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, although time is mentioned in the sentences concerning the *āgneya* and other offerings, because that [mention of time] serves the purpose of establishing the connection with the fruit and therefore lacks the status of being the object of an injunction, there is only an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) due to the mention of its constituent qualities—namely, the substance and the deity. Its role as an applicatory injunction (*viniyogavidhi*) or a performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) is merely that of a restatement (*anuvādaka*). Otherwise, it would be unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*) to assume a further intentional focus (*tātparya*) upon those [time-injunctions]. Likewise, since the sentence stating the fruit and the sentence stating the occasion (*nimitta*) function as applicatory injunctions, it would be cumbersome to postulate a performance injunction therein as well.

In the case of injunctions regarding the performance (*prayoga*), [the injunction] applies specifically to the prescription of place and so forth, because it is precisely that other subordinate factor (*guṇa*) which serves as the regulator for its application there.
For this very reason, since the application is not obstructed when place and so forth are prescribed, in every such case there is an injunction of the performance qualified by those factors.

And since performance naturally involves a connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and because it would be cumbersome to postulate a separate injunction of performance for each individual subsidiary injunction, the performance together with its subsidiaries is enjoined within the injunction of place and so forth.

Since even those things that are easy [to perform] are primary with respect to their application and are thus enjoined, the qualification of "conjunction" (sāhitya) belonging to them—by virtue of qualifying everything—connects every factor, such as place, time, and ritual action, precisely to the performance of all the subsidiaries in conjunction.

Nor should it be argued that there is no transgression of the prescribed place and so forth when [the rite] is performed with only a few auxiliaries qualified by a single primary, because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the status of being in the "prescribed place" (*deśyatva*) belongs only to that which is endowed with the entirety of the auxiliaries along with the other primaries. For in the archetype, regarding the statement on place and so forth, even the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of auxiliary and primary is accepted as qualifying the performance of the primary—according to the maxim "the substance [is located] in one place"—since this constitutes an injunction for the performance qualified by all its attributes. Furthermore, since the injunction of the attributes, being implied (*ārthika*), prescribes the place and so forth for each individual item with reference to both the auxiliary and the primary, it is established in the archetype that the concomitance is dependent upon the place and other such factors.

Furthermore, since there is no other primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), even in the absence of association with that [other primary], the attainment of place and so forth is logically established in a single primary sacrifice accompanied by other subsidiaries; thus, the accomplishment of both results is justified.
Consequently, by the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground," there is a single performance (*prayoga*) for all six sacrifices regarding the location.
By the statement "And in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [the cake] for Agni," another [element] connected to the agent is established;
this is because there is no deciding factor [to restrict it otherwise], and because those two [sacrifices] cannot be performed simultaneously.
For this very reason, it is established that across all six sacrifices, along with their ancillaries, there is one place and one agent.

There is another [type of] temporal [distinction], such as "one should sacrifice on the full moon day" and so forth, and "one offers the oblation in the evening" and "one offers the oblation in the morning," because of the difference in contradictory times and because of the difference in the primary elements that serve as the qualificands.
That supreme pair of applications, by virtue of being pervaded by the principle [of non-contradiction], is not in conflict with the application of spatial [factors] and the like.

Nor does this apply in all cases of injunctions regarding time and so forth; for if there were a single performance (*ekaprayoga*) [of the primary rite and its subsidiaries], then even in the case of "this [is performed] with an *iṣṭi* and an animal sacrifice," there would result the injunction of a single performance qualified by time, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that all rites beginning with the *āmiṣṭi* and ending with the *Soma* sacrifices would constitute a single performance. This is because, in those cases, due to the co-occurrence with the word *yat*, the injunction prescribes time alone by way of restating (*anuvāda*) the performance of each respective modified form (*vikṛti*); furthermore, since the performance injunction is permitted as an option by the very sentence of each modified form, it is impossible for those means of achieving results such as mental tranquility (*cittakṣaṇa*) to fall under the scope of a single performance injunction.
For this very reason, even the co-occurrence (*sāhitya*) found within various individual sentences is not intended to be significant, because it resides in a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

However, where there is no such indicator of a restatement of performance, since the performance itself is what is being enjoined, the co-occurrence must necessarily be observed. Consequently, the constituent parts of the sentence-sentences that constitute the object of performance possess a single place, time, and agent; yet, when there is a difference in the performance regarding specific times such as the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), this unity is not enjoined. Maṇḍana [says]: "Place and so forth are one for the primary rites."

Śaṅkara: "Time and so forth are common [to all]. Due to the requirement that the principal rites such as the Āgneya and others be connected to a single result, and due to the requirement that the auxiliary elements (aṅgas) be connected to a single service of performance (karaṇopakāra), even sentences that are distinct by virtue of their own individual purposes attain the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) by collectively producing the meaning of one great sentence.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 525). Even though there is a difference between the principal rites such as the Āgneya and others, they possess the character of being governed by the *prājāpatya* sacrifice."

Bhāṭṭa 5121: The sacrifice such as the Āgneya is the motivator only for the material (upādāna) consisting of the designation of the deity; it is not the motivator for the origination or maintenance of the deity. Bāla. pṛ. 107: In the sentence concerning the Āgneya and others, since the connection between the substance and the deity is established through direct audition (śruti) and other means—just like the act of relinquishment—it is possible for the sequence, which is presented by direct audition and the rest and expressed by an elliptical word (adhyāhṛta), to be the object of injunction. Soma. 5121: Words such as "Āgneya" are injunctions of accessory qualities (guṇavidhi), not names of rituals (karmanāmadheya).
"‘That which belongs to Agni is the cake on eight potsherds’" (Su. p.
462). By means of words such as "belonging to Agni," the section concerning what belongs to Agni [is established].

In the section concerning the Āgneya [offering], it will be stated that offerings such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni and Agni-Soma are not included because they lack the requisite capacity (asāmarthya) when compared to those dedicated solely to deities such as Agni; this will also include the discussion on the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), the portion drunk by Indra (*indrapīta*), and the ground portion for Pūṣan (*pūṣaprapiṣṭabhāga*).
The section concerning the Āgneya [offering]. Words such as *āgneya* and *āgnīṣomīya* are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), not names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*).
Their qualities would indeed be enjoined because they are expressed by the words; for the purpose is an injunction, provided they are not already established by another [injunction].
Commentary: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is unchanging at the new moon and the full moon"—such passages are heard in scripture.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are [the terms] *āgneya*, *āmīṣomīya*, and so forth, injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? If they were injunctions of accessories, then multiple accessories would be enjoined: namely, Agni, the *puroḍāśa* (cake), and the eight potsherds.
Therefore, they are not injunctions of qualities.
