This being the position reached, we reply:
that is indeed the ritual action, and its qualities would be enjoined.
For those [terms] are not distinct from the injunction of the action within that word ending in a nominal suffix;
for therein the state of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) is enjoined for the cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*).
That very [cake] becomes non-dedicated to Agni only if it is given after having been mentally resolved for someone other than Agni.
Thus, this sacrifice is enjoined in this manner.
When it is being enjoined in this way, it is not possible to enjoin it without enjoining the *argha* and the *aṣṭākapāla*.
For when a relationship is being enjoined, it cannot be said to be enjoined without enjoining the two related terms.
Therefore, these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) itself is prepared upon these potsherds (*kapāla*), whether it consists of rice or barley; this is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, the "eight-potsherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) is established here by the statement, "he bakes it on potsherds," and they do not accept what has been offered by another means.

Therefore, in this view, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). However, if they are not enjoined by the final [word], but rather the qualities are enjoined by another statement, then in that case it is a name (*nāmadheya*).
For example: "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice. Or rather: since the names and the functions of names have thus been established, an exception (*apavāda*) is now introduced.
But why is the term *davihoma* not examined right here? This has already been examined under [sūtra] 2.4.3.4. (*tatparye*).

And here [in this work], the investigation concerns those [terms] occurring in the injunctive statements (*vidhyuddeśa*); however, in that [other work, the *Tantravārttika*], at [Sūtra] 8.1.11, the investigation concerns those occurring in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as: "If one were to offer with a single [verse], one would perform a *davihoma*.
Or, once it is established that [the term] is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), the specific investigation of its particulars occurs there.
In this context, however, since the discussion concerns general principles (*sāmānya*), it has not been introduced [here].

As for the suspicion regarding a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) that arose there, that was merely a preliminary objection within the body of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*); all of this is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*).

And in the eighth [book], as before, there is the section concerning the consideration of what has not been previously established (*apūrvacintā*). But by what means is the status of names (*nāmadheyatva*) suspected for the rites such as the *Āgneya* which have already been enjoined? To this it is said:
By such statements as "it is on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāle bhavati*), ritual productions (*bhāvanā*) associated with mere substances and possessing a sequence are set forth.
And for these [offerings], sacrificial verses (*yājyā*) and invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*), addressed to deities such as Agni and others, are handed down in the sequence of their positions.
Being thus enjoined by the order of sequence, they bring to mind the deities who are the constituent parts of the ritual, as indicated by the words of the mantras themselves.
Otherwise, those mantras would not find application in the ritual action.
Mantras attain utility for ritual action either by revealing the essential nature of the action or by revealing its relationship [to other factors].
Furthermore, neither the action nor the substance is denoted by these [mantras].

If that which is denoted—such as fire (*agni*) and so forth—has its relational status unknown, then in the case of revealing its non-relationality or other such qualities, there would be the undesirable consequence of it becoming a non-auxiliary (*anaṅgatva*).

Based on the positive concomitance (anvaya) ascertained by him, it is understood thus: "Those whom they mention are surely the deities (devatā) for the constituent parts of the ritual action. And since they are designated as deities because of their predominance within the mantras, they become deities in the ritual acts as well, due to the lack of distinction [between the mantra and the act].

Since even the *puroḍāśa* and other such materials, being perceived as means to sacrifice by virtue of their fitness to constitute an oblation (*havis*), require a deity—just as a deity requires them—once the connection between substance and deity is established through inference, the names of the sacrifices, such as the *Āgneya*, are determined to be designations (*nāmadheya*) according to the principle: "And another [word] is a name because of another scriptural statement" (JS 1.4.3).

Alternatively, since the *kapāla* (potsherds) and so forth constitute the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), when the act of cutting (*avadāna*) is understood through the rule "he cuts twice from the oblation," and because the subsequent preparation of that [oblation]—such as the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*)—is established by another injunction, and once the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) is accomplished, the statement "he offers the fourfold portion" applies. Thus, when the offerings of whatever substance has been prepared are accordingly obtained for Agni and the other deities, [the term *caturavatta*] functions as a name (*nāmadheya*).
In this way, the fault of enjoining multiple meanings will not arise.
This being the position reached, it is replied:

"If they were not taught by the final word, they would not be fit to be designated as qualities by some word; rather, those qualities would have to be taught by means of an injunction regarding the portion of the oblation. To begin with, an injunction for a sacrifice is not tenable through a connection with the substance, the deity, or a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
How so? "The requirement for a mantra cannot be established on the basis of the substance's own nature. Nor is its connection with that which denotes something else understood.
By the mere statement, 'It exists on eight potsherds,' no human activity is enjoined, which would serve as a cause for recollection for the purpose of performance."
The section concerning the Āgneya [offering] would depend upon the section concerning the Āgneya.
Furthermore, the becoming of a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) cannot be enjoined for a person, because actions have specific agents.
Nor can a substance be enjoined as something to be produced in its own form, since it already exists as an accomplished entity (*siddhātmaka*), such that it could be brought about.
Moreover, neither the substance nor its operation is denoted by expressions such as "Agni and Sūrya," whereby they could even be connected through syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
There exists no connection whatsoever between those [mantras] denoting Agni and others [and the sacrifice].

Neither the sacrifice nor the sacrificial material (havis) has been determined as being the cake (puroḍāśa) or the portion (iḍā); therefore, there would be no requirement for a deity, nor any coherence with those mantras.

For if the sacrifice were first determined, then, while there exists an expectancy for a deity, the mantras expressive of a deity would be connected [to it]; however, that is not the case, as it is not so stated by the word.
Furthermore, prior to the connection with the sacrifice, the status of the *puroḍāśa* and other materials as an oblation (*havis*) is not established;
for this [status] arises from being related [to the sacrifice], and is not caused by the intrinsic nature of the substance itself.
For indeed, that substance which is connected with the sacrifice, such as milk and the like, is not denoted by the word *havis* in common worldly usage;

regarding this, there is a doubt: should one invoke those very [verses] belonging to the present context (*prakṛta*) that possess such indicative marks (*liṅga*), or should one bring in those from the *Daśataya* (the ten books of the Ṛgveda) that possess such indicative marks?

What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? Since a mantra being enjoined by its indicative mark within a specific context must be brought in, it should be brought in precisely from the *Daśataya*.
For the ten mandalas can indeed be designated by such terms as "belonging to Agni" (āgneyī) and so forth.
However, this [mantra] under discussion has been employed for another purpose; therefore, it does not deserve to be taught here as well.
For a double teaching of such a kind is certainly not logical.

Of what kind [of person] is this? One who has been instructed regarding a specific detail does not deserve to be instructed again by means of a general characteristic. How so? If that characteristic serves as its defining mark (*lakṣaṇa*), then it is defined by that specific [mark] such that "by means of this very characteristic, he performs this [action]"; in that case, he is not [further] instructed.

Or, if he is indeed instructed that "he performs [it] by means of such a characteristic," then he is not [previously] defined by it; therefore, for one of such a kind who has already been instructed, a further instruction of such a kind is not logical.

Therefore, just as in the case of the *daśatayī* [mantras], because the individual is apprehended by means of its indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is no fault even when the individual belonging to the context is apprehended. However,

if the deity is merely indicated and the individual alone is the meaning of the word, then, since the individual belonging to the context is apprehended, it would follow that the word applies to each part due to the nature of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
And here, it is only the individual (vyakti) that is the means of proof, not some such thing as a "universal" (sāmānya).
But now, why does the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) perform this denial of the universal, which causes confusion by what has been said? We say: no.
It is incorrect [to say so], because he merely states the possibility of its being a subordinate factor (aṅga). Thus, that [objection] is untenable.
That being the case, since individual instances (*vyakti*) are not explicitly mentioned, there is no fault even if they are not accepted.

Therefore, it must be stated that [the term] excludes the universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to what is under discussion. For this word "individual" (*vyakti*), being etymological (*yaugika*), does not function like a generic term (*jāti-śabda*) [as in the case of the injunction] "with an Āgneyī verse."

Furthermore, no common genus (*jāti*) is perceived here, even though the deities are of various forms and possess various meters, because the deity is one and the same, and because terms such as "āgneyī" (pertaining to Agni) are employed.
Indeed, in the two [verses] "Come to the feast, O Agni! and "I honor Agni, the bountiful Hotṛ," no commonality whatsoever is seen apart from the deity.

This [connection] with the deity does not fail; however, the generic class of the *ṛc* fails, because it is employed even in relation to substances, actions, and so forth. (Alternatively, in order to avoid a syntactical split [*vākya-bheda*], if it is said that there is merely a connection with the worship of Agni and others as they are heard in the text, the author of the Sūtras says: "The instruction would be purposeless, because the connection is not with that which possesses a fruit."

"Now, [one might argue] that by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would be a subsidiary (*upakāraka*) to the Jyotiṣṭoma"—thus he considers the general connection to be established from another source.
However, he shows that even this is not possible if it is not being enjoined:
"If the connection between the *upasthāna* and the Jyotiṣṭoma were intended to be expressed, then it would attain syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with it."

But when, instead of prescribing that [specific] attendance (*upasthāna*), the connection with the mantra is enjoined by means of a specific injunction, then the mantras would apply only to the worldly, fruitless, and pure form of attendance, overriding the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the inferred Vedic text (*śruti*). For in that case, there would be no restriction based on the context. However, in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it is appropriated by the Jyotiṣṭoma from the very beginning, there is no application elsewhere; thus, there is both purposefulness and parsimony (*lāghava*).

Alternatively, it is more parsimonious [to hold that] when the connection between the *mantras*— which serve as instruments (*karaṇa*) and constitute auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the rites such as the Āgneya— is being enjoined, the "standing near" (*upasthāna*) is also restated (*anūdyate*).
And since all [of these] have been taught, [this applies] to the Āgrayaṇa [cup], as discussed in the *Āgneyī-adhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 8.1.27–30).

In view of the non-cutting-off nature of the constituent elements (*dhātu*), through the self-reflection [of the word], there is the comprehension of its denotation as being limited by a small measure; thus, from the sentence "one should place the fire-verse (*āgneyī*) upon the post," the meaning of the sentence is understood. Furthermore, since verses such as "Come hither to the front" (*agra ā yāhi*) express a proximate object through the use of the locative case and other indicators, and since denotation cannot occur without proximity, the mention of the already established proximity is logically consistent as a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, like the general [rules], this too is not an injunction; thus, there is extreme parsimony (*atilāghava*).

Su. 1132. In the section concerning the *āgneyī* [verse] (*āgneyyadhikaraṇa*), it was stated [at Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.21–24] that in such cases as "He worships the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with an *āgneyī* [verse]," even though the verse is already employed elsewhere, only the one under discussion (*prakṛta*) in the current context should be taken, and not one brought in from the *Daśataya* collection. This is because, according to Pārthasārathi Miśra, in the *āgneyyadhikaraṇa*, the view that derivative (*yaugika*) words denote only what is proximate has been refuted. [In the case of the statement] "He worships the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with an *āgneyī*," there would be a violation of the essence of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)—which functions equally toward both the relevant (*prakṛta*) and irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*) that indicates the general relationship—in the *āgneyī* sentence.
In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, it is taught that the Aindrāgna cup belongs to the Āgrayaṇa;
in the Āgrayaṇa, the cloth and calf prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) supersede the other prescribed dakṣiṇās.

And the cloth and the first-born calf are common [to all]. The Bhāṣya states: "The Āgrayaṇa sacrifice takes place for the non-defeat of the sacrificer after the oblation has been offered; it consists of various grains: an offering to Agni of old rice, a *śyāmāka* offering to Soma, a pap (*caru*) in milk for the Viśvedevas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
In that context, it is heard: "A cloth is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); a first-born calf is the sacrificial fee."
It is obtained here by the force of the extended application (*codaka*).
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the *anvāhārya* rice remove the *vāsas* (garment) and the *vatsa* (calf), or does it not remove them?
What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is that it does not remove them, because of the absence of any reason for the extended application to take up those specific qualities.
This being the case, we reply:
the garment and the calf [are included] by virtue of their general nature;

however, because they occupy the upper and lower positions among the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), they are excluded from the re-establishment (*punarādheya*).
By the word "and" (ca), other directions are indicated.
There is the exclusion of the *anvāhārya* rice.
Why? Because of the similarity of the function.
In the archetype ritual, the *anvāhārya* rice is the object of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Here, however, a garment and a calf are to be used for that same purpose, because the word "sacrificial fee" is heard [in the text].
Therefore, there is no combination; rather, there is a displacement [of the original fee].
It is performed with the intention of expressing a state of being more easily obtained.
Vi— "The garment and the calf are to be combined, or rather, the anvāhārya [rice] is not;
because there is no contradiction, there is a combination, for there is no contradiction due to their being effects."
Bhaṭṭa: In the Śyāmākāgrayaṇa sacrifice, it is heard in scripture that "a garment is the sacrificial fee" (*vāso dakṣiṇā*);
and in the Brīhyāgrayaṇa, "the first-born calf is the sacrificial fee" (*vatsaḥ prathamajo dakṣiṇā*).
It is indeed an established conclusion that this [latter] sets aside the original *anvāhārya* (subsidiary rice-offering).

Furthermore, there is no possibility of a combination (*samuccaya*) between the ordinary and the modified forms based on the assumption that the *ānati* (prostration) has a meaning distinct from the *kraya* (purchase), as in the case of the *krayas*. This is because the purpose of the act is established solely by the attainment of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-sampatti*), and thus the prostration is enjoined as nothing more than that.
If it were performed as an independent intermediate act, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of combining rice and barley, or various sacrificial oblations (*havis*).
However, in the case of the *krayas*, there is indeed a combination, due to the scriptural injunction: "He purchases [the Soma] with ten."
Therefore, the modified sacrificial fee (*vaikṛtadakṣiṇā*) sets aside the archetypal sacrificial fee (*prākṛtadakṣiṇā*); this is established by way of the subsequent [intention].
Maṇḍana states: "The calf and so forth would be the displacers of the former.
Śaṅkara states: "Because the garment and the calf are already obtained [as part of the archetype]."
In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, there is no restriction regarding the Vaiśvadeva ritual procedure on account of the requirements of the offerings to Indra-Agni and Viśve Devās.
This is the second principle concerning the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
But by its occurrence there, the *tantra* (ritual procedure) would be restricted, just as the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) is [restricted] by the *sūktavāka*.
The commentary states: For that [offering], being simple, the *vaiśvadeva* *tantra* is restricted;
just as the animal sacrifice *tantra* is restricted by the specific direction (*preṣa*) of the *sūktavāka*.
Or rather, it is not restricted, because there is no contradiction.
The Bhāṣya says: "Or rather, it is not restricted. Why? Because there is no contradiction."
This quality is not incompatible with other oblations as well;
therefore, it is not specific (*vaiśeṣika*).
Because it is not specific, it cannot restrict [the application] to one or the other.

But the *sūktavāka* is specifically defined [as a mantra]; therefore, it is capable of restricting one or the other [of the two acts]. Furthermore, this is because it is not characterized by the nature of a general rule (*śāstra*).
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): Furthermore, these subsidiaries (*aṅgāni*) are not prescribed by the primary scripture (*śāstra*).
What then? They are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).

What follows from this? If they were prescribed by the primary scripture, then the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice would be restricted by that very [scriptural] archetype (*prakṛti*).

Alternatively, because it is not the inherent nature of heaven and earth (dyāvāpṛthivī), the repetition of the very same *prasūna* flowers is understood—by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—to be an injunction for the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, in order to avoid its meaninglessness; thus, [the rule] "therein the *prasūna* and so forth occur" is not a definition of that specific scripture.

Therefore, it is a restriction (*niyama*) for the ritual procedure already in motion. Soma [says]: By depending on the previously mentioned restriction regarding the *prasūna*, this [rule] has a connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*).
In the Sūtra, the word *tat* refers to the flower (*prasūna*).
As Viśvarūpa states: "Either heaven and earth would be the *tantrī*, or all [the gods] would be the *tantriṇaḥ*;
because the flower, through its act of sending forth, brings about the state of being the *tantrī*."

The state of being a "flower" (prasūnatva) has not been taught [as a defining characteristic], because it is free from contradiction; rather, it is accepted as being based on the fixed nature of being a *tantra*. Therefore, I suspect that the status of being a *tantra* does not apply everywhere.

Bhaṭṭa: Nor does this lead to the contingency (*prasaṅga*) that even in the case of contradictory properties such as "newly kindled" and so forth, the properties of the *dyāvāpṛthivī* [offering] alone would apply to both the *graha* and the *aditi* offerings; for when the other two [offerings] take up only the *barhis* [grass], since the state of being made of fresh flowers (*prasūnamayatva*) serves as an auxiliary to that [specific *barhis*], the other two cannot be considered contingent (*prasaṅgin*) with respect to that particular part.

Therefore, regarding contradictory properties such as "newly kindled," because the primary [offering] and the other two are the common basis (*tantri*), the single *kapāla* [offering] is indeed subject to the contingency.

However, when all dharmas are non-contradictory, there is indeed a state of being governed by the tantra, because there is no distinction from the supreme dharma (*agradharma*) due to their simultaneous commencement.
Here, since there is no contradiction among the five as in the case of the nine, it appears that even the "blazing of the nine" (*navaprajvalya*) is not contradictory.
Yet, the ritualists do not perform it in that manner.

However, in cases such as the *paśupuroḍāśa*, where the *tantra* (the common ritual framework) is taken up despite being contrary to the textual order (*ayathāpāṭha*) and so forth, there is indeed *prasaṅga* (extension of application) even regarding both the conflicting and the non-conflicting portions. Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifices, Maṇḍana states:
"In the *āgrayaṇas*, the *tantra* of the offering to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivīya*) should not occur."
Śaṅkara says:

"And here, in the case of all [the priests] being the performers (*tantrin*), in the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, the duties of the *anvāhārya* (the monthly rice-offering) must be performed for both the cloth and the calf, preceded by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
By implication, it should possess those properties because of its connection with the motive known as the "sign.

The Bhāṣya states: Regarding that very cloth and calf, there is a doubt as to whether the properties of the Anvāhārya should be performed or not. What is the prima facie view? It is not yet argued that they should be performed according to the logical principle.
"Therefore, we consider that it should not be performed.
This being the position reached, we reply:
on account of presumptive evidence (*arthāpatti*), it should possess those characteristics; and the garment should likewise possess those characteristics.
For those properties are dependent upon specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), not upon anything else;

therefore, they ought to exist in another [substance] as well by virtue of being its effect. But how is it that the cloth and the calf are its effects? By way of being the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) through the act of giving as a purchase-price (*parikraya*); for there occurs such a connection [in the scriptures], namely: "the cloth is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)" and "the first-born calf is the sacrificial fee."

Therefore, the cloth and the calf should possess the characteristics of the *anvāhārya* (the monthly sacrificial fee). Soma says: "But from the Sūtra, the cloth and the calf should have the nature of the *anvāhārya*, because of their connection with the word *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) which is caused by the purchase for the purpose of the *anvāhārya*.
Vi [ṣṇu] says: "In this case, either the duty of the *anvāhārya* is not to be performed, or it is performed."
"It is not its intrinsic nature; do not say so, for it is due to its being employed as a means of proof."

Bhaṭṭa: "The modified sacrificial fee (*vaikṛtī dakṣiṇā*), because it takes over the function of the archetypal fee (*prākṛtadakṣiṇākārya*), likewise obtains the properties of the archetypal fees such as the *anvāhārya*.
Maṇḍana: "'The calf and so forth [are the modified fee], and they possess the properties of the *anvāhārya* and so forth.
Śaṅkara: "In that case, there is the application of the properties of the *anvāhārya*."
In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, there is a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla) for Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivya).

Bhāṣya 7.1.5.23 states that in the Āgrayaṇa, regarding the cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth, there is an extension (atideśa) of the injunction for the cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth belonging to the Vaiśvadeva rite of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Furthermore, in the Āgrayaṇa, although the cloth and the calf take the place of the Anvāhārya rice, their sprinkling with clarified butter (abhighāraṇa) is set aside (bādha).
Likewise regarding the pouring over (abhighāraṇa).
The Bhāṣya states: In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice it is heard, "The garment is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)," and "The first-born calf is the sacrificial fee.
In this regard, the following point has been established: the properties of the Anvāhārya rice should be performed upon both the garment and the calf.

Now, this matter is subject to doubt: should the sprinkling be performed or not? What, then, is the prima facie view? It should be performed, because it is required by the purpose. This being the position, we reply as follows.
In that case, for whom is the sprinkling performed?

What is it that is done? For the sprinkling is performed upon the *anvāhārya* rice for the sake of flavoring (*khādimna*). Indeed, by means of the flavoring, it serves as an auxiliary in the purchase of the cooked rice.
Furthermore, there is no need for the act of eating with respect to the garment or the calf;

therefore, the sprinkling [of ghee] should not take place there. Soma says: "But here, because it serves an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), there is a need"—this constitutes the connection [to the previous discussion].
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is: "There is or there is not an over-pouring (abhighāra) here, because the application of ghee and oil is possible;
it is like the anvāhārya rice-offering. [Siddhāntin: Not so, because sweetness is impossible [in the case of oil]."

Bhaṭṭa: Since sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it would follow that it should be performed even on the cloth and the calf; however, since the rice (*odana*) serves a visible purpose and its edibility (*hṛdyatva*) is possible, one cannot assume an invisible purpose for it. Furthermore, because there is no purpose for [the cloth] being edible, the sprinkling is indeed performed [only on the rice]. Maṇḍana: "And there is no sprinkling on the cloth or the calf. Śaṅkara: "There is sprinkling on both."
The word "contradiction" (bādhaḥ) is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
In the context of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, the year to be taken is that which begins from the time of the harvest of each respective grain, and not the lunar year or other such reckonings.

In the Śruti text, "This [sacrifice] takes place for a year (saṃvatsara)," one of the various types of years—such as the lunar year established by Śruti texts like "Twelve months are a year"—is obtained as an option.
This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

In worldly usage, such as in the expression "crops ripen in a year" (*saṃvatsare sasyāni pacyante*), even a period of time exceeding the ripening of crops is designated as a "year. This is based solely on the occasion of the crop's ripening, because it is that [occasion] which serves as the defining characteristic (*upalakṣita*). Since a restrictive rule is possible [in this case], a deviation [from the standard duration] is not improper. Furthermore, the statement "beginning of the year" (*saṃvatsarādau*) applies even when there is no completion of twelve months. [Regarding the temporal markers: *parāri* refers to the previous year; *eṣamaḥ* refers to the year before that; *pūrve* and *pūrvatare* refer to the preceding years;
*parut* refers to the last year; *parāri* refers to the year before last; and *aiṣamaḥ* refers to the current year. (Amara-kośa).
In the case of the Āgrayaṇa offerings, there is a fixed rule regarding both the specific substance and the specific time; it is not a matter of option.

Having enjoined, "One desiring preeminence (āṣṭakāma) should sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa," since the time and the materials are enjoined by the immediately following sentence, there would be an option [regarding the materials], just as in the case of the materials for the Agnihotra. This being the prima facie view, the established principle is the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi rule.

If [the injunction] were to apply to multiple [offerings] across two times by way of partial application, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*); since a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) would necessarily follow, the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of all three *āmayaṇas* would be interrupted.
Furthermore, even for those [offerings] performed on specific occasions, there is also a quality of being optional (*kāmyatā*) through the statement regarding the desire for food (*annādya-kāma*).

In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, however, after prescribing the Śyāmāka-Āgrayaṇa sacrifice with the passage, "There are seventeen Sāmidhenī verses, two Ājyabhāga portions with [different] meters" (4.12), and so forth—thereby enjoining specific qualities with reference to the archetypal injunctions—and after prescribing the initiation for the Yava-Āgrayaṇa, there is a clear distinction of rites due to the scriptural statement of extended application (*atideśa*): "This is indeed my Brāhmaṇa" (4.163). Therefore, there is no option regarding the material (*dravya*), nor is there an option regarding the rite (*karman*) itself, because of the difference in the occasion (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, there is a scriptural teaching of repetition according to the difference in the solstices (*ayana*), as in: "Twice, indeed, does this sun...
(Saṃkarṣa. 3.1.16).
Oṃ: Even when one is afflicted by illness, there is no prohibition against consuming urine and other such substances, nor against eating śamī-grain.

Although a prohibition might arise for urine and so forth, as well as for *śamī* grains and other crops, due to their specific state of being cooked or unripe, there is no such prohibition because they are simply unfit for sacrifice (*ayāgayogyatva*).
Saṃkarṣa. 3.1.12.
Even when the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice has not been performed, there is no fault in eating vegetables, *aparṣā* (wild rice), and the like.

Since another scriptural statement, "One should not eat grain," establishes a prohibition against eating even vegetables and the like, and since those [vegetables] lack the fitness for sacrifice, the text begins with, "When the plants had ripened, the gods entered into a contest; Indra and Agni won them first. Following this introduction, by means of the prohibition against eating new grain, the text indicates that one should not eat cooked grains fit for offering to the gods before having sacrificed to them. Consequently, the eating of raw vegetables and green barley and the like is optional, depending on one's desire. (Saṃkarṣa 3.1.11)
Oṃ: By the scriptural statement "the rice-porridge is for Śrī," there is an injunction regarding the substance in the archetype (prakṛti).

By the statement, "Having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice with rice alone until the [next] Āgrayaṇa," this is enjoined for the period between the time of the rice-sacrifice and another time, provided that the Āgrayaṇa of rice has not occurred; for by the word *yati*, there is the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the principal rite belonging to the context.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since it is possible for the injunction to have the purpose of restricting the material for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), which are already permanently established during the intervening period, it is improper to assume a restriction on something else that is only partially established (*alpaprasaktāprāpta*).
This is because the particle *eva* ("alone") in the phrase "with rice alone" is understood to exclude barley (*yava*).
Saṃkarṣa 3.1.15: Om. There is a prohibition against eating cultivated grains when the *āmayaṇa* sacrifice has not been performed.

Therefore, the prohibition—"one should not eat with *āmayaṇa*; one must eat of the new [grain]"—applies specifically to the *phālguna* [beans], and not to the eating of rice or barley; for this is established by the specific determination made in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) which mentions the fruit and leprosy: "those which are *phālgunas*, [one should avoid them] with the other. Consequently, the eating of domestic grains other than the *phālgunas* is unrestricted.

This being the position [of the opponent]: since for an ignorant person action is impossible through a general substance, and because the general term must terminate in a specific instance—given that the activity has a specific object as its domain—even if a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) were necessary, there is no possibility of the cessation [of eating] having as its object the eating of all nine kinds of grain in general; therefore, because it is not required by the injunction, the supplementary statement lacks the capacity [to restrict it], and like the passage concerning the month of Phālguna, it is merely laudatory through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, the prohibition of eating applies to all domestic grains. [In the context of] the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, the status of being the first-fruits of the Āgrayaṇa [is established]. *Saṃkarṣa.* [Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra Bhāṣya] 857. The status of being the first-fruits of the Āgrayaṇa.
Even though the state of being unproduced (*aprasūtatva*) is set aside, since there is no setting aside of the scriptural meaning—which is merely the *barhis* grass itself—nothing becomes secondary.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: when that [quality] is common [to both], an additional quality characterized by being produced (*prasūtalakṣaṇa*) is restricted to the possessor of that quality (*guṇin*), because there is no contradiction even if it is not primary.
It is just like the rule that a student must eat from a brass vessel (*kāṃsya-bhojitva*).
There is no fixed rule regarding the preceptor.

If it should happen that both [the preceptor and the disciple] eat from a single vessel, then the duty of even the subordinate disciple is likewise upheld there. As in the case of the *barhis* grass at the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, where even if some [grass] has flowered, it is accepted because of its abundance.
And because of its being the first [to be practiced], it is primary; do not say so, for there is no loss [of the result], just as in the case of one who eats from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyabhojin*).

Bhaṭṭa: In the *Āmayana* sacrifice, three sacrifices are heard in the scripture: "A cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni; that [cake] for the Viśvedevas and the *upasad* [cakes], which are cakes on one potsherd.
Among these, it has been stated that the single-potsherd cake belongs to the Viśvedevas has the single-potsherd cake [of the model sacrifice] as its archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, in that case, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of flowers.
This [use of flowers] for the first two [sacrifices] is dependent on the extension (*atideśa*) from the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Therein, even though there are many primary [uses], because of the restriction by the secondary [rule] regarding the placement (*upanidhāna*), there is indeed no fixed rule even regarding the flowers.

For there is no such thing as "non-restriction" (*aniyama*) as a distinct category (*padārtha*) between those two, by which a restriction would be sublated due to its occurrence in only one inferior instance; rather, the mere *barhis* (sacrificial grass) is the subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that [rite].

Therefore, according to the maxim of the "one who eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinnyāya*), even if it follows the weaker [requirement], there is no fault whatsoever in not taking even the flower.
As Maṇḍana says: "Even if a quality is secondary, it should be accepted so that other qualities may also be conjoined."
Śaṅkara says: "In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, there is the *barhiḥ-sūna*.
*Sūna* means *prasūna*, that is, flowering.
In the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi, there are two Sāmans for the *sāmidhenī* verses."
Bhāṣya 10.8: (The term *āgrayaṇa* refers to a specific sacrifice [in the former sense], but hereafter it refers to a specific cup [of Soma] in the Soma sacrifice.
On the day of the *āgrayaṇa*, the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) will be performed in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
VI.2.3.1: The *ṣoḍaśī* cup is to be drawn from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel;
and that cup is drawn after the *ukthya* cup.
10.5.10: The remnant of the two [vessels] comes from the *āditya* vessel into the *āgrayaṇa* pot.
The Pālīvata cup is drawn from the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
3|2|11. The days [of the rite] prior to the Āgrayaṇa are transposed in the expanded twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha).
Ke. [Commentary].
Oṃ! At the equinox, the settling of Āmayaṇāpramatā.
Because there is no *sāman* in the *jagatsāman*, it should be treated like a *sāman* for the sake of the meaning.

The commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in the scripture]: "If the *stoma* has the *rayantara-sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the *bṛhat-sāman*, those beginning with the *śukra*; if it has the *jagat-sāman*, those beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*.
The phrase "those beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*" is the example under consideration.

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the *jagatsāman* belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*), or to the ectype (*vikṛti*)? What is the prima facie view? It belongs to the archetype because it favors the context (*prakaraṇa*). If "the *jagatsāman*" refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself—whether by some connection through a quality or an action—then it belongs to the archetype.
This being the case, we reply:
even though it is heard in connection with the Jagatsāman, that Sāman is not determined to be the Sun. Why? Because of the absence of the [actual] Sāman.
For indeed, there is no *sāman* named "Jagat" in any of the *Sāmaveda*s.
Therefore, where there is a *sāman* consisting of the "Jagat," that is [the one] "with the Jagat-sāman";
that is the Viṣuvat day.
But is it not said that the equinox occurs at the tip of the yoke?
This is no fault; it will be for the sake of desire.
Regarding the statement, "In its introduction, there is an insertion [of the word]":

Soma says—just as in the case of the phrase "on every fourth day," where the repetition (*vīpsā*) is somehow interpreted as a restatement (*anuvāda*), so too the term *jagatsāman* is somehow applied to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; thus, the connection with the example is established by what has been stated.
The compound *jagatsāma etya* is a *bahuvrīhi*.

The compound *jagattyāṃ sāma* can also be understood as a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound with members in different grammatical cases), meaning "that which has its Sāman on the *jagatī*.
Here, one should understand that the word *jagat* is a synonym for *jagatī*, or that the elision of the vowel *ī* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: regarding the phrase "if [it were] by the *jagatsāman*," since there is no such thing as a *jagatsāman*, the aforementioned Sāman would have to be designated by the name *jagat* due to its connection with the *ṛc* verse.

For the author of the Sūtra who speaks thus, only a *samānādhikaraṇa* (appositional) compound is intended. [The commentary states: "In either the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*), there may be the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa cup among the cups. The first [alternative] is due to the context (*prakaraṇa*); the other is because of the possibility of the *jagatsāman* [melody]."
Maṇḍana: "The Jagatsāman would exist in the Jagatī metre. Śaṅkara: "The Viṣuvat and Āgrayaṇa vessels.
Ke: The Sāman produced upon the Ṛg verse beginning with "vibhrāḍ bṛhat pibatu somya madhu" in the Jagatī metre is the Jagatsāman.
The precedence of the *āmayaṇa* [cup] should be performed in the *viṣuvat* day—which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—when the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* is set to the *jagat-sāman*.
(Vi. 2.3.1). The precedence of the *āmayaṇa* applies to the *dhārā-grahas* in the expanded (*vyūḍha*) twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
(Kośa 108).
Regarding the term *āghāra*:
it occurs on the ninth days of both [the *samūḍha* and *vyūḍha* sacrifices],
as well as on the fourth, seventh, and eleventh days of the *samūḍha*.
10.15.23–24: The state of having the Āgrayaṇa cup as the first belongs to the Soma sacrifice when it has the Jagatī metre for its *śyena* chant and the *upavasatha-sāman* as its chant;
and that [state] occurs in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) at the one called the Viṣuvat.
The *āghāra* libation assists the principal rite even when it is not being measured.
The reason is that at that time, the primary acts themselves do not yet exist.
However, when all the subsidiary acts have been performed, then the *apūrva*s (transcendental potencies) produced by them combine and assist the primary acts.

Bhāṣya 11.2.15–17. The first *āghāra* (libation) is without a mantra, according to the Vedic revelation: "One pours the libation while meditating on Prajāpati in the mind," and "One pours the libation silently."

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is stated in the section on the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice (Vi. 10.3.2; ŚB 8.1.15): "Having poured the *āghāra* oblation, he anoints the animal with the *juhū* ladle. This *āghāra* is a non-transitive action; it does not have a fruit as its object.
In that regard, the mention of the fruit [of the sacrifice] is as follows:
those two [offerings], the Āgneya and others, are to be inferred.
Bhāṣya 4.3.112–4: the two Āghāra libations, the two Ājyabhāga portions, the Prayājas, the Anuyājas, the Patnīsaṃyājas, the Samid-yajus, and the Sṛṣṭakṛt—these are the auxiliary elements (aṅgas).
The Āgneya, Agnīṣomīya, Upāṃśuyāja, Aindrāgna, and Sāṃnāyya sacrifices constitute the primary acts (pradhāna). [Śabarabhāṣya on Jaiminisūtra 4.4.12, p. 129–38].
The injunction "He pours the Āghāra libation" is one that has a substance as its primary object;
for by this action the substance is sprinkled, and once sprinkled, it accomplishes the sacrifice.

...this very pouring (āghāraṇa) is the primary ritual act. ...The substance is clarified butter (ājya), and Indra is the deity as indicated by the wording of the mantra. Since the pouring is conjoined with both a substance and a deity, it is therefore a sacrifice (yajati).

That [rite] is the name of the sacrifice. (10.7.14.14) "He pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon during the *upasads*" (10.7.14.14); "In the *āghāra*, he pours it upwards"—this is an injunction of a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣavidhi*).

2|2|13–16, In the *āghāra* (libation), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the properties of straightness, continuity, and upwardness, because they serve different purposes (*ahaddvārabhedāt*), and not an option (*vikalpa*).
"And in the *āghāra*, [straightness is required] because of the long stream."
In the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, as with other oblations, the commencement of the ritual action coincides with the end of the mantra.
Regarding the term "continuously" (*saṃtata*) in the injunction "he pours the *āghāra* continuously," it is used because of its long stream; that is, because it possesses a long flow.
The stream of the clarified butter (*ājya*) for the *āghāra* becomes long, beginning from a single moment until it reaches the opposite corner.

The word *vaṣaṭ* is for the purpose of providing an illustration of the previously mentioned *homa* or the *vasordhārā*. It refers to the mantra beginning with "Having commenced, the sacrifice has risen upwards," which is used in the second *āghāra* offering of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
In the case of the animal sacrifice to Vāyu, however, [it is stated]: "He pours the Āghāra-libation with the mantra *hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre*.
At the end of the mantra used for the Āghāra, there is the simultaneous occurrence of the beginning of the ritual act.
And because of the long duration of the stream in the *āghāra* offering.

The Commentary states: Regarding the *āghāra* offering in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture, "He pours the *āghāra* continuously. Even there, the extension of the action together with the mantra is not possible through momentariness.

Because of its unity, there is no continuity of action; therefore, the word "continuity" (saṃtāna) refers to a substance. It is called "continuous" (saṃtata) because it flows continuously—that is, it is maintained by a long stream—due to its state of being a long stream.

Soma: It should not be argued that even though the ritual action (*karman*) is momentary, because the activity has a single result, there is no occurrence of the syntactic connection with the word [denoting the action], since it consists of a sequence of distinct moments; for their simultaneity (*sāhitya*) is established through the possibility of a long duration. Even so, since the parts themselves are numerous, the simultaneity of a very long sequence is likewise established. Viśvarūpa: "In the *āghāra* offering, this mantra is indeed [used]; the stream is continuous. *Agrimah*.

Because there is a single action and because a continuous stream of clarified butter (*ājyadhārā*) is possible, therefore—as in the previous case—there is a conjunction of the beginning of the action with the end of the mantra.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] states: In the passage "He pours the *āghāra* continuously," since there is a single action, the injunction of its interruption is untenable; thus, the concomitance of the mantras is what is enjoined, and consequently, there is a conjunction of the beginning of the action with the end of the mantra.
This being the case, since it is impossible for a momentary action to be accompanied by a mantra composed of many syllables, [the rule applies] to the *āghāra-offering* which has a long stream,
as in the *āghāra-āhuti*.

It is said: This is indeed true; nevertheless, due to the force of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), all these sentences—through the connection of mutual substances and deities—are injunctions of actions qualified by substance and deity. Therefore, the [presence of] substance and deity is not untenable. Consequently, those sentences which the Siddhāntin maintains to be injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the Āghāra and Āgnihotra offerings—all of them consist of words denoting substances and deities connected with one another, and thus they are injunctions of qualified [actions].

And it should not be argued that this being the case, even the two sentences concerning the Āghāra and Āgnihotra would lack injunctive force because they contain words denoting substance and deity, and thus would not be mere restatements (*anuvāda*). For these two sentences are in the form of a statement of present fact (*vartamāna-padeśa*).
Nor is it necessary that they must be injunctions by virtue of being in the fifth mood (*leṭ*), since their status as injunctions is accepted on the grounds of their functional purpose (*kāryatva*).
Furthermore, there is no other quality here—whether corresponding to "upward" and so forth, or corresponding to "curd" and so forth—that could serve as the object of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
This is because it is logically consistent for the name itself to function as the cause for understanding the specific distinction being restated.
Therefore, this is a restatement of two groups of rites prescribed by the sentences concerning "upward" and so forth.
And thus, it is determined by the two mixed sentences concerning the *āghāra* and *agnihotra*.

By means of the word "or" (*vā*), he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— that the purpose of restating the two groups is that the terms *agni*, *āghāra*, and *agnihotra* are merely restatements of those groups and do not enjoin separate rites— and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
“The *agnihotra* statement and the *āghāra* statement are injunctions (*codanā*) that enjoin new rites (*apūrva-karma*), not mere restatements (*anuvāda*).
This is because the meaning of the words *āghārayati* and *juhoti*—which is their referent—has already occurred in usage and its performance has already been established.
The sense is that since the *āghāra* and *homa* offerings are obtained elsewhere [as restatements], they must necessarily be enjoined [here as new acts].”

[Objection: Is it not the case that since [the acts] are already established by the sentences concerning "upward" (*ūrdhva*) and so forth, as well as the sentences concerning "curd" (*dadhi*) and so forth—which enjoin qualified actions—the state of being "not already established" (*aprāptatva*) is unproven? To this, he says: "For the purpose of enjoining qualities"—meaning that the repeated mention of *āghārayati* and *juhoti* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of enjoining qualities such as "upward" and "curd.

[Objection: But how can the suffix (*pratyaya*), setting aside the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) which is proximate, enjoin a quality? To this, he says: "Because of its proximity to that"—that is, because of the proximity of the suffix to that quality through its non-entry into the specific verbal root-meaning; thus says the *Kutūhala*.

“Because of its proximity [to the original injunction], the repeated mention in such passages as ‘He offers the Agnihotra’—namely, the repeated hearing in ‘He offers with curd’ and so forth—is justified as being for the purpose of enjoining a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi),” according to the Kaṣṭavṛtti.
Therefore, the conclusion is that the terms *āghāra* and *agnihotra* denote distinct rituals (*karmāntara*) and are not collective designations (*samudāyaśabda*).
Ke.: The sentence regarding the *āghāra* and *agnihotra* is not a restatement of a collection (*samudāyānuvāda*).
Kau. 2|2|16, p. 206: (However,) by way of the injunction of the *āghāra* [libation], there is an injunction of ritual acts in the sentences concerning the *āghāra* and *agnihotra*.
Bhā. p. 120: *Oṃ*, the section on the *āghāra* and *agnihotra*.
The sentence regarding the *āghāra* and *agnihotra* is an injunction of distinct ritual acts; it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a collective group.
The Āghāra and Agnihotra [are not sacrifices] because they lack a specific form.
The Commentary states: "It is heard in scripture: 'He pours the Āghāra.
Likewise, there are these other [scriptural] statements: 'He pours it upwards,' 'He pours it continuously,' 'He pours it straight.'"

[The opponent argues: "Because [the terms] such as *āghāra* and *ācārya*, as well as *indra ūrdhvo adhvaraḥ* and so forth, are fit for the application of names that are qualified by a deity through the description of a mere substance.
[We reply: No, because the word *āghāra* does not qualify anything beyond the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
In that case, a specific distinction is understood through the name, where names are applied by taking up some particular feature.

Here, however, because the meaning of the constituent parts is present, the word *āghāra*—even without a conventional usage for the whole aggregate—and because it denotes mere pouring (*kṣaraṇa*), refers to a specific [act].
But is it not the case that the [general] injunction is set aside by the context?

Nevertheless, this is well said. For the *āghāra* libation does not belong to the present context; this entire section pertains to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, and there is no room for any other context.

If it is argued that proximity (*saṃnidhi*) establishes a specific connection, this too is well said [as a point to be refuted]; however, it is not so, because the sentence (*vākya*) is stronger, and thus the *āghāra* is connected even to the primary context (*prakṛti*).

Thus, when there is a conflict between the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), if it is accepted that the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) themselves are those connected with the substance and the deity— wherein some slight indication of form (*rūpa-leśa*) exists— and once the rite has been determined in that manner, how could other subsidiary elements (*guṇāntara*) be introduced by any other means? [This refers to] the section concerning the *āghāra* and *agnihotra*.
The meaning "the locus of the Āghāra and Agnihotra" is expressed by the word;
for neither from the word nor from reality is the status of the oblation (*homa*) as a locus established.
Nor is there anything to be accomplished by means of curd, because it is eternally of the nature of an instrument.
Furthermore, this scriptural statement (śruti) is stronger than both types of qualified injunctions, because when a single injunction is possible, it is illogical to assume multiple potencies;
and because, by virtue of its dual character, it can be applied indefinitely even to a remote object.

The adoption of this remote [term, *dadhi*] occurs precisely because the proximate one is impossible; thus, if both were resorted to simultaneously, there would be the fallacy of a "simultaneous conflict" (*vipratiṣiddha*) and the impossibility of [the injunction].
For this very reason, it is understood as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Since it prescribes a qualified object elsewhere, the praise [beginning with "by curd," etc. is not overly burdensome; therefore, it should not be relegated to a subordinate position.

Alternatively, since its status as having a pure meaning has been established, there is no need to perform it elsewhere after the injunction [of the primary act], just as in the case of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth. Because these eight types of *śruti* that have been shown do not depend upon one another, there is no purpose in presenting them in a specific order; however, if they must necessarily be presented in a sequence, then this is the preferable order—this is the meaning.

[He refutes the sixth type, which consists of an injunction regarding the relationship between other factors within the meaning of a verbal root: As for the claim that by the sentence "He gives two mirrors to the Adhvaryu," the relationship between the mirrors and the Adhvaryu is enjoined within the meaning of the verbal root *dadāti* (to give), that is incorrect, because of a failure to distinguish the modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*).
For in all cases, having connected the thing being restated—which is introduced by the word *yat*—with the thing to be enjoined, which is joined with the word *tat*, [the injunction is established].

Thus, in this context, if it were first enjoined that "that which he gives" establishes a relationship between the Adhvaryu and the *prākāśa* vessels, then, because this would be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the entire act of giving, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the injunction applying to the whole of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Furthermore, when an action has already been enjoined, the assumption of multiple injunctive powers for a single suffix is improper;

indeed, a relationship being enjoined necessarily implies its relata, yet the relatum itself must still be enjoined with respect to the meaning of the verbal root. Otherwise, the relatum would be a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) of the relationship itself, rather than of the action.
In this regard, it might be argued that since the suffix, while enjoining [the action], must necessarily enjoin it within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*),
then— given that the two subsequent scriptural passages are also included right here— their separate mention would be useless.

For it is not the case that in the sentences "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetamālabheta*) and "One desiring sense-power should offer curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*), the suffix enjoins the relationship [of the accessory] while being colored by the meaning of the verbal root.

The term *ālabhati* (to touch/kill), when uttered as denoting merely the natural characteristic [of the animal], does not assist in the injunction of the connection between the substance and the deity by permitting its own meaning; nor can that connection between the substance and the deity be accomplished by means of the act of *ālabhati*, because it pertains to the sphere of sacrifice (*yāga*).

If, in the establishment of a connection with another [element], the utterance of the suffix were to achieve its purpose, yet the verbal root (*dhātu*) were to effect something additional, then why would the *homa* be abandoned in the injunctions regarding curd (*dadhi*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and existence (*sattva*), or why would that which is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) be accepted? (By this, the two types of seventh-case [locative] scriptural texts (*śruti*) are also refuted by way of a consequential argument.
Therefore, the injunction of a connection with another pertains to the meaning of the verbal root.
And as before, the fact that the meaning of the verbal root is a factor (*kāraka*) and must be performed (*kartavyatā*) cannot be denied.

Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be an injunction regarding the relationship [between the two] within the meaning of the verbal root, because that relationship has not yet been connected with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
Thus, first of all, there is no injunction of the relationship in the act of giving alone.

Even if the giving were qualified by the [recipient] Adhvaryu, or the Adhvaryu were qualified by the giving, even so, because it would be a restatement of something already qualified, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

In the case of the *śuddhādhvaryu* and others, although the taking [of the gift] is implied by the scriptural mention of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), nevertheless, since the status of the recipient as a deity is untenable without the act of giving (*dadāti*), and since the relationship between the substance and the deity is precisely what is to be enjoined, it is not possible to maintain the verbal formulation that "there is a connection with something else" apart from the meaning of the verbal root.
Furthermore, since the act of giving by the *adhvaryu* is already established here by the *codaka* (extended injunction), it is the *prākāśa* and other such items themselves that must be enjoined.
Consequently, because the injunction of the relationship follows from the sense of the matter, this does not entail a violation of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

And this will be stated in the section on *jāti* (3.1.10): "Where one of the two [relata] is not already established, there alone is there a mutual injunction (*itarētaravidhi*); the connection follows from the sense of the matter. But when both are already established, or when neither is established, there is merely an injunction of the connection. Furthermore, since all three types of scriptural injunctions for connection are equal in terms of their specific suffixes, there is no distinction in their relative strength (*balābala*). Nor is there any possibility of a contradiction in inherence (*samavāya*) where such knowledge would be useful; thus, the presentation of the sequence yields but a meager result.
Therefore, according to the principle of the section concerning the *prastāva*, the reality in every case is simply the injunction of a qualified *bhāvanā*.
It should be understood that everything else has been provided by the Commentator merely as a means for those of dull intellect to grasp the subject at various points.

Furthermore, the discussion regarding proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) should be considered as pertaining to the fact that when the injunctive force resides in the *bhāvanā* itself, the factors of action (*kārakas*) serve as qualifiers of that *bhāvanā*.

But how, then, is an existing *bhāvanā* enjoined? Since it has not been obtained as something qualified (*viśiṣṭā*), it will be enjoined through its identity [with the qualification]; and consequently, it is designated as an injunction of the two qualifiers. [Objection: If this were so, then even in the case of an injunction of a ritual act already established (*prāptakarmavidhi*), an injunctive word would be capable of enjoining multiple things by means of the *bhāvanā*, just like a novel injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). Consequently, the scope of the principle "For when [the act] is enjoined, because it is for that purpose, each [qualifier] would be taught [separately]" (JS 2.1.16) would be undermined.
[Response: This is not a fault.

"Even though the injunctive force resides in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), its subservience to that [purpose] is divided; and since this pertains to the result of the qualification, there will be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) when the injunctive force mounted upon the efficient force is for the sake of the efficient force.
For when the injunctive force is mounted upon the efficient force, it is for the sake of the efficient force.

If the section on the Āghāra and Agnihotra is understood precisely as the section on the Āghāra and Agnihotra, then we shall explain that there is no syntactical split (avākyabheda) when there is an injunction of a qualifier for the purpose and so forth.

But when it is determined that "it is a qualifier of that," then, since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is connected with multiple qualifiers, if its injunctive character (*vidhitva*) is ascertained for the sake of a specific purpose, there will be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), because the injunction would apply to that one [element] alone and not to the other, just as sight does not extend to touch and so forth.
Thus, although the injunctive power resides in the same locus everywhere, it is shown to be, as it were, transferred in effect and concentrated in one place;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
As for the objection that there is the fault of prescribing multiple effects in injunctions such as the *abhyuditeṣṭi* and *kāśādī*, that is equal in all subsidiary rites (*sarvaśeṣa*).
And how it will not be so because of non-existence, we shall explain in that very section [of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra*], stating:
"This might be so, because of being qualified."

If the quality (*guṇa*) were not enjoined directly, then, because the person would not be impelled toward it, one might think that by performing the action while omitting that [quality], one’s purpose would be fulfilled. The question, “What will happen in that case? is posed with a sense of displeasure regarding the nature of the statement. The phrase, “while [the person] is not being impelled,” is an explanation of the author's own intention.
He himself explains the action [of the suffix];
with that very intention, he again provides a question and answer: "the proximity of a word denoting a quality" (*guṇavacanasaṃnidhi*).
Likewise, [he asks] "but how? with the intention of [citing] "and the traditional usage is the same" (*tulyaṃ ca sāṃpradāyikam*, 1.2.18).

"But if the object does not exist, what [is the purpose]?"—it is in this way that [the injunction] becomes purposeless, whereas when the object exists, as in the case of fish, there will be no lack of purpose.

By the statement "In that case," it is said that even though the scriptural injunction (*śrauta*) operates upon a qualified productive energy (*bhāvanā*), it will nonetheless derive from the sentence (*vākya*).
However, if it is enjoined by that [sentence], let that alone be enjoined; thus, when the meaning of the direct audition (*śruti*) is present, there is no meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
Thus he says;
by stating "this is true," he demonstrates the transfer of injunctive power (*vidhiśaktisaṃkrānti*) and [the principle] "if they have not been instructed by another.
"How? is a question accompanied by doubt, or a brief statement.

Therefore, due to its proximity to that [root], because the accessory (*guṇa*) enters into the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), it possesses the status of being something to be enjoined; or else, due to the proximity of the accessory, there is a transfer of the verbal power (*śakti-saṃcaraṇa*), or rather, because of the proximity to the attainment of the root-meaning within the *bhāvanā*, the accessory is enjoined despite the contradiction with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Regarding the word *juhoteḥ*, he says—failing to perceive that even this clear utterance of the root is intended as a restatement of the entire sentence—"If 'juhoti' is a restatement," and "Do not say 'by the word *dadhi*'"; these points should be applied according to the text of the *Vājapeyādhikaraṇa*.

(Sudhā, p. 776—As stated in the *Vājapeyādhikaraṇa* [Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.4.18, p. 339]: "If 'if he should sacrifice' (*yajeta*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), by what means is the accessory (*guṇa*) now enjoined? To provide an answer to this question, it was said: "Do not say 'by the word *vājapeya*'; for a noun-word has no injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) apart from either a verb (*ākhyāta*) or the particle 'should' (*kuryāt*). The meaning here is that the same should be stated in this case as well. [The word *chāyā* means "for the sake of the procedure" (*prakriyārtha*).]

In this regard, some slight variation in the wording is observed in Sudhākara’s paraphrase of the Bhāṣya: "The distinction is that the suffix is the injunction (*vidhi*), while the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

[Regarding the phrase] "if they were both injunctive" (the reading in the Bhāṣya being *vidhāyakau* rather than *vidhāyakam*), the intention is: "Since the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is already established, how can there be an injunction?
[This refers to the statement] "in order to ascertain that which is the sentence-meaning."
The claim that "because curd is the meaning of a word, it cannot possibly be the meaning of a sentence" also refers only to the intention of [the view that] the *bhāvanā* is qualified by the curd.
Therefore, [the sūtra] states: "Hence, there is an injunction for a different ritual act.
This should be explained in the same manner as the *upāṃśuyāja* [sacrifice] (2.1.4).
Furthermore, because the subject matter concerns the common purpose of *juhoti* and *āghārayati*, the establishment of the summary is indeed accomplished.
Here, there is a distinction from being a separate ritual (*karmāntara*) by virtue of its being enjoined;
since the substance and deity will be obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is not a different form.

Nor is it the case that there is no "how-to" (kathaṃbhāva) in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), for it is understood up until its connection with a result. Furthermore, there is no impossibility of enjoining a result for that which has an unmentioned substance and deity; for even after [the originative injunction], that [originative injunction] serves as a reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) for what was enjoined merely as a *homa*. And such an elliptical restatement (*anuvāda*) by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is accepted in cases such as these.
For this [recognition] depends on what has been previously attained; thus, recognition is sought in some way or another.
Nor does the status of the *ādhāra* as a subject matter for the *āghāra-agnihotra* follow merely from its mention in the context of another section.
The sacrificial ladles (hārās) become established as the locus for the Āghāra and Agnihotra offerings.
Furthermore, there is no notion of them being mere parts during the major repetitions of the Jyotiṣṭoma, because in both cases they are perceived as a complete whole.
And thus, as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the repetition of the performance by means of all [the mantras] together is established for both occasions.

Otherwise, however, by the principle of the "remoteness of the animal ritual" (*paśutantraviprakarṣanyāya*), [the procedure] would benefit [the sacrifice] only once performed. [This refers to the case where,] even though there is a difference in time regarding the sequence of obtaining the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) in the *savanīyapaśu* sacrifice, one might suspect that here too there is no repetition because of ignorance; having raised this doubt, the author provides an illustration of the forthcoming distinction: since from the commencement of the action until its completion there is a single time, and since the *savanīyapaśu* constitutes a single ritual act (*aikakarmya*), it is appropriate for the procedure known as the *tantra* to recur despite its remote timing, whereas in the present case [of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*], there is a difference.

(Su. Pṛ. 779) And there is no purpose whatsoever in [the two being] a single action. (He concludes the opponent's view: "Therefore, it is a restatement of the collection of the two. (He refutes the restatement of the collection on the grounds of its lack of purpose, saying: "It is replied: (ucyate).
Su. P. 779) To this it is replied: (The reading "ucyate" [it is said] is found here among the wise. "No fruit whatsoever is seen for the restatement of the aggregate;
however, it shall obtain unity of the injunction of performance, as in the case of the Rājasūya."

For just as there is a restatement of a whole when that whole is characterized by its constituent parts, so too will it be in the case of the application-sentence: "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra.
And just as in the case of "One desiring sovereignty should perform the Rājasūya," the establishment [of the whole] is achieved even without another restatement of the whole, so it is here as well.
But if this were so, then even those oblations which are not otherwise established would have the status of being primary acts.
Or, if this were a restatement of a collective whole, by what means would there be a removal of those [details]?
For no one effects such a delimitation through connection with time—as is done for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth in the cases of the *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* sacrifices—just as it is here.
[Objection: But surely the qualification "the *hotṛ*-offering in this [fire]" will serve that purpose.
No;
for they too have Agni as their deity.
Moreover, if this were the case, an undesirable consequence would follow for you.
Because there is an absence of connection with fire at the morning oblation, it would follow that it lacks the status of being an *agni-hotra* and thus cannot be a subsidiary (*aṅga*).
Therefore, even if there were a restatement of the whole collection (*samudāyānuvāda*), there would be no further qualification.

Likewise, whether there is a distinction between the various oblations of those who maintain the sacred fires, or whether the entire *agni-hotra* itself is performed as a repeated action (*abhyasta-karma*), all of it possesses equal primacy (*sama-pradhānatva*) due to the connection with the result, since the specific factor of connection with fire is present through proximity (*sannidhi*) by means of the word *agni-hotra*.

Likewise, some employ the term *agnihotra* as a common designation for all [the fire-sacrifices] (which makes the application of the word *agnihotra* appropriate by extending its scope to all subjects).

Having prescribed four oblations each for the *gārhapatya* and *ānyāhāryapacana* fires, and two for the *āhavanīya*, the text says: "He who, knowing thus, performs the *agnihotra* perfected as the *virāṭ*.
Therefore, because it serves another purpose, the injunction "he offers the *agnihotra*" is itself the injunction of the ritual action (*karmavidhi*).

Consequently, just as in the case of the sentences concerning rice (*taṇḍula*) and so forth, since the connection with the *gārhapatya* fire and other such elements serves the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), there is no reason for a difference in the ritual action (*karma-bheda*). For we recognize that very same original action in each instance through its re-cognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). But why, given that they refer to a single action, are the fires not treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpyante*) like curd (*dadhi*) and the rest? Some say:
"Because it has an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).
For even a throwing-in (prakṣepa) that is without a substrate is possible even when the substance lacks a stable foundation; thus, the conjunction with fire serves an unseen purpose.
And since all of that unseen [result] is to be postulated, the oblation (homa) is repeated.
But this being the case, even by means of the *pada* and other [mantras], the Āhavanīya fire is not excluded.
Since there is a scriptural injunction for a single offering (*sakṛddhoma*) in that context, the two oblations (*āhutī*) are not accepted;
here too, it is the same, and thus the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) arises.

Therefore, based solely on the statement "he becomes the *dirāṭ*," there is a combination [of the two acts] according to the maxim: "But in the case of those enjoined by a number, there is a combination" (PMS 1.1.2.130).
Otherwise, there would be the attainment of a result not previously established from the fires, characterized by the omission of the *āghāra* libation;
and because the nature of the act is obstructed by one [libation], the occurrence of another *āghāra* is impossible.

Even though the connection with fire has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because of the hearing of the word "all" (*samasta*), it is understood that this [connection] occurs through the realization of the *āghāra* libation; and since that is perceived directly, it is known that in a ritual act performed by one person, no other [such connection] is possible.
Therefore, an absolute option (*vikalpa*) is reached here.
Furthermore, why is there no differentiation of the ritual acts (*karmabheda*) based on number, as in the case of "he offers oblations of sesame seeds" (*tila āhutīr juhoti*) and so forth?
No;

because when there is an addition [of a new action], the number serves to differentiate the ritual acts, as in such cases as "three oblations" (*tisra āhutīḥ*) and so forth. In these instances, the number indeed functions as a differentiator of the originative injunctions (*utpatti-vidhi*).

Furthermore, when this [act] arises in relation to an action that has already been determined—as in the case of "eleven *prayāja*s"—it constitutes a mere repetition (*abhyāsa*) of what was previously established, and thus it is not capable of producing a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*).

Therefore, it is concluded that there is only one act, namely the *sarvābhibhū*, which is repeated. As for the view that there are three distinct acts because the evening and morning injunctions have multiple referents: [this is incorrect].
To this we reply:
In the sentences "He offers in the evening" and "He offers in the morning," two other factors—the time of morning and the state of the deity—are introduced by another sentence.
Now, even so, since there would be a reference to a ritual act qualified by time, there would still be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
No;

because in the case of an action characterized by a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), the deity is enjoined merely with respect to time. However, that time is not connected to the deity in its own essential form; rather, it is connected as qualified by the action belonging to that context.

Alternatively, the time [of evening] finds its application by establishing the masculine agent for the previously mentioned oblation, which is required by the deity who is the constituent of the act being prescribed.
Nor does the oblation, being obtained through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), cause a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
Nor [is there a problem with] the evening—
The section concerning the Āghāra and Agnihotra is characterized by the fact that [the sacrificer] is situated elsewhere at another time.
Therefore, Agni and Prajāpati will be the deities for the evening oblation (sāyaṃhoma);
likewise, it is established that Sūrya and Prajāpati are the deities for the morning oblation (prātarhoma).
But even so, since the two deities are presented by separate words, would they not both have to be enjoined by the sentence?

If it is argued that this is not so because there is a single agent (*ekakāraka*), [we reply: for when there is a plurality of agents, there is indeed a distinction between what is to be enjoined and what is to be accomplished. However, it has been stated that even a thousand purposes, when based upon a single agent, can be accomplished by a single effort.
To this it is replied:
"Just as even a single *kāraka* (participant in an action) may be connected with multiple words, nevertheless, because that [connection] is not repeated, the suffixes are not applied [separately]."

(The meaning of this verse is as follows: By accepting the relationship of qualifier and qualified in the expression ‘*agnaye dātre*’ (*to Agni the giver*), one establishes that the deity is Agni as qualified by the attribute of being Prajāpati. Nevertheless, because multiple factors (*kāraka*) are recited, and because both factors—Agni and Prajāpati—are heard with case-endings (*vibhakti*), their connection to the action is understood prior to the realization of the qualifier-qualified relationship. Consequently, since each factor must necessarily be analyzed separately, there arises the contingency of a prescriptive suffix for each; thus, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) is unavoidable.

In reality, however, since the deity Prajāpati is established independently, there is not even a unity of the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) by way of being a qualifier; thus, the distinction between sentences (*vākyabheda*) is quite firm.
