For it is by means of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that a *kāraka* is conveyed. And where that [ending] is one—as in "agnīṣomau" and so forth—there the operation of cognition occurs in the form of a single entity.

Furthermore, where the *kāraka* consists of multiple words connected by case-endings—as in this very instance, "to Agni and to Prajāpati"—because there is no simultaneous consideration [of both], one employs the suffix for each [deity] individually, namely Agni and Prajāpati. And since that [suffix] is not employed for those [words] that have not been uttered separately, the aforementioned refutation stands. Therefore, this is not a solution; thus it is stated: in both sentences, Prajāpati alone is enjoined as the one seated.

The Agnihotra is obtained from the very wording of the mantra itself; for by another sentence, two mantras for the deities have been enjoined, and since the deities are already obtained through those very [mantras], they are mentioned here for the purpose of praise, as it is appropriate for them to possess the status of Prajāpati immediately.

Furthermore, as for what was indicated by those two statements in the passage "And that [is] another scripture" (*tatprāyaścānyaśāstram*), that too should be understood as having the purpose of obtaining the meaning already established by the wording of the mantra. In this way, there will be no tautology with the injunction of the mantra; otherwise, there would be an unavoidable overlap with one or another of the following: the exclusion of its own meaning (*tadarthāśaṅkāparihāra*), the purpose (*prayojana*), a subsidiary injunction (*guṇavidhi*), an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), or a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*). Therefore, it is established that in that case there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

As for the claim that there is no repetition of the evening and morning *homās* because they constitute a single unitary act, it should be understood that this is not so, because—as in the case of the *Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña* and other such rites—they are known to serve the purpose of all ritual acts.

Now, if this were the case, since the evening and morning times would be equivalent as delimiters of all ritual acts, there would be an option (alternativity), leading to the conclusion that one should perform the *agnihotra* either in the evening or in the morning, but not both.
This is not so.

As long as one lives, by virtue of the injunction to perform the rite throughout one's life, when the evening offering has been made, then for one who continues to live, since the occasion (nimitta) arises again at the time of morning, the occasional rite (naimittika) will take place. This is indeed established even in this way; however, there is this distinction: when the single performance of the Agnihotra is undertaken for both evening and morning, then once the evening offering has been performed, if some misfortune should ever befall the sacrificer, the morning offering must nevertheless be performed somehow or other, in order to avoid the contingency of leaving an already commenced rite unfinished.
But in this case, since the rite is completed at evening time—just like the Jyotiṣṭoma—the morning oblation (prātarhoma) need not necessarily be performed. Furthermore:
"The performance of a desire-based rite, when intended for a specific fruit, must be joined with all its constituent parts."
"In that case, there would be another application [of the rite] by reversing the evening and morning [times].
However, regarding the position that the rite has already been performed, one must ensure its non-deficiency through effort at both times.
But how can there be an option? We reply: because of the combination [of the two times] established by the scriptural injunction."
For he speaks of what is under discussion, saying, "This [sacrifice] is indeed the *pravargya*," and "He offers [the oblation] both in the evening and in the morning.
Furthermore, even in the case of the *medaka* sacrifice, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) because of the word "and" (*ca*).
And when there is a conjunction, there is no occurrence of simultaneity (*sāhitya*), because the time is not something to be enjoined (*anupādeyatvāt*); thus, there is no contradiction.

And since, by means of another statement at dawn, this sentence has the purpose of combining [the two] times, there is no fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, that one fault does not apply. For when a ritual action is enjoined with respect to a time, it possesses the intended connection with its constituent parts (*aṅga*); thus, for the evening primary rite, only those auxiliary parts belonging to that same time are beneficial, not those belonging to other times, because of the resulting deficiency (*vaiguṇya*).
The same applies to the morning [offering] as well; this is understood from the context.
As for the objection that "it has no purpose," it is replied:

in the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*, because of the injunction of a single ritual—"He performs the *Agnihotra* for a month"—and because a single set of procedures (*itikartavyatā*) is required, the properties (*dharma*) of either the evening offering or the morning offering apply. Thus, being possessed of a single set of properties, it is performed only once. However, in the case of non-distinction [between the two], it proceeds according to the original model (*yathāprakṛti*).

Śā: "In that regard, because there is a determination of the qualifier in the full comprehension of form, and because it is to be understood through its commonality, there is no injunction for these two."
This being the position, we reply: there is no restatement (anuvāda) because the actions under discussion are not already established;
for in the sentences concerning curds and so forth, [the action] is not [established] by the potency implied by the substance.

An action can indeed be enjoined by an injunction; however, because its power is not diverted elsewhere, the injunction follows after the action. In this case, since curd and the like are not obtained from any other source, there is no possibility of the sentence enjoining a qualified action—by way of restating an injunction already established by the wording of a mantra—for the purpose of specifying [the material]. Therefore, given that it functions as an injunction, the sentence regarding the Agnihotra and so forth is a restatement (anuvāda) of an injunction for an action qualified by curd and the like; thus, there is consistency with the suffix.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is the performance of the rites enjoined by the sentences concerning curd and so forth in combination (*samuccaya*); whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the substances within a single rite, or their combination.

Likewise, according to the prima facie view, since the sentences for evening and morning—like the sentences for curd and so forth—are injunctions of separate rites, there would be no application of the evening and morning times to the rites enjoined by the sentences for curd and so forth; whereas according to the final conclusion, such application does exist, and so on.

In the *ādhāra* passage, however, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if there is a lapse in the midst of [the sequence] beginning with "after rising" and ending with "continuously," there must be a re-performance of that ritual action characterized by those specific qualities; whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since there is no difference in the ritual action itself, one should perform it having sipped water (*ācāntena*). In this regard, the Smṛti rule stating "it should be performed by one who has sipped water" (*ācāre ācāntena kartavyam*) is authoritative because it is not contradicted by Śruti.

Bhāṣya 1.3.15–7: Customary practice (*ācāra*) is sublated by a Vedic *arthavāda* indicative mark (*liṅga*), as in the section on *yava* and *varāha* (1.3.18–9). In the case of the statement, "When other plants wither, these stand up as if rejoicing," the customary usage of the word *yava* for *priyaṅgu* (panic seed) is sublated by this *arthavāda* indicative mark.
Bāla. p. 138. Customary practice is sublated by *smṛti*;
this is because [custom] lacks authoritative status.
Vārttika 3.3.74, p. 860: For those residing in Āryāvarta, the conduct of inhabitants of other regions is more excellent than that of the Mlecchas.

Bhāṣya 1.3.2, p. 581: Certain practices, when performed by some and being praised by others, attain the status of human duties (*puruṣadharma*), such as "one should not converse with a woman in her menses" or "therefore, one should not offer a weapon to a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth.
Vārttika 1.3.12, p. 164: Regarding conduct: "But certain [practices] accepted as dharma by the learned..."
Because of the commonality of the agent, their status as dharma is accepted by those who follow the Veda.
Gifts, recitations, and burnt offerings; the states beginning with that of the Mothers (mātṛśadā);
the great festival of Indra’s banner and processions at the temples of the deities;
and fasts on the fourth lunar day for all young girls.
The offerings of lamps, consecrated seats, sweetmeats, cakes, and milk-rice.

Regarding the observance of rules for the Anagnika, the Māgha-saptamī, the full moon of Māgha, the first day of Phālguna, the Prasanna festival, and so forth, there is no authority whatsoever other than the scriptures. Furthermore, the authors of the Smṛtis generally accept the authority of practices not opposed to the Vedas, stating: "The conduct of the virtuous, as well as the customs of regions, castes, and families, when they are not in conflict with the sacred traditions (Āmnāyas), are authoritative. Likewise, in the section concerning days unfit for study (anadhyāya), it is said: "After the [spring] festival, there is celebration," thereby relying on the authority of regional festivals.

And in the Veda, in the context of the Mahāvrata sacrifice, this is heard as a supplementary statement in the passage: "Having mounted the swing (preṅkha), the Hotṛ priest recites"; [it continues] "when indeed the people enter into the Great Festival (mahaḥ), then they mount the swing. The well-known meaning of *mahaḥ* as a festival is not explicitly stated [in the commentary]. (Vākyapadīya 1.3.17, p. 206).

*Sudhā-śakradhvajamahaḥ* refers to the festival of Indra’s banner (*śakradhvajotsava*). In the reading *mahā*, it is a locative compound meaning "the great procession at Indra’s banner" (*śakradhvaje mahāyātrā*). In the phrase "in the temples of the deities," the term "great procession" (*mahāyātrā*) is to be supplied as a connective word (*anuṣaṅga*).
The offering of lamps on the first day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika is prescribed.
By the mention of "sweetmeats and so forth" on the fourth day, acts such as giving and eating those items are indicated.
On the seventh day and the full moon of Māgha, the ritual to be performed at that specific time is indicated.
On the first day (*pratipad*) following the full moon of the month of Phālguna, there is a festival for the sake of spring (p.
187). Regarding customary practices (*ācāra*):

as for those things which are considered barbarian (*mleccha*), such as agriculture, service, trade, and so forth—which involve fixed and unfixed activities; and those well-known things such as drinking clay-water, using soft beds and seats, wearing jewels and the like, indulgence in desire and laziness, singing, dancing, perfumes, flowers, and so on—in these there is no appearance whatsoever of being Dharma. Therefore, it is not possible to exclude other [practices] by analogy with them.
Furthermore, because some [of these practices] have attained the status of *dharma* through scriptural authority, the community [of the learned] does not consist of all of them indiscriminately.
Rather, regarding those such as the worship of gods and Brahmins,
for which the status of *dharma* is indeed accepted, that is considered to be based on the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

For in the world, some conduct is distinguished as being "refined" (*śiṣṭa*), while other conduct is common to all living beings and is practiced even by them. Among these, that which follows only the refined in its practical form—
That alone is the true dharma, and not any other practice belonging to mere living beings. (Vārttika 1.3.17, p.
206). Those practices whose purposes are visible are authoritative precisely because of that.
"But as for those [practices] whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is an inference of Vedic words regarding them" (Bhāṣya 1.3.12, pp. 166, 168). These are the practices (*ācāra*).

Even when they have diverged, those accepted by the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) are authoritative—such as the fivefold divergence in the south: eating with one who has not been initiated, eating with one's wife, eating stale food, eating the leavings of another, and marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle or a paternal aunt.

Likewise, to the north, there are five [practices]: the fame of [the practice of] *ūrdhvakīrti*, the drinking of *sīdhu* liquor, trade in both types of shells (*dadrivya*), the profession of arms, and sea-voyaging. Having thus cited these practices which contradict the *Smṛti*—such as the taking of interest on loans and so forth—as being permitted by Baudhāyana, Āpastamba has rejected the regional authority established by the principle "one [practice is valid] in one place and another in another," stating that "it is corrupted" (as Gautama says). However, he has rightly concluded: "But both of these [regional practices] are disregarded because they conflict with the *Smṛti* of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). (Su. p. 179)
(Regarding "both-sided": the term *ubhayatodan* refers to those animals whose teeth exist on both the lower jaw and the upper jaw—namely, horses, mules, and donkeys;
transactions involving these are called *ubhayatodan-vyavahāra*).

Regarding custom (*ācāra*), a custom for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is sublated by a custom for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), just as, for example, a certain visible-purpose custom occurring at the same time as the spring festival is sublated by that spring-festival custom which serves an invisible purpose.

Bāla, p. 139: A practice that is censured (vigīta) is sublated by a practice that is accepted (adhigīta). For example, the practice of eating meat—which is censured because it is rooted in greed and other such motives—is sublated by the accepted practice of abstaining from meat, which cannot possibly be rooted in greed and the like. Bāla, p. 139: Among those things being inferred from practice, [there is] the "practice-based" (ācārakalpya) [Smṛti], [numbering] 833.
A usage that is not based on linguistic convention (*anāmnāyācāra*) is sublated by a usage that is based on linguistic convention (*āmnāyācāra*).

For example, there is a sublation of the usage consisting of the application of the word *pīlu* to elephants—which is a usage among the Mlecchas—by the usage consisting of the application of the word *pīlu* to trees, which is a usage [based on] linguistic convention.
This was stated in the *Pīlu-adhikaraṇa* (Vārtika on 1.3.18, second exposition, pp. 219–220).

"Oṃ. The substitute for the clarified butter (ājya) should consist of the same number [of oblations] because of the relinquishment of the substance.
It is heard in the scripture: 'He relinquishes that which has been circumambulated by fire as being for drinking,' and 'He completes the remainder with clarified butter.

In the inquiry as to whether this clarified butter is a substitute for the previous [substance], or whether a different ritual action involving the substance of clarified butter is enjoined, he states the prima facie view."

The *ājyasaṃsthā*—this completion or conclusion which has been described as being performed with clarified butter (*ājya*)—should serve as a substitute for the *pālīvata* animal sacrifice. Just as wild rice (*nīvāra*) is a substitute for *vrīhi* rice, so it is here. Why? Because of the relinquishment of the substance; for by the scriptural statement, "He relinquishes the *pālīvata*," there is a relinquishing of the substance in the form of an animal.
And in the absence of the primary substance, a substitute must be accepted.
Therefore, the *ājyasaṃsthā* is the substitute;
this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*),
because of the statement regarding completion.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states another reason: "He releases the animal that has been circumambulated by fire (*paryagnikṛta*)," and "He completes the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*). Here, the word "completes" (*saṃsthāpayati*) signifies completion.
From this statement of completion, it is understood that there must also have been an undertaking (*ārambha*).
Thus, from the understanding that the very rite which was undertaken is completed by means of clarified butter, we conclude that clarified butter serves as a substitute (*pratinidhi*).
Or rather, it is an injunction (codanā) because it is distinguished from other [acts] by the relinquishing of the ritual action;
thus, refuting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he states the established conclusion (siddhānta):
this must be an injunction for another ritual action, namely, "He completes the remainder of the Pālīvata [offering] with clarified butter."

Because of the abandonment of the previous rite— that is, because it is completed by that abandonment— and because it is not distinguished from, but is similar to, other rites enjoining different actions such as the *nirvapaṇa* (offering), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the number of clarified butter offerings (*ājya*) is not a substitute (*pratinidhi*), but rather a separate rite (*karmāntara*). Furthermore, he demonstrates this through the well-known non-performance of the *vanaspati* offering.
In the Siddhānta (the final conclusion), he states another argument for the view that the *saṃsthāpana* (concluding rite) with clarified butter (*ājya*) is a separate ritual act:

[he points to] the well-known absence of a sacrifice to Vanaspati—that is, the established non-existence of a Vanaspati sacrifice. By this, he demonstrates through the scriptural statement: "When you invoke both Tvaṣṭṛ and Vanaspati, or when you are about to sacrifice to these two, then the ninth *prayāja* sacrifice is for Tvaṣṭṛ, and the tenth is for Vanaspati. If the previous ritual were already completed, then there would have to be a sacrifice to Vanaspati [at that point].
In that case, the perception of non-existence is established.
Therefore, the concluding rite with clarified butter (*ājya*) is a separate ritual act and not a substitute;
this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The completion [of the sacrifice] would result from that very cause.

As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that the expression "he completes" (*saṃsthāpayati*) is not applicable when [the action] has not yet commenced (9.4.14–15)—the proponent of the established conclusion refutes that:
this mention of "completion" refers to the state of non-completion.
The previous rite was dedicated to Pātivata; this one also belongs to Pātivata alone.

Because it has that same deity—meaning that which has that very deity as its presiding divinity—or because that very deity of the previous rite is the deity of this other rite, it possesses "that-deity-status" (*tadevatva*).
Since the accompaniment of the completion of the previous rite is observed here, the word *saṃsthā* (completion) is appropriate on account of this association. Thus, one says, "he completes [it]."
Because it is that very same [rite], it should be a *saṃsthā* (conclusion).
Therefore, it is established that the *ājyasaṃsthā* is a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*) and not a substitute for the *pālīvata*.
Ke.

Oṃ. Section on the Bringing Together of the Clarified Butter (Ājya-samānayanādhikaraṇa). In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the bringing together of the clarified butter from the Upabhṛt vessel for the sake of the Prayāja offerings is the motivator (prayojaka) [of that action].
But the pouring together [of the butter] must be primary, because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The Bhāṣya states: regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "Having passed over the *iḍā*, he pours together [the butter] toward the *barhis*.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the pouring together...
Is this the instigator of the properties of the clarified butter (ājya), or is it not? What is the prima facie view? That it is not the instigator.
Why? Because this is a portion of the clarified butter intended for the Prayājas and Anuyājas that is brought forward; thus, by the previous reasoning, its status as a non-instigator is established.
This is stated:
the primary act is the pouring together [of the butter], because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
What is the indicative mark? "The clarified butters are taken four times; for here one is not about to perform the after-offerings (anuyāja)," so it is heard in the Āditya [Brāhmaṇa].
If the pouring together [of the butter] is for the sake of the *prayāja*s, then one *caturgṛhīta* portion is poured together there, and one also remains for the *anuyāja*s.

Consequently, the statement "the Ādityas conclude with the *iḍā*" applies in the absence of the *anuyāja*s. Therefore, one *caturgṛhīta* portion should be taken in the *upabhṛt* ladle for the purpose of pouring together, but not for the purpose of the *anuyāja*s.
In that case, the observation of "many" fourfold portions is appropriate; otherwise, in the absence of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), no fourfold portion would be taken in the *upabhṛt* ladle.
Consequently, the plural number in the expression "fourfold portions" (*caturgṛhītāni*) would not be justified.
Therefore, the bringing together [of the butter] is the motive.
Now, one might ask: when the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been taught, what is the resulting application? It is said: the purpose there is observed.
In the two *prayāja* offerings, there is a need for clarified butter (*ājya*) in the *juhū* ladle, but not in the empty *upabhṛt*.
The emptying of the *upabhṛt* serves an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), whereas placing it into the *juhū* serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) alone.
Therefore, the bringing together of the clarified butter (*ājya-samānayana*) for the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings employs the clarified butter contained in the *aupabhṛta* ladle.
For that [butter] is indeed intended for both the *prayājas* and the *anuyājas*, as will be stated later.

[Objection: "The bringing together is not a motivator (*aprayojaka*), because this portion of the butter intended for the *prayājas* and *anuyājas* is being brought together; thus, by the previous principle, there is no motivating force. This is the point expressed in this passage.
If this substance which is brought forward is for the sake of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, then the *prayājas* certainly employ their own substance;

how, then, could there be a lack of causal efficiency (*aprayojakatā*)? Therefore, the latter statement [asserting] a lack of causal efficiency is not consistent with the former [injunction regarding the purpose of the *prayājas*]; thus, it is untenable.

In this regard, some have interpreted the text by omitting the word *prayāja*, asserting that "this portion of what is for the *anuyāja*s is brought together. Others have interpreted the text by taking the word *prayāja* in the locative case (*prayāje*) and analyzing it [as a locative absolute], asserting that "in the *prayāja*, this portion of what is for the *anuyāja*s is brought together. Still others have formulated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) here based on the preceding [section], namely the subsequent section which states: "When he takes [the butter] in the *upabhṛt*, he takes it for the *anuyāja*s," thereby maintaining that the butter in the *upabhṛt* is taken solely for the sake of the *anuyāja*s.

All three of these views are untenable. For those [who hold the first view], the single textual passage [the word *prayāja*] is abandoned; that itself is their fault. For others [who hold the second view], an impossible substratum for the *prayājas* is specified [since it is not possible for the *prayājas*, which are actions, to have clarified butter (*ājya*) as their substrate]. And for yet others [the proponents of the third position], there is the same abandonment of the textual passage; furthermore, this is another fault: "by means of what is unestablished, that which is unestablished is sought to be proven."

Therefore, it is described differently in accordance with the subsequent text (*tasmād uttaragranthānurodhena*; however, the reading *tasmād arthagranthānurodhena* is found in printed editions other than the Ānandāśrama edition).
There are two fourfold-drawn portions (*caturgṛhīta*) in the *upabhṛt* ladle for the sake of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.
This is a compound [meaning]: "He takes that [clarified butter] for the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s."

In that case, no case-ending is heard to express the *prayāja*s; however, there must be one. Therefore (meaning "for that reason"), whatever case-ending occurs in the subsequent word should be understood as applying by *tantra* (simultaneously) to both nominal stems, because that [ending] is what is actually heard in the text.

But if another [form, namely] the dual form (*dvivacanarūpā*) were brought in as the base for the *prayāja*s, there would be the abandonment of what is heard in the text and the assumption of what is not heard.

Therefore, by the force of the plural number in "to the *prayāja*s" (*prayājebhyaḥ*), the butter from the *aupabhṛta* vessel belongs to all the *prayāja*s, and likewise that from the *jauhava* vessel.
The intention is that, because of the specific injunction "to the Prayājas," both [the general and the specific] will apply as an option.

What follows from that? To this he says: because of the statement, "He pours [the butter] into the *juhū*," at the very time when he offers the *prayāja* oblations, he brings into the *juhū* that which was in the *aupabhṛta* for the sake of the *prayājas* (for otherwise it could not be offered in that manner). This being the case, with regard to the requirement of its origin, that substance which had been taken in the *aupabhṛta* for both the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* is, at this time, "brought back across [the altar], overstepping the *iḍā*, toward the *barhis*."

Since, at the very beginning (at the commencement of the *prayāja*s), the substance intended for the *prayāja*s has already been brought together, it is not considered [to serve] both purposes; thus, it remains now solely for the purpose of the *anuyāja*s. Therefore, that which is being brought together is ineffective because it belongs to another (i.e., is intended for the *anuyāja*s), and its purpose is merely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*).

And the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: the rule regarding time is enjoined by the text, "He pours what is in the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū* after passing over the *iḍā* and the *barhis*," [meaning] at this specific time (and not at the commencement of all the *prayāja*s). Therefore, the *jauhava* butter belongs to three *prayāja*s, while the *aupabhṛta* butter is poured into the *juhū* after passing over the *iḍā* and the *barhis* for the sake of the remaining two. Even though they serve the same purpose, there is no option (*vikalpa*), because their spheres of application are distinct.
Furthermore, even in the case of the compound, the *aupabhṛta* [butter] for the two [remaining *prayāja*s] is obtained through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because it is contrary to the context, the heard case-ending is not accepted; rather, the dual number is supplied as "by the two *prayājya*s.
Therefore, it is the motivator (*prayojaka*), for the causal capacity resides in the verbal expression itself.

The commentary states: Now, why is this statement not [accepted], namely that "they are four-fold portions"? It is replied: For if it were stated, it would be supported by a reason, namely: "because one is not about to perform the after-offerings."
When it is understood that the act of bringing [the butter] together is not for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, then there is the explicit statement.
When there is the explicit statement, then the absence of the *anuyāja* offerings is not the reason.
If the reason were absent, the explanatory formula (*hetuvannigada*)—"for he does not perform the *anuyāja* offerings"—would be inappropriate.

Therefore, the act of pouring together for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the clarified butter (*ājya*) contained in the *aupabhṛta* ladle. What is the practical consequence?
When there is a pouring together for the sake of the *prayāja*, one should pour together the entire amount of the *aupabhṛta* butter, as much as is required for the *prayāja*.
If there were no functional purpose, there would not necessarily be as much [application] to the object as there is.
The Śāstra says: "Indeed, everything is for the sake of the *prayāja* because of the lack of distinction and the abundance of scriptural evidence;
since it is equal in that regard, now this [objection] based on direct audition (*śruti*) does not apply."
And because there is clarified butter (*ājya*) remaining from the *upaghāta* [offering], the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* is clearly evident.

Therefore, since there is clarified butter remaining from the *dhruvā* vessel after the *upaghāta*, there should also be an assignment for the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the clarified butter used for the *upāṃśuyāja*.
[Objection: This would not be so, because there is no remainder; it is "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*) because everything has been offered.
Having refuted the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached through the application of the Sūtra by means of the word "but" (*tu*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

In this way, there would be no taking of the remnant of the *upāṃśuyāja* for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. This is because it is "without remnant" (*aśeṣatvāt*); that is, because of the absence of any remnant of the clarified butter belonging to the *upāṃśuyāja*.
That state of being without remainder and being devoid of remainder results from giving everything.
For the clarified butter measured in four portions is for the sake of the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice;
and all of that is indeed placed [on the fire] at the very time of the offering.
And thus, because everything is taken, there is no remnant of it.
Although there is a remnant of clarified butter (*ājya*) from the *dhruvā* vessel, even so, that is not for the sake of the *upāṃśuyāja*; rather, it serves another purpose.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the rest are not to be performed from the clarified butter belonging to the *upāṃśuyāja*.
The [procedure] for the *dhruvā* [offering] should be performed with the two common [elements].
It has been stated that there is an absence of the remainder;
thus, in the case of the three-potsherd offering to Viṣṇu within the Rājasūya, one does not extend the properties of the nine-potsherd [offering].
There is no other relationship of cause and effect between primordial nature and its transformations. (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14)
The sacrificial grass (barhis) used for the Ātithya, Upasad, Agniṣomīya, and Sūta rites is one and the same.
Because the action [of the sacrificial grass] belongs to the injunction, there should be an extension of the injunction to the interval.
The Bhāṣya states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which is for the *ātithyā* is for the *upasads*, and that is for the *agnīṣomīya*.

Therein arises the doubt: Is this an instruction regarding the substance belonging to another, or is it "nirikṣaṇa" (that whose intended goal is directed toward or produced; i.e., the sacrificial grass used once in the ritual), or is it [the grass] qualified by its ritual properties (*dharma*), or is the sacrificial grass common to all?

What is obtained? The instruction regarding another's property. Why? Because this word "that" [in the phrase] "what is for the *ātithyā*, that is for the *upasad*s" functions as an instruction regarding another's property.
It is just as when one says, "The cow which belongs to Devadatta must be made [belong] to Viṣṇumitra"; [thereby] it is taken away from Devadatta and given to Viṣṇumitra.
Therefore, it is said that there is instruction regarding another's property;
yet this is not the case, for he is thus.

The principle of the sprinkling of the *ātithyā* sacrificial grass (*ātithyābarhiḥprokṣaṇanyāya*). By the principle of the sprinkling of the *ātithyā* sacrificial grass, the extension [of the ritual] is based on a direct scriptural injunction. Thus ends the third [section].
On this view, there is no single performance (*kṛtyaikya*) even for the three [rites].

However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since there is no evidence for a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of ritual properties (*dharma*) in the word *barhis*, there is an injunction of the cutting down (*nyakkya*) for all three.

Consequently, the *barhis* grass that is being omitted at the commencement of the *ātithya* rite is common to the triad; therefore, the ritual properties performed therein are also common to all, with the exception of those pertaining to the disposal (*pratipatti*).

Nor is there a lack of evidence for the *aśvavāla* grass and other such items serving the purpose of others (the three sacrifices), even though they provide assistance by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), because in the context of those items, there is the risk that they would result in serving only that [single] purpose. This is because the sentences concerning the *aśvavāla* grass and so on, by virtue of being restricted by this very sentence, have as their objective precisely that which serves as the means for the threefold transcendental result (*apūrva*). And here, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the delimiter of the objective is simply this triad; therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). By the word "barhis" (sacrificial grass), the identity with that [triad] is enjoined through secondary indication.

If it is argued that there is no difference [between this view] and the position of *dharmātideśa* (extension of properties) since the necessity of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is the same, [we reply: there is a distinction because of the *jahatsvārthā-lakṣaṇā* (indication where the primary meaning is abandoned). Since the properties of the *āśvavāla* grass and so forth belong to the *upasada* rite, and the *ātman* connected with the fruit is taken as the subject of the sentence—whether through the context (*prakaraṇa*) or through extension (*atideśa*)—even though its specific nature is being grasped, the application of the number three (*tritva*) to the *barhis* grass is justified because the threefold number is prescribed for it; thus, it is understood that even the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) performed upon it are governed by the number three. Therefore, let it be that the *tantra* (common procedure) applies everywhere.
And the connection of this chapter is incidental, arising merely from the absence [of a specific subject].

Furthermore, even the purificatory rites for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) possess a common ritual procedure (*tantratva*) through their connection with the performance of the duties of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice by means of this very knowledge.

As for the disposal of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), it serves exclusively the purpose of the *agnīṣomīya*, because the other two [offerings] are independent sacrifices (*khaṇḍeṣṭi*) and the disposal is prescribed within that context.

And this is logical: when there arises an inquiry regarding the specific effect to be produced by a manifestation (*vyakti*) of a refinement (*saṃskāra*), since the fact that the object of refinement possesses an effect produced by that manifestation presents itself immediately, it is appropriate for that [manifestation] to be the result. There is no evidence for postulating that it serves merely as a subordinate benefit (*atithyāmātropakāraka*)—which would present itself only after a delay due to occurring within a single ritual performance (*ekaprayogavṛttitva*).

For this very reason, in cases such as the *nāśīṣṭa* or *āgama*, where the *kūṭa* (the sacrificial vessel) is established as the result, since the occurrence within a single performance serves to present the effect during the process of establishing another means of presentation, only that which is presented by it is the result.
Maṇḍana: "The sprinkling and other rites do not apply to the sacrificial grasses (*barhis*).
Śaṅkara: "Those two [rites] do not apply to the *barhis*;
even that which is extended by analogy (*ātideśika*) is set aside by the force of the purpose."
Or [the third case]:

when there is the contingency of an extended (ātideśika) element being fulfilled by another extended element, as for example, the *prayāja* and other offerings intended for the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) being fulfilled by the *prayāja* and others belonging to the animal sacrifice (*paśvayajña*). Bāla. p. 132. Or, when there is the contingency of an original (aupadeśika) element being fulfilled by an extended one, as for example: "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one [verses]. In this optional (*kāmya*) additional recitation, since the purpose of the original *sāmidhenī* verses—the kindling of the fire—is accomplished through the extended *sāmidhenīs* prescribed for the obligatory (*nitya*) recitation, those [original] verses are set aside (*bādha*).

Page 133: An instance where that which is extended by analogy (*ātideśika*) takes over the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of that which is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) is as follows: when the *Śyena* sacrifice is extended [to the *Vaiśvānara* sacrifice], the designation *Audgātra* (pertaining to the Udgātṛ priest) applies because it is obtained through the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) as being a part of the *Adakabalī* [rite]. This is an instance of "taking over" (*prasaṅga*), wherein the task is accomplished [by the former]. Page 110: That which is extended by analogy (*ātideśika*) regarding the time of performance is sublated by that which is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) regarding the time, because of its direct status. Therefore, in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices and the *Sakamedha* offerings, there is only the state of being performed on the same day (*sadyaskālatva*).
*Somaprayoga* 5.1.11: The textual order (*pāṭhakrama*) that is extended by analogy is stronger than the principal order (*mukhyakrama*) that is directly enjoined.

Bhāṣya 5.1.17–18: Only when there is a conflict with the scriptural text (pāṭha) based on extended application (atideśika) does the order of principal elements (mukhyakrama) and the like possess weakness.
Bhaṭṭa 5.1.10: The self alone is the substratum of the apūrva.

Moreover, even though this [self] is devoid of actions such as moving, there is no valid objection regarding its lack of activity, because it is admitted that through a mere connection with an agent, it is also connected with actions such as reaching another location.
"The self alone is the substratum of that [apūrva], and action also resides here;
for in the doctrine of the self, this agency is established in all ritual acts."

"For it has been determined that for all [actions], such as the cutting of the portions and the casting [of oblations], the Self alone is the agent by way of volition and so forth" (Vākyapadīya 2.1.15, p. 397). "The injunction 'the Self is to be known' is not prescribed for the sake of liberation;
rather, the knowledge of the Self is observed to be a cause for engagement in ritual action."

Ślokavārttika 103: "And when its subservience [to another] is known, even that which is called a 'declaration of fruit' (phalaśruti) must be merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda); it is not a separate fruit such as heaven and the like."

Ratnākara [states]: The function of discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) regarding the otherworldly fruits such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth is the purpose of Vedic study. If, by being the cause for engaging in ritual action, it were intended for the sake of the category of karmic fruits, then the mention of fruit in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) would be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), according to the logic of the *parṇamayī* [passage], and would not be sufficient to indicate any further fruit; thus [he says] "in the unknown and the known."

Let it be that knowledge consists of worship; however, since no visible purpose is observed in either the ritual action or the person [with respect to such knowledge], and because there is an absence of scriptural authority (śruti) and so forth for any dependence on unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), it cannot be for the sake of the sacrifice (ṛtvartha). Rather, as will be stated in the section concerning grammar (vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa), its status as being for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha) alone is established by virtue of the fruits of worldly prosperity and the highest good (abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa) brought forward by the supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣa). Furthermore, the Self is not atomic.
For if it were postulated to be atomic, it would not pervade this body.
Consequently, there would be no possibility of pleasure, pain, and so forth, occurring in all parts of the body.

For when the self is of the size of an atom, then it can only preside over that specific portion [of the body] which it occupies; thus, one would perceive only those pleasures, pains, and so on located within that specific portion. Consequently, the simultaneous experience of pain in the head and the feet at a single moment would not occur. (Vākyapadīya 2.1.2.15, p. 402). The Self.
For in the original context, such as "The sacrificer takes hold of the *śukra*," it is the individual soul (*jīvātman*) alone who is designated by the word "sacrificer" as the agent of the sacrifice.
The body, however, possesses only the status of a delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*), not agency itself.
And the agency of the self consists precisely in its being the substratum for the action of taking hold (*anvārambhaṇa*).

Furthermore, such agency is not possible for one who is dead; for the cause of the production of action in the self occurs only through the limitation of a living body. (Bhāṭṭa 10.1.19). The self is distinct in each body.
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 2.1.2, page 403: The self is desired by everyone as that which is connected with the fruit; therefore, action must be performed for its sake.
Furthermore, the self is designated by the name "intellect" (buddhi), yet it is distinct from the body and other such things. 889. The distinction of the self from the body and so forth.
Bhāṣya 6.2.13:
The Self. Even the name "intellect" [does not apply] to the Person, because his essential nature is consciousness. Not [so].
"Here, eternality and unity [belong to consciousness], while differentiation is based on its objects.
(And because it is innate to the person, consciousness, the power of cognition, is eternal and one. Ślokavārttika, Śabdādhikaraṇa, verse 404.
"In the same way, like a crystal that receives a reflection, persons possess eternal consciousness despite being associated with two bodies."
The senses grasp forms and other objects presented to them...
[In passages such as] "Indeed, the Self, my dear, is to be seen," meditation—which has "worship" (*upāsanā*) as its synonym—is what is enjoined.
*Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 25. The Jaina position that the Self is limited by the body is untenable.
Or [as stated in] Vākyapadīya 2.1.2.5, page 402: "The Self is all-pervading.
Motion is not possible in the Self;
for since there is no location to be occupied or vacated by that which is all-pervading, it lacks the capacity to move."

2|1|2|5, p. 400. Since the atomicity of the mind (*manas*) of the *sulleccha* and others is established by scripture, the Self (*ātman*) is of the nature of knowledge devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa-jñāna-svarūpa*).
Furthermore, the Vedāntins maintain that the means to liberation is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) produced by the Upaniṣads, which is itself devoid of any instrumental cause (*niṣkāraka*).
Māṇi. 54: "Just as the conscious [selves] within the body composed of the great elements..."
They intend to express some meaning and do not intend to express another;
yet that internal desire of theirs is known by those who investigate the meaning of their speech through the power of the words themselves, as if it were manifesting externally.
Vārttika 1.1.13, p. 702: Because it is impossible for one who intends [to give] a substance to oneself to relinquish ownership of that substance.
Parākrama 3.1:
An establishment of the distinction between the self and the body and so forth.
Now, the distinctness, multiplicity, and establishment of the self as the grasper (the subject) in contrast to the body, senses, mind, vital breaths, and intellect are being demonstrated.
Regarding this, first of all, those who touch external objects declare that the body alone is the self;
for in this way, the identity of the body and the self is understood through direct perception itself.

That the self is the knower is beyond dispute for all theorists. In this regard, it is the body alone that is perceived as the knower in the cognition "I know. Furthermore, the referent of the "I-notion" (ahaṃkāra) is non-different [from the body], because the "I-notion" is perceived as being in grammatical apposition with the body characterized by bulkiness and so forth, as in: "I am fat," "I am thin," "I go," and "I stand."
If it is argued that this application is figurative (lākṣaṇika) and therefore does not have the body as its objective support (ālambana), we say no;
for in all cases, a figurative application is preceded by a primary (mukhya) one.
And here, no other primary referent is perceived apart from the body.

Objection: Since the body is endowed with many parts such as hands and feet (Mīmāṃsākośa 112), if the "I" appearing in the scriptures were to have that [body] as its objective support, then there would also have to be an appearance of its various parts, forms, and so forth, because it is an appearance of the body; yet this is not observed.
Therefore, the notion of "I" does not have the body and such as its cause.
It is true that there is a continuity with the appearance of parts, forms, and so forth, since such [appearances] are observed in external objects like jars perceived by the sense organs.
And this is a mental cognition (*mānasa-pratyaya*).
However, because the faculty of the mind is restricted in its capacity to grasp only internal qualities, there is no such appearance [of external parts and forms] in that case.

Furthermore, even in the case of perception by the external senses, this rule does not hold; for when there is the apprehension of a whole composed of many parts, there is no apprehension of the individual parts.
Likewise, in the cognition of air by the sense of touch, the cognition occurs solely through the locus of the tactile quality, and there is no concomitant manifestation of its parts.

Even for you, although the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) has as its object something distinct from the body, the concomitant manifestation of its qualities—such as pleasure and other attributes—is exactly the same.
Furthermore, since consciousness is perceived only in the body and is not perceived elsewhere, consciousness must be a quality of the body itself.
If it is argued that, because consciousness is unique to the body, it follows that it is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa), then it would also follow that it is preceded by the qualities of its causes.

If that were the case, then consciousness would necessarily exist in each of the constituent parts that compose the body, leading to the absurd conclusion that a single body would possess thousands of distinct consciousnesses.
And this is neither observed nor accepted.
Therefore, consciousness is not a quality of the body.
[Objection: It is not so; consciousness is indeed a quality of the body, because it is perceived only there.

Although it is not possible for [pleasure] to possess the quality of being a specific quality preceded by the qualities of its cause, nevertheless, its status as a quality of the body cannot be refuted.
Nor can its status as a quality of the body be denied by such inferences as "because it does not persist as long as the body exists," for their objects are sublated by perception.
Furthermore, if its status as a specific quality were denied, it would follow that one must admit it to be a quality of the body.

Even if consciousness does not exist in the constituent parts of the body, its perception in the body is not untenable, just as red dye—though absent in the individual components such as the areca nut and betel leaf—is observed in the resulting product due to a specific conjunction of the constituent parts.

Furthermore, it is observed that even a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) can sometimes arise without being preceded by [the same quality] in its cause; for example, when a cloth is produced from various threads of white, black, and other colors, variegation (citratva) is seen in the cloth even though it does not exist in each of the constituent parts individually.

If variegated color (*citratva*) is not admitted as the color of the whole (*avayavin*), then, because the whole would be devoid of color (*nīrūpa*), it would follow that it lacks any defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇaprasaṅga*). Furthermore, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) because even a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) such as the hardness of ice is seen to be preceded by qualities that are not its own causes. Moreover, the fact that the activity producing desire and so forth has the sense organs as its locus (*indriyāśrayatva*)—which is observed in the body—is what distinguishes the body from insentient things like a *vaṭa* tree; thus, the body itself must be sentient.
The distinction of the self from the body and so forth is understood [from scripture].

Now, if it is your view that because insentience is observed in the aggregates of other elements, consciousness is not possible even in the body, then this position is common to both of us; for since consciousness is not perceived in substances such as earth and the rest, it would likewise not be possible in a self distinct from them simply by virtue of its being a substance.
The observation of distinction expressed in such phrases as "my body" is also to be resolved by the fact that the designation of distinction in "my self" is non-different [from this]. Now,
it might be argued that the status of being a perceiver does not belong to this heart-body, because of the contradiction between one and the same thing being both object and agent.

It is not so; for even in the doctrine of a distinct self (*vyatiriktātmavāda*), how could the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) possess the status of a seer? If you argue that this is due to a difference in nature (*rūpabheda*), then that is equally true for us as well. Furthermore, the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in being connected with the fruit of an action inherent in another [substance].
This is not possible in the case of either the body or a distinct self, because [the "I-notion"] is connected with the fruit of cognition (*jñāna*) which is inherent in itself.
Therefore, since it is logical that the body itself—which is accepted by both disputants—is endowed with consciousness, there is no evidence for postulating a separate principle [of the soul].
Thus, the Sūtra states: "Earth, water, fire, and air are the principles; from these arises consciousness, just as the power of intoxication arises from yeast and other ingredients.
Otherwise, if the Self were understood to be all-pervading (paramamahat), then because it would be devoid of touch, its inferred capacity for movement and so forth would not be primary.
This too is without substance; for since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of air, the occurrence of cognition, pleasure, and so forth is impossible.
Moreover, it is undisputed that in deep sleep the self is devoid of mental modifications (*vṛtti*).
However, even at that time, the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), characterized by inhalation and exhalation, remains possible.
Therefore, since it is perceptible by the sense of touch and so forth, let them clearly accept that the *prāṇa* is nameless.
Consequently, the Self (*ātman*) is distinct from the *prāṇa*.
Let it be, then, that cognition alone is the self, because of its non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*).
Non-selfhood is observed in the body and so forth, which are pervaded by inertness; and since inertness is absent in consciousness (*saṃvit*), it also excludes non-selfhood.
Furthermore, the Prabhākaras themselves indeed accept that cognition is non-inert.

Furthermore, by those who accept that the self (*ātman*) is non-different from consciousness (*saṃvit*), the act of cognition (*saṃvedana*) is necessarily admitted as well, because its establishment is dependent upon that [consciousness]. Therefore, since all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are accomplished through the establishment of both [self and cognition] in this way, what is the use of postulating a separate reality? One might object: "The cognizer, the self, appears directly in perception in the form 'I know'.
This is not so, because that [perception] is of the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

As it has been said: "For the nature of the intellect, though undivided, appears to one whose vision is distorted as possessing the distinctions of the perceived object, the perceiving subject, and self-awareness."
This too is untenable.

If consciousness, which is subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅginī*), were the self, then because there would be no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of what was perceived on one day by another [momentary] cognition, recognition on the following day would be impossible.
For indeed, when something is seen on one day, there arises on the following day the cognition, "This is that very same thing.

And it is not appropriate to claim that this [cognition] is without a basis (*nirālambana*), because that would contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If the proofs for the absence of a basis themselves lacked a basis, then the very state of being without a basis could not be established; furthermore, [the reason] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the presence of a basis.

Now, it might be argued that recognition is possible because consciousness possesses a characteristic [of identity] through its continuity; this is not so, for if that [consciousness] were permanent, it would contradict the thesis of momentariness and result in the fallacy of abandoning one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
Alternatively, it might be argued that even though there is a difference from the preceding momentary consciousness, recognition is possible due to extreme similarity.

If it is argued that this is like the distinction between hair and so forth that has been cut and grown back again, we say no. In that case, there exists a single person who perceives the preceding and succeeding individuals and who synthesizes their similarity; however, here, because the individual instances of cognition are momentary, mutual synthesis is impossible, and thus recognition cannot be based on similarity.

Furthermore, is similarity itself momentary or stable? If it is momentary, then—being equivalent to cognition—it cannot be the basis for recognition. If it is stable, then the doctrine of momentariness is abandoned, which would constitute a contradiction of one's own tenets.
Therefore, one must accept a permanent conscious entity called consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is capable of recognition.
And that [consciousness] is all-pervading (*vibhu*), because its effects are perceived everywhere.

For instance, since cognition, pleasure, and so forth are perceived in various locations everywhere, the presence of the self (*ātman*) must be accepted everywhere; for it is impossible for a quality to exist without the possessor of that quality.

In that case, if [the soul] were to go there and then be considered as being present, it would entail the burden of postulating both the motion and its cause, since presence is observed even for that which does not move.
In the case of space and so forth, this very thing is pure: namely, the simultaneous presence in multiple locations even while not moving.
Furthermore, the self is conjoined with all corporeal forms, because it is a permanent substance devoid of atomic dimension; whatever is thus is thus, just like space and so forth.

Now, suppose the self (*ātman*) were of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*); what would be the fault? This very thing is the fault: if it were of atomic dimension, the simultaneous sensation of pain in the head and the feet would be impossible.
Furthermore, the self does not possess atomic dimension, because it is the substratum of qualities perceivable by the senses, like a jar or similar objects.
[Objection: Well then, let it be of the same dimension as the body.

For instance, the Digambaras argue: "The self has the same dimension as that in which it is perceived, because its qualities are perceived only there; whatever is thus is so, just as a lamp, whose radiance is perceived as existing within [the house], has the dimension of the house.

This is not tenable, because it has been established that the self is in conjunction with all corporeal objects; therefore, the property of having qualities perceived only in a specific location is contradictory [to the nature of the self], and the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).

For the light of a lamp situated inside a house does not have the same dimension as the house, because its dimension is smaller due to being contained within it. Indeed, it is never observed that light of equal dimension occupies the interior of a house. Likewise, the reason is also devoid of the probandum (*sādhanavikala*), for the light situated inside a house is not perceived throughout the entire house.
Furthermore, if [the self] were of the same size as the body, it would follow that it possesses parts.
For whatever substance is partless is observed to be either atomic or all-pervading;
therefore, for that which lacks both of these dimensions, the possession of parts is inevitable.
Furthermore, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the self (*ātman*) possesses unequal dimensions in the bodies of a mosquito and an elephant.
That [consequence] is only logical if [the self] has parts (*sāvayava*), not if it is partless (*niravayava*).
Thus says the Śruti: "Infinite, supreme" and "all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."
And in the Bhagavatī [Upaniṣad] it is said: "He is eternal, all-pervading, and immovable.
Thus, because [the soul] is accepted as being atomic and so forth, that should be understood as intending its initial subtlety.
Therefore, the self is indeed omnipresent.
Likewise, the self is eternal;
and although the Upaniṣads are concerned with what is to be accomplished, they declare the self to be eternally imperishable.
Therefore, because inferences regarding non-eternality contradict scripture, the [proposed] means of proof do not establish the probandum.
Therefore, its eternity is established;
likewise, it is distinct for each body.
For indeed, the perception of the distinction between selves is universally accepted.
Even those who maintain the doctrine of a single self (ekātmavādinaḥ), having accepted the perception of difference, declare it to be merely conceptual (kālpanikatvam).
Consequently, there is a disagreement among disputants as to whether this difference is ultimate (pāramārthika) or conceptual.
In that regard, it is logical that the difference is indeed ultimate, because it is established by valid means of cognition (pramāṇasiddhatvāt).
For instance, the distinction between selves is determined by perception, inference, analogy, and scripture.
First of all, through perception, the self as an enjoyer is cognized in the form "I" as distinct from another self;
and that other self is apprehended through inference as "this one," but not as "I."
Therefore, because they are cognized by distinct modes of cognition, the difference between one's own self and another's self is even clearer than that between a jar and a cloth.

Now, if it is argued that "that very same thing which is perceived as 'I' is perceived as 'this person' residing in another body," this is not so; for if the self in another body were indeed the same, then how could even a non-difference be recognized?

Likewise, just as when an action is performed by the agent of cutting, even though it is the eye that sees, one recognizes the object with the sense of touch and says, "I saw it; I am touching it," so too the self residing in another's body would recognize what was experienced by another, since the experiencer is the same single self.
Nor should it be argued that there is no recognition due to the difference between minds, for the mind is also merely an instrument.
Likewise, the plurality of selves is also understood through inference:

this self under discussion is manifold because it possesses a nature distinct from [the category of] substance, since it is the substratum of specific qualities that are not common [to all substances], just like a jar or other such objects.
Furthermore, the self must be manifold because it is the locus of the inherent cause of cognition, just like the mind.
Likewise, the self is manifold, because it is the substratum of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), like a jar or other such objects.
[Objection: But unity too can be established by inference:
"The bodies under dispute possess a self through a single self, because they are bodies, like the body of the opponent."
That is not so; for it is not accepted that all selves are omnipresent.

Therefore, since even a single self exists in all bodies, you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*). Alternatively, if the self is sought to be proven as being one by means of [the reason] "possessing a self," then because all selves exist within the body of the opponent, the example would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

Now, if it is argued that because there is a single self, [the body] is established as an instrument of experience (*bhoga-sādhana*), then, just as one and the same body is an instrument of experience for oneself, so too would the bodies of one's wife and others be instruments of experience for oneself; thus, the fallacy of the probandum being absent (*sādhyavikalatā*) remains. If it is argued that what is to be proven is not merely being an instrument of experience, but rather being the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*), and therefore the probandum is not absent—this is not correct. What is this so-called "being the locus of experience"? If it means being an instrument of experience, then the previously mentioned refutation applies.

Now, if "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) means happiness (*sukha*), and by "being its locus" (*tadāyatanatva*) you intend "the state of being inherent in happiness," then—since happiness is not inherently present in bodies—the reason would have a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*) and would constitute a counter-argument (*sapratisādhana*) that contradicts your own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
For instance: "The bodies existing at a single time, which are the subject of dispute, possess a self by virtue of their own configuration, because they are bodies, like the body of the opponent.
Nor is there an inconsistency (*anaikāntya*) with respect to bodies in other births, because only those existing at a single time are made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkṛta*).

Nor is there any deviation [in the probans] with respect to the bodies of Saubhya and others, because there is no evidence for their simultaneous assumption of many bodies, and because the accounts in the Purāṇas are of a different nature.

If you are insistent that they possess multiple bodies, then the qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣa*) must be made specifically as "bodies existing at one and the same time, such as those of Asad and others.
Furthermore, the distinction is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

For instance, the distinction between pleasure and pain is indeed perceived: when one person experiences pleasure, at that very same time another is seen to be suffering. This distinction of pleasure, pain, and so forth, being untenable without a plurality of selves, leads us to postulate such plurality.

[Objection: But this distinction is compatible even with a single self, just as within a single body there is the distinction: "there is pain in my foot" and "there is pleasure in my head"; likewise it would be in the case of another body, for in those cases there is also a connection through recollection (*anusandhāna*).
Not so; for where there is a recognized identity of object, there is also the recollection of the relationship [between them].
Where there is no recollection of the relationship, there is likewise no identity of essence.

If it is argued that the recollection is caused by the difference in bodies and not by the difference in names, we reply: even when the self is one, we observe a lack of recollection in the case of different bodies, as seen among those born of the same species.
Likewise, the infant’s desire for breast milk and so forth is due to its being based on the recollection of causes of joy experienced in a previous birth;
and this is indeed accepted as established by all disputants.
Otherwise, one might ask: why is there not a simultaneous coordination of all objects occurring quite spontaneously?
Even regarding what is experienced by the present body, there is no rule that everything experienced must be recollected.
Therefore, the fact that recollection occurs is only possible if there is a unity of the self, not merely a difference of bodies.
By this, the claim that recollection is due to a difference of minds is also refuted.
For this reason, the plurality of the self is established even through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);
likewise, it is established from scripture (*āgama*) as well:
"Two Brahmans are to be known—the higher and the lower," and "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree."
"Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating";

"Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct"; "All these selves also emerge [from Him]"; "He enjoys all desires together with Brahman"; "The One ordains the desires of the many"; "Untainted, he attains supreme equality"; "They have attained My own nature"; "The Supreme Person is another"—such are the Śrutis and Smṛtis as well.

Likewise, injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," "A King [Kṣatriya] with the Rājasūya," and "A Vaiśya with the Vaiśyastoma" imply a plurality of selves (*ātman*) by virtue of the distinction among those qualified for these rites.

Now, an objection may be raised: since for you the entire scripture (*āgama*) possesses authority only insofar as it refers to what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), its authority regarding an established fact (*siddha-artha*)—namely, the plurality of selves—is not tenable.

This is not so; for even though you are proponents of a single self (*ekātmavādin*), the scripture is indeed a means of valid knowledge regarding the plurality of selves, because it possesses authority even with respect to established facts.
For us, however, even though we are intent upon our own task, difference is established by scripture precisely because [scripture] merely restates [previously known] difference.
Thus, since they contradict the means of valid cognition that apprehend manifoldness, the scriptural texts concerning oneness must also be explained otherwise.

Nor is it the case that scripture possesses greater authority when in conflict with perception; for if that were so, the description of the Vaiṣṇava [form] being performed in some places within the Upaniṣadic passages would be inconsistent.
Therefore, the authority of scripture (*āgama*) is not superior [to perception].
Consequently, dualistic doctrines must be refuted by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In this regard, scriptural passages concerning oneness, such as "one only, without a second," have the intention of establishing that there is but one master within a single body.
Scriptural passages such as "There is no diversity whatsoever here" deny plurality; they establish that even when assuming multiple bodies, the Self is one and not manifold.
Similarly, passages such as "This is not this, not that" are intended to distinguish [the Self] from the body, the senses, and so forth.
Therefore, even from scripture, the non-duality of the Self is established.
And this being the case, the distinction between the bound and the liberated is only possible within the doctrine of a manifold self (*nānātmavāda*).

If it is argued that in the case of [the self's] unity, the distinction between the bound and the liberated is merely conceptual, then, since bondage and liberation would be illusory, the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*) has effectively established liberation.

Likewise, the self is established as the apprehender (*grāhaka*) alone during the perception of objects, not as the apprehended (*grāhya*), because it is contradictory for a single entity to be both the object of action and the agent.
If the self, as the agent in the apprehension of objects, were not manifested, then there would be no distinction between the cognition of oneself and that of another.
If it is argued that even if the state of being the grasper is not manifest, the distinction between the cognition of oneself and that of another is nonetheless established— namely,

that the distinction of one's own object of cognition arises from the production of a cognition inherent in oneself, while the distinction of another's object of cognition arises from the production of a cognition inherent in another.
Just as for that which possesses motion, cutting, or vibration, there is the attainment of another location, but not for that which lacks vibration;

so too, if it is asked how it is understood that the [cognition] residing in the body produces knowledge of the relationship between self and other, it can easily be understood through the distinction in the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) of knowledge, such as the contact between one's own or another's sense organs and their objects.
But surely, since the apprehender is also included within the self, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being perceived [by itself].
This is not so; for even that which is unperceived can be a cause, as is the case with the sense organs and other such factors.
Furthermore, the claim that "the cognition of the object is itself the cognition of the self" is the speech of one who is deluded.
Indeed, the establishment of one thing does not follow from the cognition of another, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Furthermore, the establishment of the entire order of existence depends upon consciousness (*saṃvit*); yet that [consciousness] is not itself manifested at the time when its object is manifested—how much less so its manifestation as the substrate of that [object]?

As for the claim that at the time of manifesting an object, such as "I know this jar," a triad necessarily manifests everywhere, that too contradicts universal experience; for in the manifestation of an object alone, such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth," only the object is perceived.
As for the linguistic usage of "consciousness" (*cit*), that manifestation is based on a cognition inferred from [the resulting] patentness (*prākaṭya*) and other such effects.
Furthermore, since the linguistic usage of a "knower" (*jñātṛ*) is caused by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), the self is not established through the cognition of objects.

Moreover, if the self were established from the linguistic usage "I know the jar"—just as the establishment of the object of knowledge [is established]—then the eyes and other sense organs would also be established from the cognitions of form and so forth, based on such sensory-specific usages as "the form is visual" or "the sound is auditory. If you argue that even in those cases, the usage of "hearing" and so on is dependent on the ear and other organs which are themselves established by another means of knowledge, then the same line of reasoning applies here as well: that this [usage of "I know"] is also dependent on another cognition.
Nor is there a contradiction in one thing being both object and agent, for that is possible due to a difference in form;
[specifically], it is an object in its form as consciousness (*cetanā*) and so forth, and a subject in its form as the knower (*jñātṛ*).
To this, it is replied:
In the cognition of all objects, the self must be admitted as the object of the notion "I";
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the manifestation "this has been known by me" could not occur.
And indeed, for everyone and in all cases, there occurs the manifestation "this has been known by me" regarding the cognition of an object.
If that [consciousness] were not manifest, there would be no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another.
Yet such a difference exists, both in terms of essential nature and in terms of function:
that which is cognized by oneself manifests as having itself as its correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas that which is cognized by another manifests as having another as its correlate.

This fact—that the self-cognized [object] possesses a superiority over what is cognized by another—is not possible if self-nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist; thus, this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the grasper.
But surely, this superiority can be accounted for otherwise:
the very production of a cognition inherent in itself is precisely what constitutes the superiority of the self-cognized over that which is cognized by another.
Just as for whomsoever there is movement, for that very one there is the attainment of another location;

that is not so. If cognition were merely the object being known through a cognition inherent in itself, then let that excellence belong to the unknown [object] by virtue of its being known; it would not belong to self-cognition by virtue of the cognition of another.

However, when the self is also intended to be perceived within the cognition inherent in itself, then a difference in nature and a difference in function between what is known by oneself and what is known by another become possible, since the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence would otherwise be untenable.

The distinction of the self from the body and so forth [is not established]. Furthermore, for all-pervading selves, there is no uniqueness [of cognition] based merely on its inherence in knowledge, because that would involve a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
For it is not a rule that a lamp accepted by oneself illuminates only itself and not another.

As for the claim that only the object itself is manifested and that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) pertains to that alone, whereas the linguistic usage of the self is not restricted to the apprehension of an object—that is incorrect.
For even in cases where the linguistic usage of the self is universally accepted, as in "I know the jar," the occurrence of the usage "I" cannot be explained by a cognition whose object is the self;
this is because a cognition whose object is the self would be as impossible as a poison in the mouth of a corpse.
Nor can it be established by means of inference based on mutual rebirth;
therefore, even in that case, one must say that the usage of "I" arises solely from the cognition of the object.

This being so, even where there is a usage regarding the mere object—such as "this is a jar"—there too, it is from the knowledge of the object itself that [the self] is understood as the agent in the form "my self is known. It is only because of the absence of joy or sorrow that no usage of "consciousness" occurs with respect to the self.
Furthermore, there is no rule that everything known must be subject to linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), because this is contradicted in cases such as non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa*).

Therefore, the self is not a knower of the cognition itself, but only a knower of the object; for if it were, the following perception would occur: "This is indeed a jar, yet we do not know whether it is being cognized or not, nor do we know whether it appears to me or to another.
But such is not observed to be the case.

As for the objection that—based on the cognition and linguistic usage such as "the color is visual"—it would follow that the eye itself must be cognized by the cognition of its object, that is incorrect; because there is no rule governing such a cognition, it is only the inferential knowledge of the eye and so forth that is determined.
In this case, however, another cognition is simply not possible, and it has already been stated that linguistic usage is restricted.

Furthermore, the cognition of the self does not occur through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), because it is contradictory for a single entity to simultaneously possess the status of both agent and object.
Nor can the status of agent and object be established through a difference in form, because the Self is partless and possesses a single nature as the grasper.

Furthermore, the nature of being a substance and so forth does not belong to the Self alone. [Objection: But surely, the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in being the recipient of a result produced by an action, as in the case of a village which receives the result produced by the act of going; here too, the result produced by the act of cognition is either manifestation (*bhāsana*) or practical transaction (*vyavahāra*), and both of these are indeed admitted in the case of the Self. Therefore, it lacks the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*).

Furthermore, the state of being both an agent and an object has never been observed in a single entity anywhere. Therefore, any cognition that has the self as its object and the self as its own object is as non-existent as a hare’s horn. Moreover, the current experience and linguistic usage "I know the jar" are observed; since you maintain that cognition is momentary, by the time of one's own inference it would have already passed away.
