Thus, what you have established would be merely past experience and usage, rather than current experience and usage.
Furthermore, the self is established as the apprehender even through inference.
It is universally accepted that the self appears as the apprehender in such cognitions as "I know the jar.
This appearance as an apprehender is dependent upon the cognition of the object, because it is an appearance, just like the appearance of what is known by a cognition.
Furthermore, it has already been established that the existence of objects depends upon the cognition of those objects.
Moreover, consciousness, which establishes the self, must have an object distinct from its own substratum, because it is an action possessing an object (*sakarmaka-kriyā*), like the act of cooking.

The empirical usage "I know the jar" is based on the cognition of the jar, because it arises immediately after that [cognition], just like the empirical usage regarding the jar; for it arises immediately after the cognition whose object is the self.

If it is argued that [the self] is established because it arises immediately after that [cognition], we say no; for the cognition whose object is the self is itself unestablished, being like the horn of a hare, or else it cannot be said that anything else is unestablished.

Furthermore, the establishment of the nature of the self, which is the subject of dispute, is based upon the experience of objects, because it is the establishment of the nature of the self, just like the nature of the self in a waking person. The meaning is this: just as there is no establishment of the nature of the self at the time of sleep, the establishment of the nature of the self is brought about in the state of awakening due to the perception of objects.

Therefore, it is established that "the Self is distinct from the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth; it is indeed all-pervading, manifold, and appears as one kind in every field [of experience]. (Praviv., pp. 84–97). However, the [objection regarding] the disappearance of the agent is refuted because the Self is devoid of action.
And because it is all-pervading, it is devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*).

*Bṛhatī*, p. 173. Because the self (*ātman*) appears through direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), it possesses the nature of perception (*pratyakṣatva*) even in inference and other means of knowledge. *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 185.

If the selves (*ātman*) are all-pervading (*vibhu*), then even though they are many, since every self would be connected to all bodies, why is it that one does not experience the pleasure, pain, and so forth belonging to another? Regarding this, some say: "Just as there is a restriction of pleasure and so forth even when [the self] is limited to the body alone—as in the case of the mother and the fetus suffering together—so too will there be a restriction everywhere. Even for one who maintains that the self is the size of the body (*śarīraparimāṇatvavādin*), this same fault indeed applies; nevertheless, because the self of the fetus occupies the same location as the mother, the mother’s conscious subject (*kṣetrajña*) would perceive the pleasure and so forth residing therein.
In that regard, the rebuttal offered— that [the soul] will exist in all bodies and thus there is no distinction—
is not a valid argument if it merely results in parity with the opponent's position;
for both you and he alike can be subjected to further cross-examination by another.

Furthermore, because that [self] is of the same dimension as the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*), and because the self is not admitted to exist within the internal space of the body like Brahman, there is no cognition of the self in the womb; thus, the doctrine of the self does not entail the same fault as the view that the mother's medicinal substances reach the embryo.

Therefore, it should be answered as follows: "If the enjoyability of pleasure and so forth were held to result from reaching the same location, then this fault would ensue; however, there is no such observation regarding the enjoyment of what is merely suitable. For if the very fact of the soul and pleasures occupying the same location were accepted as the cause of experience, then this fault would indeed follow.
In this case, however, there is a connection between the eyes and so forth, characterized by their fitness for the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).

In that regard, just as objects such as color and form located in the same place as the sense of touch are not perceived by it, so too would the enjoyment of the objects and qualities belonging to one person by another soul be easily grasped [as a possibility].
Therefore, because the distinction between owner and owned is established according to the doctrine of the self (*ātmavāda*), there is no fault.

Thus, because it is all-pervading, the immutability of the Self is established (*Vākyapadīya* 2.2.15, p. 404). Because [ether, space, time, and the self] are eternal, like the example of atoms (*Vākyapadīya* 1.3.8.27, p. 285), there is no engagement in actions at all without the knowledge of the Self; therefore, action must be performed solely for the sake of [attaining] knowledge of the Self.
And this will be understood by the knower of Brahman.
Now, if there were a permanent knower distinct from the act of cognition, then he who was the perceiver on one day would be the very same person who would seek [objects] on the following day.
Otherwise, indeed, desire would not be possible. To this, the Vijñānavādin replies:
"What is our conviction that it is impossible?"
In this regard, it is understood through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
First of all, we do not perceive anything other than consciousness.
That which we do not perceive, we understand to be non-existent, just like the horn of a hare.
Furthermore, it is not untenable for consciousness to exist even when that [object] is absent,
precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception;
and its momentariness is likewise established by means of direct perception itself.

Furthermore, it is not tenable that cognitions persist in a knower who is distinct from those cognitions, nor is desire on the following day possible if the cognition were impermanent, precisely because this is directly perceived.
Indeed, it is never observed that the very person who apprehended something one day is the same person who exists on the following day;
rather, what is observed is that in some cases one person desires what was seen by another, while in other cases they do not.
One person maintains that [the self] exists within a single continuum, but not within another continuum;
therefore, there must be something other than pleasure and so forth. To this, it is replied:
For the doctrine of self does not proceed for one who is without existence.

Since the person (puruṣa) has the nature of the power of knowledge, he must be conceived as eternal, omnipresent, and capable of entering another body; for even without moving, he will be joined [to a new body].

(Ratnākara: To avoid the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), a permanent person (*puruṣa*) must necessarily be established. Furthermore, for the sake of establishing his status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), he must be conscious (*cetana*);
and for the sake of attaining another body, he must be all-pervading (*sarvagata*).)
Although it is omnipresent, this [Self], even while not moving, is able to establish a connection with another body;
this alone constitutes its connection with a body, namely, the appropriation of it as the locus of experience.
Furthermore, the status of being a sacrificer (*yajamānatva*) is attained because of the state of being active from the very beginning of the undertaking.
(How is there agency for the Lord? To this he says: For us, action is not merely physical motion alone, as it is for the followers of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣikas).
Furthermore, an action is not performed by agents as something inherent within themselves;
an action is merely the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), and agency may exist even when it resides in another substratum.
To begin with, the person himself is the agent of such states as existence, knowledge, and so forth.
Even that movement of the elements which occurs therein by virtue of [the soul's] presiding over them,
and whatever action is performed by the body and the senses because they are directed toward that end—
that is performed by the person alone; why then is it said to be [done] elsewhere?
For there could be no activity of these [elements] if they were not appropriated by the Puruṣa;
therefore, because they lack independence, they possess no agency even with respect to their own movement.
While those various actions are being performed by means of the materials acquired through that [initial] karma,
the agency of the sacrificers consists in their being the causal agents (kartṛ) of the earth, the bricks, and the person.
Just as the purchase [of Soma] is performed through the medium of the skin,
here too, by signs such as "going," it is merely understood that the elements serve as the medium.
For just as there is no actual purchasing of the Self, so indeed is there no going and so forth.
And by that [agency], his agency here is established through another,
just as Devadatta’s agency exists in the cutting of wood;
so too would there be agency for the person in the movement of the body and such.
If it is argued that agency in that case consists in being engaged in another operation, then for us here as well,
the person is intended to be the instigator by virtue of possessing volition and possessing *sattva* (where *sattva-vattva* means possessing the internal organ).
Agency is common [to all] through the possession of *sattva* with respect to actions.
Furthermore, because the agent varies according to each specific action of one who intends,
there would not be uniformity in all instigating actions; for it is by means of movement that the sword-wielder is employed toward the act of cutting.
A general directs his servants by word alone;
a king, however, directs them only by his mere presence.
Therefore, even for one who does not move, there exists the agency of the self in causing movement.
Just as Devadatta possesses the quality of being a cutter,
so too is the Knower always known to us through the notion of "I.
That cognition of the Self which occurs through the designation of difference, such as "my self," [is likewise established].
In that regard, based on the knowledge of the distinction between this [self] and the Self, there is the conceptual construction "mine";
the primary meaning of this term is not perceived as anything other than the Self.

Therefore, that [diversity] would be the cause of differentiation, and differentiation would be caused by cognition. Furthermore, for those who hold the view that the self is manifold, there is the notion of "I" with respect to their bodies;
even there, it arises from the conceit of a self, as the sense of "I" is directed toward the self.
But those who have realized the manifoldness [of the self] are free from egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) regarding the body; however,
even for yogis, this cognition "I know" does not cease entirely.
If that [self] were non-existent, there would be no meditative absorption for them, nor would there be activity in instructing disciples;
yet such activity is observed, and therefore the self is inferred by them.

(Ratnākara: Not only from the words of the Upaniṣads, but also because specific rites such as the Agnihotra—which would be untenable without an eternal enjoyer—illuminate its very existence through their own nature.)
However, it is precisely that which the Upaniṣads clarify through the Śrutis and other means by virtue of its profundity:

"The Person (puruṣa) is indestructible by nature; as for that destruction, it belongs to the elements (mātrās) such as the gross elements (bhūtas) and so forth, which possess causal agency and are devoid of consciousness."

"It is without ideation and without consciousness"— thus the author of the Bhāṣya has here rightly established the existence of the Supreme Self in order to refute nihilism. And the firm understanding regarding this subject proceeds through the study of the Vedānta.

(Ratnākara: Since the authority of the Veda is established merely by its eternal non-existence [as a human composition], that alone has been demonstrated here; however, those seeking firmness [in their conviction] should strive in the hearing, reflection, and meditative contemplation (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) prescribed by the Vedānta.

*Bṛhatī*: But surely, when a difference is perceived between a cow and a Vāhīka, the figurative designation "the Vāhīka is a cow" is appropriate. Yet, we do not perceive anything other than the body here [in the case of the Veda].
"What is the intended meaning of 'we do not perceive [it]'? This very thing is the intended meaning: 'we do not perceive [it].
But surely we perceive it through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which are its effects.
[Objection: Is it not the body itself that breathes in and breathes out?"
"What do you mean by 'body,' O long-lived one?
It is this aggregate composed of the four elements. [Riju:
"But such is the established position regarding the nature of things in this matter."

The body is merely a collection of the four elements; it is not composed of all four elements, but rather the body is indeed earthen (pārthiva), while the other substances—those consisting of fire and those consisting of air—are merely conjoined with it and dependent upon it.
As it has been stated by others: "This measure [of size] is contradictory even for the conjunction of five [elements]."

For instance, this body is not composed of five elements (*pañcabhūta*) nor even of four elements; for if it were composed of both perceptible and imperceptible elements, it would follow that it is imperceptible, like the conjunction between air and a tree. As they say: "Because the conjunction of perceptible and imperceptible things is itself imperceptible, a composition of five [elements] does not exist" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.2.12). Nor is it composed of earth, water, and fire alone—even though these are perceptible—since they possess respectively non-hot-cold, cold, and hot touches; for if it were so composed, it would follow that the body possesses a touch characterized by none of those specific qualities.
For just as a cloth produced from white and black threads possesses a variegated color distinct [from its parts], so too this body would possess a distinct touch.
And since this body has a touch that is neither hot nor cold, it must therefore be composed solely of earth and air.
As it was stated by those very same [authors]: "And because of the manifestation of a different quality, it is not even composed of three elements" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.2.13).
For this reason, it cannot even consist of a single element.

Since a solitary odor residing in a single earth-atom cannot logically initiate another odor, the body would necessarily be odorless. However, since this body possesses odor, it is indeed composed of earth alone.

Those conjoined with it (*tatsaṃyoginaḥ*) are the other dependent [entities], specific effect-substances (*kāryadravyaviśeṣa*) such as the eyes and so forth, which are composed of other elements; this is to be understood from another treatise (*tantrāntara*).
Only a mere indication has been given.

By that, [it is shown that] the aggregate is composed of the four elements (*cāturbhautika*); the meaning is that these are not merely the effects of the body, but rather persist as long as the body exists, such as its growth and so forth.
Even though they are real, the appropriated [elements] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not perceived [as such].
(By this, the literal meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "as long as his body" has been shown.
However, this does not suffice to establish the impossibility [of the self] on the grounds that it is exclusively an effect of the body.)
Even through impairment, as long as the body exists, the possibility of functional activity remains;
moreover, impairment in a dead body is beyond dispute.
Therefore, it is explained otherwise.

The meaning is: "because they have not existed [previously] and have come into being [now]. If these were inherent in substances composed of primary elements (*bhūta*), then, because they would be inherent in an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), that same state would necessarily apply to the cause as well.

For the production of specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) in an effect-substance is preceded by the qualities of the cause, just as color and so forth are produced in a jar; and cognition (*buddhi*) and the other [mental states] are indeed specific qualities.

But is it not observed that even among substances there is a transformation into something solid, such as hailstones and the like? And from insentient things like cow dung, sentient creatures such as tree-spiders are born?
This objection is incomplete.
Hardness is not a distinct quality; rather, it is the loose conjunction of parts.
Furthermore, conjunction is not a specific quality [of a substance].
This point—that the production of consciousness from the unconscious exists or does not exist—is currently a subject of dispute.

In that regard, if intellect (*buddhi*) and the other qualities were present even in the causal substance, then the jars and other effects produced from it would likewise possess intellect and the rest;
yet this is not the case.

Furthermore, the reading in the *Bṛhatī*, "even though they are elements (*bhūta*), they are not appropriated" (or, according to another reading, "though they are elements, they are appropriated"), would be incorrect if [the elements] were not accepted as constituting a body. For in those cases not accepted as bodies, specific qualities such as vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are not perceived, unlike color (*rūpa*) and the other qualities [which are perceived in all elemental substances].
Regarding this, the Blessed Kāśyapa said: "From the knowledge of the cause" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.1.4).

It appears that the reading "'Not from the knowledge of the effect, nor from the knowledge of the cause'"—or rather, "'From the non-knowledge of another effect and the non-knowledge of the cause'"—is necessary, as it is explained in that very manner immediately following. However, in the original text of the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras, the reading "From the knowledge of effects, and from non-knowledge" (Sūtras 5 and 6) is observed.

The meaning of these two sūtras is as follows: because there is ignorance—that is, an absence of knowledge—regarding earth and other elements which serve as causes, there is ignorance, an absence of knowledge, regarding the body composed of them; and because there is ignorance regarding the cause, there is ignorance regarding other effects such as a jar and so forth.
Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that pleasure and the like are properties of the material elements.

For the elemental qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are perceivable by the sense organs of others, just like the elements themselves; however, pleasure (*sukha*) and the like are not [perceivable by the sense organs of others].
[Objection: Let them not be elemental qualities; what is the proof for their being distinct from those?
[Reply: Indeed, the very fact that this effect would be impossible without a cause is the proof in this case.

And since "being" (*bhūtatva*) and "causality" (*kāraṇatā*, specifically *samavāyikāraṇatā*) are established as properties distinct from one another, their being properties of different things is proven.
However, this is not established, because it is also possible for them to be mutual effects.
As for what was said—that "whatever is capable must have a corresponding correlate"—that appears merely like a statement.
How can that which is observed to possess an origin not be understood as having another related entity?
For one might think that "having an origin" implies "having a cause";
however, this is intended with reference to a dissimilar cause (*visabhāga-hetu*).
(The meaning is: this [statement] intends to show that there is a dissimilar cause (*visabhāgakāraṇa*). It does not mean, however, that origination is entirely without cause.

How, then, is it understood that this intends to show a dissimilar cause? Because in the phrase "for this is not like the moon," the word *antara* (other/different) is heard; for upon hearing the word *antara*, a relationship of a different nature is perceived.
And that very [identity] is what is being negated.

Now, one might object: "Even if there were difference, the word 'intermediate' (antara) would still be applicable. True, it would be applicable; however, it cannot be said that an effect is something other than its cause.

Granted that the text has been observed; however, the mere presence of a fault is not the reason for the deviation from the intended meaning (the reading *arthāntarāvagame* is found in the *Ṛjuvimalā*). No, for the continuity (*saṃtāna*) is admitted.
For just as a continuum is established through the relationship of cause and effect, therefore, this refers to the intention of a dissimilar cause.
Consequently, it is concluded that this web of effects has only a homogeneous continuum as its cause; there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for perceiving any fault of heterogeneity here.
Furthermore, if there were no arising from a dissimilar cause (*visabhāga-hetu*), there would simply be another state [of existence].

By this very reasoning—since nothing other than cognition and so forth is perceived, and since their occurrence is established through mutual causality—the meaning of the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is refuted, as are desire and memory; for no other [entity] distinct from cognition is observed.
Indeed, it cannot be asserted that memory and the like would not be possible if some other dissimilar (i.e., heterogeneous) entity were not seen.
For that which is perceived cannot be called "impossible.
This is what was stated [by the author]: "What is our conviction regarding something being impossible?
But what is the reason that the Commentator has presented all these means of cognition as grounds for the realization of the Self?
Through these [reasons], the notion of a self arises with respect to what is not-self.
Furthermore, ignorance must be dispelled in every way.

If these reasons were not refuted, then even in the future, students whose intellects have been led astray by hearing the Vaiśeṣika and other systems would lack the correct conceit of "I am the Self. Therefore, those reasons are refuted.

As for what was stated [Bhāṣya, p. 60], "We perceive him through breath and so forth," what is incorrect here? Since these are not qualities of the elements—because they do not persist as long as the substance itself exists—their being elemental properties has been refuted. Furthermore, since their relationship is understood through their status as substrates, and because mental states and mental factors themselves possess the nature of being substrates, it is indeed correct to say that these are qualities of the Self.

How can it be said that there is a notion of self (*ātma-buddhi*) regarding what is not-self? For [qualities] such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth are also perceived as being dependent [on a substance], and because they do not persist as long as the substance itself, they are described by the Vaiśeṣikas and others as being qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇa*).
To this it is replied: first of all, it cannot be said that breath (*prāṇa*) and the other [vital functions] do not persist as long as the substance itself;
for these consist of motion, and motion is a property of air (*vāyu*).
For in all cases, such as in the breath and so forth, there is the perception of a nature characterized by motion.
Therefore, the claim that [motion] does not exist as long as the substance exists is unproven.
This is precisely the notion of a self with respect to what is non-self.

Even those qualities such as pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest that have been put forward can be said to be merely attributes of the primary elements (*bhūtaguṇa*), because they are the causes of the modification of those elements;
for a subtle atom (*aṇu*) is not capable of modifying its own substratum.
Indeed, modification is simply a change of state (*avasthā*).
Furthermore, a state (*avasthā*) is the cause for the arising of another state;

and since a state is not distinct from that which possesses the state, it is established that pleasure and the other qualities of the primary elements (*bhūtaguṇa*) have [the self] as their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
For that which is in immediate proximity to the inherent cause becomes the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Just as the conjunction of threads is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of a cloth that inheres in those threads, so too pleasure and the like, when they produce modifications such as clarity in the eyes and other sense organs—which are the inherent substrates (*samavāyin*)—are themselves inherent in the primary elements (*bhūta*). Now, one might object: "If this is indeed the case, why was it stated [previously] that pleasure and the like manifest only within the self? To this we reply: [it was stated thus] because [the self] is the locus of experience. However, in the present context, since the discussion concerns the production of effects in the sense organs, it is appropriate to say that pleasure and the like are inherent in the elements. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, pleasure and the like are not perceived apart from the body; rather, they are perceived only when the body is present. Thus, they must be inherent in the body—that is, in the elements. Consequently, they are established as being inherent in the elements. This concludes the section on the refutation of pleasure and the like. Now, the following is considered: Is the soul (*ātman*) eternal or non-eternal? It is eternal. Why? Because it is unproduced. Just as space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and direction (*dis*) are eternal because they are unproduced, so too is the soul eternal because it is unproduced. Furthermore, the soul is distinct from the body, the senses, and the mind. Why? Because it possesses qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*), desire (*icchā*), and effort (*prayatna*). For these qualities do not belong to the body, the senses, or the mind. Since it possesses qualities, it is a substance (*dravya*). And since it is a substance, it must be either eternal or non-eternal. Because it is unproduced, it is established as eternal. Moreover, the soul is omnipresent (*vibhu*). Why? Because its qualities are perceived everywhere. Just as space is omnipresent because its quality, sound, is perceived everywhere, so too is the soul omnipresent because its qualities, such as cognition, are perceived in all bodies. Furthermore, the soul is infinite (*ananta*). Why? Because it is omnipresent. Just as space is infinite because it is omnipresent, so too is the soul infinite because it is omnipresent. This concludes the section on the nature of the soul. Now, the following is considered: Does the soul exist after death? Yes, it does. Why? Because of the Vedic injunctions and prohibitions. For if the soul were non-existent after death, the injunctions and prohibitions regarding heaven and hell would be meaningless. Furthermore, the soul is remembered by itself. Why? Because it is conscious. Just as Devadatta remembers what he experienced yesterday, so too does the soul remember its own past experiences. Therefore, it is established that the soul exists after death. This concludes the section on the existence of the soul after death. Now, the following is considered: Is the soul one or many? It is many. Why? Because of diversity in experience. For if the soul were one, then when one person experiences pleasure or pain, everyone else would likewise experience it. But this is not the case. Therefore, the soul is many. Furthermore, the soul is distinct in each body. Why? Because of the difference in qualities. For qualities such as cognition, desire, and effort differ from body to body. Therefore, the soul is distinct in each body. This concludes the section on the plurality of souls. Now, the following is considered: Is the soul active or inactive? It is inactive. Why? Because it is all-pervading. Just as space, though all-pervading, is inactive, so too is the soul inactive because it is all-pervading. Furthermore, activity belongs to the body, the senses, and the mind, which are composed of the elements. The soul, being immaterial (*amūrta*), cannot possess activity. Therefore, it is established as inactive. This concludes the section on the inactivity of the soul. Now, the following is considered: Does the soul have a beginning or is it beginningless? It is beginningless. Why? Because there is no evidence for its production. For there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish that the soul was produced at some point. Therefore, it is established as beginningless. Furthermore, the soul is eternal. Why? Because it is beginningless. Just as space is eternal because it is beginningless, so too is the soul eternal because it is beginningless. This concludes the section on the beginninglessness and eternity of the soul. Now, the following is considered: Is the soul a creator or a non-creator? It is a non-creator. Why? Because it is inactive. Since it has been established that the soul is inactive, it cannot be a creator. Furthermore, creation belongs to the Lord (*īśvara*), who is endowed with omniscience and omnipotence. The soul, lacking these attributes, is not a creator. Therefore, it is established as a non-creator. This concludes the section on the soul's status as a non-creator. Now, the following is considered: Does the soul experience the fruits of actions or not? It does experience them. Why? Because it is the enjoyer. For the soul is the experiencer of the results of its own actions, whether pleasant or painful. Therefore, it is established as the enjoyer. Furthermore, the soul is the agent of action. Why? Because it is the instigator of the body, senses, and mind. Just as a potter is the agent of the pot by instigating the clay, wheel, and tools, so too is the soul the agent of action by instigating the body, senses, and mind. Therefore, it is established as the agent. This concludes the section on the soul as the agent and enjoyer. Now, the following is considered: Is liberation possible or impossible? It is possible. Why? Because of the cessation of suffering. For when the causes of suffering—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—are destroyed, suffering ceases. When suffering ceases, liberation is attained. Therefore, liberation is possible. Furthermore, liberation is the attainment of the highest bliss. Why? Because it is the cessation of all suffering. For the cessation of all suffering is the ultimate state of bliss. Therefore, liberation is the attainment of the highest bliss. This concludes the section on the possibility of liberation. Now, the following is considered: By what means is liberation attained? It is attained through knowledge and conduct. Knowledge consists of the realization of the truth regarding the self and the non-self, while conduct consists of the performance of prescribed duties and the avoidance of prohibited acts. Through the combination of knowledge and conduct, the causes of bondage are destroyed, and liberation is attained. This concludes the section on the means to liberation. Now, the following is considered: Is liberation permanent or impermanent? It is permanent. Why? Because it is the absolute cessation of suffering. For once suffering has ceased, it never returns. Therefore, liberation is permanent. Furthermore, liberation is eternal. Why? Because it is free from birth and death. For liberation is the state beyond birth and death. Therefore, it is eternal. This concludes the section on the permanence and eternity of liberation. Now, the following is considered: Does the liberated soul retain its individuality or does it merge into the Absolute? It retains its individuality. Why? Because it possesses consciousness. For the liberated soul is conscious and therefore maintains its distinct identity. Furthermore, the liberated soul is free from all attributes. Why? Because it has transcended all limitations. For the liberated soul is free from the qualities of the material world and is thus pure consciousness. Therefore, it is established as free from attributes. This concludes the section on the nature of the liberated soul. Now, the following is considered: Is the liberated soul subject to rebirth or not? It is not subject to rebirth. Why? Because the causes of rebirth have been destroyed. For the causes of rebirth are karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Since these have been eradicated by knowledge and conduct, rebirth is impossible. Therefore, the liberated soul does not undergo rebirth. Furthermore, the liberated soul attains the state of supreme peace. Why? Because it is free from all suffering. For the liberated soul is free from the three types of suffering: internal, external, and celestial. Therefore, it attains supreme peace. This concludes the section on the state of the liberated soul. Now, the following is considered: Is the liberated soul omniscient or not? It is omniscient. Why? Because it is free from all obstructions. For the liberated soul is free from the veils of ignorance and attachment, and thus its knowledge is unobstructed. Therefore, it is established as omniscient. Furthermore, the liberated soul is omnipotent. Why? Because it has mastery over all things. For the liberated soul has attained sovereignty over all objects of experience. Therefore, it is established as omnipotent. This concludes the section on the omniscience and omnipotence of the liberated soul. Now, the following is considered: Does the liberated soul act for the benefit of others or not? It acts for the benefit of others. Why? Because it is compassionate. For the liberated soul, having realized the truth, feels compassion for those still bound in ignorance and acts to lead them to liberation. Therefore, it is
Even if it were accepted [that the self exists], this very point—that [the self] is not established as having the nature of a dharma—is the intended meaning, because of the mention of desire.
But what is the reason for accepting [this]? This is the reason:
here, certain Buddhists who are conceited about their own brilliance hold a contrary view.
What is this so-called relationship of support and supported? This is perceived merely as a composite whole.

On this point, other knowers of Brahman—the Sāṃkhyas—have maintained that we perceive a Self distinct from the body, because of the conceit of agency, memory, desire, and so forth, which extend from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the gross elements.

Therefore, one can rightly say that [the Self] "knows," as it is distinct from both cause and effect.
The cognition "one should contemplate some object of knowledge by means of knowledge" implies that the self is established as the agent.
But is it not accepted [by the Sāṃkhyas] that this [self] is devoid of activity?
And regarding the agent of cognition, this suffix [in the word] *jānāti* [is used].
(The answer: For those [Vaiśeṣikas] for whom cognition inheres in the self (*ātman*), its status as the agent of cognition is established precisely because it is the cause thereof.

Furthermore, for those [Sāṃkhyas] for whom knowledge and so forth are well-known to be attributes solely of the intellect (*buddhi*), this reason [of being an agent] applies to them by virtue of their being the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*).

For the intellect is perceived as the enjoyer by way of the Self, and as the object of enjoyment by way of its nature as knowledge. As they say: "Just as the flow of milk proceeds for the sake of the calf, so does the Unmanifest proceed for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa."

the argument that "we do not perceive any other form [of it]" remains unrefuted.

To this it is replied: "Regarding what was seen on one day, on another day there arises the cognition, 'I saw this. [Therefore, only the mere notion of "I" needs to be established here, not recognition.
Nor is the refutation of momentariness the primary aim here; rather, it is the demonstration of the existence of a self distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body.
(Objection) It is not on account of momentariness that selflessness is asserted by the opponents;
what then? It is because no [self] is perceived apart from the aggregates.

For momentariness is indeed contradictory with permanence, but not with the existence of the self (*ātman*). And here, a deceptive argument is presented by others: "The self is momentary. However, no resolution is provided against the denial of the permanence of an existing self.
No other [self] is perceived; yet, by this much alone—that there is something else—there is selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Therefore, one must simply state that there exists a self (*ātman*) distinct from the body and the instruments of action, which is graspable by the notion of "I. Indeed.
Now, this further objection is raised:
"Even if the existence of the self (*ātman*) is established, its very nature as a self is lost because of its momentariness.
(For the nature of a self consists in being an enjoyer; the meaning is that for something momentary, the status of being an enjoyer is lost.)
What kind of verbal artifice is this? Why does the "skandha-ness" of the aggregates not disappear?
For being an enjoyer is the very nature of the self, and the aggregates possess the quality of being enjoyers.

Just as the status of being an enjoyer cannot be removed from the aggregates (*skandhas*) even though they are momentary, so too is the status of being an enjoyer [inseparable] from the self (*ātman*). Therefore, this [criticism] is like setting out on a journey at night. [The author] replies: You are ignorant of the self (*anātmajña*), you who raise such objections.
"Do you know why it has been said that the aggregates are momentary?
(The opponent asks: "And why was it so stated?
(He replies: "Because of the absence of an enjoyer."

The proponent asks: "In the absence of an enjoyer, the momentariness of the aggregates—what is this, a royal decree? [The opponent replies: "This is not a royal decree; rather, it is a matter of logic (*nyāya*). How so? If an enjoyer were to exist, we have no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the effect-producing [agent] being momentary.
Why? Because a cause is indeed to be inferred from its effect."
And from this, the establishment of action [is achieved].
For whoever accepts an enjoyer necessarily accepts an action in the form of enjoyment.
When the inference of a cause is proposed based on the occasional arising of an effect, the establishment of action results from that inference.

Furthermore, the claim that action could belong to a momentary entity until the attainment of its fruit is untenable. Therefore, those who accept an enjoyer and who admit an action consisting of enjoyment must necessarily accept a stable substance.
Furthermore, if one accepts the existence of a stable substance (*sthiradravya*), there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
This doctrine of momentariness is based on the collection of effects resulting from actions.
For, in the absence of action, an occasional effect would lead to the inference of a cause possessing an adventitious nature, thereby implying that the substance itself is momentary.
If action is accepted, then because the occasional nature of effects is thereby accounted for, it is impossible to understand the momentariness of substances.
If, on the other hand, the acceptance of action is not made at all, then agency and enjoyership cannot be established.
Thus he says: "And [the objection] is raised against the agency and enjoyership of that which possesses swift action."
And by the negation of that [action], there is the negation of the self.

If one conceives that this body and its instruments are merely of the nature of transformation (*pariṇati-svabhāva*), then [the notions of] "agent" and "experiencer" [would be untenable]. Therefore, by one who desires an experiencer, action must necessarily be admitted;
and that [action] is dependent upon the admission of a stable substance (*sthiradravya*).

Considering that the stability of a substance depends upon recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the author of the *Bhāṣya*, thinking, "This [recognition] has been demonstrated as true," said: "Therefore, even when the mere establishment of the object of the 'I'-cognition is achieved, and even when agency and enjoyership are established as belonging to one distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has presented perception accompanied by recognition."

For this very reason, the proponents of selflessness repeatedly attribute momentariness and inefficacy to the self, saying: "If it were like a hide, it would be impermanent; if it were non-existent, it would not be [an agent].
Therefore, the self is the enjoyer.
While it is logical that the self is the enjoyer, its association with agency is contradicted, because the self is devoid of action.
Furthermore, because it is omnipresent, it is devoid of action.
And its omnipresence is established because it is easily perceived everywhere;
for there is nothing contradictory in the absence of movement.
Existence (*sattā*), for its part, is established for the self (*ātman*) everywhere by virtue of being easily perceived;
however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove that this [existence] is preceded by motion.
For nothing is logically untenable even in the absence of motion.
As for the perception of pleasure and so forth that occurs when the body comes [into contact with objects], that is established by virtue of the localized nature of pleasure and so forth;
and this localization of pleasure and so forth is due to their proximity to the self and the localized nature of the mind.
The fact that the self is not perceived even in a location devoid of a body is due to the localized nature of cognition itself;

that is, cognition is perceived only where it exists. [The author] refutes this: mobility was asserted by accepting the nature of action (*kriyā*), but not with respect to the perception of experience (*bhoga*).

"For what purpose is it established that 'this [notion] occurs with respect to the inner self' (pratyagātman)? For the very purpose of establishing the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva). How so? Because enjoyment is observed in the inner self.

This is the intended meaning: for if the self were an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), it would be impossible to assert that the cognition and the knower are not distinct from it; nor can consciousness itself be presented as [the self] by means of that very same consciousness.

How could that very same thing refute itself?
For it is not possible for that which is the object of refutation by something to be the refuter of that very same thing.
Therefore, this is the correct answer.
By this illustration as well—“just as someone with sight”—it is established that [the subject] is indeed distinct from the instrument.

Now, one might ask: in this case, since the agent (the person) and the instrument (the eye) are distinct from the object of cognition (form), what is the purpose of this illustration? It is because of the commonality of the absence of any other agent.

Therefore, cognition that is free from defects in its cause and non-erroneous is the reason for the existence of the self, whether there be another agent or not (for cognition exists even in the case of the self;
thus, although there is no other agent for this [self], it exists). And it has been stated: "Objects exist in the manner that they are cognized;
they do not exist in the manner that they are not cognized."
Regarding this, there is also a Brāhmaṇa passage: "When speech has become quiet.

The question is: since [the self] is occupied elsewhere as an agent, how can it be grasped in the absence of another agent or instrument? And the mention of "speech" is for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of other instruments.
The meaning of the statement, "He said, 'He has attained the light of the Self,'" has been demonstrated by way of the preceding and subsequent arguments.

(Uttara: But have you not heard, "The Self is self-luminous" (*ātmajyotiḥ samrāṭ*)? Has this also not been heard? In accordance with those two [scriptural statements], the scriptural text regarding its non-apprehensibility is relative—that is, it is based on the requirement of its being self-luminous—and it is not the case that the mention of the "Self" is explained otherwise (i.e., with reference to another person).
What is the reasoning? Because a figurative description (*guṇavāda*) is impossible if one accepts [the Self] as self-luminous, whereas its relativity is logical if it is unapprehendable.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the injunctions, "The Self is to be known," "It is to be reflected upon."
And thus, self-luminosity is established.

But if this is so, how can it be communicated to another? For this undertaking by the authors of the scriptures and the Vedas is for the sake of producing conviction in others. Self-awareness itself becomes the means [of communication].

Since it is experienced by oneself and not by another, consciousness is established as being unperceivable by others in all persons. Furthermore, the status of the teachings as "teachings" is established by way of negating the consciousness of others; thus, this is what is set forth by the statement, "not this, not this."
But surely pleasure and the like are also self-cognized; they too are not cognized by another person.
How, then, can the Self, taught to another as something distinct from them, be established?
To this, the Commentator has stated that they are indeed cognized by another through inferential marks (*liṅga*).
That is improper, as it would lead to the same consequence for the self (*ātman*) as well.
In that case too, he himself presents this inference;
therefore, how can this [argument] which destroys its own counter-position be set down by the learned? This too is a heavy burden that has arrived upon his ears.
For movement is presented as the means for eliminating defects in the cause;
however, pleasure and so forth are accessible through the eyes and other senses when there is an abundance [of their respective objects].
(What, then, is the distinction between these two? By this [inference from movement] as well, consciousness is perceived only in another [self]).
The distinction is that [it is] "by way of not being an effect" (*akāryatayā*). For movement (*ceṣṭā*) is indeed not an effect.

Therefore, the inference from movement is not an inference "from an effect," because things such as breath (*bhrama*), cognition (*jñāna*), and so forth are not effects in the sense of pleasure (*sukha*) and the like.
Therefore, the self is not perceived through its activity (*ceṣṭā*); rather, pleasure and other states are perceived through the movement of the limbs and so forth.

Consequently, the other person's self is not apprehended by another even through inference, whereas pleasure and other states are indeed apprehended; this is the distinction. But how can there be an indubitable truth [in this]? If activity is not an effect of the self, then, being unperceived by the self, how could it serve as a mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the self? Or, if it is not perceived, how can there be a question regarding the existence of another person? Thus, the suspicion of error regarding one's own self is dispelled.
(Regarding the latter: We say it is because of the non-perception of error.
When, even upon searching with effort, no error is perceived in another person, then the suspicion of error regarding one's own object is indeed removed.
For through the inference from behavior, one perceives that "my apprehension of the self is of such a kind, and so too is his"—thus a similar cognition is recognized.
It has been stated that the connection [of the means of knowledge] is not applicable when the self, which is to be apprehended, is not grasped. Therefore, this statement of the scripture is logical;
moreover, analogy is also presented here as a means of explanation.
And since the verbal report is preceded by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction between the definition and its practical application.
As for what is also said, "That consciousness should be seen as the opening of that [door]," is this not already answered by the statement, "It is self-cognizable"?
And it is not appropriate to raise again what has already been answered.
Now, if this is the intended meaning— that this is not an answer to anything else—
then to what is it an answer?
If it is an answer to nothing at all, does it become an answer simply by virtue of that?
(The opponent says: "But surely, because it is mentioned immediately after that, it is understood to be its answer.
(The partisan replies: "Because a further question is stated, it is not indeed an answer;
for an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than mere sequence."
The proponent says: This is a delusion regarding space. Both [objections] are answered by that very same [text]:
"He becomes self-cognizable"—this too is an answer based on an inferential mark (*liṅga*), as is the statement "he is this."
And its capacity to refute that has already been explained;
why, then, is there this question again?
Is there not something small [remaining]?
(Supporting this, he says: Truly, "I know this" is what is experienced; there is no postulation of another form [of the self].

(However, the apprehension of the self as distinct from cognition is not possible, because its activity is not perceived [since it is understood that the self is known while cognizing an object; thus, the apprehension of a self devoid of cognition is not possible, and therefore there must also be an apprehension of cognition]).
Furthermore, because no other form is perceived within consciousness, it is again empty.
For consciousness, when being apprehended by something, must be apprehended as having a form, since there is no apprehension of that which is devoid of form.
And therein, since no other form distinct from blue and so forth is perceived, it follows that [consciousness] itself possesses the nature of blue and so forth.
Consequently, it follows that cognitions are devoid of objects.
Therefore, since the object to be sublated remains established as being based on the apprehension of consciousness, this knot of egoism is nothing but a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The phrase "this is but a trifle" is stated once again as a further presentation.
If [the opponent] says, "You are negating the means itself," what is the intention of the respondent?

This is the intention: the verses concerning apprehension (*grahaṇaśloka*) indeed follow the nature of the primary object (*ādyānukāritā*); they do not function as the nature of the apprehender (*grāhakakāritā*). By you, non-means-ness (*anupāyatva*)—[the correct reading is *upāyataiva*]—has been presented. [How can the goal (*upeya*) be explained if it is without a means?]
This is what he says: "If you deny the means itself, it is not possible to reach the goal without a means;
this very [means] is the method for the mere cognition of what is already known.

Likewise, by the statement, "What is called white? That in which whiteness exists," what is established? This is established: that the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is not apprehended [as an external reality].

But surely, in this way, the cognition of the white [object] would be preceded by whiteness itself (and likewise, the cognition of the object of knowledge would be preceded by knowledge itself); and thus, an unintended consequence would be established.
It is not unintended.
This much has been stated by him: that although the means of attainment (*upeya*) exists, there is no consciousness of them that is not preceded by those [means].

Therefore, the state of being an object of knowledge for all cognitions is established for the Self, as expressed in the commentary: "I have seen this. Consequently, the state of being an object of the omniscient [Self] is established: "I have seen this. There is this distinction: even in inference and other means of knowledge, there is direct perception [of the Self] (because the Self appears in immediate intuition even during inference and so forth; thus, it is indeed direct perception even in inference and the like).
The difference between the means of knowledge arises from the difference in objects, not from a difference in the knower.
The nature of knowledge as a subject (*pramātṛtva*), however, cannot possibly be denied, because it is impossible to deny it (by what means?).
And this is logical, exactly as suspected, because action is directed toward an object; for an action that possesses an object (*sakarmaka*) has the object as its primary element.
As for the claim that the state of being a knower cannot be understood apart from knowledge, that is because the understanding of that [state] is dependent upon it.
As for the argument that "no other form is perceived," that too has been answered by the statement, "Granted, one might deny consciousness, but not the object.
Therefore, its status as the Self is established.
Furthermore, as for the Brāhmaṇa passage stating, "There is no consciousness after death," that has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa itself through its own preceding and succeeding context.
And thus, the firmness of the meaning is presented.
Furthermore, the expression "na caiva vidhividhanda" has also been employed.

Now, if [the word] "eṣaḥ" is used in a sense that is logically established, how is it that [one] "goes to the heavenly world" (*svarge loke yāti*)? It is established because the desire of the qualified person (*adhikṛta*) is fulfilled.

It is appropriate [to say]: "The notions of 'I' and 'mine' are misconceptions of self regarding that which is not the self. However, this should be taught only to those whose passions have been subdued (*muditakaṣāya*), and not to those bound by the accumulation of karma (*karmasaṅgin*); so it is understood. And the Blessed Lord Dvaipāyana has said in the section on secrets: "One should not cause a disturbance of the intellect in the ignorant who are bound by karma" (Bhagavad Gītā 3.26).
Therefore, the venerable Commentator has here refuted [the objection] in accordance with other scriptural statements, and not out of ignorance.
*Bṛhatī*, Straightforward Exposition, p.

147. Regarding the doctrine of the self (*ātmavāda*), as for the statement presented which contradicts perception—namely, "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhī*), goes to the heavenly world by means of the sacrifice"—it is argued that this [text] teaches through its words that the perceptible body is what is joined with the sacrificial implements.

To this it is replied: because this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and is intended for another purpose, the fault of contradicting other means of knowledge regarding its own literal meaning does not apply.
Nor is there any contradiction;

for by this it is not said that the body goes to heaven. What then? It is the Self to whom this body belongs who is designated as such through metaphorical identification with the body—because of the non-difference between the body and the embodied one—and because he is present within the body and possesses the sacrificial implements.
Or rather, the going to heaven of the Self is metaphorically attributed to the body; thus, there is no contradiction.
The word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) also denotes that very [Self] because He is the owner of the sacrifice and its agent;
nor can His non-agency be asserted—as the followers of Kapila do—because that would contradict the Śruti.
For everywhere, the designation of being both agent and enjoyer is seen in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
As in this very context: "The sacrificer goes to the heavenly world"; and as:
"He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar, [attains] the *ṛc* and the *sāman*"; and: "He who, knowing thus, by means of the doctrine of the Self..."
The reference to the milk of the sun (ādityapayas) is made as a specification,
so that it may be understood how the *caru* and the barley (*yavas*) are to be combined. In that case,
when the *caru* is being offered, the milk mixed with it is necessarily offered along with it.
This is the presentation of it:
when it is being cooked with milk, the manner in which its presentation should be performed is specified.
Therefore, this milk is for the purpose of the sacrifice, specifically for the sake of the sacrificial food (*annājya*).

Because of the similarity in form, it is called "food" (bhojana) [derived] from sacrifice (yāga). And therefore, for the purpose of offering the milk, the ritual properties of the milk (payodharma) are combined with it.
He says:
Sacrifice is not merely the act of relinquishing.
That relinquishing which is performed with reference to a deity constitutes a sacrifice.
This is what is said.
"This [offering] also is performed as a renunciation dedicated to the deity of the quarters," he says.
[The opponent replies:
"The deity of the quarters is not the milk."
A deity is not established by mere mention alone;
rather, that which is heard [to belong] to someone is the deity of that person.
And this [mention] is heard in relation to the sacrificial porridge (caru), not in relation to the milk.
It is said: because of the mention of both.
By means of both, the deity is joined together, like honey and water once they have been mixed.

Just as in the case of "curd, honey, ghee, and water—these mixed together constitute the *prājāpatya* [oblation]," so too here, although the *caru* and the barley-gruel (*yavasī*) are indicated by the locative case, the meaning of the locative itself is not intended to be significant; rather, it is merely the mention [of the substance] that is intended.
Just as when it is said, "having added curd to the rice, it should be consumed," only the mention of the rice is intended, and not its status as a locus (the vessel).
The same applies here to the substance.
Therefore, the milk is for the purpose of offering;
and the milk-heating (*payogharma*) must be performed for the purpose of offering.
And the prohibition of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is likewise.
Commentary: And by establishing this, the prohibition of certain purificatory rites for the items to be offered becomes logical, as in:
"He drives away the calves without a mantra," and "He milks the cow while it is without a strainer.
For a prohibition is appropriate only when [the rite] has already been established.
And when that is prohibited, such [an object] is likewise avoided in common usage.
The Commentary states: "When that is prohibited—meaning when there is a prohibition—such a thing is also avoided in the world. For example: 'water sprinkled with milk' and 'milk boiled with milk'."
Nor is this a property of a substance intended for cooking,
such as water used for the purpose of boiling.

If there were a prohibition in that context, then when oil has been drunk, one would not be allowed to drink water— even though water is required for the gruel and barley broth that are being consumed.
And it is not the case that milk is avoided in this world simply because it is of such a nature;
for it is intended for consumption.
Just as milk exists in the world, so too should it be here; thus have I designated it by way of general principle.
"But there is unrighteousness (*adharma*) because of non-giving; since the injunction concerns the prepared substance, there is a connection [of the milk] due to its being equal [to the curd].
(In all manuscripts, the reading found here is *adharmatvam apra*...;
however, in the Bhāṣya, the reading *adharmatvaṃ tu payasaḥ* is printed in the main text, while the variant *adharmakaṃ tu payaḥ* is shown in the marginal note.)
Since this is indeed a *siddhāntasūtra*, the word "tu" (but/however) is absolutely necessary; moreover, it is actually read in the Bhāṣya.
However, the word "tu" is not found in the universally accepted recension.
Therefore, it is clear that the universal reading is not correct.
This being the case, "tvapradānāt" (due to the addition of the suffix -tva) is obtained.

However, regarding the consideration of what the word might have been prior to that—whether it was "adharmatvam" or simply "adharma"—since the compound "taddharma" ending in "-aniścayatva" was read as a bahuvrīhi in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the first sūtra, it is appropriate to read "adharma" ending in "-aniścayatva" alone even in the siddhānta-sūtra, and not "adharmatvam," because of the resulting lack of uniformity (*vairūpyāt*).
A disagreement regarding "similarity" (*sādharman*) and "dissimilarity" (*adharmatā*) is appropriate, but not regarding "the state of being similar and dissimilar" (*sādharman-adharmatvam*).
Therefore, I have accepted the reading here as *adharma-tvapradānāt* alone;
in Vivalakara’s work as well, the reading is precisely *adharma-tvapra*.
Commentary: "But milk is *adharma* (devoid of ritual properties); its ritual properties (*pradeyadharma*) would not apply to it"—this is the meaning.
(In this context, the reading in the Bhāṣya is *adharmatvaṃ tu payasaḥ nāsya*;
the reading in the Bhāṣya-marginal-note is *adharmakaṃ tu payaḥ nāsya*.)
Furthermore, the reading in the Bhāṣya is "pradeyapayodharmāḥ," whereas the reading in the Bhāṣya-commentary (bhā-ṭippaṇyāḥ) is "pradeyadharmāḥ.
This being the case, I have inferred that the reading in the Bhāṣya itself was indeed different. Why? Because it is not given away (apradānāt).
For this [gift] is not actually bestowed.

But is it not the case that when the cooked rice (caru) is being offered, it is said that "it is caused to be given," and for this purpose, cooking in milk is prescribed? No, he says; for it is understood that this is for the purpose of ensuring that the *śruti* (direct Vedic injunction) remains intact. There is a specific requirement for the husked grains (*taṇḍula*).

For it is not the case that "the *dharma* is something other"; nor is such a purpose heard [in the scripture] regarding cooked rice and milk. How so? Because they are prescribed for the purpose of the *praṇītā* water.
But surely, since there would thus be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), this very position has already been abandoned.
It was stated that "the oblation here becomes mixed. To this it is replied:
There is no combination because of their inequality;
for the cooked rice (*caru*) and the milk (*payas*) are unequal.
From direct perception, the milk is heard as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), while the cooked rice is heard as the substance to be offered (*pradeya*).
That which is understood through the sentence as being something to be offered in milk is set aside by the direct statement (*adhikaraṇa-śruti*) [that it is the locus].
As for the claim that this results in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), that is not so; for there will be no connection such as "the *caru* is in milk."
How then? [It is said: "The sun is in the milk. Both are connected by the word "sun" (āditya). The sun—

In the section concerning "the milk of the sun" (*ādityapayas*), the two words *caru* and *payas*—which are heard as "sun" (*āditya*)—will thus have the sun as their primary referent; there will be no contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
The sun will be that which has milk as its substrate.
Therefore, the properties pertaining to the material to be offered (pradeya-dharma) cannot apply to the milk.
The subsequent [passage] would be a constant restatement (nityānuvāda).

Commentary: Now, as for what was stated [in the Sūtra], namely, "he separates the calves without a sacrificial formula" (ayujuṣā vatsānapākaroti) and "he milks the cow while it is not yet provided with the strainer" (apavitravati gāṃ dohayati).
This being the case, this does not establish the meaning [of the text].
What then? It is a constant restatement (nityānuvāda);
it restates that which already exists within this [text] eternally.
The calves are not driven away by means of the *yajus* formula because it is not something to be given; nor is the cow milked in the *pavitra* vessel. [Objection:
But is this not a useless restatement of what is already established?
[Reply: It is said:
We do not investigate whether [the sentence] possesses a purpose or lacks a purpose;

rather, we examine what is understood from this sentence. And from this sentence, it is understood that calves are not separated by means of a *yajus* formula, nor is a cow milked at the *pavitra* rite.
And that [is so] because it is not to be given away, and because it is a *yajus* and a purifier.
Or rather, it is a prohibition of what has been prescribed.
The Commentary states: "Alternatively, a prohibition of that which was indeed prescribed should be understood."
For some, it is prescribed: "He drives away the calves with a Yajus formula; he causes the cow to be milked when the *pavitra* [strainer] is present.

Its prohibition is indeed meaningful. Because avoidance is subordinate to the primary act, there would be a prohibition of what was previously stated; for that reason, it serves as a mere defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Commentary: Regarding what was stated—that when milk is prohibited, both that which is sprinkled with milk and that which is mixed with it are to be avoided—we reply: for in common worldly usage, it is logical that only that which is mixed [with the prohibited substance] is excluded; indeed, it is precisely that which is prohibited in such cases.
For milk is always used as a subordinate ingredient in food;
where it is used, a prohibition is meaningful.
Where it is not used, however, a prohibition would be purposeless, since there is no possibility of its occurrence.
But is not the *kevala* also consumed at the *paya* [oblation]?
It is said: it is called *kevala* because of its cause; that is, he who has either the *kevala-lakṣaṇa* or the *vrataudana* consumes the *kevala*.
But that [milk] is not abundant.

Therefore, because milk generally constitutes a subordinate element, the prohibition of milk is stated for the purpose that one should not eat anything joined with milk, since it is subordinate to the milk. And this is like the case of the smearings, due to the nature of the substance.
Commentary: Now, why is this another refutation? It is said:
"This should be viewed as being like the opinion [of others].
Just as it is said, "A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) must not eat meat..."

When it is said, "One should not eat," they avoid even the smear of food that has entered the ladle; likewise here too, when it is said, "Milk should not be drunk," they will avoid what is sprinkled with milk or mixed with milk.
Or rather, it is a prohibition against the taste, because this is a duty pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*).
[Bhāṣya: This is certainly not a valid rebuttal.
The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to exclude other possible interpretations.
Why? Because the vow (*vrata*) is a duty pertaining to the person. For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), the eating of meat is prohibited by the very nature of his obligation.

In that case, even for one who consumes it only to the extent that the mere taste of meat-juice is perceived, there is a fault; this does not depend on any observed effect such as the provocation of phlegm (*śleṣman*).
But it is not so in the case of the prohibition regarding milk.
Therefore, the previous resolution remains valid.
Śabara: "The sentence, by enjoining two distinct meanings—namely, the connection of the sacrificial porridge with the deity and the connection of the milk with the sacrificial porridge—is split."

"Therefore, the milk is not mixed with the properties of the *pradeya* (the substance to be offered), such as the *apākaraṇa* (the ritual act of setting aside). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: By means of the *caru* acting as the substratum and the milk, a specific distinction is established;
here, a connection between each pair of deities is also enjoined."

Therefore, the properties of the *pradeya* (the substance to be offered) apply to the milk. [Objection: Since the *daśārṇaudaura* sacrifice lacks the status of an *agnihotra*, even though the properties of its extraction (*uddharaṇa*) might apply, how can the properties of the *pradeya* apply to the milk, given that the milk serves as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) to the primary offering? [Response: This is the connection [of the argument], because it is established that the offering is seen to occur simultaneously with the cooking; for the *caru* is abandoned together [with the other ingredients], just as in the case of the injunction: "Curd, honey, the fast-food, water, and parched grains. The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Even in the case of simultaneous cooking, the offering is also seen to be simultaneous, because the *caru* is being abandoned together [with the other substances], as in the example: "Curd, honey, the fast-food, water, and parched grains."

And because the milk is mixed [with the flour], and since it is a substance intended for the sacrifice, the properties of the *pradeya* (the material to be offered) should apply to it. [The Siddhāntin] says: "The properties of the *pradeya* should not apply to the milk in the *Prāyaṇīya* offering.
They should apply as in the case of the *caru* (cooked rice), because the locative case [in 'payasi'] indicates the cause of cooking; therefore, [the properties do not follow]."

Bhaṭṭa: In the passage "The *āditya* [offering] is a *caru* of milk for the *prāyaṇīya* [rite]," because of the mention of "in milk" (*payasi*) as a locative designation, milk is not the substance of the oblation; rather, it belongs to the *caru* itself, since its connection with the deity is established through its grammatical coreferentiality with the *taddhita* suffix.
As for the milk, it serves merely as a characteristic of the substrate (*adharmatva-lakṣaṇa-mātra*); therefore, the properties of the material to be offered (*pradeya-dharma*) do not apply there.
However, the properties of the consecrated water (*praṇīta-dharma*) do apply there—so says the wise one.

In reality, however, since the *caru* is for the purpose of the *saṃyana* (the mixing), and that [mixing] is absent in the case of the *caru*, it has been stated that those [rites] also simply do not occur.

Although the apprehension regarding the attainment of the properties of the *pradeya* (the substance to be offered) cannot be otherwise [dismissed], nevertheless, in the context of the Āditya sacrifice, there is an injunction of the *yajus* and the *pavitra* by way of restating the already established *savāpākaraṇa* (driving away the calves) and so forth— such as "he drives away the calves without a *yajus*" and "he milks the cow with a non-*pavitra* [strainer]"— just as in the case of the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*, where the intention of the locative case in the originative statement (*utpattivākya*) is [to restrict the time].
This being the case, since this [passage] is justified even as a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), there is no intention to express the sense of the locative case.

In reality, however, since only the milk already established in common worldly usage would be applicable at that time, and because the duties such as heating and so forth are not otherwise established and must necessarily be enjoined, yet all other [details] are merely constant restatements, there is no intention to express the sense of the locative case.
Therefore, the properties of the object of knowledge do not apply there.
The Abhyuditeṣṭi sacrifice will be discussed in the subsequent section.
Maṇḍana [states]: “The properties of milk apply to the sun.
Śaṅkara [states]: “Milk is to be offered, not to the sun.”
*Ādityavad yaugapadyam* (simultaneity like the sun).

As for the objection that it is impossible for a single entity existing in one place to be perceived simultaneously in multiple locations: [the answer is] "like the sun" (*ādityavat*). Just as the sun, though being one, is seen as if situated in many places, so too is the word.
Bhāṣya 1.2.6.15: *Ādityavad yaugapadyam*.
Nor is it possible for seventeen *prājāpatya* terms uttered in the ritual manual to be reduced by the grammatical principle of *ekaśeṣa*, because of the recognition of the identity of the word.
Thus it has been said: "Simultaneity is like that of the sun";
here, the recognition of oneness is stated.

Or [it is like] the sun (vā. 2|3|126). The meaning of the sūtra is that simultaneity is like that of the sun; just as there is no difference in the sun despite its being perceived simultaneously in various locations, so it is with sound as well. (Su. p. 960). Furthermore, from the Āditya vessel, the Āgrayaṇa vessel comes for the sake of the two deities.
From the Āgrayaṇa vessel, [the draught] is taken from the water-vessel in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
The *Sāman* named ‘Ādityātmā’ is prescribed [in the *Anuvākya*].
Bāla. p. 72. The cups (*graha*) beginning with the Āditya are [drawn] at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

Injunctions depend upon the intrinsic nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*). (Bṛhatī). Therefore, having understood the intrinsic nature of things, their meaning should be described. (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 243).

"Oṃ: That which was first established by a low-caste person is proven by means of logic"—this is the maxim. Now, [one might object]: "It should be reflected upon through reasonings" (*mantavyaścaupapattibhiḥ*)—here the word *aupapatti* from the Smṛti; "the intellect which is well-refined" (*matiryā suparīkṣitā*)—here the word *yukta* from the Smṛti; and "it should be heard from the sentences of the Śruti" (*śrotavyaḥ śrutivākyebhyaḥ*)—here the word *śruti*. Since these do not lose their general sense, according to the maxim: "In the beginning, by the mere meaning of words dependent on reasoning," this is the meaning of every sentence.

If it is argued that since "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) is the grasping of the meaning of the Vedas through a teacher and "reflection" (*manana*) is the subsequent investigation by means of logic (*nyāya*), there would be no justification for speaking of a distinction between hearing and reflection within the context of the [logical] arguments themselves;

[the reply is: (First, at the outset, that very reality which was established and known through the hearing of the Upanishads and so forth, preceded by faith—that same [reality] is subsequently established by reflection, which consists of the investigation of logic. This is the purpose of the meaning of logic. (Ke. Adhyanta. p. 34.32–37).

The first is primary (mukhya) and the other is secondary (jaghanya). Between the primary and the secondary, whichever one remains when the other is omitted, the secondary should be dropped; the primary is to be favored. Bhāṣya 10.5.1.9. In modified forms (vikṛti), when there is an option to take either part, the inclusion of the first [elements] entails the omission of the others, according to the number [required].

For example: "The two-potherd [cake] for the Aśvins," "the three-potherd for Viṣṇu," and "the eight-potherd for Agni. Whatever the first substance of the eight-potherd [cake] may be, its ritual properties (dharmas) are to be adopted in the two-potherd [cake] for the Aśvins, and so forth.

✻ The section concerning the exception to the inclusion of the first [term]. Regarding the rule "of that which possesses sequence," it was established in that section that the inclusion of the word "first" implies the elision of others; this [present rule] concerns those numbers that do not possess such sequence.
Thus, an exception (*apavāda*) is made.
[The rule] "the first [day] is for the *ādyātvan*" is established.

Just as elsewhere the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is prescribed in the *Ādyāna* sacrifice—by the statement, "He who would be the *ṣoḍaśin-ādyāsnu* should observe the vow (*vrata*) on this night," and by the injunction, "He should not eat meat; he should not approach a woman"—the fasting of the *adhvaryu* priest is prescribed; likewise, in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, by the statement, "All the officiating priests fast," the fasting of the priests is prescribed. In the same way, here too (in the *sattra*), the refinement will belong to the officiating priests alone.
"The Āghāta [offering] has the Adhvaryu as its performer.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not performed for one who has already entered the state of maintaining the fires (*agnicayanagata*), nor for one desiring specific results (*kāmya*), nor for one who has obtained fire from a wooden drill (*vārkṣa*), nor for one who has obtained it by friction (*āpta*), because the fires are already established and because the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) would be of no further use.
(Vi. 12.1.9). The establishment of the fires is not connected with ritual acts that have already been consumed by the fires;
rather, the fires are for the purpose of all ritual acts.
Thus it is said that [the ritual] serves all purposes.
Bhāṣya 3.6.5.15: Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), [it is stated]: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fire with twelve steps; a Rājanya with eleven; a Vaiśya with twelve.
(The *prakrama* may be either one step or two steps.)
✻ The sacrificial vessels must be maintained from the very commencement of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration).
1.1.3. 14.47–40. The *ādhāna* is a subsidiary act (*guṇakarma*) that brings about excellence (*bheda*).
Bāla., p. 81. Regarding the *ādhāna*, there is an alternative view: "One should establish the fire with the eye as the cause" (*cakṣurnimittam ādadhyāt*).
One must determine the location simply by seeing it with the eye;

the establishment [of the fires] (*ādhāna*) is based on the eye. (The Bhāṣya states: "Is the establishment for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), or is the establishment for the sake of all rites? In the *Tantraratna*, within the section describing the acquisition of materials (4.1.2.12, Section 3), it is stated that the establishment is neither for the sake of the sacrifice nor for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

The *Siddhāntavārtika* in the *Tantraratna* explains the intent of the statement “the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not for the sake of a human purpose” as follows: “Just as the acquisition of property is understood through direct perception to be for the sake of a human purpose, the establishment of the fires is not so understood. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 81). The establishment of the fires is not for the sake of the *Pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices. (Bhāṣya 3.6.4.11–13).
