The re-establishment of the fires (*punarādhāna*) is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when both [fires] have been destroyed.

The act of kindling (ādhāna) does not reside in the primary rite itself; rather, it is the fires consecrated by the act of kindling that are employed in subsequent sacrifices such as the Agnihotra. (Vi. 3.6.5).
The act of kindling is the principal element, while the Sāman-chanting is its subordinate quality.

Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.2.12.9, p. 810. The establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is heard in scripture as being connected with one's wife. Just as the establishment of the fires is an accessory for the purpose of consecrating the fire, so too the oblations of the Pavamāna days are accessories belonging to the fire. The establishment of the fires is the common framework (tantra) for all ritual acts, and not performed separately for each individual act.
Furthermore, since the substance [the fire] is not established at a specific time for the sake of the ritual action, its application should serve all purposes, because it possesses its own time.
The Bhāṣya states: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn"—thus the establishment (ādhāna) is heard in the scripture.
That [fire] pertains to the primary ritual action and so forth simultaneously.
What is the reason? Because it lacks a specific fruit [of its own].

"One offers oblations in the Āhavanīya fire," "one cooks the sacrificial offerings in the Gārhapatya fire," and "one performs the cooking of the Anvāhārya mess and other rites in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire"—such is the application of those fires to ritual actions.

In this regard, it is deliberated: should the establishment (*ādhāna*) of that fire be performed separately for each distinct type of ritual action, or is there a single common procedure (*tantra*) for all actions—those pertaining to the *iṣṭis*, those pertaining to the animals (*pāśuka*), those pertaining to the Soma sacrifices (*saumika*), and those pertaining to the domestic oblations (*gṛhamedhīya*)? What is the prima facie view? Since the substance—the fire—is established at a time other than the time of the specific ritual acts, namely in spring, summer, or autumn, the performance of the establishment should be for the sake of all [rituals].
Why? Because it has its own independent time.
The time for the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice is spring and so forth. No specific time for any particular ritual action is heard [in the scripture].
In that case, no distinction is grasped as to whether the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is for this ritual action and not for that one.
Since no distinction [between the acts] is perceived, it is logical that the *tantra* (the common performance) applies.
But surely, a distinction is perceived in that the consecration (*ādhāna*) is understood as being for the sake of whichever rite is performed after the consecration?
Indeed, that distinction is perceived.

However, infinity alone is the cause. Even when [the word] refers to all objects, there must still be a prior application of it to some specific action, because simultaneity is impossible. Thus, in both cases—whether it refers to all objects or to a single object—infinity is an equal reason.
Because of its equality, it does not become a cause;
nor are the rites undertaken with respect to the *ādhāna*, as is the case with the *prayāṇa*.
If they were undertaken [with respect to it], then the undertaking of whichever rite follows immediately after it would be understood.
Since no specific distinction is mentioned regarding the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), it serves all purposes;
nor is there a restriction such as "only for this.
For when many [rites] are performed according to various conditions (*nimitta*), it is inevitable that some degree of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) will occur between them.

Since there is no fixed rule for any specific ritual action at the time of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), it is understood as being intended for all [subsequent rites] precisely because of its subsequent prescription (*anudeśa*).
Therefore, due to its independent timing, it possesses the quality of being a *tantra* (common/shared element).

For this very reason, even though this [time] is fit for performance, it is seen as a mere specific quality consisting in the particular timing prescribed for each respective *Vājapeya*, and thus it serves as a common factor for every *Vājapeya*.

Nor does it follow that because each of the six sacrifices is individually denoted by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*, there would be a contingency of repeating the *ārambhaṇīyā*—which is performed prior to both the commencement of the Full Moon sacrifice and the New Moon sacrifice—due to the difference in time; for even though they are performed separately due to the difference in time, since these six sacrifices share a single fruit and possess a single great resolve (*mahā-saṃkalpa*) from the very beginning, their unity is established.

Furthermore, it should be noted that even when times are independent, where another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) indicates that a specific individual instance is the intended object (*uddeśyatā*), repetition occurs there as well, because the remainder (*śeṣa*) is being grasped.
Maṇḍana: "The substratum for all things is one [independent] autonomy.
Śaṅkara:
"Since its very existence is absent, that [autonomy] is as far removed as possible from being the material cause."

Nor does the non-performance of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) result in a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) of the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*), because a deficiency would only occur in the absence of the fires themselves. In fact, however, since the injunctions for the seasonal sacrifices are logically established by the mere fact that the *ādhāna* has been accomplished—and thus do not themselves independently necessitate it—the one who has not performed the *ādhāna* simply lacks the qualification (*anadhikāra*) for the seasonal sacrifices; therefore, the suspicion of a deficiency is cast far away. Likewise, it is most reasonable that the *pavamāneṣṭis* are also not to be performed [by such a person].

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is enjoined by a distinct ritual injunction at a different time from the *Amāvāsya* sacrifice, there is no evidence for its being a specific qualification (*adhikāraviśeṣa*) even if it were performed once for all purposes—as in the case of the *Bṛhaspatisava* and other such rites. Consequently, the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) sacrifices could proceed according to one's capacity even without the *ādhāna*.
However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because the *ādhāna* serves to establish the necessary qualification, it is not so.
Maṇḍana states: "This [fire] is for the sake of the fire-altar; it is not a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) of the rituals."
"This is the *ādhāna* (consecration).
Śaṃkara says: 'That [consecration] is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action.
Through *ādhāna*, the consecration of the fire is effected; it is not, however, that a consecration of the ritual action itself is performed."

Bhāṣya 11.3.1.125: By means of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), one acquires a specific fire; by this, which is under one's own control, it is shown that the *ādhāna* is preceded by an *iṣṭi* (sacrifice) and that the commencement of the *agnihotra* occurs even before that.

And therefore, from the statement "one should place wet wood upon the fire of one who has established the sacred fires" (*āhitāgnim*), just as in the case of one who possesses the *āhitāgni* status, the commencement of the sacrifice (*kratu*) occurs only after the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author of the Bhāṣya [states] that although there is no hearing of mutual dependence (*nairāpekṣya*) in those respective sentences, there is no evidence for the claim that one [the *pavamāneṣṭis*] is productive (*utpādaka*) and the other [the *ādhāna*] is merely purificatory (*saṃskāraka*).

On the contrary, since it is understood from their own injunctions (*niyojaka-vākya*) that the *pavamāneṣṭis* themselves produce the *āhavanīya* fire, the production of the *āhavanīya* by the *ādhāna*—as understood from its subsidiary statements (*guṇavākya*)—is a matter of delayed comprehension.

Nor is there an option between the two being equally adoptable; for their combination is established simply by the injunctions regarding time, such as "one should offer immediately" and "one should offer after twelve nights.

According to the Vārtika school, however, since the Sāṅkhya fire-installation (ādhāna) is productive [of the fires], the fires are not established in its absence. Nor can the Pavamāna-iṣṭis be considered merely stabilizers—as in the case of the Bṛhaspatisava—because even though they are included within the performance of the fire-installation, there is no scriptural statement that the manifestation of the bhāvanā (productive operation) having the fire-installation as its instrument occurs here [independently]; thus, the assumption of them being stabilizers is untenable.
Therefore, since there is no determination of the *āhavanīya* fire apart from the *pavamāneṣṭi*, the *agnihotra* and other rites must follow immediately after that.

Furthermore, even though one has become an *āhitāgni*, the designation "one who has established the fires" (*āhitāgni*) is logically applicable to a person only after the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration); thus, the performance of those rites occurs immediately thereafter.
As for the illustrative example cited, it is intended as praise for the *tūṣṇīhoma* being an auxiliary to the *ādhāna*, and it does not indicate the prior commencement of the *agnihotra*.

For the silent oblation (*tūṣṇīhoma*) is not the Agnihotra oblation, because there is no authoritative evidence [to that effect]. Nor does it possess the characteristics (*dharma*) of the Agnihotra, because a name occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not effect an extension [of ritual details]. Furthermore, since this oblation also serves as a means for employing the fire through the act of installation (*ādhāna*), its connection with the fire is indistinguishable from that of the Agnihotra; and like terms such as *prāyaṇīya*, it does not effect an extension [of the Agnihotra's details].
Therefore, this is a praise of the *apūrva* (unprecedented) nature of the oblation (*homa*), and thus it is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the prior performance of the *agnihotra*.

Furthermore, even for those [acts] embraced within a distinct ritual application (*prayoga*), it has been established according to the view of Paurṇapātra that they function by way of incidental benefit (*prasaṅga*).

It should also be noted that the meaning of the chapter is simply the sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*), common to both direct connection (*vyavahitānvaya*) and indirect connection (*upakāra*).
Maṇḍana [states]: "The *sāṃpāvana* is the ritual action here;
the *oṃkāra* is superior to the *agnihotra* and other sacrifices.
Thus, the *agnihotra* and other such sacrifices are to be performed as the highest [duty].

This is the principle: "Because the time for the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived," as stated in [Jaimini Sūtra 6.8.21]: "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity, because the time for that fire-consecration has not yet arrived."
The phrase "the case concerning the slaughter of animals for scattering [the hair]" (avakīrṇapaśuvadhi-karaṇa) should be considered and examined (6.8.4.22).

The logical meaning is that prior to marriage, the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is not possible for a religious student (brahmacārin), because at that time the proper period for the establishment of the fires has not yet arrived.
Ke.

The necessity of *ādhāna* (the formal establishment of the sacred fires) is determined from the statement, "One should not go [on a journey] without having established the fires" (*anāhitāgnibhir na yāyāt*).

Su. p. 915. Regarding the view that *ādhāna* must be preceded by an *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering), there is the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the *paurṇamāsī-tāgnīṣomīya* oblation of the Brāhmaṇa prior to the Soma sacrifice;
however, some authorities maintain that only the *paurṇamāsa-iṣṭi* itself is postponed.
There is an option between having the *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering) as the predecessor and having the *soma* sacrifice as the predecessor for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration).
The statement regarding the priority of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice.
The Commentary: The priority of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice is traditionally handed down in connection with the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the priority of the *iṣṭi* and the priority of the *soma* sacrifice to be taken as optional alternatives, or is it the case that the priority of the *iṣṭi* alone must be observed?
What is established? It must be that the *iṣṭi* comes first. Why? Because of a scriptural statement (*vacana*).

This statement is as follows: "The New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are indeed the chariot of the gods; he who, having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, sacrifices with Soma, dwells at the very end on the chariot-track of the gods"—the meaning is that he stands [there] for the sake of completion.
Thus,
there is no excessive burden of scriptural authority.
Therefore, the sacrifice must indeed be preceded by the *iṣṭi*.

Because there is a statement regarding the transgression of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) for the *Soma* sacrifice which is to be performed after the *Ādhāna*, that [statement] would otherwise be purposeless.
The Commentary says: We accept that the *Iṣṭi* must come first;
however, for these [sacrifices], the *Soma* sacrifice comes before the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*.
Why? Because of the statement regarding the transgression of seasons and constellations in the case of the *agnyādheya*:
"He who, intending to sacrifice with Soma, should establish the fires (*agnīnādadhīta*), must not wait for a constellation.

This means that he who establishes the fires in order to perform the Soma sacrifice need not wait for a constellation nor even for a season; rather, he should establish them immediately—thus, immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is expressed.

Otherwise, the statement regarding the transgression of the season and the lunar mansion would be meaningless. If immediate succession were not intended, then disregard for those two [the season and the lunar mansion] would be declared only in cases where they have been specifically mentioned. Therefore, there is indeed an immediate succession between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna).
Moreover, the present tense suffix is clearly manifest in the expression "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*).
When that [suffix] is intended to express the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, it does not intend to express the present time; in that case, this word would be contradicted.
Therefore, it is understood that there is an intention to express immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
Objection: Soma should be performed even before the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
How so? Because of the statement: "One who intends to sacrifice with Soma should establish the sacred fires" (Ṣoḍaśin).
This indicates that the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) must be preceded by an *iṣṭi*.
For it is heard in scripture that Soma [is to be performed] after the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*);
and that is possible only when [Soma] possesses a unique status distinct from other rituals.

If one were to sacrifice with Soma after the time of the *ādhāna* (and even before the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s), rather than after the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s, then there would be a non-common relationship [between the person and the sacrifice]. Otherwise, the person would be sacrificing by means of all [rites], including the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, animal sacrifices, and the *dhanvan* sacrifice. In that case, the qualification "one who intends to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*) would not be appropriate. Furthermore, there is no such person who does not sacrifice at all with Soma, in relation to whom this qualification could apply.
For the Soma sacrifice is indeed obligatory.

(He states the meaning of the sūtra: And the prohibition regarding seasons and constellations is only applicable when there is immediate succession to the establishment of the sacred fires (and not otherwise).
For the time for the Soma sacrifice has been prescribed [in the rule]: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in the spring."
If that [Soma sacrifice] were prohibited, for what purpose would there be its injunction?

If, however, the prohibition of time refers to the Soma performed after the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration)—and not [to the rule] "one should not ask"—then the injunction of the spring season becomes purposeful with respect to the time following the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices (as it is ordained: "Having sacrificed with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, one should sacrifice with Soma").
(He concludes: Therefore, there are two times for the Soma sacrifice: before the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and after them.

(While this is the case regarding the legal topic, there arises a doubt: after the consecration (*ādhāna*), should the Soma sacrifice alone be performed without doing anything else, or should something else also be done in the interval? When this doubt arises, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that nothing else should be performed because of the understood immediate sequence between the consecration and the Soma sacrifice; to this, he states another position: Nor should it be thought that nothing else is to be performed after the consecration and that the Soma sacrifice alone is to be performed. Rather, even after performing the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, the Vrātya-animal sacrifice, and the Agnihotra, the Soma sacrifice is to be performed prior to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); with reference to this requirement, the specific qualification "one who intends to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*) is indeed justified as being non-common (*asādhāraṇya*).

(The Commentator does not accept this view, and thus says: According to what the Commentator has stated, the Vrātyapaśu sacrifice exists because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice; the Pavamāna offerings also certainly exist because they are purificatory rites for the fires (*agni-saṃskāra*).
However, the Agnihotra does not exist [in that state].
As for those who believe that the Vrātyapaśu exists only under the view that the Iṣṭis must precede [the Soma], we do not know what their basis is.
Ratna:

And because of the statement regarding that purpose, there is no lack of distinction; thus, it has that as its purpose. Bhāṣya: In this way, there is immediate succession between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna).
Why?
Because it is stated for that purpose.

For it is said: "He who, intending to sacrifice with Soma, should establish the sacred fires"—thus, everyone who intends to sacrifice establishes the fire, and by means of Soma alone does he establish it more excellently.
There would be no distinction regarding the Soma sacrifice;
otherwise, there would have to be a distinction such that the sequence between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the fires (agnyādhāna) constitutes this difference.
Furthermore, for one who intends to perform the sacrifice, there might be a doubt arising from the proximity [of the rites] due to the specification of the time for the Pavamāna oblations.
Commentary: The time for the Pavamāna offerings of one who intends to sacrifice with Soma is specified:
"He who, intending to sacrifice with Soma, establishes the sacred fires (agnīn ādadhīta), should offer [the Pavamāna oblations] at the three [full-moon days] before the end of the year.
Indeed, there is no one who does not intend to sacrifice, since it is prescribed for everyone.
Therefore, it is understood that [the Soma sacrifice] is to be performed immediately after [the Iṣṭi].
For one who intends to perform the Iṣṭi, the Soma sacrifice comes first because it serves that purpose.
Commentary: This sūtra is explained as stating the purpose.
The office has expired.

What is the purpose of this reflection? [It is to establish that] for one who has not yet performed the *iṣṭi*, there is the *soma* sacrifice; and for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) performed without a specific motive, the *soma* sacrifice must precede it.
This is because the *soma* sacrifice is intended for that purpose.
If, however, the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) were for the sake of the Soma sacrifice, then the Soma would necessarily have to precede it;

because there would inevitably be an intervention by the Soma Pavamāna offerings and the vow of silence (*vāgyama*), it would be impossible to enjoin immediate succession to the fire-laying. Thus, even from the perspective of the purpose (*artha*), the Soma does not precede the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Consequently, since there is no sublation of the scriptural sequence (*vācanika-krama*) here by anything else, this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) as a counter-argument.

In the sentence "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*), since both the Soma-sacrifice and the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) are already established by other sources as being characterized [by certain requirements], it is the consecration itself that must be enjoined in relation to the Soma; otherwise, there would be a lack of syntactic unity (*vākyabheda*).

In this regard, the Pavamāna-iṣṭis do not constitute an interruption, because they are part of the consecration and because they serve to establish the eligibility for the Soma-sacrifice following the Vrātya-animal sacrifice. Furthermore:
"Is the sequence of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-iṣṭi*) and the Soma-sacrifice fixed, or not?"
Uttareya says: No, because there is no scriptural statement regarding the immediate sequence of the Soma sacrifice after the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*).

Commentary: In the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), it is heard in scripture: "He who, intending to sacrifice with Soma, should consecrate the fires—let him not inquire about the lunar mansion.

However, it is not possible to enjoin the immediate sequence of the Soma sacrifice by means of that [text], because no such immediate sequence is explicitly stated, and because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, it is merely the disregard for the prescribed time that is enjoined with reference to the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).
The phrase "one who intends to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*), however, is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
By means of that [restatement], [the connection is made] with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

Regarding the fact that the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) must be preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice: since the originative injunction for the establishment of the fires is found in the text "The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) at the establishment," the establishment of the *āhavanīya* fire proceeds from the *gārhapatya* fire itself.
Saṃkarṣa:
Having considered the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) regarding the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), it is understood that the *sāmans* belong to another Veda;
however, because of the connection between the subsidiary and the principal acts, the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is also understood.

For if this origin [of these mantras] were in the Yajurveda alone, then the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) would be based solely on their own form. But since these [mantras] originate in the Sāmaveda, where loudness (*uccais-tva*) would naturally apply by virtue of their own form, the whispered nature is based on contact with the primary sacrifice; thus, it is a property of the primary act. (Vārttika 3.2.19, p. 810). Regarding the fire-laying (*ādhāna*): "Wearing linen garments, the two [husband and wife] should lay the fires."
In this context, the dual number expresses the intention of the couple. In a single act of consecration (*ādhāna*), the qualification belongs to one man alone together with his wife;
it does not belong to two men.

VI. 6.1.5. Regarding the *ādhāna* (fire-laying), the "unlimited" nature (*aparimitatva*) of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) constitutes a different number than the previously mentioned range ending at eleven.
Bhāṣya 6.1.122: Regarding the *ādhāna*, the "unlimited" nature of the sacrificial fees means they exceed one thousand;
there is no fixed rule because there is no specific distinction [stated].
Commentary: Regarding the statement "an unlimited amount is to be given," [the word] *aparimita* has been established as referring to another ritual alternative (*kalpāntara*).

Now, this is being questioned: is "unlimited" that which is less than a thousand, or is it more than a thousand? What, then, is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule, because there is no specific distinction.
No specific rule is observed here regarding whether [the number] is more than a thousand or less;
since no such rule is observed, it may be as one desires, and whatever is done is correct.
Therefore, there is no fixed restriction.
Or it may be more, because of its proximity with others due to having many referents.
The word "or" (*vā*) in the Bhāṣya serves to exclude that alternative position.
It is not the case that there is more or less than a thousand.
What then? It is precisely more. Why? Because the word "aparimita" (unlimited) has many meanings;
for it has been stated that people employ this word in the sense of "many."
Multiplicity is relative; something is called "much" only in relation to something else that is less than it.
Without such a relation, this [notion] would be incomplete.
For example, a son exists only in relation to someone, and not otherwise.
In this matter, the determination is made by considering both what is under discussion and what is proximate; and the "thousand" is proximate.
Therefore, that which is more than that is "immeasurable.
And the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is likewise.

Commentary: How is it so? In that regard, the phrase "the supreme is indeed the immeasurable" indicates that which exceeds a thousand. Śā [explains]: "For the meaning of 'much' is relative; since it is mentioned immediately after 'thousand,' it must therefore be more than a thousand."
Soma: The connection [of this topic] arises from the specific investigation mentioned previously.
Vi: Even prior to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), there is a plurality [of fires], as the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices are prescribed.
The Pavamāna-iṣṭis at the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) are intended for those [fires] specifically enjoined;
nor is there a single performance, but rather a performance connected with many.
Therefore, simultaneous performance is understood.
Regarding the statement, "The oblations are common," this is a restatement (anuvāda).

In that context, because of the injunction that "for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), all the oblations are to be prepared together," the *tantra* (common procedure) applies to the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) as enjoined by the scriptural declaration.
Therefore, with respect to that, there is a restatement (anuvāda).

In the case of the obligatory (nitya) performance of the Soma sacrifice, there is a single ritual procedure (samānatantratā), whereas in the optional (kāmya) performance, there is a difference in procedure. Although there is a disparity in the materials used in the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, there is no such disparity in the Pavamāna-iṣṭis; thus, the connection [of the present topic] has been stated.

Vi— "Is there a single *tantra* for the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices, or is there a difference? The first [position] is that there is no difference because of the non-distinction of the locus of the goal (*sādhyadeśa*) and so forth; the last [position] is that a difference is stated regarding the optional (*kāmya*) rites. Bhaṭṭa—The *pavamāneṣṭis* have multiple primary elements (*pradhāna*). Because of the injunction of a single performance (*prayoga*) qualified by those specific times, in the passage: "One should offer [the oblations] in a year, or in twelve days, or in four days; they are to be offered on a day," it is beyond dispute that they must be performed as a single performance, just like the rule: "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* [offering] on the full moon day."

For this very reason, in the statement "the offerings are to be prepared on the same day" (*aho nirupyāṇi*), if one accepts the meaning that "on the same day" (*sadyaḥ*) refers to being proximate to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), then even if one accepts merely the sublation of specific times such as a year, a single performance-injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*) is nonetheless necessary because of the necessity of a specific time in the sentence concerning the year.
And precisely by enjoining proximity to the *ādhāna* for that [single performance], the status of a single performance is established even in the case of the "same-day" (*sadyaḥ*) view.
For this very reason, the restatement (*anuvāda*) "they are to be prepared together" (*saha nirupyāṇi*) is also consistent.

Thus, although simultaneity (*sahatva*) is prescribed for the regular performance (*nityaprayoga*), by the principle of "separateness despite connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*, 4.3.15–17), simultaneity is enjoined for the sake of a specific result—just like [the simultaneous offering of] curd and other substances—in the passage: "He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), for him all [the oblations] should be offered together.

This being established, there is further heard in scripture: "He who should desire, 'May I become more prosperous and better at each successive stage,' for him, having offered to Pavamāna, he should offer the two subsequent oblations to Pāvaka and Śuci on a single layer of sacrificial grass (*samānabarhis*)."

In that case, because the *pavamāna* [laud] is characterized by occurring after the *laghu* [rite], and because the three— *pāvaka*, *śuci*, and the *samānatantra*— constitute a single performance for the sake of the fruit, the three do not share a single performance. Nor should it be argued that, since the three are enjoined together in the obligatory (*nitya*) performance, here in the optional (*kāmya*) performance only the sequence of the principal [rites] itself is enjoined for the sake of the fruit— just as in the case of curds and so forth— because if that were so, it would be impossible to refer to the two subsequent [rites] as having the same sacrificial vessel (*samānahavīṣtva*).

Nor does the difference in the performance (*prayoga*) entail an impossibility of the grammatical suffix *-lyap*—which requires a common agent—as there is a difference in agents; for even when there is a difference in the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) due to the distinction between their selection (*varaṇa*), maintenance (*bharaṇa*), and so forth, this is possible either by virtue of the unity of the agent in the form of the patron (*yajamāna*) who presides over them all as a single entity, or simply because they are based upon that one person.

In reality, however, since the injunction for the *dāna* (gift) occurs precisely within the *pavamāneṣṭi*s—which themselves follow immediately after the injunction for the *ādhāneṣṭi*s—the required purpose is accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) right there, and thus there is no separate selection or maintenance of priests for the *pavamāneṣṭi*s.
Therefore, although there is a temporal difference in the performance, the unity of the agency remains, and thus the use of *-lyap* is justified; enough of this.
Maṇḍana: "There is a common procedure (*tantra*) for the Pavamāneṣṭis.
No, says Śaṅkara: "In those sacrifices, the fruit does not arise from a subordinate factor (*guṇa*)."
That is the principle of *tantratā*.
At the *ādhāna*, the *pavamāneṣṭis* are performed not even upon one consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭis*, but only upon one consecrated by the *ādhāna* alone.
The fire of the *vāsāgni* is the archetype (*prakṛti*).
It should be performed with speed.
[Objection: There are the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, beginning with "First, to Pavamāna," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the Pavamāna-iṣṭis be performed in a fire consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, or not?
What is established? Indeed, for those Pavamāna-iṣṭis, the fire consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis should come from the archetype (prakṛti).

Why? Because of the force of the extended injunction (codaka), as in the case of the "swift" [sacrifice]. Just as the fore-offerings (prayāja) occur swiftly by virtue of the extended injunction, so too should the fires consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis likewise occur.

Or rather— there is the deliberation that, according to the principle of the section [beginning with] "In that case, however, there would be rapid offspring" (10.1.4.6), those [sacrifices] are not to be accomplished by means of the fire consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis. In that regard, since it has been established by the rule "In the iṣṭis, it should be the archetype of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" (8.1.4.11) that the Pavamāna-iṣṭis have the Darśapūrṇamāsa as their archetype, just as the Prayāja offerings and so forth are extended [by analogy], so too [are they extended] to the Pavamāna-iṣṭis in the Pavamāna-consecration.

Because the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is not subsidiary to everything, and because there can be no reference to two things to be given together when they are not consecrated simultaneously, it must be stated that the phrase "that indeed belongs to him" (*sa hi tasya*) refers to a state of coexistence; for this phrase is heard as being connected with the *āhavanīya* fire, by virtue of its referring to a collective plurality.

"Whatever third light there is, that very one is obtained by him"—this is stated in another Śruti passage concerning the Āhavanīya fire. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), [the siddhāntin replies]: because the word "third" refers to the space on the northern altar (auttaravedika), and because it is impossible for the singular number in the phrase "for he is his" (sa hi tasya) to denote a plurality of fires, the meaning is simply that "that Gārhapatya fire is the source (yoni) of the Āhavanīya. Thus, even for the officiating priests (ṛtvij), the preparation of those two [fires] occurs from that very same world.
(Saṃkarṣa 3.2.3).
Because the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is not subsidiary to everything.
Regarding this, they recite: "A Brāhmaṇa should consecrate the fires in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn.

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the mention of the Brāhmaṇa and others for the purpose of an occasion (*nimitta*), such that the consecration belongs only to a Brāhmaṇa and the spring and other seasons are enjoined for him; or is the consecration itself enjoined for the Brāhmaṇa and the others?

Having, in the preceding section, incidentally determined the difference in the application of the *avabhrtha* [concluding bath], we shall now establish the difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) based on secondary qualities (*guṇa*), which is the subject at hand. Herein, the first intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) is as follows: It is established that when all subordinate words (*upapada*) are heard, an injunction (*vidhi*) that has shifted its focus toward the meaning of those subordinate words requires a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the root-meaning.

That too requires a restatement of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), because of its connection with the meaning of the qualifying words "spring" and so forth in the injunction, "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should lay the fires. Nor is the fire-laying unestablished, for it is established by implication through the Agnihotra and other rites. For indeed, the Agnihotra and other rites are accomplished by means of the *āhavanīya* fire, according to the Vedic revelation: "What one offers in the *āhavanīya*... And since the *āhavanīya* fire exists only for one who has performed the fire-laying—as indicated by the rule "The *āhavanīya* belongs to one who has laid the fires"—the fire-laying is established by such implication. Thus, the fire-laying is indeed obtained.

Alternatively, since the act of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is already established by the injunctive statement itself—"He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire"—which possesses an unimpeded capacity for injunction, the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* and other classes is intended to indicate the occasion (*nimitta*), in order to enjoin the times such as spring (*vasanta*) as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that act.

Furthermore, this is not an injunction expressed in the present tense; for an injunction is established through a connection such as "He who, knowing thus, overcomes his rival enemy," or "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire. Thus, the injunction is distinct from the mere description of the present state.
As it has been said: "Is the laying of the fires [required] by implication, or by the general statement?
Therefore, there is a repetition of the recitation for the purpose of indicating the specific castes as the cause."

(Vārttika, p. 588) Now, is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) a Brāhmaṇa qualified by the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), or is it the fire-laying qualified by a Brāhmaṇa? In either case, since there would be a reference to a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). To this it is replied:
In the injunction regarding an unattained object, the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because they are already attained [in other contexts].

Even there, since the qualification is redundant and the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is a qualifier of the action, and because the Brāhmaṇa alone serves as the occasion (*nimitta*), there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Nor can it be argued that both the occasion and the time are included in this sentence by virtue of being conditions for rising (*uddeyatva*).
This must be stated:
because time is connected with action and the occasion (nimitta) is something to be performed, their coexistence is possible due to their distinct natures.

Therefore, just as in the case of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), where—despite the absence of a person [as a primary factor]—the mention of Brāhmaṇas and others in connection with the *ādhāna* serves as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it follows that the specification of the spring season is an injunction for the *ādhāna* occasioned by being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth.

This being the position reached, it is replied: This would indeed be so, if the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) were obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) from that which is heard in the text.
For here, in the statement "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring," the establishment is understood to have a fruit accruing to the agent, on account of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

And since the Āhavanīya fire is the fruit of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), this sentence-meaning pertains only to the position of restatement (*anuvāda*): "That which results in the Āhavanīya for the agent should be performed by a Brāhmaṇa in the spring.
Nor is such an *ādhāna* obtained through these very acts as the Agnihotra and so forth, simply by implication (*ākṣepa*), even though that might be the case.
For by them, the *āhavanīya* fire is implied, but not the continuous connection with the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) ceremony;
because it is possible for one who has consecrated the fire by one means to acquire it through others, such as purchase (*krayaṇa*), and so forth.
Nor should it be argued that, due to the observation of a specific qualification within the restatement (*anuvāda*), only such a [fire] connected to the *ādhāna* is implied.
Even when doubt exists, a determination may arise from the observation of a restatement (anuvāda).

For example, regarding the rule "Having made [the word] *irā*, one should sacrifice," there is a doubt as to in what position the word *irā* is to be inserted; however, because of the observation of a restatement of a prohibition in the form "Not with *girā*, not with *girā*," it is determined that the word *irā* is to be inserted in the place of the word *girā*.

In the present case, however, since the injunction for the ritual (*kratu*) is impossible without the *āhavanīya* fire due to the force of the application (*viniyoga*) stating "One offers in the *āhavanīya*," let there be an implication (*ākṣepa*) for the employment of the *āhavanīya*.
And since it cannot be obtained from itself, it refers only to the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) as qualified by the spring season and so forth.
Now, one might object: let there be no restatement of the established fact that the seasons are heard [in the injunction];
for there is an explicit injunctive statement, namely, "He who, knowing thus, lays the fire," which contains the word *āgneya*.

In that case, since the act of *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) which results in a fruit for the agent is already established [by other means], the sentences concerning spring (*vasanta*) and so forth would merely restate it (*anuvāda*) and enjoin only the fruits such as springtime for the specific occasions (*nimitta*) of being a Brāhmaṇa and so on.
This is not so; for this would be the case only if there were an injunction in the form, "He who, knowing thus, performs the *ādhāna*.

What is it, then? It exists as a statement in the present tense (*vartamāna-apadeśa*), forming a single syntactical unit with the injunction regarding the collection of materials (*saṃbhāra*) which is subordinate to the *ādhāna*.
This entire passage is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
For it is heard [in scripture]: "He thus overcomes his rival enemy," because the act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*) is not subordinate to anything else.
The immediate succession of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and the *soma* sacrifice is established by the text:
"He who, knowing thus, consecrates the fire, pours out water."
Furthermore, the injunction "he establishes" (*ādadhāti*) is heard here as an unmistakable, direct (*pratyakṣa*) prescription.

This being the case, there can be no implication (*ākṣepa*) of the *agnihotra* and other such rites from this [text], nor is it possible to assume that the statement in the present tense is itself a prescription.
As it has been said: "When a direct prescription exists, an inferred one is not perceived."
"Therefore, there is no capacity for attainment in the case of [statements concerning] objects or present time" (Vārttika, p.

Consequently, since there is in no way any object to be attained, the mention of Brāhmaṇas and others in sentences such as those regarding the spring season (*vasanta*) is for the purpose of indicating a causal condition (*nimitta*); rather, distinct acts of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) are enjoined, characterized by differences in agent, time, and accessory details.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the introduction of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) will be explained right here in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* by describing the injunction: "One who knows thus lays the fire"?
Why, then, is there a different discussion here?
[Response: It is said:
For in that case, since the scriptural mention of the desire (*kāma*) pertains to the primary action and is common to all four castes,

when the Śūdra’s eligibility is established by the force of that [desire], then— in order to justify that eligibility— the scriptural mention of the desire itself will imply the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) as being connected to all four castes.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that even a Śūdra has the right to perform the *āhitāgni* sacrifice—on the grounds that the injunction "one establishes the sacred fires" (*agnim ādhatte*) denotes the establishment of fires common to all four castes, and since the sentences concerning spring (*vasanta*) and so forth merely prescribe specific times, the establishment of fires performed by a Śūdra would fall within the scope of this injunction—the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established as follows: Even if the mention of the desire for results (*kāmaśruti*) does not exclude other castes, there is no contradiction in its being restricted to them; however, the Śūdra's eligibility cannot be established here by implying a specific type of fire-establishment through the sentences concerning spring and so forth, which are already settled in this section.
Therefore, this section is intended to refute the possibility that the mention of "Kamī" (the desire for results) establishes an eligibility for Śūdras that exceeds the limit of the four castes.
Furthermore, it would be redundant to say that everything established by this section has already been set forth [elsewhere].

As for the purpose: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even though [the Śūdra] is excluded, there would still be a status as a constituent part of the ritual action characterized by the subsequent purchase (*krayaṇa*) and so forth.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the status of being an auxiliary to the ritual acts exists only after the fire-laying (*ādhāna*).

The Sūtra, moreover, states: "Even regarding the fire-laying, the statements concerning purification are not for the purpose of indicating a specific occasion (*nimitta*), just as before; because the fire-laying is not a subordinate part of everything (*asarvaśeṣatvāt*), there is no implication [of its application] due to the absence of its being a subordinate part of the ritual acts, unlike the Āhavanīya fire.
In the second interpretation (*dvitīyavarṇaka*), however, it is because it is a subordinate part of everything (*sarvaśeṣatvāt*).
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the meaning is that [the fire] is not subordinate to water, because it is the remainder of all the requisites.
According to the Tautātitas, it is because [the fire] is not a remainder of everything in the context of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration).

The Śruti text—"A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring," "A Rājanya in summer," and "A Vaiśya in autumn"—states that the Brāhmaṇas and others are the *nimitta* (conditions) for the fire-establishment (*ādhāna*), but this text is not one that establishes the performance of the fire-establishment itself. Regarding this point, the Siddhānta (concluding view) is stated in response to the Pūrvapakṣa (prima facie view) in the Sūtra: with respect to the fire-establishment, the sentences concerning spring and so forth enjoin the fire-establishment as qualified by the Brāhmaṇas and others and by spring and so forth; they do not merely indicate specific times through a connection with conditions for an already established fire-establishment.

Because the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not a subsidiary to all [rites]—since it lacks the status of being a subsidiary to every ritual—and because the injunction for the laying of the fires is not heard as having the character of applying to all rituals;
therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *śruti* and other means of proof establish the laying of the fires for the Brāhmaṇas and others.
Bhavadeva, however, has explained "all" and "not all" differently.
In this regard, it has been explained through another interpretation that [the term] "all" refers to the entirety of everything, meaning the entirety of all the requisites (*sarvasambhāra*).
Since the principal rite (*pradhāna*) belongs to the Yajurveda along with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*), the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) must be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

Vārttika 3.3.15, p. 890: The *vāravantīya* chant, prescribed in the Sāmaveda for the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), is obtained as being to be recited loudly; however, it is set aside by the requirement of whispering (*upāṃśutva*) resulting from its being enjoined in the Yajurveda. Bāla, p. 140: The time for the fire-installation is set aside when there is a desire to perform the *sadyahsoma* sacrifice immediately, due to the constraints of the season, lunar mansions, and so forth. Vi. 5.4.15: By the principle of the fire-installation (3.6.11–13), the *prayāja* offerings and other such elements become subsidiaries of the archetype (*prakṛti*); thus, they are extended [to the ectype] by analogy.
However, it has been established that the *māneyī* [offering] is not an integral part (*karmāṅga*) of the ritual action.

Vārttika 3.6.16–17. Once the Āhavanīya fire is established through the combination of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices, the *agnihotra* oblation is subsequently performed in that fire.

Bṛhatī 5.2.19–25. If the sacrificer should die at some point between the *ādhāna* and the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice, there would be the undesirable consequence of cremating him without sacrificial vessels; therefore, the sacrificial vessels must be maintained from the very commencement of the *ādhāna*.
VI. 11–14. Only one who has performed the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) is entitled to perform the *sattra* sacrifice, and no other.
VI. 6–15. Like the vows of the *ādhāna*.

The vows of the *ādhāna*—that is, the vows of one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*)—are commenced immediately after the *ādhāna* itself; they do not depend upon the performance of the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices. Similarly, the *agnicidratā* rites must also be performed immediately after the *cayana* (the piling of the fire-altar). This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

*Vṛtti* 5.3.10–28: One intending to perform the Soma sacrifice immediately after the *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration) should offer the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) before the end of the year. *Bhāṣya* 5.4.13–18: There is a sublation (*bādha*) of the initiation (*dikṣā*) prescribed for the general *Ādhāna* by the initiation prescribed for the *Punarādhāna* (re-consecration).
*Vṛtti* 10.3.15–33: It is the opinion of some that the injunctions for the *Sāmans* of the *Ādhāna* should be inferred from certain branches of the *Sāmaveda* scripture.

Su. P. 1184: Although the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the *Soma* sacrifice are in reality part of the Yajurveda, they are treated as belonging to the Sāmaveda for the sake of a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvā-cintā*). P. 1137: The sequence between the establishment of the fires and the *Soma* sacrifice is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the establishment of the fires. [Section 930: The Topic on the Establishment of the Fires (*ādhānādhikaraṇa*)].
There is [a rule] regarding the transgression of seasons and constellations; Bhāṣya 5.4.13.6. However, the *tūṣṇīhoma* (silent oblation) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration);
Bhāṣya 5.1.19. According to the Vārtika, the *pavamānahavīṃṣi* (oblations to Pavamāna) are also auxiliaries of the *ādhāna*.

*Soma* 5.1.9: This *tūṣṇī* (silent) oblation is enjoined as something entirely new (*apūrva*) by virtue of being an auxiliary to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration). Since there is no authority for a mantra, the statement "it should be offered silently" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). As for the deity, in an unspecified case, it is Prajāpati.
The ritualists, however, consider this to be an extension (*atideśa*) of the *agniṣṭoma*.
In that case, there is also an injunction for silence (*tūṣṇīka*). Nevertheless, evidence must be sought for its status as a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Bhāṣya 10.8.15: According to the principle of the sentences concerning the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and other rites—namely, that "the sentences regarding *ādhāna* and so forth serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) by means of establishing the refinement of the fire which is an auxiliary to the sacrifice"—so too the *upanidhāna* (placing near) has its expectancy satisfied by the fruit of the sacrifice situated at a distance, through the emphasis on establishing the agent who serves the purpose of the sacrifice.
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 24: There is a lapse of the refinements such as *ādhāna*.
In the *abhijyana*, there are two optional *āgneya* offerings.
Bhāṣya: [The fire] is obtained from its actual presence; it is not inferential.
Regarding the section on the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna):
[the fire] is obtained through direct existence, not through inference.
Therefore, there is no "attainment" (*prāpakatva*) of the meaning of the two present-tense words.
First of all, there is no attainment of the meaning [of the *arthāpatti*] by way of restriction,
because it is easily obtained even through other means such as receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), since those [offerings] placed by other persons are not restricted by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

When there is an explicit statement (*pratyakṣavacana*), there is no other way for it to be established; thus, there is the acceptance of a substratum obtainable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Even the phrase "one who knows thus" (*ya evaṃ vidvān*)—referring to the present tense—obtains the power of injunction (*vidhiśakti*) when found in Vedic passages concerning Brāhmaṇas and others, because of the presence of the explicit injunctive suffix (*liṅ*). Therefore, it is not the case that this [passage] is merely subsidiary to an injunction already established by an explicit injunction elsewhere; rather, the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) qualified by being performed by a Brāhmaṇa and so forth is enjoined precisely as something not previously established.

"What is the similarity based on the cause? (Bhāṣya)—this refers to the intention that there is no connection with words such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth. "The simultaneous utterance of the Brāhmaṇas and others with the injunctions regarding the spring season and so forth"—this is because, once the capacity of the injunction to connect word with word has been established, [the mention of the Brāhmaṇas] serves as the cause for the result.

"But surely, even by means of the Ādhāna and other rites for the Brāhmaṇas and others..."—this is intended to show that when [the rite] is not otherwise obtained, its application through specific Ādhānas and so forth becomes possible.

The other [opponent], however, negates their status as being prescribed because they are already established, saying: "But it is not that the connection of these [fires] with the *ādhāna* (fire-installation) is unknown. The question "By what [means] is it established and known? is a challenge regarding the source of that establishment.

The other, however, thinking, "Why should I put forward another stronger direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) right at the outset even while refuting this?", says: "It is the scriptural statement of desire (*kāmaśruti*)."

When the capacity for attainment (*prāpaṇaśakti*) is challenged with the angry question, "Which [Vedic] texts regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*) [attain this result]?", [the author], thinking that [the opponent] does not even know its essential nature, shows [the answer]: "The injunctions for the fruits of the Agnihotra and so forth" (this is the implicit commentary). Anticipating the objection, "How can that be attained by those [texts] which are intent on something else?", he demonstrates the implication (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, according to the principle "that which is born of action [is grasped by action], like the sacrificial post" (7.3.9.28), the *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is grasped by actions such as the *Āhavanīya* because it is the means for another [action].

And since it is impossible for all [the injunctions] to apply simultaneously, there is a qualified injunction; thus, with reference to the combined requirement, he states the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
This being the position reached, we reply:
even though they are already established as prior, the scriptural texts serve as the means of bringing them forth.
How so? Because it is not subsidiary to all [rites].
For if the establishment (*ādhāna*) were subsidiary to all ritual acts (*karman*), then it would either be implied by them or not;

however, according to the very principle stated in *Jaiminīya Sūtra* 7.3.9–129, "Or rather, its form [is determined] because it is not subsidiary," since the taking up of the Āhavanīya and other fires is already concluded, there is no reason whatsoever to establish that the establishment is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of those [rites].

Regarding this, he will state [later] that "or for all purposes" (3.6.1.156), and that will be explained as being because they serve the purpose of all ritual acts (*sarvakarma*). To the question, "What follows from this if it is so?", the opponent considers that even a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) can be implied by way of *anyathānupapatti* (presumption based on the impossibility otherwise). However, the proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) says, "But the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) is not [implied] by the scriptural injunctions regarding desires (*kāmaśruti*), because those fires are obtained through those [injunctions]," since presumption (*anyathānupapatti*) is the sole means of proof [for such an implication]. He continues, "Is it not the case that the fire-laying is also a means for obtaining the fires?"
In that context, only name and form (*nāmarūpa*) are grasped, such as the *vakṣyatva* (the state of being what will be spoken) which serves a worldly purpose.
However, the *āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires are not worldly means.
Therefore, their means must necessarily be derived from the Veda itself; since there is no means other than the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), that [means] is also resorted to.
It is said: No,
because it is inconclusive.
For the fires possess means such as purchase and so forth for the performance of the sacrificial acts;
and by all of these, the scriptural injunctions regarding desires are rendered complete through the mere acquisition of the Āhavanīya and other fires.
Therefore, since the establishment (*ādhāna*) is established here as an absolute necessity, there exists no restriction that would interrupt this.
In this regard, it might be argued that the *āhavanīya* and other such fires cannot be acquired through other means, because their status is contingent upon consecration (*saṃskāra*).
To this, it is replied:
"It is true that three kinds of grain are obtained from the first sowing;
subsequently, there are three varieties of rice, for which no other means of acquisition is described.
For just as rice and the like do not arise without cultivation, yet they are not harvested by all men, since they can also be obtained through purchase and other such means."
Thus, first of all, in the present case, these [fires] are established by means of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration); others, however, obtain them through other means.
And so, just as in the case of the *vaṭa* tree and others, which serve as the substratum for the *ādhāna*.
There is no instruction regarding the immediate offenses;
in the section concerning the immediate offenses,
there is no instruction regarding the immediate offenses.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is not heard [in the text]: "He closes his fists, restrains his speech, and announces the initiated one," nor is it heard: "He washes his hands and spreads the grass-bundle. Regarding this, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—based on the sequential order of the recitation—is that the closing of the fists and the restraining of speech are for the purpose of announcing the initiated one, and likewise, the washing of the hands and the spreading of the grass-bundle are for that same purpose. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is precisely the opposite: that the closing of the fists and the restraining of speech are for the sake of all ritual acts, and the washing of the hands is for the purpose of touching all the ritual materials.

The Sūtra, however, is for the purpose of refuting the reason for the prima facie view, namely immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). In the case of immediate sequence, proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is the factor; here, the injunction (*codanā*) is the authority.
And thus it has been said: "In the case of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), there is an injunction, yet no injunction, no authority;
for it is sublated by a stronger indicative mark (*liṅga*) and by the context (*prakaraṇa*), and because the sentences are complete in themselves."

Because the sentences recited in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice— namely, "he clenches his fists," "he restrains his speech," "he announces the consecrated one," "he wipes his hands," and "he spreads the grass-bundle"— are each complete in themselves through their respective groups of words,

these are indeed distinct sentences that are independent when separated. Therefore, the acts of clenching the fists and restraining speech serve the purpose of all the ritual actions, and do not consist merely of the announcement of the consecrated one.

Likewise, for one who rinses his hands, there is the mental visualization (*adhyālambana*) of all objects required for the ritual, but not merely the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the spreading of the grass-bundle (*ulaparājistaraṇa*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the reasons.
This sūtra is intended to demonstrate the reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The strength of the *prakaraṇa* (contextual connection) [prevails] by the maxim "proximity is not an injunction" (*ānantaryamacodanā*), Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 1.4.12, p. 166. By this maxim, "proximity is not an injunction," since proximity is not a cause for the cessation of cognition, it has been stated in the section on performance (*anuṣṭhādhikaraṇa*) that [the former prevails] due to its proximity. Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1112. Even if there is proximity, if the second maxim—"proximity is not an injunction"—[applies], then the third maxim is far removed.

*Soma* 2.1.16: In a case where there is a requirement for a primary element (*sākāṅkṣa-pradhāna-sthale*), the qualification consisting of the cessation of the cognition of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa-buddhi-pivṛtti-rūpa-adhikāra*)—which is found in the mantra for the purification of vessels recited in proximity to the *Sānnāyya* sacrifice—is common to the *Āgneya* and other offerings as well. Furthermore, by the principle "Proximity is not an injunction" (*ānantaryam acodanā*), this qualification is stronger than mere immediate proximity (*avyavahita-saṃnidhi*), just as in the case of the *Prayāja* offerings; therefore, it does not belong exclusively to the *Sānnāyya*. *Kau.* 1.3.12, p. 123: Because of the rule "Proximity is not an injunction" (3.1.14.24), the sequence characterized by immediate proximity (*ānantarya-lakṣaṇa-krama*) is not a factor that effects application (*aviniyojakatvāt*).
Su. pṛ. 457: Satisfying a requirement through immediate sequence occurs when a requirement exists.
Bhā. 3|1|14|24: It was stated in the section on "immediacy" (3|1|14|24) that the order consisting of immediate sequence is not a factor for application.
Su. pṛ. 1072: In the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is not accepted that order characterized by immediacy possesses the power of application.

Page 1193: It is possible for sequence characterized by immediate succession (*ānantarya*) to be a factor of application (*viniyojaka*), because even when there is immediate succession, it is equal to the case where there is no context (*prakaraṇa*)—which would otherwise render the specific proximity (*saṃnidhi*) meaningless.

Page 1067: Regarding the application of sequence characterized by immediate succession, since that [sequence] is equal with respect to both the preceding and the succeeding items, there is no logical necessity for a restriction such that "only the preceding belongs to the succeeding," rather than "the succeeding belongs to the preceding.
Page 1066: The Section on Immediate Succession (*Ānantaryādhikaraṇa*).
The washing of the hands is a subsidiary act (*adhikaraṇa*).
The clenching of the fists, the washing of the hands, and so forth, belong to the entire context (*prakaraṇa*).
The objection regarding immediate sequence.
The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "He closes his fists, restrains his speech, and announces the consecration";
likewise, "Having washed his hands, he spreads the grass-bundle."
In this regard, there is a doubt: are the clenching of the fists and the silence intended for the purpose of the announcement (*āvedana*), or are they to be included within the entire context?
Likewise, is the lowering of the hands intended to spread the *ulapa* grass, or to perform all the ritual acts within the context?
What, then, is the prima facie position? The lowering of the hands is for the purpose of consecrating the hands, and the speech [utterance] is for the purpose of consecrating the person.
Therefore, there exists an expectancy as to which specific items are to be consecrated by these two acts.
When this expectancy exists, it is satisfied by immediate proximity.
Therefore, because of their immediate sequence, the purpose of the speech, the clenching of the fists,
and the lowering of the hands is for the sake of spreading the grass-bundle (*ulaparāji*).
This being the case, we reply as follows.
"There is a connection with all the purposes of the sections.
Why? Because of the split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
How is there a split in the sentence? Because two distinct meanings are being expressed.

For the word "āvedayati" does not occur in the sense of "he should announce one who has been initiated," nor does "stṛṇāti" occur in the sense of "in order to strew. Furthermore, both the spreading [of the grass] and the pouring down [of water] are enjoined; likewise, the clenching of the fists, silence, and the announcement are all enjoined.
And there is no mutual relationship whatsoever among these; nor is there the principle of immediate sequence (*ānantarya-adhikaraṇa*).
When there is an expectancy for the meaning of the words regarding immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), that immediate sequence becomes the cause for their syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
Therefore, such characteristics belong to the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself.
Alternatively—the sequential application has been established immediately preceding this. Now, its exception is being formulated.

The making of the two fists and the speech of the sacrificer are performed by the sacrificer, while the announcement is performed by the officiating priest; in that case, how is that which depends on the subordinate parts (aṅga) invoked?
This is not a fault;

for even when [the action] is for the sake of another (*ādhyarthya*), the sacrificer remains the agent by virtue of being the instigator (*prayoktṛ*). Alternatively, regarding that which is to be announced there by the initiated person, the other two are considered subordinate (*aṅga*) to it, and thus they are subject to doubt.

But why, when the sequence of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is equal, is the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) attributed only to the preceding [act] and not to the subsequent one? Some say: "The mention of the preceding [act] first is precisely for the purpose of demonstrating that there is no fixed rule. Alternatively, among all expectations, the expectation expressed by the word "what" (*kiṃ*) arises first. And when there is such an expectation, the consideration of what was performed previously occurs because it is consistent with being an auxiliary; therefore, having the expectation, "What is to be done with the making of the fist and the speech? [the subsequent act] presents itself as, "He announces the initiated one" (*dīkṣitam āvedayati*).
And there is no reason for its transgression.
Furthermore, it is possible to conceive that even this [act] possesses a purpose derived from something else; therefore, it is logical that it exists solely for the sake of that [other purpose].
In the same way, the washing of the hands is for the purpose of spreading the layer of *ulapa* grass.

One should proceed with the strewing of the *ulapa* grass on the altar in the middle of the *vedi*, using upright grass for the curd; this is the strewing of the *ulaparāji*. (Sudhā: From the root *lū* preceded by *ut*, the suffix *kapad* is applied; due to the prescribed elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel and the following consonant, and because the letters *k* and *n* are designated as *it*, they are dropped. Thus, the word *ulapa* signifies grass suitable for upright cutting, such as fragrant grass and the like—this is what is expressed by the word "upright" (*ūrdhva*). In the sense that "a line (*rāji*) is made by means of *ulapas*," a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) is shown.)
On page 1067, the word *rāji* is explained as denoting a "line" (*rekhā*) or its synonym, "a form" (*ākāra*), which is why the term "long" (*dīrgha*) was mentioned.
However, in the *Kutūhala*, it is stated that *ulapāḥ* are dry grasses known by that name; their *rāji* is simply a row (*paṅkti*).
The ritualists, however, take up only a single handful of *darbha* grass separately.

In all cases, fitness (*yogyatva*), intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), and syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) are stronger than the primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) as determinants of application (*viniyojaka*). Therefore, everything belonging to the subsequent section is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to that which concludes later than what precedes it.
Due to the absence of compatibility (*yogyatva*), the mutual connection between the act of clenching the fist and the verbal expression is not established;
for there is no mutual dependence between two things that both serve as primary purposes. Therefore, one must not go too far by disregarding this lack of compatibility.
This being the case, we reply:
"First of all, syntactical unity is not observed; yet the semantic competency is equal.
At that time, the intermediate manner-of-being (*kathaṃbhāva*) is not understood."
Indeed, two statements cannot constitute a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatva) without some supporting reason that would override the context;
as for semantic compatibility (yogyatā), it is equal whether [the mantra] serves the immediately following rite or all rites, though it is more appropriate when it serves all.
For attention is certainly more useful when directed toward many ritual items; thus, let them be performed in whatever manner is possible.
Furthermore, no intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) exists here.
If it were the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the preceding [rite], then the subsequent [rite] alone would obtain as its subsidiary (*aṅga*).
But this cannot be the case, because the portion consisting of the goal (*sādhyāṃśa*) is not yet complete.

Nor can that *kathaṃbhāva* (the requirement of "how" to perform) be fulfilled by what follows [in the subsequent procedure], because its purpose has already been accomplished by the state [of the primary act]. In this way, it proceeds through each subsequent stage until the main act (*pradhāna*) is reached. Therefore, whatever desire for a subordinate quality (*guṇakāma*, such as the *godohana* vessel) arises in the interval, it connects with everything preceding it (meaning everything below), and does not extend as far as the main act itself, because the intermediate *kathaṃbhāva* has already been completed.
It is said:
"If indeed two qualities were understood from the name itself, even though they are obtained through the sentence..."
The manner of being of the principal subject, however, is immeasurable;

this has been explained in the section on *anupaṅga* (2.1.16), which states that after mentioning a connection with another [subject], it continues until the very end [of the context, both before and after the principal].
But if this were so, would it not follow that the intermediate context (*prakaraṇa*) of everything would be utterly destroyed?
It is said:
"When a different context has been recognized by means of marks such as the location (*sthala*) and so forth, that very same [context] is again desired to be connected;
this is what is meant by an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*)."

For in all cases, such as those beginning with the *prājāpatya*, there is a subsequent reference after some subsidiary element (*aṅga*) has been mentioned; thus, there arises the assumption of an intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) extending up to that point.
Otherwise, there would indeed be a lack of systematic order, because it would follow that all subsidiaries would be mutually related as subsidiaries to one another.
However, where there is no such subsequent mention, everything must be determined as being for the sake of the primary rite (*pradhāna*) alone.

Regarding whether this [subsidiary] belongs to the principal act alone or to the principal act together with its subsidiaries, the distinction will be stated starting from the sūtra, "Because of the specific context, that which is connected belongs to the principal" (3.1.19).
Therefore, in this case, it is determined through suitability (*yogyatā*) that the acts such as clenching the fist (*muṣṭikaraṇa*) pertain to the principal act along with its subsidiaries.

If, however, it were heard in the text as "to announce" (*āvedayitum*) or "to strew" (*staritum*), then there would be an application (*viniyoga*) based on syntactic unity according to Pāṇini 3.3.10, "The suffixes *tumun* and *khul* occur when another action is for the sake of the preceding action"; but this is not the case here.
Therefore, there is the quality of having all purposes [fulfilled].
And because the sentences are complete:
the commentary states that a single sentence is one that is fully perfected by its own respective collection of words.
938. Or else, meaninglessness (*anarthakya*) is a defect of the sentence; likewise for others, and so for all those that have been cited.
Therefore, this matter is quite clear: there is a lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) when there is a division [of the sentence].
Therefore, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
Consequently, because there is no distinction in the connection and because there is no distinction in the performance, the application [of the rule] is throughout the entire context (*prakaraṇa*).
Or rather—furthermore, immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is not an authoritative means of proof.

Since the characteristic of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is observed in each of these [sentences] individually, but not in all of them together, even for that reason there is no mutual subservience (*anyonyārthatā*). Śabara says: "Because of their infinity, when it would follow that they are subsidiary only to that [specific act]—either by virtue of syntactic unity or from a subordinate context—it is stated in reply: 'Indeed, by means of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), their subservience to all [acts] is understood.'"
And since order is weaker than both [the previously mentioned authorities], it applies in every case accordingly.

Since the sequence of mantras beginning with the *ājyabhāga* was previously established by means of direct statement (*śruti*), the present discussion constitutes an exception (*apavāda*) regarding that sequence.

The purpose is as follows: according to the final view (*siddhānta*), if by chance one fails to perform the washing of the hands and other such acts at their proper time, and subsequently remembers them after having performed several subsequent items, they must be performed there to ensure the non-defectiveness (*avaiguṇya*) of those subsequent items. However, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [they would have to be performed] immediately after the item [previously] performed.
The principle of "uselessness and its constituent parts" (ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya): the word *yūpa* would be meaningless.
If it is argued that [the word *ūrdhvapātra*] will function through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we say no;
for there can be no indication when there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or when another [more direct] mode of application is possible.

Furthermore, in the case of the view that [the *ūrdhvapātra*] is not a subsidiary (*anaṅga*), there is no instance of indication at all, because the genitive case denotes mere relationship (*saṃbandhamātra*), and thus it is appropriate even for that which is not a subsidiary, insofar as it is merely helpful (*upakāraka*).
For he does not state only the relationship between part and whole;
even that which is not a constituent part, such as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), is an auxiliary to the *Vājapeya* sacrifice because it serves the purpose of its parts.

As for the claim that the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) functions as an applicatory injunction due to the [otherwise] meaninglessness [of the connection], that remains no different when applied to the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) as well.

And therefore, O Lord of the Treasure, because it is an act of performance consisting of seventeen cubits, we grasp that which we perceive to be the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the *vājapeya*; such is the effort regarding the animal’s tethering-post (*paśupāśa*).
However, there is also this inquiry: "What if there were a direct sacrificial post for the *vājapeya*?
But when none is perceived, then another alternative is resorted to.
Furthermore: "Even when there is a connection with the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is not determined;
for that [connection] is not manifest merely by way of a direct relationship."
(He explains the word *yathā* as follows: First of all, it has been stated that being seventeen cubits in length is not directly applicable [to the sacrifice].
Even a mere relationship, if unspecified, cannot be understood from the phrase "of the Vājapeya" alone;
for since the meaning of the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is not connected to that [Vājapeya], it is far removed [from the context].

Therefore, its aforementioned status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) merely restates the succession of authorities (*adhikāra-pāraṃparya*). For he will say this in the passage "If it is argued that [it applies] even from afar, because in that sentence it has that purpose" (3.1.13–14): "Just as, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the ritual duties (*dharma*) are enjoined only for the sake of assisting that [primary act], and not directly upon the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) alone.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: "The placement of the seventeen-cubit length upon the upper vessel [is established].
To this, it is replied:
