This would indeed be so if there were a connection with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
That is not [the meaning] derived from the Vājapeya-śruti, because that [Vājapeya-śruti] is indeed a direct scriptural statement (śruti).

The genitive case has as its meaning mere relationship; it does not depend upon the status of being a subordinate or a principal member, nor does it require an uninterrupted connection, as in the case of "Devadatta's kingship."
The sacrificial post (yūpa) assists the Vājapeya sacrifice by means of the animal victim;
since its connection is merely with the ritual (ṛtu), there is no figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
The word "sacrificial post" would only be figurative if it were connected to the tall vessel (ūrdhvapātra).
The connection is with what immediately precedes, and the integration is with the principal element;
this is for the sake of favoring the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*), and not by external [elements], because that would contradict the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
Therefore, the integration is precisely: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is seventeen cubits long."
And that [wooden post] is connected to the Vājapeya sacrifice by virtue of the context;
therefore, this [mention of it] will be a restatement (anuvāda) of the Vājapeya's [post].

They say that the connection [of this section] follows immediately after the determination of the specific application of the *saṃskāra* (preparatory rites) for the *soma*, because there now follows the determination of the application of *guṇas* (accessory qualities).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since a height of seventeen *aratnis* and so forth would be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) in relation to the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*), the Vājapeya, due to its unsuitability there, it is applied to its subsidiaries (*aṅgas*).
Thus: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the Vājapeya may be seventeen *aratnis* long."
The measurement of the substance is an auxiliary of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
however, because it would otherwise be purposeless, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), this becomes an auxiliary of the *ṣoḍaśin* rite.
In the case of the *khadira* post, the height of the vessel (*ūrdhvapātra*) follows the ritual action through the connection with the word "at the top" (*agre*).
[The sacrificial post] serves as the means for the *urodga* [offering], and through the *urodga*, it serves as the means for the ritual action;
because it belongs to the Soma sacrifice, there is no sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in the Vājapeya except for the animal sacrifice.
Bhāṭṭa: "The sacrificial post of the Vājapeya is seventeen *aratnis* in length."

In this context, because it is more proximate, because it is the primary element, and because it is grasped by the thematic context (*prakaraṇa*), the state of being seventeen cubits long is enjoined by the genitive *śruti* with reference to the *vājapeya* sacrifice, and not with reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, if it were qualified by the *vājapeya*, there would be a restriction to that specific qualified locus.

Therefore, the state of being seventeen cubits long, being enjoined with reference to the *vājapeya*, finds its place through the mediation of its own constituent parts; the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) because it is something to be accomplished.

This being the position reached, since there is no evidence for the term *yūpa* (sacrificial post) to be used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*), the term *yūpa* indicates its own function (*svakārya*), and with reference to that function, the measure of seventeen *aratnis* is enjoined.

Although both the substance and the measurement of *aratnis* are already established through extension (*atideśa*) by way of possibility, nevertheless, because enjoining the number as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those two would result in a violation of the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratā-bhaṅga*), the specific substance itself, characterized by that number, is enjoined by means of the previously operative injunction, just as in the case of the rule "those wearing red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣāḥ*).

Since there would be purposelessness regarding the actual nature of the sacrificial post's function, the term "of the Vājapeya" is a restatement (anuvāda) based on the context, by means of an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that [the post] is a means to the *apūrva* of the Vājapeya; thus, through this indication, one obtains a sacrificial post connected to the *apūrva* of the Vājapeya.
Furthermore, the genitive case is appropriate even when there is an indirect connection, as in the expression "this belongs to Devadatta’s son.
Moreover, because the connection is mediated, this does not constitute a fault, especially when compared to the alternative of figurative usage (*gauṇatva*).
Maṇḍana: "The rope is subordinate to the sacrificial post for the sake of the animal.

Śaṃkara: "When [the primary] is purposeless, there is the descent [of the requirement] to its subsidiary parts" (the nature of the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). When a connection through direct relation is impossible, a connection through indirect relation occurs, provided that the injunction would otherwise result in being purposeless.

In the section [of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra*] beginning with "Because of meaninglessness, in its subsidiaries" (*ke. ānarthakyāt tadaṅgeṣu*), there is a connection of the seventeen-cubit length—which has become a subordinate quality (*guṇa*)—with the Vājapeya sacrifice; this is the principle of "meaninglessness in regard to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*).

The *nyāya* (maxim) will be explained in the section [of the *Tantravārttika*] beginning with "Because of meaninglessness, [it applies] to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyāt tadaṅgeṣu*). [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.4.9.4]. The meaning of the *sūtra* on the maxim of "meaninglessness and its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) is: "That which is meaningless with respect to the primary object [of a rite] finds its application in its subsidiaries. This indeed constitutes the very nature of this maxim. [Kevalānanda].

(The reason for the application of the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*): Since an injunction, even when operating through the *bhāvanā*, possesses the nature of enjoining what has not been previously established, it cannot have its purport (*tātparya*) directed toward that which is already established by another source; therefore, it is logical for the purport to descend upon a subordinate element (*guṇa*) according to the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*.
As stated in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* (p. 775):

"And because the portion consisting of the *revatī-vāravantīya-sāman* is a subordinate element, it falls within the scope of the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*; thus, [the injunction], beginning to establish its connection with those subordinate elements..."

p. 861. (This principle is where and how it does not apply) The principle of *ānarthakyatadaṅga* (uselessness of that which is a subordinate part) does not apply when another way to avoid such uselessness is possible. Su. p.

Even by means of the principle of *ānarthakyatadaṅga*, since the truthfulness (*satyatva*) pertaining to the ritual action cannot be established, there is no application of that principle in what is called the second [case].

For this very reason, it will be stated in the tenth [book] (Vārtika 10.8.2.5) that the principle of *ānarthakyatadaṅga* does not apply to instances of the locative case, such as "not in the Soma sacrifice" (*na saumye 'dhvare*). Regarding the phrase *ānarthakyatadaṅgeṣu*, it is not introduced by means of the primary [act], but rather relies upon its subsidiaries.
For that which is enjoined as being for the sake of assisting the primary, it is postulated that it assists even when situated within a subsidiary of that primary.

Or [it may be argued]: "By the principle of the preceding section (3.1.2.13–14), even though the *upāṃśutva* (low-voicedness) is known to apply to those [verses] prescribed in the Yajurveda, because it is impossible there, it descends to the *vāravantīya* which is being inserted into its subsidiaries according to the *ānarthakya-tadaṅga* principle. This should not be said;
for since the possibility of direct insertion exists immediately after the cessation of the non-prescription of that [quality], the *ānarthakya-tadaṅga* principle does not apply here.

Ku. 3.1.28, p. 313: It has been stated that the principle of "uselessness [implying] its being a subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) does not apply without a relationship established by a genitive case.
Vā. 3.6.125: The *upavīta* (sacred thread) is neither directly enjoined nor implied by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
And that [sacrifice] has the *śyena* as its archetype, not the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
The maxim "because it would be purposeless, it applies even to its subsidiaries" does not apply here;
for when something is impossible in the primary act, it is applied to the subsidiaries by implication.

And in this case, the *nivīta* position is possible in relation to the *pradhāna* (the primary act) itself. [Dpu. 10.4.1.1, p. 1906]. This is not a case for the principle of "uselessness [of the primary] with respect to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakya-tadaṅganyāya*).

For in all instances, even when there is a cognition of the incompatibility of one word with another word that is heard, the fact that verbal comprehension occurs is an empirical reality, provided there is no cognition of incompatibility; thus, the determination of incompatibility is merely an obstacle [to comprehension].

However, where there is a verbal cognition through a *kalpita* (imagined) word, in that case, regarding the imagination of the word, the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*) alone is the cause. This is because, even when the absence of a determination of non-competency exists, the non-arising of the imagined word in the absence of the knowledge of competency is a matter of experience. Therefore, since due to the absence of the knowledge of competency regarding what has been reached [by the context], the word expressive of what is heard therein is not imagined within the context, how could there be an application [of that word] to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) in the event of its impossibility?

In all cases where there is no deviation from one's own intended object (*svodeśya*) regarding its being a means to the *apūrva*, there is an entry into the context (*prakaraṇa*) for the purpose of defining it as a means to the *apūrva*; as in the case of "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), and so forth.

For this very reason, in such instances, the principle of "uselessness [of the main act] leading to its subordination" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) applies. But in the present case (in the passage concerning the Pavamāna oblations, or in the discussion regarding the knowledge of their distinctness, namely, "The sacrificial vessel is made of Varaṇa wood"), since the status of being an unerring means to the *apūrva* is already presented by the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) itself, how could there be an application of that principle of subordination? Thus says the Vārttikakāra.

Bhāṭṭa 3.1.12. (This is an exception [to the previous rule]. Having relied upon the establishment of the method of performance for the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) and *upasaṃsthāna* (concluding rite) by means of the principle that "what is purposeless is subordinate to what has a purpose" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), and having deliberated on their specific details, an exception to the principle of "what is purposeless being subordinate" is now made [under the sūtra]: "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*).

(As for its non-existence [as a separate entity]): Since the subordinate mantras (*anuvākyās*) would result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) if they were connected directly to the primary act, their status as subsidiaries to that act is established—either through their sequential order or by the mention of the *atrātā*—as explained in the *Vāraṇādhikaraṇa* (3.1.12) regarding the application of the principle of "meaninglessness and its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅga*).
Sūtra-pṛ. 1065.
(Now, the subjects accomplished by the principle of "meaninglessness and its subsidiary" follow in the order of the letters).
Furthermore, that sequence of phonemes is not to be observed in the initial syllables of the sentences, but rather in the *sthala* syllables.

In the injunction for the *adhigṛ* sacrifice, "The father does not grow old, nor the mother," since the cognition of the *pṛṣṭha* and other [stotras] is perceptible, a prohibition is impossible; therefore, by the principle of "uselessness [leading to its application to] its parts" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), it is understood to apply to the word itself. Or rather: [the sequence is to be observed in the *sthala* syllables].

1|2|144. Since the measure of seventeen cubits (*saptadaśāratni*), which is understood as belonging to the *Vājapeya* sacrifice, is impossible therein [in the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*], it has been stated that it descends [as a rule] to its subsidiaries (*aṅga*) by that same principle. Now, since the descending step (*abhikramaṇa*) and the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavyāna*) have been established as duties to be performed by the agent who is a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga-bhūta-kartavyatā*), there arises this inquiry: Does the descending step descend to all the subsidiaries because it belongs to the entire *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, or does it belong only to the *adhvaryu* priest in the *prayāja* offerings and so forth? And as for the wearing of the sacred thread, does it descend to the mere cause—the reason for its being a subsidiary of the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses—or does it belong to the entire *Darśapūrṇamāsa*?

The maxim of "uselessness [leading to application] to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*) is concluded from the consideration that [the injunctions] apply to all *liṅgas* (indicatory marks) which have become parts of those [subsidiaries]. (Su. p.

109). Nor does the application of the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya* occur solely because the primary sacrifice lacks a substratum; for it will be established in the *Revatyadhikaraṇa* that the status of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) does not fall within the scope of the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*.

Kau. 1.2.22, p. 45: The mantra "iṣe tvā," though traditionally recited as an auxiliary to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), is employed as an auxiliary to the cutting of the sacrificial shed (śālā) by means of the indirect scriptural injunction known as *itikaraṇa*, namely, "With 'iṣe tvā,' he cuts the shed."

And here, in this section known as *adhikāra*, there is no contradiction with the order of the direct Vedic text (*śruti-krama*) because the status of being a direct auxiliary to the sacrifice is not understood; for since the sacrifice is already occupied by another mantra possessing a clear indicative mark (*spaṣṭa-liṅga*), it cannot be directly connected to it. Consequently, by the principle of "uselessness [leading to connection] with its auxiliaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), when the application extends to the subsidiaries, its status as an auxiliary to the *puroḍāśa* (cake-offering) is established in accordance with the name (*samākhyā*). (3|1|7|14, p. 356). Since properties of sound such as loudness (*uccais-tva*) can be incorporated into an action, they are included as auxiliaries to that [action] by the principle of "uselessness."

The others, however, hold that when a factor (*kāraka*) is not intended to be expressed and only the quality (*guṇa*) is meant, that quality—supported by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) within its specific context (*prakaraṇa*)—descends to the substances through the principle of "uselessness [leading to application] in its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), and thus they consider it to serve all purposes.

But that view should be disregarded, because in the present context there is no inclusion of qualities connected to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and because the principle of "uselessness in its subsidiaries" is applicable only when the status of being a subsidiary to an action is established; since the grounds for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) are absent here, the objection lacks foundation.

PMS 3.1.6.12, p. 691. Even if, due to the impossibility of its own lack of an object, one were to somehow—by the principle of "uselessness [of the whole] applies to its parts"—assume that the designation *audgātra* has as its scope only the subsidiary parts;

Bhaṭṭa 3.7.24: In the rule *kartari śap* (Pāṇini 3.1.68), the term *kartari* is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). Since it is not possible for an agent to exist elsewhere within the arrangement of the word itself, it is understood through the principle of "uselessness" (*ānarthakyāt*) that the operation applies to the word.

In this context, the meaning is: "when a *sārvadhātuka* affix denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) follows. (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.4.143, p. 922). By accepting that the word *kartṛ*—through the principle of *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya* (the principle that when a term is meaningless in its entirety, it denotes its constituent parts)—denotes a word that expresses the agent, it is explained as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the form of the *sārvadhātuka*.
(See *Siddhāntakaumudī*, p. 1417: *kartṛ kṛt*, *sārvadhātuke yu*). Butter that has not yet become curd is called *ājya*.
Because it is impossible for multiple meanings to be enjoined simultaneously, only a specific quality is enjoined as subordinate to the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Nor is there a lack of attainment of the primary element. Therefore, "due to the purposelessness [of the injunction], it applies to its subsidiaries."

Thus it is established. [Vārttika 3.8.2.38] Now, since *na* is a particle (*nipāta*), it lacks the capacity for syntactic connection with a verb; and if one were to admit such a connection with a verb, it would follow that the verb itself—which is the primary element—would undergo a change of meaning. Therefore, by the principle of "the uselessness of the whole when its parts are already meaningful" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), it is understood that *na* connects with the qualifiers of the action. Consequently, in the case of "One should not eat the *kalañja*," the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that what is being enjoined is the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to abstain from eating.

Bhaṭṭa [comments]: Regarding the sūtra *āghāne 'pi tatheti cet* (3.8.20.38), which aims to refute the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by raising an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*), [the opponent argues as follows]: Since the Pavamāna-iṣṭis are not subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice, they do not fall under the scope of the principle that "what is useless [for its own purpose] belongs to its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). This is because it is accepted that even by means of mere assistance (*upakāramātra*), the dimensions such as the *aratni* and *prādeśa* descend upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) during the year-long rite (*saṃvatsarasādhya*). Thus, mere assistance falls within the scope of that principle. Consequently, the Soma sacrifice does not occur at the end of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Furthermore, those [iṣṭis] cannot be grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) as being required [by the Soma sacrifice].
Moreover, in this case, the scriptural meaning (*śruta-artha*) is much more remote (*viprakṛṣṭatara*) from being a subsidiary part of that [Soma sacrifice].

And it has been stated that the principle of "uselessness and its application to the subsidiary" (ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya) does not apply unless there is a relationship to be established by the genitive case.

[Vārttika 3.6.125] Since the Jyotiṣṭoma has *soma* as its substance, the animal-related duties (paśudharma) serve no purpose for it; thus, under the rule "uselessness and its application to the subsidiary," they descend only to the subsidiaries. Because there is no distinction in their status as subsidiaries, they descend to all three [of those subsidiaries]. Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that "the injunction applies equally to all three," the following is stated in reply:

3|6|7, p. 1043. There is no evidence for the performance of the animal-sacrifice rites on the day of fasting (aupavasathya), prior to the understanding that they are auxiliary to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

Even though they are mentioned there [in that context], because their status as auxiliaries is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) aided by the principle of "uselessness otherwise" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), their performance is recognized at various points according to their different times, even with respect to the animal substance.

(Thus, regarding the prima facie view: Kau. 3.3.5.12, p. 336. Since the characteristics of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) belong to the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), and because they cannot have a direct connection as characteristics of the animal sacrifice due to their belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, they serve to produce the animal sacrifice according to the principle of "uselessness [otherwise] leading to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). Furthermore, since there is no reason—given what will be stated later—for any one among them to override the specific context (*viśiṣṭaprakaraṇa*), and because there is no distinction [among them], the first prima facie view is that they apply to all [the sacrifices].

Bhāṭṭa 3.6.17: If [the vessels] belong to the Pavamāna-iṣṭis as a subsidiary (*aṅga*), then, because of their connection with the sacrifice, even though they cannot directly apply to the primary act of fire-installation (*āghāna*), the vessels nevertheless apply to the Pavamāna-iṣṭis—which are themselves subsidiaries of the fire-installation—by the principle that "what is useless [for the whole] belongs to its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Śābara 3.1.12: Vessels made of *vāraṇa* wood and *vaikaṅkata* wood, which are not for the purpose of offering oblations (*ahomārtha*) and are known to belong to the sacrifice, [are used] at the fire-installation.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is that, setting aside the general context (*prakaraṇa*), it should be understood—on the grounds of "uselessness" (*ānarthakyāt*)—that these [mantras] belong to which specific sacrifice, namely the Pavamāna offerings.
(Vārttika 3.1.212, p. 736). In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *pāśa*-mantra ending in the plural number.

Nor is there an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the general connection; for the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, when assisted by the principle of "uselessness and its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), serves as the means of establishing the general connection with the sacrificial animals (*ṛtupaśu*).

Bhāṭṭa 9.3.15: Since the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote only the principal [sacrifices], they apply—by virtue of the principle "because of meaninglessness" (*ānarthakyāt*)—exclusively to the principal oblations alone.
Therefore, the intention refers only to the principal oblations;
such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Or [it may be argued]: by the principle that "the suffix [denotes] only that which possesses an unapplied Vedic function" (PMS 3.1.48), and by the rule "the causal factor related to that [bhāvanā] approaches [it] up to the third [element]" (PMS 2.2.3.6, p. 486), [the lamp] would be connected to the bhāvanā.

However, because the connection with the act of giving (*dāna*) is primary for the two lamps denoted by the word *prākāśa*, the injunction of the connection with the lamps applies to the qualifiers themselves, as they enter [the injunction] through the principle of "uselessness [of the whole] leading to its parts" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). Thus, due to their being qualifiers, there is an injunction of the connection with the lamps.

Among these modes of expression—namely, the injunction of a connection with another [priest] while intending the primacy of the Adhvaryu himself through the relation of being subject to command (*vidheyatva*) in the case of the *madhyeṣu* qualified by giving; or the injunction of a connection with the lamp while restating the Adhvaryu alone by not intending the act of giving—it is impossible to distinguish which one constitutes the intended meaning of the sentence. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 869). This is because, according to the principle of "uselessness and its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), there is a mutual connection perceived between the two properties themselves: the nature of being a command (*praiṣatva*) and the impossibility [of that command].

(Maitrāvaruṇa issues the *preṣya* and the *anuvāka*—in this context): According to the principle of "uselessness [leading to application] in its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), although the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) descends upon the mortar and pestle, it is prescribed by the sentence specifically with reference to threshing (*avaghāta*).

Since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) which serves as the qualificand is already obtained from the injunctive sentence itself, and because it is capable of being the subject of what has been enjoined, it descends only upon the qualifiers by the principle of "uselessness [leading to application] in its subsidiary."

*Kau.* 2.2.3.6, p. 175: "The state of possessing cows is *gomatva*. In that regard, since the cows are qualifiers of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), they are not grasped by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) because they are absolutely distinct from that person. Nor is any other quality (*guṇa*) possible there that could be denoted."

Nor does the word *puruṣa* obtain this non-difference by being stated as "the state of being real" (*tathyabhāva*). Therefore, by means of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), it relies on the connection with the meaning "in those [rites] which are subsidiary to that [main rite] because they would otherwise be purposeless" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). Vārttika 3.6.122, p. 670. Since the context of the Maṇḍūka-hymn (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.103.1–10) makes it known that it pertains to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is placed within the *cayana* (the piling of the fire-altar), which is a subsidiary part of that sacrifice, according to the principle of "being purposeless [without that]."

[Kau. 2|1|6|23] And it is accepted that the *manotā* mantra, which is connected with the mention of the limbs of the animal, is obtained at the *savanīya* [offering] even though it is not directly included there—because it has already been obtained at the *jyotiṣṭoma* due to its belonging to the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), and by the principle of "uselessness [leading to application] in its parts" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*)—even when not explicitly included as a constituent part.

[3|1|2|22, p. 206] When a connection with the primary rite is impossible, it is indeed desired that a ritual property (*dharma*) may apply through a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) that is itself not directly included, provided it is presented by the primary rite;
as in the case of the *manotā* mantra and the *savanīya*.

Page 209, 3|1|2|22: When, however, there is the *āgneya-savanīya* animal sacrifice in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, then—since the *manotā* mantra is connected to the *jyotiṣṭoma* due to its belonging to the *mahāprakaraṇa* (the great context), and since it is understood to be a means for the heart and other organs being cut out (*avadīyamāna*)—and because the mantra would otherwise result in purposelessness (*ānarthakya*) in that [general] context, its application is restricted to that very [sacrifice] by means of the *prakaraṇa* (context) assisted by the principle of "purposelessness and its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), which serves as the authority for establishing the general connection with the *savanīya*.

Bhāṭṭa 10.4.22: Or rather, since the Agniṣṭut sacrifice is produced by the Agniṣṭoma-stotra, even though it cannot be the substratum of that which is termed "being produced" through an indirect relationship, it nevertheless applies to the Agniṣṭoma-stotra according to the principle of "uselessness [leading to application] in its subsidiary parts" (as stated in the *pūrvapakṣa*).

Kau. 2|2|126, p. 282: Since the *ṛtantara-sāman* lacks a direct connection with the Soma sacrifice, the designation "*ṛtantara-sāmā*" results in a relationship through the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* by means of the principle of "uselessness [of the primary] leading to its subsidiary" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), as this is the only way it can be logically appropriate. Soma. 2|3|1: In cases such as "of the *vājapeya*," the principle of "uselessness [of the primary] leading to its subsidiary" applies only where the connection is explicitly heard.

If, however, there were no specific other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing that the animal (*paśu*, namely the *savanīya*) is a means to the *apūrva*, then—by the principle of "uselessness [of the main act] leading to its being for the sake of its parts"—these [details] such as the measurement would pertain to all animals, since they are encompassed by the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*).
But this is not the case, because by this [text], they are for the sake of the *agniṣṭomīya* animal.

Bhāṭṭa 3.6.17: Although there is no specific qualification (adhikāra) for the Pavamāneṣṭis because they are recited in a different section [of the text] and thus lack a proximate indicator (upasthāpaka), nevertheless, by virtue of the qualification for the primary sacrifice (pradhāna-adhikāra), the Pavamāneṣṭis—which are related to that primary sacrifice—are brought to mind even though the primary portion [of the qualification] is set aside. Thus, according to the principle of "uselessness [leading to inclusion in] its subsidiary" (ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya), there is no contradiction in the fact that the *vāraṇa* wood and other materials serve that purpose. Kau. 3.1.2.22, p. 206: Since the *vāraṇa* wood and other materials, which are heard in scripture as means of accomplishing the sacrifice (*yajñasādhana*), cannot be directly employed as sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*), they must, by the principle of "uselessness [leading to inclusion in] its subsidiary," be employed in the sacrifice itself in the form of the Pavamāneṣṭi.

The principle of "uselessness and its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*). When it is argued that [the rule] applies because of the maxim "that which is obstructed by uselessness finds its place [elsewhere]," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) is as follows: Since the sentence "one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," read within the context of the Fire-laying (*ādhāna*), establishes that the Pavamāna oblations are subsidiaries of the Fires, they cannot be subsidiaries of the Fire-laying itself; thus, the principle of "uselessness and its subsidiaries" does not apply here. Consequently, the Vāruṇa and other such oblations are subsidiaries of all sacrifices.

Bhāṭṭa 3.1.12: By the principle of "uselessness [of the primary] and its being restricted to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), the application of the *vāravantīya* chant to the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* is indeed appropriate.

Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.26, p. 283. Since the sentence enjoining the connection between the quality (*guṇa*) and the fruit (*phala*) requires the context (*prakaraṇa*) to obtain a substratum (*āśraya*), it depends upon that context; thus, once subsidiariness (*aṅgatva*) toward the context is established, it is possible for it to fall under the scope of the *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*. Therefore, by virtue of its suitability, the *vāravantīya* descends into the *stotra*. Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 871.

One should not argue that the *vāravantīya* chant can serve as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice by means of the principle of "uselessness [of the main act] when its parts are available" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), through the accomplishment of the stotra which is itself an auxiliary of the sacrifice; for there is a disparity between the two cases. In the *vājapeya*, the twenty-seven-spoked chariot pole directly attains the status of an auxiliary to the *vājapeya* through its five sets of five spokes, which are themselves its parts. However, how could the *vāravantīya* chant attain the status of a constituent factor (*kāraka*) of the sacrifice through the medium of the stotra, which is merely an auxiliary? This is because the relationship between an action and its constituent factor is, by nature, a direct connection.
Ku. 2|1|2|27: By the principle of *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*, the connection with the *stotra* [is established] for the *vairūpya* and so forth, which are heard as being connected to the sacrifice;

however, there is no universal application (*sarvavidhatva*) for that which has descended [into the ritual] by the principle of *ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*, because if that were the case, the fourfold intonation (*cātuḥsvarya*) would result even in the *yājyā* and other such parts, leading to an undesirable diversity (*vairūpya*).

Bhāṭṭa 10|6|6: In the rule *ānarthakyatadreṣu* (3|1|1|8), this principle does not apply (i.e., "he does not perform the two *padyas*, nor in the *soma*"), whereby a prohibition regarding the *soma* might occur.

By the genitive case in "of the Vājapeya," a relationship is established; seventeen cubits are prescribed for that [relationship]. Since this is merely a relationship and not a relation of subordinate and principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva), it finds its application in the sacrificial post (yūpa).
But here, Soma is heard as the substratum (ādhāra), not merely by way of a general relationship.

The meaning of the Bhāṣya passage, "For the possession of sacrifice is equal," is this: if these were preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*), then no fruit would need to be postulated; but since these are sacrifices, fruit is therefore postulated for them.
This being the position reached, we reply:

Even that which was previously [connected] with ordinary words is indeed connected even with something unprecedented (*apūrva*), provided there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), despite being separated by intervening words that are otherwise unconnected.

Furthermore, there exists a connection between the *āmana-homas* and the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries: "If one were to offer before the *prayājas*, one would place oneself outside of one's kinsmen; if after the *anuyājas*, one would fall away from the heavenly world" (*Yajñamce juhoti, madhyata eva sajātānām ātman*). Since the *āmana-homas*—being referred to in the middle—are grasped by two related words (the reading is *saṃbandhi-pada*), it is established that the *āmana-homas* are employed for a specific purpose (*kṛta-prayukta*).

Soma: Just as the *soma*-cup is used for the purpose of eating because it serves as a vessel for the *saumya-caru*, so too here; thus, the connection with the illustration is established by direct perception.

For even though in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) serves a non-primary purpose, since the *darvihomas* constitute a new ritual (*apūrva*), it is untenable to enjoin only the mantra by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the enclosing-stick.

Furthermore, because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) involves excessive complexity (*gaurava*), even if the mantras for the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi-mantra*) were intended for the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice, they could not be connected [to it] due to the intervention of unrelated words—namely, those expressing the *paridhi*-mantras found in the Taittirīya recension such as "May I be pre-eminent among my kinsmen, thus he lays the enclosing-sticks" (*sajāteṣu bhūyāsam iti paridhīn paridadhāti*)—or by the mantras for the enclosing-sticks in other recensions. This is according to the maxim: "When there is an intervention, [the mantra] is supplied by ellipsis (*anuṣajyate*). Nor is it proper to argue that, despite the impossibility of ellipsis, these mantras possess primacy because they yield results such as prosperity (*āryādi*).
Thus...
Otherwise, even the *prajāpati-homas* and the like would have to be considered primary for that very reason.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: rites such as the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice, which possess a fruit, would be primary in relation to other rites such as the *āmanahomas*, which lack a fruit.

Why is it that those [latter] lack a fruit? Because the absence of *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection) has been stated as the reason—specifically, because of the impossibility of *anuṣaṅga* due to the intervention [of other words], and because in the absence of *anuṣaṅga*, the possession of a fruit is impossible.
Or rather: "Because of its primacy, the Āmana-homa is a subsidiary of the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice";
or else, "Its primacy arises from ignorance [of its true nature], whereas its status as a subsidiary would be for the sake of a result."

Bhaṭṭa: Having introduced the topic with the text, "One desiring a village should offer the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas," it is heard [in the scripture]: "He offers three oblations with the verses beginning 'āmana-syāmahe devāḥ'.

In that case, since the Āmana-homas possess the character of being part of the Sāṃgrahaṇī, their status as its subsidiaries is established by mere proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), even though there is no formal context (*prakaraṇa*) because the Sāṃgrahaṇī is a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

"If one were to offer before the *prayāja* oblations, one would place oneself outside of one's kinsmen; if one were to offer after the *anuyāja* oblations, one would fall away from the heavenly world; therefore, one offers in the middle"—this is because of the scriptural statement regarding its occurrence in the midst of the archetypal (*prakṛta*) subsidiaries, and because that [connection] is established through the context (*prakaraṇa*).

However, in reality, it should be understood that this is not "context" (*prakaraṇa*), because there is no evidence for the connection being established through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) or syntactic contiguity (*anuṣaṅga*).

Since the purposefulness [of these rites] is thus established, there is no assumption that they serve as independent fruits through the connection with the word "desiring a village," because there is a lack of evidence for such a claim; rather, they must be accepted as being merely subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) to the act of encircling the sacrificial altar with the *iṣṭadhra* and *paridhi* sticks.
Therefore, these are indeed connected with the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice, and not intended for a fruit like the *Saumya* offering.
Consequently, they should be performed by all [the sacrificers] among those who possess the *prajā* (offspring).
But it is not the case that the Āmanahoma belongs exclusively to other Āman sacrifices.
Maṇḍana states: "The Āmanahoma is a subordinate element (guṇa) of the Sāṃgrahaṇī.
Śaṃkara states: "The Āmanas are subsidiary parts of the Sāṃgrahaṇī."
The power of injunction is obstructed by the vocative case, as in "O Ahibudhnya, protect my mantra" (*ahe budhniya mantraṃ me gopāya*).

[Vārttika 3.1.6.1] "These two [the optative and the imperative] are said to depend on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the capacity for addressing and so forth. [Vārttika 3.1.37, second half of the verse].

According to this principle, [the mantra] "amītra" (or "amīn vihara")—by virtue of its power as an address (*āmantraṇa*) and its power as an injunction (*praiṣa*)—will be explained as having the sense of indicating the existence of a sign (*liṅgasattva*).

(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1098) Mantras whose injunctive power is impaired by the presence of the word *yat*, an address, or the second person (*uttama-puruṣa*), even when they are stated to be means for accomplishing dharma, do not lead to the postulation of a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), despite their repeated recitation through such words as "and with those [verses] the gods sacrifice and give. (Śabara-bhāṣya on Jaimini-sūtra 2.1.30–31)
Or [it is said]:
"For one suffering from illness (āmayāvin), in the milk that has turned sour, for one suffering from illness; the fourth Atirātra is named Āyu."
*Bāla*, p. 34:
The *sāman* named Āmahīyava is sung in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice during the Mādhyandina-pavamāna, upon the three verses in the Gāyatrī meter beginning with "uccā te jātamanasaḥ. (Vi.
9.2.6, varṇaka 2).
That alone is *āmicā* where curd is poured into heated milk.
Bhāṣya 4.1.9.23. When curd is placed in milk, the word *āmicā* is employed.
Or rather,
the curdling of that milk is the motive for the addition of the sour milk, not the whey.
If there were a single final purpose, everything would be equal.

The *Bhāṣya* states: In the *Vaiśvadeva* section of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it is heard: "He pours curds into the heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā*; for the *vājins*, the *vājina* [remnant]. Therein arises a doubt: does the pouring of curds into the heated milk serve as the means (*prayojaka*) for the *āmikṣā* but not for the *vājina*, or for both?
What is established? That both [are the motive].
Why? Because it is understood that when something is performed, that for which a purposeful result is accomplished is the motivator (prayojaka) of that action.
And when the bringing of curd is performed, both results are accomplished.
The curd and the whey as well, and from that very same source, the horse as well.

In that case, it would be performed for either one if there were a reason for a definitive determination. Since no such distinction is perceived, it is understood that the bringing [of the substance] is for the sake of both.

Therefore, this single [act] is employed for both, as it is the means of accomplishment (*niṣpatti*). Regarding the word *sarva* (all) in the Sūtra: it should be understood by considering the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that is about to be stated. The meaning is that this Sūtra is to be explained according to the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application), based on the entire prima facie argument to be stated—namely, that "everything from the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), the whey (*vājina*), and the purchase of Soma up to the mixing (*saṃyavana*) and pouring out (*ninayana*) is accomplished by this single act; thus, because it is the means of accomplishment, the bringing of the curd (*dadhyānayana*) and the bringing of the water (*āpyānayana*), etc., would be equally the motivators (*prayojaka*) for the *praṇītā* and *apraṇītā* waters."
That which possesses a purpose is the motivator.
And curdled milk and whey possess a purpose. Therefore, the bringing of the curds is motivated by both.
And that [the primary substance] is capable of accomplishing both. Since the mixture would not be produced without them, the primary substance would be the motivator.
The Bhāṣya states: "It is not the case that both are motivators."
"The curd is the motivator.
Why? Because that which is produced from both the curd and the milk is the *havis* (sacrificial oblation).
If that were the *havis*, it would not be understood as a distinction that both [the curd and the milk] are produced from those two alone.
What, then, is the oblation? It is milk mixed with curd.
Why is this so? Because it is said, "That [mixture] belongs to the Viśvedevas," and not that whatever is produced from it [is the oblation].
But surely, because of the indication of the feminine gender, the *āmikṣā* is the oblation; and that is produced from it.
And there is the *vājina* oblation; that too is produced.
To this it is replied: "No," for that very milk, when heated and mixed with curds, becomes the *āmikṣā*.
Therefore, the feminine gender is not a fault.
He asks: "If the oblation (*havis*) is milk mixed with curd, why then is it said that the *āmikṣā* is the motivator?
It is replied: [as follows].
Regarding *āmikṣā*, curd and milk are prescribed.
How is this understood? Because it is produced through a mixture;
for in that case, a taste is perceived belonging to both the mixed curd and milk.
Therefore, in that case, there is the inference: "curd and milk. As for *vājina*, its taste is pungent. He said:
When curd is being poured into heated milk, both things occur:
the milk is mixed with the curd, and it is also separated from the whey (*vājina*). In that case, because of the scriptural mention of mixing (*saṃsarga*), there is no separation (*viveka*).
Whence is this [known]? It is said:
"The connection with the curd is expressed by the word; the separation from the milk is not expressed by the term *vājina*."
And the name "sāra" attains syntactic unity with the previously mentioned word.
In the alternative view, the bringing of curd into the milk would have to serve the purpose of indicating the separation of the whey (*vājina*);
and when there is no difference between direct statement (*śruti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is the more appropriate.
Therefore, the bringing of curd is for the sake of the *āmikṣā*.
Furthermore, the word *āmikṣā* is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
That alone is *āmikṣā* wherein curd is poured into heated milk.
Therefore, the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) is the motivator (*prayojikā*), while the whey (*vājina*) is not a motivator.

[The *Ṭup-ṭīkā* states: That which is referred back by the pronoun (*sā*) is [the substance] in its capacity as a deity (as indicated by the statement "it belongs to the Viśvedevas"). And by that pronoun, the immediately preceding principal element is referred back.
And that [principal element] is the motivator of the bringing of the curd (*dadhyānayana*).
(The three items previously mentioned in the preceding sentence are *payas* [milk], *dadhi* [curd], and that which is *ānīyamāna* [being brought].

Among these,) the verb *ānayati* [brings]—because it is a purificatory act (*saṃskāraka*) with respect to the other two (*dadhi* or *payas*) and because it is subordinate (*śeṣabhūta*) to them—is not referred back even though it follows immediately. (If it is argued: "Since *ānīyati* is an action (*kriyā*), it should be referred back due to its primacy," the author replies: And because it is unfit for connection with the deity (*devatā-sambandha*) [the action cannot be referred back]; for indeed, an action cannot be offered in sacrifice by aiming at a deity. (Someone says: But *dadhi* is the primary element in the act of bringing, because it is designated by the accusative case.
Because it is designated in the locative case, milk (*payas*) is also a subordinate element of that [sacrifice] (an alternative reading is *taccheṣabhūtam*;
thus, it is not a correlative reference).
The milk being pervaded by curd (the meaning is: because it is that which is being pervaded) is the primary element (*pradhāna*).
Therefore, that milk is the object [of the action] qualified by the act of pouring in;
therein, by the very force of the context, the curd is necessarily subordinate (*śeṣabhūta*).

Therefore, the meaning is "that which is being brought. In the preceding sentence, the accusative form *dadhi* (curd) refers back to *payaḥ* (milk), which is the primary subject; and since that [milk] is the primary subject, it is referred back by means of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

That [milk] is connected with the deity. And the wording of the mantra shows that the milk itself is connected with the deity—(there is an alternative reading: *tadeva*—that very thing is connected with the deity)—as in: "May they enjoy the suitable milk" (*juṣantāṃ yujyaṃ payaḥ*). Here, the word *payas* ("milk") joined with curd (*dadhi*) is expressed by the term *āmikṣā*, which is in grammatical apposition with the pronoun.
"Thus let them enjoy," "thus let them serve"—this is the meaning of the mantra.

Since the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) alone is the motivator for the addition of curds as the primary means of accomplishment, he states this result: [he] refutes [the objection] that if the milk here were connected with the deity, then [the term] would be qualified; [he says] even this is not the case, just like [the verb] *ānaya* ("bring").

The extension [of the rule] is established by the principle: "Or rather, it is milk, because it is the principal substance" (8.1.10), since there is no difference in their status as subordinate qualities.
To express that purpose, he says: "The root *ā-nī* [is used] in the sense of two [things]" (2.4.22).
But Maika says that this [conclusion] is not established if curd (*dadhi*) is the primary element.

In that case, although one object is pervaded by the action, [the curd] is not the object of refinement (*saṃskriyate*) with respect to that [action]; rather, even though it is the primary element, it assumes the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*) with respect to the other [milk], just as the curd is refined when it is brought for the sake of [making] curd.
When curds are poured into milk, as in the expression "he leads the goat to the village," the word *āmikṣā* is employed by the speaker with the intention of expressing its primary status;
for this very reason, it also possesses the feminine gender.

(He demonstrates this very point: If the goat (*ajā*) is understood as the object of the action because of the feminine gender of *āmikṣā*, then in that state [the goat is] intended; therefore, it is the primary element, and the village is for its sake.
Alternatively, because it is already established, [the word] "that" (*tat*) refers to both [the goat and the curd].
Because of a certain reason, this village holds preeminence;
therefore, in the phrase *ānayati-kṣāyām* ("in the bringing"), the flavor of milk (*payorasaḥ*—this is the reading) is perceived, and a specific goat is intended for that purpose.
In that case, there is no [grammatical connection] between the two words ending in the accusative case and the curd (*dadhi*), which serves as the agent of refinement (*saṃskāraka*).
As for the statement that even *vājina* is indeed milk—this determination is based on the word (*śabda*) because of its commonality; however, what is it based on in reality?
To this he says: "Both [the *nābhyā* and the *vājina*] are not present in the female [animal].

By this, [if one were fruit-bearing and the other fruitless, then the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) would have spoken with the intention of referring to the fruit-bearing one: "The *nābhyā* is determined to be milk, and the other is not."

But where both [actions] result in a different substance, namely the oblation (*havis*), as stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "In this case, the second case-ending at the end of *dadhi* and *payas* does not have a purposeful function; therefore, there is no determination [of the object]," this is recited by way of its meaning.

However, where one of those is specifically designated as the substratum (*ādhāra*), then the other is [the object], namely the oblation—[is it] milk mixed with curds? Milk and curds [are the object] ending in the second case, because they are that which is to be placed (*ādheya*); thus, that which is indicated by the locative case means "that which has been prepared" (*saṃskṛta*).

[The opponent] says: "In the case of [the injunction] *tate payasi* ('when the milk is poured out'), etc., [the milk] is led away! And therefore, the latter part of the *Codya-bhāṣya* states: 'The word denotes a relation (*saṃsarga*)'.

Because it is that which is pervaded (*vyāpyamānatvāt*), the other [substance] indicated by the locative case is indeed subordinate (*pradhāna*) therein. This is what has been stated: for that which a word aims at (*para*) is the meaning of the word;
and here, [the milk] is not [that which the word aims at]."
The state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇa-bhāva*) follows as an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatvāt*). This word is intended to express a conjunction (*saṃsarga*).
For if curd and milk were to become the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) by being conjoined, then only the act of cutting (*cheda*)—that is, division (*vibhāga*)—is performed.
Therefore, according to this general principle, the word would be intended to express the connection [of the milk] with that [act].

However, regarding the status of milk as the sacrificial offering (*havis*), the text shows that in this case, milk is the primary object of the action (*pradhānakarman*). How so? Because the word is directed toward the preparation (*saṃskāra*) [of the milk], it is the word itself [that denotes the primary object], and not the connection. (The fact that milk is a qualifier is understood through the locative case; how then can it have primacy? Because it too is something to be prepared.)

Therefore, he says: "And [the word] for milk has a refinement" (meaning that it undergoes a transformation). He demonstrates this: "The locative case has two meanings" (the locative case has two senses). By the very word [denoting] curd, [it is established] with respect to the milk;
and that [curd], being the object of refinement, has two forms when designated: because it is the substratum, it is subordinate, and it does not exist apart from its connection [with the milk].

Therefore, by this means, because [the object] is that which is pervaded (*vyāpyamānatva*), it is the primary element (*pradhānabhūta*)—[this being so] for the sake of accomplishing the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the action—and since there is an abundance of refinement, it is called "become" (*bhūta*) [as found in the reading of the text]. Regarding that, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), intending [to show] that the verb *ānayati* takes two objects (*dvikarmaka*), says: "The connection is verbal (*śābdaḥ saṃsargaḥ*)," because the second [object] is required by that which is pervaded.

In the other case [the view that it is for the purpose of preparing the *vājina*], the meaning [of the word] is "that which is being pervaded" (*vyāpyamāna-svarūpa-artha*), and that is what is grasped; however, on the view that it is a subordinate factor (*guṇa-pakṣa*), the pouring of curds into the milk would have the purpose of distinguishing the *vājina*, but this is not the case because such a purpose is not required.
Therefore, the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "by that which is qualified by the act of bringing," is untenable.
[This is because] the status of being a preparatory act (*saṃskāraka*) applies to the milk.
That which is understood through the word, setting that aside, another [unheard] thing is designated as "māṃ kṣeti.
The mantra— "juṣantāṃ yujyaṃ payaḥ"— is made into a remnant of the *vājina*.
Therefore, because of the connection with what has not been heard [in the primary injunction],
it follows that *āmikṣā* is indeed milk; thus, there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the oblation for the Viśvedevas is milk.
(Although there is no word whose literal meaning is abandoned— neither the bringing [of the curd] being employed for the Vaiśvadeva offering nor for the sake of the *vājina*—
and thus it has no application elsewhere, nevertheless, regarding the bringing of curd that is being enjoined...)

Soma: [The *saṅgati* (logical connection) arises] from the investigation of the combined meaning previously stated: [namely, that] when the [sacrificial] horse (*vājina*) is not explicitly heard as being subsidiary to [the *āgneyī* brick], then by means of that [horse], the word [‘āgneyī’] also possesses an implicit intention (*tātparya*) toward what is not explicitly heard. This is the connection.
In the *Tantrasāra*, it is stated regarding the definition [of *lakṣaṇā*] in the case of bracelets and the like being modifications of gold:

"It is not proper to abandon what is explicitly heard (*śruta*) for the sake of an implicit intention toward what is not heard (*aśruta*), just as [one does not lose] the nature of gold even when there is a modification of gold, or the nature of clay even when there is a modification of clay such as a jar. This is the intended meaning of the *Bhāṣya*.

The state of being milk belongs to the *āmikṣā* only when it exists as a modification (*vikāra*), and not because of the primary application of the word "milk" to the *āmikṣā*. It has been stated that there is neither difference nor non-difference between the two types of milk. Prior to the *vājina* sacrifice, the commentary on the *vājina* states: "And it is not logical that both [the substance and the deity] should be the motivators [of the action]."

In this case, there is no scriptural statement to the effect that "the *vājina* should not be prepared again by bringing in curds," nor is it the case that this [curd] is the motivator (*prayojaka*). If there is no motivator, there is no purpose.
Therefore, since it is used for the sake of the substance (*dravyaprayuktatvāt*), it is postulated that the *vājina* serves as the motivator.
In that regard, there is the principle "in one case, by way of logic, there is elision.

According to the statement, "When the motivating factor (*prayojaka*) is established as having all [its requirements], the instruction of the purpose does not apply even when another motivating factor exists," the performance of that [rite] with ghee prepared by a smooth [process] is appropriate for the Sūtra.
And it is not the case that no distinction is understood.

How is it understood? [The Sūtra says: "Because both are produced from the bringing of curds; because all are praised by the primary term. It is logical that the primary term praises both the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina*, since both are equally prompted by the bringing of curds.
First of all, its status as the motivator (prayojaka) is known due to its priority.
Alternatively, by the phrase "in one [instance] of milk," it is intended that there is simultaneous determination.

Since that [first factor] exists as the motivator (*prayojaka*), the charge of futility (*ānarthakya*) has been avoided; therefore, the second [factor] is not the motivator. Furthermore, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the whey (*vājina*) is not produced subsequently (*anuniṣpāditva*); rather, both are established simultaneously. Nor is it the case that being produced subsequently constitutes "subsequent production," for the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) is primary and the whey is secondary. Indeed, there is no such thing as "subsequent production" merely because of being produced later.
Therefore, the curdled milk (āmikṣā) is the motivator.

Furthermore, by means of the primary word, the state of being produced without its own purpose—namely, for the sake of the final accomplishment—is attributed; and thus the curdled milk is praised: "Curd and ghee are indeed a couple."

Now, since it is possible for both [the curd and the whey] to be determined simultaneously, that which is perceived as mixed together—like the scum (*maṇḍa*) and the cream (*mastu*)—is indeed the *garbha* (the embryo/interior).
Since there is no contradiction even in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), its status as a cause is not undermined. Thus, the *āmikṣā* is contained within the *garbha*.

And regarding the embryos of the *mithuna* (pairing): it is the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina* that are the motivators (*prayojaka*), not the embryos. Therefore, the *āmikṣā* is the motivator. Furthermore, since the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of both is equal, the *āmikṣā* alone is the motivator.
We consider this: what is the purpose?
If both were the motivators, then here it is the *āmikṣā* (curdled milk) that is the milk, because of that word, because of the mantra, and because of its essence.
Generally, when curd is mixed with milk for the sake of the *vājina*, the curd must be brought [as a separate substance].

Now, since the *vājina* is produced as a secondary by-product (*anuniṣpādi*) primarily due to the predominance of the milk, the *vājina* is not the motive factor (*aprayojaka*); therefore, even if the *vājina* is omitted, there is no omission of the bringing of the curd.
In the case of the *dadhyānayana* (the bringing of curd) qualified by heat, as long as it remains expectant [of its purpose] and thus meaningless, it must be supplied with a motive.

Therefore, for the sake of avoiding meaninglessness, the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) is the motivator; for it is heard in scripture: "He brings curd; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* (whey) is for the *vājins*. And the *āmikṣā* is produced from the bringing of curd.

In that context, once the objection regarding the single purpose of bringing curd—namely, that it serves both for the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina*—has been refuted, there remains no connection with the *vājina*. In the deliberation as to whether this [bringing of curd] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) or whether it is the *āmikṣā* alone, the following is considered: "The *āmikṣā* has a sweet secondary taste and is solid in form. In the sentence concerning the bringing [of curd], only the bringing of curd having milk as its substratum is heard; therefore, that [curd] is something distinct from the milk, for the latter is a substance consisting solely of a sweet taste."
"But neither milk nor curd possesses primacy [as the object], because primacy belongs to that which is expressed by the locative case; therefore, the bringing is prompted by both.
To this it is replied: "Because at that time, it is milk that is denoted."

Nor is it the case that, because the root *ā-nī* (to bring) takes two objects, the *payas* (milk)—which is the object being acted upon—is referred to by the word *tat* (that) and thus enjoined as the *vaiśvadeva*;
for [the word *tat*] refers to that which has attained primacy even over the curd (*dadhi*) by virtue of being the subject of the mantra.
Furthermore, from the grammatical description of roots that take two objects, it is understood that the milk (*payas*) possesses the status of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).

In the case of *payas* (milk), it is not [the object] on dry land (*sthala*), because it possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) and a qualification (*adhikāratva*). Rather, it is merely a relationship dependent upon a liquid substance, caused by its essence as a fluid. And when there is the intention to express milk itself as having become solidified, since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply to the mere relationship—as in "in the milk" (*payasi*)—the rule "and that which is unexpressed" (*akathitaṃ ca*) applies, as in *āmikṣā vatte payasi* ("curdled milk is in the milk"), where the *āmikṣā* is associated with the deity.

Thus, because there is no evidence for primacy [of the flour] due to the application of the accusative case as a result of its connection with an action, and because the hearing of the locative case in the present context leads to the understanding that the locus is intended, the second [accusative] case would consequently apply to the flour. However, the status of the flour as the primary element is understood precisely because of its utility;
for what is called *āmikṣā* is not merely curd and milk, since it is a distinct entity due to the presence of qualities such as thickened flavor and consistency.
Moreover, there is a designation by distinction [in the Veda]: "for her [is] curd, for her [is] whey, for her [is] *āmikṣā*, for her [is] *vājina*.

Furthermore, because of the rule "after *go* and *payas*, the suffix *yat*" (Pāṇini 4.3.160), the word *payasyā*—ending in the suffix *yat*—is a synonym for a derivative (*vikāra*), just like [the words] *gavya* and *payasya*.
As for the phrase "may they enjoy that which is enjoyable," it refers to the derivative, just like the word *dhānya*.

Therefore, since there is no object to be aimed at (*uddeśya*) in its own sentence for the act of bringing curd (*dadhyānaya*), and since it must be admitted by implication that it is for the sake of *āmikṣā*—the milk mixed with curd—and because the status of being produced is common to both, it is understood that it is also for the sake of the whey (*vājina*). Thus, [one might argue] it serves as the motive for both. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: In the statement "That indeed belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*sā vaiśvadevī*), the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) refers back to what has been mentioned in the preceding context. It is determined that *āmikṣā* is what was primarily indicated in the previous sentence, and not some other thing.
Furthermore, the essence (*rasa*) consists of the sweet and sour forms; it is these two alone that are determined, and thus it is not a different thing from those.
The process of solidification, like that of nectar and the like, is indeed possible even when there is no difference [in essence];
the separate designation [of the parts] is also due to a different state.
Furthermore, the traditional rule regarding the suffix -tva denoting a modification is also restricted to states, in accordance with those specific words.

Therefore, *āmikṣā* is not a different thing, but rather curds or milk; furthermore, the specific distinction regarding it will be determined in the eighth [book] (2.4) for the purpose of establishing a particular extension (*atideśa*).

Thus it is established that, because the understanding of the objective (*uddeśya*) in the form of *āmikṣā* occurs within its own sentence, the preparation (*ānayana*) is indeed connected to that [objective], and not prompted by the whey (*vājina*), since the whey is perceived as a different thing due to the absence of the word "that" (*tat*) referring to it.
Even if it were produced by that [preparation], there is no comprehension of its being the subordinate element (*śeṣin*).

And for this reason, because that [sentence] possesses the quality of *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic ellipsis-filling), and since its occurrence is established as being like the first [sentence], it is understood that there is a necessity for *anuṣaṅga*. Furthermore, even in its absence, since it is understood that one relies on the method of recitation employed by another, the role of the *vājina* (the whey) as a connector (*yojaka*) should not be postulated, as that would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). The practical application (*prayojana*) is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since this *vājina* would be a primary ritual act (*arthakarma*), it would attain equal status [with the *āmikṣā*]; consequently, there would be no extension (*anatideśa*) of its details to the modification (*vikāra*) of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because it functions as an *anuṣaṅga* and is thus subordinate to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, there is an extension of its details to that modification.

However, Someśvara argues that even in the Siddhānta, for one who asserts that the *vājina* is a subordinate act (*arthakarma*), the extension (*atideśa*) [of ritual details] would not be established within its specific context, because the *āmikṣā* sacrifice would be understood as the primary model.

Furthermore, in his view, the statement "the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) are six" would result in being an unestablished restatement (*anuvāda*) due to a lack of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*).

As for the purpose stated by the author of the Bhāṣya and others—that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if the whey (*vājina*) is lost, it would be produced again by adding curds, just as in the case of the loss of the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the rite is completed with clarified butter (*ājya*)—that has been set aside because it applies equally even to the prima facie view, since the completion with clarified butter on the occasion of the destruction of the oblation and so forth will be established by the force of the injunction in the sixth book (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 6.4.6). Maṇḍana [Miśra] says: "The curd-mixture is the motivator (*prayojikā*) of the curds.
Śaṅkara says: "The curds and so forth are not for the sake of the whey."
12. *Āmikṣā* is not a distinct entity from curd and milk, but rather [consists of] either curd or milk.
Even therein, the specific distinction—that it is indeed milk—will be determined in the eighth [book] (8.2.4) for the purpose of establishing a specific rule of extension (*atideśa*).
Bhaṭṭa 4.2.9: *Āmikṣā* is the motivator for the bringing of curd.
That which, having been determined as the object to be given, possesses the status of being that which is to be bestowed, is the motivator (prayojaka) for that [action].
4.1.12. *Āmikṣā* is simply milk that has become thickened through the addition of sour [substance].
In it, the milk is abundant; the curd is small in quantity.
In that case, curd is used as the substance from which milk is to be solidified;
however, in the absence of curd, it may also be prepared with another sour substance such as sour gruel (kāñjika) and the like.
Even in that instance, the term *āmikṣā* is applied.

The rule regarding curd (*dadhi*) serves the purpose of [establishing] the number eight in the eighth [chapter]. Bhāṣya 8.2.4.22. In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, there is *āmikṣā* dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa (11.2.16.163). *Āmikṣā* dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa (26–27). "The *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa, and a barren cow as the sacrificial fee"—this is the fourth *aveṣṭi* sacrifice in the Rājasūya.
Bhāṭṭa 11.4.3: Curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) is the motivator for the production of whey (*vājina*), but not for both production and preservation.
Bāla. p. 106: "Curdled milk is for the Vaiśya" is the vow during the consecrations (*dīkṣā*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

Bhāṣya 4.1.8.8–9; 6.1.7.28; 12.1.14.30: Curdled milk is a modification of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, because of the scriptural injunction: "One who has not sacrificed with Soma should offer the *sāṃnāyya* after the [Soma] sacrifice."
5|1|8|129. When milk that has been boiled is mixed with curd, it becomes twofold in a short time.
Of these, the portion that has become solidified is *āmikṣā*;
the portion in the form of pure water is *vājina*.
Some say: "The learned one indeed speaks of *āmikṣā* as being conjoined with the deity;
because of its proximity to the word *āmikṣā*, it is that very [word] which provides the object."
This is the principle (*nyāya*) [Vārttika 2.1.123, p. 534].
It is not so;
for the *āmikṣā* belongs to Varuṇa, because it is the substrate for both [the curd and the whey].

For it is said that the *taddhita* suffix expressing the deity refers only to the substance; since the specific substance denoted by the word "this" (*asya*)—which is present as the subject of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*)—is connected with the deity by means of the *taddhita*, there is no lack of purpose for the other word. According to this same principle, the other word serves to provide the substantive required by the proximate qualifier, as in the case of the word "āmikṣā. This has been stated in the *Nyāyasudhā* by means of the *Vārttika* itself: "In this case, there is no [additional] meaning, as there is in the case of 'blue lotus' (*nīlotpala*). etc. (Su. p. 475).
Regarding the fruit pertaining to the next world (956): it is taught that when something other than [ordinary] milk is mixed with milk, the milk becomes solidified after a suitable period of time.
Furthermore, when *ātañcana* (the act of curdling) is applied by means of another substance besides curd, the milk likewise becomes solidified.
Therefore, because of its thickened state and because milk is the primary substance of curdled milk (*āmikṣā*), milk alone is the material cause, not curd, nor both.
Consequently, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to milk applies to the curdled milk;
this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And there is the favor of the dharma.
In the Siddhānta, he states another reason:
the very nature of the dharma, which consists in its being performed at once (sadyaskālatā), is indeed its favor.

The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is to be performed on the same day [sadyaskāla]. If it were accepted that *āmikṣā* is a modification (*vikāra*) of milk, then, because of its long duration, the favor of the "same-day" rule would not apply to the curd;
therefore, *āmikṣā* is a modification of milk.
And so it has been said: "In some cases, there is a conformity with the established meaning through the auxiliaries in relation to the primary elements;
in some cases, it resides in those [auxiliaries] that are subordinate to the primary elements; and in some cases, it exists by itself."

Now, although it is true that linguistic mastery arises solely from the usage of elders, nevertheless, one must abandon the capacity of all words to denote an object as connected to an action (*kāryonvitābhidhāna*).

Instead, based on general linguistic mastery, one must accept the capacity to denote an object as connected to something else that is desired, appropriate, and proximate (*ākāṅkṣitayogyatāsaṃnihitānvitābhidhāna*), because in sentences containing injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like, it is precisely the action that exists in such a state.

The postulation of specific capacities for all words is based on their being understood as connected [with a meaning]. If one were to postulate specific capacities merely because they are understood at the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating unheard-of words to supply ellipses, such as in the case of "the door, the door," since connection is observed in linguistic acquisition only with that which is present in the verbal expression.

Therefore, just as in the *Holākā* section, when a particular practice is established by the mere postulation of a general rule, there is no need to postulate a specific rule; so too here, there is only the postulation of a capacity for this much—namely, the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth.
That is incorrect.
The capacity to denote an object as connected with an action (kāryānvitābhidhāna) is not to be postulated merely on the basis of what is observed in the linguistic usage of elders.
What then? It is in accordance with the way one's own mental continuum develops [understanding].

And within one's own continuum, it is understood that it is precisely the action—qualified by numerous attributes—that serves as the cause for engagement; this is how the meaning is determined even in the case of a sentence used in everyday communication.
Furthermore, there is no linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) regarding one's own mental continuum, nor regarding this or that [object] alone, nor regarding what is merely proximate to a word.

In the *Holākā* section, however, because of deviation [in practice], and because there is no evidence for postulating a verbal [injunction] that would specify particular regions and so forth, let there be the postulation of a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*).
For in that case, there is no cause for restriction other than the mere fact of being a performer, since everyone is a performer.
And thus it has been said: "The Vedic revelation, whose denotable objects such as 'east' and so forth are not fixed,
does not attain validity at all through the determination of the connection between those denotables."
Likewise, it has been stated by the venerable author of the Vārttika: "But here there is no accompanying word (upapada) whatsoever that follows established usage,
by which a specific agent seen in that region could be inferred."
(Vā. p.
246) By thus asserting the *holākādhikaraṇa* principle, he has made it known that [the opponent] is ignorant of both philosophical systems.

Now, it might be argued: just as in instances such as "Bring the cow," the connection with a task to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*) is understood, so too in instances such as "The cow goes," the connection with an already established fact (*siddhārtha*) is likewise understood.

Therefore, since both types of usage are observed, the expressive power (*śakti*) is determined to reside in the mere presence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors common to both, and not in the task to be accomplished alone.

Just as in the case of "Devadatta’s son," we observe the use of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhakti*) both when there is a direct relationship and when there is an indirect relationship; therefore, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the genitive case resides merely in a relationship that is indifferent to being either direct or indirect, encompassing both possibilities. And just so, since we observe the use of the accusative case (*dvitīyāvibhakti*) for both what is desired (*īpsita*) and what is not desired (*anīpsita*), its expressive power resides merely in the state of being a recipient of the result produced by an action, which encompasses both cases; it does not reside solely in what is desired, as the Bhaṭṭa maintains.
That [position] is incorrect.

To begin with, according to one's own linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*), it is understood that all words have as their primary purport only connection with an action to be accomplished (*kāryānvaya*). Subsequently, when a purport toward an already established fact (*siddhārtha*) is perceived, it is not capable of subverting the purport toward connection with an action—which was understood at the time of proficiency and is otherwise unaccounted for—since the realization of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) can be explained through the function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) regarding the meaning. Objection: Even that which was understood at the time of proficiency, being focused on the necessity of an action (*kriyākāryatva*), is indeed subverted later when the understanding of an established fact (*bhūtārtha*) is reached; the same will happen here as well.
Reply: Not so.

Even for one who understands the meaning of the stable element (*sthāyin*) later, that understanding is not otherwise established; for indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the like occur only with respect to a meaning already previously understood.
There is no prior understanding of something unprecedented (*apūrva*), because it is separated by [the notion of] the unprecedented.
However, there is indeed a prior understanding of the action as the thing to be accomplished (*kārya*).

Since that which is established as non-deviant (*ananyathāsiddha*), being understood subsequently, sublates both the unprecedented (*apūrva*) and the previously understood—even though it is merely a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇika*) of the action-result (*kriyākārya*)—the primary status belongs exclusively to the unprecedented result (*apūrvakārya*).
This is not the case here; thus, there is a disparity.
As for the illustration regarding the meanings of the genitive and accusative case-endings, that is entirely irrelevant.
