For in that case, no one perceives—either by necessity or otherwise—the direct relationship or the indirect (paramparā) relationship of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), nor the status of being desired (*īpsita*) or undesired (*anīpsita*) of the accusative (*dvitīyā*), such that [the genitive] would have to be considered primary for the sake of its literal meaning alone.
Since they are perceived without such necessity, it is more appropriate that they possess a common (general) meaning.
Alternatively, these [terms] may be intended in this way.

If this were distinguished [as the sole rule], then upon the acquisition of linguistic proficiency, it would be understood that all words have as their primary purport only the connection with an action (kārya);
however, this is not so, because in cases such as "A son has been born to you," proficiency is acquired through words whose purport is an established fact (siddhārtha).

For just as, immediately after hearing the words "Bring the cow," one observes activity directed toward a specific object and thereby infers the cognition of a specific object as an effect produced by the word; so too, immediately after hearing a sentence announcing the birth of a son, one observes in the father the horripilation, tears, and other such signs. For one who has already acquired linguistic competence through the knowledge of the birth of a son obtained by other means of knowledge, there is likewise possible the inference of the birth of a son—an established entity that is the cause of joy—produced by the word. Thus, what is the necessity of [restricting] the relation to an effect? In this way, the acquisition of the meaning of all words occurs.
That is not tenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpa*).

Is this acquisition of the meaning of a word for one who has never previously engaged in verbal usage, or for one who already understands the meaning? In that regard, for one who has never previously understood it, there would be no comprehension of the specific [cause], just as there is none when inferring the cause of joy from its effect.
For just as the birth of a son was understood there as the cause of joy, so too [is] the delivery of the womb of a pregnant woman... [subhagāgarbhavimoka-]... understood as the cause of joy.
There is no evidence for the restriction that the word [‘son’] conveys only the birth of a son, as there are numerous disturbances such as easy delivery, auspicious birth, and so forth.

Nor is there evidence for it being understood according to the meaning [of the context], because even for a word whose meaning has not been previously established, its reference to an action (kāryaparatva) is understood in accordance with previously established linguistic usage. Furthermore, since a figurative sense (lakṣaṇā) is possible only when a primary sense is unattainable, it is more appropriate that the word’s purpose lies in conveying a connection with an already established fact.

Thus, since it is established that all words—by virtue of their etymological derivation—are directed toward a task (*kārya*), even the *arthavādas* must be admitted to have the task as their ultimate purpose; for, while they possess a requirement for a task, they lack any independent task of their own, and thus their status as having the task as their purpose is asserted through syntactic unity with the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) due to their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*). However, this is not tenable, as it would incur the previously mentioned objections.

Therefore, because they form a single syntactical unit with the *arthavādas*, the injunction (*codanā*) lacks the capacity to convey [the truth], and its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) is established.

Therefore, although the authority of the injunction (*codanā*) was established in the first chapter, it is now addressed again by being established as non-expressive [of meaning] due to the force of its syntactic unity with the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*); thus, there is a logical connection. (This is the final position according to the Prabhākara school. To this, it is replied:
First of all, it is understood that for all words, the natural tendency to refer to an action (kāryaparatva) is established through linguistic derivation (vyutpatti).
While this might occasionally be obscured by defects in what is called an explanatory passage (arthavāda),
such a thing is not possible here in the case of an eternally faultless statement.
Therefore, one must follow that manner by which its orientation toward the task (*kāryaparatā*) is possible.

And although it has no other purpose than the communication of meaning for the sake of the injunction regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), nevertheless, it will serve its purpose through the communication of excellence (*prāśastya*).
This is because excellence, like sequence (*krama*), functions as a secondary indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) that is capable of contributing to the cognition of a specific task.

[Objection: Since the performance of multiple ritual acts by a single agent is impossible without a specific sequence, it is correct that the sequence should be construed [with the injunction] because its connection is required as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the performance. However, excellence (*prāśastya*), consisting in the form of being a means to a result and so forth, is established by the injunction itself; it is not required in the same way as the sequence. How, then, can it be construed? [Response: Not so. By the force of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the requirement for connection is generated—just as in the case of a "red cloth"—and thus the construing is logically established.

Nor should it be argued that there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for one who is already attached [to the act], because since excellence (*prāśastya*) is understood through the injunction itself, there is no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

For even when there is no person qualified for the action (*adhikārī*), as in "one should feed a Brāhmaṇa," we observe the connection of words such as "one" (*eka*)—which denote singularity and so on—even though they appear in the accusative case, by virtue of their forming a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*) with the rest of the statement, even in the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Therefore, this is the principle of the *adhikaraṇa*: even when the word’s own sense does not naturally require an injunction, and even when there is no other [direct] means [to express it], the word’s intention is to convey a connection [of meaning] through the force of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), by arousing an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) even though it is entirely useful for engaging in activity.

And that excellence (*prāśastya*) is what is indicated (*lakṣaṇārtha*); either each word of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) indicates it individually, or—given that all words denote their own meanings as connected to an action—it is because they do not denote [excellence] by themselves that, for the sake of establishing the logical principle, the meaning of excellence first arises as something indicated.

Therefore, since the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) of the caravan leader itself has its purpose in action (*kāryaparatva*), its validity is established. (This concludes the refutation of the Prabhākara view.
Thus, both the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) are untenable.
For instance, that which has been described—the claim that all words have action (*kārya*) as their sole purpose—is first of all incoherent.

Because, just as in one's own continuum it is understood that the cognition of a specific action (such as bathing or drinking) is the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*), so too it is indeed understood that even established entities (*siddha-svarūpa*), such as contact with the body of one's mother, possess causality (*hetutva*).

Just as, immediately after hearing a command such as "Bring the cow," one observes the specific activity of the elder who is the agent of the injunction and—setting aside the understanding of a specific action—concludes that the word's purpose lies in conveying a specific action because of its co-occurrence with the injunctive term and the resulting understanding of its meaning; likewise, when a son is arriving from afar, immediately after hearing the words "This son of yours has arrived," one observes the father’s facial expression brightening and so forth, and—setting aside the established cause of joy residing in the father—one indeed perceives that such words have the purpose of conveying the connection with an accomplished fact (*siddhārtha*), since their presence is invariably concomitant with that state.

Now, when the astrologer had declared, "The kingdom shall be yours in Mālava," although the understanding of that future event was a cause for joy, the understanding of the lineage of Siddhārtha is a cause for joy for everyone because it reveals the reason for that joy.

If that is so, then even for you, since there is deviation [from the rule]—as seen in the fact that after hearing such a statement, one may still observe the activity of setting out to go to Mālava and other places—how can it be the case that in all instances the sentence is intent upon connection with an action (*kārya*)? Alternatively, even if this [sentence] does not express an action, the initiation of activity occurs either by supplying the word "action" (*kārya*) or by determining an action through the power of one's own intellect. Similarly here as well, it is possible for the understanding of a completed entity (*siddha*) to be the cause of joy, either by supplying words that indicate the fitness for the kingdom of Mālava residing within oneself, or by determining the fitness for the kingdom and so forth through the power of one's own intellect.
Therefore, even though the causes of joy are infinite, the principle established by the case of Siddhārtha is not contradicted.

Furthermore, just as in your own position the determination of a specific [meaning] is achieved through the observation of words referring to a qualified object, so too in my view it will be established through the employment of words immediately following the observation of the connection with a qualified entity.

Now, if the son’s departure—which is the cause of joy for the father—and the words expressing the eagerness and so forth that are the causes of the son’s joy were not perceived from that sentence, then even in cases such as "Bring the cow," there would be an incidental [purpose] based on the possibility of communicating effects such as the excellence of qualities residing in the cow immediately after seeing the cow.

[This is because of the principle: "The Veda has action as its purpose. [This is because of the principle: "The Veda has action as its purpose. [This is because of the principle: "The Veda has action as its purpose. [This is because of the principle: "The Veda has action as its purpose. (160–161)

Thinking it to be the bringing of the cow, one would not determine that it teaches another action. Herein lies the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Of those [words] which have attained that state... [the action...]

And through the distinction of insertion and extraction (*āvāpoddhāra*), you have understood that each respective word has its own specific meaning; this is also our view, as concluded by the statement: "The Vedic collection [is authoritative] because it is for the sake of [dharma]" (1.2.12).
It is exactly the same.
Therefore, at the very first acquisition of linguistic knowledge, it is precisely the connection with an action that is [established];
thus, its authority is demonstrated as being solely for the purpose of action, just like a Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
Because we observe that even in the case of established lineages (siddhānvaya), it is merely through expectancy, semantic competency,

and proximity; at that time, the capacity of all words lies in conveying meanings other than those [already] connected to the means of achieving the goal, such as the explanatory passages (arthavāda) which have established meanings.
And because it establishes one or another form among the various things to be done (*kartavyatā*), its purpose is action (*kriyārthatva*). This is integrated [with the definition].
Therefore, as Śālikanātha stated: "Whatever is required and appropriate..."
It is possible;
and even in the case of the Veda, it does not attain proximity through the connection with an action, but rather by way of the praise of that which is to be enjoined.
Accompanied by that [word], the meaning is established as being for the sake of action (kriyārthatva),
because it generates enthusiasm for activity toward its own object and because it is not known as an injunction regarding an action.
Thus [it is said] (Vākyārthamātṛkā, p. 5).
For it is understood from the *arthavāda* that there is a connection with praise.

Nor can it be argued that [the text] has the purpose of praise through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for even in your own view, this alone is correct— that the syntactic connection of words denoting existing entities (*bhūta*) is established even without secondary indication, rather than [assuming] such a connection for all words based on their capacity for action (*kārya*).
[The phrase] "the state of being dependent on positive concomitance" (anvayaparatva).
Furthermore, let it be for now that [this is established] through the linguistic usage of elders (vṛddhavyavahāra), because [of their authority].
Nor can there be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) on the grounds that the status of the sentence as an injunction would otherwise be untenable;
for when words associated with an injunctive term function to convey a meaning connected to the task to be accomplished,
it is impossible for them to constitute an injunctive sentence because their meanings would be mutually distinct.
Even though such is the etymological derivation, nevertheless, in cases such as "the cow goes" (*gaur gacchati*),
if it is intended in this way— that the understanding of the required meaning [occurs] through superimposition—
then how could the comprehension of the connection with an unestablished object be figurative (*lākṣaṇikī*)? For the primary meaning has already been understood.

The injunction regarding the *yan* (the *svādhyāya*), by enjoining the study of the entire Veda, [indicates] the meaning directly; for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs only when the direct meaning is untenable. And here, there is no such connection with a [specific] action (*kārya*).
In these [Vedic] discourses, not perceiving the intended meaning,
the primary sense is understood through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise for what is to be performed (*vidheya*), because there is an absence of words denoting an action (*kārya*).
Nor is it the case that...
It brings about the state of being directed toward a required object;
that is correct.
[The word] *vidhi*—

Even in the absence of an expressive word, since it is observed that the comprehension of meaning occurs from a word uttered even without a connection to an action— given that the status of having an accomplished object (*siddhārthatva*) would otherwise result for that which [is connected] to the injunction— it is impossible [for the injunction to apply].

Because it would be fruitless. As it has been said: "The scripture is purposeful when [the meaning] is already attained" (Pāṇini 6.2.18). It must be stated that only that which possesses a connection established through fitness is figurative (lākṣaṇika).
Likewise:
"Thus, no means for the study of those [Vedic passages] intended for the comprehension of meaning is prescribed."

Since it is appropriate in all cases for the injunction to be connected only with a person who desires the intended fruit, and since the cognition of the meaning arises from the Veda— whether through oral hearing or through inference from written characters— it follows that in the case of obligatory duties (*nitya-adhikāra*), where such desire is impossible, the injunction must be connected at least with the person as such (*niyojya-mātra*).
Because it would contradict the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of direct perception (*darśana*).

The restriction (*niyama*) regarding study is like that of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the word] being used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*).
Therefore, it also follows that [the Veda] has as its ultimate purpose the lineage of Siddhārtha (the Buddha).
Even for one who does not know the means to the unprecedented (*apūrva*), and since [the result] does not manifest through perceptible means,
the word [of the Buddha] must necessarily be accepted in that regard.

Therefore, there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition regarding all words; nor is there, in this case as well, a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of that which accomplishes the unseen (apūrva), because:
Because explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are intent upon establishing a connection with the action to be performed, they are subordinate to the injunctive statement; furthermore,
because the study [of these passages] is not recited within the context of the sacrifice,
nor is the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood [recited therein].

Thus, for her [the opponent], both the lack of authority and the authority of the two positions regarding the established doctrine (pūrvasiddhāntapakṣa) are untenable; for, by means of the connection with a sacrifice that has been commenced, the status of being for the sake of the *apūrva* is indeed not possible.
Because the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) lacks a necessary connection with ritual acts (*kratu*). Furthermore,
even if all words were intended to convey a connection with an action, nevertheless—
If it were regulated by the mere act of performance, then it would apply to the acquisition of wealth as well.

Since explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable; for if it were regulated by the sacrifice due to its being an auxiliary to the sacrifice, an over-extension (*prasajyeta*) would follow.
For just as in the case of the expression "bring the cow," [the meaning is understood] through the observation of worldly usage;

furthermore, if this were a rule regarding the sacrifice (*kratu*), then the fact that study has only the act of learning as its purpose would be understood, just as in the case of the injunction "you shall dwell with the Adhvaryu."
The recitation (*svādhyāya*) itself, when performed, brings about prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
This being so,
even though there is a connection with an injunctive word in the phrase "yet" (*ye tu*), we observe its usage [to indicate] the effect.

On that day, it was understood that the student, upon being initiated into the sacrifice (*kratūpanayana*), is intent upon the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other such duties.
By this, through [the process of] linguistic comprehension (*vyutpatti*), this has been fully realized: that—

Since there would be futility for all [words] if actions and the Veda that illuminates them were not understood, it follows that only those words capable of connection with an action have the purport of action, and not those that are incapable. To this, he says: "In this case, 'non-hearing' (an-ākarṇanam) would result"—this is a great calamity that befalls the proponents of restrictive injunctions (niyamavādins).
Furthermore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are not capable of being connected with an action in any manner whatsoever.
Moreover, since the inferred scripture has not been studied, its study must be performed;
thus, [the injunction] exists, because the two modes of being a cause—namely, origination and establishment—are otherwise impossible.
Therefore,
there would be the undesirable consequence that the composition of all the *smṛtis* by the authors of those works would be rendered useless for one who is already pure.

Since [the status of] being "other" (paratva) is impossible, let there be non-authoritativeness for the explanatory passages (arthavādas) themselves— just like sentences such as "the tip of a finger"— and likewise for the entire performance of Vedic rites such as the *śrāddha* by one who has not studied the Vedas.
Since that [prohibition] is superimposed as part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), there is the consequence of it applying to the whole.
Furthermore, for one who has not studied the prohibitory texts, [there would be no knowledge of] the substances prohibited.

The lack of authority of the Veda is an object of extreme ridicule; for even when one performs [the rites] with the very same understanding as one who has studied the Veda, no transgression would occur— just as in the case of a mosquito.
Burning arises from a fault, and one is seized due to delusion;
likewise, because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) would otherwise be purposeless,
for even an act in the form of cessation serves as a cause for avoiding transgression when that is the case.
The validity of the entire Veda.

Therefore, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*), [the objection] is prior. Now, as for the statement, "For those who do not study [the Veda] become outcasts (*vrātya*)," this subsequent censure is fitting only for one who behaves like a sluggish stream.
The restriction applies to the person, not to the knowledge of the meaning.
Therefore, this is the sense: for a twice-born man, [the study of] his own Veda...
likewise, because it establishes excellence, the established conclusion is also achieved through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by way of attention to that presentation.
"One should indeed study, and not fail to study, so that one may come to know"—
this [position] is simply untenable.
In your view, excellence (*prāśastya*) is [established] by being made known through negation (*vidhūta*).
Although this injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) possesses a purpose by way of the avoidance of sin (*pratyavāya*),
it does not require [excellence], because it is not in need of anything further (*anatirikta*).
Nor is it the case that [the meaning] is different [from the words],
because even so, meditation is observed to arise from an external expectancy; thus, by the principle of having a purposeful object,
another [meaning] is established through the arousal of expectancy, provided there is no additional object.
Knowledge alone grasps that which is to be cultivated; and thus, there is no qualification even for one who has merely heard [the teachings],
because it is impossible for them to give rise to the required expectancy.
For there is no further expectancy once the word *rakta* has been uttered, because those who have acquired knowledge are satisfied by its very nature as a class-term (*jāti*). However,
the word *rohit*, being a term of specific color (*ruci*), gives rise to an expectancy.
First: the references to the Śruti are not sufficient to imply a connection with Vedic knowledge for a Śūdra.
Thus.
In worldly usage such as "one should feed a Brāhmaṇa," [the singular] applies even to a collective group;
and since a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) may be intent upon other means [of livelihood], the meaning there [in the Vedic injunction] follows by implication.
This is seen in the use of the singular number in expressions such as "eat the food."
The restriction applies to the knowledge, but this injunction is not for the purpose of restricting that [knowledge].
Likewise,
because of its nature, there arises an expectancy for a single word through the purpose of removing doubt.
Because the knowledge of a purposeful meaning is produced by the cultivation of study,
it possesses the capacity to prompt action;
however, there is no such purpose here.

Furthermore, since that [literal sense] is impossible in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) where the primary meaning is intended, there is a disparity between them by way of direct denotation (*śruti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Enough of this excessive elaboration.
Therefore,
because it is inconsistent that the authority of the *arthavādas* arises solely through their syntactical unity with the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*),
everything must be described according to the sequence of the *Vārttika*.
That is correct.
This being so, the injunction for Vedic study [serves] to avoid transgression.
For in this *codanāsūtra*, the authority of the entire Veda is indeed the thesis being asserted.
For even though the fulfillment of the purpose (*caritārthatva*) is the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*),
it is nevertheless [the case that] the determination of the meaning of words everywhere occurs through the synthesis of the preceding and the following.

Is there an activity [of the scripture], or not? If there is, then the injunction regarding what is already perceived becomes fruitless. And in this regard, [the sūtra] "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" [establishes] the entirety—
Thus, it is not possible for the knowledge of an object that has not been perceived to be produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
First, it was explained that the study of the Vedas, specifically regarding the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*), is the cause for the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*).
It is not [the case] by way of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), because that is undesirable.
And that [means of knowledge] consisting of the aforementioned characteristics is possible only if the entire Veda is the authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding Dharma.
And because it is impossible for that [object] to exist without being transcended;
if, on the other hand, it does not exist,
then it is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Likewise, later on as well, regarding that which is denoted by the *Autpattika-sūtra*—
namely, the isolated *bhāvanā* alone— there arises an expectation for a means [of accomplishment] seen in the world;
and because of the reason stated as "due to independence" (*anapekṣatvāt*), there follows the necessity of the relationship between words and word-meanings.

When the knowledge of the meaning is connected with that which has been performed, even the knowledge of an existing fact produced by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be connected [to the injunction],
because the production of those [results] constitutes the justification for the authority of the entire Veda; however,
the knowledge of the meaning intended by the person [is not so connected] through the injunction.
Because even the numerous investigations that will be undertaken [later] have the Veda alone as their object;

therefore, the primary [function] of the *arthavādas*— [Note: The provided fragment appears to be a portion of a philosophical argument (likely from a Mīmāṃsā or Vedānta commentary) concerning the status of *arthavādas*. The translation reflects the logical structure of the Sanskrit.]

And this is precisely the ultimate prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this section: since there is no possibility of perceiving [an injunction] directly, there is an occasion for the postulation of the unperceived; thus, the secret is that "whatever is possible" [must be accepted]. Therefore, because the Veda—the sacred tradition—is connected to an action in the form of something to be performed (*vidheya*), and because the study of the syllables follows the capacities understood from common worldly usage, the name-mantras (*nāman*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) existing separately would otherwise be purposeless. However, by means of the sequence of grasping the enjoined actions, they become causes for the knowledge of objects desired by persons; therefore, that alone constitutes their "purposefulness. Consequently, it is said that this [Veda] is not non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*).

Thus, it is accepted as something to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), but not the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) such as heaven and so forth. Nor is it stated with respect to what is already attained—for when the visible is present, an injunction is purposeless—and therefore the knowledge of the meaning is not the object to be cultivated by the *bhāvanā* which is constrained by the injunction; rather, because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, the injunctions serve the purpose of praise (*stuti*). Otherwise, there would be a doubt regarding the determination of the intended meaning of the Veda, since there would be no other means than the injunction for the study of the Veda itself.
For it is precisely because pronunciation is dependent upon the teacher that it is called "study" (*adhyayana*).

This is the intended meaning: this would indeed be so if, by way of praise, the fact that pronunciation is directed toward the meaning were possible for the names of words; however, it would not follow that the *arthavādas* lack the purpose of being for the sake of the enjoined action (*vidheya-kriyā*).
For the injunction [is satisfied] by the mere pronunciation.

Is it not the case that what is established by worldly linguistic usage is that the name of a word is itself the verbal *bhāvanā*? And that [verbal *bhāvanā*] is indeed the objective *bhāvanā* (arthabhāvanā), which requires an end, a means, and a manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). Furthermore, the fact that words have meaning as their primary purpose is established even in the case of human speech; however, in the Veda, there is a requirement for something further.

In that context, the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) consists of human activity; since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding the connection, this [activity], which is established by the general rule (*utsarga*), remains unsublated. Furthermore, having taken up the means (*karaṇa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) follows from the Sāṅkhya [tradition] and worldly custom—so what is the need for an injunction (*vidhi*)? Not so. For the meaning of words is twofold: the simple (*kevala*) and the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*). Even when the primary force of the word is directed toward the simple meaning, it brings about the knowledge of the excellence of the object (*viṣayaprāśastya*), which generates enthusiasm for action in accordance with the general rule. Thus, it effects the qualified meaning.

And it is observed in the world that in transactions such as buying and selling, the inclination toward activity and the intensity of effort arise from the utterance intended to convey a specific meaning; this invariably produces the knowledge of the excellence of the object [of the transaction].
For example, "This cow is to be bought"—this is established through the assumption of a co-utterance [with a specific intention], and not otherwise.

For instance: [1] when a cow is described as "having many offspring," "yielding much milk," or "having beautiful calves"; [2] or when, in a context where [terms] such as "this is to be bought—a cow, a horse, a man, or an elephant" are mutually connected, the word "man" does not denote a man in general, but rather "this man [is selling] my elephant"; [3] or when, among various objects, a word is uttered with the intention (*tātparya*) of conveying a specific meaning—as in "This is no mere Brāhmaṇa, but Vasiṣṭha"—then even by means of the secondary function (*jaghanyavṛtti*) of implication (*arthāpatti*), as in "This cow is swift," and so forth.

Likewise, in common worldly usage, there are sequences of words that express existence, non-existence, or the half [of either], such as "The man is also a mighty elephant by his other activities. Even through the function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), when there is the communication of excellence (*prāśastya*) regarding a qualified object, there arises the cognition of that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

Likewise, just as in the case of words such as *akṣa* which have multiple meanings, the status of being a sentence [is determined by context], so too here, the determination of a specific meaning for the *arthavādas* through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise is not produced by the inherent nature of the word itself; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that every sentence—regardless of its form—would result in the comprehension of a meaning simply by virtue of being a sentence that serves as the locus for what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), thereby fulfilling the requirements of the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) and its procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Rather, it is produced solely by the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) in uttering them. Thus, they indeed serve the purpose of action.

Furthermore, in the case of the physical act of producing meaning, when the word "cow" is uttered as in "he says 'cow'," there is no cognition of the object; rather, there is primarily no connection with the objective, the means, and the procedure (sādhya-sādhana-itikartavyatā). Instead, because the utterance is directed toward the word itself, there is primarily a cognition of the word alone, since the injunction does not apply to anything else.
It is only the injunction, along with its accessories, that is understood through syntactic connection.

Therefore, the cognition of a qualified object is not produced by the intrinsic nature of the word, nor is it due to the absence of excellence resulting merely from its utterance; rather, it is not produced by the intrinsic nature of the utterance itself, but is not untenable because it has as its purport the cognition of a qualified object. Now, let it be that in common worldly usage this occurs through the force of human intention, and that this purport of utterance arises because in the world people [use words] otherwise, for a word may have another meaning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Just as [words] are uttered by the power of a speaker's intention (*abhiprāya*), so too in the Veda, which consists of utterances for the purpose of knowing specific meanings, how is it that even through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *arthavāda*, only excellence (*prāśastya*) is understood because of its connection with an injunction? Thus, even though it has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), it possesses "being-for-another" (*paratva*).
Not so.
This would be the case if, in the Veda, the person were the primary factor, such that [the Veda] were established by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*).

But surely, if the utterance were the cause for the comprehension of meaning, then the injunction to study would be [rendered] purposeless. For that injunction—"One's own Veda is to be studied"—is understood to have the meaning as its primary purpose, since such a result is perceived once the meaning is grasped. If the injunction to study were itself dependent on the understanding of meaning, then the very act of studying would be required by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of the study; and if the injunction were already intent upon the meaning, then the conclusion that utterance is merely for the sake of recitation would follow. Thus, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).
Although study (*adhyayana*) is proximate as the meaning of the verbal root, it is likewise not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*).

For, following the power understood from common worldly usage, [the author] rejects the status of being a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) in the aspect of the objective (*bhāvyāṃśa*) and assigns it to the instrumental aspect (*karaṇāṃśa*).
And thus, it is performed.

And since it is established from the worldly perspective that a person should accomplish their desired goal through the study consisting of the grasping of syllables and so forth during recitation, the knowledge of the meanings of words uttered in sequence certainly arises;

however, because there is no means of determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—given that the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) has action as its purpose—it fails [to establish the meaning of non-injunctive texts]. Furthermore, in the case of the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), a clear split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) occurs.
However, in the case of the fire consecrated by the *ādhāna* rite, once its intended meaning (*tātparya*) has been ascertained, it becomes integrated [with other injunctions].

Therefore, this fault does not apply here; for while there is an ascertainment of the truth according to another injunction—namely, "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire"—this is merely an ascertainment of the fact, since the intended meaning established by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) already exists.
Moreover, in this case as well, there is no such ascertainment [of meaning through integration], so there is no circularity (*itaretarāśraya*).
Nor should it be argued that there is a disparity because there is another long-term injunction [for study].

Once the study of the Veda has been completed, the knowledge of the meaning occurs at a later time following one's familiarity with Mīmāṃsā and other sciences; likewise, for all words, the knowledge of their specific meanings occurs after the recitation of the text.

Therefore, how can it be said that the purpose of the recitation is the knowledge of the perceived meaning, since it was stated that there is no determination of the knowledge of specific meanings without an intention directed toward communication?

Regarding the rule for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*): since the study of the Veda proceeds through the sequence of grasping the syllables and so forth, the purpose of that study is the comprehension of meaning; and by that sequence, even at a later time, it is not contradictory that the *svādhyāya* (Vedic text), which has ascended to a connection with its constituent parts (*aṅga*), serves as the cause for the understanding of meaning. Because such recitation is possible even then, there is no fixed distinction between the primary (*pradhāna*) and the auxiliary (*aṅga*). Furthermore, since there would be a lapse in the recitation if the rule of study were absent in the case of the Veda, the comprehension of meaning is established by that very rule.
Thus, even by that [recitation], the possibility of recitation exists, and therefore the distinction between the auxiliary and the primary remains intact.

For even in the world, the cognition of a specific meaning does not occur immediately after hearing a word; likewise, the order of performance is not determined by the order of recitation. Rather, it occurs in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, where the sequence is established through the possibility of syntactic connection inferred from the words recorded in the *smṛti* texts.
Likewise, just as in a single sentence [one finds] "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu," so too here; thus, it is not untenable.

Now, one might object: since the status of the Veda as something to be accomplished through study is understood even from the use of the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) in passages such as "by transgressing the second case-ending" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 25.4.4), and because the expression "he who is the Adhvaryu is the Hotṛ" is possible with the nominative case, how can the knowledge of the meaning also be established as the goal to be accomplished, given that the nominative occurs first?

For within a single sentence, it is not possible for the word *hotṛ*, the particle *eva*, and the instruction [of the *adhyupadeśa*] to simultaneously have the character of a ritual act (*kāryalakṣaṇa*),
because the coexistence of two things to be accomplished (*sādhyadvaya*) would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Likewise, in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), regarding the fifteen-fold [stotra] dedicated to Indra, even with the four handfuls of the archetypal rite (*prākṛta*), [the objection] "four" is not so.
This might be so if this were an injunction regarding the dual nature of the goal, as in the case of "he makes the fists" (*muṣṭīr nirvapati*, Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.8.2).

But here, since it is observed that the very comprehension of the meaning is the goal to be accomplished, there would not be a sublation of the primary [text] by the subsequent [text] at the outset, provided that which has first arrived is already refined;
and thus it is not the case for the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) either.

For him, there would result a total collapse of the meaning of the entire Veda, since the purpose of the injunction for its recitation would remain unascertained prior to the performance of that act of recitation, and because the injunction for the recitation would be undermined by the fact that the text has no other purpose than its own meaning. Furthermore, there would be the fault of the non-establishment of the status of being a "thing to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) due to the lack of utility for that which is not employed in a ritual application (*viniyoga*) through direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.
Such being the case, [the Vedic texts] would have their meanings established according to their respective applications by virtue of being used exactly as they are recited.

Furthermore, once it is determined that study is directed toward meaning— since the injunction [of study] is syntactically connected [to the Veda] and thus, by the force of logical reasoning, establishes the desire [for meaning] and so forth— and once it is established that the entire Veda has as its object a desired purpose, then, because a literal sense is impossible for the *arthavādas*, one must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Now, one might argue that, by following the sequence of syllables and so forth, and keeping in mind the necessary utility for the desired goal, the injunction of study has as its purpose the communication of the fact that the subject matter is what is required.

Furthermore, even by means of the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), the understanding that they possess a required meaning cannot occur without the apprehension of the words themselves. If the understanding of their required meaning were dependent on the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Therefore, the cognition of their having a perceptible purpose is authoritative, just like presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Not so.

For, in accordance with worldly practice, even the portion consisting of the *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) adopts the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of excellence (*prāśastya*) regarding the object to be enjoined immediately after the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) itself; this is because it is established that its purpose is to convey the required meaning through the application of logical principles.

Therefore, it is proven that the *arthavādas* possess authority by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunctive statement, through the medium of communicating excellence.
And that excellence, being indicated, is not denoted by each individual word,
because the cognition of excellence does not arise from each single word;
for indeed, the understanding of excellence is not attained from the word *vāyu* alone.

What then? [The answer is: The purpose is the understanding of the praise characterized by the swiftness of the whole [sacrifice], as in the statement, "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity. Just as the authority of explanatory passages (arthavādas) serves as a purpose, so too, in the case of the passage "The pebbles are smeared," since there is no other means of knowledge to specify [the substance], any substance whatsoever that serves as a means of smearing would be adopted. However, when the authority of the explanatory passage is established—as in the explanatory passage "Ghee is indeed brilliance" (tejo vai ghṛtam)—the praise of ghee leads to the adoption of ghee itself for the sake of its purpose.

The Sūtra, however, states that because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction through the subject matter of the injunction, the explanatory passages (arthavādas) are authoritative for the purpose of praise. [Tautātita:
Oṃ. Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless; therefore, they are said to be non-eternal.]
This sūtra is intended to present the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that explanatory passages (arthavāda), the Purāṇas, and Vedic utterances are not authoritative.

Since the Veda (āmnāya) is for the sake of action—that is, because it aims to communicate actions consisting in the production of engagement with objects that are means to the desired or the undesired—those Vedic utterances that do not have that as their purpose, being devoid of such communication of action, are "meaningless" (anarthaka); that is, they are void of meaning, lack the capacity to produce a cognition of an object, and thus are non-authoritative.

Therefore, the lack of authority for certain Vedic statements implies that all statements—meaning all words—are either useless or lack authority. Some say: "Prescriptive statements (vidhi-vacana) are not authoritative because they are merely informative, like explanatory passages (arthavāda). Furthermore, there is a contradiction with both scripture (śāstra) and perceived reality (dṛṣṭa). "Scripture and perceived reality" means *śāstradṛṣṭe*; that which is seen through scripture is "seen by scripture" (*śāstradṛṣṭa*).
[The objection] "from form" [is raised].

Regarding the statements "the mind is a thief" and "speech is a liar," an opposition to observed reality was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) in the second sūtra; this [present] sūtra is for the purpose of refuting that.
This is a supplementary portion (*śeṣa*) of the injunction: "When gold is in his hand, he then takes the cup."

"Just as thieves have a concealed form, so too is the mind"—this is a figurative statement based on its nature. "Speech is a speaker of untruth"—this is a figurative statement based on its predominant tendency; for speech generally speaks untruth, and thus it is called a "speaker of untruth."

An action is performed by first forming a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and then uttering a mantra with speech; yet those two—speech and mind—are subject to defects, whereas gold is free from defect. Therefore, at the time of taking up the portions of the oblation, gold should be held in the hand.
Since this is something to be enjoined, there is a [logical] connection.

The term "guṇavāda" (figurative description) is carried over here from the previous sūtra, and its application must be determined according to the context. In the case of the mind, it is a figurative description based on its form; in the case of speech, it is based on its predominant tendency.
Thus, one meaning is that it is a designation for the quality of gold.

The statement "the thief is a speaker of untruth" is a figurative description (*guṇavāda*), meaning it is a word used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). This is another interpretation. Because of its great distance [from the primary meaning], this is the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) intended to refute the first position (*pūrvapakṣa*) mentioned in the second sūtra.

"Therefore, it was only the smoke of the fire that was seen by day, not its flame"—this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is a praise for the injunction of the morning *agnihotra* mantra: "The sun is light, light is the sun, svāhā. The praise consists in the statement that the *sūrya*-mantra alone should be recited, on the grounds that "the fire goes to the sun at dawn. The claim that the fire is invisible by day due to its distance is a figurative usage (*gauṇaḥ prayogaḥ*).
Similarly, the statement "Therefore, fire alone is seen at night, not smoke" is for the purpose of praising the evening injunction of the mantra "Agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā.

Since the sun deposits its own light within fire at night, fire is visible at night due to the abundance of brilliance, and not smoke; thus, this usage is figurative (*gauṇatā*). This being the case, there is no contradiction with perceived reality (*dṛṣṭavirodha*).
"Far and moreover far" means *dūrabhūyas*; the state of being so is *dūrabhūyastvam*.

Because the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) heard in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is connected with each [term] individually, it is established that "distance" (*dūratva*) and "abundance" (*bhūyastva*) are separate reasons.
This is due to the fault of the other [the opponent], and because the agent sees his son.
The following is a *siddhānta-sūtra* intended to dispel the doubt raised by the *pūrvapakṣa*:

"And we do not know this—whether we are Brāhmaṇas or non-Brāhmaṇas"—it is heard in the scripture: "O gods, you are fathers; O fathers, you are gods; being who I am, I sacrifice; I do not overstep that from which I am. This [statement] is figurative (*gauṇa*) in view of the difficulty of knowing one's own Brāhmaṇahood when the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) is being recited.
How so? Because of the transgression of the woman—that is, the mother—due to the possibility of the mother’s infidelity.

If it is argued that Brahminhood consists solely in having a Brāhmaṇa for both mother and father, and that this is easily understood by taking the case of those who possess the "field" (kṣetrin), [we reply] that in such cases, the son is seen to belong to the actual progenitor.

Having begun with the statement, "The son belongs to the progenitor, [not to the owner of the field]," and continuing with "The sower of the seed leads away the son," Āpastamba and others have determined that the son belongs to the one who performs the sowing of the seed, and not to the owner of the soil (*kṣetrin*). Thus,

even for such a person who is not a Brāhmaṇa by birth, the praise [of becoming a Brāhmaṇa] is applicable through the recitation of mantras such as "The gods are the fathers," because it occurs immediately [upon the performance].

Regarding the second aphorism, "And because of contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures" (*śāstradṛṣṭavirodhāt*), this aphorism is intended to refute the defect stated at the end—that there is a contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures. The term *ākālikam* means that which occurs at an improper time, at a covered time, or at a slightly improper time; or alternatively, it means that which occurs at the same time. Its meaning is that [the result] is momentary, non-perishable, pertaining to this world (*aihika*), and easily attainable. The desire for such a result is demonstrated by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "For who would know that? (*ko hi tad veda*). Thus, there is no contradiction with the heavenly bliss seen in the scriptures.

The meaning is as follows: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is enjoined that "one should make windows (atīkāśas—meaning *liḍakī* or *jharokhā* in the vernacular) facing the cardinal directions" according to the scriptural injunction regarding the eastern sacrificial hall (*prācīnavaṃśa*). For by making windows, one obtains an immediate and temporal benefit, namely the removal of the distress caused by smoke.
Furthermore, even if one does not obtain the bliss of heaven through the Jyotiṣṭoma, the easy attainment of some worldly sovereignty would be possible simply by seeing it through the windows.

But in the absence of openings (atīkāśa), even that [the aforementioned result] would not occur; therefore, openings must be made. Thus, there is scriptural authority stating, "For one [opening] serves the same purpose as all," and so forth. And in this way, since the injunction regarding the openings is a commendatory passage (arthavāda) for the sake of the primary rite, there is no contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures.
Regarding this, Bhaṭṭapāda has stated two readings: *ākālikepā* and *akālikepsā*.
In this regard, the formation of the word *ākālika* is established by the rule *ākālikadācyavacane* (Pāṇini 5.1.114).

The intention of the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Mahābhāṣya is as follows: "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to birth and "end" (*anta*) refers to destruction; when the expression of their being simultaneous is intended, the word *samānakāla* ("simultaneous time") undergoes the substitution *ākāla*, and subsequently, with the addition of the suffix *iyap*, the word *ākālika* is formed.
However, the author of the Mahāvṛtti, having rejected the suffix *iyap*, [proposes] *ākālā-*...

Intending the formulation of the rule as *dāca-tava-cane*, the derivation of the form is accepted by performing the *prāg-veṣṭhaj* suffix after the word *ākāla* itself—meaning "the time of eating" (*āhuta-kāla*) or "the time of going" (*īṣ-kāla*)—which functions as the governing term (*adhikārika*).
The meaning of the word as "that which is about to happen soon" (*acirabhāvitva*) is common to both positions.

Regarding the reading *akālikā*, the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda himself has demonstrated its etymology as follows: "In common usage, *kāla* refers to remoteness (a long duration of time). That which exists therein is *kālika*, derived by adding the suffix *ṭhañ* according to Pāṇini 4.3.11 (*kālat ṭhañ*). That which is not *kālika* is *akālika* (meaning short-lived or perishable).
This is a statement of praise for knowledge.
It is a *siddhānta-sūtra* intended to refute the doubt raised in the *pūrvapakṣa* by the rule "because there is likewise an absence of fruit" (*tathā phalābhāvāt*).

That which is called the "Garga-trirātra-vedānumantraṇa-vidyā," stated here as the cause for beauty in the afterlife and possession of offspring, is the praise (*praśaṃsā*) of both the Garga-trirātra and the vedānumantraṇa; this is the *Sudhā* commentary.

Here, because the words "vidyā" and "praśaṃsā" are seen in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is determined that they are two separate words. In the *Kutūhala*, however, it is explained in the third person: "The *vidyā* is the praise of the Garga-trirātra by means of sacrifice."

In the *Subodhinī*, however, it is explained as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound: "the praise of one who knows the *Garga-trirātra* [rite] regarding the *vidyā*," similar to a praise of a sacrifice (*kratustuti*).
Therefore, according to both views, the unity of purpose (*aikapathya*) is to be understood in the *sūtra*.
The quality of being "entire" (*sarvatva*) pertains to the qualification (*ādhikārika*).
This is a *siddhānta-sūtra* intended to dispel the doubt raised by the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) argument stated in the sūtra: "It would be for another purpose" (*anyārthatvam anyat*).

Regarding the statement, "By the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one attains all desires," the term "all" (*sarva*) should be understood as pertaining to the specific context (*ādhikārika*), the particular section (*prākaraṇika*), and the subject of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*).
Just as in the case of the statement, "All Brāhmaṇas should be fed," it refers to all those who have arrived at the house, but not to every single Brāhmaṇa residing on the face of the earth.
The meaning is that by means of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), whatever desire is obtainable, all those desires one obtains through the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Therefore, there is no fault of it having another purpose.
Since the fruit arises from the ritual action, there would be a distinction in the fruit according to its measure, as is seen in the world.
This is a *siddhānta-sūtra* intended to refute, by means of another method, the statement in the sūtra "anyārthatvam anyat" (the other [result] would have a different purpose).

Because there is scriptural mention of the production of results such as heaven through actions like the *pūrṇāhuti* sacrifice, since those actions vary in their degree of smallness or greatness according to their measure (*parimāṇa*), and in their quality (*sāra*) according to being more excellent and so forth, there will be a distinction among the results—that is, a gradation of results.
This is "like in the world."

Just as in the world there is a gradation of fruits according to the gradation of service and so forth, so it is here; and consequently, through the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), all fruits such as heaven and the like become small,
whereas through the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other rites, they become greater than those.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the phrase "by measure" (*parimāṇataḥ*) in the Sūtra, the two words "or by essence" (*sārato vā*) are found only as a marginal variant reading in the printed *Kutūhala* manuscript.

However, in the *Sudhā*, it is stated: "Since one would not engage in giving substances of high quality even when the sacrifice could be accomplished by giving substances lacking in quality, the inclusion of the term 'essence' (*sāra*) in the Bhāṣya exceeds the Sūtra."

The commentary states as follows: "Even though it is an injunction (*vidhi*), nevertheless there is purposefulness (*arthavattā*) by way of measure (*parimāṇa*) or essence (*sāra*), because of the distinction in results.
By means of a small action, the result would be small in measure or lacking in essence;
by means of a great action, the result would be great in measure and substantial in essence.

From a greater action, there would result a fruit of greater magnitude and higher quality. By this, even that which is easily understood [is shown]: "The ornament itself perishes when its middle part is severed. Therefore, it appears that according to the Bhāṣya, even those two words not found elsewhere should be accepted as parts of the Sūtra, as they are sanctioned by the Bhāṣya.
Nevertheless, because it is generally not found [in the Vedic corpus], this [type of statement] is not included in the Sūtra.
As for the other two, as has been stated:

regarding the proof of the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the two other reasons mentioned in the two Sūtras—*abhāgipratiṣedhāt* (1.2.15) and *anityasaṃyogāt* (1.2.16)—the response to those two is exactly as previously stated.

"The fire is not to be piled on the earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in the sky"—this prohibition of what is non-participatory (*abhāgin*), namely of that which has not even been reached, such as the intermediate space and so forth, as well as of the dual number, would be purposeless; thus, this is a reason for [the Veda's] lack of authority.
But that is not so, because it serves as a eulogy (*stuti*) for the injunction that "having placed gold on the earth, the fire is to be piled.

As for the claim that the mention of individual entities possessing birth (*janmavatīnāṃ vyaktīnām*) in the Veda is a reason for its lack of authority, that too has been stated to be not a source of fault, because it refers to universals (*jāti*), and because universals such as "Bharata-hood" are eternal.
In every respect, even *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) are authoritative regarding *dharma* by way of praise and so forth;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Among these, passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" are supplements to injunctions (*vidhi*) because they are equal in status to what is to be enjoined; whereas passages such as "He wept" are supplements to prohibitions (*niṣedha*) because they serve to censure that which is to be prohibited.
Such is the distinction.
[Question: Why? [Answer: Because the Veda has action as its purpose; for this reason, it is placed upon the head.

(Symbol) "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their purpose are useless"—this is merely what is stated in the scripture (*śruti*). It is said that whatever does not serve the purpose of enjoining anything is [therefore] purposeless.

(Symbol) This is the logical principle (*nyāya*): "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their purpose are useless; therefore, they are declared to be non-eternal."

Why is the authority of other portions of the Veda—distinct from those explaining injunctions (*vidhi*)—not accepted in their capacity to produce results such as the *iṣṭi* sacrifice? Otherwise, in accordance with the maxim "the purpose of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is [to enjoin action]," all the great Vedānta statements (*mahāvākya*) would fall into futility.
(Sanātanadharma-pradīpa, Prāmāṇya-prakāśa, p. 51).
[Symbol] We are capable of explaining the purpose of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), but not of questioning the sacred tradition itself.
Such is the principle (*nyāya*).

Even though the status of being a commendatory statement (*stāvaka*) is established by the injunction (*vidhi*) alone even without an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the Pūrvamīmāṃsaka accepts this status of being a commendation solely for the purpose of establishing the meaningfulness of the *arthavādas*, according to the principle that "the Veda [is not meaningless]" (*āmnāyasya...*), because otherwise they would be useless.

(The meaning of the Sūtra is: *āyan* is the substitute for *ph*, *ey* for *ḍh*, *īn* for *kh*, *īy* for *ch*, and *iy* for *gh*, provided that these are the initial elements of suffixes beginning with *ph*, etc. — Bhāṭṭadīpikā 3.3.8.

Regarding the term *āyudha* (weapon): 969. The principle of the results such as longevity (*āyurādiphalanyāya*).

In the case of the term *āyudha*, there is a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in its sense of being an instrument of war; there is a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) in the mere sense of being an instrument [in general].
(In passages such as *yajñādyāni* etc. Maṇi, p. 164.

The word "weapon" is well-known to apply only to weapons; it is applied to the wooden sword and others by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because these too are instruments, just like those [actual weapons].
Or [it is so] because the word "weapon" (āyudha), when restricted to sacrifice and the like, is used figuratively for the means of accomplishing other actions.
(Symbol) The Principle of the Fruit Beginning with Longevity (*āyurādiphalanyāya*).

In the *sūktavāka* formula belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, when there are multiple sacrificers in a *satra* or similar rite, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*).
[The rule states: "The modification should occur in that which is primary."
Commentary: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the Sūktavāka [mantra]: "With the Sūktavāka, he throws the prastara [grass-bundle] into the fire.
Therein, this is recited: "This sacrificer (yajamāna) desires long life.
Regarding this, the meaning is subject to doubt: in a modified sacrifice (*vikāra*) performed by another agent, should the word "sacrificer" be modified (*ūhitavya*), or not?
What is established? It should be employed without modification;
in this way, its functional capacity is maintained.
Furthermore, it does not here denote something inherent.
For here, in the case of "the sacrificer prays for long life" (*yajamāna āyur āśāste*),
no visible purpose for the sacrificer is produced by that prayer for long life.
Therefore, the benediction for long life is not to be removed.
The blessing is distinguished by the sacrificer; even when uttered by a single sacrificer, it becomes as if heard [and fulfilled] by all.
Just as it is said, "The two sacrificial posts are commensurate with the sacrificer," so it is in this case as well.
"Having reflected thus, it should be employed without modification.
This being the position reached, we reply:
there should be a modification; that is, an adaptation (*ūha*).

"In that which has him as its principal" means "in that which has the sacrificer as its principal. How is there a connection with the sacrificer? It is heard in scripture thus: "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*.
If the *sūktavāka* does not reveal the means for that throwing of the *prastara*, then the *prastara* would not be thrown by means of the *sūktavāka*.
The result of the throwing [of the *prastara*] is stated to be the prayer for long life.
The sacrificer prays for long life through this ritual act; thus, it is by the sacrificer that the *prastara* is thrown.
In that case, if the sacrificer—who is the primary agent with respect to the result—were not mentioned, then the throwing would not have been performed by him.
Therefore, all [the priests] being assembled together should be mentioned as the guests;
and when all are being mentioned, there occurs a plural expression.
Consequently, the modification (ūha) belongs to the sacrificer.
Ṭup—This is a counter-example.

(In the preceding sūtra it was stated, "And because it is for the sake of another, there is modification"; this is a counter-example of that mention of "for the sake of another," whereas in its own sense, it occurs as such).
Alternatively, this is a different topic (*adhikaraṇa*). [Āmī. Ko. 122]
It is commenced by means of *śakti* (capacity).
[The proponent of the *āśīḥ-kāma* view says: "This sacrificer desires long life"—thus, the fact that longevity is the fruit is not known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, a connection between the sacrificer and the benediction (*āśis*) must be stated for the sake of the injunction (*aṣṭa*).
In that case, the benediction connected with the sacrificer must be recited;
and that [benediction] indeed occurs even when there is only one sacrificer. Therefore, there is no modification (*anūha*).
(The author states the established conclusion: This is not so.

Because of the indication by the instrumental case in the injunction, "He throws the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka*," the *sūktavāka* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the throwing.
Furthermore, it neither reveals the act of throwing nor is it an instrument for that act.
And having heard it, its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) is determined.
Therefore, that which is manifested by the *śruti* is connected with the instrument (*praharaṇa*).
And by that [instrument], the deities (Agni and so forth) and the fruits such as long life (*āyus*) are manifested.
In that context, the deities attain the status of being the means (*sādhana*) for the action, while longevity and so forth attain the status of being the ends to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Therefore, longevity and so forth are the fruits. Furthermore, the fruit of an action accrues to the agent.
Therefore, the sacrificer is the primary factor with respect to the fruit;
the modification (*ūha*) follows from that which is the primary factor.
[Question: Where is this section? [Answer: It is found as a separate section in the Bhāṣya.
In the *Vārttika*, however, after stating "this is a counter-example," it is said, "or rather, this is a different section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The same is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā*. And that [section] has been placed at the end of the thirteenth section, beginning with the sūtra "But when [the act] is enjoined... (*codite tu*).
Regarding Soma’s statement that there is no modification (*anūha*) of the word *yajamāna* just as there is none for the word *yajñapati*, the connection is as follows:

Since the status of longevity and so forth as the fruit [of the sacrifice] is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their status as the fruit must be inferred solely from what is revealed by the mantra. the knowledge of medicine for one who is ill is found within the science of healing (*vaidyaka*)."

Or [as stated in] Bhāṣya on Jaimini Sūtra 13.8.24, page 162: "One desiring long life should offer a *caru* oblation dedicated to Prajāpati consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇala* [berries]; he places four *kṛṣṇalas* at a time.
Bhāṣya.
The *Āyuṣyasūkta* is the hymn recited in the Sāmaveda beginning with "May we attain long life, may we attain long life for all people; may we attain long life for the sovereignty of so-and-so.
This is the principle of the rotation of the buckets on a waterwheel (*āraghaṭṭaghaṭībhrāntinyāya*).

Starting from sunrise, the vital breath (*vāyu*) moves through two *ghaṭikās* (forty-eight minutes) in each of the six channels (*nāḍīs*); thus, over the course of a day and night, twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths occur according to the scriptures.

And it has been stated by the Abhimuktas in the *Pātañjala* section of the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*: "The breath flows through one channel for two ghaṭīs at a time; the rotation between the two channels occurs again and again, like the turning of a waterwheel."
The release of wild animals in the Aśvamedha sacrifice. Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa 6.27.

The principle of the forest [animal], the principle of the wild beast. In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, regarding the wild beast (parasva)— that is, the wild animal used in the sacrifice— there is a prohibition of the subsidiary rites subsequent to it, by virtue of the injunction that prescribes the performance of the subsidiaries up to the rite of carrying fire around (paryagnikaraṇa).
Regarding the abandonment of those animals for whom the fire has been carried around, it serves that same purpose as the placing [of the bricks], as stated in the Bhāṣya:
"In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, they recite: 'One should sacrifice the parasvats to Īśāna.
With reference to that, it is heard: 'They release the wild animals after the fire has been carried around them.'"

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the immolation of the *araṇya* animals for the purpose of their disposal—that is, for the purpose of discarding the substance—or is it a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual, meaning that those animals, having been consecrated by the rites up to the *paryagnikaraṇa*, are to be discarded? What is the prima facie view? This is a disposal of the substance, and the immolation is indeed for the purpose of disposal. Why? Because by enjoining the disposal thus obtained, the text confirms its existence and thereby excludes [the completion of the ritual].
Otherwise, [the suffix] would merely restate what is already established by the general rule (*utsarga*).
The suffix would express the existence of the sentence-meaning, which is a prohibition;
however, direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection (*vākya*).
This being the case, there is a connection with a deity in the act of seizing:
animals belonging to another must be seized with reference to Īśāna, and having performed the rite of carrying fire around them (paryagnikaraṇa), they are to be released—
just as in the case of the *upadhāna* bricks.

Just as in the case of the statement, "This indeed is the direct eye; he who places the *caru* in this manner [places] the *caru*," the taking up of the *caru* is solely for the purpose of placing it;
so too here, the touching (*ālambha*) will be for the purpose of relinquishing (*utsarga*).
Or rather, there is a prohibition of the remainder because, due to the absence of a purpose, it is not connected here.
Commentary: Or rather, the prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action is stated in this sentence. Why? Because of the absence of purpose.
If the act of "sacrificing" (ālabh) were for the sake of relinquishment (utsarga), there would be no purpose whatsoever for the sentence, "One should sacrifice a parasvat for Īśāna."

How so? At the very time of the sacrifice, the Adhvaryu priest would know: "These will not be given to Īśāna. For one who knows this, the resolve does not arise: "It should be taken up in order to give to Īśāna. Since its purpose is thus already accomplished, this statement becomes meaningless.
This very intention is thus logically established: [the animals] must be given to Īśāna.
Therefore, it is understood that by the verbal expression "they are to be immolated" (*ālabhya*), the act of giving itself is enjoined.

And when the giving is enjoined, then the scriptural statement—"they release them after they have been carried around the fire"—serves to enjoin a specific manner of releasing by way of restating the general act of releasing (*utsarga*).
But how, then, is a specific rule established here? Is it that the time for the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite is [the same as] the time for the *utsarga*?
No, he says;
for no word expressing time is heard here.
When one specific time is prescribed, other times are excluded, but not other injunctions.
Now, is it to be discarded like the *paryagnikaraṇa*?
That too is not the case.
For here the injunction of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) is not being stated;
if that were the case, then all the ritual acts—both those preceding and following the *paryagnikaraṇa*—would be prohibited once it has occurred.
How then [is it understood]? It means that "once the *paryagnikaraṇa* has been completed, [the animal] is to be released."
"What is [the purpose] in this state?"—he says, "No; this is obtained from the injunction itself: 'it is the animal for the Utsarganīya'."
Furthermore, this word is not expressive of a prohibition of another state;

for when the time for the *utsarga* (releasing) has arrived, it is precisely at that point—after the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) has been performed—that the act occurs. If, however, there were a prohibition of the state itself, then the ritual items would be prohibited either after the *paryagnikaraṇa* or before the *utsarga*, but certainly not those that follow (*parāñcaḥ*).
What is the purpose of that? It is so that this [animal] becomes exactly as it was when the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) had been performed.
But surely, that accessory is already obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
It is said in reply: [it serves to ensure the animal remains in that state].
Furthermore, this state of his is heard for the purpose of enumerating specific auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). By means of these very auxiliaries, there is the performance of other auxiliaries.
Thus, those [elements] obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) are enumerated, so that they do not become auxiliaries from any other [sources].
If it is asked, "How can this word alone effect such an exclusion?
we reply that it is indeed capable of doing so.

How? Because the archetype (prakṛti) is rendered free from expectancy by the directly stated (pratyakṣa) sentence regarding those specific subsidiaries; thus, there will be no syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) with the remaining subsidiaries through the indirect application (codaka).
Therefore, it is a prohibition of the remainder of the ritual action.
Furthermore, because the word [“saṃsthāpayati”] refers to what has preceded, the expression “he completes with clarified butter” would not be tenable if [the sacrifice] had not already commenced.
The Bhāṣya states: "And because the word refers to what has preceded, [it means] that preceded by the commencement of the sacrifice, one completes the remainder with clarified butter."
If this sacrifice has been commenced, then it is appropriate that one "completes" it;
for this [act] is similar to the completion of a sacrifice, being another sacrifice itself.
For if the previous sacrifice had not been undertaken, there would be merely an act of relinquishment, and in that case, it would not be similar to the completion of a sacrifice.
Therefore, it is not tenable that he "concludes" [the sacrifice].

For this reason as well, there is a prohibition of the remaining rites. As for the statement, "He concludes the remainder," this is an observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding its being a sacrifice; it is understood through the logic of the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*).

How is that so? However, another rite, such as the *pārśva* [offering], has the same scriptural injunction (*śruti*) regarding the abandonment in the forest (*āraṇyotsarga*). In that context, it is heard: "He completes the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*)."

In that case, because the act of lightening [the burden] has been completed, the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is untenable; and due to its absence, the verbal root *saṃsthāpayati* ("to conclude") is likewise untenable. Only the suffix remains in its pure form.
Since there is no remainder or number, the instrumental case ending in "with clarified butter" (*ājyena*) is also of an untenable meaning.
What remains is merely the nominal stem "clarified butter" (*ājya*).

When there is a connection between these two—the base word *ājya* and the verbal suffix—and the verbal suffix expresses the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*), the clarified butter (*ājya*) becomes the most desired object (*īpsitatama kāraka*), as in "one should make the clarified butter" (*ājyaṃ kuryāt*).
Nor is this a mere injunction for the production of clarified butter, because that would be purposeless.

Therefore, the injunctive statement regarding performance (*prayoga-vacana*), which requires another term to complete its sense, connects with the proximate term *pānīyatva* found in the sentence concerning the carrying of fire around the sacrificial animal (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Thus, when water has been exhausted, one should perform an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*);
and because of the connection between a substance and a deity, this constitutes a sacrifice.
(This is a distinct sacrifice.)

[The author] states the application of the words "saṃsthā" (conclusion) and "śeṣa" (remnant), which are in the accusative case: "And that [sacrifice] possesses both a beginning and an end"; thus, by implication, the verbal roots *saṃsthā* and *nirvap* (to offer) are employed as its constituent parts (*aṅga*) in their respective forms.

Since it has fewer duties to perform than the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), and being performed immediately after it, it is as if it were a remnant of that; therefore, the word "remnant" (*śeṣa*) is meaningful. Consequently, the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is indeed appropriate.
(Therefore, it is an injunction for a separate rite.

Thus, the section being concluded, the observation of an indicative mark from the preceding section follows: A comparison with the completion of the remaining [rite] is appropriate on account of similarity, provided that the former is also indeed a sacrifice.
However, if it is merely the disposal of the substance, then—due to the absence of similarity—it would not be logical [to say] "he completes the remainder."
And this is established because the same logic applies even to the *āraṇyakas*.

Since activity is caused by [prior] impulsion (*pravṛtti*), when there is a prohibition, there would be no performance of the ritual refinements (*saṃskāras*), because they are brought about by that [impulsion], just as there is no taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*) when the *prayāja* offerings are prohibited.
*Bhāṣya*: This is a sūtra stating the purpose [of the discussion].

If the relinquishment of the substance (*dravyotsarga*) were enjoined, then there would be no ritual action (*akarma*) for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). Why? Because the performance of the purificatory rites has sacrifice as its cause.
