In that case, if there is a prohibition and consequently an absence of sacrifice, why should the purificatory rites be performed? For they are indeed brought about by the sacrifice.

Just as in the absence of the *prayāja* offerings, the vessel intended for them is not taken up and the drawing (*grahaṇa*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is not performed; so it is where it is heard in scripture: "Those [offerings] are without *prayājas* and without *anuyājas*. This is the principle of the *āraṇyanyāya* (the logic of the forest-food), namely, the principle of the consumption of forest-food.
In that case, clarified butter is not taken for its sake;
likewise here too, the consecrations (saṃskāras) should not be performed.
Or rather, it would be a mere act of cutting, which would result in the total abandonment [of the substance].
Commentary: But when there is the position that it is a prohibition of the remainder of ritual acts, even then, one might ask: "Should the purificatory rites not be performed?
This is not so;
the performance would take place under the view that there is no interruption.
For at that time, it occurs in the sacrifice;
therefore, all the constituent elements of the sacrifice must be performed.
If it were not a sacrifice, then it would be a non-action.
There would be the total abandonment of all formative factors (saṃskāras);
however, in that case, the sacrifice (yāga) still takes place.
Therefore, according to the position that prohibits the remainder of ritual action (karmaśeṣa), everything must be performed.

It is argued that even substances such as Soma and milk do not possess the status of an oblation (*haviṣtva*) because there is simply no injunction for a sacrifice; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) with the example.
Mādhava states that the word *paraskha* denotes a specific species of wild deer.

As for the meaning of the sūtra: the animals designated as "encircled by fire" (*paryagnikṛta*) are intended for the act of immolation (*ālambha*) prescribed by the sentence concerning the Lord of Fire (*agner īśānavākya*), just as the preparation of rice-porridge (*caru*) is for the purpose of the placement (*upadhāna*) enjoined by the rule "he places the porridge"; it is not, however, for the purpose of a sacrifice (*yāga*).
Touching is contact; sacrifice is the taking hold of what belongs to another.
Or, the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering] belongs to the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, not to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
[The Ārambhaṇīyā] belongs to the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
It may be so, because time is not exhausted;
the word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the prima facie view.
Thus, there may be the *ārambhaṇīyā* in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
Because the time of life—that is, the duration of one's lifetime—is not a subordinate element (*aśeṣabhūta*).
The time of life is not a subordinate element of the primary action;
rather, it is a property of the agent.

However, the time for the archetype (prakṛti), namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices, is [fixed]. Thus, since each lunar phase (parvan) constitutes a separate performance, the modified sacrifices (vikṛtis) do not fall within the framework of that [archetype], and therefore there is no case of "incidental benefit" (prasaṅga). Consequently, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the Ārambhaṇīyā offering should be performed in the modified sacrifices.

And because of the distinction between the commencement [of the archetype and the ectype]. The *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering], which is to be performed at the commencement of the archetype, must also be performed separately at the commencement of the ectype; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The present sūtra provides another reason for this:
because there is a distinction between the commencement of the archetype and that of the ectype, the *ārambhaṇīyā* must be performed separately for the purpose of commencing the ectype.
For when there is the commencement (*ārambha*) of the primary rite (*prakṛti*), the modification (*vikṛti*) has not yet arisen; therefore, the commencement of both is distinct.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the reasons.

Which [rite]? The *Ārambhaṇīyā* [offering], because it is common to all performances or because it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatva*), should be performed only once at the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

However, it is not the case that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* must be performed earlier as such, on the grounds that the activity directed toward the great resolve (*mahāsaṃkalpa*)—"I shall perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—is in fact produced by the desire directed toward the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, and thus possesses the nature of that resolve with respect to the *dīkṣaṇīyā*. This is because that desire takes the form "May the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice together with its subsidiaries arise for me"; although the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is an object of that desire in its capacity as a subsidiary, it is not an object of it in its specific capacity as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.

Therefore, since the purpose in the form of the door [of the sacrifice] is lost, it is established that this [Ārambhaṇīyā] is not to be performed at the commencement of the Jyotiṣṭoma, nor at the commencement of the Dīkṣaṇīyā;
and this has been explained by us in detail precisely in the ninth [book], at [sūtra] 9.1.11.
Maṇḍana says: "And the Ārambhaṇīyā is [performed] at the Dīkṣaṇīyā."
Śaṅkara: "The commencement [is performed] by means of the Ārambhaṇīyeṣṭi.
Regarding the Ārambhaṇīyā: there is a re-performance of it in the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, such as the Saurya sacrifice and others.
[Objection: The Ārambhaṇīyā should not occur in a modification, because it falls within the time of the archetype (*prakṛti*); how much less, then, for its sake?
(Note: In the Bhāṣya manuscript, the phrase "atrāśaṅkate" is printed as an introduction preceding the sūtra.
This is indeed present in the Kalkattā manuscript and in the Vitarkarīyā as well; however, it is printed within the commentary on the preceding sūtra.
Furthermore, in that preceding sūtra, it was stated that the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) must be performed.)
And following that is the discussion on the *ārambhaṇīyā* [introductory rite].
This being the case, the two words "here" (*atra*) and "one objects" (*āśaṅkate*) are entirely inconsistent both previously and subsequently;
therefore, those two words have been omitted here.

Bhāṣya: Regarding the modified (vaikṛta) rites, there arises the inquiry whether the *ārambhaṇīyā*—the rite marking the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa—is to be performed or not. It is stated that it is not to be performed. What is the reason? Because they fall within the time-period of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
The time for the archetype, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, is defined by the injunction: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives."
In the midst of that, the modified rites (vaikṛta-karmāṇi) fall;
why, then, for its sake?
Because the Ārambhaṇīyā, performed at the beginning, is for the purpose of the application (prayoga) of the entire life-long sacrifice (kṛta-yāvajjīvika).
It has been stated: "Because of the connection with a single commencement, there is no further commencement, since the application lasts for as long as one lives" (9.1.135).
Thus, that very [application] will accomplish the task for them by way of *prasaṅga* (extended application).
Therefore, there should be no distinction among them.
Or rather, it may be [performed], because time is all-encompassing.
Bhāṣya: Or rather, the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering] should be performed in the modified sacrifices (vikṛti).
Why? Because it is obtained through the extended application (codaka).

But was it not said that [the performance] would follow as a consequence because of falling within the interval of the *prakṛti*? No, for the time of life-long observance (*yāvajjīvaka*) is not a residual part (*śeṣa*) of the *prakṛti*.

It has been stated [in the sūtra] "Or rather, it belongs to the agent, because of its connection with the scriptural injunction" (2.4.12) that this [observance] is for the purpose of being performed by the agent; such is the nature of the restriction. Likewise, this is the time:
whereas the time for the archetype is the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices.
Therefore, according to their respective views, the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) are included within the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Consequently, the *ārambhaṇīyā* offering does not apply to them. Otherwise, a fault was stated; otherwise, the resolution is given.

The objection was stated on the grounds that the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice has a lifelong duration (*yāvajjīvaka*); the resolution is that it is occasional (*naimittika*). Furthermore, resolutions are possible even under the alternative view, because of the distinction regarding its commencement (*ārambha*).
Commentary: The commencement of the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) is distinct.
When there is the commencement of the material cause, at that time the modification has not yet arisen;
for it is impelled by desire or by a causal occasion (*nimitta*).
Therefore, there is no performance of it at the commencement of the archetype;
and because of the difference in the commencement, there would be a difference in the *ārambhaṇīyā* occasioned by that [commencement].
Consequently, the *ārambhaṇīyā* should exist in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*).
Soma: The connection [of the topic] is established by the fact that the same objection raised previously arises here as well.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering] should not be performed in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because since the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) is to be performed throughout one's life, the modified sacrifices fall within that same period; thus, since the Ārambhaṇīyā has already been performed for the sake of the archetype, its requirements can be met through "extension" (*prasaṅga*) into the modified sacrifices.
Vi: "The Ārambhaṇīyā should not be performed in the Saurya and other such [modified sacrifices], just as [it is not performed] in the case of the [repeated] performance."
How many purposes are not for the sake of the performance [of the sacrifice], such that from them there would be an undertaking?

Bhaṭṭa: According to the method stated in the ninth chapter (nauamika-adhikaraṇa), since the Ārambhaṇīyā is known as the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and because it is established that its commencement applies to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) by means of extended application (atideśa), the Ārambhaṇīyā must indeed be performed.

Nor can there be any suspicion that this [benefit] is established through *prasaṅga* (extension), on the grounds that once it has been performed for the archetype (*prakṛti*), it assists all applications (*prayoga*) because its assistance is understood to persist until the end of another Darśapūrṇamāsa performance, and thus it is logically possible for it to assist the *vikṛtis* (modifications) performed during that interval. This is because this [benefit], which constitutes the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, is not known to belong to the second and subsequent performances.
Furthermore, this matter has been explained in detail precisely in the ninth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].
Moreover, the view of the authors of the *Tantraratna* and others, who claim that it belongs to all performances, has been refuted.

Therefore, since the benefit produced by the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is destroyed precisely when the commencement of the aforementioned [main] rite is performed, it serves no purpose to remain present throughout the performance of another *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice; thus, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* must be performed separately for each commencement of a modified (*vikṛti*) sacrifice. However, for those such as the author of the *Tantraratna*, who maintain that the *anvārambhaṇīyā*—once performed—is for the sake of all performances, the occurrence of *prasaṅga* (extension of the benefit) in the modified sacrifice would be unavoidable.
Maṇḍana: "The Ārambhaṇīyā [rite] should be performed in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti).
Śaṅkara: "The Ārambhaṇīyā [rite] in the modified sacrifice.
There is an exclusion (bādha) of the Ārambhaṇīyā in the Anumati and other offerings belonging to the Rājasūya.
From the principal [act] when conjoined with others, the result would cease for all [of them], because they are not auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
Commentary: There is the Rājasūya sacrifice, [enjoined by the rule]: "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya.
In that [sacrifice], the *iṣṭi*, animal, Soma, and New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-homas*) constitute the principal acts.
Regarding the iṣṭi sacrifices such as the Anumati and others, there is a doubt: should the Ārambhaṇīyā rite be performed, or not? What is the prima facie view? It should be performed;
for it has been stated, "In the case of a different cause, the rule should apply by extension to all rites" (10.1.12).
This being the case, we reply:
as the primary element, it ought to exclude those things connected with other primaries.
Why? Because the Jyotiṣṭoma is enjoined there by all its constituent parts, as in the statement: "One performs the Agniṣṭoma first."
It must be recited by way of a common application (*tantra*) for each of the principal rites under discussion.
For here, the context is common to each principal rite by way of such a *tantra*.
Therefore, since the purpose of the commencement is already accomplished through the *anumati* offerings and others, the *ārambhaṇīyā* offering need not be performed.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The Jyotiṣṭoma is enjoined there by all [the texts] as having both [purposes].
How so? The Jyotiṣṭoma is connected with the fruit through direct scriptural statement (śruti).
And it is not logical for it to serve two purposes in the absence of an explicit injunction.
Nor does there exist any means of valid cognition such as inference or the attainment of an effect [to establish it].
Therefore, the designation "perception" (pratyakṣa) is improper;
rather, one must state that there is simply an absence of the object.

Objection: Is it not the case that the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-varaṇa*) is for the sake of all the principal rites (*pradhāna*), and therefore the *ārambhaṇīyā* will apply to those principal rites such as the Āditya sacrifice? Reply: It is said in response:
even so, because its function is non-archetypal (*aprākṛta-kāryatva*), there is its exclusion.
Just as there is the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of sprinkling on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) when there is a sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Soma: The Commentator, in the section on the *Rājasūya*, established the conclusion that the function of the introductory rite (*ārambhaṇīyā*) is replaced (*pratyāmnāna*) by the injunction of the *Agniṣṭoma* in the statement, "He performs the *Agniṣṭoma* first.
That is incorrect; since the aforementioned sentence is appropriately explained as being intended to prescribe the sequence (*krama*), it cannot be a case of replacement (*pratyāmnāna*).
Because of its existence [in the model sacrifice].

Therefore, the Vārttikakāra has established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is a sublation (*bādha*) precisely due to the removal of the door; it should be understood that this very point was also stated by the author of the [Śābarabhāṣya] (*granthakāra*).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: according to the position of the Bhāṣyakāra, the *ārambhaṇīyā*—which is connected to the Soma-sacrifice—would be excluded even from the principal (*pradhāna*) Iṣṭi sacrifice, because the *ārambhaṇīyā* is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*), given that the Agniṣṭoma is enjoined as being for the purpose of all undertakings (*sarvārambhārthatayā*).
According to the view of the Vārttikakāra, however, since the commencement of all [the rites] is common and lacks the specific character of the *iṣṭi* alone, [the question arises]:

"Does that [commencement] not apply to the Anumati and other [sacrifices], or does it? Because the commencement belongs to the principal (*aṅgin*), and because the door [to the sacrifice] is lost, that [commencement] would not belong to the *iṣṭi*."
That [Ārambhaṇīyā] is the introductory rite.

Bhaṭṭa: In cases such as the Rājasūya, where there are principal sacrifices consisting of *iṣṭis* that are connected with other principal acts, even though those [individual *iṣṭis*] possess primacy, their performance is possible through a resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as "I shall sacrifice with this particular *iṣṭi*"—which takes the form "May this particular *iṣṭi* be accomplished"—even if it is not generated by a desire characterized by the property of being a Rājasūya (such as "May the Rājasūya be accomplished for me"). Consequently, because they lack the status of being objects of activity whose intended goal is delimited by those specific *iṣṭis*, the Ārambhaṇīyā is not performed prior to them.

Nor can one say, "I shall not sacrifice with the Rājasūya," prior [to the performance], because it is a great resolve (*mahāsaṃkalpa*); for even that [resolve] has as its object of activity (*pravṛttiviṣaya*) that which is delimited by the status of being a Rājasūya, and thus it lacks the status of being an object of activity whose object of intention (*uddeśyatā*) is delimited by each of those specific sacrifices [that constitute the Rājasūya].

Indeed, the property of being a Rājasūya (*rājasūyatva*) is not the delimiter of the modified nature (*vikṛtitva*)—as characterized by the archetypal nature (*prakṛtitā*) residing in the Darśapūrṇamāsa—because it is over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), since it also exists in the Soma-sacrifices.

For this very reason, in cases such as the Cāturmāsya or the Āgrayaṇa sacrifices, where the property of being a "Cāturmāsya" and so forth is not over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), there is no deficiency even if one assumes distinct extended applications (*atideśa*) for each individual sacrifice, provided that [the class-property] serves as the delimiting factor of the objective referent (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). In reality, however, even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the status of being a *Darśapūrṇamāsa* is not the delimiting factor of the objective referent; rather, it is the specific sacrifices such as the Āgneya and others. Furthermore, due to the unity of time, the performance is carried out by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Thus, the statement "I shall sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" has the same meaning as "I shall sacrifice with the Āgneya and other [constituent] sacrifices."

Consequently, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as the Cāturmāsya, the very nature of each respective sacrifice (*yāgatva*) is the delimiting factor for the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*); and because the time is identical, the performance is conducted by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Furthermore, the expression "I shall sacrifice with the Cāturmāsyas" has the meaning "I shall sacrifice with those respective sacrifices," and thus there is no contradiction whatsoever. Therefore, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* [introductory offering] must indeed take place upon the commencement of that [modified sacrifice].

In the present case, however, even though each respective *iṣṭi* and so forth possesses the status of being the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatā'vacchedakatva*), the *anvārambhaṇīyā* [is not required] because each respective *soma* sacrifice also possesses the status of being the delimitor of the objective.
For in the archetype (*prakṛti*)...

By the statement "one who is about to undertake the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsāvārambhyamāṇaḥ*), the qualifying injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices is understood; at the time of characterizing the means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), the qualification of the objective (*uddeśyatā-viśeṣaṇa*) must be intended as that which is delimited by the non-delimiting nature of the causality defined by the effect residing in the transcendental result of the primary sacrifice (*prakṛta-apūrva*). Consequently, because such an objective is absent in the Rājasūya, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is not performed there.

For this very reason, even the desire in the form "May the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices be performed for me" does not constitute the constituent of the objective (uddeśyatā) in the archetype (prakṛti). Otherwise, since even the first constituent element of the initial performance of the Agnihotra would have such a desire as its object, the Anvārambhaṇīyā rite would undesirably apply there as well. Therefore, it should be understood that after such a desire [for the archetype], a subsequent desire arises in the form "May the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices be performed," and that alone constitutes the constituent of the objective.
Maṇḍana: "And that [initiation] should not be performed in the Rājasūya sacrifices.
Śaṅkara: "It is so even in the Rājasūya sacrifices.
[This is] the prohibition of the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering].

The injunction regarding the *ārambhaṇīyā* and other such rites—which, having attained syntactic unity with the time, place, and so forth prescribed by extension (*atideśa*), serves the purpose of the sacrifice—is an injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).
Bāla. p. 13.
The section on the *ārambhaṇīyā*.
Bhāṣya 9.1.11–14: The Ārambhaṇīyā Principle (one).
There is the sublation of one Ārambhaṇīyā by another Ārambhaṇīyā.
But it should be [performed] with the true essence, like the *prayāja* offerings.
Commentary: There is the *ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice.

"One who is about to undertake the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap (*caru*) to Sarasvatī, a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvat, and a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Bhagin, he who desires: 'May I be fortunate and an eater of food.'"
"Some say it should be performed as if it were permanent" (so it is stated).

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: Should the Ārambhaṇīyā rite be performed at the Ārambhaṇīyā [of the Soma sacrifice], or not? What is the prima facie view? In that case, it should be so, just like the Prayājas.
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing doubt; indeed,
there is no doubt that the Ārambhaṇīyā [rite] ought to be performed at the commencement [of the sacrifice].
Why? Because of the sūtra: "In another context, due to extension [of the rule], the rite should be performed for all actions" (10.1.11).
Just as with the *prayājas*, so too with the *ārambhaṇīyā*.
[The opponent] says: But surely, for that [first *ārambhaṇīyā*] there is another *ārambhaṇīyā*, and for that...
Furthermore, for the sake of that [first] *ārambhaṇīyā*, another would have to be undertaken; and for the sake of that one as well, yet another—thus the *ārambhaṇīyā* would never reach a conclusion.
And the meaning of the scripture must be something established.
To this, it is replied:
In all these cases of non-proximity (*anayasthā*), the determination will be established by implication (*sāmarthyena*).
The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "On the same day"—this is the implication.
For these [rites] are for the sake of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, and because they share the same time, they must be performed on that very day.
Therefore, on that day, as many times as it is possible to employ [the mantra], so many times it is employed; thus, there is no lack of fixed rule (*avyavasthā*).
Or rather, it is not so, "because of the impossibility.
The *Bhāṣya* states: the position expressed by "or rather, not" is refuted.
The Ārambhaṇīyā [rite] would not be applicable to the Ārambhaṇīyā itself.
Why? Because that [Ārambhaṇīyā] is not yet established within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
and the establishment of what is already established occurs only through its status as the primary act.
Thus it has been stated:
the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices must be performed by one who has undertaken the Ārambhaṇīyā.
Therefore, since it is the archetype (prakṛti), the Ārambhaṇīyā itself must also be performed by one who has undertaken the Ārambhaṇīyā.
Therefore, would there be an *ārambhaṇīyā* in relation to the *ārambhaṇīyā* itself?
And that is not so;
for even without performing another *ārambhaṇīyā*, it is understood that by performing the *ārambhaṇīyā*, one is indeed engaged in the commencement (*ārambhaṇīyā*).
Therefore, there should not be an *ārambhaṇīyā* [introductory rite] for the *ārambhaṇīyā* itself.

Moreover, the lack of fixed order (*avyavasthā*) that would be understood through the syntactical connection (*vākya*) regarding the *ārambhaṇīyā*—resembling a bubble on water—is sublated by the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) [of the injunction].
In the absence of such a position, there is neither lack of fixed order nor sublation.
Therefore, there is no *ārambhaṇīyā* [rite] in the *ārambhaṇīyā* itself.
The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "For that [rite] is not established within the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; and that which is not established is accomplished only as a primary act" (this is the *Bhāṣya*).
If you think it is like the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth, then [the answer is] regarding that.
Why? Because the Ārambhaṇīyā is performed outside the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, whereas the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites are not.
Therefore, this [objection] is incorrect.
Furthermore, this Ārambhaṇīyā is enjoined as an auxiliary (aṅga) that fulfills the requirement of "how" (kathaṃbhāva).
And that [offering] requires the ritual details (*dharma*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
yet those two, prior to their formal prescription, are devoid of the *ārambhaṇīyā* offering.
This is like the case of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
Commentary: For this reason as well, we understand that it must be exactly so.

Why? Because when this single sentence prescribes the *ārambhaṇīyā* [introductory rite], it does not [at that time] prescribe it for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. It would thus be prescribing it for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices as if it were not already prescribed for them.
And one might extend [the rule] as if it were prescribed for the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering];
however, that which is uttered only once is not capable of performing this.

Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no *ārambhaṇīyā* in the *ārambhaṇīyā*. Soma says: because here, since it is for its own sake (*svārthatayā*), a separate commencement is possible, and because the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) has been stated. But the meaning of the Sūtra is that in that *ārambhaṇīyā*, it (the *ārambhaṇīyā*) should exist, just like the *prayāja*s and so forth.

Vi—Is it present in that [sacrifice], or not? Even if it were present, because it is commenced separately from this [original sacrifice]. It is present. Do not say so; for there is no injunction [of it] by way of extended application (*atideśa*) due to incapacity. Bhāṭṭa—Even though the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is excluded from the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), another *anvārambhaṇīyā* need not be performed at all.

Regarding the resolve, "I shall perform the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice," even though an activity generated by a desire in the form "May the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, along with their ancillaries, arise for me" is possible, there is nonetheless an absence of being an object of activity whose intended goal (uddeśyatā) is delimited by the nature of the Anvārambhaṇīyā itself.

For this very reason, the Anvārambhaṇīyā is not performed in the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, nor in the Pavamāna-iṣṭis which constitute the Vaiśvānara-Pārjanya section that forms an ancillary to the first of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Furthermore, the Anvārambhaṇīyā itself does not require another Anvārambhaṇīyā, according to the principle established regarding the third Pavamāna-iṣṭi.
Likewise, in the Vaimṛdha sacrifice as well, there is no Vaimṛdha offering.
Maṇḍana states: "And one should not perform that [Vaimṛdha] at the time of its own commencement. Here, "its own" refers to the Ārambhaṇīyā.
Śaṅkara: "It has been commenced within oneself. That is, within the *ārambhaṇīyā* [rite].
This is the *ārambhaṇīyā-nyāya* (the second).
Even though the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa) are repeated, the introductory rite (Ārambhaṇīyā) is to be performed only once at the beginning, not with every repetition.
[Objection: In the case of a repetition of the sacrifice, the Ārambhaṇīyā should be repeated, just like the fore-sacrifices (Prayāja).
[Commentary: There are indeed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, as stated in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."
In that context, there is the *ārambhaṇīyeṣṭi* (inaugural sacrifice). It is prescribed as follows:

"One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvat, and a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Bhagin; one who desires, 'May I be an eater of food,' [should do so]; some mention the offering to Agni Bhagin as being obligatory.
Furthermore, the repetition of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives."
In this regard, concerning the repetition of the *iṣṭi*, there is a doubt: does the *ārambhaṇīyā* also repeat, or not? What is the prima facie view? That it should repeat.
"It must be performed repeatedly. Why? Because in this way, the injunction regarding the performance will be upheld, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.
Just as the *prayāja* offerings, being constituent parts (*aṅga*), are repeated, so too should the *ārambhaṇīyā*, being a constituent part, be repeated.

The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "Or rather, it may occur even in a single part" (6.1.12). Thus, in all these sections, it is stated that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) applies even to the lifelong performance.

In that context, since the *ārambhaṇīyā* is heard [in the injunction for the Darśapūrṇamāsa] by way of its first constituent element, it is beyond doubt that it belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Should this [introductory rite] be performed for each individual performance (*pratiprayoga*), or once for all performances (*sarvaprayogāṇām*)? What is the reasonable position? First, it should be performed for each individual performance.
Why? Because there is a distinction (*bheda*) among the performances regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), which implies repetition (*āvṛtti*).

Therefore, even the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering] should be repeated [in each performance]. Because it is connected with a single commencement, there is only one commencement for as long as the lifelong performance lasts.
The Commentary states: the word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position.

This is not so; as for what was said, that "the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering] should be repeated," it should be performed only once. Why? Because of its connection with the commencement: it is connected with the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
The commencement of all ritual applications (prayoga) is common to them all.

How so? Having established the sacred fires (agnyādheya), one forms a resolution (saṃkalpa): "At every lunar festival (parvan), the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) must be performed by me.
Having thus resolved that the New and Full Moon sacrifices must be performed, the Ārambhaṇīyā rite is carried out.
This very thing is its commencement, namely, the conclusion;

and that is common to all ritual applications because they are performed throughout one's life. Alternatively, if commencement means the initial undertaking, even so, by that first undertaking, all the applications are accomplished.

Therefore, the *ārambhaṇīyā* should be performed only once. [Ṭup-ṭīkā]: Or rather, it should be performed once. Why? Because, having performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), one makes a resolution (*saṃkalpa*) regarding all [the rites]: "The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices must be performed by me for as long as I live, at each respective time. And that resolution is common to all performances, because its specific characteristics are identical to those of the constituent parts (*aṅga*).
And the preceding volition (*saṃkalpa*), subverting the state of indifference, becomes determination (*adhyavasāna*)—that is, of the form "do this.
And determination is the category [of action] (*padārtha*), namely the category of undertaking (*ārambha*).
And it has been stated that this is common to all.
Therefore, it should be performed once.

[The author] shows the alternative view through the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which is explained by its very wording: "In this regard, even if the first performance (*prathamapravartana*)—namely, the *agnyanvādhāna*—is the commencement (*ārambha*), nevertheless, all ritual applications (*prayoga*) become accomplished by that which was performed for the first time" (this is the reading in the root text of the *bhāṣya*; the reading in the *bhāṣya* cited in the *ṭup-ṭīkā* and the *ratna* is *ārambhaṇīyāpravṛttena*).

(The author of the Bhāṣya, however, has placed [the action] after the end of the *yājyā* verse; because of dissatisfaction with this, the author of the Vārttika refutes the previous explanation while demonstrating that dissatisfaction: This is not correct.
Time is indeed the occasion (*nimitta*) for the ritual act; therefore, it impels that act to be performed.
Prior to the time of the full moon, the ritual action is not performed, because the occasion (for it) is absent.
And that [occasion] impels only one performance (and not another).
Having cast aside his indifference on the preceding day, the person performs either the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) or the determination (*adhyavasāna*) precisely because of that [occasion].
And that [procedure, such as determination and so forth], belongs to one [single] performance alone, not to a second or subsequent one, because there is no cause for it.

Furthermore, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is connected with the performance, not with the action itself (i.e., the essential nature of the ritual act). And because of the difference in performance, there is a difference in the procedure.
And if [the sacrifice] were prompted by the ritual act (*karman*), then, since the acts of all the sacrificers would be one and the same, there would be only a single performance;
yet this is not desired.

For it has been stated that after performing the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), one resolves with all [the priests]: "The New and Full Moon sacrifices must be performed by me on every lunar festival (*parvan*)."
"And that [intention] is not grasped as a specific feature of all ritual applications.
To this it is replied: It has already been stated that intention itself does not apply to all ritual applications, because of the absence of a cause.

(But surely, since a common resolve arises immediately after the *āghāna* rite, it cannot be set aside; therefore, he says: "And the learned man is qualified [for the rites]. And he knows: "The obligatory rites must be performed by me, and the optional ones [must be performed] by one desiring results" (if there is a desire for results, this is merely a cognition at that time; he does not actually form such a resolve at that very moment). That resolve which belongs to this person subsequent to the *āghāna* (as you have stated)—that resolve is like [a mere mental state], and is not, in the ultimate sense, two distinct ritual performances (*prayoga*).
Therefore, this [explanation] is not satisfactory;
hence, another explanation is provided by the author of the Bhāṣya.
[He states the alternative explanation: "If the desired result is accepted, there is the performance of the Prayāja offerings and the Ārambhaṇīyā."

(Thus, having explained the section (*adhikaraṇa*) in that manner, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), being dissatisfied with it, provides another explanation. [Śābarabhāṣya]) The Bhāṣya says: Or rather, it is thus.

Regarding the first point—that it is the "commencement" (*ārambha*) as a ritual act—this is the summary: does the *ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice properly perform the commencement for the two *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices in their first constituent part, or does it effect the connection with commencement for the person who is about to commence, i.e., for the agent who is about to engage in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices for the first time? What is the prima facie view? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it should belong to the commencement of those two [sacrifices]. If it were connected to the person, one would have to assume a result [for the person].
Therefore, [the rite] begins with the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
If this is so, then because of the difference in commencement, if the desired result were to follow, it would occur at every commencement,
just as in the case of the offspring resulting from the performance.

In the *Ṭup-ṭīkā*, regarding the statement "one who is beginning the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," the suffix *-śānac* denotes the agent. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the word "beginning" (*ārambha*) denote the preparatory rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, or does the word "beginning" denote the instigation of a person who has not yet engaged in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices?

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains: although this [suffix] *śānac* denotes the agent, nevertheless, because the assumption of a fruit would otherwise be required, the *Ārambhaṇīyā* is not for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), but rather for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

(For if it were for the sake of the person, a fruit would have to be assumed. And if it were for the sake of the agent, it would have to be repeated at every performance; however, because it is connected with the "commencement" (*ārambha*), it is performed once, since the commencement occurs only once throughout one's lifetime.
The commentary states: It ought to occur only once.
Why? Because of its connection with the person's undertaking.
It is prescribed when the person undertakes the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Why? Because by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) "one should offer" (*nirvapet*), a connection with an agent is established.
In that case, the expression denoting human effort becomes intended for inclusion (*vivakṣita*).
Otherwise, since the injunction would be accomplished merely through the meaning of the word, the expression denoting the agent's effort would be unintended.
That which is already established by the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) is merely restated.
As for the result that must be postulated in connection with the agent, that will indeed be postulated.
A person who has performed the Ārambhaṇīyā rite will be included by the injunction of performance.

If this is so, then because of the application of the *tantra* (the single performance of a ritual procedure), when a person has performed the *ārambhaṇīyā* at one commencement, he remains one who has performed the *ārambhaṇīyā* throughout his life-long practice.
When first undertaking the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), he becomes one who has performed the *ārambhaṇīyā*.
Since he has become one who has performed the *ārambhaṇīyā*, he will be perfectly qualified even when undertaking the New and Full Moon sacrifices in the second and subsequent performances.
Now it is said: [the phrase] "commenced on the same day" applies [to the first performance].
And in the second and subsequent performances, one who has already performed the *Ārambhaṇīyā* on that same day [is not the one referred to].
To this, it is replied:

Even in subsequent performances, since the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are commenced on the very same day, that person who has performed the Ārambhaṇīyā will remain fit [for the sacrifice]; therefore, the Ārambhaṇīyā is to be performed only once.

The *Ṭup-ṭīkā* states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): The Ārambhaṇīyā, which renders the person fit for the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, is subsumed by the *ṛtu* (the seasonal ritual).

Furthermore, the person who is denoted by the present participle (*śānac*) in the phrase "one who is beginning" (*ārambhamāṇaḥ*) is referred to by the word "offering" (*nirvapaṇena*) as being the one for whom the *ārambhaṇīyā* is established by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) containing that participle.
Otherwise, if the *ārambhaṇīyā* were merely a ritual act (*kārya*), the participle would be meaningless.
(How so? Even if the word "should offer" (*nirvapet*) were uttered alone, the *ārambhaṇīyā* would still serve the purpose of the action of beginning.

(Regarding the question: "How is it here?"—in the statement concerning the great performance (*mahāprayoga*), namely in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*), the injunction (or inclusion) will be by means of that which expresses the action (*bhāvavacana*), because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). (To explain what follows from this in the present case: And that [injunction], being performed externally (to the performance), effects a connection of the person with the undertaking (*ārambhayoga*).
And since that [undertaking] is unitary, it cannot be determined that "this person is fit for this performance" and "that person is not," because no distinction is perceived among all performances.

And if it were performed as part of the *tantra* (common procedure) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, then it would follow that it makes fit only that performance whose *tantra* it belongs to, and not another; thus a distinction would be understood. But such is not the case.
Since no distinction is perceived, however, once performed, it benefits all [performances] and therefore need not be repeated.

[Objection: But surely, because the *Ārambhaṇīyā* is produced on the same day as the *luṭ* (the future tense marker indicating the commencement), a distinction is grasped: it makes fit only that person for whom the *Ārambhaṇīyā* is performed on that same day.
It is said:

regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya first refutes this objection with the following passage: "Even in the case of subsequent performances, since the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are commenced on the very same day, that person has already performed the Ārambhaṇīyā; thus, he will certainly be fit [for the sacrifice]. We, however, refute it in another way.
The claim that [the suffix] is enjoined for the same day is not tenable.
The suffix *luṭ* arises when there is a general reference to a future time.
But surely the meaning of *luṭ* is sublated by its being restricted to a non-immediate future time?
(Therefore, it must exist only in the sense-field.
It is said: this is not tenable.

If, however, the *luṭ* suffix prescribed for the non-past (*anadyatana*) were not to find its own scope (*ādhāna*), then it might indeed be sublated. But here, even while being prescribed for the non-past, the *luṭ* suffix certainly finds its own scope; therefore, it does not sublate [the other]. Consequently, *luṭ* applies both to the non-past and to the past (*adyatana*), whereas the *luṭ* suffix itself [as a specific marker] applies only to the non-past.

Furthermore, if the *luṭ* suffix were restricted only to the present day, then the word "bhaviṣyat" (future), being also formed with *luṭ*, would likewise be used only for the present day; in that case, there could be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) between [the term] "bhaviṣyati" and "anadyatane" (not the present day). Nor is this comparable to the passage "One who intends to sacrifice with Soma should establish the fires" (*somena yakṣyamāṇo 'gnīn ādadhīta*), because in that case, having performed the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), one performs the Soma sacrifice and other rites.
As it is said: "In the case of repetition, the subsidiary (*aṅga*) is repeated without abandoning the primary (*pradhāna*);
therefore, for the sake of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is repeated like the *prayāja* offerings."
It is said:
"But this factor, which is the cause of commencement, is common to all;
because it is common, that [result] also becomes common."
But in the second explanation: "Even in the view that it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), the possession of a fruit would follow.
Therefore, the *anvādhāna* [would have to be performed] because of this;
for since it is a part of these two, upon its repetition, it undergoes repetition precisely because it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of them."
When it has been argued that [the sacrifice] must be performed in its entirety because it is like the *pradhāna* (the primary rite), the following is stated in reply:
Indeed, no specific ritual act (*padārtha*) is denoted by the word "commencement" (*ārambha*);
rather, it refers simply to the initial instigation of an agent who has not yet begun acting.
In this regard, the following applies:

the word [denoting] the agent of the action being commenced is expressive [of that agent] by its very direct denotation (*śruti*); likewise, the *luṭ* suffix is also expressive of its own meaning by its very direct denotation.
The first [performance] belongs to the commencement itself; many [repetitions] do not belong to a single action.
Therefore, the Ārambhaṇīyā [offering] is not repeated.
The connection [of this topic] is that this inquiry arises from the context of the commencement of the Soma sacrifice.
The formal resolve (saṃkalpa) made by a ritualist, "I shall undertake the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; with them, I shall perform the sacrifice for [my] patron," is not based on logical necessity.

According to the view of the Vṛttikāra: "In every performance, is there an 'undertaking' (ārambhya) or not? It does not exist as a subordinate element (aṅga); therefore, it would not be a property common to all [sacrifices], like the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna)."

According to the Bhāṣya view: "When human effort occurs at the commencement of the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary fire-arrangement), it is the first [act] because it possesses a fruit; the other [acts] have separate fruits due to their connection with merit.
The Bhaṭṭa school: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One who is commencing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices should here perform the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* [offering]."

In this regard, it is first of all indisputable that this [initiation] is not directly for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)—as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—because the meaning of the two words "the Darśapūrṇamāsa being commenced" is already established.

Nor is it occasional (*naimittika*), like the *medana-homa* and other such rites which have commencement as their occasion, because its status as something to be commenced is understood from the future passive participle (*luṭ*) prescribed when a verbal root meaning an action is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*).
This much is beyond dispute.
It is considered what constitutes the meaning of the term *ārambha* (commencement) as it enters into the scope of the subject matter (*uddeśya*).

Since the result [of the ritual] accrues even to the minute particles of the Sūtra-author through repetition in every performance, the body of this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*) is not concerned with that; for [the result] is utilized in the eleventh [chapter], whereas here it is not utilized for the *ūha* (modification).

In that regard, since among the ritualists (*yājñika*) there is a well-known convention that the first ritual act (*padārtha*), consisting of the *anvādhāna* (placing of fuel), marks the commencement of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, the act of *agnyādhāna* (establishing the fires) itself is the meaning of the term "commencement."

And that *anārambhaṇīyā* is prompted by its specific purpose (*tatkāryaprayuktā*), rather than being [defined] by the form of being the "first ritual act" (*prathamapadārthatvena*) such that it would be carried over—as in the previous case—to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) lacking the fire-installation (*agnyādhāna*), on account of its being known as the "commencement. Nor should it be argued: "Since the fire-piling (*anvādhāna*) is also denoted by the term 'commencement' precisely because it is the object of prompting what has not yet begun, and not by virtue of being the 'fire-piling' itself, how is it not the subject matter of the previous section?
For in the case of the fire-piling, the status of being the object of prompting what has not yet begun with respect to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is sublated.

For instance, the general absence of activity regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices on the part of a person [indicates] either that the person has no activity directed toward the Darśapūrṇamāsa, or that the object of such activity is those [sacrifices]; it does not mean that the person is directed toward some unspecified object, because such a definition would be over-extensive (atiprasakta), as it would apply even to activities like the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) or eating.

Consequently, the status of being the object of the verbal root *ci* (to pile) in the sentence concerning the re-piling (*punar-citi*) belongs only to the Darśapūrṇamāsa and not to the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*), because there is a distinction between the subsidiary and the primary rites, and thus a distinction between the two acts directed toward them.

However, the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is not heard here [in the text] in such a way that it would be included as a constituent part of the rite of commencement (*ārambha*) by virtue of being designated with an accusative case—as in the rule "those [offerings] are to be performed in a whisper" (*tā upāṃśu kartavyāḥ*).

Therefore, since that [accusative] is sublated in the case of the fire-piling (*anvādhāna*), the word "commencement" (*ārambha*) refers to Rudra according to the consensus of the ritualists (*yājñika*). Furthermore, the accusative case has the sense of the genitive; that [usage] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Consequently, the *ārambhaṇīyā* (initiatory rite) is for that purpose [of the Darśapūrṇamāsa] and should not be transferred to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) that lacks it;
therefore, since the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) occurs with every performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, it must be repeated.

This being the prima facie view, the Commentator (*Vṛttikāra*) established the following conclusion: the *anvādhāna* is not the constituent element (*padārtha*) of "commencement" (*ārambha*), because even in the Jyotiṣṭoma—despite the absence of that [Darśapūrṇamāsa *anvādhāna*]—the term "commencement" is employed in the statement, "And indeed, the sacrifice is commenced by means of the deities."
However, the *ārambhaṇīyā* is a specific form of determination (*adhyavasāya*) synonymous with the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that "this must be performed by me.
Its purpose is to be fulfilled even in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) that lacks the fire-installation (*anvādhāna*), because it exists [there] as well; therefore, it must indeed be performed.

Furthermore, in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), since the resolve is made only once for all ritual applications throughout one's life after the installation of the fires, the *ārambhaṇīyā* is performed only once.
That is not so;

for, since the occasioning cause known as "living" (jīvana) exists at that very moment, the lifelong applications—which are contingent upon that cause—are determined to be applicable at those respective times.
There is no evidence for a determination that applies universally to all [occasions].

In that regard, just as when one son has been born, the Vaiśvānara offering is performed, and it is not non-conclusive that it may be performed again upon the birth of another son, so too here, due to the difference in determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is no necessity for performing [the rite] only once.
Therefore, this is the conclusion established by the author of the Bhāṣya and others: the word *ārambha* does not denote determination.
In that case as well, the term "commencement" (*ārambha*) is employed precisely in the sense of setting in motion what has not yet been set in motion.
Therefore, commencement is simply the instigation of what has not begun;
however, the word "commencement" is applied to the constituent parts (*padārtha*) by virtue of their being the objects of that instigation.
Therefore, that [Anārambhaṇīyā iṣṭi] does not have that [commencement] as its purpose;

nor does it do so directly, but rather, because the agent is the same through the use of the present participle suffix (śānac), it serves the purpose of the commencement by means of the agent, just like the act of being commenced. Thus, it has the commencement as its purpose through that intermediary.

Although the term *darśapūrṇamāsau* [is in the accusative case] because of its being the object [of the action], and since the status of being the object of an instigation directed toward an activity not yet commenced can only be possible by virtue of being the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves, it follows that the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* is to be performed precisely in the middle of the first performance; thus, the phrase "one who is commencing the *darśapūrṇamāsa*" would be applicable.

Nevertheless, since the aforementioned meaning is already established by the mere reading [of the text], the question regarding the redundancy of the two words implies that the accusative case is intended to express the status of being the objective reference (*uddeśyatva*).

Therefore, since even the performance of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is directed toward the primary rite (*pradhāna*), the status of being the object of an instigation to engage in an activity not previously undertaken—directed toward the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—belongs only to the very first performance of those sacrifices; thus, the *Ārambhaṇīyā* is a subsidiary of that [first performance].

Nevertheless, the status of being the object of an instigation toward the aforementioned subject matter consists in being the object of an activity directed toward those sacrifices at the time of the conclusion of the activity directed toward the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*.
And this is not possible for anything other than the first constituent element (*padārtha*) of the first performance of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*.
Because everything other than that [first performance] which is intended for that [sacrifice] exists at the same time as such a destruction (of the Apūrva).

Therefore, since the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*—if it were to indicate the means to the *apūrva*—would lack its own primary referent (the first performance) and would instead consist of other referents such as the first performance and so forth, the *ārambhaṇīyā* must indeed be modified (*ūhya*) in the *vikṛti*. Furthermore, because the suffix *-luṭ* (future tense) prescribes the grasping of such a primary referent, the status of being a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*) of the performance is not established.
Furthermore, in the case of a second or subsequent performance (*prayoga*), there is no non-performance [of the rite] because the object is not delimited by the aforementioned property (*dharma*).

For here, in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the objective status (*uddeśyatā*) with respect to the performance does not belong to them as specific individuals (*tattadvyaktitvena*); if it were so, then—because they would be objects of a performance whose objective is delimited by that individuality and which is not simultaneous with the property of the performance directed toward that [first] objective—they would also possess the status of being the first object belonging to a second performance. However, since the term "Darśapūrṇamāsau" (the two sacrifices) is heard [in the injunction], the delimiting factor of the objective status is the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice itself.

Furthermore, in both cases, the Āvaśyaka rite must be characterized by an objective (uddeśyatā) determined by a case-ending that specifies the action; otherwise, since even an activity directed toward bathing in the Gaṅgā could be considered an activity having as its objective the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices in a general sense—namely, "let the prescribed action occur"—the Ārambhaṇīyā would undesirably apply there as well. Therefore, the objective status of the first ritual item is established solely by its being the object of an activity delimited by the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which occurs at a time not simultaneous with the destruction of that [first] activity.

In this context, if there were a desire characterized by generality (*sāmānyākāraka*), then even after performing a bath in the Gaṅgā, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice would not be required during the first performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Therefore, there must be a specification of the first delimiting factor (*prathamāvacchedaka-vivakṣā*).

Furthermore, since the aforementioned desire could arise even when one performs a bath in the Gaṅgā while in the midst of the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsakāṇḍa*), there must be a specification of the second delimiting factor (*dvitīyāvacchedaka-vivakṣā*).

In reality, however, even when one performs a bath in the Gaṅgā with the desire "May the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices be accomplished for me," there arises the undesirable consequence [that the sacrifice has begun]. To avoid this, it is necessary to include only that activity toward a specific object—such as the *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) and so forth—in the definition of the delimiting condition (*uddeśyatā-avacchedakatva*) for the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, such that the linguistic usage "the Darśapūrṇamāsa have been commenced" occurs only when that particular object has been performed. Since the exclusion of the aforementioned case is thus established by that very requirement, the intention to specify the delimiting condition is solely for the purpose of excluding the individuality (*tattad-vyaktitva*) of those specific instances from being the delimiting condition of the objective.
Therefore, since it is commenced only upon reaching that [state] and possesses the aforementioned characteristics, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is not required for a second or subsequent performance.

[Objection: But in this case, since there is an engagement with an intention (*saṃkalpa*) such as "I shall sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma together with its subsidiaries," and since there is an engagement directed toward that which is delimited by the status of being the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, does it not follow that the *anvārambhaṇīyā* would be required prior to that?

If, however, it should be suspected that the aforementioned [initiatory] activity does not apply because the objective (uddeśyatā) there is qualified by being the object of a desire in the form “May the Jyotiṣṭoma with its auxiliary parts come into being,” and thus it is delimited by a qualified property, then [we reply]: because it is an intermediate resolve (avāntara-saṃkalpa) of the form “I shall perform the Dīkṣaṇīyā,” the Anvārambhaṇīyā would necessarily have been performed previously; for that [intermediate resolve] is the object of a well-defined activity, and since the activity directed toward the object of an intermediate resolve is produced by a desire in the form “May the Dīkṣaṇīyā come into being for me,” it has as its objective that which is delimited by the nature of the Dīkṣaṇīyā.
If it is argued that, in the same way, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* would also apply to the *rājasūya*, the *iṣṭis*, the *paśubandhas*, and so forth, we say no.

Even though a desire in the form "let the *dīkṣaṇīyā* arise" does not occur, an activity directed toward the object of such a resolve as "I shall perform the *dīkṣaṇīyā*" is possible precisely by way of having the qualified whole (*sāṅga*)—namely, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice—as its mode, in the form "let the *Jyotiṣṭoma* with its subsidiaries arise. Since such a resolve, being a form of determination (*adhyavasāya*), lacks the status of being the object of an activity whose objective reference (*uddeśyatā*) is delimited by the nature of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* itself, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is excluded solely due to the loss of the means (*dvāralopa*). This is because the absence of the *anvārambhaṇīyā* in the *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), and so forth belonging to the *Rājasūya* will be explained in the tenth book (10.1.2.4).

Likewise, since activity in rites such as the Vaiśvānareṣṭi is possible only through a desire of the form "May Soma be born to me" directed toward the very purpose of Soma and so forth, the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I shall sacrifice with the Vaiśvānareṣṭi" must also have an objective (*uddeśyatā*) delimited by the Vaiśvānareṣṭi itself. Therefore, it should be understood that even in that case, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is not performed, because the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* is connected to the *ārichāchamasa* (the cup for the *ārichā* verses), and thus the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is excluded precisely due to the loss of its mediating function (*dvāralopa*).

However, the status of being the *darśapūrṹṇamāsa* sacrifice arises from its being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) within the mental conception (*icchā*) in the form "May the *darśapūrṇamāsa* with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*) come into being"; thus, there is the distinction that it falls within the scope of the defining characteristic of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedakakoṭipatva*).

Therefore, it is established that because the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is an initiation (*ārambha*) of the aforementioned kind, there is modification (*ūha*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), and furthermore, it is not an auxiliary part (*anaṅgatva*) in subsequent performances (*dvitīyādiprayoga*).

As for the claim that the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice, performed at the commencement of the first performance, benefits all performances—it cannot be argued that because the term "being commenced" (*ārabhyamāṇa*) refers to the present time, it must therefore apply only to the second and subsequent performances since they are understood to be performed on the day of the main rite (*pradhāna-dina*). This is because the term refers merely to the future time common to both the current and subsequent performances; it does not refer exclusively to the present time. Otherwise, the use of the *luṭ* suffix in the rule "the *luṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of the future (*bhaviṣyati*) and the present (*adyatane*)" would be untenable.

Therefore, it has been stated that at the commencement of the first performance, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice itself is indeed the provider of all assistance. Now, [one might object]: "In that case, would not the intermediate apūrvas (transcendental potencies) be denied? [The answer is: No, as long as the person who performed the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice remains alive, it continues to provide assistance to the sacrifice.
Thus, the intermediate apūrvas are not negated.
We do not deny this.

Although, at first glance, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like are not capable of establishing the *niyoga* (the mandate) as something distinct [from the action], because—just as in the case of acts such as threshing—they function merely as restatements (*anuvādaka*) of the *niyoga* pertaining to the qualification (*adhikāra*) as expressed by the words; nevertheless, it is logically consistent that these momentary intermediate *apūrvas* (transcendental potencies), which do not produce the *niyoga* of qualification, remain unperceived. Thus, subsequently, due to the absence of the *apūrva* of qualification, those intermediate *apūrvas* which are to be accepted and heard are admitted as being denoted by the optative suffix. This very point has been demonstrated in the section concerning the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.
Indeed, we shall explain later how the acceptance of intermediate *apūrvas* is based on this very principle.
And those intermediate *apūrvas*, which do not exist as such through the word itself, are brought forward by means of their respective governing forms (*adhikāra-rūpa*).

[Objection: If that is the case, then in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, the restriction of speech (*vāg-niyama*) would not be prompted by an intermediate *apūrva*; rather, it would result in being prompted by that [final] *apūrva* alone, as in the case of the rule "one threshes with two [stones] that have been sprinkled" (*prokṣitābhyām avahanti*).
No;
because it is for the purpose of determining its own nature (*svarūpa-niścaya*).

Although intermediate apūrvas lack dependence on another state (*parabhāva*), nevertheless, duties such as the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) serve solely to determine their own nature, since one understands the connection with the nature of the intermediate apūrva related to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice from the injunction: "One should not recite [the mantra] at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*."
Nor is it logical for them [the objects] to possess the characteristic of being manifested by ignorance through the abandonment of their own nature.
Nor can there be an inference based on their own nature, because the establishment of a thing's own nature is not cognizable by anything other than itself.
All of this is established as being cognizable only through verbal testimony.

However, since acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) are established by other means of knowledge even without sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), their essential form is accomplished even in its absence; thus, if they were for the sake of their own essential form, the performance of the restrictive injunction (*niyamaniyoga*) would be improper. Therefore, because it is inherently light (*laghu*), there is no room for the postulation of a qualification (*adhikāra*) in the case of subsidiary rites (*prayāja*) and the like, which involve light performance. By that same principle, it should be understood that in the case of the originative injunctions (*utpattiniyoga*) regarding the primary rites (*pradhāna*), there is an absence of an intermediate instrument (*karaṇa*).

For one who does not accept that intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), there would be no distinction between causes in rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Likewise, the properties (*dharma*) belonging to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices would apply to the *upaśuyāja* and others, because they are all prompted by the ultimate transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*) and because there is no difference in their status as the substratum for that result. However, when there is a distinction in the intermediate operation, a systematic restriction (*vyavasthā*) is logical; otherwise, the instrumental character (*karaṇatā*) of the *āgneya* would be of one kind, while that of the *upaśuyāja* and others would be of another.

Even though the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] are established means through direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*), their status as means is determined by the specific arrangement of the ritual (*dharma-vyavasthā*) according to another [principle].
The same applies to the two *pārṣaṇa* oblations.
For this very reason, there is sublation (*bādha*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

For it is not the case that the *saurya* sacrifice possesses the same status as the means to the *apūrva* of the *āgneya*; thus, due to the absence of a connection with the archetypal (*prakṛta*) door, there is no sublation of the two *pārvaṇa-homas*.

Furthermore, those who assert that intermediate *apūrvas* exist but do not take the form of means—on their view, these do not constitute intermediate operations—and thus the entire range of objections raised by the ancients does not apply.

Indeed, it is because of the absence of a cause for the production of a distinct effect that something possesses the status of an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*); otherwise, even the *āśrama* (the fire-altar) and so forth, being produced by the *kṛṣi* (the *kṛṣi-saṃskāra*), would incur the undesirable consequence of having the status of an intermediate operation like the *navama* (the ninth day).

Now, if this were the case—that is, if there were a lack of qualification (*adhikāra*)—then there would be no extended application (*atideśa*) to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites. It is replied: [this is not so].

Even for those who lack a specific qualification [for the primary ritual], the expectancy as to "how" (katham) is indeed appropriate, because their actions are not different in nature from those of others and because they serve as a means for attaining the ultimate goal.
But if this is so, then a subordinate context (avāntaraprakaraṇa) has been admitted;
for it is a well-known tenet among the Mīmāṃsakas that a context consists in the expectancy regarding "how" a duty is to be performed.

There is no such thing as a "subordinate context" (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) as a means of proof (*pramāṇa*), because so long as those intermediate *pūrva*s (preliminary rites) are not understood, the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*)—since it has not yet grasped the entire class of constituent elements that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*)—does not distinguish between them. Subsequently, because all of them enter equally into the sphere of the qualified person's entitlement (*adhikāra*), they do not stand in a relationship of mutual subservience; thus, there is no possibility of application by way of subordinate context.

However, as for those intermediate *apūrvas* that have been assigned to the sentences and so forth at the beginning, they are established therein; there is no transition [of their results] into the supreme *apūrva*.
[Objection: But in this case, would it not follow that the rules for the Soma sacrifice apply to the *prayāja* offerings and the like?
[Response: This is not a fault.

If those who lack an entitlement were to possess an inherent expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) just like those who do have an entitlement, then it would indeed be so. Furthermore, this expectancy is natural because [the object] is something to be performed.
But how can there be both non-actionability and actionability? Surely you have never heard such a thing before!
[He was] heedless.
For it was indeed pointed out by the teacher that [the place] was secluded.
Indeed, whatever a person understands with absolute necessity as "this is my duty," that is to be performed.

That which, being previously unestablished, is employed for the sake of accomplishing that [apūrva] is the "kārya" (the thing to be accomplished). And in the case of the supreme apūrva, it is understood as an independent kārya. This quality of being a kārya resides primarily in that which possesses the fruit.

Because there is no disregard for the fruit, it is "to be accomplished" (*kārya*), as has already been explained. Therefore, the distinction between what is to be performed and what is not is established.
Furthermore, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding "how" (*katham*) arises only with respect to that which is to be performed, not with respect to the mere fact of something being an effect.
Therefore, the extension (*atideśa*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites occurs precisely because they possess the status of being expectant.
You have not correctly understood our position.
For our established conclusion is that there is indeed a purpose [for such inquiry].
However, for those who lack the qualification [to engage in Vedic study], there is no natural expectancy for such an inquiry.
Yet, the possibility of other causes [for such inquiry] is not denied.

In that regard, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is postulated on the grounds that the *prayāja* and other elements are to be performed daily. Even when naturally devoid of expectancy, an expectancy arises due to the intervention of another factor; for example, although the two words "the cloth" (*paṭaḥ*) and "is" (*bhavati*) are naturally devoid of expectancy, an expectancy toward "red" (*rakta*) arises because of the utterance of the word "red. Otherwise, the unintended consequence would be "a red cloth is being produced" (*raktaḥ paṭo bhavati*).

Thus, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, since there is no other reason to establish an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics belonging to the Soma sacrifice. Consequently, it is established that in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, one obtains the status of being subject to optional injunctions.

As for those who maintain that the subsidiary injunctions possess a mandate by accepting the principle of "mandate for one already mandated" (*adhikṛtādhikāra*), for them, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, the person entitled to perform them would—according to the logic of the *Rātrisatra*—be only one desiring the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Therefore, the possibility of a "mandate for one already mandated" does not arise.
It may be thought that the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the manner of performance is fulfilled by the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*).
Let there be no such fulfillment; however, while the purpose (*prayojana*) is fulfilled, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not.

Since the words of the *arthavāda* fall within the domain of the means of knowledge, lest their function be indirect (*parokṣā vṛtti*), it is appropriate that only one who desires the fruit described by them be the qualified agent (*adhikārī*).

However, because those [subsidiary acts] lacking a specific qualification are understood through the mere proximity to a qualified injunction (*sādhikāra-vidhi*), they possess a purpose for that [primary act]. Since there is no further expectancy for a qualification, the words of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) result in being merely explanatory.

Likewise, in cases such as "the milk-vow for the Brāhmaṇa," since a qualified agent is obtained within the very sentence itself—just as one who has set out to eat is subject to the rules for acquiring food—it is impossible to postulate a separate qualification for one already engaged in the primary act; otherwise, the milk-vow and the like would fall into the state of being independent.

Likewise, even though the injunction "one should not speak of another" is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no possibility of its inclusion in that context, because it is understood that the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs to the agent of the prohibited action. Similarly, in the case of "one offers the oblation when [the ladle] is broken," since the occasion (*nimitta*) constitutes a specific qualification, the *homa* does not attain the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—provided that no other occasion is postulated—because it serves as a qualification for the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Nor is this a means [to the primary result], because the word "broken" (*bhinna*) is etymological (*yaugika*); thus, while it applies to the primary substance (*prakṛti*), the qualification belongs to the one who is already qualified by the occasion itself.
Thus, because that which is separate from the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not employed [within it];
for only that which is proximate to the context and is employed therein [belongs to it],
and there is no employment of what is separate.

Alternatively, when there is a requirement for an entitlement (*adhikāra*) and one begins to postulate such an entitlement, why should it be postulated through the proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) of the purpose? It would be better that there be an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying) of the directly heard word of entitlement. For when the word of entitlement is heard in the principal sentence and is connected with the principal act, those proximate [sentences] whose entitlements were not heard become connected by means of the intervening word of entitlement; thus, they no longer have a requirement for an entitlement. This is the primary argument for rejecting *anuṣaṅga*. However, the statement that it is "better" is merely a supplementary point.
This is the connection: thus, through such reasoning, there is the desire for fulfillment, which is precisely the satisfaction of that desire.

Furthermore, since in each individual case—such as "He offers the *samidh* oblation"—the person authorized for the primary rite is understood to be the same, and since the *samidh* and other subsidiaries are each individually a means (*upāya*) to the primary rite, there would have to be a separate set of procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) for each.
For in that case, the intermediate injunctions (*avāntaravidhi*) would establish each of those subsidiaries as a distinct means.

Since it is impossible for the supreme apūrva (transcendental result) to possess the status of an instrument when it is already obstructed by [other] instruments, one must assume its status as a means precisely through its role as a generator of the instrument.

Therefore, disregarding that status as a means and relying instead on the fact that each [rite] alone effects the assistance to the instrument, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) among the *samit* offerings and the rest.
However, since the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) merely grasps their being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), if that [qualification] were not connected with them in another way...
The "connection with the qualified person" (adhikāra-sambandha) means its entry [into the injunction].
However, since there is subsequently a connection of that [subordinate act] with the sentence again through the two-night sacrifice, there is no further entry [into the primary injunction].

Thus, when the remote auxiliaries (ārādupakāraka) have first been connected to the qualified-person-injunction by virtue of being for its sake, and the assistance to the instrument has been established by the injunction of the qualified-person-injunction as something to be performed, there is no assumption of a generative capacity toward that [instrument] on the part of the qualified-person-injunction.

Furthermore, since they are momentary, it is impossible for them to exist simultaneously in their own essential nature; thus, they cannot collectively produce an assistance [to the sacrifice], and therefore the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is not accepted as something distinct.

In this way, even without an *apūrva*, the production of assistance for the instrument (*karaṇa*) is established through the mediation of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the substance and the deity within the substrates. Thus, there is no evidence whatsoever for the existence of an *apūrva* when it is not explicitly heard in the scripture.
Moreover, what you consider "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) in the case of a visible garland is not actually seen by you.
For that very purpose, it has been shown:
