the sacrifice does not directly benefit the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*), but rather through the medium of the portions consisting of mantras and ritual procedures (*tantra*) which constitute its own limbs (*svāṅga*).
Nor is it possible for those two [substance and deity] to be applied there [in the sacrifice] unless they have entered into the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the sacrifice.

And without an intermediate apūrva, there can be no entry into the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of the sacrifice; thus, the *avadya*, *śrāvaṇīya*, and *avāntara-apūrva* are established. Furthermore, their status as unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is not the purpose [of the action].
For in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice, it is not merely the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the substance and the deity that is the motivating factor.

In that case as well, in the instance of substances, deities, and preparatory acts, it should be understood that only the injunction (*apatti*) is the motivator; for in a sacrifice, the substance serves the sacrifice directly.
However, the application of the substance is governed by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*);
the scripture does not support any intermediate means (*dvāra*) for the substance.

However, even though it is not irrelevant to the context, there is no application (*viniyoga*) of a substance [directly], because it lacks the capacity to produce an assistance for the instrument (*karaṇa*) directly.
Its connection with the verbal root’s meaning (*bhāvārtha*) as the producer occurs through indicative power (*liṅga*), name (*samākhyā*), and position (*sthāna*).
Furthermore, the application of the accessory (*guṇa*) and the deity (*devatā*) occurs through syntactical connection (*vākya*), because the causes of application are distinct.

Since those two [the agent and the object] are indeed useful as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the means (*aṅga*) and its realization (*sādhana*), their application as *kārakas* is not contradicted.

As for the number—such as in "one offers eleven *prayāja*s"—which is inherent in the highest order [of verbal action], it is prescribed as being based on desire (*kāma*), because it is impossible to enjoin actions that have already perished.

Although a qualification pertaining to the subject of a statement (*uddeśya*) should not be intended [as significant] for fear of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*), and thus the collective performance (*sāhitya*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is not intended, nevertheless, because that [collectivity] resides in distinct individuals, the result does not accrue to each one individually, but rather to the entire group alone.

Since there can be no realization of that [result] without repetition, study proceeds by way of repetition as a matter of necessity. Furthermore, in the case of a rule that confers entitlement (*adhikāra-vidhi*) based on the favoring of the original sequence (*prākṛta-krama*), there is a fulfillment [of the requirement].
Furthermore, that which is inherent in the action as it arises is not something to be enjoined;
for it delimits the actions being enjoined, and it is not possible for it to be enjoined in that way.
Since it is already obtained through the performance once many [actions] have been enjoined, it does not require a separate object of injunction.

Even though those two meanings are not directly subordinate (*avidheya*), they do not fail to assist because they are expressed; thus, they are indeed [subordinate]. However, that which is denoted by a distinct nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—like the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) and so forth—is not enjoined as a cause for the ritual action.

On the other hand, regarding this which is denoted by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), although it has a connection with the meaning of the nominal stem by virtue of its own power, nevertheless, if it were connected to that alone, a connection with the "cup" (*graha*) would not be possible through context (*prakaraṇa*), general indication (*sāmānya*), and so forth. Therefore, it is determined that its connection to the state of being the "appropriator" (*grāhakīyāvasthā*) is what constitutes its functional subordination (*aupādānikī*).

For that which has already been enjoined, a subsequent single offering is not possible unless it is delimited; thus, there is a requirement for a number that serves as its delimiter. Furthermore, since a number requires a substratum (*āśraya*) so that its connection with the understood agent may be established, the injunction (*vidhi*)—by virtue of the proximity of that state—postulates such a substratum. This is recognized by the Mīmāṃsakas as an injunction characterized by "appropriation" (*upādāna*), which is synonymous with "implication" (*ākṣepa*), because it brings about the existence of the [action] itself. Thus, the injunctions regarding qualification (*adhikāra*), application (*viniyoga*), and performance (*prayoga*) are established.
And the very fact that the injunction as it is perceived is untenable is the seed [of this argument].
An injunction accompanied by a qualification (sādhikāra), such as "One should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," being unintelligible in the absence of a supporting rationale (*upapatti*),
implies its originative injunction (*utpatti*).
It has been stated many times that a mere momentary sacrifice, independent of its origination (*utpatti*) and application (* viniyoga*), is not capable of establishing the qualification (*adhikāra*).

Since performance is impossible in the case of the *Viśvajit* and other such sacrifices without a qualification, the impossibility of the injunction (*vidhi*)—which is of the nature of an action (*kārya*)—being understood [as complete] is the seed for the postulation of a qualification. Furthermore, since the meaning of the injunction is perceived as being connected with a number, it brings about the state of being integrated into the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) in order to justify that connection; thus, the injunction which is the goal to be accomplished within the qualification applies precisely to the occasion (*nimitta*).
That which is called "performance" (anuṣṭhāna) implies the purpose of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

However, in the case of an injunction for desire (*kāma-adhikāra*), since the fulfillment of the desired object depends upon that [instrument], the mental inclination (*mānasī pravṛtti*) remains unimpeded even prior to the actual performance; thus, the injunction is not the motivator (*aprayojaka*).
In the case of both types of auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), the sacrifice itself (*ṛtu*) is the motivator, because they serve as the means to its completion.
For whatever is the effect of something, that alone is its motivator (*prayojaka*).
In the case of ignorant persons, it is precisely this effect that serves as the cause for performance.
And those who know the truth maintain that whatever is implied by an injunction for the sake of its own accomplishment is the "to-be-performed" (*vidheya*).
[Objection: In that case, even in the Viśvajit and similar sacrifices, the qualification (*adhikāra*) would also have to be enjoined by implication.
[Response: It is said:

the qualification has no function in the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*); rather, the implication of the qualification is for the purpose of establishing the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*).
Thus, because it is not implied for the sake of its own accomplishment by the injunction, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the sequence is not something to be enjoined.

There is no denotation whatsoever of a sequence belonging to the fifth book [of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra], nor is it possible for such an unexpressed sequence to possess either a syntactic (*vākyika*) or a material (*aupādānika*) status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*).
Furthermore, an injunction regarding that which has already become a residual element (śeṣa) is not capable of implying [a further requirement].
As for the sequence denoted by the word "first" in the statement, "The first draught belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," that is indeed an application (*viniyoga*) and thus a basis for being enjoined;
for this very reason, it does not fall under the category of the implied.
Furthermore, regarding the fifth [point], as for the Vedic sequence beginning with "Having initiated the Gṛhapati, [he initiates] the Adhvaryu," there is no explicit statement of that [sequence].
How, then, is it understood?

For even when the suffix *ktvā* occurs elsewhere, because it denotes an action performed by the same agent (*samānakartṛka*), that which is employed first—even though it is what is being enjoined—is understood from that very point, since the suffix *ktvā* is heard there.
Alternatively, once the status of being "to be employed" (prayojyatva) is established, the failure of the purpose (arthavipatti) is likewise understood in that same way.
Since speech is understood as expressing the manner of application, and since performance follows that very manner, the sequence is also understood to be of such a kind.
Any suspicion regarding the expression of meaning and so forth in the case of [the word] *artha* and others is simply untenable.
Even for that which is not explicitly stated, its status as a means of comprehension has indeed been considered in various authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*).

If sequence (*krama*) were not a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) with respect to the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*), how then could it possess the character of being defined by Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*)?

Being an object of injunction is not the cause for having the character of being defined by Vedic injunction, because that would result in the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) of this status to the qualification (*adhikāra*).

If it is argued that the definition of *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is that which conveys a meaning not otherwise established (*avidheyārtha*) as connected with that [injunction], then the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*), being likewise connected with the sequence [of actions], is also determined; thus, its status as being defined by *codanā* remains uninterrupted.
For the performance-injunction is indeed understood as the performance itself as grasped through a specific sequence.
It is for this very reason that there is an insistence on the rule regarding the commencement of what is not a subordinate element (*anaṅga*).

Because, in the absence of that [direct statement], one follows the application [of the rule], since the specific application is to be accomplished by a rule qualified by the object of the application.
(Thus, in this way, the two-fold nature of the teaching of dharma is both based on dissociation and based on inclusion.
In that regard, it is not applied according to the respective qualification.

Rather, the application (viniyoga) depends upon the qualification (adhikāra), because even in a general sense, the application is established by relying on the qualification; for even in the view that the application is preceded by the "grasper" (grāhaka) in order to establish the systematic arrangement (vyavasthā) for each specific section (prakaraṇa).

And although the capacity to grasp [an injunction] belongs to one who possesses a qualification (*sādhikāra*), nevertheless, once a qualified person such as "one desiring heaven" has been identified in a general sense, and the capacity to grasp has been established so that the act of grasping is concluded, then—among the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) that have been enjoined—the qualification belongs to that desirer of heaven who is capable of performing them, with respect to the meaning of the injunction delimited by those subsidiaries and seeking the task to be accomplished. Thus, there is a subsequent restriction to a specific qualification.

For this very reason, even those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the *anvadhyas*—which involve the inspection, hearing, and stepping over the sacrificial limbs—as well as for the *pañceṣṭis*, which possess the characteristic limb of the three *ādheyas*, and for the *ādhvanīya* and other sacrifices.
This should be inferred by oneself: because those aforementioned [persons] lack the natural capacity to accomplish the purpose of such injunctions.

However, for those whose natural capacity has not departed—such as those with impaired vision who are nonetheless capable of performing specific injunctions, and those whose sense organs are directed toward particular injunctions—they certainly do possess the entitlement.

Is it not the case that their eligibility (*adhikāra*) simply does not hold, because that [eligibility] is based on the accomplishment of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), and that [accomplishment] depends upon all the constituent parts (*aṅga*)? True; the eligibility for desire (*kāma-adhikāra*) would indeed not exist, because its object is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the fruit along with its procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
For one who desires a fruit has no eligibility toward the cultivation of the fruit when only a single means (*karaṇa*) is present.

It is generally accepted that all instruments (karaṇa) experience their status as instruments only when accompanied by their respective procedures (itikartavyatā). Therefore, if the constituent parts (aṅga) are not performed, the status of being accompanied by the procedure is lost. Due to this contradiction, and because the object [of the injunction] would otherwise be non-existent, the qualification (adhikāra) of those desiring [the fruit] would simply vanish even regarding the primary object itself.
[Thus ends the line according to the seal.
Regarding the phrase "among those who are poorly learned," something is to be inferred.

Consequently, in the case of the non-performance of the ritual along with its ancillaries (this is the reading), it refers to the state of being accompanied by the required procedure (*setikartavyatākatva*).
(This is the conclusion of the preceding [section].

Because of the contradiction [arising] from the logical sequence [of the injunctions, such as the "looking at the clarified butter" (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*)], and because of the absence of a subject matter [due to that contradiction—namely, because in the absence of the act of looking at the clarified butter, the subject matter, which is the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual, would not exist], the possessor of the qualification [the result of the ten-fold entitlement] is also untenable; thus, there is indeed a collapse of the qualification [for one desiring heaven, since qualification exists only when a specific result like heaven is possible, and in this case, that very qualification collapses]. This applies to those who possess desire [the aforementioned persons, etc.].
The meaning is that those such as the *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference) do not have the qualification for the ten primary rites (*daśādikarma*).

[In this regard, the learned are the authority: Since qualification (*adhikāra*) pertains solely to the objective of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) when there is a causal occasion (*nimitta*), even if there is no formal conclusion (*anupasamhāra*) due to ignorance, there is no arising of qualification because the object has been lost.

The section concerning independence (anapekṣatādhikāra) conveys at that time precisely that which is to be enjoined as something to be brought into effect; however, the general rule is that [the injunction] is established only upon the accomplishment of all its constituent parts (aṅgas). By this very same principle of qualification, in the case of a secondary qualification based on a causal condition (nimittādhikāra), the primary meaning of the scriptural teaching (śāstrārtha) [is maintained].
The teacher is the collection of constituent parts (*aṅgakalāpa*).
Some others consider the causal basis (*kāryanibandhana*) to be the [authoritative] source; however, others regard it as the capacity (*yogyatā*), which is beyond dispute.
As for proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), it was previously established by the Buddha.

For instruction indeed occurs separately for each section for those who are ignorant; by that very same *apūrva* (unprecedented result), the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *apūrva* is brought to mind through a specific indicative mark (*liṅga*), because the application (*viniyoga*) is preceded by the apprehension of the *apūrva*.
For if it were so, that [archetype] would bring its own assistance into proximity.

For this very reason, the experts in the true nature [of ritual] maintain that the connection with the qualification—namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*).

For when an injunction such as "He should sacrifice with the *samidh*s" is directed toward the sacrifice by means of the text, and since that [sacrifice] has already been presented by the primary injunction itself, the injunction regarding the *samidh*s and so forth applies to it; at that time, because it is prescribed while being thus referred to, the *samidh*-injunction pertains to the sacrifice itself, just as the benefit (*upakāra*) exists in the archetype (*prakṛti*). This is because, in cases such as the Viśvajit sacrifice, the injunction regarding the *samidh*s and so forth is operative throughout all sacrifices.
Thus, since the relationship of assistance has been established, by which category of entity (*padārtha*) is the instruction produced? It is not settled [by the agent].

For at that time, the word "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not refer to the *darśa* sacrifice; rather, it subsequently denotes the nature of an action (*kriyātva*) that is distinct from the directly assisting (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)—which consists of the form of the ritual action characterized by the object of prescription as defined by the deity, through the exclusion of either the substance or the deity—and which is an indirect assistant (*ārādupakāraka*).
There is a distinction between that which assists by way of direct conjunction (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and the *Atithyā-iṣṭi*.

Regarding the ritual action such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it is established that the *Atithyā-iṣṭi* must be performed. The term "action" (*kriyā*) is employed to exclude things that are merely of an accomplished nature (*siddharūpa*).

Murāri (Bhāṣya-pṛḥ 1162): "The quality of being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakārakatva*) belongs to the element of renunciation (*tyāga-aṃśa*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others.

Bhaṭṭa (4.1.7, pṛḥ 93): "The quality of being a remote auxiliary is set aside by [the quality of] being an integral part of the sacrifice (*sāmavāyikatva*). This is an instance of sublation where [the sublated rule] was not previously established (*aprāptabādha*)."
Or [it may be so], because of being an indirect auxiliary (ārādupakāraka), since the status of being an integral auxiliary (sāmavāyika) is more highly esteemed.

[Śābarabhāṣya] 3.3.10.20: Even though the apūrvas of the subsidiaries, which reside in the self [of the sacrifice] and assist by being connected with the primary acts through co-inherence in a single purpose, are established as indirect auxiliaries because they lack the status of being subordinate to a substratum (āśraya). Page 398.
In the case of indirect auxiliaries, the relationship between the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices must be inferred, as must their specific assistance.
Mīmāṃsā, p. 209: In cases where there is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) is the means of application (*viniyojaka*). On p.

209, because the taking of the primary sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as a substance by an indirect auxiliary member has been refuted by the principle stated in the Vārttika (2.1.38, p. 407): "For the connection with rice is equal for both the sacrifice and the threshing, according to the scripture."
Su. Pṛ. 638: But that [deity] which is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāriṇī*) is not abandoned; therefore, it is external (*bahiraṅga*) to the sacrificial material (*havirdravya*).

Bhāṣya 8.2.17.132: There are three types of exclusion of indirect auxiliaries: exclusion of indirect auxiliaries belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*), exclusion of indirect auxiliaries belonging to the ectype (*vikṛti*), and exclusion of indirect auxiliaries belonging to rituals that are neither archetypes nor ectypes.

Examples of these have been provided by me [in the Bālakrīḍā], page 20. "The quality of being an indirect auxiliary (ārādupakāritva) is set aside by the quality of being a direct auxiliary (saṃnipatyopakāritva) when there is a possibility of their coexistence, but not otherwise. [Śābarabhāṣya] page 728. "The quality of being an indirect auxiliary is set aside by the quality of being a direct auxiliary, as in the case of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) and so forth."
Bāla, p. 140: Even though redness (*āruṇya*) is a quality (*guṇa*), it is connected to the action by means of delimiting the substance *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow). Su., p. 1028:

The connection of redness with the substance—which is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) as being possible with the action (in the form of purchase)—is set aside because the connection indicated by syntactical context (*vākya-lakṣaṇa*) is weaker.
Vā., 3.1.6.2, p. 685: Redness is applied to the three-year-old female calf (*trivatsā*), which has not yet been obtained for all the substances used in the purchase.

Bhāṭṭa 3.1.6, p. 199: The quality of redness (āruṇya), being a means for the purchase, pertains only to the one-year-old cow (ekāyanī), which is the cause of the purchase. This is the principle of the "simultaneous application" (pādikā ārtinyāya) regarding the qualities of redness and the substance of the cow.
"The shallow cup; and it [belongs] to both offerings.
He says, "If [the wind] turns away from the two directions..."
It is said:
the comparison is unequal;
it is not so.

The qualification is not accepted; for you, there is also the qualification by means of the oblation (*havis*). In that case, having designated the substance by means of the word "cow" (*go*), its bringing forward is enjoined;
[but] this does not obtain.
That is now explained:
we accept [the application] by means of the oblation (*havis*).
For even in that case, if this [quality] had not existed, the word "white" (*śukla*) would certainly not have been used for it.
The qualifier would be meaningless if there were no object to be qualified. "Of whom..."
He dried it up.
However, in that context, the act of bringing is qualified by both adjectives;
whereas in the case of "one should remove distress" (*ārtim ācchet*), since there is no such qualification, it is understood to mean "anything whatsoever."
The primary [cause] is stated. Here, however, it refers to a substance characterized by being fit for the oblation when it has suffered damage (*ārti*).
In that case, everything indeed suffers some degree of damage, at least insofar as it has been consumed.
A vessel of five śarāvas should be prepared.
But what is the reason for [using] the principal [measure], namely, "the twinkling of an eye" and "the thought"?

In that context, the word "of whom" (*yasya*) serves as a qualifier when it is combined for the purpose of expressing the cause (*nimitta*); however, when it is for the sake of another, it is stated separately,
[and] in the case of the eternal (*nitya*), it is not [so].

( It is enjoined ); therefore, because of the simultaneous connection of the word *havis* and the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) according to the principle of the *praheka-lpa* (3.1.13).
[The Bhāṣya] says, "If the qualification is not relinquished" (meaning: let there be no qualification by *havis*), thereby rejecting the status of *havis* as a qualifier.

Thus it has been stated: "Indeed, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) does not desire that the oblation (*havis*) be a qualifier; rather, the substance connected with distress (*ārti*), which is denoted by the term *upapāta*, is the cause for the *pañcaśarāva* offering. This is because, at the outset, it was declared that the oblation qualified by distress is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, he says: "(If a connection of the word *ubhaya* with distress is not desired, let there be no connection even with the oblation"—thus he expresses the connection with the word that serves as a qualifier. [This introductory passage is found in both the manuscript and printed editions of the commentary.]
However, this passage is not found in the *Āraṇyakabhāṣya*. For here, only the lines of the *Bhāṣya* itself have been commented upon.

In that regard, at this point, the intended line is as follows: "If the word *ubhaya* (both) expresses a connection with the word qualifying the oblation (*havis*) by its own form, then the intention is that mere distress (*ārti*), independent of its connection to the oblation, would result as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*)."
[Objection: But surely it is not logical for that alone to be the cause, because it is eternal.
Therefore, how can this objection be raised? To this he says:
"Thus" — having grasped the distinction that the collection of verbal roots (kriyāpada-gaṇa) attains the status of being the cause, the objection is raised.

(Regarding the statement that there would be a syntactical split [vākya-bheda] if one were to qualify the specific cause: since there would be a syntactical split if either of the two—either the distress (*ārti*) or the oblation (*havis*)—were to qualify the other, the term "both" must include the cause itself, as well as the inclusion of the other two; thus, without grasping this distinction, [the opponent] has raised the objection). [The Siddhānta-bhāṣya states: "We consider the oblation to be the qualification. (He explains the intention behind that): Without a connection to the distress of the oblation, there is no cognition of the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).
(Therefore,) it is said: "the qualification of the oblation."

Thinking that the term *paramatathā*—whether as a qualifier or not—is being refuted, [the author] speaks of it as a qualifier of the oblation (*havirviśeṣaṇa*) out of disregard [for its literal status], since in every way the refutation of the causality of the two [terms taken] alone is established. However, in the ultimate sense, distress (*ārti*) alone is the qualifier of the oblation.
Thus, the accomplishment of the connection between the oblation and distress is the occasion (*nimitta*) for the fivefold division.

For the direct statement (*śruti*) is able to express the connection with that [root-meaning]; however, it would have to express the connection with the oblation (*havis*) by means of syntactical context (*vākya*). (The author states the intention of this commentary: Because of its being something to be performed (*kartavyatva*), the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*)—since it is heard subsequent to [the root]—expresses the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) of that very [root-meaning] through direct statement (*śruti*) in the ultimate sense.
And since that [sacrifice] does not attain its existence without the factors of action (*kāraka*s), the injunction (*vidhi*) also operates upon those *kāraka*s for the sake of that [root-meaning].

Since an action (*kriyā*) requires a cause for its result (*phala*), he prescribes the action for those [who possess it]; thus, because the agent, the result, and the cause are required by the injunction itself, they are intended to be expressed (*vivakṣā*).

However, as for the qualification of the oblation (*havis*)—namely, its "twofoldness" (*ubhayatva*)—since that is neither the action nor a means to it, it is not referred to by the injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*).
[Objection: But let the oblation qualified by "both" be the cause; it need not be qualified by "distress" (*ārti*).

Therefore, he says: If, in this way, the cognition of the occasion (*nimitta-pratyaya*) arises through the oblation (*havis*) qualified by distress (*ārta*), then because the injunctive statement regarding the occasional rite (*naimittika-prayoga-vacana*)— namely, the word "one should offer" (*nirvapet*)— requires that very [oblation],

any other word (*padāntara*) which is observed to be not connected with the occasion (such as "both," *ubhaya*) becomes a separate sentence (*vākya*), because of its delay (it arrives later, after the injunction has already been established).

(He states another interpretation of the commentary: Alternatively, the word *liṅga* (indicative mark) signifies the cause (*nimitta*), as in the phrase "one should take" (*ācchet*). This indicates that the cause belongs specifically to that [act] whose purpose is distress (*ārtyartha*), because it is heard [in the text] immediately following that. In that case, if one were to accept the mere verbal testimony (*kevalaśruti*) [without regard for context], there would be an absence of causal status because distress alone is constant (*nityatvena*). Thus, even when the oblation (*havis*) is qualified by distress, the verbal testimony is not excessively impaired, just as when rice (*dhānya*) is prescribed elsewhere [as the material], there is no impairment of the verbal testimony in the statement "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*brīhīn prokṣati*).

But when there is a connection with the state of being the sacrificial offering (*havirbhāva*), the meaning of the verbal root is not enjoined (it is not designated as the occasion), nor does it [serve] elsewhere (the meaning is that it does not become the occasion even by way of being a qualification of another).

Therefore, it is not required by the statement of the occasion and duty (*nimittakartavyatāvācana*) expressed by the word "one should cut" (*ācchēt*), nor by the occasional rite (*naimittika*) expressed by "one should offer" (*nirvapēt*); hence, it is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

Now, [the author] explains the objection in the *Bhāṣya*—beginning with "But why is it that pain qualified by two words is not understood as the cause (*nimitta*)? and ending with "Therefore, it is understood that pain qualified by both is the cause"—as follows: Just as the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the word *havis* and [the word *ārti*] is accepted according to the ultimate sense of the Vedic revelation (*paramārtha-śruty-āgama*), even so, in the absence of knowledge of both words, one must accept whatever Vedic revelation is possible [based on what is actually heard].

Therefore, by virtue of that distress (*ārtyā*), not only is the oblation (*havis*) qualified, but both [the oblation and the deity]—being joined with one another—are qualified by the state of being the oblation (*haviṣ-bhāvatve*).

(This is precisely what the *Bhāṣya* statement "distress qualified by both" (*ubhayaviśiṣṭā ārtiḥ*) intends; the word "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) refers to the relationship, and it is explained as establishing the meaning: "both [the oblation and the deity] as qualified by distress. )

Or rather, [the author] says that what was heard is indeed logical: "Alternatively, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) failed to grasp the distinction that this is a qualification of *ārti* (distress). What, however, did he grasp? From the previous [Siddhānta] Bhāṣya, which states, 'The cessation of distress is also understood there,' he grasped that *ārti* qualified [as its absence] is the occasion (nimitta)."

If this is so—that is, if the cessation of distress (*ārtinivṛtti*) alone is the cause—then just as the cessation of distress, being qualified by one [word] (*havis*), exists as expressed by the Vedic text (*śruti*) and does not disappear, so too the cessation of distress of this [person], being qualified by the second word (*ubhaya*), does not cause the Vedic text to be abandoned.
To this, it is replied:

With the commentary beginning with "First, this must be asked of those dear to the gods" and ending with "therein it can be set aside by a specific statement expressing a prohibition," the author of the Bhāṣya now sets forth his underlying intention: An action (whether as a fruit or as something to be refined) is enjoined by stimulating its cause; since that which qualifies those two is not a constituent part of the ritual act (*kriyā*), it was previously stated that such a qualification is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*).

(But surely both words [in the compound] are merely the cause (*nimitta*) and not qualifiers of the cause; therefore, how can there be no intention to express [the distinction]? To this, he says: Here, the substance qualified by distress is the cause; that substance, whether separate or combined, is so by virtue of its form as an oblation (*havis*). Therefore, whatever substance possesses the form of an oblation, each of those is established by the word as being the cause.
Just as in the case of "One should not touch a cow with one's foot," every cow whatsoever is not to be touched with the foot, so it is here as well.

Furthermore, even though the word "both" (*ubhaya*) is connected with the oblation (*havis*), the affliction (*ārti*) qualified by both is not at all perceived [as the cause]. (This introduces the Bhāṣya passage from "ityādi" up to "tasmād ubhayaviśiṣṭā ārtir nimittam. Now, why is this point raised again when its meaning has already been established by the previous statement that "the word 'both' qualifies the oblation"? (It is replied: [The following is the response: It is for the purpose of showing that the word "both" does not qualify the oblation, but rather qualifies the affliction (*ārti*). For if the word "both" were to qualify the oblation, then the affliction would not be understood as being qualified by both; consequently, the affliction alone would be the occasion (*nimitta*). However, since the word "both" is intended to qualify the affliction, the affliction is indeed understood as being qualified by both. Therefore, the affliction qualified by both is the occasion. This is what is being stated here. Thus, there is no repetition. Furthermore, the word "oblation" is mentioned here in order to indicate that the word "both" does not qualify the oblation. Otherwise, one might think that because the word "both" is used in proximity to the word "oblation," it must qualify the oblation. To prevent such a misconception, the word "oblation" is explicitly mentioned here. Therefore, the objection regarding repetition is unfounded. Regarding this, the proponent of the objection has stated that "by being connected through distress (*ārtyā*), it will qualify the sacrificial offering (*havis*)," just as in the case of the statement, "Let a white cow be brought. Here, the word "white" qualifies the cow which is being connected with the act of bringing;
thus, by implication, it serves as a qualifier for a single action, setting it apart from blackness and so forth.

When such equality between the example and the illustrated case—that is, between the qualifiers of the thing to be taken up (*upādeya*) and the thing to be designated (*uddeśya*)—has been urged, the other [the respondent] explains the distinction: "The illustration is unequal."
By these words and others, he shows the summary of that meaning: when action is primary, because it is being enjoined, its qualification is intended;
but when the action is subordinate, that which is the qualification of the primary [substance] is not intended.

(The mention of the "principal" [pradhāna] is also indicative of the "cause" [nimitta]). Here, however, by means of the words "Moreover" (*apica*) and so forth, he rejects [the view] after first accepting a connection with the oblation (*havir*). (He states the rejection: "The oblation is referred to by the word *ārti* (distress), but not the word *ubhaya* (both), even though it exists.

(Thus, when the connection with distress has been rejected because of its lack of connection with the property of the principal—) "Now, because of its connection with the case-ending that serves as the locus for *ārti*."

(He explains by summarizing the Bhāṣya from "ityādi" up to "aśvasya śraityaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ bhavati"): By this (Bhāṣya), the fact of having the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktimatva*) and syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) are presented as the grounds for the word *ubhaya* being connected with *ārti*.
(He illustrates the single case-ending: *Ātaḥ* is the substratum of the oblation; the case-ending that occurs there is seen in the other word (*ubhaya*) as well.
Therefore, by whichever case-ending the oblation (*havis*) is connected with the term "affliction" (*ārtyā*), by that very same [case-ending] both [the affliction and the word "both"] are connected.
(He explains [this] in terms of proximity: Just as the oblation is connected with the affliction revolving in the mind, so too are both [connected], because their presence in the mind is equal.

(He explains [this] in terms of syntactic unity: Since both [the affliction and the word "both"] occur within a single sentence, the word "both" would otherwise be purposeless; for when it can be meaningful through its connection with the affliction, it is not proper to assume it is purposeless.
Having thus set forth the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he provides the refutation.

(In this regard, he states the intention of the commentary on the refutation of the first objection: Because of its connection with the same case-ending, the relationship [defined by the sentence] would be with the *havis* alone, and not with the deity.

(He refutes [the objection regarding] immediate proximity: as in the example, "The king’s wife, Devadatta’s man"—just as the king, while being connected to the wife, is not connected to the man despite their proximity because his expectancy is satisfied, so too is the case with both words.)

(He resolves the objection regarding syntactic unity—) as in the case of "he goes by a white horse, covered with a cloth," where whiteness, though connected with the cloth even within a single sentence, is not a qualifier of the horse because it is not required [by the horse]; likewise, since the *ātman* (self/essence) belongs to the oblation (*havis*), the word *ubhaya* (both) is not connected with *ārti* (ruin/injury).
(He begins to explain this very point by raising an objection—the principle of *ārti*.)
The principle of distress (*ārtinyāya*).

It has been stated that there is no connection between "one who desires" (*kāṅkṣan*) and "one who is worthy" (*arhatin*); however, that is incorrect, because by this sentence—namely, "if both oblations of one should suffer damage"—the connection with distress has already been established.

Furthermore, the word "both" (*ubhaya*) is connected with the oblation (*havis*), not with the essential nature of the oblation itself (lest it lead to the undesirable consequence of [the rule applying even when] there is no distress). Rather, it is connected with that form by which the oblation becomes the locus of distress. Therefore, it is connected with the oblation as qualified by distress.
Just as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of rice grains is connected with the portion that leads to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), and not with the mere nature of the rice grain.
(Concluding the objection: If this is so, then it is logical that the distress (*ārti*) is qualified by both [the rice and the sprinkling].
It is replied:

In that case (regarding the sprinkling), because of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is possible to indicate by implication (*lakṣayituṃ*) that which pertains to the *apūrva*, just as the distress is indicated in the form of the rice.
In this case, however, since there is no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to be brought into the context, indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is impossible.

First, there would be a connection with "distress" (*ārti*); then, for that which is colored by it—that is, for that which is colored by distress—there would be a connection with both [the offering and the deity]. In this way, indirect indication would occur. And such being the case, because the word for the oblation (*havis*) is uttered twice, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

(The first utterance of the connection with *ārti* is: "the oblation which has been spoiled" (*yat havissāt ārte*). Then, for the sake of connecting that [oblation] with both [the cow and the calf], there is a second utterance: "that oblation which was spoiled, if that is both [the cow and the calf]"—thus the Commentary explains. In this way, having refuted the attachment of the word "both" (*ubhaya*) to *ārti* by means of the previously stated method, [the author] asks: why does the connection not occur with the oblation as qualified by *ārti*, according to this passage of the Commentary: "it might be said that the connection of both is with the oblation characterized by *ārti*"? By this, he asks why there is no connection with the oblation as qualified by *ārti*.

(He) says: "And this being so, the two previous faults are avoided; (he states the two faults as: there is no connection of the *ārti* with both [the act and the substance], but rather with the pure oblation (*havis*) alone.
But the other (the proponent of the established view) says: "'*Na ācchet*'—this word is employed as a qualifier of the oblation.
Now, is it not improper that the *ārti* should thus function as the occasioning condition (*nimitta*) for the oblation?

If the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified were reversed, then because distress (*ārti*) would necessarily exist [at all times], there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it is eternal, which would strike at its being caused by a specific occasion.
It is replied:
this passage does not aim to refute that distress is a qualifier of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); rather, it is stated from the perspective of another's opinion.
It qualifies the oblation (*havis*).
(He explains this very point: "In what way, indeed, might the oblation be connected with both words?"—it is by this portion that it qualifies [the term].
[As stated in the Bhāṣya: "Now, the gift characterized by the form of the oblation..."—here, the word "both" (*ubhayam*) and so forth is supplied.
In this position, *havis* is the qualifier and both [the *dadhi* and *payas*] are the qualificands.
Subsequently, the *havis*—qualified by both—is connected with the verb *āśrayati* (is contained).
Even so, that same syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) remains (due to the double utterance of the word *ubhaya*).

(He states the intention of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "Just as from a verb [the others are subordinate]" and ending with "both words denoting the oblation should be uttered for the purpose of qualifying the distress"—thereby explaining the intent: In that context, by setting forth the various modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*) which will be discussed later, he explains the distinction between the subordinate and the principal nature of the verb.
When the verb is the principal element (that which is to be enjoined), its qualifier—the case-ending—is intended; when it is subordinate (that which is to be enjoined), it is not intended.
(He states the essential meaning of the Bhāṣya: That which is being enjoined by two words is uttered for the sake of another.

Therefore, this is the meaning of the [Bhāṣya]: where the meaning of a verb is uttered for the sake of its own prescription, there the qualification is intended; but where it is uttered for the sake of prescribing something else—as in "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where the oblation (*homa*) is mentioned for the sake of prescribing the connection with curd—there there is no connection with a second word, because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Having thus explained the distinction, the various modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*) are set forth.

By the commentary beginning with "Now, if the utterance is not repeated," the word *havis* is treated as a *tantra* (a term used once to serve multiple purposes). (The meaning is that, through the word *tatra*—which is a common synonym—the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "that which performs it is [the agent]," and the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object;

thus, the connection of the word *havis* with both the words *ārti* and *ubhaya* is shown by way of *tantra*). By the commentary stating, "In this way, if the word *ubhaya* were connected with *ārti*, it would not be qualified by *havis*," the word *ārti* is treated as a *tantra*.
"If it were connected with the word *havis*," [as stated in the Bhāṣya], the word "both" (*ubhaya*) is supplied and thus governed by the term "both.
(He states the refutation in all cases: Therefore, the defect mentioned in the section on the Vājapeya—characterized as repetition—is present.

When it is argued that "the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) applies to both [the new moon and full moon sacrifices]," it is said: "Whatever is auxiliary to the sacrifice persists as long as its occasion remains."
To that extent it is the object of apprehension; anything other than that is not intended to be expressed by the words "heard" (*śruta*) or "understood" (*mata*).

Just as the word *havis* is connected with the verb *ācchet*, so too both words [of the compound] are connected with that very [verb], because they are not mutually related; they are not connected with *havis*, since nouns that are already mutually related are connected with the verb.
Therefore, the mere appearance of the *havis* is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).

The two-fold condition (*ubhayapada*) should be construed in this way: neither the overflow of the evening milking alone is the cause, nor the overflow of the morning milking alone; rather, both together, independently of one another, constitute the cause.

Since the condition for the *soma*-disturbance—the complete burning of the sacrificial cake—is included within the body of the causal definition because it is explicitly stated in the scripture, what need is there to mention the "twofoldness" [as a cause]? This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) by way of a question. Now, an objection: the sentence "whose both... is recited following the introductory statement, "whose evening milk or morning milk might be spoiled."
And in that case, only this much is intended by the phrase "for whom both [are spoiled]," because the context (prakaraṇa) establishes that "he should offer an excessive oblation" (havirātimācchet).

Thus, even though the context is available, since there is no operation of the word [itself] toward that end, and because it would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda), the five-platter sacrifice (pañcaśarāva-yāga) applies only when both oblations are spoiled.

[Objection: "Since there is no established conclusion (*siddhānta*) on this point, this investigation is untenable. [Reply: True. This is not recorded as "whose milk is in the evening"; rather, it is investigated by taking into account that the milking in the morning and evening is recorded within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
And since the statement "the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) would perish" is not part of that context, and because it cannot be obtained from the context, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

[Objection: But is this not redundant with the section on the *prahā* (3.1.7), since the desire to express a qualification of the subject (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa-vivakṣā*) was already stated in the *tantra*?
It is said:

Having accepted that both [terms] function as qualifiers, we do not investigate here whether they are intended or unintended; rather, we investigate whether "duality" (ubhayatva) is included within the causal factor (nimitta) or not. If it is included within the causal factor, then because the essential nature of the causal factor is intended to be expressed, the duality included therein is also intended; if not, then it is not.
Therefore, there is no tautology.

Now, in Helārāja’s commentary on the *Vākyapadīya* (3.1.92), while explaining the passage of Hari: "Either singularity or plurality is intended for some; however, duality would be intended for the sake of conceiving them as distinct classes," [the following objection is raised]: "If that were so, then even in the case of the rule *yasyobhayam*, if duality were intended, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of the occasioning condition (*naimittika*) for one or the other."

Anticipating this objection, [the author] replies: in that context, mere duality is not what is heard; rather, it is a collection (*samudāya*) consisting of two parts. This is because the word *ubhaya* is derived from the specific numeral [root *ubha*] through the substitution of the suffix *tayap*, according to the rule "after a numeral, *tayap* is used in the sense of a part" (*saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*). Thus, it denotes a collection composed of two constituent members.

Furthermore, since it has been stated here that "because the meaning of the word *ubhaya* (both)—which refers to a whole through its parts—is destroyed even upon the destruction of a single part, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is not applicable even when only one [of the two] is destroyed," [it might be argued: "Even if the intention is to express 'bothness,' the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) should still take place upon the destruction of even one. This is true;

however, although the term denotes a collective whole, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *havis* (oblation), and because the oblation is in fact primary, the expiation applies only when both oblations are destroyed, not when only one portion is.

In the case of the *pañcaśarāva* offering prescribed for one who has suffered loss, whether it be due to the exhaustion of two milch-cows or the destruction of even one, let it be performed immediately with the two oblations that have been sprinkled;
for the mere utterance of the word "oblation" (*havis*) constitutes the determining cause (*nimitta*).
If there is no intention to express both [the conditions], then [the rite] would take place even upon the destruction of one;
thus, "even when one is destroyed and two are not, the *odana* should be offered.
Having stated the expiation for the destruction of each of the curd and milk individually, [the text continues]: "For whomsoever both sacrificial offerings (*havis*) should be spoiled..."
It is traditionally taught: "One should offer an oblation of five-śarāva-measure rice for Indra.

In this context, mere distress (*ārti*) cannot be the occasioning condition (*nimitta*), because since some form of distress always exists for someone at all times, it would be eternal and thus unfit to serve as an occasioning condition.

Therefore, as in the case of the phrase "when the sacrificial ground has not been measured," there is no dispute that, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the distress regarding the sacrificial material (*haviḥ*) is the occasioning condition.

Therefore, that very duality itself enters into the category of the occasioning condition (*nimitta*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because otherwise the two terms [of the compound] would be rendered redundant; indeed, the offering of both oblations (*ubhaya-havis*) alone is the occasioning condition.
For there is no purpose such as grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) or the like, as there is in the case of dual number and so forth.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the following is established]: according to the principle of the "single vessel" (*grahaikādhikaraṇa*), even though the specific intended object (*uddeśya*) is a qualification of the occasion (*nimitta*), it is intended to be significant (*vivakṣā*). Moreover, since the word "both" (*ubhaya*) can be explained as meaning "each one," and since "duality" (*ubhayatva*) does not enter into the category of the occasion (*nimitta*), the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies even when only a single oblation (*havis*) is destroyed. In reality, however, the occasion is simply the destruction of "both."
Nor is it the case that its status as a cause is untenable because it is eternal;

The formal discussion (*adhikaraṇa*), meanwhile, is conducted as a hypothetical inquiry (*kurvācintā*) regarding the status of the oblation.

In reality, however, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in words such as "oblation" (*havis*) even in both [the opponent's and our own] positions, because it is logically possible for all word-meanings to undergo mutual connection only after their connection with the verbal root (*ākhyāta*). Bālakrīḍā, pp. 19–20. Exclusion by implication (*ārthī parisaṃkhyā*) is of two kinds: exclusion of what is already obtained (*prāpta-parisaṃkhyā*) and exclusion of what is not yet obtained (*aprāpta-parisaṃkhyā*).

In this regard, the *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) that restricts what is already established possesses three defects, whereas the *parisaṃkhyā* that restricts what is not yet established is free from them;
moreover, it is designated as *parisaṃkhyā* by virtue of its result.
Regarding these, there is no example of the former at all in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Bhāṣya* and the *Ārtika*.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, it exists in the fifth alternative regarding the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.

But according to the internal opinion of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is sometimes established, as for instance in the tenth book (*daśama*) [at 10.5.13–14], where it is heard in the context of the *agni-raśmi* two-night sacrifice: "The *vaikhānasa* chant is the *sāman* on the first day; the *ṣoḍaśin* is on the latter."

In this regard, since the *dvirātra* sacrifices of the highest class have the *atirātra* as their concluding rite (*saṃsthā*), the model *atirātra* (*prakṛti-atirātra*) applies, and the *ṣoḍaśin* cup would thus be obtained as an option among sixteen alternatives. However, by another scriptural statement not recited in the *Āraṇyaka*, "The *ṣoḍaśin* is taken on the later day of the *dvirātra*," the *ṣoḍaśin* is made mandatory. Consequently, by the word "later" (*uttare*), there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the *ṣoḍaśin* specifically for the *dvirātra* of the Agnirasa school. Therefore, according to the statement of other commentators, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in other *dvirātra* sacrifices, the *ṣoḍaśin* remains optional.
The Śabarasvāmins did not accept the restrictive injunction (parisaṃkhyā), because it entails three defects.
Regarding the Vaikhānasa sacrifices, they accepted the statement "the Ṣoḍaśin is in the latter [part]" as an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
Furthermore, the phrase "with seventeen" is also not a restrictive injunction of what has already been obtained.

Although the author of the Sūtras stated in that context, "Or rather, it is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), because of enumeration" (3.7.6.33), and the author of the Bhāṣya likewise explained it in that manner, nevertheless, the author of the Vārttika stated at the conclusion of that section that the scriptural mention of "seventeen" serves the purpose of a summary.
This has been demonstrated by us in the *Śāstradīpikāprakāśa*.
Therefore, the example of a restrictive injunction regarding what is already established is strictly from the Smṛti: "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten."
An example of an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) that has not been previously established is "imāmagṛbhṇan" (RV 10.85.14).
[Bālakrīḍā, p. 25]. The efficient force (*ārthī bhāvanā*): the efficient force is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātāṃśa*).

Now, what is this *ārthī bhāvanā*? If it is argued that it is "the activity to be performed" (*kartavyavyāpāra*), this is not so; for then even the sacrifice (*yāga*) and other such acts would incur the status of being *bhāvanā*, since they too are activities. Nor is this a desirable consequence, because [the sacrifice] is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) and thus cannot be the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).
If this is argued, [the author states the view of the *Nyāyasudhākṛt*: ] here he says:
It is true that the sacrifice is not the *bhāvanā*; rather, the *bhāvanā* is that effort directed toward the sacrifice which is produced by the desire for heaven.
And that very [effort]...

It is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātāṃśa*); for when the verbal suffix "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is heard, the cognition "one should sacrifice by means of a sacrifice" arises. Furthermore, since we observe the use of the verb "to do" (*karoti*) in the case of one who performs actions such as walking with deliberate effort—as in "Devadatta performs walking"—but we use the expression "he does not do this; rather, his movement is produced by the wind and so forth" in the case of something vibrating due to the wind, the meaning of "to do" is indeed effort (*prayatna*).

Furthermore, co-referentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "to do" (*karoti*) is observed in verbal forms: "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) means "one should effect by means of a sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*); "he cooks" (*pacati*) means "he effects cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*); and "he goes" (*gacchati*) means "he effects going" (*gamanaṃ karoti*).
Therefore, because of this co-referentiality with "to do," effort (*prayatna*) is the denotation of the verbal suffix.
Nor should it be argued that the usage "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*) is untenable due to the absence of effort in the chariot.

Since the effort residing in the horse that draws [the chariot] can be attributed to the chariot because it is logically consistent with its application, even in the view where *bhāvanā* is defined as a general activity (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*) conducive to the undertaking of another [action], there is no occurrence of an activity distinct from "going"; therefore, the usage "the chariot goes" is merely figurative.
Consequently, effort alone is the meaning of *bhāvanā*.
As they have said: "But it is impossible to say that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is something other than effort;
therefore, we desist from the discussion here regarding its being denoted by the verbal suffix."
(He states the mixed opinion: Others say this: "The operation of the producer (*bhāvaka*) which is conducive to the coming-to-be of that which is to come-to-be (*bhavitṛ*) is *bhāvanā*;
that is to say, such an operation by which, once performed, the instrument (*karaṇa*) becomes capable of producing the result.
That alone is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*khyātā*)."

Indeed, when one hears the verbal suffix in the expression "he cuts with an axe," such a cognition arises: "The axe is so employed that, when that operation is performed, cutting occurs by means of the axe.

Similarly, the meaning of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" is this: "One should be so engaged by means of the sacrifice that, when that operation is performed, heaven results from the sacrifice.

And what is that operation? From [the mundane perspective], it is the raising, lowering, and so forth; and from [the Vedic perspective], it is the placing of fuel on the fire (*agnyanvādhāna*) and so forth.

When there is an expectancy for the nature of the action (*kāryabhāva*) following the satiation of the Brahmins, it is subsequently understood in its specific form; however, in its general sense, it is understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) itself as being conducive to the employment of other factors.

In the sentence "The chariot goes to the village" (*ratho grāmaṃ gacchati*), by means of the verbal suffix, only an activity conducive to reaching the village is perceived, because of the cognition that "the chariot is pervaded by the act of going," and that "when this activity is performed, the reaching of the village occurs as a result of the going.
But here, mere going is not the meaning of the verbal suffix, since that is already expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

In this regard, when the expectation arises as to "What is this operation?", it is subsequently understood as consisting of the disjunction from and conjunction with a preceding and a succeeding intermediate space, based on such usage as: "The chariot goes to the village after having disjoined from the eastern region and conjoined with the northern one," and "He cuts with the axe in both ways."

(He says that even in cases such as *yate* ("he exerts"), where the action has a conscious agent (*cetana-kartṛka*), the application of the definition occurs only according to the view of the opponent [the Mīmāṃsakas], and not according to the view of the [Vaiyākaraṇas] who hold that [the effort] is not present: Likewise, in the case of "Devadatta exerts himself" (*devadattaḥ prayatnate*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is simply an activity conducive to effort—namely, "Devadatta acts in such a way that effort arises"—and not effort itself, because that [effort] has already been expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).
And when there is an expectation for a specific kind of activity, desire and so forth are understood subsequently, since both [the root and the suffix] are not restricted to a single meaning.

And thus, because it is present everywhere, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is simply the general activity conducive to another's material cause (*upādāna*), and not mere effort alone; for that [effort] is absent in instances such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*) and "Devadatta exerts effort" (*devadattaḥ prayatnate*).

Indeed, the authors of the *Vārttika*, in the section on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), have accepted the cognition of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) by distinguishing between the parts [of the action] and acknowledging the distinction between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*).

In reality, just as the Vārttikakāras’ demonstration of the cognition of *bhāvanā* (productive activity) in the case of the word ‘*bhavati*’ (*it comes into being*) was for the sake of a specific refinement (*atiśaya*), so too here, in cases such as ‘the chariot goes’ (*ratho gacchati*), that demonstration is likewise only for the sake of a specific refinement.

For no one has the experience that “the chariot performs going,” “the person performs effort,” or “the jar performs becoming. Therefore, the purport of this treatise is that, regardless of other specific substrates, the general sense of operation (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*) alone is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in all instances.

In the examples provided, the understanding [of the meaning] is established even without a formal definition: the operation of going as it exists in the case of Indra, the operation of effort residing in a person, and the operation of coming into being residing in a jar.

Nor is it appropriate to claim that these are merely figurative, for when a primary sense is possible, resorting to a figurative one is improper. Furthermore, the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is indeed an operation conducive to the acquisition of something else, and not mere effort alone.
The intended meaning is simply this: "activity-ness" (*vyāpāratva*) is the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), not "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*).

As for the fact that being conducive to the undertaking by another is the delimitor of the denotable capacity, whether that is understood there through direct expression or through implication is another matter. Furthermore, the root *karoti* occurs in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with verbal suffixes whose agents are both sentient and insentient.
Thus, it is established that *bhāvanā* has as its meaning an activity conducive to the undertaking by another.

And that very same [activity] is expressed by the verbal suffix in the phrase "he should sacrifice" as "he should bring about" (*bhāvayet*). When there is an expectancy for what is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), heaven and so forth are connected as the object to be brought about.

In the sentence concerning the sacrifice and the animal, it is an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāgavidhi*), not an injunction for a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), because of the connection between the substance and the deity.
This is because, in a context where no preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is under discussion, there is no word denoting a ritual action.
The Bhāṣya states: "Something is studied as an independent injunction (*anāramyādhīta*): 'One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu.'"
