Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, they recite: "One should sacrifice a ewe" and "He offers four handfuls.
(In this context, the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] is reached by assuming syntactical unity between the first and third sentences, and between the second and fourth sentences.)

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: there is a doubt: Is the act of seizing (*ālambha*) in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), and is the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices also an injunction of a subordinate quality; or rather, do these two acts not pertain to the archetype (*prakṛti*) beyond what is explicitly stated, or are these two actions accompanied by sacrifice (*yajimat*)? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That they are injunctions of subordinate qualities for the archetypal acts of seizing and pouring out. Why? Because they are not words denoting a distinct action (*akarmaśabdatvāt*).
There is no word here that prescribes an action.
But surely [words such as] "one should sacrifice" (*ālabheta*) and "one should offer" (*nirvapet*) exist; yet these two are not prescriptive.
Only one who speaks of a meaning not already known is prescriptive.
Nor are the meanings of these two [terms] known as "the animal is to be sacrificed" or "the offering is to be performed";
therefore, they are merely restatements (anuvāda).

For what purpose are these restatements? They are for the purpose of enjoining a white animal for the *ālambha* (the act of touching/sacrificing) and a *caru* (oblation) for the *nirvāpa* (the act of pouring out).
Therefore, there is no separate *ālambha* nor a separate *nirvāpa*;
rather, these are merely injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the original acts.
Nor is it heard in the context of any specific ritual that "one should sacrifice a white animal" (*śvetam ālabheta*) or "one should offer a caru-oblation" (*carum nirvapet*).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: since those [injunctions] studied outside of a specific context (*anāramyādhīta*) pertain to the archetype (*prakṛti*), are the qualities of whiteness and the *caru* prescribed as attributes for the very archetypal acts of sacrificing and offering? Or do they refer to two distinct rituals (*karmāntara*) as far as the text indicates? Or rather, are they [acts] involving a sacrifice (*yajimat*)?
In this regard, the principle of what is studied outside of a specific context serves as the basis for the doubt and is intended to establish the first position, which has not yet been stated.
The principle of the immolation and the offering (*ālabhanirvāpanyāya*):

How so? If, first of all, the immolation and the offering were heard of as being enjoined with reference to the archetype (*prakṛti*), then there would follow only a continuation of the cognition of the archetype; thus, no suspicion of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) would arise.

However, when there is a discussion concerning an independent injunction (*anārambhya-vāda*), because qualities such as "white" and so forth are to be adopted, a doubt arises whether a quality is being enjoined by way of a reference to something already established elsewhere, or whether, due to the absence of identity, a distinct ritual action is being enjoined. Likewise, in this case, the injunction of a ritual action involving sacrifice (*yajimat-karma-vidhāna*) appears to be almost settled by the sūtra: "And because of the connection with a substance, the injunction [is] of the animal and the soma" (2.3.16–17).

Since there is no original sacrifice (*prakṛtayāga*) [to which these acts could refer], and because an injunction of a quality such as "white" is possible even for an action inherently connected with a substance—provided it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—the question arises: how can this be?

Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds by asserting that since the two acts of immolation (*ālambha*) and offering (*nirvāpa*) do not belong to the context (*aprakaraṇāt*), one must accept only those components belonging to the original sacrifice (*prākṛta*).

The refutation of that view will likewise proceed thus: due to the absence of a context and the lack of any specific defining characteristic (*asādhāraṇalakṣaṇatva*), there is no cognition of the two original acts as having a form distinct from worldly ones.

In the case of injunctions regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*), because the acts of slaughtering (*ālambhana*) and offering (*nirvāpa*) are mentioned as qualified by those qualities, what is the prima facie view? Just as in the *Ayana* sacrifices, where the sentences are intent upon connecting qualities and there is an absence of words enjoining a ritual action (*karmavidhi*), there is no distinct action (*akarmāntaratva*), so it will be here as well; this is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*).
Furthermore, since that [injunction] is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the mention of the "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is for the purpose of determining its scope.

Alternatively, even though this much is heard in the section defining the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), nevertheless, because the injunctive word is not subsumed under the ritual action, this repeated mention is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
That which is the offering-spoon (*sruk*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is to be made white and used for the slaughter (*ālabhya*);
and the oblation (*caru*) is to be prepared, measured by the *caru* vessel, or [measured] by the cooking-pot (*odanasthālī*).

Furthermore, regarding those desiring prosperity (*bhūti*) or Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), the statements "the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices [are] for all" serve as restatements (*anuvāda*) of what is already established.

Similarly, in the case of the injunction "to Vāyu," since the quality of being dedicated to Vāyu (*vāyavyatā*) applies to every wooden pole (*vanaspati*), the mention of the "pole" (*īṣā*) is merely a figurative restatement (*anuvāda*).
Likewise, in the case of "to Sūrya," this is a restatement of that which is already dedicated to Agni, due to the commonality of having a deity characterized by brilliance (*tejas*).
Therefore, it is argued that a quality (*guṇa*) is being enjoined.
Or rather, as much as has been stated, because the ritual action (*karman*) is rooted in direct scriptural revelation (*śruti*).
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "And this is not the case, namely, that these two are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) for the archetypal rites (*prākṛta*)."
What then? A different *ālambha* (touching/sacrificing) is enjoined, not a different *nirvāpa* (offering/pouring).
If both *ālambha* and *nirvāpa* were enjoined, then those two would not be the original (archetypal) ones that are enjoined.
If they are not enjoined, then the original ones are indicated by the statement, "that *ālambha* and *nirvāpa* which ought to be performed."
Therefore, having indicated those two [the *śvetam* and *carum*], they would have to be enjoined;
and since both purposes—desire for prosperity (*bhūti*) and desire for Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*)—would be objects to be enjoined, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Alternatively, that word which is injunctive would be exhausted by being used for the purpose of indication; thus, due to the absence of an injunction, not even one of the other two could be enjoined.
If it is argued that the very same [act] is what is to be obtained, and by that very act the quality is enjoined— so that there is no mutual relationship characterized by injunction—

then if it is said that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) while the suffix is intended to be injunctive, such that "that which is the act of killing (*ālabhambha*) must be performed with this quality," even so, the original [Vedic] act would not be indicated, for there is also a worldly act of killing.

When the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is being determined, the archetypal (prakṛta) act is restated; for that which is to be performed must be established by scriptural injunction (śruti), not by worldly practice.

Therefore, a mere restatement of the archetypal act is not tenable; rather, only the acts of touching (ālabhana) and pouring out (nirvāpa) as far as they are expressly stated must be performed as something new (apūrva), because the ritual action is rooted in direct revelation (śruti).
For it has been stated that "the Veda is indeed the root of ritual action," namely, "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (1.1.2).
Therefore, in another ritual action—or rather: "If the acts of immolation (*ālambha*) and offering (*nirvāpa*) are not accepted as being subject to an injunction..."

Therefore, there would be an injunction of qualities, and those two are considered here to be the objects of injunction. The word "vāyavya" (dedicated to Vāyu) disregards the previous deity; rather, when the word expressing the result is accepted, the suffix is heard [as signifying the injunction].

For if the acts of immolation (*ālambha*) and offering (*nirvāpa*), as well as the quality of whiteness (*śvetatva*), were enjoined [separately], then the word expressing the result would indeed be purposeless.

Even if it were a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the attainment of all desires, the mention [of the act] as if it were obligatory (*nityavat*) would be problematic because [the attainment of all desires] is only occasional (*pākṣika*).
Alternatively, if it were a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Furthermore, if a connection between a quality and a fruit (*guṇaphalasambandha*) were being enjoined, even then, since the [act of] "touching" (*ālambhya*) and so forth—which is the subject under discussion—is not established as something to be performed, one would have to establish that connection through the sentence itself, and thus the sentence would be split.
However, there is no fault whatsoever in [the view that] it is distinguished by its qualities (*guṇa*).
Therefore, it is stated in the Sūtra: "Because the action has its root in direct revelation (*śruti*).
Here, the action is rooted in revelation by virtue of being what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), whereas the quality is not.
For that [act] would indeed have the characteristic of being without an injunction;
or rather, it would be exactly as stated, not involving a sacrifice.
Why? Because the action has its basis in direct scriptural statement (śruti).
For it is not possible to determine that "this person sacrifices" unless he is impelled [by a scriptural injunction];
nor is anything here unaccomplished without that [impulsion],
since the designation of primacy is justified solely by the fact that the acts of immolation (*ālambhana*) and offering (*nirvāpa*) possess fruitfulness.

There is no authority whatsoever for the claim that because something is seen to be subordinate in one instance, its primacy in another instance— though even if it were expressly stated by scripture— should not be accepted;
for the status of being subordinate or primary follows the scriptural injunction, not the method of seizing (*ālambhana*) or offering (*nirvāpa*).
These two are inherent.

Furthermore, the mention of "dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavya*) and so forth in all these cases is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since the presence of a deity in substances can be established in some way or another.
Alternatively, whatever has been intended by someone as being dedicated to Vāyu becomes a cause of prosperity when it is employed in the acts of touching and so forth.
Furthermore, because this is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is no excessive burden even if that [quality] is omitted.
Alternatively, one may simply enjoin the wind (*vāyu*) alone, clearly specifying it as "the wind" or "the eternal" (*nityam*).
Moreover, it is not necessarily the case that a deity must be the object of dedication (*uddeśya*) only in the context of a sacrifice (*yāga*).
For wherever it is mentioned, it is not contradicted when being pointed out there.

Therefore, whatever is white is to be touched by the Vāyavya [offering], as determined in accordance with the injunction as far as it has been stated. Having stated that there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) if the word expressing the result were connected to the subordinate quality (*guṇa*), the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) now speaks even while accepting the abandonment of that [result].
"Or rather, as for that word which is injunctive," and so forth.

His intention is this: that which he asserts regarding the application of those statements not connected to a specific context (*anāramyavāda*) to the archetype (*prakṛti*)—namely, [Sūtra 3.6.1.1–8]—"this is not based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*).
How then? By way of the door (*dvāra*)."
Regarding the *āvasadhyā* fire:
as for the repetition [of the rite], it would occur because of the difference in time when there is an intervention, as established in the section concerning the *āśīḥ* (benediction) at sūtra 10.1.2.

In the Gavām Ayana sacrifice, the performance consists of four Abhiplava ṣaḍahas and one Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha each month. By the rule, "When the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha has concluded, [the midday meal] is eaten from clarified butter," the eating at midday at the end of the ṣaḍaha is prescribed. Once the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha has been performed in the first month, at the beginning of the second month, four Abhiplava ṣaḍahas are performed.
Then again, there is the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha].
Thus it is with the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍahas*.
And likewise, when there is an interposition—that is, an intervention—of the *abhilava* [ṣaḍahas] between the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍahas*, a difference in time is clearly evident.

Thus, since there is a separation [of the sessions], due to the difference in time, there would be a repetition of the midday meal (*madhyāhnaśana*) at the end of each *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, rather than just once at the end of all six-day periods. Therefore, the eating occurs every month. The mention of "sūtra-sūtra" (thread-thread) is for the purpose of indicating a distinction in performance from what was stated in the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*).
"O Āśālā, this sacrificer is yours"—this is the constant designation; "when the sacrifice is designated"—this is the constant restatement.
"O Āśālā, this sacrificer over there is yours"—thus [it is said].

The principle of the weakness of the substratum (āśrayadaurbalyanyāya): 1014. Regarding the relationship between the substratum and the dependent (āśrayāśrayisaṃbandha), it should be understood that even though [certain factors] lack the status of being instrumental (karaṇatva) in rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, their status as the substratum (āśrayatva) is nonetheless established.
There is no uniform injunction (samānavidhitva) regarding the desire for a specific quality (guṇakāmanā) together with the substratum.

Bhāṣya 3.6.16.41–47: When the substratum (āśraya) functions, that which is dependent upon it (āśrita) also functions; just as when a cloth is pulled, the painting supported by it is also pulled along. 8.1.4.122: The principle of the weakness of the substratum (āśrayadaurbalyanyāya).
The meaning of this principle is that when the substratum is weak, that which is dependent upon it becomes even weaker.

The principle regarding the relative weakness of suffixes such as *ṇyut* and others—based on the rule that "the suffix *ṇyut* [is applied] after roots ending in *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, and after those well-known for expressing desire" (*pītvadhikaraṇa*, Vārttika 1.3.4.9, p. 218, l. 19)—though struck down by the section concerning the non-contradiction of the learned (*śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*, 1.3.13.5–7), is revived once again.
This was stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). (Kauṇḍinya 1.3.5.10, pp. 80–81). This is the determination of the definition of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*).
In the second [section], the *indriyakāmādhikaraṇa* (2.1.2.1–26), the connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and the fruit of that quality was stated.

[Regarding this,] those ritual acts which, by means of a portion [of themselves], take recourse in another's substance, deity, or both, and thereby consecrate them, are called "recipients" (*āśraya*).

In that context, after raising an example, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering]: it is not a valid example [for the present discussion], because since its purpose is purely visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*), it cannot be connected with an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Regarding this, he says: First, the *mantra* (beginning with "ayāṭ abhiḥ," etc. has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) because it proclaims the chosen deity.

(He further states that the sacrifice (*yāga*) also has a visible purpose: When there arises the possibility of disposing of the scattered material (the *puroḍāśa* and so forth, which remains after the offering) without any restriction, it is disposed of by means of the sacrifice.
(Therefore,) even that casting of the material into the *āhavanīya* fire has a visible purpose alone.
Therefore, because the substance is being consecrated by means of the sacrifice, it is not equal to the others (such as the *samid* offerings).
Even the *samid* offerings and so forth are not examples [of this], because in their case the action alone is primary, while the substance and deity are subordinate.
The animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) offering also benefits solely through the consecration of the deity.
However, there is no evidence that the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) constitutes a separate sacrifice from the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*).
For it is the animal sacrifice itself that is extended by means of the omentum, the heart, and other parts; moreover, that [animal sacrifice] does not serve as the substratum [for a distinct act].
Therefore, this [offering of the omentum] is also not an example [of a distinct sacrifice].
(The *uttamaprayāja* is also to be excluded by the principle of the animal-cake offering [*paśupuroḍāśanyāya*].

It concludes as follows: An example [of this] occurs where the substance has not yet fulfilled its purpose, while the deity is either already worshipped or intended to be worshipped, and another sacrifice is also mentioned;
for instance, the throwing of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) into the fire with reference to a specific deity has no other purpose than the production of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*).)
Therefore, these have an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).
Hence the author of the Sūtras says: "In the case of the dependent [rites], their existence is understood as the purpose without distinction;
the meaning is that they are enjoined after the sacrifice."
“The existent is taught for the sake of the to-be-accomplished” (Bhāṣya): the existent substance brings about the to-be-accomplished action; thus, the unseen result [arises] from the action.
Alternatively, although the sacrifice benefits the deity by refining it, nevertheless, by attaining the status of an instrument, it becomes the substratum [of the unseen result], and not otherwise.
Therefore, “the existent is taught for the sake of the to-be-accomplished.”
"But regarding this injunction, there is no commencement of anything new; rather, it is enjoined by way of abandonment.
Commentary: "In this injunction, however, there is no commencement of something unprecedented (*apūrva*).
Since this verbal expression is distinct [from others], that which has a perceptible purpose does not entail an *apūrva*."
That which indeed has an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha) is therefore called *apūrva*.
This [other] relies on a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
For when this sacrifice is performed, the deity is remembered, and in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering as well, the substance is disposed of.
Nor is an *apūrva* enjoined here by any other word;
therefore, the sacrifice itself is the purificatory act (*saṃskāra*).
However, where substance and deity are subordinate elements dependent upon a substratum—as in the case of the *samidh* offerings and others—there an *apūrva* exists.

Furthermore, where the substance or the deity is the primary element—as in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the animal sacrifice, the *puroḍāśa* cake, and so forth—there is no *apūrva* because the purpose of the action is for the sake of that [substance or deity], and thus the status of being the substratum (*āśrayatā*) serves that end.
Or rather, when there is a desire to prepare the substance (*dravyacikīrṣā*), the verbal root-meaning (*bhāva*) is subordinate; for subordination arises from the status of being a substratum.
According to the Bhāṣya, there may indeed be an *apūrva* in such cases.
Even though there is a desire to effect the deity, the sacrifice possesses a subordinate status toward that purpose of refining the deity, as it serves to present the substance.
By means of the mantra, the deity is remembered therein.
For when the unseen [effect] is produced by that mantra, another unseen purpose is heard in the injunction regarding the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
For him, nothing visible is seen; however, because it rests upon a deity, it is understood that what pertains to the deity arises from that [recitation] as an unseen potency (*apūrva*).

(The author states the intention of the Siddhānta-sūtra, *dupū*, namely: *svitkṛtvā*—"having performed": That which is the mention of the deity by means of the mantra serves a visible purpose, since remembrance is required there.
But the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is for the sake of the unseen, and therefore it results in an *apūrva*.

The first *prayāja*, the *paśupuroḍāśa*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and so forth—these, which refine the substance and deity belonging to another [rite], are considered: do they serve only that purpose, or do they also serve the purpose of producing the *apūrva*?
In this regard, it is argued: "It is proper for a single action to have only a single purpose;
since a visible result exists, an invisible one should not be postulated, and therefore no *apūrva* exists here."
It is said: "The recollection of the deity [arises] from the mantra; the preparation of the substance [arises] from the casting [into the fire].
But for the portion consisting of the renunciation (tyāga), there is no purpose whatsoever other than the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
Therefore, although they serve an unseen purpose through the portion of renunciation, they are thus [considered] to serve both purposes.

Just as in the case of *soma*, the means-status (*sādhanatva*) of gender and number is established through the visible door of the delimitation of the substance, so too it is for the final *prayāja* offerings and others; thus, because this is directly perceived, the application of the analogy is appropriate.

Although the act of throwing (*prakṣepa*)—unlike the dedication to the deity—is not a constituent part of the sacrifice (*yāga*) because it is not included within the denotation of the word "sacrifice," nevertheless, since that which is to be thrown is to be performed by way of being relinquished with a dedication to the deity, it is understood as if it were a constituent part of the sacrifice; it is on this basis alone that the refinement of the substance (*dravyasaṃskṛti*) arises from the act of throwing.

Now, if the utterance of *svāhā* were solely for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), then, due to the absence of an intermediate *apūrva*, the mere sequence prompted by the *apūrva* of the subsidiary rites would be established; consequently, the purpose of that *apūrva*—namely, the production of the substance—would consist of actions such as stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*). Furthermore, in the case of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), if there were no *apūrva*, the principle of the substratum connected to the *apūrva* would not apply, and the term *āśvavāla* [would be meaningless].

If it is argued: "Since there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rules [to this sacrifice], the purpose characterized by such an extension is not possible; furthermore, regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt*, there is no purpose for establishing that [extension]. Just as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because it is a disposal (*pratipatti*), there is an omission in the event of the loss of the portion intended for it, so too in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because it consists of a single part of the substance and thus lacks the capacity to motivate the use of the substance, there is no difference in the resulting omission"—this is true.

Even in the absence of the function of joining substances such as the northern half [of the cake], if there is a purpose for the unseen (adṛṣṭa), then for the sake of accomplishing that unseen result, there is a practical purpose: the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering must be performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) as prescribed in the rule, "If all one's sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) should be lost, or if both are spoiled by fire, one should sacrifice to those deities again after calculating [the portions] with *ājya*.
The same applies to the flour-smears (*piṣṭalepa*) and the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: those [actions] which, being perceived through their constituent parts, depend upon substance (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*) as a means of refinement (*saṃskāraka*) are called "dependent" (*āśrayaṇa*). That which is brought about in them is the "state" (*bhāva*), which is the meaning [of the verbal root]. It is the *apūrva* (unprecedented merit) that is perceived, by other [means] such as *yajati* and *juhoti*; thus, it is said to be "without distinction" with respect to the purpose of the *apūrva*. [Regarding the term *viṣkṛt*: it is exhausted in the refinement (*saṃskṛti*), and is not useful for the subsequent *apūrva*.]
It is logical that there be a single purpose in one [moment]; therefore, their cessation occurs sequentially.
The consecration of the deity occurs through the mantra; the consecration of the substance results from its casting [into the fire].
That which arises after the act of renunciation (*tyāga*) is like the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*).
Therefore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent offerings serve a dual purpose.

Bhaṭṭa [says]: Regarding the injunctions "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and "he offers oblations" (*juhoti*), where these are heard, since the root *yaji* denotes a sacrifice consisting of a substance qualified by the dedication to a deity, the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) functions as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) by way of producing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). However, the act of dedication (*uddeśa*) functions as an auxiliary to that very sacrifice by way of producing a visible effect. For this very reason, the deity, which is a subordinate element of the dedication, is weaker than the substance, which is a subordinate element of the relinquishment.
In the case of pouring into the fire (*prakṣepa*), however, it serves merely to consecrate the substance that is a subordinate element of the relinquishment.

However, in the case of the *juhoti* offerings, the other two [the *āghāra* and *pūrṇāhuti*] are merely subordinate parts (*aṅga*) to it by way of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭavidhayā*), or else they are equally primary (*samapradhāna*) along with the act of pouring.
For this very reason, the established position is that in both cases the mantra serves solely to reveal the deity who is a constituent part of that [act].

However, in cases such as the *svāhākāra*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the cake offering (*puroḍāśa*), and other oblations like the *vājinejyā*, where either the substance or the deity is directly associated with the act through the act of throwing (*prakṣepa*), the dedication (*uddeśa*), or the mantra—such as the deities Āgneya and others in the case of the *svāhākāra*, *sviṣṭakṛt*, and animal sacrifice being associated by means of both mantra and dedication; or in the *sviṣṭakṛt* where the substance belongs to that [deity] through the act of throwing; or in the *piṣṭalepahoma* and similar rites where the substance itself belongs to that [deity] through the act of throwing—the authority for this is stated in various places and will be explained further on. As for the element of renunciation (*tyāga*) therein, it serves solely an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Nor is there any harm in its being purposeless on the grounds that it is merely a part of a larger ritual act (*padārtha*), because since it is itself a prescribed act (*vihitapadārtha*), its constituent parts also possess an inherent requirement for a purpose, as they are implied by the necessity of the whole. Therefore, even this [act], being for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), serves as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the casting-in (*prakṣepa*) and so forth which yield a fruit; or, through the sequence of the substance to be consecrated, it produces an invisible effect (*adṛṣṭa*) precisely upon the substance and deity to be consecrated—just like sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other such acts—and thus it is rightly classified as a "directly contributing auxiliary" (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*). This is the correct view.

This being the case, since there is no evidence for the portion consisting of the act of renunciation (*tyāga*)—which is perceived as a specific element—to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the act of throwing [the oblation] (*prakṣepa*), and because the assignment of the deity (*devatādeśa*) depends solely on a visible purpose and does not require an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭopakāra*), the portion of renunciation must, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), function as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) like the *prayāja* offerings.

However, there is this much distinction: since it subsists upon a substance and a deity employed by another, it cannot independently imply its own specific substance and deity in the absence of those employed by another.

For this very reason, in the case of the *ekakapāla* (single-potsherd) offering, there is indeed an omission of the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, because the substance that serves as the agent of the action has been destroyed; since the causal condition (*nimitta*) is absent, it is impossible to conclude the rite even with clarified butter (*ājya*).

Furthermore, in the *cayana* (fire-altar construction) and similar rites, or in a non-sacrificial context, although there is a scriptural injunction for the application of the *prayāja* and other offerings, there is no sacrifice involving the utterance of *svāhā*.

However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), if all the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are destroyed, completion is achieved with clarified butter according to the scriptural statement: "If one's entire sacrificial food should be destroyed, or if it is burnt by fire, one should perform the sacrifice by enumerating these deities with clarified butter."

However, in the case of being an auxiliary by way of embellishment (*saṃskāra*), since there is no object to be embellished, the rule is that it is simply omitted, as in the case of the *iḍā* offering; this is the distinction. Maṇḍana [states]: "The *sviṣṭakṛt* would be a new transcendental result (*apūrva*). Śaṅkara [states]: "There exists a substrate for the new transcendental result."

10. “*Āśrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, *yaja*, *ye yajāmahe*, *vauṣaṭ*”—this seventeen-syllable [formula] is Prajāpati; it serves a visible purpose consisting in the recollection of the ritual elements of the sacrifice. (Saṃkarṣa. 2.3.1). Regarding the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when the established order is transgressed:
because optional elements are accepted from the very beginning.
Vārttika 2.4.23: "The *upabhṛt* ladle is made of *aśvattha* wood.
Here, the scriptural mention of the result—"He obtains the Brahman-speech"—is a mere explanatory praise (*vāda*), not an injunction of a result.
Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.3.1.12–14: The *Āśvalāyana-kalpasūtra* is indeed of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
And it is authoritative because it is rooted in the Veda (Vi.

since the long-characterized leaves of the *kāśa* grass resemble the mane of a horse, the word *āśvavāla* is used figuratively (*gauṇatva*) for the *kāśa*.

*Saṃkarṣa.* 3|2|14: The *āhavanīya* fire, the *purītat*, and so forth, serve solely the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). *Bhāṣya* 4|1|21, Section 2: Even though the Brāhmaṇas residing in Āhicchatrā and Mathurā are not [of the highest] caste, drinking liquor is improper conduct (*anācāra*). *Vārttika* 11|3|17, p. 204: "They burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) with the fires and the sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*). Regarding the section on those who have maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), it is stated here that the disposal (pratipatti) of the fires is the subject matter.

Regarding the perpetual duties of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), such as "one should not place split wood [on the fire]," these apply only to the *āhitāgni* in his fires; in that case, the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices need not be awaited.

Just as the vows are prescribed for the sake of the person with reference to the occasion of the *āghāna* (fire-consecration), so too are the duties regarding the non-deficiency of the fire (*agni-cchidratā*). As stated in Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 5.3.10: "Like the vow of one who has established the fires.

Regarding the vow of one who has established the fires, such as "One should place a piece of wood that has been cut [as fuel] upon the fire" (or "one should add it," according to the Vārttika), these duties pertain only to one after the *āghāna* has taken place.
There are thirty oblations in the Vaiśvadeva section:
nine *prayāja*s, nine *anuyāja*s, the two *ājyabhāga*s, and eight *havis* offerings; one takes portions for Agni and sacrifices to the *vājina*s.
(Bhāṣya 12.1.1.4). Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, and thirteen on the new moon day.

(There are five *prayājas*, two *āghāra* and *ājyabhāgas*—namely those for Agni and Agnīṣomīya—one *upāṃśuyāja*, one *sviṣṭakṛt*, and three *anuyājas*; thus, there are fourteen oblations in the Full Moon sacrifice.
In the New Moon sacrifice, however, there are thirteen because of the absence of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
For each oblation in this group of offerings, the drawing of the material occurs once.)

Where many *darvihoma* offerings are performed in succession, there too, because that which was once taken at the beginning of the group serves as the offering for all deities, there is a single performance (*tantratā*), just as in the case of the *upavasatha* where the three sets of five are previously assigned.
Nor is there a need for the completion of each individual oblation,
since it is possible for the *aurava* [oblation] itself to be replenished again and again.

This being the position reached, [the filling] is for that purpose alone, because what was taken prior to the time immediately preceding the first offering is a specific portion of what is being taken.
However, since the swelling (*āpyāyana*) is not possible without an explicit scriptural statement, there is a single drawing for each oblation.
(Saṃkarṣa 2.4.7)

Practices such as the *āhīnaivuka* and others are not to be performed by Southerners alone; rather, they are duties for everyone, independent of the performer's region. One who performs the *agnihotra* in the Deccan, whether facing east or north, certainly performs the *āhīnaivuka* and other rites.
(*Āhīnaivuka* refers to the worship of the *dyukṣa* [heavenly] with hands and so forth, as handed down through one’s own family tradition.)
Section on Invocation (Āhvānādhikaraṇa).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra for the oblation is to be employed in its primary sense for invocation, and not for the act of threshing.
If it is argued that the same applies to the summoning as well, the Bhāṣya states: "The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices exist.
In this regard, the following is recited: 'O preparer of the oblation, come!'—thus he summons while striking [the mortar] three times."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this mantra enjoined with reference to the act of striking (*hanti*), or does the word *hanti* indicate its time? How would it be enjoined with reference to the striking, and how would it indicate the time? If the connection were made thus—"striking [with the words] 'O preparer of the oblation, come' (*haviṣkṛdehi')"—then it would be enjoined with reference to the striking.
But if it were "while striking he calls out," then it indicates its time.

What, then, is the prima facie position? "The invocation as well [is like that]. Just as the *aindrī* verse is taught in relation to the *gāyatrī* and so forth, in exactly the same way, the mantra is taught in relation to the *han* [action].
In this way, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is upheld; otherwise, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The connection would be between the verb *hanti* and the mantra, not between *hanti* and the mantra [as a whole].
This being the case, the word *āhvayati* is a restatement (*anuvāda*);
it means "he performs the summoning."
For he who says "come" is the one who causes [someone] to come.
In that case, the mantra will effect its purpose by making something understood through some quality;
therefore, it is not to be employed for the act of summoning.
Or rather—thus it is established with its exception that the primary function of mantras is such [as previously stated].
Beyond this, the following is investigated: what is the scope of the general rule (utsarga), and what is the scope of the exception (apavāda)?
In that regard, when the sacrificer’s wife prepares the oblation (*haviḥ*) by saying "O preparer of the oblation, come," the mantra is incapable of manifesting that act of summoning.

Should he be employed for that very purpose, since there is no contradiction in the conjunction [of the acts] being a matter of time while he is threshing; or rather, because of the scriptural statement, the meaning is otherwise, and since the threshing is already previously established, it is merely the calling out?
If, by the words "O preparer of the oblation, come," it is enjoined that "he calls out while threshing," then the threshing is subordinate to the calling out.

Now, the word "avaghnan" (while threshing) is connected with "āhvayati" (he calls out), and thus, by the very form [of the sentence], it is understood that the mantra is to be recited at the time of calling. Having thus restated the mantra as occurring at the time of calling, the word "thrice" is enjoined. Consequently, because the word "avaghnan" serves the purpose of indicating its own specific time, there is no statement of an improper meaning; therefore, the mantra is used according to its true sense. What is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? Because of the favor shown to the direct Vedic text (*śruti*), and because the act of calling is already established by the very form of the mantra, the agenthood in the preparation of the oblation (*haviṣkaraṇa*) belongs somehow to the one who is "threshing. Thus, there is an improper meaning [if taken literally]. Furthermore, there is a communication [of the meaning] through the connection with a secondary quality (*guṇa*).
No, because it is taught as a prescription for time. The Bhāṣya states: "It is not the case that this is taught with reference to the act of killing.
What then? It would be a designation of time.
Why? Because in the injunction "he recites three times," the triple recitation is prescribed by means of the mantra.
If the mantra were prescribed within this very sentence, the sentence would be split due to the prescription of multiple qualities.
Therefore, the connection is not "striking [the grain] in this manner."

How then? [It is said: "While threshing, he causes [the wife] to announce. But surely, on this view, both the mantra and the time are being enjoined; would that not result in the same fault? We say: no.

At the very time of threshing, the *haviṣkṛt* is summoned by means of the purpose; in that context, this very connection is restated, while the mere triple repetition is what is enjoined. As for the claim that the word has the purpose of indicating time, this is not a fault.

For indication (lakṣaṇā) is worldly; moreover, since the mantra is already obtained for the purpose of summoning by its very form, it too is merely restated. And the threshing, enjoined by another sentence, is capable of indicating the time.
Therefore, it is to be employed in the invocation.
Or rather: "Because of its being subordinate to the repetition of the three [mantras], no mantra is enjoined here;
furthermore, the suffix -śatṛ occurs in a sense of characterization (lakṣaṇa), and that which is already established is merely restated."
For in the case of the word "avaghnan" (beating), the agent, which is subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root, is understood as being connected with a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
because of the suffix *śatṛ* [prescribed] by the rule "lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.126). Therefore, there is no violation of the direct Vedic text (*śruti*).
Therefore, having restated all of this, it is "thrice" that is enjoined, and nothing else, because that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Furthermore, since the time is already established by its inherent fitness (*yogyatva*), it too is not enjoined;
rather, it is said that for this [act], the injunction consists merely in its being expressed (*abhidhāmātra*).
"Or that which arises from the third repetition of the practice;
when the practice has been prescribed, that time is here enjoined by implication. (The meaning is:
when the third repetition of the practice has occurred, that [time] is enjoined in this sentence by the means of valid cognition known as *arthāpatti*—presumption.)
And likewise, in the passage "the practice is lifelong" (2.4.11), the mutual relationship between time and practice as the basis for the injunction has been explained.
This is because of the absence of [other] qualities.
The Bhāṣya states: this is the sūtra following the word [in question].

(He states the grounds for doubt: Now, why does he not say that they thresh because of a quality? For the act of threshing produces the oblation; therefore, [the one who performs it] is the *haviṣkṛt* (oblation-maker).
What will be the result of this? Since the threshing is already established by the very form [of the word], the mantra will merely prescribe the threefold repetition.
Thus, there will be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
(The answer is stated: It is said in reply: Since there is an absence of the [necessary] quality (*guṇa*), a figurative designation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*) is not possible.
For a snake does not understand, "I am being called"; in that case, the calling would have to be directed toward the snake itself.
The invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* by the sacrificer’s wife serves a perceptible purpose;
therefore, the mantra [used] is "hanti" (he slays).

Or rather—regarding what was said, that the act of slaying itself will be the *haviṣkṛt*, it is replied: "Because of the absence of the subordinate quality (*guṇa*), there is an absence of the *haviṣkṛt* mantra when [the act of slaying] is mentioned."

(Since the unconscious act of threshing lacks the quality characterized by being the object of an address and so forth, there is an absence of the mantra that illuminates the *haviṣkṛt* [the preparer of the oblation]. Or rather, it may be based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the capacity for addressing and so forth.
Alternatively, this sūtra follows after the previous section:
"But because it refers to the repetition of the three [verses], no mantra is prescribed here."
It is said that [the word *haviṣkṛt*] refers to the deity because it is of the nature of form (*rūpa*). Even if you somehow imagine its status as the "maker of the oblation" (*haviṣkṛt*),
nevertheless, the term "he calls out" (*āhvayati*) in that mantra would be redundant.
The vocative case and the imperative mood constitute the middle [category].
In a mantra, all of this would be purposeless if it were intended solely for the act of threshing;
however, because the wife is insentient, it is meaningful [only] in relation to her.
Therefore, it is from the very form [of the word] that its status as an *avaghāta* (beating) follows;
and also because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The Bhāṣya states: "And there is an indicative mark: 'Speech indeed is the *haviṣkṛt*; he thus calls speech itself.'"
Furthermore, there is no similarity between speech and the lower millstone;
however, there is a similarity between the sacrificer and his wife,
for she is female, and "speech" (*vāk*) is a feminine noun.
"One who threshes is neither a woman, nor a man, nor a neuter.
But surely, there is also a feminine word for "threshing" that is used here? To this we reply:
The word for "threshing" (*avahanti*) is not necessarily feminine; it also exists in the masculine as *avaghātaḥ*, and in the neuter as *karma*.
Furthermore, there is a similarity between the wife (*patnī*) and the act of threshing in its essential form, while [the similarity] with the word is through its grammatical gender (*liṅga*).
Therefore, the gender of the wife is more appropriate [as a designation] for the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation).
Or rather—thus, the word "vāk" will be established as having a gender that is exclusively feminine in its meaning;
otherwise, since the word for action (kriyā) and so forth does not possess the feminine gender, how could it be conceived in any way as a property of the word characterized by a non-exclusive gender?
Therefore, [the conclusion is] "you are the one who summons."
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction of the injunction in the instruction.

The Bhāṣya says: "If the mantra were present during the threshing, there would be a contradiction with another injunction, namely: 'He threshes while reciting, "The Rakṣas is struck down,"' and 'He threshes while reciting, "The Yātudhānas are struck down.
In that case, because [the mantra] would be absent [on certain occasions], the scriptural statement which prescribes it as a constant rule would be obstructed."
Therefore, the term *avacana* has the sense of indicating time (*kālalakṣaṇārtha*).
Alternatively, there would be an improper contradiction with other mantras for threshing (*avaghāta*);
however, if it refers to the invocation (*āhvāna*), there is no such contradiction, as this [mantra] itself serves that purpose.
Śabara: According to the principle of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate in a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*).
However, for a mantra, its conformity with the actual facts (*tathyathārthatva*) does not incur any fault, because it is based on a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*).
Therefore, the mantra is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the act of threshing (*avaghāta*).

This being the position reached, it is replied: "Since repetition three times is not invariably established by the recitation—because in some places it is recited twice and in others once—it is therefore enjoined as a constant rule. It cannot be a contingent restatement (anuvāda), because that would contradict its status as a constant injunction."

Therefore, in this case, there is a threefold repetition; otherwise, if it were different, the injunction of the mantra would not be possible due to the consequence of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
However, while the mantra is connected to the act of summoning (*āhvāna*), the word "hanta" functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Therefore, because of the prescription of the threefold repetition, the mantra is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the invocation (*āhvāna*), and it does not have a meaning other than that [invocation] in the context of threshing (*avaghāta*).

Soma: But surely, since the invocation is also established as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the injunction would be one of a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*); how then can there be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)?

Nor should it be argued that the invocation is not to be enjoined because its purpose is already established by the fact that threshing is understood to be performed by the wife—based on the statement, "She stands near the *haviṣkṛt* and threshes"—and thus the invocation for the sake of threshing is already implied by the sense of the matter.

If it is argued that because the unstruck [sound] (anāhatā) may arrive spontaneously, there is no possibility of its being constantly obtained through summoning, and thus an injunction (vidhi) is possible— this is not so;
for the summoning is established as a constant requirement by the very wording of the mantra, "Come" (ehi).

As for what was stated in the *Nyāyasudhā*: "If it is accepted that [the deity] is obtained through the wording of the mantra, then there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the application of the mantra would depend on its obtaining the invitation, and the obtaining of the invitation would depend on the wording of the mantra."

Furthermore, even though the invocation (*āhvāna*) is already established by constant application, and the spreading (*prathana*) is established by the force of the name *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) despite being obtained through the syntactic requirement of the sentence "He spreads the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with [the mantra] 'Spread yourself wide,'" both are nevertheless subject to injunction here. This is for the sake of establishing that the spreading is performed by the Adhvaryu—thereby making possible the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "It is the sacrificer himself whom he thereby spreads"—and for the sake of making possible the explanatory passage "It is speech itself which he thereby invokes," which would otherwise be untenable if the Adhvaryu's agency were not established. Thus, their status as objects of injunction is necessary.
Therefore, it should be understood that the injunction is for the act of recitation (*japa*) as qualified by the repetition three times, rather than being an injunction regarding the time [of day].
(This is the first part, a paraphrase of the meaning of the *Sūtranayasudhā*’s statement: "It is not an injunction regarding time. In that regard:

Since it must be stated that the mantra containing the word ‘ehi’ (come), which is eternally recited, always assists in the ritual (*ṛtu*), and since that mantra lacks a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), its application to the rite is established through the power of the mantra’s own capacity; and because it is appropriate for the act of summoning (*āhvāna*)—which is obtained by reflecting on the mantra’s efficacy—to serve as the medium (*dvāra*), the connection of the mantra with that summoning, which serves as the medium, is established there by the very force of the mantra’s application to the rite. Thus, there is no room for the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, the fact that the summoning is to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest is established simply by the force of the mantra being recited in the *Adhvaryu-kāṇḍa*; otherwise, a separate injunction for the summoning for that purpose would be redundant.
As for the mantra "uru prathasva," its recitation is prescribed in the *Ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa*; however, this does not establish that the spreading [of the altar] must be performed by the Adhvaryu priest.
For even when another person recalls the purpose of the rite through a mantra recited by the Adhvaryu, it is possible for that other person to perform the spreading.

In the present case, however, because the word "ehi" (come) is employed, the act of summoning—being associated with the word "ehi" in a mantra recited by the Adhvaryu—is necessarily the duty of the Adhvaryu; thus, there is a difference [between the two cases].

Furthermore, since the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can somehow be made consistent even with the injunction of the mere triad of repetitions, there is no need to accept the injunction of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) for that purpose; thus, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) alone is appropriate (p.

213). Nor can it be argued that there is an inequality between the two positions—namely, that for the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), the term *avaghnat* (beating) involves figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereas for the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), it would fall on the inferior term *āhvayati* (invoking)—for such a distinction is untenable.

In the case of *avaghāta* (threshing), because the suffix *śatṛ*—prescribed for the agent of one action that indicates another action according to the rule "the suffix *śatṛ* is used after a verb when it indicates another action and is not used in the sense of a characteristic or a cause"—is understood to have the purpose of indicating another action, it is logical that the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) applies even to the word *avaghnan*, which is heard first and conveys its own primary meaning as a subordinate element.
The meaning of the Sūtra is: the invocation (*āhvāna*), and even the mantra used for the invocation, would likewise be non-literal (*ayathārtha*), just like the *aindrī* mantra.
Viśvarūpa states: "Having addressed the *haviṣkṛt* with the words 'Come, O preparer of the oblation,' one should say this three times while threshing."
The application [of the word *hanti*] would be either to the act of threshing or to the invocation for threshing;

otherwise, as in the case of the *aindrī* mantra, the term *hanti* would have to be used figuratively based on the mere presence of the mantra-text. For the threefold [repetition] obtained through the recitation is merely a figurative expression for the act of striking (*han-*).

Indeed, repetition should be prescribed for the three; likewise [for the others]. Application, syntactical split, and being subordinate to the invocation by virtue of indicative power—the logic of the *aindrī* mantra does not apply here because of the absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); rather, it proceeds primarily with the *bārhaspatya*.
Therefore, this mantra is for the purpose of summoning (*āhvāna*).
Regarding the section on summoning (Āhvānādhikaraṇa):
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, according to the Bhaṭṭa school, it is revealed in scripture: "O preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), come!—thus he strikes three times."

In this context, this mantra is not a subsidiary part of the invocation (*āhvāna*), because its non-existence [as such] is understood from the statement: "She approaches like a husband; she brings the gods hither.
Therefore, by means of the particle *iti*, it belongs specifically to the threshing (*avaghāta*).
Consequently, in this sentence, there is an injunction for the act of threshing qualified by the threefold repetition and the masculine mantra.
And in the case of the wife’s statement, there is an injunction for a separate ritual act based solely on its specific quality.

Regarding those two acts of threshing, although they are dependent upon the object to be refined by the rule "one threshes the rice-grains," there is an option between them because their purpose is visible.
Furthermore, in the act of threshing performed by the wife, the mantra "Avarakṣo divaḥ" is to be recited.
Therefore, by this statement, this mantra is enjoined for use specifically in the secondary sense (*gauṇa*) of threshing.
The demonstration of its secondary nature should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.

Regarding the manner of this secondary application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) even in the case of threshing, it is stated at the end of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the *Kaustubha*: "It should be understood by somehow attributing agency—as in the expression 'the pot cooks'—and by superimposing consciousness upon the insentient object, accepting the meaning: 'O threshing! Come, become fully accomplished.'"
And the statement "it is *āhvayati*" (he calls) is a restatement intended to indicate the capacity [of the mantra] for the meaning of calling, by means of the rule "tadādyaca" (Pāṇini 1.1.73).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since the application of the mantra is possible in its primary sense of calling, there is no evidence for assuming a figurative sense for either the mantra itself or the word *āhvayati*.

Furthermore, because the act of calling is necessarily established through the very act of taking up [the vessel], as indicated by the words "sadyāsam" and so forth, which prescribe the application based on the wording of the mantra.
However, the meaning of "patyeva" is not that [the mortar] itself stands up and does not call out; rather, it means "only by the husband (pati) and not by another.
Therefore, this does not indicate the absence of that [calling].

Consequently, since the mantra is already established for the purpose of calling by its very indicative power (*liṅga*), and since the act of calling occurs at the very time of threshing as an auxiliary to it, the term "threshing" (*avaghnan*) is also a restatement (*anuvāda*). Thus, only the tripling (*tribhyāsa*) is enjoined, and there is no application of the mantra to the secondary sense of threshing.
Maṇḍana: "The mantra 'O preparer of the oblation, come! does not involve the act of killing.
Śaṅkara: "The preparer of the oblation is indicated by the time [of the action].
As for the suffix -i (the *iñ* suffix), just as it is established in the sense of offspring, so too is it established in the sense of the agent of an action."
(Regarding the passage "Babara Prāvāhaṇi," etc. Bhāṣya on Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.23, p. 129.

The verbal root *ikṣ* is sometimes used even for the object, as in the cases of *yajir* and *yajatiḥ*. Therefore, it should be understood that when the word is expressed, the meaning is apprehended through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Vākyapadīya 2.1.12, p. 379. The maxim of the sugarcane stalk (*ikṣudaṇḍanyāya*).

Just as there is an excellence of flavor in every joint of a sugar-cane stalk, so too does the cultivation of friendliness gradually attain excellence. As it has been said: "Just as there is a specific excellence of flavor in every joint of a sugar-cane stalk, so it is with the cultivation of friendliness; however, for those who are the opposite, it is the opposite."
Thus [ends] the *Sāhasrī*, 324.
Om. The Principle of Sugarcane Juice (*ikṣurasanyāya*).
In products such as jaggery and sugar, different natures and characteristics are observed even though they are equally modifications of sugarcane;
it is the same elsewhere. Summary: This is the "Sugarcane Juice Principle" (ikṣurasanyāya).

Just as sugarcane juice, though abundant within, is seen to be extremely impure on the outside, so too Māyā, though possessing many forms internally, is seen externally to be of that very same nature; and that which is its most stainless form is like the sugar derived from sugarcane juice.

And just as the sweetness of sugarcane is manifested in sugar, whereas elsewhere it is less distinct due to contact with impurities, so too everything is manifested in the pure Sattva of supreme sovereignty.
(Sāhasrī 97)

Oṃ. The Principle of the Transformations of Sugarcane (*Ikṣuvikāranyāya*). Just as even among the transformations of sugarcane—such as juice, molasses, and sugar—their distinct forms are seen solely due to the varying degrees of the removal of impurity, so too should it be understood regarding *sattva* and the other qualities.
*Sāhasrī*.
Desire (*icchā*). For desire is the longing for an object previously experienced;
it is *bṛhatī*, p. 164.
Desire arises spontaneously toward human goals such as heaven, sons, cattle, and so forth.
For desire occurs only toward an intended object that has been previously experienced (Su. p. 31).
Just as there is not a repeated desire for those sweet tree fruits to the north of Mount Mera which have never before been perceived by us,
nor indeed does a desire arise in one perceiver for an object perceived by another person; yet,
there does arise on another day a desire for what was perceived by someone else.
Bhāṣya 2.1.15, p. 63: "We perceive the self through desire" (the meaning is that the self is perceived by means of the mark of desire).
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 2.1.15, page 63:
"Desire has as its cause the ascertainment of its respective causal factors" (Maṇi, page 28).

Therefore, another means of knowledge must be sought for these—either another scriptural passage or a logical principle (*nyāya*). In the absence of such a means, that [statement] becomes like the sight of a mirage.

However, the application of two designations occurs based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and formal designation (*vyapadeśa*). The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: the word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position.

The application of the two collective terms—namely, these two designations, ‘paurṇamāsī’ and ‘amāvāsyā’—is to distinct groups.

The word *indra* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for the *gārhapatya* fire either because of its similarity in being a means of accomplishing sacrifice, or because of its sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Bhāṣya 2.2.14: because the word *indra* denotes sovereignty.
A single action—namely, *yajati* (sacrifices), *dadāti* (gives), and *juhoti* (offers)—is like a rainbow, not mentioned by the three grammatical roots (*dhātu*).
(This is the prima facie view.
Vārttika 2.1.1, p. 463.
Just as a rainbow (indrāyudha) appears through the combination of the three elements—red, white, and black—so it is here.
The sacrifice to Indra and Soma (aindrāsomīya) is a modification (vikṛti) of the sacrifice to Indra alone (aindra), because it has Indra as its primary face.
A sense-faculty (*indriya*) is that which makes known; it makes known an object in proximity to itself by its mere existence.
*Ke*: A sense-faculty, such as the eye and so forth, is indeed nothing other than each respective substratum (*pratyadhiṣṭhāna*).

And that [perception] is distinct from other means of knowledge, such as the ocular (taijasa) and so forth; this is the view of the Bhaṭṭas (Bhāṭṭa 9.1.10). A sense organ produces cognition only with respect to an object that is in immediate proximity.
Straightforward. Page 204: The sense organs are capable of self-experience.

"Oṃ! By the two senses, the tongue and the genitals, the entire world is indeed destroyed—alas, from Brahmā down to the smallest insect! This is the maxim.
The sense is that this entire world, including all insentient things and living beings, has been led solely toward the pursuit of the enjoyment of sense objects by beginningless ignorance.

[The term] *sāhasrī* [is used] because the sense organ (*indriya*) is the cause for perception in all cases. *Maṇi*, p. 19: "For one desiring sense power, one should offer the *agnihotra* with curd; whoever should desire sense power, he should perform the oblation with curd.
