Su. P. 855: Regarding the *indriyakāmahoma* (the oblation for one desiring sensory power), since a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) cannot be a means to a result without a substratum (*āśraya*), and since there is no evidence for the oblation—though understood through the context—to serve as that substratum in the absence of an explicit injunction, the very form of the oblation understood from the context becomes established as the substratum by means of an injunction extended by the "inconsistency" (*anupapatti*) of the injunction enjoining the connection between the subordinate factor and the result. Thus, the sentence "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) alone is taken [as the basis]. And this has been refuted.
Moreover: "The curd is a qualification of that oblation in the tenth alternative;
and since it is also [required] for one desiring sensory power, it is not thereby determined [as the sole means]."
(Regarding the ten substances in the *sudhāyyā* [oblation]: "Milk, curd, sugarcane juice, ghee, honey, soma, meat, as well as oil, and water—these indeed are the ten.")

Thus, even if curds and the other substances were to be combined permanently in the oblation, then—even though the ritual action is diverse—it might somehow be conceived as being enjoined by the mention of a single part.
However, since curds and the others are optional, each one individually possesses the status of being an accessory to the oblation according to the tenth alternative.
Therefore, even when the sentence concerning curds is examined, curds are seen to be only optional.
Furthermore, that [offering] is heard of as being permanent in the context of the *indriyakāma-homa*;
therefore, for this reason as well, it is not recognized [as the same act].
Nor can it be restated by the words "when one should offer with curd," because the result is not something to be enjoined.
For this is the mode of expression here: "If one desires sense-faculties, then one should perform the oblation constantly, characterized solely by curd.
And since such a [rule] is not obtained from any other source, it is distinct.

Now, it has indeed been asserted that the measure of the oblation (*homa*) is the same; and from the conviction regarding that [measure], non-difference is established. That substance which is not recognized [as being the same] does not serve as a cause for the difference of the ritual action (*karma*).
Therefore, it is that very same ritual action which is enjoined for the sake of the fruit, with the addition of a mere accessory (*guṇa*).
This is not so.
Why? Because "the injunction of a single purpose regarding an action already established was previously refuted;
moreover, in your view, the contingency of an injunction for multiple [purposes] would follow here."
"A sentence that prescribes both the connection between the curd and the oblation and the connection between the oblation and its fruit would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) must necessarily be accepted.
Consequently, it is established that this is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*)."

Just as, when by implication there is the possibility of using various indefinite substances, the restriction to *dadhi* alone is established— thereby postulating an optional nature of the substance because it excludes the application of injunctions for rice and so forth— and since that [use of *dadhi*] is not obtained from this sentence in any way whatsoever, there is the status of a separate action (*karmāntaratva*) resulting in a fruit from the *homa*.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is adopted:
"Even though there is a word for a quality here, it is the action that is enjoined more extensively;
for a fruit is heard in this context, and [the status of] being an action is appropriate."
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that every word denoting an entity (*bhāvārtha*) is the locus [of the injunction].
For it is established therein that words consisting of verbal roots (*ākhyāta*) are connected with the word denoting the fruit, not words denoting substances (*dravya*) or qualities (*guṇa*).
Therefore, because the fruit is connected with action, when there is a mention of the fruit—
An action is enjoined when it is [otherwise] absent; a subordinate element (guṇa) is not enjoined in respect to an action that is already established.
How so? "Because it is already established, the subordinate element does not require a further injunction.
Even under the view that there is an injunction for what was not previously established, the mention of a result would be purposeless."

In this case, while there is indeed a word for an action (*karmaśabda*) that lacks a specific quality (*aguṇa*), a quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined; yet that quality does not exist [independently] where it would apply, nor is any other distinct object (*arthāntara*) heard in the text.
Furthermore, even a substance (*dravya*) is not present here, because curd (*dadhi*) is already established by another sentence, and because an additional result (*phala*) is being prescribed.
Therefore, he says: "A result is heard here, and it is logical that it belongs to the action."

In this regard, regarding the question, "Is the fruit of action indeed seen?", there are two ways in which it appears: as a division of sentences and as a single sentence. Among these, he first considers the position of the division of sentences: "First, we say 'no'; for this is not established by this visible [fruit]," and so on. Following the shadow of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) because it is intent upon refutation, the question is only this much: "What?"—the meaning being, "Is it reasonable that [the fruit] is 'what' [i.e., uncertain]? The other says: "For the fruit of action is indeed seen [as rice and so forth from plowing and so forth]."
To this, we reply: "No.
The commentary from "If" onwards refutes [the objection] by raising the doubt itself, up until the point where it concludes: "Therefore, this does not apply to such cases.

(Having thus refuted the position that there is a split in the sentence, he introduces the position of syntactic unity: In that case (in what follows), how then can the fruit be rightly derived from the oblation? Such is the definitive question of the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*).
And since that [conclusion] appears ill-connected immediately after the summary of his own words, this alternative construction is appropriate.

(In this view, he applies the Bhāṣya: When the proponent of the prima facie view has stated, "And that [result] is logically connected to the ritual action," the proponent of the established conclusion, fearing the meaninglessness of the word *dadhi* (curd) and considering the word to be incapable [of denoting a result] because the principle of the section on "actions whose purpose is to bring about an entity" (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*) does not apply here, asks: "For is the fruit of a ritual action seen [in the world], such as from plowing and so forth? By this logic of general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), he implies that you consider the fruit to arise from the oblation (*homa*).

Although it has been established that inference and the other means of knowledge lack the capacity for such [matters] because Dharma is accepted as being defined solely by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), nevertheless, since their status as causes for determining the meaning of the Vedas has not been denied, inference is presented here for the purpose of determining that meaning. However, the opponent—whose mind is still permeated by the arguments of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (the section on the meaning of the verbal root)—objects and says: "Do not impose such a misconception upon me; I am certainly not saying that there is inference when the Word exists.
Nor is what we do not accept established by this 'inference from general observation' (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*), for it is unproven (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."
Because inference is vitiated by faults such as contradiction (*viruddha*) and others.

How so? If it is stated, "The *homa* sacrifice possesses a fruit, because its possession of a fruit is observed," then it is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it falls short of the intended meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

If, on the other hand, it is stated, "because the possession of a fruit is observed in the case of agriculture and the like," then it lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).

Now, if it were to be postulated merely by its shadow, even without the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), that would be indistinguishable in the case of substances.

Or, if it were to be postulated through analogy (*upamā*) by way of similarity, that similarity exists between the oblation and agriculture and so forth in terms of their nature as actions—resulting in the increase of fruit—but not in the case of a substance, because a substance is non-actional in nature.

Thus, having considered that even in this case there exists some degree of similarity between the substance (*dravya*) and [the *kūpa*], if that [similarity] is rejected on account of a more proximate intermediate similarity, then one might likewise reject the *homa* by reference to something even more proximate. Thinking thus, he says: "The *homa* is also dissimilar to the *kūpa*, because of the difference in the nature of the means (*sādhana*), the form (*svarūpa*), and the result (*phala*). Now, if some slight similarity is admitted, that same [similarity] exists in the case of the substance as well; for it is not eternal, since it possesses distinct properties such as being a substance (*dravyatva*) and being an effect (*kārya*). This is the explanation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Now, since similarity is relative, if something else exists that is more similar than a substance, then when that [more similar thing] is taken into account, the [substance] becomes clearly remote [in its degree of similarity].

Therefore, when actionhood (*kriyātva*) is considered in relation to plowing and the oblation (*homa*), because it is remote, the substance—though endowed with qualities such as being existent and non-eternal—is said to be dissimilar.

This being so, even though both are actions, there is a requirement for a consideration of intermediate similarity between plowing and the oblation on the one hand, and eating for the sake of curd and going on the other.
Because of the great distance [between them], there would be no similarity at all, and thus it would be without a cause.
And it has been said: "In this case, no supreme similarity is observed between plowing and the fire-oblation;
because some slight similarity is seen even in other substances, there is no certainty."

Nor is this established; for it has been stated that the attainment of all properties—whether by means of analogy (*upamāna*), which measures mere similarity, or by inference (*anumāna*)—is not independent of the logical pervader (*vyāpaka*) as explained, because it would lead to the absurdity (*prasaṅga*) of all things being names.

Thus it has been said (ŚBh 11.2.12, p. 17): "Indeed, Devadatta’s dark complexion does not necessarily entail Yajñadatta’s dark complexion. Likewise: "Having seen the possession of a dewlap and so forth in a cow similar to a gavaya, the [properties] such as the fruit [of the sacrifice] do not undergo modification in the original [rituals]."

"If that which has been observed as the cause in the established instance (dṛṣṭāntadharmin) is understood to be likewise the cause in the subject (sādhya-pakṣa), then it is indeed a prover of that [subject]. From this statement, some conclude that the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is that the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer exists only between effect and cause.
However, that is incorrect.

For it is well established that even among properties that do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship— such as impermanence and being produced— the relationship of indicator and indicated exists.
Furthermore, even between cause and effect, the cause does not indicate [the effect] in the same way that the effect indicates it, because the cause can exist in a state where there is deviation.

Therefore, it should be understood that the logical mark (*liṅga*) itself—when observed as the pervaded (*vyāpya*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and being apprehended for the sake of conceiving the possibility of its being a means of cognition (*gamaka*) for the pervader (*vyāpaka*), which elsewhere constitutes the probandum (*sādhya*)—is what is called the "cause" (*kāraṇa*).
This has been explained in the section on the reason (*hetu*).

And thus Viṣṇu [the author of the Nyāyabhūṣaṇa] clarifies: "Therefore, even that which is similar [to the reason] must be examined as to whether it is a prover (*sādhaka*) or a non-prover (*asādhaka*)."
If, then, this effect is stated on the basis of a cause that has been examined and asserted— namely,

by inferring in the sentence "for one desiring sense-organs" (*indriyakāmasya*) that "this action possesses a fruit, because it is an action, like plowing and so forth," or "this fruit is achievable through action, because it is a fruit, like rice and so forth"— and then [the opponent] renders this inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by stating a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*),
namely: "When the action has ceased, another substance such as a cloth is seen to be the fruit of substances such as threads and their conjunctions."
The mention of "cessation" (*uparata*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction from ritual action (*karman*).
For it might be suspected that even here [in the Veda], one might state that the fruit has action alone as its cause.

Therefore, he says: in the sentence concerning the desire for sensory power (*indriyakāma*), "curd possesses a fruit because it is a substance, like a thread; or rather, sensory power is produced by a substance, because it is a fruit, like a cloth."

Furthermore, he states that [the reason] "because agriculture does not fail" is contradictory (*viruddhatva*). For in this very way, this reason establishes either that action possesses a fruit or that the fruit is produced by action; likewise, it establishes either that the fruit has a visible purpose or that the fruit is a dissimilar indicator. Therefore, since all possible faults of a logical reason would apply to such a relationship of cause and effect, this [reasoning] does not hold in any case. How then is it said that a proper fruit arises from the *homa*? It is explained as follows: [The opponent asks: "But how can there be a proper fruit from the *homa*, given that the *homa* is imperceptible (*parokṣa*)? [The author replies: This is not so. Even though the *homa* is imperceptible, its fruit is perceived through inference (*anumāna*). Just as the existence of fire is inferred from smoke, so too is the existence of the fruit inferred from the *homa*. Furthermore, the *homa* is not like agriculture, for it is not dependent on external factors such as rain and the like. Moreover, the *homa* is not like a seed, for it does not produce a fruit after a long interval. Rather, the *homa* is like a sacrifice (*yajña*), which produces its fruit immediately upon completion. Therefore, because the *homa* is similar to a sacrifice, it is established that a proper fruit arises from it. Thus, the objection that the reason is contradictory is refuted. Consequently, the statement "because agriculture does not fail" is not a valid reason. This concludes the section on the contradiction of the reason. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "If the *homa* is imperceptible, then its fruit must also be imperceptible. [The author replies: This is not so. Even if the *homa* is imperceptible, its fruit is perceptible. For example, when one performs a *homa* with the desire for wealth, wealth is indeed perceived. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished. This concludes the section on non-establishment. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-conclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "Even if the *homa* is performed, the fruit may not arise due to obstacles such as sins. [The author replies: This is not so. If the *homa* is performed correctly, the fruit necessarily arises. For example, when a seed is sown in a field free of obstacles, the sprout necessarily arises. Similarly, when the *homa* is performed correctly, the fruit necessarily arises. Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive. This concludes the section on non-conclusiveness. Now, the following is stated regarding the contradiction (*viruddhatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "If the *homa* were to produce a fruit, it would contradict the scriptural injunctions regarding the exhaustion of merit. [The author replies: This is not so. The scriptural injunctions regarding the exhaustion of merit refer to the exhaustion of the merit of previous actions, whereas the fruit of the *homa* is a distinct result. Therefore, there is no contradiction. This concludes the section on contradiction. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-eternal nature of the relationship between cause and effect. [The opponent says: "If the *homa* is impermanent, then its fruit must also be impermanent. [The author replies: This is not so. Even if the *homa* is impermanent, its fruit is eternal. For example, although the sun is impermanent, its light is eternal. Similarly, although the *homa* is impermanent, its fruit is eternal. Therefore, the reason is not contradictory. This concludes the section on the non-eternal nature of the relationship between cause and effect. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-perception of the relationship between cause and effect. [The opponent says: "Since the relationship between the *homa* and its fruit is not perceived, the reason is unestablished. [The author replies: This is not so. Although the relationship is not perceived by the senses, it is established through inference. For example, the relationship between fire and smoke is not perceived by the senses, yet it is established through inference. Similarly, the relationship between the *homa* and its fruit is established through inference. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished. This concludes the section on the non-perception of the relationship between cause and effect. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-existence of the relationship between cause and effect. [The opponent says: "Since the *homa* and its fruit do not exist simultaneously, there is no relationship between them. [The author replies: This is not so. Even if they do not exist simultaneously, a causal relationship is possible. For example, the relationship between a seed and a sprout exists even though they do not exist simultaneously. Similarly, the relationship between the *homa* and its fruit exists even though they do not exist simultaneously. Therefore, the reason is not contradictory. This concludes the section on the non-existence of the relationship between cause and effect. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-universality (*avyāpti*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason 'because agriculture does not fail' is not universal, as it does not apply to all actions. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason applies to all actions that are intended to produce a visible fruit. Therefore, the reason is not non-universal. This concludes the section on non-universality. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-relevance (*aprāptakālatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is irrelevant because it is stated at the wrong time. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason is relevant because it serves to establish the conclusion. Therefore, the reason is not irrelevant. This concludes the section on non-relevance. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-finality (*anigrahasthānatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is not final because it does not lead to a definitive conclusion. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason leads to a definitive conclusion through the process of inference. Therefore, the reason is not non-final. This concludes the section on non-finality. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-definitiveness (*aniścayatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is not definitive because it allows for doubt. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason removes doubt by providing certainty. Therefore, the reason is not non-definitive. This concludes the section on non-definitiveness. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-validity (*apramāṇatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is invalid because it lacks a basis in scripture. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason is valid because it is supported by logical inference. Therefore, the reason is not invalid. This concludes the section on non-validity. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-usefulness (*anupayogitva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is useless because it does not contribute to the understanding of the subject. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason contributes to the understanding of the subject by clarifying the relationship between cause and effect. Therefore, the reason is not useless. This concludes the section on non-usefulness. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-completeness (*asampūrṇatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is incomplete because it lacks certain elements. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason is complete because it contains all necessary components. Therefore, the reason is not incomplete. This concludes the section on non-completeness. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-coherence (*asaṅgatitva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is incoherent because it contradicts other statements. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason is coherent because it is consistent with the overall argument. Therefore, the reason is not incoherent. This concludes the section on non-coherence. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-clarity (*asphuṭatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is unclear because it is expressed in ambiguous language. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason is clear because it is expressed in precise terminology. Therefore, the reason is not unclear. This concludes the section on non-clarity. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-brevity (*adīrghatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is too long because it is unnecessarily verbose. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason is concise because it expresses the essential meaning without redundancy. Therefore, the reason is not too long. This concludes the section on non-brevity. Now, the following is stated regarding the non-elegance (*arucitatva*) of the reason. [The opponent says: "The reason is unattractive because it lacks aesthetic appeal. [The author replies: This is not so. The reason is elegant because it is logically sound and pleasing to the intellect
Alternatively, the question ends precisely with the particle *iti*.
The answer is conveyed by the word "it is said" (*ucyate*), which refers to that fruit, as established by the introduction of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (the section on the meaning of verbal roots).
Therefore, it is logical that the fruit results from the oblation (*homa*).

And as for the statement "the curd is the fruit," which is stated even though its meaning is already established as improper—that is for the purpose of refuting the notion that [the two options] possess equal strength.
For at some point, even the curd might be considered proper;
moreover, the curd would be incapable of accomplishing both purposes.
To begin with, curd cannot possess causality independently of an action, such that it could be connected solely with the result.
Therefore, [the action] must be enjoined in both cases; yet that is not possible. [Objection:

But is it not like the case of a blanket and a person? This is said with the intention of referring to a connection with an incidental action, for the purpose of refuting the incapacity of the thing itself.
Or rather, it is seen that by the opponent's statement—taken as it was heard—that "curd is capable of both," it is in fact the capacity of the thing itself that has been stated.
We do not say that it is improper for one thing to have two purposes;

nor do we intend to deny the capacity of the thing. Rather, even though the thing is capable, since its performance has not been so enjoined [otherwise], curd must necessarily be enjoined as serving both purposes.

But this is not the case, because establishing multiple relationships would result in the fallacy of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). When a proximate possibility exists, a remote meaning is enjoined;

thus, here, since the proximity of curd to the oblation exists while the connection of curd with the fruit is remote, if both were enjoined simultaneously, one would have to accept both possibility and impossibility at once.

Therefore, when one of the two must be abandoned and the attainment of the result [of the sacrifice] is possible through its abandonment, even curd (*dadhi*) is connected with the oblation (*homa*) due to its proximity; that [oblation] is also connected with the result. Thus, when the result is joined with the ritual act, the status of it being a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is established.
"But because of the inequality of the two sentences, it is understood as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of that [act].
Commentary (*bhāṣya*): The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that the previous position is reversed.
It is not a separate action, but rather the fruit arises from a subordinate quality (guṇa). How so? Because these two sentences are not equivalent.

In the case of "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the fruit is expressed in grammatical coordination with the action: "One desiring heaven should bring about [the result] by means of the oblation."
The statement, "One desiring sensory power should offer with curd," expresses a connection with a subordinate element (guṇa).
For here it is not understood that the oblation is to be performed for the sake of sensory power;
rather, it is that the oblation is to be performed with curd by one who desires sensory power.
The connection of the oblation with curd is for the sake of [attaining] sensory power; it is not the origination of the oblation itself.
"Whoever should desire sensory power, he should perform the oblation with curd"—what word here expresses the human effort? We say: the word "juhuyāt" (he should sacrifice).

But surely, by direct statement (*śruti*), it expresses the human effort as being connected only with the oblation (*homa*), while by syntactical connection (*vākya*), it expresses its connection with the curd (*dadhi*). Nor can syntactical connection override direct statement.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the simultaneous connection with both, for the sentence would indeed express it in that way.
To this it is replied:
those who would adopt this position of yours would subvert the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
In our position, however, only the meaning of the verbal root—namely, "one should sacrifice"—is subverted.
In your view, however, the word [denoting the fruit] arises from the *kratu* itself, as if from curdled milk (*dadhi*). And it is understood that they recite this without making it authoritative;

for it has been stated that "this does not extend [the application]," as in the sūtra: "For the traditional transmission is equal" (1.2.18; the reading there is *tulyaṃ ca*). Therefore, the fruit is not mentioned in grammatical coordination with the ritual action (*karman*).
But when [the verb] is mentioned in conjunction with a quality (*guṇa*), there is no possibility of error whatsoever.

For it must necessarily be stated that "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*) for the purpose of enjoining the relationship between the curd (*dadhi*) and the one desiring sense-faculties (*indriyakāma*).
Now, even if it were so stated, the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) would not be understood in isolation; nor is there any purpose in stating it in isolation.
And that [action] is connected with the oblation; therefore, it is repeated. We say: no.

Even though it is connected with the oblation, it is still the very meaning of "doing" (*karoti*); there is merely a distinction regarding its connection with the oblation, but it does not sublate the meaning of "doing. For one who desires sensory power, [the injunction means]: "One should perform the effort connected with the oblation and connected with the curd."
But if this is so, does it not follow that this fault arises: namely, that the fruit is obtained as connected with the oblation?
It is replied: the capacity of the word "juhuyāt" (one should sacrifice) is such that it expresses an effort qualified by the oblation.
However, the oblation (homa) is not enjoined here as a means;
rather, it is understood from the sentence that a specific effort, characterized as the end to be achieved, is based upon the curd (dadhi).

For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti stated: "The accessory (guṇa), being based on the oblation, will accomplish the fruit, just as a king's servant, depending on the king, performs the king's work."

Therefore, the result arises from the curd: "He who desires sensory power should produce sensory power by means of curd. How so? By this procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belonging to the Agnihotra. Why is this so? Because the curd, as the means of accomplishing the result, stands in need of a procedure.
And because this procedure is in close proximity, and because the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice), which is the indicative mark of the injunction, is observed;
and precisely because this meaning of *juhoti* is a restatement (*anuvāda*), it must therefore be injunctive.
Nor is there any other injunction for the *homa*.
Therefore, it is not a separate ritual act;

Or rather—this is supported by those [passages] in which it has been established in the *Bhāṣya-artha-adhikaraṇa* that the result arises from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in external sentences.
How so? "For as long as the capacity of the injunction remains unexhausted, it is drawn toward the meaning of the verbal root."
That connection with the fruit would belong to the meaning of the verbal root, as it is understood.
But when there is an injunction regarding the connection of a quality, the mention of a fruit that occurs therein is touched by that very injunction; therefore, it attains syntactic unity with it.
The status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) of the *bhāvanā* itself transfers to various elements according to their respective purposes.

For example, when the fruitful *bhāvanā*—which has transferred its focus to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—attains that end, it then makes the meaning of the root the instrument (*karaṇa*), while everything else becomes subservient to that purpose.
And this [transfer] does not occur in cases such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*," because there the name (*nāman*) is capable of displacing the injunctive force.
In this case, however, because the word "curd" (*dadhi*) lacks the characteristic of being a name for anything else, it must necessarily be enjoined;
thus, its injunctive force falls upon the meaning of the verbal root.

Consequently, when the fruit is perceived in a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) that restates the meaning of the root as required, it is determined that the curd is the instrument (*sādhana*) of that [operation], not that the oblation (*homa*) is the instrument.
For it is not possible for things that are not being enjoined to possess the status of a means (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, it has been stated (at 2.1.16) that when there is the introduction of another thing to be enjoined, it is not logical to enjoin a matter that has already passed.

And just as there is no injunction of the *homa* because the injunction is implied by the word "curd" (*dadhi*), so too, due to the consideration of the word denoting the result (*phala-pada*), there is no injunction of curd with respect to the *homa*; rather, [the injunction applies] to the productive activity toward the result (*phala-bhāvanā*).

"Therefore, [the question arises: 'What is the fruit of the curd? Which word here expresses the human effort? Since the words "curd" (*dadhi*) and "fruit" (*phala*) cannot directly be the objects of an injunction because they consist of the nature of *bhāvanā* (productive activity), and since the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) must be expected [to express the effort], and because the application [of the effort] depends upon that [suffix] (as per *PMS* 2.1.14), one who considers that the root-meaning must therefore be abandoned in favor of the fruit asks this question.

The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*), however, distinguishing between the fact that the meaning of the suffix is what is enjoined and the fact that the root-meaning is merely restated (*anuvāda*), says: "One should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*).
"Now, is this not the opponent's own intention, clarifying that this connection with the oblation is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)?

How so? "There would be the prescription of many meanings when the prescription of a few meanings is possible;

When a minor noble injunction (*āryavidhi*) is possible, it prescribes only that much and disregards an injunction involving great effort.

Furthermore, since the oblation (*homa*) serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) toward the result, when the relationship [of the curd] with the established injunction—"One should effect the sense-power (*indriya*) by means of the oblation"—is untenable because of the equality [of status] with the curd acting as the instrument, one must necessarily resort to a possessive indication (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*), namely: "by means of an oblation characterized by curd (*dadhimat*)."
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for that [quality].
Nor is it possible for the word "curd" (dadhi) to function as the name of an action (karma-nāmadheya) in the absence of a basis for its application (pravṛtti-nimitta).
Thus, this word "curd," deprived of both [possibilities], would result in being entirely meaningless.

And thus, because the word "dharma" (in *dharmya*) is sublated by the acceptance of the soldiers (*sainika*), the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) regarding the meaning of the verbal root is set aside; for in the alternative view that it refers to the quality (*guṇa*), there would be no sublation of anything. To avoid that [objection], he says: "It must necessarily be stated that 'one should offer oblation'.

How so? "The connection between curd and the sense-faculty cannot exist without the cognition of a productive operation (bhāvanā). Nor is it possible for this [curd] to be uttered by any verbal root without [the mention of] an object."
Because it possesses the nature of being a suffix (*pratyaya*), it must necessarily be uttered to enjoin a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) qualified by curd and the sense organ.
And since that [suffix] cannot occur in isolation, and because it is untenable for it to be conceived apart from a verbal root (*dhātu*), it must be uttered following some verbal root.
Consequently, when any verbal root might have been adopted, the adoption of the *homā* (oblation) obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) was accepted.
Furthermore, its connection with curds—which consists of the relationship between substrate and superstratum—is obtained through the context itself and is thus merely restated.

And just as it will be explained (1.1.14) that the case-ending does not have number alone as its sole purpose, but rather, when uttered for the sake of conveying the mere grammatical relation (*kāraka*) in words such as *mahān* and so on, it causes the number to be understood as unintended due to its inseparability; likewise, here too, the verbal root, when uttered for the sake of favoring the suffix, causes its own meaning to be conveyed despite being unintended, because it must be articulated.

For it cannot be said that its sole purpose is merely the communication of meaning. VI. 3.4.17: Regarding the injunction for the laying of bricks (*iṣṭakopadhānavidhi*): "In the context of reciting the mantras obtained from the section beginning with ‘The vital breath (*prāṇa*) of that [fire-altar] which is present before is the Bhautrāyaṇa,’ one says, ‘He lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks.
By the word *prāṇabhṛt*, the bricks are indicated through the medium of the mantras. VI. 3.4.18: The *iṣṭi* sacrifice is preceded by the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*).

VI. 6.5. Because of its connection with the commencement [of the sacrifice], the *ārambhaṇīyā* offering—which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*)—is excluded from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites that are subsidiaries of the Soma sacrifice, since the commencement belongs to the principal (*pradhāna*). The *ārambhaṇīyā* is not to be performed for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites.
Because of the connection with the commencement (*ārambha*).

From the text, "One who is about to commence the *darśapūrṇamāsa*," it is understood that the sacrifice is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* by way of its commencement; however, there is no such commencement for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites occurring in the midst of the Soma performance.
Commencement, indeed, is the first action directed toward the primary rite (*pradhāna*).

Primacy in the performance (*kṛti*) consists in being a performance belonging to its own class (*svasajātīyakṛtitva*), occurring at the time of the injunction’s execution (*vidhānakaraṇakālavṛttitva*).
This "belonging to the same class" occurs either directly or through a lineage (*sākṣāt paramparayā vā*), such as by way of being a *nodeyyaka* (one who does not give).
Therefore, such an initiation (*ārambha*) does not exist in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.

Because that [Dīkṣaṇīyā] is not known as a Jyotiṣṭoma, it is merely an *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering); and that commencement (*ārambha*) is connected with the primary rite (*pradhāna*), since the commencement is joined with the primary.
Since such a commencement is absent in the Dīkṣaṇīyā—which is itself a subsidiary (*aṅga*)—the *Ārambhaṇīyā* is excluded from the subsidiary Dīkṣaṇīyā due to the loss of its occasion (*dvāralopa*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *Ārambhaṇīyā* is set aside in the case of the Dīkṣaṇīyā and similar rites.
The *iṣṭi* is a sacrifice (*yāga*);
that same [sacrifice], when augmented by the act of pouring (*āsecanādhika*), is a *homa*.
Bhāṣya 6.8.17: The *iṣṭis* include the *adhvarakalpā*, the *sarvapṛṣṭhā*, the *mṛgārā*, the *sumanā*, and so forth.
Sūtra 1.1.4.23: The *iṣṭis* do not exist for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).
Bhāṣya 6.8.12: The *iṣṭis* are those such as "One desiring progeny should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," and others like them.
In that case, the procedure belongs specifically to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, not to the Soma sacrifices, nor is there an option between the two.
(8.1.4.19). The optional *iṣṭi*s, which are modifications (*vikṛti*), consist of eleven potsherds;
the archetype (*prakṛti*), however, is the Darśapūrṇamāsa and so forth.

Vi. 1.2.13: The *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices (*paśus*), and optional *soma* sacrifices are not to be performed according to the order of the text; they may be performed according to one’s desire. Bhā. 5.3.1.22–36: The *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices can also be performed even prior to the performance of the *agniṣṭoma*. Vi. 5.3.14: Even though the modified (*vaikṛta*) *iṣṭis* have the same time as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, they do not depend upon the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
And there is no contingency of simultaneity.
Bhāṣya 1.2.1.15:
because the *iṣṭis*—that is, the optional *iṣṭis*—are the principal elements, there is no remainder left unperformed.

There is an omission of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiatory offering) in the case of an *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice) when the deceased is the performer. Regarding the *iṣṭis*—whether optional, obligatory, or consisting of archetypes (*prakṛti*) and modifications (*vikṛti*)—their performance occurs only on the festival days (*parvan*), because it has been stated: "He who sacrifices with an *iṣṭi*, with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma, [sacrifices] on the new moon day or the full moon day."
VI. 1.2.12: Regarding the performance of *iṣṭis*—whether optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not the restrictive factor;
rather, it is either the desire (*kāma*) or the occasion (*nimitta*) that serves as the restrictive factor.

5|3|12. In the *iṣṭis*, the following are the indicative marks (*liṅgas*) that serve as bases for extension (*atideśa*): 1) the designation of the deity by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*); 2) having a single deity; 3) having two deities; 4) having an herb as its substance; 5) having clarified butter (*ājya*) as its substance; 6) having milk (*payas*) as its substance; 7) having curd (*dadhi*) as its substance; 8) having a substance that is frothy and clear (*unmīlaviśada*); 9) having a substance produced from the five [products of the cow] (*pañcaprabhava*); and 10) the presence of the *nirvapati*-mantra. These are stated in the eighth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*].

Vāla-pu. 119: Even in the case of *iṣṭis* that lack specific indicative marks (*aliṅga*), such as those [other than] the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the application of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* injunction is established—just like the "grain from the cooking pot" (*sthālīpulāka*) example.

Furthermore, this is established by injunction preceded by reasoning (*nyāya*); and that reasoning is the same for all modified rites (*vaikṛta-karman*), whether they possess indicative marks (*liṅgavat*) or lack them.
Bhāṣya 7.1.4.12: In *iṣṭis* such as the *aindrāgna* and others, there occurs a connection with the indicative marks of the archetypal form (*prakṛti*), namely the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

What, then, is that indicative mark of the original nature (*prakṛtiliṅga*)? It is the instruction regarding the deity through a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the possession of eleven potsherds (*kapālavattā*), and the word "he offers" (*nirvapati*). For example: "One should offer an eleven-potsherd cake to Indra and Agni," and "An eleven-potsherd cake for Indra and Agni. According to the principle stated in [Mīmāṃsā Sūtra] 8.1.4.11, "The application of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) occurs in the case of the *iṣṭis*," the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that the fruit, the restrictive rule, the agent, and the collection [of subsidiaries] belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices are applied to the *saurya* and other such offerings.
Bhāṣya 8.1.3.10: There should be the application of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [rites] to the *iṣṭis*.
In *iṣṭis* such as "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Agni," there should be the application of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

For in the injunction, there is a connection with the characteristics of the archetype (*prakṛti*) through the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the instruction of the deity, the possession of potsherds, and the word "nirvapati" (he offers).
In the archetype (prakṛti), it is stated: "An eight-potherd cake for Agni," and "He pours out the oblations with the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle.
However, in this [ectypal] case, it says: "One should pour out an eleven-potherd cake for Indra-Agni.

Regarding the solar sacrifice (*saurya*), there are the indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as: "One should pour out a pap (*caru*) for Sūrya" and "Generally, one offers a *kṛṣṇala* berry at the *prayāja* offerings."
Even in the case of those [rites] that lack specific indicative marks (*aliṅga*), the proof is established by the analogy of "a single grain from a cooking pot" (*sthālīpulāka*).

In which [rites], such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others belonging to the Soma sacrifice, is there an absence of the fire-laying (*agnyādhāna*) performed at the New Moon sacrifice or for optional purposes?
Bhāṣya 12.1.10.19: The refutation of the objection regarding this very point;
12.1.12.24–28: The accomplishment by way of *prasaṅga* (extension) of the *patnīsaṃyāja* ritual belonging to the Soma sacrifice in the *iṣṭis* such as the *prāyaṇīyā*;
12.1.13.19: In the modified (*vaikṛta*) *iṣṭis*, the original (*prākṛta*) material and deity are set aside.
10|7|9| 58–60: In all *iṣṭi*s, the *nāriṣṭa* oblations are observed to be performed;
in them, the utterance of *svāhā* also occurs.

8|1|5|18: In those *iṣṭi*s that are constituent parts of the Soma sacrifice, there is no accomplishment by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) of the consumption of remnants or the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to the Soma ritual.

12.1.17.33-34: In the *iṣṭis* that are subsidiary to the *soma* sacrifice, the requirements for the altar of the *darśa* sacrifice are fulfilled by the altar of the *saumika* sacrifice through the principle of *prasaṅga* (incidental application).
12.1.18.8-9: Among the *iṣṭis* of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, certain *iṣṭis* are prescribed for the full moon day of Kārttika.

It is undisputed that, according to the logic to be explained later, by virtue of the scriptural injunction "he who [performs] an *iṣṭi*," these [Kārttika *iṣṭis*] must have the same harvest-time as other *iṣṭis*.
Bhāṣya 5.1.11: The extension of the ritual properties of the *iṣṭi* does not apply to the *soma* sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 8.1.13–10: In the *saumika* rites such as the *iṣṭiparvan*, the preparation of the sacrificial materials (*dravyatvaraṇa*) pertaining to the *darśa* sacrifice must be performed.
12.1.8.15, 40–41: Because they are preceded by the *iṣṭi*, the modifications of the *soma* sacrifice do not involve the remnants of what has already been performed.
Bhāṣya 5.4.15:

Because it is preceded by an *iṣṭi*, the *homa* (oblation) is not a remnant of what has been performed; it should take place when the fires have been consecrated, as it is a new (*apūrva*) rite, since the laying of the fires (*adhyādhāna*) is subsidiary to everything.
"One desiring offspring should cause [him] to sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ*; having taken four portions of clarified butter, he should recite the *caturhotṛ*."
"One should offer in the eastern fire for the sake of the *artha* [purpose], and in the northern fire for that same *artha*.

Although the *artha*-offering is not a remnant of what has been performed (*akṛtaśeṣa*)—and thus is not a remnant of what has been performed (*kṛtaśeṣa*), and for that very reason is also *apūrva* (an independent rite)—nevertheless, because all *homa*s are preceded by an *iṣṭi*, it should take place only in the fires consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭi*s.
This is because the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is a subsidiary to everything, being a subsidiary to all Vedic rites, and because the *pavamāneṣṭi*s follow upon the *ādhāna*.

Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the Caturhotṛ-homa is performed in fires consecrated by the *ādhāna* and the *iṣṭis*. However, because the text mentions it as being of the nature of an *iṣṭi*, it indicates that it should be performed in fires consecrated by the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Rejecting the prima facie view reached in the Sūtra by means of the word "but" (*tu*), he establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta).

The Caturhotṛ-homa does not take place in consecrated fires, because of the statement: "These Caturhotṛ-formulas are indeed the sacrifice for one who has not established the sacred fires. This indicates that the Caturhotṛ-mantras—the homas performed according to the sequence of the Caturhotṛs—occur in unconsecrated fires, since they are preceded by the *iṣṭi* (the primary sacrifice), and thus the remainder of the ritual is not yet completed. Because they are preceded by the *iṣṭi*, the remainder of the rite is not yet finished.

[Objection: In that case, how is it consistent with the statement, "This indeed is an *iṣṭi*," which speaks of its being an *iṣṭi*? To this he replies: Its status as an *iṣṭi* is merely a figurative praise (*stuti*) of this *homa*. For one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there can be no real *iṣṭi*.
Therefore, for one who has not established the fires, the *caturhotṛ-homa* is a worldly (*laukika*) sacrifice.
But it is an instruction, because it conveys something not previously known.

If it is argued that this indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), and therefore [the injunction] must be understood as a restatement (*prāpti*), he says in response:
the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is that this is not merely an indicative mark;
because it is something new (*apūrvatva*), being unestablished by any other means of knowledge, this is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*).
Therefore, the oblation is also [performed] by way of its being unconditioned,
because it is common to all without distinction.

The proponent says: That injunction would apply to all the *caturhotṛ* oblations, both those that are remnants of non-performed acts and those that are remnants of sacrifices, because there is no distinction; for this is the rule for the *caturhotṛ*s, and no specific qualification has been stated here to the effect that it applies only to those that are remnants of non-performed acts.

Therefore, [the rule applies] to all; however, because of the absence of the state of having performed [the rites], this is an exhaustive specification regarding one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). By using the word "or rather" (*api vā*), he sets aside what was stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and establishes the conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In the section concerning the *iṣṭi* and the *rājasūya*, because the injunction is one, there is a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice;
only by virtue of a specific scriptural statement would there be a separation of the *pravāraṇa* rite.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other such rites, however, there is a distinction of ritual acts due to the difference in intermediate injunctions (*avāntara-codanā*). Thus, the example of the *vipra* (the Brahmin) is seen. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the *iṣṭi*, *rājasūya*, and *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, there is a repetition of the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) according to the requirements of each performance.
Section on the Iṣṭi and Rājasūya:
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya, and other sacrifices, there is a repetition of the subordinate acts in accordance with each respective performance.

In the case of the *iṣṭi*, *rājasūya*, and *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, there should be a state of *tantra* (commonality of performance) for the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) because they belong to a single ritual action.
Commentary: From the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there are two groups: the *darśa* and the *pūrṇamāsa*.
Similarly, in the *rājasūya*, there are the *iṣṭis* such as the *anumati* and others, and the *soma* sacrifices such as the *pavitra* and others.

The Vaiśvadeva and other seasonal festivals (*parvan*) also occur during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. In this regard, it is deliberated whether the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) are to be performed by a single common procedure (*tantra*) for both the New and Full Moon sacrifices, as well as for the *iṣṭis* and *soma* offerings in the Rājasūya, and the seasonal festivals in the Cāturmāsyas; or whether they are to be performed separately. What is the prima facie view? That in each case, there is a single common procedure.
In one consecrated by the *iṣṭi* sacrifice (1072), the desired object is the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, for one consecrated by the *iṣṭi* (or consecrated by the *pavamāna-iṣṭi*).
Oṃ. There is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of the *iṣṭi* and the *soma* sacrifice.
(*Iṣṭi* here refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Oṃ. At the conclusion of the *iṣṭi* (specifically at the end of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*), the state of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) occurs; and since the staff and other items serve merely to manifest that state, the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣitadharma*) commence precisely at the conclusion of the *iṣṭi*.
Oṃ. The *iṣṭi*, *agnihotra*, and *soma* sacrifices constitute the fundamental archetypes (*mūlaprakṛti*).

Vi— "The status of being a primary archetype (*mūlaprakṛti*) for the *iṣṭi*, *agnihotra*, and *soma* sacrifices does not exist, or rather it exists; this is not due to their being non-existent, but because of a lack of discernment.
As in the world, there is a twofold [assistance]: that which is directly contributory (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and that which is indirectly contributory (*ārādupakāraka*)."
Thus, the designation [of these] as the primary source (mūla-prakṛti) is established among the six.

If it is argued that, because [the sacrifice] is non-worldly (*alaukika*), it is impossible to determine that "the assistance is complete with just these many constituent parts" (*aṅga*), and therefore the status of being a primary archetype (*mūlaprakṛtitva*) does not exist in the *iṣṭi* and other such rites—
this is not so;
for they resemble worldly [actions].

Just as in worldly intellectual activity, rice is the instrument (*karaṇa*), while the husking and so forth are its directly contributing factors (*saṃnipatyopakārin*), and the stool, lamp, and so forth are its indirectly contributing factors (*ārādupakārin*);

likewise, in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), sacrifice (*yāga*) is the instrument, the threshing and so forth are the directly contributing factors, and the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are the indirectly contributing factors.
Therefore, it is not entirely worldly in nature.
Just as in the case of worldly [rites] it is based upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too in the case of Vedic rites it should be based upon direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Therefore, the *iṣṭi*, *agnihotra*, and *soma* sacrifices possess the status of being the primary archetypes (*mūlaprakṛti*). (Vi.
8.4.3, Varṇaka 2)
"Oṃ, the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) is for the sake of the iṣṭis, because of the context.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the establishment of the fires is for the sake of the iṣṭis or for the sake of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis—or indeed not at all—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
the establishment of the fires should be for the sake of the iṣṭis, namely, for the sake of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis.
Because of the context, since it is recited within the context of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice;
for whatever is recited within the context of something serves that purpose.
Or rather, it is not so, because those [mantras] serve that purpose.
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not for the purpose of the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices;
for those very *pavamāneṣṭis* themselves have that [fire] as their purpose, whereas the fire has a different purpose.
The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is for the purpose of refinement, and the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices are also for the purpose of refinement;
thus, they possess mutual subsidiarity (*parasparāṅgatva*).
Therefore, the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices are not for the sake of the establishment of the fires.

"And because of the observation of an indicative mark. This sūtra provides another reason for the established conclusion that the Pavamāna-iṣṭis are not [parts] of the fire-installations (*ādhāna*). "This animal, once consecrated, indeed decays."

That which is Agni— these very oblations of the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), namely the *pavamāna* oblations— one should offer in the course of a year. By that means, indeed, he does not grow old.
"Therefore, he makes this [Agni] new again"—this is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the Pavamāneṣṭis being for the sake of Agni.
For it has been stated here that by means of these sacrifices, Agni becomes new again;
thus, their purpose is known to be for the sake of Agni.

And because it is for the sake of the fires, it is not for the sake of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration). The particle *na* is used for the purpose of adding another reason. Ke. Oṃ: In the repetition of an *iṣṭi*, the *ārambhaṇīyā* should be repeated at each *prayāja*.

At the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Ārambhaṇīyā offering is prescribed: "One who desires, 'May I be an eater of food,' should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Viṣṇu, a caru-oblation to Sarasvatī, a twelve-potherd cake to Sarasvat, and an oblation to Agni at the Agniṣṭoma. Regarding the deities of the obligatory rites, they state, "They prescribe [the Ārambhaṇīyā] for the [Darśapūrṇamāsa]. Furthermore, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa, a repetition is heard in the scripture: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives."
Regarding the question of whether the *ārambhaṇīyā* (opening rite) should also be repeated in those two repetitions, or not— in this discussion, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

When there is a repetition of the sacrifices, that is, when the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-iṣṭi*) are repeated, the *ārambhaṇīyā* should be repeated, just like the *prayāja* offerings.
Just as the *prayāja* offerings repeat in each performance of the *darśa*, so it is here;
or rather, because of the connection with the single commencement, there is no repeated commencement, since the performance lasts for as long as one lives.
With the word "or" (*vā*), he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering] should be performed only once at the beginning;

because it is connected with the commencement, as the *ārambhaṇīyā* is connected specifically with the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Furthermore, "commencement" refers to the undertaking for the duration of one's life, and thus there is only one such commencement throughout the lifelong performance.
When there is elision of a case ending, the ablative is used.
Since the commencement of the lifelong performance does not vary,
therefore the *ārambhaṇīyā* offering occurs only once together with the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Ke.: "The understanding that what is desired is that which is to be accomplished [arises from the rule]; for 'whatever is desired is accomplished. Su., p. 890. "The object intended to be obtained (*īpsita-karma*) is of four kinds."
The term "second case" (dvitīyā) is to be understood as referring to the gem in the context of breaking.
"That which is the most desired means of accomplishment is expressed by a word ending in the second case.

1073. Because it is inappropriate to intend (*vivakṣā*) even the qualification of the intended object (*īpsitoddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*), let alone the qualification of the cause (*nimittapadoddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*), [regarding] God’s being the cause of the world. *Bhāṣya* 6.4.6. The maxim: "For envy is an obstacle to discrimination. (*īrṣyā hi vivekaparipanthinī iti nyāyaḥ*).

"Envy is impure toward the objects mentioned by others; it is also born from malice. It is an "obstacle" (*paripanthin*)—meaning an enemy—to discernment (*viveka*), that is, to the discrimination that "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted.
The meaning is that when envy exists, discernment does not arise.

[The word] *sāhasī* [is used]. 944. "Oṃ! He offers [the victim] to Īśāna while looking at it; he releases those that have been roasted. Thus, according to the principle of the Gṛdhra-sacrifice portion for Īśāna (*gṛdhramedhīyājabhāga-nyāya*) [in Jaimini Sūtra 10.3.9.24], because of the removal of the extended application (*codaka*), there is an implied prohibition of other auxiliary parts. *Soma*. 9.1.12.1. Oṃ! *Īśvara* (the Lord).

Having accepted the Lord as known through the authority of the Upaniṣads and other sources, His very will—taking on various forms—is the meaning of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) in the Veda and constitutes its purport (*tātparya*).

(Thus some [say]). *Rahasya*, p. 15. "Oṃ! This one is indeed capable of being praised along with the quarters, since they establish themselves according to the quarters; they become possessed by the quarters; having taken hold of the body established in the quarters, they praise. Thus, the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, which is heard of as being accompanied by joy for the purpose of establishing the directions and is included within the *Rājasūya*, [is the subject].
Śābarabhāṣya 9.1.4.3. Oṃ! The refutation of the Lord’s being the cause of the world.
"The world is beginningless, and it has no creator whatsoever"—this is stated in the *Bīja* [chapter] of the *Ślokavārttika*. (Ṛju-vivaraṇa, p.

141). Here, certain individuals—whose minds are inclined toward the doctrines of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda, whose intellects are deceived by an excessive faith arising merely from encountering scriptural passages concerning creation and dissolution found within the *arthavādas*, and who proclaim God to be the cause of everything, including the body and the universe—declare as follows:
We observe that everything is possessed of parts, having acquired its existence through the conjunction of parts, and is thus modern [in origin]. And this includes the body, the world, and so forth;
for these are produced rapidly through the conjunction of parts.
Even the dyad (dvyaṇuka), as a composite whole, must be initiated by the conjunction of two atoms.
And the conjunction between atoms is produced by mutual action.
Furthermore, this action in the atoms is understood to arise solely from the conjunction with the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
As it has been stated: "And because this action is established by inference" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.1.23).
Furthermore, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is insentient.
And that which is insentient cannot, on its own, bring about any effect without being presided over by a sentient being, just like an axe or similar tools.
Nor is it appropriate that those very *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) who are [the objects] should themselves be the presiding agents over their own unseen merits and demerits (*adṛṣṭa*),
because they are ignorant.
For it is observed that one who knows both an object and the capacity of that object is the presiding agent, just as a carpenter is with respect to his tools.

Furthermore, the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are not capable of knowing, either by their own nature or through their power, the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) inherent within them; therefore, a conscious being distinct from them is postulated.

By virtue of that excellence of consciousness, it is understood that bodies, worlds, and so forth—which arise from a succession of effects beginning with binary atoms (*dvyaṇuka*) produced by the conjunction of their respective atoms caused by specific *adṛṣṭas*—are possessed of a beginning.
Likewise, it has been established that everything accumulated is subject to destruction.
Thus, how can there be a beginningless succession of conventional usage?
This [objection], which even attempts to subvert the position of the opponent, was set aside by the Blessed One, the author of the commentary, as it does not succeed in refuting our side.
For instance:
Even if this desire were to be fulfilled, it must still be understood how all composite wholes could dissolve simultaneously.

We consider that it should be accepted—on the basis of what is observed—that at this very moment, some things arise while others perish; for such is the inference from experience. And who can deny the continuity of the traditional usage of the elders?

Furthermore, if the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are not the presiding agents due to the absence of knowledge, then how could another be the presiding agent? For in that case as well, knowledge would not arise.

[This is because] cognitions arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind, dependent upon unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and assisted by the respective conjunctions of the sense organs with their objects.
Furthermore, the status of being a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not tenable with respect to unperceived factors.

If it is argued that there exists another cause for that [effect] which is unperceived, that is not so; for it is impossible to infer another unperceived cause while setting aside the perceived causes.
Inference follows what has been observed in all cases. Even when arising from a general rule, the mind does not function by subverting what has been observed.
But is it not also observed that "that which is insentient does not act without being presided over by consciousness"?
Now, it has been refuted.

Regarding the truth that there is a fallacy in both cases, one must ask: what exactly is being refuted? In this regard, because it concerns a specific subject, our own inference of another cause for the arising of knowledge is to be respected; it is not, however, the [inference] of the proponents of God (Īśvaravādins), which concerns an extremely general subject—that the insentient is presided over by a sentient being.
This is because a specific inference possesses greater force.

This has been stated by the venerable author of the Vārttika: "Since that which has well-known constituent parts is established without distinction, it is more powerful than [an inference based on] the similarity of the sense-organs with the object to be proven and the perception of what is seen;
just as there is sublation of a general rule by a specific scriptural statement."
"Thus, this inference is sublated by another inference.
By this, the following [position] is also refuted: "The intellect of the Lord is eternal."

Since whatever intellect exists is both produced and perishable, the intellect of the Lord must likewise be of that same nature. Furthermore, [he would require] a substratum for that intellect as well. (Mīmāṃsākośa 1.3.5)
It must be said:
for whatever kind of superintendence is observed in the case of tools such as an axe—namely, the conjunction of the hand and so forth—that very same kind must be inferred even when it is unobserved;
yet that is not possible.
Likewise, what else is there for the activity of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) other than the acquisition of its own nature?

Just as in the case of an axe, [its activity consists in] its conjunction with wood and so forth; and the acquisition of its own nature by the unseen force is established precisely through the performance of sacrifices and other rites.
Therefore, the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*) has not been refuted even by us.

This is because if the relationship between words and their meanings were of the nature of a convention established by God, it would result in the loss of the authority of the Vedas.

Bāla, p. 7. The Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda). For indeed, in this world, there exist entities that have a well-known conscious agent as their creator, such as palaces, palace gate-towers, archways, and so forth.
An example of that which has its opposite well-established is atoms and the like.
An example of that whose agent is doubtful is threads, the earth, mountains, and so forth.

These, being subjects of dispute, have an intelligent agent as their creator because they are effects and because they have non-intelligent material causes; for whatever is an effect or has a non-intelligent material cause is entirely possessed of an agent who perceives it, such as a palace and the like, and so too are threads, the world, and so forth.
Therefore, these too must be preceded by an intelligent perceiver.
The mention of "arrangement" (*saṃniveśa*) and so forth is for the purpose of indicating the two previously stated reasons;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and atoms (*aṇu*).

Furthermore, it is not unestablished that the earth and other elements are effects; for their status as effects is established—like cloth and similar things—by virtue of their being possessed of action or being composed of parts, provided they possess magnitude.

If it should be thought that [the argument] proves only that [the world] is preceded by something non-intelligent, then this would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For even our opponents accept that the entire collection of effects arises from karma, and since karma is a cause that is sequentially non-intelligent, the world has a non-intelligent cause.
But if [the world] were preceded by an omniscient being, the pervasion of the reason by that [omniscience] would not be established as faulty;
furthermore, the example would be devoid of the probandum,
because potters and others are not omniscient.

Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "possessing an origin" (*upattimattva*) or "having a conscious material cause" (*cetanopādānatva*) is observed precisely with respect to things like pots being preceded by a non-omniscient being.

Nor is it correct to say that the mere state of being preceded by an intelligent being (*upalabdhimatpūrvatvamātra*) is the object of the proof, while its specific qualification—being preceded by an omniscient being—is established from that [reason] because it is the object of that [qualification].

For if this specific qualification were not pervaded by the reason, how could it be established? If it is established, how can it not be the object [of the reason]? And if it is the object, how could the cognition of it not reach its own substratum?
This is incorrect;

for even when there is a pervasion of the universal alone, the universal— though it includes the particular— is inferred in the subject of the thesis by virtue of its being a property of that subject (pakṣadharmatā).
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.
To explain: even the inference of fire does not have the mere universal of fire as its object, because that [universal] is already established prior [to the inference].
Nor does it have a mountain qualified by that [fire] as its object, because since the universal of fire lacks a relation with that [mountain], it cannot logically function as its qualifier.

Otherwise, just as cows [are inferred] from the conjunction with a cow-pen (*golasa-samavāya*), fire would also necessarily follow on a mountain due to its conjunction with fire-in-general (*vahni-sāmānya-samavāya*).

And since there exists a relation of "conjunction-with-that-which-is-inherently-connected" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*) between the mountain and fire-in-general, one might object: "In that case, this [inference] cannot be established without first apprehending the specific fire conjoined with the mountain; therefore, there must be an inference of the specific fire as well.
But if that were so, the previously mentioned fault would necessarily follow.
In the same way, this very [argument] should be shown regarding the inference of the sense-faculties as well. For instance,
even there, no action whatsoever having the sense-faculty as its instrument is perceived.
Indeed, actions such as cutting and so forth are not accomplished by means of the sense organs, because cutting and the like are not themselves sensory faculties;
nor is it possible for actions characterized by the discernment of color-form and so on to have cutting and the like as their instruments.

And for this very reason, although action in general depends upon instruments despite being non-pervasive, the specific instrument characterized as the sense organ is established by virtue of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Likewise, here too, although that which possesses origination and has an insentient material cause is measured merely by an agent who provides the material cause, the instruments, the recipient, and the purpose, the establishment of that [agent] in his specific form occurs by the force of *pakṣadharmatā* regarding those things under dispute.

Otherwise, even the general property (*sāmānya*) desired by logic would remain unestablished, because a thing devoid of particulars is impossible, and no other particular can be logically justified. Furthermore, for one who is not omniscient and lacks the knowledge of distinctions such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), the state of being a supervisor is impossible. Therefore, although the fact of having an intelligent agent as its cause is the object of the logical inference, nevertheless, because that specific [agent] possesses the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), it is an inference whose object is a particular. Thus, the aforementioned fault does not follow.

Since the deficiency of properties in either the subject (*sādhya*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) constitutes the application of *utkarṣa* (excessive attribution) or *apakarṣa* (deficient attribution), and because this is common to all inferences, it serves as a reason for rejecting the validity of inference in general.
Thus, it is established that those things under dispute have an intelligent agent as their creator.

In this context, the means of accomplishment is stated by the word to be dependent on the established [object] that is desired, because its scope regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth is dependent upon that [established object]. Whatever has its scope regarding the material cause and so forth dependent on something else, that is a means of accomplishment dependent on the establishment of that thing; for example, smoke has its scope regarding the material cause and so forth dependent on the establishment of a specific fire, and thus its establishment is dependent on that [fire].
"One" [is the subject];
and there is also a traditional scripture (*smṛti*).
"Driven by the Lord, this person goes from birth to death toward his own pleasure and pain, either to heaven or indeed into a pit. Furthermore,
the arising of the knowledge of the Lord does not depend upon the body and the senses.
For there is a scriptural passage beginning with: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes and hears without ears.
He knows the universe, yet there is no knower of Him. They call Him the foremost, the Great Puruṣa.
And so forth.
Thus, through both analogy and scripture, the Lord’s status as creator and his omniscience are established.

Because we observe effects characterized by innumerable immobile beings and so forth, it must be established that there exists a Lord (Īśvara) who possesses eternal consciousness alone regarding all objects and is endowed with the six qualities.
Indeed, the entire universe does not arise from this much alone;

One who desires to make a jar, or even one who merely intends to do so, does not become fit for the commencement of the jar if he makes no effort due to laziness regarding the procurement of its materials and so forth.
