Now, if it is argued that those [causes] do not operate because they are unperceived, and that therefore one will assume them to be like a jar or similar objects;
then, just like knowledge, both the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and effort (*prayatna*) must also be accepted as existing.
Moreover, in that case as well, knowledge is employed for the sake of a specific desire to act.

And since that [creation] occurs through a difference in effort (*prayatna*), it is precisely the difference in the cause, namely effort, that is the direct cause for the arising of manifestation; how then could that be possible without it? For rice does not get cooked merely by blowing on it while tossing the grains, without fire.

If you think that both the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) and the effort exist in the Lord *sui generis* (by Himself), then are these two eternal or non-eternal? If they are eternal, then what is the use of the Lord’s knowledge, since it would be useless for producing desire-to-act and effort, as those two, being eternal, do not depend upon any further causes for their own production?

Furthermore, cognition, like effort, is not directly an auxiliary factor for the material cause of the effect. Indeed, it is through a specific effort that there occurs the presiding over [the agent] and the grasping of the material cause; however, at the moment [of action], cognition or the desire to act has no utility whatsoever, because a means that does not produce any distinction in an object whose action has already been accomplished fails to function as a means. Thus, the omniscience of God is dismissed. If, on the other hand, [effort and cognition] are non-eternal, then their cause of production must be stated.
But surely, eternal cognition itself exists as the cause for its own production;

so what need is there for another cause? Oh, what a mistake! That he should conclude by saying, "Cognition arises from cognition alone, without depending on desire and effort, which are the non-inherent causes [of the conjunction] with a particular self.
If that were the case, he might as well produce cream even from rice that has no starch!

If it is argued: "The liberated self indeed possesses conjunctions with those [minds]; therefore, for that purpose, two efforts—one of desire and one of exertion—proceed simultaneously there to produce such an effect," then we ask: are the minds and their conjunctions impelled by the desire and effort while being presided over (*adhiṣṭhita*), or while not being presided over? If they are not presided over, then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule right there. Furthermore, presiding is simply impossible without an effort.

If it is argued that "the presiding over those [atoms] arises from a desire to act produced by another effort, and there is no infinite regress because the stream of desire to act and effort is beginningless," then how is it that the Lord—who possesses unimpeded knowledge and aversion—remains inactive even when the collections of merit and demerit among the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) and the atoms in the world have reached their full development?

Even if [the soul] remains for some time and then desires to act or exerts effort, since that desire or effort has been produced by a prior desire or effort, how could there be a presiding over the subsequent desire or effort, or over the minds or their conjunctions? Thus, due to the lack of presiding, effort and desire cannot be produced from the conjunctions of the mind [with the soul].

Or, if they were produced, how could "being an effect" or "having an insentient material cause" fail to be a valid reason [for proving the existence of a sentient creator], as these would then be subject to deviation?

Nor is it correct to say that, like the light of the sun, the Lord’s mere knowledge alone constitutes His effort, such that through the conditioning of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) this [effort] comes to be;
for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

For there would be the conditioning by those respective adjuncts only when there is the state of having those respective things as objects, and there would be the state of having those respective things as objects only when there is the conditioning by those respective adjuncts.
Because that which is being produced does not take up its substrate as its material cause, and because it arises from that substrate [as a distinct entity].
Furthermore, the refutation of the position that cognition is non-eternal will be explained immediately below.

How can such a distinction—one that cannot withstand scrutiny—be applied to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) merely on the strength of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)? For that which is itself not logically tenable is incapable of establishing anything else.

What, then, is the status of a universal that is established through inference when no particular instance exists? Must its status necessarily be maintained? Surely, that which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be accepted, provided that an inference for it is possible. As for that which is not so possible—let the doctrine of God (Īśvara) stand as an example of such an inferential claim.
Its production is simply that of an atom.

But is it not a contradiction to say that what is established by valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) is untenable? If that is so, then there is a contradiction with what is established by valid means of cognition regarding resistance (pratighāta).
Let it be so, in order to avoid contradiction; however, this is not an invalidation of what is logically established. What then is this refutation of the proof?
It is not a refutation of the proof.

The name of that proponent is one who, in order to avoid specific qualifications such as "having assistance" or "being without assistance," employs a proof that establishes the general property of being preceded by an intelligent agent—which is like a flower in the sky—residing in earth and other [elements].
Yet, no such specific qualification is possible, upon which the general property of being preceded by an intelligent agent could depend while residing in earth and the rest.
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the destruction of all inference.
Because these inferences have as their object a possible particularity;

for it is not the case that a specific particularity belonging to the mountain or its constituent parts is impossible, nor is it impossible that a part of the fiery sacrificial vessel (caru), whose nature has been perceived, is the means for the perception of color,
given that the capacities of the causes for producing variegated color and shape are perceived here and there.

Therefore, just as a person who brandishes a sword toward the sky—which cannot be cut by that sword—is restrained [by the law], but not the sword or the sky itself; in the same way, when "being an effect" or "having a non-conscious material cause," aided by reasoning (*tarka*), reaches its full development, they establish that the Lord (*īśvara*) alone is the cause of the conjunction of the *kṣetrajña* (the conscious soul), atoms, and so forth, for all things.

The Doctrine of God.)
The statement "the noble one who speaks of omniscience" (sarvajñatāvādāryaḥ) is to be seen in verse 22 of the *Vidhiviveka* treatise within the *Vindau*.
Therein, the refutation of the Lord (īśvara) as conceived by the Naiyāyikas is established by means of the refutation of omniscience.
Ke.

The Naiyāyikas hold that inference (*anumāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the existence of God (*īśvara*). Maṇi [Śrīharṣa] maintains that the Veda alone is the means of valid cognition for establishing the existence of God, and nothing else.
Refutation of the view that God is known through inference.
Now, the inferential nature of God is refuted.

Some propose the following inference: "The subject under dispute possesses a creator, because it is an effect; whatever is an effect has a creator, as for example a jar; and this [world] is likewise."

In this context, the subject (*pakṣa*) is the earth, mountains, sprouts, and so forth, whose creator is doubted; the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is the pot and such, whose creator is well-known; and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is space and such, whose creator is unestablished.
Nor should it be said that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is unestablished, because its establishment follows from the fact of having parts (*sāvayavatva*).

But [an opponent might object]: the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), for whatever is an effect is seen to have a corporeal creator, just as a pot and the like have a creator such as a potter who possesses a body. Thus, "being an effect" establishes only that there is a corporeal creator, whereas what you wish to prove (*sisādhayiṣita*) is a creator who is bodiless.

The counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is things such as a jar, which possess a corporeal creator—the opposite of having an incorporeal creator. Since the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*) and in the counter-example, it would be contradictory (*viruddha*).
This is not so; for if "having an incorporeal creator" were indeed the probandum (*sādhya*), then it would be contradictory.

For us, however, setting aside the distinction between having a corporeal creator or an incorporeal creator, the probandum (*sādhya*) is merely "having a creator" (*sakartṛkatvamātra*). Otherwise, if "existence as a creator" were the probandum, there would be a dilemma: is it existence as a perceptible creator, or existence as an imperceptible creator? If it were existence as a perceptible creator, there would be a mere vacillation regarding the probandum, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total annihilation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, one must state that the probandum is simply the mere existence of a creator, excluding the specific qualities of being perceptible or imperceptible; and even so...

[Objection: "But for us as well, since agency belongs to the *kṣetrajña* alone by way of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), there is indeed agency [of the world]; thus, you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). [Reply: Not so. Since it is impossible for the *kṣetrajña* to possess the knowledge required to preside over merit and demerit, agency itself is not possible for him. Therefore, by means of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)—namely, the agent characterized by proficiency in the direct perception of merit and so forth (which is synonymous with the logic of a *siddhānta* established through the force of the context)—there is established an agent who is skilled in the construction of this diverse universe.
But surely, agency is not possible even for one who is distinct [from the body], since he too possesses the power to directly perceive dharma and adharma;
and being presided over by that [consciousness], he would be conscious like the *kṣetrajña*.
Nor can that direct perception have dharma and adharma as its objects, because it is a direct perception, just like any direct perception commonly accepted as such.

Furthermore, his external sense organs do not have dharma and adharma as their objects, because they are sense organs, like the sense organs of people such as ourselves. His internal organ, the mind, likewise does not function independently in the external realm, because it is an internal organ, like the internal organs of people such as ourselves.
Nor can his will and knowledge be eternal, because they are will and knowledge, like the will and knowledge of people such as ourselves.
Furthermore, even that body cannot be eternal because it is composed of the elements (*bhautika*), like the bodies of ourselves and others.
Nor can he possess a non-material, divine body, because it would still be a body, like the bodies of ourselves and others.
And because he would lack any purpose, he could not be an agent.

"This [Ishvara] cannot be the creator of the world because he is conscious, like the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul)," and so forth— by means of hundreds of such arguments, they deny his capacity for the creation of the world.
But surely this is merely the manifestation of faith in the non-human origin of the Vedas on the part of those who study the scriptures of logic and the Vedas!

For instance, is all this collection of inferences stated by accepting that supreme [entity] as having distinct characteristics, or without so accepting it? If it is by accepting it, then there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the property (*dharma*) for everyone.
If it is without accepting it, then there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Now, perhaps there is scope for the reasons (*hetu*) stated by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*):
[The claim that] God is established through inference:
this is not so; for even the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is indeed nothing but inference, differing from it merely in its mode of expression.

Therefore, if that [reductio] is accepted, there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends [the subject]; if it is not accepted, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus, the previously mentioned objection remains exactly as it was.

Furthermore, it is undisputed that every effect, beginning with atoms and so forth, which possesses the first quality [of sound] and is insentient, must be presided over by a sentient being. As for the motion of the atoms, however, it arises from the conjunction of the soul with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); and that unseen force produces its effect only when it is presided over by a sentient being.

To explain: that which is subject to doubt is indeed presided over by a conscious being (cetana) and is capable of producing an effect, because it is insentient (acetana). Whatever is insentient is observed to be presided over by a conscious being and capable of producing an effect, such as an axe or similar tools; and this [the world] is likewise; therefore, it is so.

Since a presiding agent must possess the nature, power, and effects of that which is presided over, the presiding agent—possessing eternal will, knowledge, and other qualities—is established by the force of the property residing in the subject (pakṣadharmatā), just like the specific fire on a mountain that is not perceived.
Consequently, for one who possesses knowledge, there is no dependence upon a body or sense organs.

Furthermore, there is no consequence of knowledge being impermanent like the knowledge of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), because the color and other qualities of earth-atoms are impermanent, yet this does not entail that color and other qualities are impermanent in the atoms themselves. Nor is there an absence of inherence for that which is distinct by virtue of residing in the knower of the field, because it inheres in a knower of the field that is conjoined with atoms conjoined with distinct [qualities].
Indeed, the relation of "inherence in what is conjoined with what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyogisamavāya*) is possible for the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, the presiding agent (adhiṣṭhātā) is established as distinct from the individual soul (kṣetrajña). Alternatively, the inference is as follows: that which is the subject of dispute is produced by an intelligent agent who possesses knowledge of the material cause, the instruments, the assembly of factors, and the purpose, because it is an effect, like a jar and so forth. Thus, if it is argued that the Lord (īśvara), who is distinct from the individual soul, is established by inference alone— [Response: No, because of the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). It is not that the Lord is not established at all; rather, he is established by the scriptures (āgama). However, since the scriptures are accepted as authoritative only for those who acknowledge the existence of a Lord, they cannot serve as a means of proof for one who does not accept them. Furthermore, even if one were to employ an inference, it would result in proving what is already established, because the existence of a creator is already proven by the fact that the world is an effect. Moreover, there is no such thing as an "effect" that is devoid of a beginning in time (anādi); therefore, the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha). Furthermore, the reason is contradictory (viruddha), because it proves the opposite of what is intended. For instance, in the case of a jar, the potter is indeed the agent, but he is not the agent who knows the material cause, the instruments, the assembly of factors, and the purpose; rather, he is merely the agent who fashions the clay. Therefore, the reason is contradictory. Consequently, this inference is not a valid means of proof. As for the claim that the Lord is established by scripture, that too is untenable, because the scriptures are not accepted as authoritative by those who do not acknowledge the Lord. Thus, the existence of the Lord is not established by either inference or scripture. Rather, the Lord is established solely through the grace of the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is the witness of all. This is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "O best of the twice-born, the Lord is not perceived by the senses, nor is He reached by inference. He is known only through His own grace, O sage, to those whose minds are purified. And in the *Bhāgavatapurāṇa*: "The Lord is not perceived by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the mind, nor by the other senses. He is perceived only by the self (ātman) when it is purified by devotion. Thus, the existence of the Lord is established solely through the grace of the Supreme Self. Therefore, the aforementioned inference is not a valid means of proof. Furthermore, the scriptures themselves are not a means of proof for one who does not acknowledge the Lord. Hence, the existence of the Lord is established solely through the grace of the Supreme Self. This is the conclusion.
To this it is replied:
inferential knowledge of God is not possible, because inference has as its object only a general agent;
therefore, there is no establishment of [an agent] distinct from the world.

As for the argument that "the earth and so forth have an agent because they are effects, like a pot," this is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since even the *kṣetrajña* (individual soul) possesses agency with respect to merit, demerit, and the like, due to its nature being pervaded by agency.
As it has been said: "Since that [agency] is established for all perfected beings (*siddhas*) through their actions, it is a proof of what is already established.
If it is argued that only an intelligent agent is to be proven, even then it remains a proof of what is already established, because the quality of intelligence also exists in the *kṣetrajña*.

Now, if what is to be proven is not merely the state of having an intelligent agent as creator, but rather an intelligent agent who possesses knowledge of the nature, power, and effects of the material cause, instruments, and so forth, then the example is deficient in respect to the probandum.
This is because even for all things that originate, the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) serves as an instrument;
and for a jar, too, that [unseen merit] is the instrument, while atoms and the like are the material causes.
Furthermore, since the potter does not possess knowledge regarding that [effect], the reason suffers from the fallacy of being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*).

Moreover, what is intended here as the probandum (*sādhya*)? Is it "having a creator such as non-existence" (*asadādikartṛkatva*), or "having a distinct creator" (*vilakṣaṇakartṛkatva*)? If it is "having a creator such as non-existence," then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
If, however, it is "having a distinct creator," then the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the property to be proven.
If it is argued that what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is merely the state of being an agent common to both [the Veda and ordinary speech], we reply: no, because such a commonality does not exist.

If it is further argued that even though the general property of agency (*kartṛtva-sāmānya*) is present, a distinct [divine] agent is established by virtue of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), we say: not so, because this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For there is no proof of a general property that is common to both. [Objection:
But in that case, wouldn't it follow that all inference based on the characteristic of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*) is destroyed?

For instance, since an effect is occasional (*kādācitka*), when "action" (*karman*) is used as the objective basis (*sādhana*), it is precisely an action distinct from substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) that one intends to prove.

Even there, if one considers the dilemma of whether the effect is of the nature of substance and so forth, or something distinct from them: if it is substance and so forth, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); if it is something distinct, there is the lack of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*); and if the probandum is merely a cause common to both, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). These [objections] apply equally. [Reply: It is not so. In that case, the implication of a distinct property (*vilakṣaṇadharma*) is appropriate by virtue of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), because there is no absence of a distinct property as long as one does not overstep the essential nature belonging to the class of causes.
In this case, however, there is a distinction for you as well, due to the transcendence of the essential nature of the class of agents.
To explain: the agent commonly accepted, such as a potter, possesses a body, is subject to merit and demerit, and has non-eternal desire, knowledge, and so forth;
whereas the one desired by you is bodiless, devoid of merit, demerit, and the like, and possesses eternal desire, knowledge, and so forth.

It is not tenable that, by means of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), there could be an implication of qualities such as the capacity for action—which are to be established [by inference]—that are of a different nature from those found in the class of creators like God, who are omniscient, omnipotent, and so forth. Furthermore, the reason "because it is an effect" (*kāryatvāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), since it is not established in relation to the earth and other such things.
As it has been said: "Just as now, so too everywhere, a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) is required."
Thus [it is said].
Now, if it is argued that "being an effect" is established because of "having parts," in that case, having parts is not the determining factor for being an effect;
for even in the absence of having parts, one observes that things such as cognition are effects.
Therefore, the possession of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) alone is the determinant of being an effect (*kāryatva*).

Now, if that very [possession of prior non-existence] were to be the reason (*hetu*), then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*), because the possession of prior non-existence is not established for the earth and so forth.

But surely both having parts (*sāvayavatva*) and possessing prior non-existence may be determinants; therefore, being an effect is established by means of having parts, since it is accepted that [the former] is a probans even when [the latter] is partially present.

It is not so; for in the case of things that can be produced, being an effect is observed through the property of having parts, as in the case of a jar and the like. However, in the case of things that cannot be produced, one cannot establish "being an effect" by means of the general property of having parts as a reason for every individual instance, because the subject [of the inference] would be contradicted.

This is just as corporeality, although pervaded by impermanence in jars and the like, cannot establish impermanence in atoms where destruction is impossible—such is the nature of the inference regarding God.
Moreover, this reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*). To explain:

in cases such as a jar, where "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is observed to be pervaded by "having an agent" (*sakartṛkatva*) as its specific cause, it is observed everywhere that this is pervaded by "having a corporeal agent" (*vigrahavatkartṛkatva*), as seen in the case of a potter and the like. Therefore, while establishing "having an agent," the property of being an effect establishes it specifically as qualified by corporeality.
Objection: Is it not observed that even one who is bodiless possesses agency in the act of impelling his own body?
Reply: Not so; for even in that case, agency exists only in one who is situated within a body, since the body itself is the object of the action.
Indeed, impelling is caused by volitional effort (*prayatna*), and such effort is impossible for one who is bodiless, as it is impossible in the case of liberated souls.

Now, if it is argued that agency in the assumption of a body by one who is bodiless is observed only through the taking up of another body after the enjoyment of a previous body—since the simultaneous assumption of two bodies is impossible—we say:
not so. For even in that case, a subtle body exists; thus, upon the abandonment of the previous body, agency belongs everywhere to the embodied being alone.

Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the total annihilation of all inference, because we accept a property as a valid reason only when it is observed in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and is non-deviant, just as smoke is pervaded by fire.

If it is argued that because heat and the like are non-pervasive and deviant with respect to fire, "being fire" is specifically accepted as the probandum later on, and that "not being a mountain" is likewise pervaded— this is not so, because even on a mountain, fire is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is further argued that "having a location other than that established by inference" is also a limiting condition (*upādhi*) due to its non-deviance— this is not so, because at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no recollection of a location other than that established by inference occurring spontaneously.

Therefore, when "having an agent" is being proven, it is necessarily "having a bodied agent. Since everything that lacks a bodied agent constitutes the counter-example (vipakṣa), the reason (*hetu*) of "being an effect" exists in both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the counter-example; thus, because it proves a contradictory meaning, the reason is "contradictory" (*viruddha*). Furthermore, what is intended by the proponent (*vādin*) to be proven is "having an incorporeal agent," yet the property of "being an effect" is pervaded by "having a bodied agent. Consequently, this very reason is one that proves the opposite of the specific property of the probandum (*sādhyadharma-viśeṣa-viparīta-sādhana*), and likewise, it is a reason that proves the opposite of the specific property of the probandum.

For, when the subjecthood of things such as mountains—which are impossible to produce—is established, and their status as effects is known to be pervaded by the state of being producible, as in the case of pots and the like, that [status of being produced by an intelligent agent] is also proven.
Likewise, since the state of being an effect is pervaded by having a conscious soul (*kṣetrajña*) as its agent, that too is proven.
Similarly, since the state of being an effect is pervaded by having an agent who possesses unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), that too is proven.
Likewise, it also establishes that [the world] is pervaded by having a creator who possesses impermanent desire, knowledge, and so forth.

Now, if the probandum is established merely through the general property of "having a creator" while setting aside all specific details, then, because there is no such thing as a creator who is a mere generality, the probandum would be devoid of its essential nature (*sādhyavikala*).

By virtue of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), the implication of a specific [cause] implies only a specific conscious entity (*kṣetrajña*) whose nature is consistent with the nature of being an agent, and not one of a contrary nature. Just as when "being fire" is to be proven, the presence in the subject implies a specific kind of fire characterized by qualities such as heat and burning, and not a contrary kind characterized by qualities such as minuteness.
Furthermore, this reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For it is the state of having an intelligent creator that is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*). In this regard, the earth, mountains, and so forth constitute the subject (*pakṣa*); things such as pots constitute the similar instance (*sapakṣa*); and everything other than those things with an intelligent creator constitutes the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). The property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) exists in all three of these categories—in the subject (the earth, etc.), in the similar instance (pots, etc.), and in the dissimilar instance (as well). Therefore, the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*) is unavoidable. Furthermore, this reason (*hetu*) is one that functions through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For instance, what is intended by this "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) regarding the earth, mountains, and so forth? Is it the state of being an effect characterized by having previously been non-existent (*abhūtvā-bhāva-lakṣaṇa*) in the case of the whole (*avayavin*) such as the earth and mountains; or rather, is it the production of certain parts in succession while the whole itself remains indestructible? Since we do not accept the latter definition of "being an effect"—that which is characterized by having previously been non-existent—the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

In the case of "being an effect," characterized by the successive production of several parts, there exists both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). This is because such a nature of being an effect is impossible in things like mountains and the earth, and because of the absence of any other [instance]; furthermore, since it resides only in the subject (*pakṣa*) and lacks the existence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), it cannot be a purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekin*).
Moreover, the reason is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
For instance, by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the very fact that the earth and so forth lack an agent is ascertained; therefore, this inference is sublated by non-perception.

For example, the inference that "the head of a rabbit has horns because it is the head of a four-footed animal, like the head of a cow" is sublated by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Now, if it is argued that because the creator of the world is established by inference and is bodiless, he lacks the fitness for perception—therefore, due to the absence of non-perception of a fit object, there is no sublation of the inference—then, in that case, since the horn of a rabbit is also established by inference, it would likewise be unperceivable due to its [supposed] subtlety like an atom; thus, there would be no sublation of the inference even in that case.

If, because horn-like things are seen to possess color, magnitude, and so forth, they possess perceptibility there [in the world], then here too, since the agent-class possesses a physical body, it would be perceived as something possessing the perceptibility of being apprehended by the senses; yet it is not perceived. Therefore, the contradiction with non-perception is unavoidable.
Furthermore, this is an inference that contradicts another inference.
For instance: the earth and so forth are without an agent, because they are not produced by a body, like space.
If it is argued that this pervasion (vyāpti) is conditioned by the absence of an agent [in general], then there is no contradiction, as both [conditions] may serve as the probans.
Likewise, the subject of dispute is produced by a conscious agent (kṣetrajña), because it is produced by a conscious being, like a jar and the like.

Likewise, the earth and so forth do not have a bodiless creator; for the purpose of this [inference] regarding Īśvara is absent, as it has been stated that the designation of action follows from being an effect, like a jar and the like.
Likewise, the earth and so forth [are established] through eternal effort, will, and exertion; "desires are not to be performed" is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Nor is it the case that these do not have a creator possessing knowledge, because they are effects, like a jar and the like.
Thus, the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) concerning exertion and purpose are indeed injunctions (*vidhis*).
Or [it may be argued]: "It is like space and so forth, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*).
As it has been said: "Because of the absence of an object for such inquiry, it is like the *sūktavāka* mantra;
and in the *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice), there is that which is an object of cognition and so forth, being non-contradictory and not directly perceived."
Since the purpose of its existence is inconceivable according to this aforementioned reasoning, who indeed would postulate such an Ishvara, even when all other [causes] have been refuted?

Thus, since all the fruits mentioned in the *sūktavāka* cannot be accomplished through performance, and because these [other] inferences would have either a visible (*dṛṣṭa*) or an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) characteristic, your inference— [namely] that "there is no mention [of the fruit] while one lives, because the blessings for long life (*āyurāśis*) are for that purpose" (10.2)— is more powerful. Furthermore, according to [the rule] "this [inference] is equal to the context" (25.61), it applies only to long life (*āyus*).

The designation of action has been stated [at Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.2]. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word *agnihotra*—whose purposefulness with respect to the traditional corpus (*samāmnāya*) has been stated—is a source for dharma (*dharmapradeśa*), and there is an extension of dharma (*dharmātideśa*) from the obligatory *agnihotra*.
This is the principle (*nyāya*) stated as "the designation of action" [at Jaimini Sūtra 7.1.1].

Just as there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants from the six-day sacrifice (*ṣaḍaha*), so too here—in the *avabhṛtha* of the Vāruṇapraghāsika—is there an extension of ritual properties (*dharma*) from the *avabhṛtha* of the Soma sacrifice.
Why? Because the principle has been stated: "It has been said... it would be so" (*uktaṃ ... syāt*). (Bhāṣya)
"But the priority of the word has been stated" (1.1.8.29) [this is the *nyāya*].

Even if, on account of the eternity of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-nityatā*), one were to postulate an beginningless succession of human compositions, nevertheless, because the *nyāya* "But the priority of the word has been stated" remains established, grammar—even if it were composed by many persons—does not attain the status of being based upon the Veda (this is the *pūrvapakṣa*).
Vārttika 1.1.8.24, p. 257: "But the priority of the word has been stated."
But in the case of the Vedic sentences, there is no possibility of anyone having a different intention or being mistaken;
nor is there a speaker who might state them otherwise, for all persons [rely on the Veda].
This is because, as stated in the phrase "but it has been said," one relies solely on what is heard in scripture.
Page 699, 1.1.13: It has been stated that the Vedic corpus exists for the sake of ritual action; therefore, everything therein must be for that purpose.
In the Vedic corpus, there are such injunctions as "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "One should sacrifice with the *balabhid*," and "One should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*.
Regarding these, a doubt arises: are terms such as *udbhid* injunctions of accessory materials (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)?
In this regard, the Prābhākara, out of a desire for consistency, has described the section (*adhikaraṇa*) as follows:

In injunctions such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," there is first of all no qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) involving an indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), because that would entail the fault of excessive injunction (*vidhigaurava*) and the defect of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Nor is there an injunction of both [the instrument and the action] separately, because that would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
In that case, if one of the two were to be enjoined, if the sacrifice (*yāga*) itself were enjoined, then the accompanying word (*upapada*) would be redundant.

Nor is it possible to enjoin an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) by referring back to a sacrifice enjoined elsewhere, because in every instance where such an accompanying word is heard, the injunction of a ritual action (*karmavidhāna*) is impossible.

Therefore, even against one's will, one must admit that the injunction of an accessory pertains to a worldly sacrifice of the Mothers (*mātṛyāga*)—[note: "sacrifice to the Gaṇas" (*gaṇayāga*) is written in the margin].
And this being the case, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that even the Veda lacks authority because it depends upon other means of valid cognition.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*), it is indeed a name (*nāmadheya*), as stated in the Bhāṣya.
That [prima facie view] is incorrect.
For when multiple injunctions depend upon a single injunction of purpose, it brings about the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).
Thus, the status of being a definition pertains only to the primary meaning, and not with reference to invalidity.

This [position], out of fear of the excessive burden of injunctions and the necessity of figurative indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), results in resorting to the unauthoritativeness of the Veda; it appears like choosing death out of fear of the exertion of eating.

Nor does resorting to a worldly *gaṇayāga* (group sacrifice) result in liberation from figurative indication, because since no deity prescribed by the Veda is sacrificed to, that *gaṇayāga* lacks the status of a primary sacrifice.
Or, let there be some way or another for this quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) to rest upon a worldly rite; even so, there is no lack of authoritativeness.
This is a trivial argument, since validity is established even for worldly actions based on [worldly] sources, as in the rule: "One should eat facing the east for the sake of longevity.
Thus, the section (adhikaraṇa) is introduced exactly according to the Vārttika.
For, in the first pāda, the validity of the entire Veda with respect to dharma was demonstrated by way of its being an injunction (codanā), through the removal of all other doubts.

Since that [arthavāda], which consists of explanatory praise, might be suspected of lacking authority with respect to dharma because it is included within the injunction (codanā) yet lacks direct utility toward it, its authority was established in the second pāda by demonstrating how each part serves a specific purpose through its inclusion within the injunction.
In the third pāda, however, it was demonstrated that there indeed exist such explanatory statements (vāda) that serve as the source for Smṛti and established custom (ācāra).

Now, although the specific utility of the names with respect to *dharma* has been generally described as being included within the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*), it was not previously established; therefore, this is introduced once again.

Here, although in the Bhāṣya this appears to be a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of the preceding and following sūtras, nevertheless, because the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) intended for the preceding sūtra does not appear there and because two distinct investigations are required, the venerable author of the Vārttika has treated these as two separate investigations, having inferred the prima facie positions accordingly.

In this regard, first, the intention of the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) is as follows: Even though terms such as *udbhid* occur within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), they do not fall under the category of injunction because they merely introduce the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Furthermore, because they lack the status of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), they cannot be considered explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, because they do not function as reminders of what has already been enjoined, they lack the status of *mantras*.

Therefore, since they do not serve the purpose of action (*akriyārthatva*) through the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), the words such as "Udbhid" and so forth would indeed be useless; thus, the threefold nature of the Veda [would be undermined].
As it has been said: "For one who asserts that only a portion of the Veda is authoritative, [words like] Udbhid and the like would be even more [problematic] than that."

Or there is the pointlessness of matters not applicable to the *dharma* and so forth; [as it says] in the rule "the non-usage of *yuk*, *uktha*, *artha*, and *nāman*" (Pāṇini 2.3.60), when the *ukthya* hymns are displaced.

This is from the commentary on the sūtra *bhivādeśraddhe* (Pāṇini 8.2.83). Viśvasāhasrī, p. 483. Nor does it follow that there would be the undesirable usage *vikalpati pacati*, because since that [meaning] is already expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, the noun expressing that meaning (*ukthārthanāman*) is not employed.
Rahasya, p. 88. The mantra *ukthaśā yaja somasya* applies where there is only the taking up of the cup (*graha*) and the offering (*homa*).

Saṃkarṣa. 2|3|12. The *ukthya* (a specific type of *soma* sacrifice) is an optional modification (*saṃsthā*) of the *agniṣṭoma*. This cannot be performed prior to the *agniṣṭoma*. Bhāṣya 5|1|14|39–42. The *ukthya* is the second *saṃsthā*.
In that context, following the Agniṣṭoma stotra, there are three additional Ukthya stotras;

thus, there are fifteen stotras in total (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 3.6.16). Regarding the statement "The Ukthya has the Vairūpa Sāman," the Vairūpya Sāman is to be placed in the Pṛṣṭha-stotra of the Ukthya sacrifice.
VI. 10|6|16: "The *ukthya* hymns are dedicated to Indra and Agni" (*ukthya-yāga* has Indra and Agni as its deities).

Bhāṣya 3|6|17|8: For the *ukthya* hymns, the *saubhara* is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* chant. In that case, the arrangement of the *nidhana*s—namely *hīṅ*, *ūrdhvaḥ*, and *ū*—is established respectively for the sake of the fruits of progeny, food, and heaven; however, there is no separate fruit for the *nidhana*s apart from the *saubhara* itself.
2|2|13|28-29. In the Ukthya sacrifice, there are two sets of five *savanīya* offerings dedicated to Agni and Indra-Agni.
Vi. 9|1|8. The prohibition regarding the *atigrāhya* cups in the Ukthya applies only to the modified (*vikṛti*) Ukthya, not to the archetypal (*prakṛti*) Ukthya.
Saṃkarṣa. 3|1|3. It is stated that for a Kṣatriya in the Ukthya, the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is accompanied by the *stotra* and *śastra*, as indicated by the phrase "even in the Ukthya."
And in that case, it is accomplished by means of the very words of the *ukthya* stoma;
nevertheless, there is no omission of the *ukthya* chants and recitations (*stotra-śastra*).

(Bhāṭṭa 10.1.12). In the *ukthya* sacrifice, regarding the two *savanīya* animals at the *agniṣṭut*, in the verse "prāsmā agnim bharata," there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word "asmai" (to him) into "ābhyām" (to these two).
(Consideration of the ritual application: in reality, because the Savanīya animals are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Agniṣṭomīya animal, this belongs to this day.
Vi. 9|1|8. There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the chants (*stotra*) belonging to the Ukthya to the Pañcokthya and other such rites.
Bhāṣya 8.3.5:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the three Ukthya cups are drawn even before sunset.
If, by chance, the Ukthya cups were to be drawn after sunset, then the Ṣoḍaśin cup, which follows them, must also be postponed.
VI.

Regarding the *ṣoḍaśi-graha* which follows the *ukthya*: even though it is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the act of drawing the cup (*grahaṇa*), because the act of drawing is a direct constituent (*saṃnipāti*), it serves as the basis for the *ārādupakāra* (indirectly contributing) stotras. Due to its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), the sequence (*krama*)—as an internal attribute—is stronger than the external stotras. Therefore, for the sake of favoring that [sequence], the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *ṣoḍaśin* is necessary. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, according to *Soma* 5.1.18, the time for the performance of the portion of the *ṣoḍaśin* is after the repetition of the *ukthya* chants.
Therefore, by the time of that [principal rite], the time of its subsidiary is sublated;
[that is,] by the time of the practice of the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup], the time of the subsidiary, the *stotra*, is sublated; hence, the *ṣoḍaśin* is to be postponed. (Ṭup. 5.1.1)

The quality consisting of the Ukthya form transforms the permanent Agniṣṭoma termination into another termination. (Vi. 3.6.16). The ten-night period of the twelve-day sacrifice, being completed each day with the Ukthya stotra, reaches the state of being performed one hundred times when repeated ten times.
Thus it is with the five Ukthyas.
VI. 8.1.4. When there is a displacement of the Ukthya stotras, there is also a displacement of the Ṣoḍaśin stotra, because the Ṣoḍaśin is connected with the Ukthyas.
Bhāṣya: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the Ṣoḍaśin, it is heard in scripture: "One takes that [cup] away from the faces."

When the Ukthya-stotras are postponed due to some divine or human obstacle, there arises a doubt: should the Ṣoḍaśin then also be postponed, or not? What is the prima facie view? It should not be postponed. Why? Because at that time, how could there be a Stotra for the Ṣoḍaśin? For it is prescribed: "At the time when the sun has half-set, one begins the Stotra of the Ṣoḍaśin."
Therefore, regarding the displacement:
this being the position reached, we reply:
the *ṣoḍaśī* cup, too, is to be displaced.
Why? Because of its connection with the Ukthya.
For the Ṣoḍaśin has a connection with the Ukthya, as it is said: "He draws it after the [Ukthya] cups.
Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśin is to be displaced.
As for what was said—that there will be no omission of the *ṣoḍaśin* at its own time—it is replied:
if one follows the sequence of the hymns (*stotra*), the sequence of the principal acts (*pradhāna*) would be displaced.
Therefore, the sequence of the hymns must be observed.
It is not possible to favor both [alternatives].
For it is heard in scripture: "Having either taken up the *graha* or having lifted the *camasa*, he introduces the *stotra*."

Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśī* is to be displaced. [The *Ṭup-ṭīkā* states—beginning the section: But surely, by this specific statement, "the *stotra* at the time when the sun has half-risen," the sequence of the *ṣoḍaśī* following the *ukthya* (which was previously established by the general statement, "having either taken the cup or having lifted the *camasa*, he begins the *stotra*") is set aside. It is replied:

Both the state of following the Ukthya sacrifice and the state of being at the time of twilight can be accommodated; therefore, because there is no contradiction, there is no conflict between the general rule and the specific rule.
Furthermore, in this case—where the phrase "due to divine or human force beyond one's power" is not heard as a qualifying clause—there exists no relationship of general and particular.

(How so? For a scriptural injunction (*śāstra*), having regard for the relative strength of divine or human factors, does not act merely for the sake of general qualification. (Consequently, since it is impossible to accomplish both the "time of twilight" (*samayādhyuṣitatva*) as a subordinate element of the hymn (*stotra*) and the "subsequent occurrence after the *ukthya*" for the cup-drawing (*graha*), there must be non-interruption regarding one or the other; thus, the inquiry as to which is to be set aside is appropriate.
The cup-drawing (*graha*) is an internal factor (*antaraṅga*) because it assists the sacrifice directly, being a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakārin*);
the hymn (*stotra*), on the other hand, does not assist the sacrifice directly (because it is an indirect auxiliary, *ārādupakārin*).
Therefore, between these two [times], the time that is internally related [to the sacrifice] should be followed (since the word "time" actually denotes the sequence itself).
For this reason, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "If one follows the sequence of the stotras, the sequence of the principal acts is contradicted.
Alternatively, when the Ukthya chants are postponed, the sacrifice itself—namely the Ṣoḍaśin—is postponed in this manner, because the Ṣoḍaśin chant also depends upon the Ukthya.
When the *graha* is being taken, the sacrifice reaches its conclusion, just as it does with the *avadāna*.
The time for the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin-graha* occurs after the performance of the *ukthya-yāga*.
Therefore, by that time (the time of the performance of the *graha-yāga*), the time for the subsidiary element (the time of the *stotra*) is superseded.
"Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśin is to be displaced.

Śā—(Regarding the doubt as to whether the Ṣoḍaśin is displaced when the Ukthya cups are displaced, or not: "In that case, displacement is not appropriate because of the inclusion of the time for the Stotra;

for if there were displacement, its Stotra would be deprived of its own proper time. However, even though it is a sequence, this [displacement] is stronger because it is subordinate to the primary act."

"Time, being subordinate to the hymn (*stotra*), is weak and thus deserves to be set aside. Soma [replies]: "When the ritual action is grasped through time, the sublation of sequence is established by *kaimutya* (a fortiori)"; this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*) because of the counter-objection. Even though the state of following the *ukthya* is merely a subordinate part of the act of drawing the cup (*grahaṇa*), since the act of drawing is an *saṃnipātin* (directly contributing factor), it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the *ārādupakāraka* (remotely contributing) hymn; therefore, because sequence is stronger with respect to the hymn—which is external due to its being a property of that which is internal—it is necessary to favor that [sequence].
In the Jyotiṣṭoma (Soma. 5.1.18):

"When there is an advancement of the Ukthya, is there no advancement of the Ṣoḍaśin, or rather is there an advancement?"—or else, as in the previous case regarding the drawing of the Ṣoḍaśin cup, there is no advancement of the time for the stotra.

[The opponent argues: "Because the cup (*graha*) is manifested as being subordinate to its constituent parts (*aṅga*), the time for the hymn (*stotra*) should be set aside when the cup is displaced [from its position] by means of the hymns. [Bhāṭṭa’s response: Upon reflection—whether due to a divine or human error—if the *ukthya* cups are displaced, should the *ṣoḍaśin* hymn also be displaced or not? In this deliberation, because the time prescribed by the injunction, "At the time when the sun has half-set (*samayādhyuṣita*), one begins the *ṣoḍaśin* hymn," would lack authority [if the displacement were ignored], the displacement [of the hymn] follows.

Furthermore, because the sequence following the Ukthya is enjoined by the statement, "He takes that Ṣoḍaśin [cup] when turned away," and because the time of the Stotra is subsequent to the taking of the cup according to the statement, "Having taken the cup," the time of the *samayādhyuṣita* (twilight) must conform to that; for by the statement, "That which is turned away," there is an injunction regarding the performance of the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice itself as occurring after the Ukthya, and thus there is no contradiction even if the taking of the cup precedes the Stotra.
For this very reason, since the cup has not fallen into the hands of others, the sacrificer himself indeed takes it.

Or, let it be that [the rule] pertains to the drawing of the cup (*graha*); even so, because the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is prescribed in the Taittirīya recension for all three pressings (*savana*), the statement "him, turned away" (*taṃ parāñcam*) refers to a different pressing.

Or, let this [statement] also apply to all cases; nevertheless, since the phrase "or the cup" (*grahaṃ vā*) has a general scope, there is no contradiction whatsoever in performing the hymn (*stotra*) at the time of twilight (*samayādhyuṣita*), even when the cup is drawn after the *ukthya*.

If, however, it were argued that because [the rule] possesses both general and specific forms, and because it does not apply in the case of a divine transgression since its subject matter is the scripture as it stands, all matters possess equal force; even so, since the sequence following the *ukthya* is to be adopted as a temporal order, sublation (*bādha*) is logically established according to the principle of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇanyāya*). Therefore, the logical conclusion is indeed the favoring of the time when the sun has set (*samayādhyuṣitakāla*). Nor is the time weaker in consideration of the order of the principal act simply because it is subordinate to a subordinate element, for both are equally subordinate elements.
And because the drawing [of the cup] (*grahaṇa*) begins with the offering (*pradāna*), like the cutting off (*avadāna*), it constitutes a single ritual act here;
such being the prima facie view, the sequence of that [offering] is stronger because the drawing possesses an internal status as the means for determining the repetition of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
In reality, however, "him, turned away... [is the scriptural basis].

Regarding the connection of the *ukthya* with the *iṣṭoma* (1086), even in the case of the statement "in the *ukthya* and so forth," this too refers solely to time; therefore, due to its being more internal (*antaraṅga*), it is indeed more appropriate [to take it as time]. Nor can the favoring of the time for the *stotra* be established even if the drawing of the cup (*grahaṇa*) is performed at a later time, because in that case there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting both the fact that the *stotra* occurs after the drawing of the cup and its proximity to the principal act (*pradhānapratyāsatti*). Consequently, it is logical that only this single factor—the subversion of the time fixed by the *samayādya*—should be set aside.
Therefore, it is established that there is also an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*) of that [rite].
Maṇḍana: "The upward displacement of the *ṣoḍaśin* is desired. Śaṅkara: "And the upward displacement of the *ṣoḍaśin* must be stated."

"Oṃ. Because of its connection with the Ukthya and the Agniṣṭoma, [the Ṣoḍaśin] should be without Stotra and Śastra; for when there is a numerical [limit], there is an absence of [further] recitation.
The Ṣoḍaśin cup, being drawn in the archetype (prakṛti), should be without Stotra and Śastra—that is, devoid of hymn and recitation.

Because of its connection with the Ukthya and the Agniṣṭoma, it is stated: 'One should draw it at the Agniṣṭoma for a Kṣatriya; it may also be drawn at the Ukthya'; thus, the Ṣoḍaśin is to be taken at the sacrifice characterized by the Agniṣṭoma form."

For if the *stotra* and *śastra* were present, the ritual would be completed with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup as its *śastra*, and thus there would indeed be a change in the number [of chants], which would be their proper placement.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: just as in the case of "it becomes golden" (*kaustambhaṃ bhavati*) and so forth, the use of a *bahuvrīhi* compound in such instructions as "the *vairūpa* exists" and "the *ukthya* is possessed of the *vairūpa*"—having set aside the specific mention of the *vairūpa*—indicates that the *vairūpa* and other such elements, though mentioned by the *bahuvrīhi* term, serve a dual purpose, in order to avoid the redundancy of the *bahuvrīhi* expression itself.

Furthermore, according to the logic of the *Kautsa* and others (*Śabarabhāṣya* 10.4.9), since there is an absence of previously mentioned *sāmans* for which the number would be equal, how could there be a restriction based on a specific similarity when there is the possibility of their insertion into whatever [stotra] they might enter?
This is because the statement "here indeed they insert" is a general rule (*sāmānyavākya*).

For here there is no injunction of the *vairūpa* and other *sāmans* by way of restating the previously mentioned stotras—which would result in their insertion into all stotras, as in the case of the rule "the cups are dedicated to Agni" (*āgneyā grahāḥ*).
Moreover, by the principle of *ānarthakyatadañjyāya* (3.1.9), that which is heard as being connected with the season (*ṛtu*) is connected with the *stotra*.

Furthermore, that which has descended [to a specific application] via the principle of *ānarthakyatadañjyāya* does not have universal applicability; for otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*vairūpya*) of the fourfold accentuation (*cātuḥsvaryya*) applying even to the *yājyā* verses and so forth.
Therefore, when it follows that the placement could be anywhere, it is restricted by similarity (*sādṛśya*).

Or, even if it were like the *trivṛt* and other *stomas*, such that it too possessed the character of being enjoined for all [the *pṛṣṭha* chants], nevertheless, it is only for the sake of avoiding the futility of the injunction "recite" (*brūhi*) that its application to the *māhendra-stotra* is established.

For this very reason, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), even under the alternative view that the sentence "they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" is an injunction for the *pṛṣṭha-grahas*, the *kaṇvarathantara* does not find a place in all the *pṛṣṭhas*.

However, since in the two sentences "The *pṛṣṭha* is the *bṛhat*" and "The *pṛṣṭha* is the *rathaṃtara*", the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two *sāmans* and the word *pṛṣṭha* would otherwise be rendered meaningless, it must be concluded that for the sake of avoiding this, even the *kaṇvarathaṃtara* and others—which are designated as coreferential with the term *pṛṣṭha*—are intended for its specific function; thus, they are to be inserted into the *māhendra-stotra* alone.

In passages such as "The *bṛhat* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*," neither an injunction for the *sāman* by way of restating the *stotra*, nor an injunction for a *stotra* qualified by the *sāman*, is possible; for both the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara* are already established through their recitation alongside the *vāmadevya* and other *sāmans*.
Furthermore, the *stotra* itself is already established by another means as something to be accomplished by those [sāmans].
Therefore, in order to avoid this redundancy, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* on the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa* that the *kaṇvarathaṃtara* and others perform their own specific functions.

Thus, here too, the placement of the Vairūpa and other [sāmans] in the Māhendra-stotra is solely for the purpose of avoiding the futility of their designation as Bahuvrīhi compounds. Maṇḍana states: "The Vairūpa is the means of accomplishing the Pṛṣṭha. Śaṅkara states: "And the Vairūpa is indeed in the Pṛṣṭha."
Among the *saṃsthās* such as the *ukthya*, only the *agniṣṭoma* form proceeds as the primary one.

And where there is an injunction for specific features such as the *ukthya*, only the properties (*dharma*) of those specific forms apply there. (Vārttika 3.1.16.47). That which is occasioned by the *ukthya* and other *saṃsthās*—namely, the *ukthya-graha*, the *stotra*, and the *śastra*—is non-original (*aprākṛta*). In that case, whatever extension of properties from other *grahas*, *stotras*, or *śastras* might otherwise apply based on a desire for certain qualities (*guṇakāma*), that does not occur.

In the *ukthavākya*, by means of the injunction prohibiting the remainder of the ritual action, there is the bringing of a bull (*ukṣan*) with a different name every year in the *pañcaśāradīya* sacrifice, which is an *ahīna* rite.
(Bhāṣya): Words such as *uktha* and others denote age.
Or [as stated in] Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 3.1.6, page 679:
"The hearth (ukhā) is the fathers. One yokes that hearth with the mantra: "Yoking first the mind..."

Having prepared [the fire-pan] with the mantras prescribed in the *Pāṭhakrama* beginning with "ityādi," and having placed the fire within it, one should set that *ukhā* upon a sling for six or twelve months. Having tied that disciple—[placed] between two gold plates (*suvarṇarukma*)—to one's own neck, one should maintain that primary fire for a year and subsequently fill it with bricks such as the *paśu* and others.
(Vi. 4.4.6) The *ukhā* is the vessel for the *sāṃnāyya*.

"The *ukhā* (pot) exists for the purpose of boiling the milk for the *agnihotra*, for the sake of the constant sacrifice, and for the purpose of maintaining the fire in the *ukthya* rite" (Bhāṣya 8.2.12–14). Having prepared the *ukhā*, [the clay] is mixed therein.
That fire is permanent in the Agnicayana ritual (Vi. 10.4.17).
In the case of the *ukhā* (fire-pan), there is a combination of the optional and the permanent, because the desire [for a specific result] is observed in the injunction.
In the Agnicayana sacrifice, the Ukthya fire is maintained for a year.
The fire that exists in a large, square, earthen pan (*ukhā*) used as a receptacle for embers is called *ulkha*.
In that very context, the fire beginning with the *āṣṭaupajña* is also associated with fruits such as the attainment of food and nourishment.
There should be a combination of these two fires—the optional and the obligatory—within the fire-pan (ukhā).
But is it not the case that the optional fire sublates the obligatory one?
No.

In the context of *niyoga* (application) or *niyojana* (employment), this desire (*kāma*) is heard [in the scripture]: "Having fetched [the fire], one should place it [on the altar] for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Thus, the fulfillment of the desire occurs through mere application, and not through the act of offering (*homa*).
As for the offering, however, it is indeed obligatory (*nitya*) in relation to the *ukhya* fire.
And thus, because their purposes are different, there is no relationship of sublation between them;
furthermore, because both fires are present in the cauldron (*ukhā*), they are to be used in combination.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the case of the *ukthya*, there would be a performance of the rites even for those who have not undergone consecration, because the word has been uttered [as part of the desire-based and obligatory ritual]. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says this.
Moreover, if there were a sublation of the obligatory *agni* by the optional one, then once the optional is established, the obligatory would simply not exist.
And if the obligatory did not exist, the ritual action and oblation would take place in the unrefined *āghāra* vessels themselves, which lack the purificatory rites such as the *ādhāna*.
In that case, the universal applicability (*sarvārthatā*) of the *ādhāna* would be contradicted.
Therefore, there is a combination of the optional and the obligatory, not a sublation [of one by the other].
And because that [fire-laying] is for the sake of the deity—

since that fire-laying, when established in the mind, is for the sake of the deity, meaning it is for the purpose of securing the deity— if the obligatory [fire-laying] were absent, the securing of the deity would not occur.
Therefore, there is a combination of the optional and the obligatory rites; the obligatory is not sublated by the optional.
This is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). Or rather, there is a modification, for the reason stated therein.

The word "vā" (or) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). There would be a modification (*vikāra*), that is, a sublation (*bādha*) of the obligatory (*nitya*) fire-altar by the optional (*kāmya*) one, such as the *āghā* and so forth;
this is because of the reason already stated.

The reason has been stated for that which is called "uktahetu" [in the rule]: "But the occasional (*naimittika*) is a modification of the original (*prakṛti*)," as the reason was stated there [in the *Tantravārttika*]. It was stated therein that "the occasional sublates the permanent (*nitya*). Therefore, the conclusion is that by means of the *āghāra* and other such [occasional rites], the optional (*kāmya*) *ukthya* sublates the permanent one; there is no combination (*samuccaya*).

Regarding the statement that "there would be ritual action even in the case of non-consecrated fires" (Sūtra 18), as asserted by the opponent, he replies: "On account of the scriptural injunction. By the force of the scriptural injunction, ritual action—namely the *homa* offering—would take place even in non-consecrated fires, that is, in fires such as the *āghāra* which lack the formal consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*).

There is also a fault regarding the combination (*saṃsarga*). Regarding what was stated in Sūtra 17, "In the case of the *ukhā*, there is a combination of the optional and the obligatory," he says this in response: if there were a combination with the optional fire (*kāmya*) that has been offered from a tree-top while it is blazing, there would be a contact between that fire and the fire used for the sacrificial hearth (*vaihārika*).
Moreover, there would be a fault in their combination;
in that case, an eight-potherd cake would have to be offered to Agni Śuna.
Therefore, there is no conjunction of the optional rite with the obligatory fire, but rather its supersession.
If it is argued that this is due to a scriptural injunction:

if the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) should say that contact with fire is not a fault because of a single scriptural injunction prescribing the maintenance of both the obligatory and optional fires in one and the same pan (ukhā),
then the same would apply to the other case as well.
On this point, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) says:

By the force of the scriptural statement, contact with fire is not a defect; likewise, by the force of that very statement, the oblation (homa) would also take place in the other case—namely, when the fires have not been consecrated and have been merely brought forward.
