Soma should belong to the Brāhmaṇa because of his superiority. Commentary: Regarding this, the meaning is established in that very context—that there is both the state of being preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice and the state of being preceded by the Soma sacrifice.

Now there is a doubt: do all three castes have the option of being preceded by the *iṣṭi* sacrifice or preceded by the *soma* sacrifice; or is it that only the Brāhmaṇa must be preceded by the *soma* sacrifice; or is it that the *Paurṇamāsī* is postponed for the Brāhmaṇa, such that both ritual options apply to him; or is this a separate rite performed after the *soma* sacrifice; or is it that one *havis* is postponed for the Brāhmaṇa, such that both options apply to him? What is the prima facie view? That all three castes may be preceded either by the *iṣṭi* or by the *soma*. Why? Because there is no distinction made.
We do not perceive any distinction whatsoever.
This being the case, we reply:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the Soma sacrifice should come first.
Why? Because of the exaltation (*utkarṣa*).
For an exaltation is heard in scripture: "The Brāhmaṇa indeed has Agni as his deity; having sacrificed with Soma, he becomes one whose deity is Agni-Pūshan.
That very oblation which belongs to the Full Moon sacrifice, he should then offer it subsequently; at that time, he becomes one whose deities are both."
For what speech indeed would one not follow? Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Soma sacrifice must necessarily come first.
Or rather, it is the Full Moon sacrifice [that comes first], because of its connection with the direct Vedic injunction (śruti).
Commentary: Regarding that which was stated—that for a Brāhmaṇa the Soma sacrifice must necessarily come first—in that regard...
For him as well, both alternatives apply.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
Indeed, no specific distinction regarding the two alternatives is recorded for the Brāhmaṇa.
But was it not just stated that there is the superiority of the Brāhmaṇa?
We say: no.
The displacement applies only to the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice.
This is because of the direct scriptural connection (*śruti-saṃyoga*): regarding the *paurṇamāsī*, there is the text, "That which is the *paurṇamāsa* oblation.

Since that which is expressed by the words is authoritative, no logical inference (*nyāya*) can override it; for the principle holds: "When two equal things are mentioned, if one part is displaced, surely the other part must also be displaced."

Because the entire [rite] has a single purpose. The Commentary states: Regarding the claim that "only the Full Moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī) is displaced," in that case, there would be a displacement of the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual.
In this way, there is a connection with the fruit;
otherwise, there would be no fruit, because the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) is only a single part [of the rite].
If only that part were postponed, the remainder performed previously would not yield a fruit.
Because it is only a single part and because it lacks its own fruit, even the highest [part] would not be performed.
However, when the whole is being displaced, the fruit comes into being.
Therefore, by implication, there is a displacement of the whole.
In this way, the entire instruction will become meaningful.
Therefore,
for a Brāhmaṇa, there is the excellence of performing the Soma sacrifice first.
Or rather, it may be an injunction for another purpose.

The Bhāṣya states: This is not the case that there is a transference of the whole; for if a transference of the entire collection were thus postulated in the absence of an explicit statement, then this rite named "Evam-nāmaka" would have to be something entirely different from the Soma sacrifice.
Thus, it will not be necessary to assume an unmentioned result for a single part.
However, the name may apply to both rites as one, just as "akṣa" refers to dice or "pādāḥ" refers to feet.
Or rather, another rite possessing the characteristics of the Paurṇamāsī is being enjoined.
This injunction of ritual action arises from the Vedic revelation; it therefore sublates the [previous] sentence. Consequently, this is a distinct ritual act.
[Duhkha: If the Full Moon sacrifice alone were postponed, the fruit would not be attained.
If both were to be displaced, the displacement of that [latter] would not have been heard [in the text].
Therefore, another rite is enjoined subsequent to the Soma sacrifice;
thus, because it is an injunction of a rite, it is a direct scriptural statement (śruti).
Otherwise, the time subsequent to the Soma sacrifice would be enjoined for the Paurṇamāsī rite;
in that case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), because the sacrifice itself would not be enjoined.
Therefore, due to the injunction of a sacrifice, it is a distinct ritual act designated as "Paurṇamāsī."
Alternatively, the designation [of "both"] is common to both actions; for a Brāhmaṇa, both ritual procedures (kalpas) apply. However, due to the context, it should refer to time.
Commentary: There is no evidence that this is a designation for a different ritual action;
rather, it is directly perceived as a designation for the ritual action under discussion. And that which is supported by evidence is what should be accepted.
[Otherwise] there would be the fault of injustice and lack of purpose.

Furthermore, if one were to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when grasping the term "dharma," that figurative sense would have to be postulated despite the possibility of following the direct literal sense (*śruti*).
Moreover, its specific form is not understood.
Because it is expressed as having a form, it is a different ritual act.
Therefore, the mention of the ritual under discussion by its well-known name must be for the purpose of prescribing the time.
Furthermore, because it possesses a fruit, there is a complete elevation [of the entire procedure].
And the same applies to the Brāhmaṇa passage. As for the claim that [the result] exists because of the scriptural statement and so forth, it is replied:
where no fruit is heard, even in the case of a sentence and the like, [it must be supplied].
Furthermore, there is no mention of a fruit (phala) here.

As for the claim that a fruit must be inferred, such a fruit does not exist without a scriptural statement; in that case, one would have to assume a word expressing the fruit and thereby establish syntactic unity with it.
However, there is direct syntactic unity with the word expressing time.

In the context of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsaprakaraṇa*), that which is heard [in the text] is not capable of establishing a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). Therefore, since the sentence has fulfilled its purpose by enjoining the time for this sacrifice already established, it is incapable of enjoining another ritual action. Furthermore, because it would lead to numerous undesirable consequences, the extension of ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*) has also been explained [as being unnecessary].
When a specific application is possible, it is improper to rely on a common term, as that would result in assigning multiple meanings to a single word.
Therefore, there is an extraction (*utkarṣa*) of the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice.
Consequently, because the fruit is enjoined in connection with that [sacrifice], the *darśa* sacrifice must also be extracted.
The *Parṇamāsī* [sacrifice] is superior to the *Soma* sacrifice, according to the statement of the Brāhmaṇa.
Commentary: The discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) thus far established remains unfinished;
another point of inquiry will be addressed in between by means of the two subsequent sūtras (15–16).
...the reply to what was stated [above]:
It is not the case that the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is postponed;
rather, only the Paurṇamāsī is postponed after the Soma sacrifice.
Why? Because of a scriptural statement.
This statement is: "Whatever oblation is first in the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice, that one should offer subsequently in exactly the same manner.
There is no overburdening for a scriptural statement.

Therefore, only the full-moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī) is displaced. As for the objection that there would be no fruit [for it], the fruit will indeed arise from the aggregate itself; this is known from the scriptural statement. Thus, there is no fault.
Or rather, it is one [offering] that is displaced by virtue of the force of the word, prior to the complete prescription of the Full Moon sacrifice.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, only one oblation is displaced, not the entire Full Moon sacrifice.
Why? By virtue of the force of the word."
One oblation is displaced; the word is capable [of effecting this].
It is heard in scripture: "Whatever is the first oblation of the Full Moon sacrifice. That which is expressed by the verbal statement is brought about by that very statement; nothing else can be so.
Everything prior to the Soma sacrifice is prescribed; therefore, that which is displaced by a specific injunction occurs after the Soma, while that which is not displaced must occur before it.
Consequently, one oblation should be displaced.
For a Brāhmaṇa, both ritual procedures are valid.

Since the postponement of the *iṣṭi* is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, therefore he must have the *Soma* sacrifice first; however, for both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, both [the *iṣṭi* and the *Soma*] are required.
It is not the postponement of the entire *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice.
However, "that very Agniṣomīya sacrifice, which is referred to by the word 'this' (adaḥ),
having been made into an oblation, remains established as something else obtained through the *yathāprāpta* method;
therefore, even for a Brahmin, it would previously have existed [as such], though devoid of that [specific] portion."
Therefore, even in its absence, two ritual procedures (kalpas) [are applicable] for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya respectively;

because the subsequent [word] serves to grasp the intended meaning of that [preceding] word as the basis for excellence (utkarṣa), and because otherwise there would be the contingency of a syntactical split (vākyabheda) regarding the specific location.

Furthermore, the determinant of the objecthood (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*) is not like the sacrificial offering (*havis*) dedicated to the deities Agni and Soma; for otherwise, it would follow that [the *upāṃśuyāja*] would not be performed subsequent to the sacrifice.

Nor is it the state of having those deities, or the state of being a primary sacrifice (*prakṛtayāga*) having those deities; because if "having those deities" were a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), then in the case of its modification (*vikṛti*), where the deity is dependent, it would follow that the status of occurring after the *soma* sacrifice could not be extended (*atideśa*). And if it were a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), then even the *upāṃśuyāja* dedicated to Viṣṇu and Prajāpati would incur the consequence of occurring after the *soma* sacrifice.

However, there exists that property which is the delimitor of the causal efficiency (kāryatāvacchedaka) characterized by the exclusion of Agni and Soma as deities, and which is co-extensive with (vyāpya) the delimitor of the status of being a means to that apūrva. Indeed, such a property exists—namely, the property of being the *ājyabhāga* offering and so forth, which serves the purpose of the *āgneya* sacrifice—in order to avoid deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases where there are optional means such as *vrīhi* rice and the like. This has been stated in their respective sections (3.1.17–18) in the Kaustubha.

Although, in the case of injunctions for preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as threshing, the [property of being produced by Agni] does not enter into the delimitation of the scope of the objective (*uddeśyatā*), because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), nevertheless, here it is necessarily the objective due to the force of the meaning (*arthāt*).

Consequently, since the two properties delimited by being produced by Viṣṇu and Pūṣan do not possess the status of being the delimitors of the objective—given that even their own subordinates (the respective deities) lack the status of being the delimitors of being produced by Agni-Soma, which is the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*—they cannot serve as the delimiters of the objective.

In the case of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), however, there is no contradiction regarding its being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the objective (*uddeśyatā*). This is because the very nature of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—which serves as the delimiting factor for the instrument of the transcendental result (*apūrva*)—is itself the delimiting factor for being produced by Agni and Soma, and it is also pervaded by itself (*svavyāpyatva*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that when a specific qualification (*adhikṛti*) is governed by a single deity, the status of that specific qualification—which is the delimiting factor for being produced by that particular deity—is reduced to a property pervaded by that deity; thus, since the aforementioned state of being pervaded exists, there is no contradiction regarding its being the delimiting factor of the objective.

And here, even though they possess qualities that are not to be adopted [as independent acts], there is no suspicion of their being separate rites, because they are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Maṇḍana says: "These two [rites] belong to Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Brāhmaṇas at the animal sacrifice.
Śaṅkara says: "That [rite] also belongs to the three castes."
That is the alternative view.
In the section concerning excellence (utkarṣādhikaraṇa), the status of the time as a subordinate element of the Soma sacrifice is established.
Bhaṭṭa 5.4.3.
The maxim is that "the superior [seed] bears fruit in inferior soil.
Thus, the worldly maxim is followed by the superior one;
such is the worldly maxim, as for example, the sight of a king reflected in a charioteer.

Thus, regarding inferior objects such as the sun and so forth, one should practice the perception of the superior [Brahman] by thinking, "This sun is Brahman," and not the reverse. This is the principle: "The perception of the superior in the inferior is fruitful" (Śāṃbhā. 4.1.4.1; Vas.).

Nyāyani. 1|3|12|13 Vas.: By the maxim "the inferior is to be viewed through the superior," supported by the scriptural statement, the two occurrences of the word *iti*, and the inference that "only the superior is to be meditated upon because it is directed toward a specific fruit—just like [meditating on] a king and so forth"—the [opposing] argument is refuted.

4|1|4|1 Vas.: Whether Brahman is the primary object or not, since the scriptural authority that "Brahman alone possesses the fruit" is established, the worldly maxim that "one should practice the view of the superior upon the inferior" need not be set aside.
Ābharaṇa. 4|1|4|1 Vas.
X. The maxim of the snake whose coils have been uprooted;
the existence of the world for one liberated while living;
a compendium.

Just as a serpent whose venomous fangs have been extracted no longer harms anyone, so too, once the root [of ignorance] has been destroyed, the world-process (saṃsāra) is no longer capable of causing affliction even though it continues to appear to one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Ke.:
The *prayāja* is a preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*).
Mā. 10|1|17| 14–15: In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *anuyāja* and other rites are performed with the highest voice (*uttamayā vācā*, i.e., loudly).

The injunctive power is set aside by the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*), as in "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) and "O Śukra, I take you for the sacrifice" (*śukraṃ tvā śukryā... yajñapaye gṛhṇāmi*).

Vārttika 2.1.6.13: Mantras possessing the power of injunction through the use of the first person, the word *yat*, the imperative (*āmantraṇa*), and so forth, do not prescribe a subsequent ritual act.
Śabara-bhāṣya on Sūtra 3.1.12.1, p.
649: In the final fore-offering (*uttama-prayāja*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is an injunction of deities based on the wording of the mantra.

From the context, together with the sequence, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) is understood. (Dvādaśalakṣaṇī 10.1.17–18). In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *uttamaprayāja-nigada* is seen to have deities that are common to all [the offerings].
(Bhāṣya 10.1.1).
Excluding the *uttama* (last) day, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is prescribed as ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
This concerns the investigation of the meaning of the statement: "On the subsequent day of the two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*), [the *agniṣṭoma*] is taken. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 9.1.129–32).
Murāri; *Mīmāṃsākoṣa*, p. 130, 1.34:
"In the statement ‘He milks the later ones,’ the milking of all the cows is enjoined."

VI. 1.1.9: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the application of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] occurs only with the two Kakubh verses produced by the first [verse] of the two [verses] beginning with "tvāmiddhi" and "sa tvaṃ naścitra.
Bhāṣya 9.2.6:
[This applies] also to the two subsequent [verses], as stated in the subsequent [section]. 1096. Regarding the subsequent [verses], the same principle holds.

25–28: Regarding the two *uttara* [verses] as well, the chanting (*gāna*) belongs only to the *uttara* of the *kaṇvarathantara*, which is prescribed as the means for the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* in the *vaidya-stoma*, and not to the *uttara* of the *rathantara*.
10|4|23|48–49: The chanting of the two *uttara* verses is performed with the *yonisāman* according to the *uttara-arṇava*.
12|13|1–32: The *yoni* [verse] and the designation of the name are likewise applied to the two *uttara* verses.
In the phrase "Oṃ uttarayogyāyati," by the word *uttara*, there is the inclusion of two verses from the two *uttara-yoni* sections of the *Uttara-grantha*.
But the subsequent status is understood as being occasional due to its immediate sequence;

The Bhāṣya states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they recite: "He sings the Rathantara on the two *uttarā* verses," "He sings the Bṛhat on the two *uttarā* verses," "He sings the Rathantara over the *kavacī* verses," and "Whatever he sings on the *yoni*, that he sings on the two *uttarā*s.
Regarding this, it has been established that [the singing] should be performed on similar verses.

Now, however, this is doubted: whether it is between the *yoni* and the *uttarā*, or between those found in the *Uttarā-grantha*, or whether only those found in the *Uttarā-grantha* are to be adopted?

What is the prima facie conclusion? That there is no fixed rule, because there is no scripture that establishes such a restriction. This being the position, we reply: it is an occasional (naimittika) injunction; therefore, it applies to those [verses] collected in the latter part of the text.
Why? Because of the designation (*samākhyā*) and because they are part of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Uttaragrantha.
[The opponent] says: Even regarding substances, syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than designation and context;
therefore, it follows that there is indeed no fixed rule.
To this it is replied: For all words denoting proximity do not express any meaning whatsoever without depending on another word.
Therefore, another word is required; and that [word] must be either the one under discussion (*prakṛta*) or the one proximate (*saṃnihita*).
Otherwise, a sentence whose meaning is incomplete would be non-expressive of any object whatsoever.
However, when there is the inclusion of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it does not require another word;
its meaning becomes complete through the mere hearing [of that name].
Therefore, the word "proximity" (saṃnidhi) must be understood as that which is to be determined;
it is employed in the subsequent term.
For when technical names (saṃjñās) are being apprehended, there is no requirement for proximity to another word.

Regarding the statement, "One sings the *Rathantara* on the two *uttarā*s," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the word *uttarā* to be a numeral. Thus, from the sentence, "That which is [sung] on the *yoni*, one sings on the two *uttarā*s," it is understood that there are two verses—the *yoni* and the two *uttarā*s.
However, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), [it is understood that] the two verses are those found at the conclusion of the *Uttarā* collection.
And a direct statement (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). (This was stated for the sake of emphasizing this point.

Now he states the ultimate truth: Alternatively, because of the statement "whatever [is prescribed] for the *yoni* [verse], that [applies] to the two following [verses]," it applies to the *yoni* and the two following verses; or rather, it is due to the statement itself regarding what is contained within the *Uttarā* collection.
Therefore, because the word *uttarā* is a numeral, there would be no restriction [as to which texts are meant].

However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word *uttarā* is well-known in common usage (*rūḍhyā*) for a specific book, based on such usage as "the *uttarās* proceed" or "we study the *uttarās*.

[Objection: But it is indeed conventional (*rūḍha*) even in the sense of a number; what then is the distinction? [To this he says: When this [book] called the *Uttara-grantha* is taken, then among those things being taken, because it is a word denoting proximity (*saṃnidhi*), the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) must be expected.
In that case, the cognition is delayed; in the other case, however, it is not delayed.
Regarding the repetition of the same object, the Commentary states:
"And upon those very [verses], the *sāman* found in the *Uttara-grantha* should be practiced."
In this way, the word *tṛca* will have a single meaning. They apply the term *tṛca* by relying on some particular universal (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

When this is stated, if there is a specific number in a particular instance, otherwise all numbers would apply everywhere; for in that case, there would be an absence of conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*).

Therefore, since the term *tṛca* is uttered for those [verses] that have the same meter (*samānacchandaka*) and the same deity (*samānadevatā*), only those included in the *Uttaragrantha* are to be selected. Soma says: "Let it be that in the previous case there was a restriction because of the existence of specific determining factors, such as the particularity of the *saṃśara* and the secondary characteristics; thus, there was the rule that 'the Sāman-singing must be performed only on those with the same meter.
But here, since there is an absence of such specific determining factors, it is said that there is no restriction."

This is the connection with the illustrative example (*prāyudāharaṇa*). If it is argued that, since [the term *yoni*] is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍhatve*), there would be no restriction such that only those *ṛc*s recited in the *Uttaragrantha* as the respective *yonis* are to be taken—and not any *ṛc*s whatsoever found anywhere in the *Uttaragrantha*—because there is no rule to that effect, we say: do not say so. The recitation of the *yoni* in the *Uttaragrantha* is not for the sake of establishing the essential nature of the *yoni*; for its essential nature is already understood from the very fact that it consists of the name of the meter (*chandas*).

Rather, the *yoni* is recited in conjunction with other *ṛc*s precisely so that it may be restricted to those [verses] recited in the *Uttaragrantha* which serve as the *yonis* and their corresponding *uttaras*. Thus, because it functions as a restrictive rule in that very way, [the objection does not hold].

The meaning of the scriptural statement (*śruti*) is as follows: the quality of being "subsequent" (*uttaratva*) is understood to be purely occasional (*naimittika*), based on the name itself; because of immediate sequence, it is perceived as being free from any intervention caused by the requirement of a correlative.
Vi [rtika]: "Whether in the *chandas* or in the subsequent [verse], there would be an ascent of the melody (*gīti*).
Since there is no distinction, there would be an option (*vikalpa*); however, it is otherwise, because it is determined by the name."
Regarding the phrase *uttarayogyāyati* (1097):

there is a doubt as to whether the term *uttara* refers to both [the *yonigāna*] and the two *uttara* verses (in the case of the *Chandoga* and *Tāṇḍya* schools), or whether it refers to the two verses named *uttara* (in the case of the *Ṛk* verses) for the purpose of inferring (*ūhana*) the Sāman chant.

The Bhaṭṭa school maintains: In the rule "He chants on the *yoni*; he chants on the two *uttaras*," the doubt arises as to whether the word *uttara* includes both the *yonigāna* and the two *uttara* verses recited in the *Uttaragrantha*, or only those two *uttara* verses recited in the *Uttaragrantha*.

Since the word *uttarā* (the latter) is seen to function as a term denoting proximity in such instances as "he places the grass-bundle to the north (*uttaram*) of the sacrificial grass" and "he milks the latter cow silently," that which is recited immediately after the *yoni* verse is indeed the *uttarā*.
Consequently, because the *bṛhat*-yoni is recited in the *Yoni-grantha* immediately after the *rathaṃtara*-yoni, the singing of the *rathaṃtara* is performed upon that [latter].

Furthermore, since in the *Uttarā-grantha* the verse "na tvāvān anyaḥ divyaḥ na pārthivaḥ" is recited immediately after the *rathaṃtara*-yoni, the *rathaṃtara* may optionally be sung upon that verse as well.

This being the position reached, [the author states]: In the case of the northern and southern sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) of the *Bṛhadyoni*, the rule regarding the northern milking of cows (*uttaragodoha*) applies; in the *Varuṇapraghāsa* sacrifices, there is a common procedure (*tantra*) for the performers other than the *abhyaryu*.
1112|13|14–42: In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, there is a repetition of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings belonging to the northern and southern sacrificial halls (vihāra).
1112|13|149–50: The word "prior" (pūrva) is conditioned by what follows (uttara), and the word "subsequent" (uttara) is conditioned by what precedes (pūrva).
10|1|4|127: The sequence of the prior member's meaning is established through the operation of the subsequent member's meaning.

In the case of the Citrā sacrifice, regarding the statement "Sarasvatī and Sarasvant [are the deities]," the justification for the sequence of their preparation is that the order of the subsequent elements—namely, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses—is followed; thus, first comes Sarasvatī and then Sarasvant.

(Bhāṭṭa 5.1.7). It will be stated later (5.1.5) that the sequence of the preceding elements is determined by the sequence of the subsequent elements. In the Agniṣṭoma, the *uttaravedi* (high altar) is prescribed during the middle *upasad*.

In the *Saṃkrama* (2.1.26), regarding the *uttaravedi*: among the things to be accomplished, the *uttaravedi* is understood as being independent of ritual consecrations (*śāstrīyasaṃskāra*), namely as a fertile field (*urvarā*). A fertile field is one that yields all kinds of crops.
(*Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa* 10.1.15). The *uttaravedi*.
The latter half of the chapter: the prohibition of the latter half by means of the injunction for the *jarīti* [chanting] ending with the locative case (*paryadhikaraṇa*).
In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, at the *parakhyāga* [offering],
according to Bhāṣya 9.4.13.51–55, the transformation into *āi* occurs only before the vowel *e* at the beginning of the second half [of the mantra].
(Bhāṭṭadīpikā)

By the principle of the *uttarārdha-adhikaraṇa* (1.1.9.47–53), as long as there is a nominative case ending (*prathamā-anta*)—such as in "may life be perfected by the sacrifice" (*āyur yajñena kalpatām*) and so forth—a distinction is established; thus, there is no suspicion that [the number] should terminate at three alone according to the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*.
(Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya 2.1.6.48, p. 128). Furthermore, it is accepted that when other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) exist, even elsewhere, the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* principle does not apply.

For example, in the case of "he places the *iṣṭakā* bricks with the *āgneyī-sūkta*," this mention of the *āgneyī-sūkta* extends as far as it goes, and the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* principle does not operate therein.

Bhāṭṭa 10.6.18: "He offers the initiation-oblations (*dīkṣāhuti*). Here, due to the plural number, there is a distinction between the acts (*karmabheda*). Furthermore, because of the sixfold recitation of the mantras, according to the subsequent principle (*uttaranyāya*), since there is a distinction between the acts, the principle of the *kapiñjala* section does not apply.
10|3|4. With respect to the offering (*tyāga*), the northern half [of the *puroḍāśa*] is subordinate; with respect to the casting [into the fire], it is primary.

Bhāṭṭa 4|1|13. From the northern half, he gives the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion. Bhā. 3|5|4|17. The casting of the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the northern half—or rather, from the whole sacrificial oblation (*havir*)—is not the motive [for the action]; however, the casting of clarified butter (*ājya*) is the motive.
Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*):
Bhaṭṭa, *Mīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya* 4.1.13, the latter half of the chapter.
In the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is not prescribed for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
Because of the connection with that which exists when there is the hearing of a substance from a single part.
The Bhāṣya states: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He cuts off [the portion] for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half.
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Agni the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, while other cakes are not motivators, or is both the case?
What is the prima facie conclusion? "Since there is a single division [of the ritual], all [the priests] should share equally.
This being the position, we reply:
a substance of this kind, when it constitutes only a part [of the whole], would not be the motive for the action.
Why? Because of the conjunction with that which already exists.
An action in one part does not necessitate the whole.
The thought occurs there: "A part of the already existing whole is to be taken up," and not "the whole is to be taken up."
Just as when one says, "Give this man a piece of sugarcane," or "Give him a fragment of a sweetmeat," it is understood that one should not take up the entire sugarcane;

rather, it is understood that one should take a piece from the existing sugarcane, and a fragment from the existing sweetmeat. Therefore, the substance is for another purpose, and its subsequent portion is what should be given.
And there is another purpose for the *puroḍāśa* cake;
therefore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is not the motive [for its preparation].
If it is argued that this is because of the specific designation "from that which has another purpose," [we reply: no.
The Commentary: If you view it thus—that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the *puroḍāśa* cake is not a motive [for its performance]—this is not so;
because that *puroḍāśa* cake is specifically designated for Agni.

Another sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) must be prepared for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, from which the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion is intended to be taken from the northern half. Since that cake has already been dedicated to Agni, the sacrificer does not own it; how then could he give it to another deity? How, then, can there be a designation toward Agni? Regarding this, it is heard in scripture: "The Agnirasa sages, indeed, went from here to the heavenly world; they approached with glory. They said, 'Be dear to the *puroḍāśa*, be dear to Bṛhaspati, be dear to Āditya'; but he was not dear to them. They said to him, 'Be dear to Agni'; then he became dear."
"Since the cake for Agni on eight potsherds is constant at both the new moon and the full moon," therefore it has no connection with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
If this is so, then from that [cake], another substance must be produced by implication.
For there can be no subsequent portion of a substance that is not whole.
[The *Ṭup-ṭīkā* states: Since the entire [substance] is designated for Agni, how could its subsequent portion be joined with the other? Therefore, another substance must be produced by implication.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering belongs to the latter part of that [rite].
No, because of the proximity of the remnant (*śeṣa*).
Commentary: This is not so.
For the remainder is proximate.
That which, when not adopted, would cause the purpose to remain unaccomplished, is implied by the sense of the matter.
And since the remainder is proximate, the taking of the subsequent portion is accomplished.
Therefore, a substance should not be produced from the [intended] purpose.
Whatever substance is already present for another purpose, from that very substance the northern portion (uttarārdha) must be taken.

For it is heard in the scripture that the northern portion is for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, but not that it belongs to "that specific substance," and yet no such practical distinction is made on this basis.
For every [portion] is the latter half of something;
this [latter half] requires what is proximate, and what is proximate is for the sake of another.
Therefore, the sacrifice to Sviṣṭakṛt is performed from that substance which constitutes the latter half.
And for this reason, it is not the motive; as for what was said—that one who lacks mastery is unable to give—that is now addressed.
[End of] the latter half of the chapter.
[End of] the latter half of the chapter.
This general rule is stated for the purpose of providing the remaining details;
it is possible to perform it.
For giving (*dāna*) is indeed the establishment of another's ownership preceded by relinquishment (*utsarga*).
And it cannot be performed by one who lacks authority.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: The phrase "from the subsequent portion" implies that, through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the scriptural mention of the subordinate (*śeṣa*), it impels the principal (*śeṣin*).
And that principal which is thus impelled exists.
And it is not heard [in scripture] that [the cutting] is from the northern part of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Therefore, because they reside in a substance that has already been presented by another, the northern part of the cake and the [act of] cutting are not motivators [for the performance of the rite],
due to the nature of the ritual action.
Commentary: It is heard in the scripture that the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt is caused by the ritual action (karmanimitta).
How so? "The gods said to Sviṣṭakṛt, 'Carry our oblation (havya) [to the gods]. He replied, 'I choose a boon; let there be a portion for me.'"
They said, "Choose!
He replied, "Let me take a portion from the northern part of the *sakṛt-kṛta*.
This is a praise, meaning that this portion belongs to one who performs the ritual action, and it is taken from the northern part.

If it is said that [the horse] is from the northern part of the offering to Agni (*āgneya*), then there exists this similarity with the portion intended for the ritual act: "This is the oblation for Agni which you indeed carry.
Since such similarity exists, the praise is appropriate;
however, if the horse were merely a causal factor (*prayojaka*) and not similar, the consistency of the praise would not be possible.
Therefore, the sacrifice of the *sviṣṭakṛt* for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* is not the motive [for the offering].
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The Commentary states: "There is an indicative mark: 'In that he cuts portions from all the oblations, therefore this food of manifold forms is collected here within the belly.'"

If [the substance] is taken from a material intended for another purpose because it is present, then it is logical that the portion is cut from all [of them] due to the specific circumstance of their proximity. However, if it were the motivator [of the action], the portion would be cut from only one;
therefore, for this reason as well, it is not the motivator.
Likewise, there is this further indicative mark: "He cuts the *iḍā* from the remnant" and "He sacrifices the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the remnant.
Now, one might argue that this should be an injunction;
we say, no.
There is no injunctive suffix here;
for even in the present tense, it is said "this.
Śā— "There is no connection of the oblation intended for Agni with another deity."
"Having made [the offering], the deity of that [oblation] is from the latter part"—thus it is said.
(When it is argued that one should cut off the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion [from the first part],) it is replied:
"Of those [verses] which are recited over the upper placing and which express a meaning requiring completion..."
The meaning is not determined prior to the connection with that which is to be expected;
for even the meaning of one thing may be connected with another through verbal statement and through comprehension, and thus there is no contradiction.
Therefore, from the very oblation intended for Agni and others, the *sviṣṭakṛt* [portion] is taken from the northern part.

Soma: The connection [of this section] is established because of the following counter-argument: whereas in the previous case it was possible to take the white and red parts of the animal (paśu) intended for the heart and other organs—and thus the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering was not a motivator (*aprayojaka*)—in the present case, it is possible to take the upper portion of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) under discussion; therefore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is indeed a motivator.

According to the principle stated in the section on "The Offering of All" (*sarvapradānādhikaraṇa*, 3.4.14), because the entire *puroḍāśa* cake has been made for Agni, the sacrificer possesses ownership over it; consequently, he is incapable of relinquishing it by dedicating it to another deity. Therefore, one should prepare another *puroḍāśa* and offer that other portion from the northern part to Sviṣṭakṛt.
However, in this case, since there is no connection with another deity at the outset, taking the original [cake] is not defective.
Nor is there a contradiction regarding the remnant for Sviṣṭakṛt, as the text states, "He cuts off the Sviṣṭakṛt from the remnant" (*śeṣāt sviṣṭakṛto 'vadyati*), provided another *puroḍāśa* is used.

(Thus it should be stated: "In the passage, 'He causes the remainder to be consumed with clarified butter,' the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the word 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) can logically refer to another sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) within a different ritual action.

If the sentence 'the northern portion' were to convey its own meaning independently, without regard for the connection to the context under discussion, then it would serve as the motivator for a different substance.
But this is not the case."

Because the term "northern half" (*uttarārdha*) is dependent [on another], its meaning is understood through the cognition of its locus as "the northern half of this," which results in the sentence-meaning being established. Thus, when the expectation arises as to "of what?", it refers only to the northern half related to the context—the Agneya cake that is proximate—and not to any other sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: An action such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, which involves a portion of the substance, is not the motivator (*aprayojaka*) because it exists only when the *āgneya* cake and other such items have already been enjoined, due to its connection with them. The commentary (*vi*) states: "Is the *sviṣṭakṛt* the motivator for both the cake and the subsequent portions, or does it depend upon the primary [sacrificial elements] for its own accomplishment?"

[Objection: Since the *uttarārdha* (northern portion) is mentioned in its primary sense [as a part], let it function only as a subordinate element (*upajīvya*) for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) offered to Agni and others. [Bhāṭṭa Reply: In cases such as "He cuts off the *uttarārdha* for the *sviṣṭakṛt*," where there is no mention of the accusative case, there is no evidence for it being a mere disposal (*pratipatti*). Therefore, since the *uttarārdha*—which is heard in the scripture as the source (*apādāna*)—is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) with respect to the sacrifice, the sacrifice is indeed the motivator (*prayojaka*) for that *uttarārdha*.

And since it exists as a correlate, it is quite easy to understand that it refers to some substance whatsoever that is its own counter-correlate. Nor is there a lack of independent expectancy on the part of the present *puroḍāśa* simply because it is a whole (*avayavin*), for the present [topic] concerns the section on the rising, the speech-utterance, and so forth, following the division of the upper half.

Because one's own duty (*svakārya*) is assigned to all [means] through its application elsewhere, there is no restriction; according to the reasoning of Patañjali, the authority of the scripture (*āgama*) arises from the Lord himself. Furthermore, since the knower of the yoga of speech does not depend on [external] comprehension, there is no possibility of the fallacy that [texts such as] "by means of throwing" (*prakṣepeṇāsya*) and so forth would result in being mere false tradition (*apasmṛti*). [This is the flaw in the view of some].
How could comprehension be possible?

Even in the case of the *prakṣepa* (the act of throwing), its status as a *prakṣepa* [is established] by its very nature (*svarūpeṇaiva*), since it depends upon a purpose; furthermore, because if both the subordinate (*guṇatva*) and primary (*pradhānatva*) natures were admitted for the latter half [of the mantra] through a division of parts, the fault of heterogeneity (*vairūpya*) would result. [For example, in the mantra: "Rising, he says, 'O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires!'"—even if one were to admit that this refers solely to the primary action, the use of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) remains unavoidable.

In the mantra "uttiṣṭhan" (rising), the connection is for the purpose of time (*kālārtha*), and not for the act of rising itself; therefore, it is established that the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice is merely a subsidiary act (*arthakarma*), just like the injunction regarding the mantra [for obtaining] progeny and so forth.
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, [in the section concerning rising and the release of speech], he is the prompter (*prayojaka*) of both the latter half [of the sacrificial cake] and its constituent part.

This being the case, it should be understood as follows (Bhāṣya 3.1.4.10): "While rising, he says, 'O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires; perform the vow,' and thus he releases his speech. Even if [the injunction] were merely for the sake of the purpose, nevertheless, because it possesses a correlative relationship, when there is an expectation for a correlate, since it is correlated with the mantra, it does not have the character of an implied reference (*ākṣepa*) therein in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice during the command to spread the fires, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).
And since there is a connection with the subject matter through the act of undertaking [the vow], the mantra is thus consistent.
Furthermore, in the injunction for the giving of the vow consisting of the drinking of milk, the "vow" (vrata) is the remainder;
therefore, it is indeed dependent upon that.

For this very reason, the mantra "śeṣāsviṣṭiṃ kuruta" (perform the sacrifice with the remnants) is applicable; however, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "when rising or when speech has been released" is not appropriate [for that context]. And thus, there is the abandonment of the latter half [of the verse].

Therefore, since an application of two things that are incapable [of mutual relation] is impossible, one must resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indication) out of necessity; even though it is enjoined as a subordinate (*guṇa*), the time is prescribed by accepting the capacity for comprehension residing in the primary (*pradhāna*).
Furthermore, there is no harm in assuming another sentence (*vākyāntara*) in accordance with this, even if the act of throwing into the fire (*prakṣepaśaṃ*) holds primacy.
Even by means of the scriptural injunction for sacrifice, the assumption that it serves as the motivator for retention is set aside by the section concerning rising and the release of speech;
rather, out of fear of prolixity, it is inferred from that very [injunction].
For this reason, it is an inferred instrument (*anumitakaraṇa*).
The section concerning the emission of speech (*vāgvisarga*).

Since it is logical to assume that the very act of rising and the emission of speech serve as the motivators for holding [the breath], this conjunction—being inferred in the absence of a direct injunction—is intended merely to indicate time.
This is according to the principle: "Because of the application of mantras to the act of moving forward (*abhiviharaṇa*) and so forth," since the result of the inference has been perceived.
For this very reason, it is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "he cuts off all the oblations together"—is also consistent because of its primary importance.
For this same reason, even the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt is a subsidiary part of the principal rite; therefore, there is the rising and the dismissal.
[The action] has been completed.

Being thus, the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt is also mentioned therein; the Bhāṣya states: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: 'Rising, he says, "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires. Because there is no difference in the fact that [the action] is to be performed, therefore that [offering] does not belong to the whole, nor to the northern half."
"Perform the vow in such a manner"—thus the instigator utters these words;
however, regarding the throwing of the clarified butter, the instigator releases [the speech] with the words "it shall be so.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the rising [from the vow] and the release of speech already established?
Is the mantra an injunction regarding form (*arūpadeśa*), or is the connection intended for the sake of time (*kālārtha*)?
On this point, Maṇḍana [holds that] the performer [is enjoined] for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

The principle of the previous section (pūrvādhikaraṇanyāya) is extended [by analogy]. In this case, the prima facie view (pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ) is that Śaṅkara holds that the Sviṣṭakṛt offering of the Āgneya and other sacrifices is not a motivator (aprayojaka).
That is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here;

where there is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), that is the established conclusion here. The *rathaṃtara* should be sung according to the syllables of the second half [verse], not according to the syllables of the *yoni*; for it is said, "He recites while rising, saying 'O Agnīdh, kindle the fires! and "Perform the vow! according to the syllables.

Bhāṣya 9.1.132–133: The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the word *uttara* is used here in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*), as in the expression "he releases speech" (*ity evaṃ vācaṃ visṛjati*).

[The opponent objects: "Because there is no etymological derivation (*lakṣaṇābhāvāt*), it is well-known in the text [as a conventional term]: 'the subsequent [part] proceeds' (*uttarā vartate*), 'we study the subsequent chapters' (*uttarān adhyāyāpāmahaḥ*).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the connection is: "while rising, he recites" (*uttiṣṭhan anvāha*).
The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is established by the statement, "One releases speech at the place [indicated] by the rule *vrataṃ kuruta* (ŚB 9.1.1.33).
The final conclusion (siddhānta) is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) according to the principle that "the authority of the sages increases progressively."

And although it is possible— on the grounds that these are stated by Kātyāyana and thus have the human goal as their primary purpose— to say of such [injunctions] as "one who knows the application of speech" (*vāgyogavid*) or "one should rise" (*utthāna*) that "the *āgnīdh* priest should spread the fires," [implying] "he will spread the fires by means of rising," and "fire is enjoined";
or [of the injunction] "perform the vow" (*vrataṃ kuruta*), [implying] "it is the speech that is designated."

Nevertheless, the statement would then have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, if it were assumed that the two mantras serve the purposes of rising and releasing speech, then the other mantra prescribed [for that occasion], "Those which are the bulls of the speech of animals," would be sublated. Moreover, if the two mantras were enjoined with respect to rising and the release of speech, they would both result in having an unseen purpose.
But in the case of sending, the two have a visible purpose;
therefore, it is by way of indication (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the release of speech here, it is proper that either the sacrificer or the bull among the animals [should do so].
Regarding the word "vācaḥ," it is because of the measurement [indicated] by another mantra.

As for "vā"—because it is an *atideśa* (extended application) sūtra, everything should be applied according to its own meaning from the preceding [text]. Soma asks: "What is the purpose of these two mantras in the secondary arising or the release of speech (*vāgvisarjana*)? In the previous case, it was stated that [the mantra] serves the purpose of indicating the time (*kālārthatva*).

And now, as for the application (*viniyoga*): the distinction is that [the mantra] applies to the primary [rite] through the *abhiviharaṇa*, the vow (*vrata*), and the *preṣa* (directions), even though the procedure for crossing over is also present.

Furthermore, because it is not subordinate to anything else, its application is there in the direction for sprinkling the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and in the direction for performing the vow; however, the instruction regarding the mantra was not understood there, whereas here, such is not the case, as the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) exists.
Rather, the connection of the two mantras with rising and the release of speech is for the purpose of indicating the time (*kālārtha*).

By the commentary statement, "The fire is kindled by rising," it is established that "rising" is indicated [as the application], because the two mantras are enjoined for use both in that act of rising and in the utterance of speech.

When this [mantra] becomes an auxiliary to the act of rising due to the direct injunction according to the rule from the previous section (*pūrvatatra*)—"In the case of a meaning [not otherwise obtained], it is by direct statement" (3.1.12)—then, in the absence of a formal command (*praiṣa*), there is no scope for the rules governing commands; rather, its application is restricted to the secondary sense (*gauṇa*) according to the principle of the instrument (*karaṇanyāya*).

And thus, in the case of the *vahniṣva* [praiṣas] (Prāptakālādhikaraṇa, 3.1.11), since the Adhvaryu has moved to the place of measurement (*mānadeśa*), it is impossible for him to perform the spreading of the fires (*viharaṇa*) and the subsequent actions such as the *abhiviharaṇa* without rising from his seat; therefore, these actions must be performed by the Āgnīdhra alone. Consequently, both of those [actions] are intended to be the function of the Āgnīdhra, and thus the act of rising is taught only in a figurative sense (*gauṇyā*). Likewise, the root *kṛ*, meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*), can be made manifest through words such as *amīt*.

Having derived the word *kuṇuta* from the verbal root, since even eating is of the nature of injury (*hiṃsā*), there is the verbal expression "perform this vow" (*vrataṃ kuruta*). [The phrase] "may speech be satisfied by the mixing" means: "Perform this vow consisting of milk, barley, and so forth; eat it. In reality, because of its dependence on speech, the agency in the performance of the vow belongs to the mouth; thus, by means of this mantra, the agency—which is actually the speech containing the emission—is figuratively attributed to the agent. It is possible to express that [agency] through metaphorical usage. In that context, "perform the vow in the morning"—the plural number is appropriate there because of the distinction between the locations such as the palate and so forth. Thus, [this refers to] time.
Furthermore, the plural number is used due to the difference in substrata such as the palate and so forth.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

[The opponent argues: "Just like the *aindrī* mantra, here too, because there is an absence of qualities that could serve as the basis for applying the mantra to secondary meanings (3.1.13), and because there is an absence of the mantra's own qualities, and because of the absence of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the connection understood through syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*) is merely a conjunction for the sake of time; therefore, it is stated that this would result in the mantra serving only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*)."

It is not the case that the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa*) [indicates the agent], because its application is established even by the word itself; rather, the application is primarily determined by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). We shall explain later how this is possible even without the sending of another.
(And this is not the final conclusion.)

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: even regarding the acts of rising and releasing speech, it is possible to perceive both the summoning and the simultaneous observation; the time for the ritual act belongs to you, and not for the attainment of the mantra. Thus, "for in that case the sentence would be split"—this is the indicative mark found in the Bhāṣya on the section concerning the *praiṣas* (3.1.10–11, p. 1126). Some indicative mark is also to be known: (*Su-vi*: "While rising, he says 'I shall praise the Agnis'"; p. 1098). Some indicative mark is also to be known: (*Su*: "Reciting 'Perform the vow,' he releases his speech").

Even in the absence of a direct indicative mark (*liṅga*), the sūtra concerning the absence of secondary qualities (*guṇābhāva*) establishes that the two mantras are to be enjoined as times for the *Āgnīdhra* and the *Agnyanvādhāna*, respectively—namely, the time of rising and the time of speech.

Although they lack the capacity to directly manifest the acts of rising and the release of speech through their primary function, it is appropriate to employ figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the time in the injunction.

Since the capacity exists there due to the non-difference between the meaning of the mantras and the time, and since the scriptural application (*śrautaviniyoga*) is thus established, the injunction itself is capable of removing any doubt.
Due to that impossibility, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication); thus, at that time, the capacity of the portion of the mantra other than the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix is enjoined.

Even though the *loṭ* suffix, which indicates the object of an injunction (*praipaviṣaya*), is possible, Bhaṭṭa-Soma explains it as follows: because of the heaviness (*gaurava*) of the rising and the release of speech, one relies on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the similarity with the act of summoning (*āmantraṇādi*) when saying, "Rising, he recites: 'O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires! and likewise, "Perform the vow," by which he releases his speech.

According to the principle of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices (*vā. 3.1.16*, p. 757), regarding the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* rites: "Having brought forward the *praṇītā* waters, he restrains his speech while about to give the *preṣya* call"; the intention is that this [restraint of speech] and the [use of] mantras should be explained as being for the purpose of the primary acts indicated by the indicative marks of the sūtra.
It is heard in the scripture: "He releases [his speech] along with the *haviskṛt* call.
In that case as well, just as before, the application of the mantras is to the primary acts, and not to the secondary acts of rising and releasing speech.

Even though it is directly perceived, the statement of the Brahmin can be accounted for as a prescription regarding time; therefore, there is no absence of an indicator for a secondary sense (*gauṇa*),
nor is there any contradiction with the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*).
