This discourse [concerning names] is of two kinds: one which praises the purpose or the injunction, such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity";
and another which is a mantra that illuminates the enjoined matter at the time of performance, such as "I cut the barhis-grass, the seat of the gods," and so forth.
Therefore, these terms beginning with *udbhid* must serve one of these purposes.
In that regard, first of all, it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), for it is a supplement to what is to be enjoined; it is not a mantra,
because there is nothing of that kind to be manifested by it.
By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
The quality of being an *udbhid* is enjoined for the sacrifice.
Why? Because it is not apprehended as something already established [as a name], because an injunction of a quality is purposeful, and because it brings about a specific result.
This status of being for the sake of sacrifice is neither understood in common worldly usage nor established by the Veda;
therefore, it pertains to a subordinate quality (guṇa).

If it were an injunction of an accessory (guṇa-vidhi), then the ritual action would not be enjoined. And when the ritual action is not enjoined, the injunction of an accessory therein would be purposeless.
We say: no.

The injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) in the archetype *Jyotiṣṭoma* becomes purposeful [only if it is not a name]. If it were a name, then "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would mean exactly the same thing as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" (*udbhidā yajeta*); no specific quality would be enjoined. And in the case of an injunction of a quality, by virtue of its connection with a quality, it enjoins an additional matter.

Words such as *udbhid* and others will thus possess meaning; therefore, the initial position reached is that they are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). Or rather—once the authority of the Veda, together with tradition (*smṛti*), has been established, and the occasion for explaining the meaning of sentences has now arrived, why is the inquiry into names introduced before the definition of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is finished, and by what connection? Some say: "Are words like *udbhid* a means of knowing a quality, or are they names of actions?"
That is not correct;
for if that were the case, the entire treatise would consist solely of the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For in every case, this is investigated: "Is this sentence an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for this meaning, or for another?

Even those investigators who explain these two sūtras as belonging to a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) by postulating them as the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) positions must state what established conclusion is intended by the sūtra "The Veda is the authority for this" (*uktaṃ samāmnāyaidamarthyam*), which prescribes a meaning consistent with the prima facie view.
For the statement that there is no such thing as "thisness" (*aidamarthya*) regarding the Veda cannot be a non-injunction (*anidharma*) of the *udbhid* and other such terms.
Therefore, this pair of sūtras should be explained as the *uttarapakṣa* (concluding arguments) for both of the aforementioned *adhikaraṇas*, whose *pūrvapakṣas* have been inferred.

Therein, first of all, taking the *udbhid* and others as examples, a doubt is raised: do these serve a purpose regarding *dharma*, or not? What, then, is the initial position (*prāpta*)? [The answer is: they are useless, because "the Veda has action as its purpose" (*āmnāyasya kriyārthatvāt*).

And it is said: "Because the Veda is the sole authority for dharma, [words like] *udbhid* and so forth would be redundant; [otherwise], they would result in meaninglessness due to denoting things not useful for dharma. (The meaning is that because they denote things not useful for dharma, they would result in meaninglessness.)

In the reading "the dharmas are not employed," the meaning is that because they are [merely] names, they attain a state of pointlessness (*anarthakya*) that exceeds [the utility of] the Veda. (Sudhā, p. 313). Indeed, these do not fall within the scope of injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth, because they do not convey the objective (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). To that extent, they are not denotable by *codanā* (Vedic injunction), as there is an absence of the cognition of them through direct revelation (*śruti*). They are distinct from *arthavādas* (laudatory passages) because they do not function as indicators of the nature of ritual acts (*karmāśraya*). Since they lack factual correspondence (*yathārthatva*), they fail to fulfill the function of a mantra. And since there is no other purpose for the Veda [in their case], those of this class are indeed non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*).
Thus it is said.
To this, it is replied:
"Because the entire Veda consists of three parts, according to the reason already stated..."

The first point—that the *udbhid* and so forth lack the status of authoritative means of knowledge—is established; however, this is indeed undesirable, as it contradicts [the opponent's] own position.
Furthermore, because the specific [quality] is already established, the name will not be prescribed as an injunction, and thus [the opponent's argument] collapses.

And when, by some means or other, words such as *udbhid* are established as denoting specific [substances], then, because they would necessarily denote a universal that is inseparable from something else [the sacrifice], the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice") would become redundant.

Furthermore, there would be parsimony (*lāghava*) if the injunction were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), since it would be an injunction following upon the mention of the sacrifice (*yāgānuvāda*).

If this is so—that because of the presence of a quality, the injunctive power [of the sentence] does not enjoin an action—then an action is not enjoined; and if the action is not enjoined, of what would the quality be enjoined? Thus, [the sentence] would be meaningless. Therefore, he says (in the Bhāṣya): "In the archetype, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma."

Now, if it is argued that under the view of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the phrase "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" would also be directed toward that [quality], and thus the ritual action would remain unenjoined; we reply: since there is no other way to understand it, this will be a single injunction of the ritual action.
Furthermore, once that [action] is excluded, it is impossible to enjoin a quality through an injunctive word; therefore, the word *Jyotiṣṭoma* alone is the name.

Alternatively, that one [injunction] is the prescription of an action qualified by a quality (*guṇa*), while the others are prescriptions of qualities by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to an existing action.

But if this is so, then all injunctions regarding the *ekāha*, *ahīna*, and *satra* sacrifices would not be distinct from the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself, since they would fall within its context (*prakaraṇa*) as mere prescriptions of its qualities.
Thus, because there would be no separate actions, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* could in no way be the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Thus, according to some, by the word "that" (tat) [in the phrase *tad uktvā*], the name itself is intended; this is according to the view of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), as indicated by the word "he said" (*āha*).
Alternatively, it is called the "archetype" (*prakṛti*) because it is being performed (*prakriyate*); the meaning is that the Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion is the archetype.

Alternatively, since terms such as "Now this [is] Jyotis" (*athaiṣa jyotiḥ*) lack any connection with an instrumental case-ending—which would indicate the status of an accessory (*guṇa*)—they cannot function as injunctions of accessories; therefore, they unilaterally serve as names of rites (*karmanāmadheya*). And in relation to those, the Jyotiṣṭoma is the archetype (*prakṛti*). [Objection: But surely, because the Jyotiṣṭoma is already occupied by Soma or by the Jyotiṣṭoma itself as part of its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), it is improper to enjoin other accessories within it.
[Reply: Because they are optional (*kāmya*), rites such as the Udbhid will act as superseding factors (*bādhaka*).

And because in the case of a permanent application (*nitya-prayoga*), the purpose belongs to the original quality (*pūrvaguṇa*) alone; or else, even though the rite is enjoined with specific qualifications, if one extracts its mere essential form (*svarūpamātra*) and enjoins it with another quality, it does not differ from the original (*autpattika*), since otherwise no other course is possible, and thus [the opponent] considers that there is an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, it would be a name (*nāmadheya*), because it is not injunctive of something new at the time of the origination [of the rite].
The Commentary: This being the case, we reply. By the word "also" (api ca), the previous position is overturned. We maintain the thesis that this is a name (nāmadheya).
In this way, it will prescribe a sacrifice other than the Jyotiṣṭoma for a purpose not already established;
the direct Vedic statement (śruti) will denote a distinct sacrifice.
Otherwise, the direct Vedic statement [would have to denote] the Udbhid and so forth.

One who intends to speak [of the word *udbhid*] would indicate that it possesses the quality of being "udbhid" by means of the sacrifice, as in "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice *udbhid*.
The meaning of the term *yajeta* (one should sacrifice) is "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice.

For the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and since *udbhid* and so forth are also indicated with the instrumental case ending, they too are instruments. In that context, the coordination is consistent through the status of *udbhid* as a name of the ritual action, as in "by means of the *udbhid*-sacrifice."

If it were a word denoting a substance (*dravyavacana*), there would have to be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the indication of the possessive suffix (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*). And when there is a choice between direct statement (*śruti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is more authoritative.
Therefore, it is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).
[Objection: Would one not be abandoning the well-established status of denoting a substance and asserting the unestablished status of denoting an action?
[Response: It is said: its status as denoting an action follows from the indication by the third case ending.
Why? Because the third case ending occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes an instrument; how then could it not denote a sacrifice?
Therefore, one might infer from this that it expresses a sacrifice.
This is not correct.
If, upon the mention of the instrumental case, the cognition of a sacrifice were to arise from words such as "udbhid," then this might be so;
however, it is not our cognition that is being stated here, and therefore [your position] is incorrect.
If you argue that the use of the instrumental case would otherwise be inexplicable, let it remain inexplicable if you wish.
It will never be expressive of a sacrifice even when [the connection] is not understood;
therefore, it must be an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).
And if it were a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) [of the sacrifice], [it would be improper].
"Better that there be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or a forced interpretation (*haṭha*), rather than the postulation of something not established.
Furthermore, if it were the name that is being enjoined, then it would not be a sacrifice;
if it were the sacrifice, then it would not be the name; and if both were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
It is said: the name will not be prescribed as an injunction;
for "udbhid" and the others are merely restatements (anuvāda).

Why? If it is argued that [the name] is due to attainment (*prāpti*), then it is replied: because of the capacity of the word *ud* and the capacity of the word *bhid*, the word *udbhid* denotes an action.
Since the manifestation (*udbheda*) or disclosure (*prakāśana*) of cattle is performed by means of this, the sacrifice is called *udbhid*.
Thus, from the conquest of the quarters comes the Abhijit; from universal conquest comes the Viśvajit.
This applies everywhere.
Therefore, these are names of rituals.

It might be argued that [a word] which does not produce a specific modification in the performance of an action is meaningless; however, even a name is meaningful by virtue of its connection with a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, it is established that words of this class are names of actions (*karma-nāmadheya*).

Alternatively—that is to say, when at the time of origin (*utpatti*) in the first instance, a word such as *udbhid* is not definitively established as denoting something other than an action, then, because it occurs first in Vedic usage, it must be a name by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Alternatively, by enjoining a previously unknown action (*apūrva*) in this manner, it will become purposeful.
Or rather, the doubt as to whose name [this is] is being addressed:
it belongs to that from whose origination the *apūrva* is accomplished; that is to say, it belongs to the sacrifice.
What is the reason?
"For an attribute being enjoined must pertain either to the fruit or to the action;
or it would be understood as a qualified injunction—but in every respect, [this] is not tenable."

First, regarding the injunction with respect to the fruit (*phala*), there are the following defects: the injunction of a connection with another word, the postulation of an intervention (*vyavahita-kalpanā*), the subordination of the verbal root (*dhātu*) to another purpose, the loss of the inherent meaning of both [the root and the suffix], and the fact that sacrifice (*yāga*) would be understood through the *laṭ* suffix and other such forms which are entirely unestablished in that sense.
Likewise, regarding the injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇa*) with respect to the sacrifice, the word for the fruit becomes meaningless.

Furthermore, if it were intended as a qualification of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* already established by the principle of universal desire (*sārvakāmya*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), remoteness from the operation of the suffix (*pratyaya-vyāpāra-viprakṛṣṭatā*), and the highly improper option between the verbal root, its derivative meaning, the non-edible, the sacrifice, and the Soma vessel.

Likewise, in the case of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there are the following defects: the subordination of everything [to the qualified object], the postulation of multiple injunctive powers (*vidhiśakti*), the figurative indication of the sense of possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the abandonment of the understood grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and the sacrifice of something unfit for consumption.
Therefore, it is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
This is shown by the Bhāṣya: "Otherwise, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would denote [the names] *udbhid* and so forth" (the reading in the Bhāṣya is *khani* and so forth).

And just as there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* [in the word *yāga*], so too would the nominal stem (*taddhātu*) [denoting] sacrifice be indicated [by the suffix].

(The commentary shows another reading for the word *śastra*: "or it would be indicated by the form *vakṣyantī*"). Having explained the capacity of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), he demonstrates that this very same point is understood even from the connection with the case-ending (*vibhakti*) by means of the passage beginning with "one should effect [the result] by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*).

Furthermore, in such passages as, "In both an injunction and a restatement, since the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the word ending in the third case [denoting that] situated near it does not lose its expressive power" (Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa 3.1.6.2, p.

679), because it is accepted that the *kārakas* are the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), how can it be said that "[the suffix arises] from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting the instrument"? This is not a fault.
The intention is that [the suffix] indeed denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Alternatively, whatever meaning the word "instrument" expresses, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the very signifier of that.

For by means of a *kṛt*-derived form, it is the substance (*dravya*) itself as qualified by its functional capacity (*kāraka*) that is expressed, and not the isolated power (*śakti*), as is the case with a case-ending (*vibhakti*).

And likewise, the connection with other *kārakas* is observed in such expressions as "the instrument by means of the instrument" (*karaṇaṃ karaṇena*) and "for the sake of the instrument" (*karaṇāya*).

Otherwise, since a substance would be controlled by only one *kāraka* already expressed by its own case-ending, it could not enter into a connection with another *kāraka*. For a capacity (*śakti*), however, there is no other capacity.

Therefore, since verbal derivatives (*kṛdanta*) denote a substance qualified by a capacity (*śakti*), it is established that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses the meaning of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
By this, the following is stated: the third case suffix must arise from that nominal stem which denotes the instrument in this sentence.
And it will be explained later (2.1.12) that in this context, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the instrument for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of the result, not the substance (*dravya*).

Mīmāṃsākośa 142: Consequently, the word *udbhid* denotes the sacrifice; thus, being in the instrumental case-ending, it will form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). However, if it were to denote a different object, it would be incoherent. But [it may be argued]: "The fact that it directly denotes a substance has been presented; how then [can it denote a sacrifice]?"
It is sublated by the inference of its being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), as in the case of the *vrīhi* and *homa* offerings.

Just as in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with *vrīhi* grains" and "one should sacrifice with *soma*," the use of the instrumental ending is not contradictory even when there is a difference in grammatical coreference (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—since these are sentences where the sacrifice itself functions as the instrument—so it is here as well.
The term "*haṭha*" refers to a green substance that has long covered the water of an ancient pond.
Just as that [water], even while being pushed aside, repeatedly covers the water again by its own will,
so too any other independent activity is known as *haṭha*.
This is what is said:

"From the cognition of the word 'lotus,' there arises doubt; however, through well-known [synonyms] heard separately, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indicated. Once it is firmly established, it is determined that the primary meaning is not discarded."

For words such as *vrīhi* (rice) are extremely conventional (*atyanta-rūḍha*); since they cannot attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) without abandoning their own primary meanings, and because there is no other recourse, they are understood as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

However, as for those like *udbhid*, which are etymological (*yaugika*), it is possible for them to denote an action (*karman*) by the very same means through which they denote a substance (*dravya*). Thus, while direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) remains indifferent [to the matter], it is not improper for inference (*anumāna*) to dispel ignorance and doubt.
For this is the means for retaining the meaning of all words: namely, well-known grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Furthermore, the primary instrument in the sacrifice, having acquired its own nature, is able to cause the nominal stem to take itself as its object. Moreover, "Because there is a restatement of the meaning of the case-ending, there would be brevity in the injunction regarding the name."
The status of being that which is to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*) belongs to the quality (*guṇa*), as well as to number and the grammatical relation (*kāraka*).
For on your view, one would necessarily have to assume a certain injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) of the suffix even with respect to the meaning of the case-ending.
Therefore, by way of its constituent parts, there is established usage (*prasiddhi*) for [the term *karman*] even in the sense of the object (*karman*).

If it is argued that even the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices would incur this name because they too bring about the manifestation of their own results, we say no; for the specific object [of this term] is determined by its grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "knowledge" (vidyā), which explains its constituent parts.
Furthermore, there is no syntactic co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) of this term with the Jyotiṣṭoma and the like.

Alternatively, by the force of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), this very act of "piercing" (*udbhedana*)—which has this specific [act] as its object—is the cause, and there is no other such thing; thus is the determination established, just as the word "cow" (*go*) has as its cause the specific act of moving with the nose lowered (*sāmānādagragamana*).
The explanation of the phrase "because it is not injunctive" (*avidhāyakatvāt*) is: "it will not enjoin a name.
[The cognition arises] in the form of a relationship between a name and the named.
Section 1.1.1: The *udbhid* Topic.
In this *udbhid* topic, there is weakness because it depends on another word expressive of the thing to be enjoined (*uddeśya*).
The third [type] consists of those that enjoin a *bhāvanā* (efficient force) with another instrument (*karaṇa*) while indicating the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*),
such as "He offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).
Here, because the status of being enjoined does not reside in the meaning of the verbal root, but rather in something else, it is even weaker than the former.

The fourth [type of injunction] is the injunction of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) wherein one thing is performed for the sake of another, while accepting that the verbal root has the sense of "being correct" (*sādhutva*).
An example is: "One desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*).
Here, because the meaning of the verbal root is not proximate even as the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*), it is weaker than the previous case as well.
The fifth [type of injunction] is the prescription of a cultivation (bhāvanā) characterized by a specific quality and a specific instrument,
such as "one should sacrifice with Soma.
Because it involves the additional assumption of an injunction for a qualification, it is weaker even than that [the preceding type].
The aforementioned [offering] is for the sake of another,
as in: "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya."
But this [interpretation] is the weakest of all.
Thus, if one were to enjoin a sacrifice qualified by the attribute *udbhid* for the sake of a result, there would be excessive complexity due to having to resort to six types of methods;
furthermore, because the attribute would not be syntactically connected to the sacrifice, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the possessive sense (*mattvartha*).

For when the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) is already occupied by the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*)—an object denoted by the same word—the status of being the instrument cannot belong to a subordinate element (*guṇa*).

Therefore, if one were to assume that this [subordinate] is connected to the sacrifice, a connection between the sacrifice and a *kāraka* (syntactic factor), as well as a mutual connection between *kārakas*, would be impossible; thus, in the case of "one should sacrifice with *soma*," the possessive indication (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*)—namely, "by means of a sacrifice characterized by *soma*"—would necessarily result.

However, in reality, even in the example, the connection of *soma* with the *bhāvanā* occurs through its status as the instrument, and this will be explained there [in the section on *soma*]; moreover, it is logical.

Even though the instrumentality [of the sacrifice] is already occupied by a single instrumentality, it is possible for another distinct form of instrumentality to be understood as a qualifier (*prakāra*) within the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
For the instrumentality of the sacrifice is not defined by the productive urge itself, but rather by heaven (*svarga*).
Therefore, just as that instrumentality—though defined by something else—is connected to the productive urge as a qualifier, so too is the instrumentality of *soma* defined by the sacrifice.
In both cases, since the one who determines the truth is understood through a partial cognition, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Although in this view there is no possessive indication (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*), nevertheless, the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the assumption of a separate injunction for the qualifier and so forth—which would entail an injunction of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by both the accessory (*guṇa*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*)—cannot be dismissed.

And just as there is a possessive indication in the form of "both" (*ubhayetā*) even when the form [of the word] is intended for the purpose of connecting with the efficient force of each individual, so it has been stated in the *Kaustubha*.

Thus, even in the second and third prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), accepting the method of the lowest injunction (*jaghanya-vidhi*) leads to a fault. Furthermore, in the case of the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and the curd-oblation (*dadhi-homa*) and so forth, that [method] is accepted precisely there;
for since those terms are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in those specific senses, it is impossible for them to function as names (*nāmadheya*).

In the present case, however, just as there is an engagement with the digging by means of a particular method (*yoga*), so too the fruit is "broken open" or produced by that very same method; thus, by way of etymology, [the term *karman*] applies even to the object. Consequently, because it serves as the basis for the second injunction through its connection with the name, there is simplicity (*lāghava*).

Nor is the verbal root *bhid* restricted in its expressive power (*śakti*) solely to "cleaving," since the root is listed in the Dhātupāṭha simply as *bhid*. This is because the grammatical consensus (*siddhānta*) is well-known among scholars that the mention of "cleaving" is merely an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its potential meaning.

Therefore, because the term is used even in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇa*) as well as "taking up" (*upādāna*), its application is equal [to both]. Nor does it have the meaning of a name (*nāmadheya*), because it serves a purposeful function through the act of mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Furthermore, there is an instance where the action is performed without a specific fruit, such as: "Having completed the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, one offers the *Vaiguma* on the full moon day."
And in the present case, the purpose is precisely the injunction of a distinction in number.

For otherwise, since there would be the addition of a quality and a fruit to the very action under discussion, it would not constitute a separate action. Nor does the assumption of a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) for a new action follow from the fact that the etymological sense (*yoga*) of "causing the emergence of a fruit" is over-extended; for if all terms were both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*), the cause for such an assumption would have to be established as prior usage, which is not assumed here.
The purpose [of this discussion] is clear.
Śaṅkara: "And the status of being a name belongs to *udbhid* and others.
In the *udbhid* section, the status of being a name is accepted in order to avoid the implication of possessive indication (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*).
Soma.

Page 70, line 11416: In the *Udbhid-adhikaraṇa*, it is established that both qualities (*guṇa*) and ritual actions (*karman*) can be denoted by words through their etymological derivation from their constituent parts; furthermore, regarding terms such as *udbhid* which are not found in other [standard] treatises, there is an inquiry as to whether they are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*).

Kau. 11412, p. 188. However, in the case of a construction involving *vaiyadhikaraṇya* (different grammatical coreferentiality) with *udbhid*, there are two possibilities: either a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the fruit, namely "one should effect the fruit by means of a quality residing in the sacrifice," or a prescription of a quality for the ritual action (*karma*), namely "one should perform the sacrifice by means of a quality. In both cases, because the root *yaj* lacks a connection between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), and because one must set aside what is expressed within the same word (*samānapadopāttatva*) to prescribe a quality expressed in a different word (*bhinnapadopāttaguṇa*), the quality would be subordinate to something else; this constitutes the fault of "confusion of the prescriptive and the prescribed" (*vidhividheyaviparyaya*).

On the other hand, it is established that in the case of a prescription of a quality for the ritual action, there is a syntactic connection with the word denoting the ritual action (*karmapadānvaya*).

[Objection: It is not [correct] to say that the Kṛṣṇajayantī is optional (kāmyā) because it is understood to have a connection with a fruit; for, as in the cases of the Citrā and Udbhid sacrifices, since there is a connection with a fruit independent [of other rites], this would result in a difference in performance (prayoga-bheda). Furthermore, in the Udbhid-adhikaraṇa, it is untenable to suspect that the name [Udbhid] is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).
In the *Guṇakaraṇikābhāvanā* (the meditation on that which has a quality as its instrument), the meaning of the verbal root is construed as the object (*karman*);
this is the instruction regarding the *udbhid* section in the *Udvāha*.

But it is not [denoted] as an instrument (*karaṇatva*), because that would result in a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) contrary to the primary meaning. This has been established in the *Udbhid* section (*Kauṭilīya* 2.1.16, p. 198). Nor does the name "Agnihotra" produce a cognition characterized by a mode of offering belonging to a different class; for otherwise, there would be no occurrence of the same syntactical application (*samānaprayoga*) with other instances of the root *hu* (as in "he offers the Agnihotra").
Rather, [the capacity to produce cognition] belongs to the word *udbhid* precisely as a non-differentiated act of sacrifice (*homatva*).

Since the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) was established in the *Udbhid-adhikaraṇa* by the very absence of ancient usage, a combination of etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*) is not admitted.
(PMS 1.4.124, p. 80). Furthermore, the connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) when [the word] functions as a name is explained in the *Udbhid-adhikaraṇa*.

114|11 (p. 158): Even in passages such as "fifteen others," since the injunction of a substance qualified by a number—by way of restating the ritual realization (*bhāvanā*) of the hymn—is subsequent to the connection with the primary *bhāvanā*, it has been established in the *Udbhid* section that this constitutes a "qualified injunction" (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

114|13 (p. 185): Although in all cases there is an injunction of a qualified *bhāvanā* based on what is perceived, the sixfold methods [of differentiation] explained in the *Udbhid* section are established solely through the distinction of the objects [of the fruit].
Furthermore, it has been stated that their relative weakness increases progressively.
2|1|1 (p. 198): The extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics of Soma sacrifices to unmanifest sacrifices such as the *Udbhid* and others.
Bhāṣya 8|1|12–16. Sacrifices such as the *Udbhid* must be performed only after having completed the *agniṣṭoma* form, even though they occur subsequent to the first day of the *atirātra*.

Bhaṭṭa 5|1|13. Furthermore, regarding those words such as *udbhid* which are etymological (*yogika*), since their status as denoting a substance (*dravyavacanatva*) is established by the very same manner in which their status as denoting an action (*karmavacanatva*) is also established, it is not improper to dispel ignorance and doubt through inference for those who remain indifferent despite [the matter] being established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddha*).
Or: [See] Vāla. p. 141. In cases such as *udbhid*, the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is set aside by the direct denotation (*śruti*) of the name.
This is because, in the section concerning explanatory passages (*arthavādādhikaraṇa*), the general authority of names such as *udbhid* has already been established.

*Soma*, 1.2.1, p. 13. Having rejected the view that words such as *udbhid* and others—which are etymological (*yaugika*)—are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) due to the fault of implying possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), it was established [in *Sūtra* 2.1.1–2] that they are names of rites (*karmasaṃjñā*) because their application is possible through etymology (*yoga*) with respect to the ritual action. *Ku.*, 1.4.14, p. 99. The authority [of the Veda] is established by the fact that words such as *udbhid* are names of sacrifices (*yāganāmatva*). *Vi.*, 1.4.1. It was established that words such as *udbhid* serve the purpose of religious duty (*dharmopayoga*) by virtue of being names, based on their usage as well-known technical terms among practitioners of sacrifice (*yājñika*).
Su. Pṛ. 390. Regarding the *udbhid* [example]:
In passages such as "Now this is the Jyotis," there is, according to your own position (the Siddhāntin), no evidence whatsoever for the establishment of doubt.

First of all, the *udbhid* [example]—namely, the *Udbhid-Adhikaraṇa*—does not apply because, being a conventional term (*rūḍha*), it lacks the quality of having multiple simultaneous applications (and thus, where there is a conventional term with multiple simultaneous applications, that is the scope of the *udbhid* example).
PMS 2.1.12 (p. 250): "One desiring to perform malevolent magic (*abhicaraṇa*) should sacrifice with the *śyena*.

In this case, because there is no *mattvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of the sense of possession) based on the syntactical relation (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—namely, that one should effect the killing of an enemy by means of the *śyena* which is an instrument for the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice—the word *śyena* is already firmly established (*nirūḍha*) as referring specifically to a particular bird. Since the word *śyena* is not well-known in any way whatsoever as denoting a ritual action, the *udbhid-nyāya* does not apply here.

Ku. 114|15, p. 97: Regarding the statement, "One desiring the Vājapeya should sacrifice with the Vājapeya," this [section] is commenced to challenge and then resolve the status of the term *vājapeya* as a name (*nāmadheya*), even though its status as such is established through the method of *udbhid*.

114|16, p. 98: In the case of the *Āgneya* and other [offerings]—such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni"—since there is no other scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) regarding them, and because the status of being a name for the ritual action is not well-known, it is possible for them to be the subject of the *udbhid*-method, which consists in having an equal application in both respects.

Kau. 114, p. 211: In the case of the passage "one practicing sorcery [should sacrifice] with a hawk" (*śyenābhicaran*), [the word *śyena*] is not established as a name (*nāmadheya*) because it functions through its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), just like *soma*, *dadhi*, and so forth. Kau. 114, p. 214: Furthermore, the status of *samit* as a name is not established by the principle of "being distinguished" (*udbhid-nyāya*), because there is an absence of equal application (*tulyavad-vṛtti*) in both cases.

Vi. 114.3, p. 430. At the conclusion of the rite (*udghāpana*), there is the completion of the vow (*vratasamāpti*).

The instruction regarding the *udvāha* [is given].
In the section on the fire-altars (agniprakaraṇa), regarding the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings that have arisen, it is stated: "One offers these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* [oblations];
[they are] for the rites of marriage" (11.3.4); thus, even though it occurs at the beginning [of the section], it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating that one offers them.

(*Poḷā*, *bendūra*—so it is called in the vernacular).
