The attainment of the meaning of a word occurs only by way of being subordinate to the benefit [of another]. Bhāṣya 3.7.1.22;
Even an action becomes something to be accomplished by action through the form of assistance; for that [status of being a subordinate] is characterized by assistance.
Vārttika 3.1.1.20.
Indeed, that [status of being a subordinate] has assistance as its defining characteristic.
That which assists something is subordinate (*śeṣa*) to it.
Bhāṣya 3.1.12.
When a direct assistance is possible, it is illogical to assume an indirect assistance.

When there is an extension of the auxiliary benefit (upakāra), modification (ūha) is then conceived; for example, in the archetype (prakṛti), having taken the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) and ending with the gratification of Brahmins, one considers how these will provide assistance.
Bhā.
It is that which is beneficial.
For indeed, no substance that does not provide benefit can belong to anything else.

Thus, the Commentator will state in various places in the Upaniṣad: "That which benefits something is its subordinate (*śeṣa*)," and "That which exists for the purpose of benefiting something is called subordinate" (p. 658). "Upa..."
"The character of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) consists in being a cause" (PMS 3.1.12), and so forth.
Vārttika 2.1.2.12, p. 656: For that which is heard as being helpful to the primary (*pradhāna*) is also helpful when it remains within a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of that [primary].
"Furthermore, it is the practice of the virtuous that those who provide assistance must be assisted. (Vākyapadīya 1.2.12, p.
The introduction (upakrama) is more powerful than the conclusion (upasaṃhāra),
because it is not yet contradicted by anything else.
Furthermore, the introduction often takes the form of a question.
As in the example: "What is the name of this river? What is the name of this mountain? What is this fruit? (Bhāṣya 2.3.4.11).

When a sentence begins with a general statement, that beginning is established as referring to a specific [object] by the force of the conclusion (*nigamana*), because the conclusion serves to provide that specific detail which was left unexpressed by the beginning.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 529). A sentence begins with a general statement that requires a specific [qualification], and it is by the force of the conclusion that it is fixed upon a specific [object].
Bhāṣya 1.4.1.24: Following the introduction (upakrama), which is stronger because no contradiction has yet arisen, the conclusion (upasaṃhāra) must be interpreted in accordance with it. Vi.
3.1.15: Some hold that the conclusion is stronger than the introduction because it serves as its explanation;
for an explanation is necessarily posterior.

Regarding *parākrama* 71: some maintain that, according to the principle of the "simultaneous cutting" (*apacchedanyāya*), the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) is stronger than the introduction (*upakrama*). However, there is no need for an introduction that has already attained self-sufficiency (*nirākāṅkṣa*) to follow the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*), as established in the section [of the *Tantravārttika*] beginning with "by a word whose own meaning is connected" (2.3.7–8). Regarding the superiority of the introduction, some argue it is due to its lack of prior contradiction; yet others hold that this is not universally true, because the initial impression arising from the first hearing (*āpātajapratyaya*) does not necessarily prevail.
72. Where there is no expectation for the introductory statement (*upakrama*), there one does not follow the subsequent conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) even if it is contradictory to it.

442. Since the introductory statement is determined to have the Veda as its subject matter, it is appropriate that the words *ṛc* and so forth occurring in the conclusion function in accordance with it.

(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 523). When the introductory statement gives rise to doubt, the conclusion is the cause of determination, as in the passage: "One places the smeared pebbles; ghee is indeed brilliance," and so on.
Even following the *arthavāda* situated at the beginning, the primary [injunction] is also to be interpreted in three ways; this is the principle of the *upakramādhikaraṇa*.

However, if there are mutually dependent *arthavādas* and injunctions that are internally contradictory and occur both at the beginning and the conclusion, then "relying on which one should one interpret the other?"

Regarding the doubt expressed in the *Upakramatantra* (1135) concerning the section on "commencement" (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), the logical structure of the principle found in the context of commencement is as follows:

Since the arising or the operation of a subsequent cognition is independent of its predecessor, it is not tenable that the destruction of a sublated cognition should occur through the sequence established by the commencement [of the latter].

It is said that since both the injunction (*vidhi*) and the mantra function only through mutual dependence, the principle of the superiority of the injunction occurring at the beginning (*upakrama*) is indeed appropriate;
this is stated in the *Sanātanadharma-pradīpa*, Vivāha, p.
192, according to the maxim that within a single sentence, the conclusion must be consistent with the introductory portion (*upakrama-tantra*).
Nyāyamālāvistara 2.3.2.92:

The principle of the subordination of subsidiaries (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*) is an exception to the principle of the opening statement (*upakramanyāya*), as seen in passages such as "He who [desires] with the *iṣṭi*," and so forth. In reality, however, even the principle of the opening statement does not apply there; for the injunction, which is vast in its verbal meaning, is directed toward the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of all matters by the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). Since this has been established in the section concerning the determination of context (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*), the words "iṣṭi" and so on function merely as restatements (*anuvāda*), and thus that [principle of the opening statement] is absent.

*Kau.* 3.1.12, p. 313: Since there is no requirement for a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), even perceptual error does not require the Śruti; thus, because there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the principle of the opening statement (*upakramanyāya*) has no application here.
*Advaita.*, p. 355:

Even though the principle of the conflict between a subordinate and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*) sets aside the principle of the opening statement, one should observe that the establishment of the present doctrine is accomplished only by means of that which possesses primacy (*prādhānya*).

Some (Śaṅkarabhaṭṭas), in order to establish this [sentence concerning the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, etc. as an example of a conflict between a subsidiary and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*), assert that the sentence-rule (*vākyanyāya*) alone applies to the *iṣṭi* sentence, etc., and thus claim there is an absence of the principle of the opening statement (*upakramanyāya*). That is rejected;
for since it is more appropriate to assume a single sentence (*ekavākya*) due to the lack of connection [otherwise], there is no evidence for accepting their position.

Furthermore, although it appears from that text that when there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the principle of the opening statement (*upakramanyāya*) alone prevails, whereas in its absence the principle of the conflict between a primary element and a subordinate quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*) applies—this [view] has been disregarded because, even in cases such as "he offers four handfuls," where there is syntactic unity, the Pūrvapakṣa is formulated on the grounds that the handfuls (*muṣṭi*) are primary and thus take precedence over the seventeen-potsherd rice-offering (*caru*); and in the Siddhānta, since both are connected to the action, they lack primacy, making it difficult to establish [the former's superiority]. Thus, it was set aside.

Therefore, although the principle of the conflict between the quality of a subordinate member (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*) constitutes an exception to the principle of the opening statement (*upakramanyāya*), it should be understood that the establishment of the present doctrine is accomplished precisely by means of that which has attained primacy.
(Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1.12, p. 316).
The superiority of the opening statement (*upakramaprābalya*) is also easily established in the case of the Vaiśvānara passage.

*Parākrama*, 471–2: Regarding the principle of the predominance of the opening statement (*upakramaprābalyanyāya*), they say as follows: "In every instance where a word oversteps its own primary meaning, contradiction (*virodha*) is the cause; and that [contradiction] is observed in the case of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Furthermore, at the stage of the opening statement, the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*) is not known to be contradictory. Therefore, it is logical that the opening statement functions in its primary sense. *Parākrama*, 9: By this very principle of the predominance of the opening statement, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established even in the section concerning the acceptance or rejection of dice (*akṣapratigrahaheyadhikaraṇa*).

51. This might be a case where the initial statement (*upakrama*) prevails due to its superior force, were there a requirement for accentuation based on the origin (*utpatti*) and application (*viniyoga*) [of the mantra], such as in the rule "the *ṛc* is recited aloud" (*uccaiḥ*). However, since time and so forth are qualifiers of the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), they are required [only] at that stage; therefore, the accentuation determined by those [qualifiers] alone possesses superior force. (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya, 3.1.12, p. 320). The principle of the superior force of the initial statement will be discussed under the sūtra "Or rather, the Veda [is primary], because of the observation of the majority" (3.1.2).
Su. Pṛ. 526:

When the meaning of a word in the concluding portion is determined by the force of the opening statement, there is a sublation of the dharma consisting of the cognition of the word's primary meaning through the adoption of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as [in the case of the word *ṛc* and others] due to the influence of the opening of the Veda.
"The Vedas mentioned at the beginning can be restated by means of the words 'Ṛk' and so forth occurring in the conclusion, because the Ṛk and others are parts of the Veda.
This is the logical principle (nyāya).
The prowess of the section concerning the commencement of the Vedas: 412.
That which stands at the commencement sets aside the conclusion.
*Aprāptvādhaḥ*.
Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 860.
The Section on the Opening (Upakramādhikaraṇa).
The principle of the section on commencement;
the principle of commencement; the principle of the superiority of commencement.
The principle of following the introductory statement;
the section concerning the introductory statement of the Veda;
because the beginning and the conclusion constitute a single syntactical unit.
The entitlement [to the designation] would arise from the Vedic revelation (śruti).

The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is revealed: "The Ṛk is performed loudly, the Sāman loudly, and the Yajus in a low voice. Regarding this, there is a doubt: do these words apply with reference to the class (jāti) of the Ṛk and so forth, or do they apply with reference to the Veda?
What, then, is the established position? It should be that there is an authority for the genus (jāti).
Why? Because of the scriptural testimony (śruti).
For it is from the mere hearing of these words that we comprehend the genus.

In the section concerning the commencement [of the sacrifice], the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is connected with the genus (*jāti*) that has been established; for there is no word that serves as a governing authority (*adhikāraka*) for the Vedas.
Furthermore, those *ṛc* verses that have transcended the *Ṛgveda* will be recited loudly (*uccaiḥ*) in the *Yajurveda*.
Otherwise, both properties would be optional alternatives for that very *ṛc*, and in that case, there would be a contradiction [of the rule].
Furthermore, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is thus upheld;
otherwise, if there were a connection with the Veda as a whole, the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) would apply to every sacrifice.

Therefore, these words have their application determined by the context of origin (*jātādhikāra*). Or rather—having thus described the application by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*), the application by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*) is now introduced.
An example therein is the sentence: "The *ṛc* is recited loudly," and so forth.
"If, therefore, the quality of being an *ṛc* or the quality of being a *yajus* is to be established, one should go to the Gārhapatya fire and offer with the words 'bhūḥ svāhā'.
And so on, including "if from the Yajus, if from the Sāman," and so forth.

In that context, regarding the injunction of the properties of loudness (*uccais*) and whispering (*upāṃśu*), as well as the injunction for the Homa sacrifice known by its own name due to its great importance, is there indeed a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) denoting [the terms] independently of their connection with preceding or following words?

Regarding these, is there the inclusion of the *ṛk*-class and so forth—defined by the rule "wherein the arrangement of quarters occurs according to the sense" (*PMS* 2.1.35)—or rather, the inclusion of all the Vedas consisting of mantras and brāhmaṇas?
Whence arises this doubt? From the discrepancy between the opening and the conclusion of the single sentence;
for at the beginning, the Vedas are heard.
In the conclusion, however, there are the classes of *ṛc* and so forth.

In this regard, a doubt arises between two possibilities: whether the word "Veda" occurring in the opening [sentence] signifies the class (*jāti*) as a subordinate component, or whether the classes of *ṛc* and so forth occurring in the conclusion signify the collection including the *Brāhmaṇas*.
And this [doubt] is to be resolved through objection and refutation, just as in the case of the statement, "The pebbles are smeared."
If that is so, then since this has already been covered by that very [section on] *aktādhikaraṇa* (1.4.13), this [present discussion] need not be undertaken.
This is not a valid objection;
for it was stated there that the authority of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) applies only where there is doubt.

In this case, however, because the term *viśuddheśvarī* refers to a specific class of mantras—such as those beginning with the letter *ga* and so forth—which are beyond doubt, the purification (*viśuddhi*) itself is indeed free from ambiguity.

Therefore, having begun with the premise that one must adopt one of the two alternative positions by means of a restrictive interpretation (*vyavaccheda-kalpanā*), the question arises: what is the prima facie position? It is that, according to the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding those [mantras], the *viśuddheśvarīs* possess equal status in their respective applications (*adhikāra*).
Furthermore: "Just as a substance-universal and its action are not mutually contradictory,
so too the Vedas are not contradictory with the meanings of the supplementary statements regarding particulars."
It is not possible in any way to designate a Brāhmaṇa as a "Veda" by using the term *Ṛk* and so forth.

However, the word "Veda" is capable of referring even to a single part [of it], because it is observed that collective terms are applied to their constituent parts, as in the expression, "The village has arrived. Furthermore, the learned apply this very term even more emphatically in that context, saying, "We study the Veda," or "The Veda exists."

Moreover, those who study the Brāhmaṇas do not speak in such a manner. Furthermore: "Since there is a fixed order for one who is born, the determination of dharma is superior; however, because the Vedas are mixed, there would be a confusion of that dharma."
For indeed, certain *ṛc* verses are recited in all three Vedas as well as in the *yajus*.

In that case, if "Veda-hood" were the cause for the connection with *dharma*, it would not be known which specific *dharma* should be performed regarding such [verses], or else an improper option (*vikalpa*) would have to be resorted to; furthermore, the designations of different Vedas would be equivalent due to their commonality.
However, this fault does not apply under the view that the genus (*jāti*) is the defining factor.
For two universals cannot be inherent in a single collection of phonemes (*varṇasamūha*).
Moreover, the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is thus preserved.
Otherwise, since the Veda pertains to all sacrifices such as the Dvirātra, Pañcarātra, and Satra, the Dharma following the Veda would override the specific context and become universal.

[Objection: But surely, even though the section on "the born" (*jāta*) is under discussion, this [objection] is equal [to yours], because—just like the Veda—the *jāta* exists in other contexts as well.

[Response: If you argue that the restriction here is due to the absence of any reason to overstep the *jāta* currently under discussion, then that same [reasoning] applies equally to the case of the Veda, because of the determination that "the Veda is only as much as is contained within the context."
This is not equal [to the case of the *sāman*].

Why? "Because it possesses a composite structure, it does not exist in the context from which it is produced; because the Veda is a great collection, it is not completed within the archetype (*prakṛti*)."

If that which is produced in the collection of all-pervading [qualities] and so forth were to be distributed [among them], it would not be fully completed within its material cause; therefore, that too would be like the Veda.
Vedic status eternally resides in collections such as the Kāṭhaka, which consist of mantras, brāhmaṇas, and tarkas, and which pertain to many sacrifices.
Indeed, there are collections of sentences consisting of feet, words, and sections (*parvan*).

(The *ṛc*s are those bound by feet; the *yajus* are collections of words; the *sāmans* are the *brahmans* of the sections). Here it must be noted that the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), by employing the word *parvan* in the sense of a "portion" (*bhakti*)—as in the phrase "a portion of a *sāman*"—was criticized by the authors of the *Vārttikas*, who stated that this was "a lapse due to negligence."
In this context, however, the word *parvan* is used by the venerable authors of the Vārttika as a synonym for the word *bhakti*; thus [it is said]:
"For even those who have heard the scriptures stumble on the path when their vision is clouded by passion.
Furthermore: "Within each of those [Vedas], there exist collections of Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman for us."
Just as aggregates such as forests were previously endowed with a universal.

In this way, the commonality of these collections is called the "universal" (jāti). Indeed, it is precisely this universal that has been described by the authors of the Bhāṣya as being produced from a collection; the commentator has explained it therein as arising from the aggregate.
Furthermore, since a word consists of two phonemes, the genus "word-ness" (gośabdatva) is not postulated;
for if it were like a sentence, how then could there be genera such as Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman?

In the *Upakramādhikaraṇa*, it was determined in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that just as the genus called "sentencehood" (*vākyatva*) cannot be postulated— since it arises from the cognition of a relationship between word-meanings with distinct parts, which depends on the sequence of phonemes in a collection of words consisting of phonemes, meanings, and expressive effort produced by different articulatory locations and efforts, or on the sequence of phonemes themselves according to the logic of "wandering-ness" (*bhramaṇatva*) and so forth— likewise, the properties of being a *ṛc*, a *yajus*, or a *sāman* cannot be postulated based merely on the hearing of phonemes in a particular sequence or with specific accents.

[The opponent argues: "By means of the well-disposed [organs], the places [of articulation] such as the throat, and the instruments known as the modes of pronunciation—by both of these efforts acting as manifestors (*vyañjaka*), because they occur sequentially, one cannot postulate a genus-form (*jāti-rūpa*) called 'sentencehood' (*vākyatva*) in the collection of letters (*varṇa*), or of syllables (*akṣara*) consisting of a collection of letters, or of words (*pada*) consisting of a collection of syllables, or even in the final letter of a sentence. This is because, unlike the case of 'circling' (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth, there is no simultaneous occurrence; nor is it possible to perceive [such a genus] through other letters, because that would contradict the two designations of 'word' (*pada*) and 'sentence' (*vākya*). As stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*, since the components of a sentence—which are words—would have to be grasped through perceptions (*pratyaya*) consisting of the apprehension of their forms, and the word-meanings and the relations between words and meanings would have to be remembered through recollections, and because there is an intervention by the mutual expectancy of word-meanings, it is impossible to grasp a genus due to the failure to connect with the substrata of that genus. Therefore, just as [the sentence is not determined], it is impossible to postulate the *Ṛg* verses and so forth as being of the nature of a genus. This is the meaning.

(Page 1170) "Rather, that which is designated as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, consisting of a collection of things having a single purpose, is a universal of a collection; there is no such thing as a [real] genus (jāti)."
Just as for those [words] whose meaning is derived etymologically (*yaugika*), a universal other than the genus (*jāti*) is accepted,
so too is the universal of the collection (*samūhasāmānya*) considered a genus characterized by its own generic nature.

And even in common worldly usage, the established meaning of the word *jāti* as "that which is born" should be explained in exactly this way; or rather, it is the Veda [that establishes it], because of the observation of its predominant usage.
The Commentary (Bhāṣya): This is stated with reference to the Veda. Why? Because of the observation of the majority (prāyadarśana). What is this "observation of the majority"?
In a passage that is predominantly Vedic and begins with the Veda, these words are heard being concluded: "Prajāpati alone was this [universe] in the beginning.
He performed austerity. From him, having performed austerity, the three Vedas were created."
Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya—
these practiced austerity. From them, as they were practicing austerity, the Vedas were emitted.

Beginning with the statement, "The *Ṛgveda* from Agni, the *Yajurveda* from Vāyu, and the *Sāmaveda* from Āditya," it is heard at the conclusion: "The *Ṛc* is recited loudly, the *Sāman* loudly, and the *Yajus* in a low voice.
This must be because [the performance] is to be done in a low voice and so forth by means of these aforementioned [Vedas], and not by means of the *Ṛg* and other [classes of mantras] as such.
How is this understood? Because it is heard in the concluding portion of the sentence.
Since these Vedas originated from Him, they must be performed in a low voice (upāṃśu) and so forth by means of them;
furthermore, the conclusion must also be made with words denoting "Veda" such as "Ṛk" and the rest.
Otherwise, the sentence itself would not be logically consistent.
In that case, they would indeed be meaningless.
Therefore, [the author] says, "These are the governing topics" (*adhikāra*).

Or rather—[the author] asks, observing that this is not equal to those other instances of "observation of the majority" (*prāyadarśana*) mentioned in the commentary: "What is this [that is said] 'on account of the observation of the majority'? (*kim idaṃ prāyadarśanāt iti*)?

(He demonstrates the very incomparability [of the cases]: For in the sūtra "And because of the statement regarding the majority" (*prāyavacanācca*), it is stated that where there is a majority of primary elements (*pradhāna*) and other primary elements are present, [the rule applies] because of the statement.

Similarly, in the sūtra "Because of the observation in the context of the majority" (*viśaye prāyadarśanāt*), it is observed that where there is a majority of purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) such as the *godohana* vessel and others, this [rule] is seen to apply there.
However, it cannot be said here that where there are other Vedas, these [metres] such as the *Ṛk* and so forth are observed there.
"For there are no Vedas apart from these [mantras], with which they might be confused upon their occurrence.
Therefore, there is no observation of predominance here.

To this, he states the answer (the Bhāṣya): "In a context predominantly Vedic, at the commencement of the Veda, and in a mind permeated by the impressions generated by the cognition of the Veda, [one thinks]: 'These words are being heard.'"
To that effect [it says]: "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this" (and so forth).
As for the argument that, because the Veda is more powerful than the Arthavādas, the word "Veda" must refer to its constituent parts, we reply:
the power [of the Veda] is of a different kind altogether, being connected with all the Arthavādas.
That [nature] of cognitions, by virtue of being the primary means of valid knowledge, is indeed something other [than mere appearance].
For those explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that are heard after the injunctions are weak;
whereas those heard before them are stronger because of their primacy.
Indeed, for every word, the cause of contradiction lies in its overstepping its own primary meaning.
Furthermore, contradiction is recognized when the counter-positive is perceived.

Thus, in this context, when such scriptural passages as "The three Vedas were born; Agni was the Ṛgveda" are heard, there is no utterance of the Ṛgveda and so forth at the time they are said to have been "born," by the perception of which the word "Veda" could be understood as signifying its constituent parts.
Therefore, first of all, the intellect is pervaded by that very Śruti.

Now, since the words "Ṛk" and so forth, while intending their own primary meanings, do not cohere [with the context], they are forced to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Consequently, there is weakness regarding the pure reality of the primary meaning; thus, even though the knowledge of the primary Veda from the *arthavāda* is sublated, the knowledge of the pure Veda [prevails]. This is the section concerning the beginning (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), according to the principle: "Or rather, the primary [meaning] prevails because of the characteristic of the initial injunction. This is how it is established.
Only the section concerning the commencement (upakrama) would be grasped;
this is not so.
"Where indeed the superiority of the earlier and the later is perceived,
and where there is the arising of cognitions independent of one another."

For when contradictory meanings are heard that reside in separate sentences and are mutually independent, the priority of the earlier over the later arises; because the earlier has already attained its own nature through the sublation of the subsequent, whereas it would be impossible for the later to attain its own nature without the sublation of the earlier. However, this does not apply where there is a hearing of [words] that are mutually dependent as part of a single sentence. In that case, syntactic unity occurs by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
Furthermore, the subsequent [element] requires that which is either consistent with itself or superior to what was previously understood.
Therefore, that which is neither superior nor consistent is not present in that sentence at all, because it is not required.
And since a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) cannot be established by means of what does not exist, the priority of the former prevails.

Therefore, since the injunction (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) here have the same subject matter, for as long as the Vedas are mentioned in the *arthavāda*, it is understood that "this is something to be enjoined. Consequently, there is an expectation regarding the name [of the Vedas] as to what among them is to be enjoined, but not [an expectation] as to which [Veda] is for what purpose,
according to the principle of the introductory section (*upakramādhikaraṇa*).
But this does not apply to *śruti* and *liṅga*.

Because of the investigation into the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) suitable for the application of *liṅga*, there is a connection with the section on the beginning (*upakramādhikaraṇa*) within the chapter and the book.

As for the immediate sequence: since the application cognizable solely through the authority of *śruti* has already been examined, the occasion for examining the application cognizable through the combined authority of both [śruti and liṅga] is now clear.

Thus, because the beginning and the conclusion form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), it is determined that this is a Vedic duty; such is the application by syntactical connection (*vākya-viniyoga*).
Bhaṭṭa: Having thus explained the application by indicative power (*liṅga-viniyoga*), the application by syntactical connection and the others are now explained here.

Thus, in this context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the injunction "The Ṛc is recited loudly" (*uccairṛcā kriyate*) and so forth, there arises a deliberation as to whether the words *ṛk* and so on—which serve to identify the subject—intend only the *mantras* known as Ṛgveda and so forth, or rather, by virtue of the corroborative explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the introduction stating "The three Vedas were born," they intend all *mantras* that constitute parts of the rites enjoined in the Ṛgveda and other Vedas through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In this reflection, because the word "Veda" (*veda*) found in the introductory passage is subordinate to the primary injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), and because the principle of "contradiction between the subordinate and the principal" (*aṅguṇavirodhanyāya*) dictates that the purpose of the figurative indication is grasped by the primary statement, the word "Veda" itself must be taken as figuratively indicating its constituent parts, namely the Ṛgveda and so forth.
In reality, however, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even when the word "Veda" refers to its parts, because the property of being a Veda (*vedatva*) resides in each individual part.

Otherwise, upon hearing the single syntactical unity with the other scriptural passage, a logical fault would not arise. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: by hearing the word "Veda" at the beginning, this much is understood: surely, since the Veda is being praised here, its status as the subject (*uddeśyatva*) or the thing to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*) must necessarily be intended within the sentence.

And since the qualities such as "high pitch" (*uccais*) are to be enjoined therein, it is understood by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that the *ṛc* and so forth are the subject (*uddeśya*).
In reality, however, the word *ṛk* and so on is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), and its purpose is to exclude other [Vedas].

Consequently, because the word *veda* occurring in the opening statement—which has not yet encountered any contradiction—serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the words *ṛk* and so on, based on their status as those [mantras], for the mantras that constitute parts of the rites prescribed in the *Ṛgveda* and the others.

Nor can there be a sublation by a subsequent [text] through the investigation of the delimiting factor (*apacchedaka*) of what was understood from the opening statement (*upakrama*), because that [subsequent text], being dependent on the praise of the injunction, must necessarily form a single syntactical unit (*tadaikavākyatā*) with its purpose; thus, you would have to accept that the subsequent [text] does not even arise when there is a contradiction with the prior. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the opening statement on the grounds that "Veda-ness" (*vedatva*) is fully present (*paryāpti*) in the *Ṛg* and other Vedas, because Veda-ness—being a specific property residing in a collection consisting of the constituent parts of the mantra—is fully present only in that whole and not in each individual part. Otherwise, the requirement of the injunction for study would be fulfilled merely by studying a single sentence.

Even upon hearing the word *śrudastha-kapada*, it is not untenable [to apply the rule], just as there is a prohibition regarding parts such as *dhuntāka*. Furthermore, the distinction between the prohibition and the injunction in such cases should be observed in the *Kaustubha*.

Therefore, in accordance with the introductory context (*upakrama*), the high pitch (*uccais*) and other such qualities belong specifically to the mantras that are constituent parts of the rites enjoined by the *Ṛgveda*. Thus, since the status of being a Veda (*vedatva*) is not pervasive enough to apply to the entire section, the sentence, or the individual words, it is logical that the sentence is subsumed within its scope by the context. Consequently, because the prescription of accents is understood through the sentence—which enjoins the constituent parts of the rites delimited by the status of being a Veda—there is no harm even if the context is set aside. As Maṇḍana says: "The *Ṛgveda* prescribes [the mantra] to be recited loudly."
Śaṅkara: "The Vedic dharma is yours.
In the *Upakramādhikaraṇa*, it was stated that the status of the accents as Vedic dharma is determined by another principle (*nyāya*), without relying on the opening statement (*upakrama*) alone.
Parākrama: [Agrees].

Because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) occurring at the beginning is explained exactly as it is heard due to the absence of any contradiction, and because the principle regarding the conflict between a subordinate element and its primary (*aṅgaguṇavirodha-nyāya*) has been established in the *Upakramādhikaraṇa* (Jaiminisūtra 3.3.14) as having a different scope—namely, that which pertains to the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) and its own supplementary portion;

and because the redundancy of the *Upakramādhikaraṇa* with respect to the *Adhapratigrahe’dhikaraṇa* (Jaiminisūtra 3.4.15–17, p. 376) has been refuted, since the latter serves to resolve further doubts.

3|4|15|37, p. 377: By the principle of the *upakramādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the opening statement), the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) indeed has the giver as its primary referent (in the case of the *akṣapratigraha-adhikaraṇa*). 3|4|15|37, p. 377. Nor should it be argued that, by the principle of the *upakramādhikaraṇa*, the statement regarding the one with qualities (*saguṇavākya*) possesses greater authority because it is not contradicted [by anything prior].

This is because the logic of the *upakramādhikaraṇa* applies to cases where the concluding portion (*upasaṃhāra*) is established otherwise, whereas in the present case, that is not the situation. (Advaitasiddhi 2.4.1365). Since the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) is dependent upon the injunctions of application (*viniyoga*) and origination (*utpatti*), and since these two precede it, they possess greater force by virtue of the logic of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa-nyāya*)—because their basis is more rapidly presented and thus lacks any prior contradiction.
(By the logic of the *upakramādhikaraṇa* itself).

*Kau.* 3.1.2.9, p. 320. The nature of the principle of the section on the beginning (*upakramādhikaraṇa*) is that "the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) must be interpreted in accordance with the beginning. Since the conclusion must have a meaning consistent with the beginning, its status as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is maintained; because the conclusion derives its very existence through the consideration of the beginning, the beginning possesses greater force (*prābalya*).

Since it will be stated in the third [section] that the concluding statement must conform to the opening statement, it is not proper to determine the meaning of an injunction in the opening based on an explanatory passage (arthavāda) in the conclusion.
Anticipating this objection, [it is said]:

according to the principle of following the opening statement (*upakramānurodhanyāya*), [the word] refers to the *upa* [vessels], just as [the word "arrow" refers to the reed] in the case of the *śara*. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 523, 1141)
Because the principle of following the opening statement (*upakramānurodhanyāya*) pertains to cases where the opening is unambiguous.

This is established in *Nyāyanirṇaya* 3.4.18–19 (second section), in the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*, in the section concerning the opening of the Vedas (*vedopakramādhikaraṇa*), and in the section concerning the acceptance of stone (*aśmapratigrahādhikaraṇa*). The conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) is interpreted in accordance with the opening.
Regarding *parākrama* 1:

"If the sacrifice is afflicted from the perspective of the *Yajus*, [one should offer] with the mantra ‘bhuvaḥ’ into the southern fire"—since the status of this expiation as belonging to the Vedic dharma is established in the third [book] (*Tarkapāda*) in accordance with its introductory statement, [as stated in] *Kau.* 1.2.14.44, p. 84.

Furthermore, because the opening statement serves as the cause for the subsequent production [of meaning], one must accept even the fruit mentioned in the supplementary portion of the sentence by means of its abandonment alone, according to the principle of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice.
Parākrama 471:
There must be a single unified syntactical connection between the opening and the conclusion without contradiction.
Parākrama 412:
The relationship between the introduction and the conclusion exists through the state of being a single coherent statement in terms of their preceding and succeeding parts.
Parākrama 4312.

Even though there are many properties that serve as the grounds for the application [of terms] and which are not established by the reality [of non-duality], they must be sublated because they contradict the non-duality taught in the Vedānta texts, as understood through the uniformity of their opening and concluding sections;
this is according to the maxim: "One should abandon the earth, but not oneself. (Parākrama 561)

If one begins [a rite] but does not complete it, the learned (śiṣṭas) would immediately thereafter condemn him, saying, "This is a base man who merely initiates. For the learned censure those who, having resolved upon an oblation for the gods, do not carry the sacrifice to its conclusion.
Therefore, it must necessarily be completed.
Bhāṣya 4.3.124, beginning with: "When a ritual act for the gods performed according to the scriptures is not brought to completion, there is censure by the learned;
this is what is called *upagamana*.
For *upagamana* is the attainment of that which has not yet been attained."
For one who has attained that, it is not possible.
[In the passage] "the attendants" (*upagāḥ*), there is a distinct technical designation based on its etymological derivation (*yaugika*).
(Who are the *upagās*? They are those who sing along with the *udgātṛ*, *stotṛ*, and *pratihartṛ* in accordance [with them], emitting a firm tone with the sound "ho"; thus they are called *upagās*.
Who? VI.3.7.14. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the *upagās* are some among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) (the sacrificer as well).
Bhāṣya 3.7.120:
"And the *upagātṛ*s [are included] because of the observation of indicative marks;
the *udgātṛ* and others are the principal singers."

And there are certain others called *upagātṛ*s (accompanying singers). Standing near the principal singers (*mukhya*), they sing with a single monotone (*ekaśruti*), uttering "aho. They are so named because they cover the intervals of the principal singers' pauses and provide assistance to the singer with a steady, low-pitched voice, like that of a lute-player.

In the inquiry as to whether these [upagātṛs] are distinct from or non-distinct from those who are officiating as priests (*ṛtvijyamāna*), when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—based on a departure from the Sūtra—is that they are distinct because of the difference in words, this is the Sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of bringing forward another reason, namely "because of the connection with the act of singing" (*uttyasaṃyogāt*).
The *upagāḥ* are the singers (*upagātāraḥ*); they are not distinct from those officiating as priests.

Because of the connection with the act of choosing (*varaṇa*); because in the sentence enjoining the choosing, there is no connection with the *upagānas*; because there is an absence of a name [for them]; and because there is no injunction for the choosing [of them].
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The prohibition of the Adhvaryu from singing the *upagāna*, namely "The Adhvaryu should not sing the *upagāna*," is an indicative mark that the [singing] belongs to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), since a prohibition must be preceded by a prior application [of the rule].
Therefore, there are no other *upagātṛ*s (accompanying singers).

Regarding this, the *Chandoga-sūtra* states the distinction: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) sing the accompaniment with the syllable 'ho', while the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) does so with the syllable 'o'.

On this point, the *Sudhā* commentary explains: "Like the *śamitṛ*, the *upagātṛ*s are not distinct [from the officiants], because they are connected to the act of appointment (*varaṇa*) from its very origin, and because the word *upagātṛ* is applicable to those mentioned in the context by virtue of its etymological meaning (*yaugika*). This is the meaning of the sūtra.
Regarding this point of curiosity: some ritualists (yājñika) believe that the *upagātṛ*s are distinct from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
This is not correct;

for in the *Kāṭhaka*, within the section on the sacrifice of the World-Creators (*viśvasṛjām ayajña*), after enumerating [the priests] with the words "Tapa was the householder" (*tapa āsīt gṛhapatiḥ*) and so forth, it designates the *upagātṛ*s as being none other than the officiating priests themselves.
Therefore, we consider that those who join in the singing (*upagātāraḥ*) are not included among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

As for the prohibition, "The *adhvaryu* should not sing along," there will be no fault because it will apply to the attainment [of the rule] regarding the *abhiṣṭoma* chant, namely: "All those who have been commissioned (*prasūtāḥ*) should sing along with the *adhiṣṭhima*.
(Ke.)
In the case of the *upagas*, it should be like the *śar* [grass], due to the connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Regarding the *mahāvrata*, it is heard in scripture: "They sing the *upagāna* on the shoots.
In the archetype, it is heard: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) sing the *upagāna*."

In this context, regarding those who perform the *upagāna* (the act of accompanying singing), it should be like the case of arrows (*śara*) in the ritual of covering; just as arrows set aside the ordinary *kuśa* grass, so too do the *palya* women set aside the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at the *Mahāvrata*. This is because of the connection with the indicative mark of the archetype (*prakṛti*), that is, due to the relationship with the indicative mark of the archetype. For in the archetype, namely the *Abhiṣṭoma*, there is indeed singing.
Regarding the *upagas*, as in the case of arrows (1142): the *upagāna* (responsive singing) is performed by the female singers (*upagānakartrībhiḥ*).
This has been stated here concerning the wives in the *Mahāvrata*.
Thus is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
"But because it would be purposeless, there must be something additional.
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta):
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the prima facie view.
By means of the singing by the wives (*patnyupagāna*), there is no exclusion of the original singing (*prākṛta-upagāna*);
rather, while the singing obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*) remains in force, the singing by the wives would be additional.
The meaning is that there should be a conjunction of both.
Conjunction is necessary because otherwise the injunction would result in being purposeless.
It has been stated: "They sing along with the wife; they sing along with *kāṇḍavīṇās* and *piccholās*."
Or, this "upagāna" (accompaniment) belongs to the musical instrument, or it is the accompaniment of the musical instrument;
in either case, the term "upagāna" occurs with a different meaning from its ordinary sense.
Therefore, there is no connection with the indicative mark of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, there is a combination;
this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Who [holds this view]?

In the passage "upageṣu śaravat" (10.4.18–19), regarding the Mahāvrata rite in the Gānaveda, after introducing the statement "drums resound in the quarters," the text teaches that the wives "sing along" (*upagāyanti*). It is stated therein that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of these prescribed (*atidiṣṭa*) songs with the [already established] songs; thus, the *upagātṛ*s (those who sing along) are not distinct from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). (Bālakrīḍā, p. 178).
[The view that] the *upagātṛ*s (accompanying singers) are [distinct from the priests] because of the observation of their characteristic marks.
The Commentary states: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there are those called *upagātṛ*s; they convey a distinct number due to the difference in terminology, and thus they are other than the *adhvaryu*s.
This being the position reached, we reply as follows.
Some of them alone might be [the singers].
Why? Because of the enumeration [of specific priests] and because the word is etymological.
This is an indicative mark (liṅga): "The Adhvaryu should not sing."
If there were others besides these, he would not prohibit the Adhvaryu, since [the office] would not have been applicable [to him].
But because he prohibits him, we understand that [the prohibition applies] to one among those very persons who are mentioned in the context of the appointment.
Soma—The connection is from the preceding section.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: others are not the *upagātṛ*s (accompanying singers), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "One should not sing along with the Adhvaryu. Since there is no possibility of other [priests] singing along with the Adhvaryu, a prohibition would be inapplicable; therefore, it must be assumed that this is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), as there is no other way [to account for the text].

Vi— "Others may be the performers [of the recitation] after the [verses] have been uttered, or not; as it is in the world, so it is here as well. It is not so, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) that 'the Adhvaryu is not [the performer]'."
Bhaṭṭa: Likewise, the *upagātṛ*s (assistant singers) mentioned in connection with the *soma* sacrifice are also included among those chosen.

Nor should it be argued that because the *upagātṛ*s are well-known in the world as being subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) to the *gātṛ*s (principal singers), while these [others] are of equal status, they cannot be included.
For even among equals, mutual assistance is appropriate, since they perform the functions of both the commander (*praiṣa*) and the one commanded (*praiṣya*).
This is also seen to be the case for artisans who are employed by their masters.
In that context as well, because the *upagāna* belongs to the Sāmaveda, the *subrahmaṇya* is fixed [as one], even though the three [priests] beginning with the *udgātṛ* are occupied with singing.
Others, however, hold that they are not fixed, in accordance with other scriptural statements such as "the *adhvaryus* sing the *upagāna*" and "four sing the *upagāna*."

For this very reason, because of the statement "the Adhvaryu should not sing along," these two [are excluded]. Maṇḍana says: "The upagās are considered to be those mentioned in the context. Śaṅkara says: "And the upagās are likewise considered [to be so]."
Likewise, as in the case of the *śamitṛ*,
the role of the *upagātṛ* (accompanying singer) is prohibited for the *adhvaryu*, according to the rule: "The *adhvaryu* should not sing as an *upagātṛ*" (*Vi.* 3.7.14).
Some perform the *upagāna* only as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
sometimes the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) does so, and occasionally even the wife (*patnī*).
However, it must not be performed by the *adhvaryu*.
Some [say]: "At the Mahāvrata, the women sing along (*upagāyanti*) with *piccholās*, *kāṇḍavīṇās*, and *āpāṭālikās*.
(Mānava Śrautasūtra 10.4.18)

In the Mahāvrata rite occurring within the Gavāmayana sacrifice, there is a combination of the wives who act as subordinate singers (*upagānakartrī*) with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who act as subordinate singers by virtue of extended application (*atideśika*).
In the *upagas*, there should be [the use of] arrows, because of the connection with the characteristic mark of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Commentary: In the *Mahāvrata* sacrifice, it is heard: "The wives sing along (*upagāyanti*), they sing along with *picchola* lutes, they sing along with *kāṇḍavīṇā* lutes, they sing along with *āpāṭālikā* lutes.
However, in the archetype, it is stated: "The priests (*ṛtvijas*) sing along."
In this case, it is obtained through the principle of extension (*codaka*).
Regarding that, the following point becomes subject to doubt: are the priests who are singing as accompanists excluded by the phrase "the wives sing along," or are they not excluded?
In this regard, it is further considered: is this "singing along" a form of vocal singing (*gāna*), or is it a form of instrumental accompaniment (*vāditra*)?

In this regard, what is the doubt? Is "gānopagāna" (singing with accompaniment) singing accompanied by another song (*upagāna*), or is it singing where the accompaniment (*upagāna*) is itself the singing?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That the original [archetypal] element is set aside.
Thereupon this is described: "Singing and accompanying singing. The wives sing and thus augment the singing.

The singing (*gāna*) itself is already established as being in the vernacular (*prākṛta*); what is prescribed here is the addition (*upacaya*), which is the meaning of the prefix *upa*. Therefore, it is "singing with accompaniment" (*gānopagānam*). Alternatively, the term *upagānam* means simply "singing" (*gānam*).
For the word "gāna" is well known in the context of the two songs performed by the body [the singers].
Therefore, this is the *upagāna* of the *gāna*;
that is, the secondary singing (*upagāna*) belonging to the primary song (*gāna*).
When either of these two occurs, then the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) proceed with the wife.

Therefore, due to the connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), that which is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) is set aside by what is directly heard in the text (*pratyakṣa-śruta*), just like the *śara* grass.

For example, when it is said, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara*," the *śara* grass, being directly heard in the text, sets aside the *darbha* grass obtained through the extended application; so it is here as well.
"But because it would otherwise be purposeless, there should be an addition.
The Commentary states: "The word 'but' (tu) sets aside the previous position; it does not mean cessation.
There should be a combination (samuccaya)."
This is now considered:
Is this singing a supplement to instrumental music?
For there is indeed instrumental music here, such as "drums resound in the quarters," and so forth.
Regarding the term *upagāna*, it refers to the singing that accompanies an instrumental performance.

How so? For by means of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the verbal root-meaning is expressed through the *śruti* (direct audition). The existence (*sattā*) of the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*), being remote, becomes weak due to the remoteness of its meaning.
Therefore, because it is the meaning of a prefix that is being enjoined, its injunction is set aside by the injunction of the existence of the root-meaning.
Alternatively, this is a figurative expression for accompaniment (*upagāna*);
for thus it is said: "The wives accompany [the singing]," and "They accompany with lutes made of bamboo."
There is the sounding of musical instruments such as the *kāṇḍavīṇā* and others;
and in the singing of stringed instruments, there is the sound of singing.
Therefore, instrumental music is a form of accompaniment (*upagāna*).
In this regard, whether the singing is subordinate to the instrumental music, or the instrumental music is subordinate to the singing, in either case there is a difference from the ordinary meaning.
Therefore, they are to be combined.
Why? Because otherwise it would be purposeless.
In this way, the injunction will not be rendered meaningless;
the meaning is that the injunction will be upheld.
Therefore, there is a combination [of the two].

Soma: Since there was no injunction for the *āmantra-homas* in the previous context of the *anuyāja* rites, their non-performance was acceptable; however, here, because of the statement "they sing along" (*upagāyanti*), the wives are enjoined to perform the original (*prākṛta*) singing. Consequently, the original singers—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—are excluded. This constitutes the connection [of the present case as a] counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). The meaning of the Sūtra is: In the case of the *upagas*, because of the connection with the act of singing along, there should be an exclusion of the original performers, just as *kuśa* grass is replaced by *śara* grass. Vi: "The statement 'the wives sing along' excludes the officiating priests."
Or rather, this increase in the chanting of the Sāman would arise from the beginning of the section (kāṇḍa) and so forth.
Indeed, the sounding of kettledrums revolves within the mind;
therefore, the singing accompanied by lutes and other instruments would be appropriate for it.
(At the end of *Taittirīya-saṃhitā* 7.5.8, there are two additional verses in the Mīmāṃsā section; these are presented here because of their particular utility.

They are as follows: "Is the singing of the wives (*patnīnām upagānam*) to be understood as [an action] performed by those who possess knowledge? Or is it appropriate that it be withheld, since singing is a bodily act?"

Singing, which makes the accents and consonants manifest, is prescribed like the *graha* cups; the increase of musical instruments is due to the *sāman*, and there is a combination because of their proximity.
(Bhāṭṭa: Regarding the Mahāvrata at the end of the Gavāmayana sacrifice, having introduced the subject with "The kettledrums resound in the quarters," the scripture states, "The wives sing along.
Here, the word "wives" (*patnyaḥ*) is used in accordance with Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

In the archetype (prakṛti), when the singing is performed by the *udgātṛ* and others, the rule "the priests (*ṛtvij*) sing along" prescribes a form of singing consisting of accompaniment (*upagāna*) performed by the priests. In this regard, there arises a deliberation: do the wives, being enjoined here by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the archetypal accompaniment, exclude the priests; or, because they are connected with a non-archetypal accompaniment, do they not exclude them? Upon such reflection, since accompaniment is prescribed in the archetype and is thus obtained here by extension (*atideśa*), the wives enjoined here by way of a restatement of that [accompaniment] exclude the priests.

Nor can there be a suspicion that, if singing (*gāna*) is the intended object (*uddeśya*), another increase (*upacaya*) in that same location is not intended; for since prepositions (*upasarga*) are understood to connect with one another, the formation of a qualified intended object is logically possible.

Nor, even so, is it the case that because of the direct scriptural instruction, "In the quarters the drums resound," an increase performed by the wives—which would otherwise be excluded—is rendered possible;

for since such an increase is enjoined as having its means (*sādhana*) specified by the text, "They sing along with *kāṇḍavīṇā* lutes," it is impossible for the word "singing" (*gāna*)—which is well-known in common usage to refer only to vocal music—to refer to the sound of drums.

Because the meaning of the prefix *upa-* (increase) cannot coexist with the mutual proximity of the wives [to the singers] during the morning chanting (*prātassavana*), and because there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if multiple things were enjoined,

the wives— being enjoined as agents for the act of chanting (*upagāna*) which is archetypal (*prākṛta*)— exclude the priests. Furthermore, in the archetype, there is no "increase" (*upacaya*) of the chanting that consists of vocal singing (*śārīragīti*).
It must be asked: since [the singing] consists solely of vocal (śārīra) song, how can there be an injunction for the *kāṇḍavīṇā* and other instruments therein?
[The answer is: because there is no evidence that the increase of vocal song occurs only within the body (*śārīra*).

Therefore, since there is no injunction regarding their being means in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no harm even if they are not bodily (*aśārīra*) here, given that the *kāṇḍavīṇā* and others are enjoined despite the increase being bodily.
Or, let it be that even here [in this context] it possesses a bodily nature; however, what is prescribed here is merely the accompaniment of the *kāṇḍavīṇā* and other instruments.
And by virtue of suitability, while playing the *kāṇṍavīṇā* in unison with the singing, they should perform the ordinary *upagāna* (responsive chanting) with their mouths.

This being the position reached, first regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*): in the statement "the priests sing along" (*ṛtvija upagāyanti*), it is not merely the act of increasing (*upacaya*) performed by the priests that is enjoined by way of restating the *sāman*-chanting performed by the *udgātṛ* and others. Rather, because the meaning of the prefix [in *upa-*] implies the existence of chanting, that which is performed by the priests is enjoined. And when the expectation arises as to whose [chanting] is to be increased, it is connected with the *sāman*-chanting, since that is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).

Furthermore, since no other means of accomplishment is prescribed for the *gāna* which consists of accumulation (*upacaya*), its very nature as the *sāman*-chanting under discussion must be relied upon.
Consequently, because such *sāman*-chanting—which conforms to specific sounds such as the *tālu* (palate) and so forth—is accepted as being of the nature of *sāman*-chanting, it is called *upagāna*.
Moreover, the inclusion of *kāṇḍavīṇās* (flutes) therein is not possible, as their nature as *sāman*-chanting would otherwise be untenable.
Therefore, in this context, immediately after the *upagāna*, that which employs instruments such as the *kāṇḍavīṇā* is enjoined.

And since the word "singing" (*gāna*) can be applied even to the playing of strings, the *upagāna* may indeed be performed with the *kāṇḍavīṇā* as its instrument. Furthermore, this is not an augmentation of the original *sāman* chanting; rather—

Upadeśa: 1146. Upanaya: "The wise have declared that [the definition] is its denotation, which excludes both similar and dissimilar classes" (Vivaraṇa, p. 239; Kaṇikā, p. 240). Om. *Udaya*, *vidhi*, and *codanā* are synonymous.

Bāla, p. 4: Oṃ. The instruction (*upadeśa*) has been examined through six types of deficiencies (1–6). Vi. 7/1/1: An instruction regarding what ought to be done pertains to matters that are possible and so forth. Bhā. 6/2/4/49: Furthermore, an instruction being imparted even to those of dull intellect becomes fruitful.
Moreover, all [beings] are of dull intellect when compared to someone [superior].
(10.4.2.4.49). Where a textual composition that explains the collection of meanings required for a specific purpose is recited, that is *upadeśa*. (Vi.
7111, in the context of the introduction). For indeed, even from delusion (*vyāmoha*), there arise instructions (*upadeśāḥ*).
When there is no delusion, [the application] arises even from the Veda;

Bhāṣya 1.1.2.2, p. 16. In that which consists of the excellence of the sixfold instruction (*upadeśa*), extended application (*atideśa*) is postulated (the six means—direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth—are *upadeśa*;
Vārttika 3.6.7–9). Through direct instruction (*upadeśa*), the origin of the ritual action is understood, not through extended application (*atideśa*).
2|1|2|21 p. 525. An extended application (atideśa) is weaker than a direct injunction (upadeśa).
Therefore, in the *avabhṛtha* bath belonging to the *vāruṇapraghāsa* sacrifice, Varuṇa’s sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is set aside by means of the husks (*tuṣa*) and the scrapings (*niṣkāsa*).
Vi. 7|3|5. Furthermore, the status of direct injunctions as such is established through the negation of other [conflicting] cognitions.

*Bṛhatī*, p. 180: Because they fall within the scope of extended application (*atideśa*) preceded by direct instruction (*upadeśa*), and because they belong to the seventh and subsequent sections (*paṭṭaka*), [the treatises] await the first six sections which consist of the investigation of direct instruction.

*Vārttika* 3.1.1.1, p. 651: This very same [principle] applies to the status (*gati*)—that is, the authority (*prāmāṇya*)—of the instructional sentences found even in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. 1.3.1.2, p. 166: The sequences of the meaning of the *Śruti* and the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) are the objects of direct instruction.
*Ḍupa* 5.1.1.1, p. 1287: Furthermore, when there is direct instruction (*upadeśa*), even extended application (*atideśa*) does not operate.

*Vārttika* 2.1.2.1, p. 390, l. 26: "The maxim that 'the relative strength and weakness [of rules] is reversed regarding direct instruction and non-instruction' is an exception to the principle that 'between the dependent (*upajīvaka*) and the basis (*upajīvya*), the basis is stronger.'"—*Saṃgraha*.
In the case of whether there is an authoritative teaching or no such teaching, the relative strength and weakness are reversed.

For instance, it is observed that regarding the moon and so forth, verbal testimony—which teaches an extremely vast magnitude—sublates perception, which apprehends a limited magnitude (the size of a thumb).

Furthermore, it is observed that in the case of space (*ākāśa*), there is a sublation of the very perception that serves as the basis for inference—namely, the perception of its counter-correlate, color such as blue—by means of an inference establishing the absence of blueness and the like, based on the teaching that space has sound as its sole specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*).

The rash one [should act]. 404. According to the instruction, according to the designation, and according to the indicative mark, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) must each perform their respective duties.
Bhāṣya.
And when direct instruction (*upadeśa*) is impossible, there occurs extension (*atideśa*).

Vārttika 3.6.16.41, p. 1061. But as for the *anugrathya* [verses], since all direct instruction is absent (due to the absence of *śruti* and so forth), their application will occur solely through extension. Vārttika 3.6.7.19. Furthermore, that which is impossible cannot be fit for direct instruction.

Bhāṣya 6.1.5: *upadeśivadbhāvaḥ*. "Upadeśa" means the instruction [regarding] a suffix (*pratyaya*); that which possesses this is "upadeśī. That which functions similarly to an "upadeśī" is "upadeśivat."
The state of being that [is expressed by the suffix -tva].
Soma 3.3.8: "And the placing [of the potsherds] is for that purpose;
therefore, the ritual act of placing the potsherds should not be performed for the sake of the Saurya [oblation]."

Because of being for that purpose: since the placing of the potsherds is for the sake of cooking the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and because that [purpose] is absent in the case of the cooked rice (*caru*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), the term "non-performance" (*akriyā*) is carried over [from the previous rule].
By the analysis of the compound as *tādarthyāt* ("because of being for that purpose"), the hearing of the word *athaḥ* from the preceding sūtra is referred back.
That which has that as its object or purpose is "tadartha";

the state of being such is "tadarthyam. Of what? Of the *upadhāna* (the placing of bricks). There is a simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) by means of the collection of eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapāla*) and so forth.

Bhāṣya 5.2.3.14–5: In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the mere act of placing (*upadhāna*) the *naivāra* oblation is enjoined by the statements, “There is a *naivāra* oblation” and “He places the oblation.
[This is] like the act of placing.

Just as in the passage, "This indeed is direct food; he who places this *caru* [oblation] [therein]," the placing of the *caru* is solely for the purpose of being placed [as a brick], so too is the placing of the *naivāra-caru* in the *cayana* [altar-building rite]. Bhāṣya 9.1.2.31.
Application (*upanaya*) is the subsumption of the reason—which has been shown by the example to be invariably concomitant with the property to be proven—into the subject (*sādhya-dharmin*).

Ratnākara, p. 223. Application is the statement that establishes the subject as possessing the property qualified by pervasion; for example, "And so is this" (the subject, which is the locus of the reason pervaded by the property to be proven).
Maṇi, p. 39.

Upanayana (1147). Regarding the section on the Upanayana-homa: Upanayana is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of Vedic study, because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the boy who is the agent of that fruitful study. *Śāstradīpikā*, Tarka-pāda, p. 6. Upanayana is enjoined by such injunctions as "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa," as qualified by the spring season and qualified by the agents such as the Brāhmaṇas. *Viṣaya-vicāra* 2.3.1. Upanayana.

"One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn" (Bhāṣya 6.1.7.33). The initiation (*upanayana*) is enjoined by the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) verbal suffix in the injunction for making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*). And the injunction for Vedic study has that [initiation] as its scope, because the subject matter of the injunction for study is study performed by one who has been initiated.
It has been stated that initiation (*upanayana*) is the subject of the injunction for Vedic study because it does not pertain to [other] objects of experience.

This being the case, the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) impels [the student] by way of its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), whereas the injunctions for ritual acts (*karmavidhi*) impel him merely through their utility.
(Ṛjuvimalā, pp. 8–9). Even prior to initiation, liquor must not be drunk and a Brāhmaṇa must not be killed.

"After the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), [rites] such as salutation and rising to greet others are taught; prior to initiation, one is said to have freedom of action, speech, and eating" (Vājasaneyi-prātiśākhya 6.2.6.22). Regarding the initiation ceremony, the *smṛtis* prescribe the bright fortnight, the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*), and auspicious times as the proper periods.
VI. 6|8|5. Because the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*) has knowledge as its purpose.
One is brought into the presence of the teacher for the sake of knowledge, not for some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), nor to build a difficult wall or the like.
Bhāṣya 6|1|7|35. And at the very time of initiation, his instructions are given [such as]: "One should not speak untruth."
Bhāṣya 3.4.4.2. Oṃ. The Section on the Upanayana Oblation. The Upanayana oblation is to be performed in the secular fire (laukika-agni), not in the Vedic fires (śrauta).
One should study after the initiation (upanayana), because of its connection with the oblation (homa).
The Commentary states: They recite this [text]: "One should offer oblations with the *abhi* verses upon initiating him.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is this oblation to be performed in fires consecrated by the rite of fire-laying (*ādhāna*), or in unconsecrated fires?
What is established? That one should establish the fires upon initiation (*upanayana*), because [the fires] are consecrated.
Why? Because of the connection with the *homa* (oblation) regarding the *āhavanīya* fire: "When one offers in the *āhavanīya*, by that he becomes satisfied and pleased for him.
Therefore, these *homas* occur after the time of the establishment (*ādhāna*).
Or rather, it should take place in the common fire, as in the case of the Sthapati-isti, because of the sequence of knowledge and action.
The Commentary states: "It is not the case that one must offer such [oblations] only after having established the sacred fires (ādhāna).
What then? It proceeds in the common fire itself."
Why? Because they follow the sequence of knowledge and ritual action.
These oblations are for the purpose of acquiring knowledge;
and only one who possesses knowledge has the qualification for the consecration (*ādheya*), by virtue of his capability.
Therefore, this [consecration] cannot be understood as occurring at a time subsequent to the *ādhāna*, as is the case with the *sthapatīṣṭi*.
Furthermore, the *ādhāna* is connected with a wife.
The Commentary states: "And the *ādhāna* is heard in scripture as being connected with a wife."
Furthermore, the taking of a wife occurs after the acquisition of knowledge;

for that reason as well, the prior occurrence of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) is not tenable. Moreover, there is no ritual action subsequent to the consecration, for its connection is indeed with ritual actions.
The Commentary says: Here it is argued:
that activity prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) shall be for the sake of ritual action (karma);
and by virtue of the scriptural statement, that which follows the establishment of the fires is for the sake of offspring (apatya).
"In both cases, this fault will not arise, just as in the case of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
To this it is replied:
"And marriage is not a ritual act at a time subsequent to the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna)."

Why? Because the ritual act belongs to the collection [of fires] such as the Āhavanīya. Furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is for its own purpose; thus, there is a restrictive rule.
Therefore, it is not the case that the taking of a wife must occur at both times.
"If it is argued that it is like the *śrāddha* ceremony," the Commentary says: Here he [the opponent] objects:

"Just as the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is performed by both one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and one who has not (*anāhitāgni*), so too is the taking of a wife"—this which was stated must be refuted.
No, because it contradicts the Śruti.
Commentary: This is not so;
for there would indeed be a contradiction with the Śruti.
If this were done while performing the rite of marriage, it would be contradictory to claim that what is heard [in the texts] as occurring after the acquisition of Vedic knowledge is performed first.
If you argue that this is a different matter altogether,
we say no.
This is a restriction of time for one who has not yet attained the purpose;
and the initiation ceremony is for the sake of ritual action.
Therefore, it is prohibited on the second day.
Because it serves all purposes, one need not employ it solely for the sake of a son.

The Commentary says: Now, it might be argued that prior to the consecration (ādhāna), it is for the sake of ritual acts (karma), and after [the consecration], it will be for the sake of offspring (apatya).
Since this is so through those very [acts], there is nothing lacking for him.
It is said: this is not so;
for she is intended for all purposes, and will not serve merely for the sake of offspring.
Thus it has been said: "Because there is no difference in the enthusiasm for the fruit.
For this reason also, there is no taking of two wives.
Moreover, it is stated thus in all cases: "One should not be excessive in dharma, artha, and kāma."
This being the case, she would be transgressed;
therefore, for this reason as well, there is no taking of two wives.
There is only one wife, for the sake of ritual action and for the sake of offspring.
Section 1148: The Oblation for the Initiation (Upanayana-homa) and the Procedure for Initiation;
and from that [it follows] that [the study of the Veda] occurs subsequent to the acquisition of knowledge.

Therefore, these oblations are not performed because they are consecrated by the rite of fire-installation (*ādhāna*). However, there is the attainment of the second [fire] through the drinking of Soma; therefore, one should take hold of it.
Commentary: This is accepted—that prior to initiation (*upanayana*), there is no wife.
As for what was said—that there is only one wife—that is not accepted as final.

Just as the Smṛti states, "She must not be transgressed in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma," and "One should not take another wife while the current wife is endowed with dharma and progeny," even so this is likewise recorded in the Smṛti: "In the absence of either [of these qualities], one may take another."
Therefore, one whose wife is neither endowed with virtue nor endowed with offspring may take another;
thus he provides an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the drinking of Soma:
"A drinker of Soma does not take a second wife," which thereby indicates the existence of a second wife as well.
"But regarding the Pitṛyajña, it is understood [to be performed] before the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), because it is seen [in the texts].
Commentary: Now, how is it that the Pitṛyajña has two times?
It is said:
For a scriptural statement is seen there:
"It should be performed even by one who has not established the sacred fires.
Therefore, the Pitṛyajña takes place prior to the establishment of the fires.

Viśvarūpa says: "As for the fire-oblation performed at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), whether it be in the Vedic or the worldly fire—since it was previously stated that [the Vedic fire] is absent, let that oblation take place in the Vedic fire."

The initiation of one who has been brought near [to the teacher] should be performed with the knowledge of lightning; for one who is not so initiated, it is not [performed]. In the absence of a Vedic fire, the oblation is offered in a common (laukika) fire.

Bhaṭṭa: There is no dispute that the oblations (*homa*) which constitute the act of initiation (*upanayana*)—whether performed by the teacher (*ācārya*) or by the student (*māṇavaka*)—are for the purpose of consecrating the student by means of the initiation.

Among these, as for those performed by the teacher, even though the teacher may be one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), since they fall under the category of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the fires), they should not be performed for the sake of the teacher;
rather, these are to be performed in the ordinary (*laukika*) fire.
But those [acts] for which a human agent is the performer are even more so [excluded],

because the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) is the motivator (*prayojaka*) not only of the injunctions regarding the seasons but also of the oblations that constitute an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the initiation (*upanayana*). Even if it were a motivator, the fire-installation cannot be performed prior to the initiation, as it lacks any means of inducing knowledge [of its procedure], just like other ritual acts.

Furthermore, even if it were an injunction [of study], the assumption of both [the student and the householder] as qualified persons would be untenable, because it is impossible for them to exist in the relationship of husband and wife. And since marriage is prescribed after the return home (*samāvartana*) by the rule "having bathed, one should desire a wife," it is impossible [for marriage] prior to that time.
Nor can the timing be sublated merely to suit a specific purpose.
Otherwise, this statement would result in being devoid of any subject matter.
Nor can it be a prescription regarding the timing for taking another wife for the sake of offspring, as indicated by the passage beginning with "In matters of dharma and artha... and so forth.

Upon careful consideration, [marriage] is not for the sake of *dharma* and other goals either, because another wife is impossible; furthermore, even regarding the act of marriage, since its own independent time is prescribed, the injunctions concerning the seasons (*ṛtu*)—just like the injunctions for the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) and Vedic study—lack the capacity to necessitate the act of marriage.

For this very reason, for one who is dispassionate, there is no act of marriage for the sake of ritual action, but rather only the transition to another stage of life (*āśrama*). Otherwise, if the fire-consecration were performed prior to the initiation (*upanayana*), would it not entail the loss of the prescribed time for the consecration due to the birth of a son, or the loss of the prescribed time for initiation due to the occurrence of the *adhvarṣa* [period]?

Therefore, these [fires] are also merely worldly (laukika). Maṇḍana says: "One who is not initiated should perform the homa in the worldly fire. Śaṅkara says: "And those who have undergone initiation [should do so] in the worldly fire."
3. The *upanayana-homa* (initiation oblation) is to be performed in the common (*laukika*) fire, and not in the *āhavanīya* fire. (Vi.
6.8.2). Regarding initiation and study, the rites are obligatory (*nitya*) by virtue of their result.
Alternatively, their status as obligatory is established by the statement, "From this point on, one is subject to censure," and by the prohibition, "Those who do not study become brazen."
Maṇi, pp. 4–5: Only after the initiation ceremony (upanayana) are the actions prescribed by the Smṛtis to be performed.
Bhāṣya 6.1.121–22: After the initiation ceremony, the Vedic matters are recited;
