When the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) poured into the ladle of the venerable deity is being carried toward the *āhavanīya* fire, a hand or some substance must necessarily be placed on top according to established practice (*ācāra*).

In this context, because of proximity, the rule "having grasped a fuel-stick (*samidh*) by its handle, he runs after [the oblation]" is understood to have this very purpose, since it prescribes an object required by that practice.

Therefore, the statement "he wears it over [the left shoulder]" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established—just like the *upavīta* rule and so forth—based on the principle that "there is the observation of an indicative mark for something that exists" (as per the previous logic).
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"In the case of wearing [it], there must be an injunction itself, for there is no source of its prior establishment."
Because of the incapacity for concealment, [the fuel-stick] does not follow from the practice (ācāra) as something superior.

It is true that concealment should be performed according to practice, but in that case, the fuel-stick (*samit*) would not even be applicable there, since it could only be restricted by proximity (*saṃnidhi*).
For in that context, only the hand would be applicable due to its fitness, not the fuel-stick.

But surely, by the force of the scriptural injunction regarding the *somacamasas* and so forth, whatever [portion] would otherwise be purposeless [is set aside]; likewise here too, whatever [portion] will be excluded by the *pracchinnam*. This would indeed be the case if, even when there is an indication of their respective sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), [the rule applied] to the *upavatī* and *prabhavatī* [verses].

The maxim "even for that which serves as a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa), [the rule] applies to the secondary indicator itself" is well known; for example, in the injunction "one should arrive every day at the time of the *śakla*," when a specific time has been taken as a secondary indicator by the mention of *śakla*, even if on a certain day the moon does not appear, it is not understood that the time indicated by it does not exist.
(Rasāyana, pp. 21–22)
This very same principle applies to *upalakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) and the principle of *lakṣaṇapāya* (the disappearance of the defining characteristic).

The discussion regarding this [principle] is found in the section on the *Upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice even when there is only one sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), as noted in the *Cintāmaṇi*.
Oṃ, the principle of the non-departure of what is to be characterized (*upalakṣaṇīyānapāyanyāya*) (10.8.18.69).
This is indeed the principle of the non-departure of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇapāyanyāya*).

For even though [the result] actually comes into being after the subsequent [cause], the elaboration of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by the mere possibility [of the effect] through the principle of the non-departure of what is to be characterized, even prior [to its actualization].

Furthermore, if it is argued that—by the principle of the "removal of the indicative" (*upalakṣaṇapāyanyāya*)—the injunction regarding time actually intends only a specific time for the performance (*anukartavya*), and thus there is a sublation of the time, then this is not an injunction of time at all. [As stated in] *Soma* 5.1.18: "That [is to be given] to the chief of those who are ignorant. As for the objection that, when an indicative is introduced, it is improper for a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) to serve as an example, that is a challenge based on the fact that even an indicative functions as a qualifier.

Or rather, there will be the status of an example by virtue of some commonality; [the example] "milk that has been drained" [serves as an illustration] by way of being inexpressible and by way of being a differentiator.
*The maxim of the disappearance of the indicator*.
"Even when there is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is a means of indication (*upalakṣaṇopāya*).
According to this principle, it is a substance (*dravya*).
For an indicator, being unperceived, becomes the object of the cognition that "it does not exist."
For one does not entertain the apprehension that "it does not exist" regarding that which is absolutely unperceivable.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 248. Oṃ *Upalā*.
The sprinkling of the curd and the parched grain is prompted solely by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), not by the act of killing.
Mānava Śrautasūtra 9.1.12–13:
"One should employ the *pratipad* verse beginning with *upa tvā* for a sacrifice where the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*-stotra."
The *upavatī* is a *ṛc* verse containing the word *upa*, such as: "Sing forth to him, O men! (*upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ*).
Oṃ. The *upavatī* and *prabhavati*, which are occasional (*naimittika*) and original (*prākṛta*) *pṛṣṭha-pratipads*, are not to be performed in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *saṃsava*.

In the case of the *ubhayasāman* [sacrifice], there should be an optional application of the rule based on the specific characteristic (*naimittika*), because of its equality. The Commentary states: There are sacrifices characterized by both *sāmans*, such as "one should perform both at the *saṃsava*";
and it is also heard in the *Apaciti* sacrifice that "one should perform both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*."

In this regard, there are two [prescriptions]: one conditioned by the *rathaṃtara* and one conditioned by the *bṛhat*, namely: "One should employ the *upavatī* as the *pratipad* for that which has the *rathaṃtara-pṛṣṭha*; one should employ the *iyavatī* for that which has the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha*. Herein arises a doubt: should either the one conditioned by the *rathaṃtara* or the one conditioned by the *bṛhat* be performed? Is it an option (*vikalpa*), or should only the one conditioned by the *rathaṃtara* be performed, or should only the one conditioned by the other be performed? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It should be performed according to either condition; it is an option.
Why? Because the application [of both rules] is equal;
there is a combination of contradictory options. Indeed, there is no reason for determination to the effect that "it should be performed with this specific cause" and "not with that specific cause."
And it is not possible to perform both alternatives;
therefore, there must be an option (*vikalpa*). Or rather, it should be restricted by the primary [alternative].
Commentary: As for what was stated—that the attainment is equal and there is no reason for a decisive conclusion—we say that there is.
The primary characteristic of the *rathantara* is its being first in sequence.
Thus it has been said: "Or rather, the primary [act] [applies], because of the prior injunction, as in the case of the *choka*. (12.1.8.23).
Or, due to the destruction of the occasion (*nimitta-vighāta*), there should be a ritual act for one who has undertaken the sacrifice.
The Commentary: The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position.
Because there would be a contradiction between both causal conditions (*nimitta*),
the condition pertaining to the sacrifice itself (*kratu-nimitta*) alone is adopted.
That being the case, this [sacrifice] is neither one characterized by the *rathantara* *pṛṣṭha* nor by the *bṛhat* *pṛṣṭha*.
In that context, the *pṛṣṭha* stotra is accomplished by means of both the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara* [sāmans].
Therefore, the introductory verse (*pratipad*) should not contain the word "water" (*upa*), nor should it contain the word "death" (*mṛtyu*);
rather, it ought to be something else entirely, motivated by the [specific] season.

Soma: Because the *kāva* [sāman] lacks the character of being a *pṛṣṭha*, it cannot serve as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the performance; however, since the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans], which are connected to the *saṃsava* and other rites, are related to the *pṛṣṭha*, it is possible for them to serve as the occasion. Thus, the connection with the appropriate counter-examples is established. Viśvarūpa: "In the Gosava sacrifice, do the *upavatī* and *apratirathā* [stotras] both exist, or not? If they do, is there an option between them, or is only the *upavatī* [to be performed]?"
Because there would be two distinct causes for the conceptual construction, there would be a contradiction if they were combined;
due to the primacy of the Rathantara, it is appropriate [to apply it] only to that which contains the word "upa."
In the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), there is a motive for each individual [element], but here, in the case of the two combined, they are subordinate; therefore, both are not motives.

In the absence of the original cause (nimitta), even when the occasioned rites (naimittika) are performed according to their specific rules, the *upavatī* and *aprabhavatī* [verses] remain as they were; and the *upavādya* is likewise.
The verse beginning with "upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ" is the *upavatī* ṛc; the verse beginning with "prayujo vāco agniyaḥ" is the *agni-yavatī* ṛc.

Bhāṭṭa: In modified sacrifices such as the *saṃsava*, the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* sāmans—both of which are obtained from the archetypal model (*prakṛti*)—is heard in scripture: "In the *saṃsava*, one should perform both the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*."

In this regard, according to the view that those two [Sāmans] serve as the means for a single *pṛṣṭha-stotra* through an option (*vikalpa*), then, since both are combined (*samuccaya*) in this very same stotra according to that view, it is beyond dispute that they are recited by way of repetition (*abhyāsa*) within a single stotra during the *saptadaśastoma*, each serving as the substratum for its respective Sāman through division. Furthermore, that division—namely, that the *rathaṃtara* is used in certain verses and the *bṛhat* in others—is to be understood from the statements of the authors of the Kalpasūtras.

However, even according to the view that there is a distinction between the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*s not achievable by the two *sāman*s, there is still no combination (*samuccaya*) of the two *stotra*s, such that one might suspect the performance of two *stotra*s characterized by the *sadas* and *daśa* stomas.

Rather, since the two *stotra*s are already obtained as alternatives (*vikalpa*), the injunction concerns the specific combination of the two *sāman*s and their respective substrates within a single *stotra*. Therefore, it should be understood that even in that view, there is no difference in the actual performance.

For this very reason, those attributes of *sāman* such as closing the eyes (*saṃmīlana*) and so forth must be performed at that time; thus, there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*) of these as well.
However, regarding those [attributes] pierced by consciousness (*cidviddha*), there is an option (*vikalpa*).
This too is certainly beyond dispute.

However, those [rites] which are prescribed as contingent upon the *bṛhatsāman* or the *rathaṃtarasāman* being the cause—such as the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup and so forth, or as in the rule:

"One should make the *pratipad* of that which has the *bṛhat* as its *pṛṣṭha* possess the word *agra*, and that of the *rathaṃtara-pṛṣṭha* possess the word *upa*"—in these cases, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has the *bṛhat-sāman* as its *pṛṣṭha*," the *agravatī* [verse] is prescribed with reference to the *pratipad* belonging to that [rite], based on the context of the *vahiṣpavamāna* chant, contingent upon the presence of the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha* within the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Because of the possibility of being designated by the genitive case, there is the cognition of it being a causal condition (*nimitta*).

When a doubt arises as to whether those two [rites] are to be performed here in the *Saṃsava* sacrifice and others, or not, since there are two causal conditions, the two contingent rites (*naimittika*) also become applicable.
Since their simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*) is impossible, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

This being the case, since the status of being a cause (nimittatva) conveyed by the word "yadi" is occasional, and since this occasionality is due to the mutual contradiction between the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*, it is understood from the archetype (*prakṛti*) that the causality of the *bṛhat* consists in its obstructing the *rathaṃtara*, or the causality of the *rathaṃtara* consists in its obstructing the *bṛhat*.
Therefore, because the mutual contradiction constitutes the strength of the cause, there is no modification whatsoever resulting from the removal of that [contradiction].
Furthermore, because the contradictory elements are of the nature of a single alternative (*vikalpa*), they are not both performers of the *citrā* sacrifice.

Therefore, the status of being a cause (nimittatā) exists in both cases, just as it does in the archetype (prakṛti), because of their belonging to the same class; however, where there is a restrictive rule (niyama), there is opposition due to sublation (bādhaka). But where there is an absence of the two kinds of opposition, even though the Rathantara and so forth exist, they do not possess the status of being a cause.

For this very reason, in the Viśvajit and other such sacrifices, although other *stotras* exist—such as "the Rathantara is sung when the moon is in the Pañcamāna [nakṣatra], and the Bṛhat when in the Ābhīśava]—there is no rule regarding the precedence of the cup for Indra-Vāyu (*aindravāyavāgra*) and so forth.

Consequently, those occasional (*naimittika*) ritual properties do not apply in the Saṃsava and similar rites due to the absence of conflict and the absence of the specific occasion (*nimitta*). This has been established in the *Kaustubha* under the section on the Rathantara-chant.

And therefore, in that case, the recipient of the gift is indefinite, as is any substance whatsoever that has been offered. Maṇḍana says: "It would apply when there is equality in terms of being the locus of the ritual. Śaṅkara says: "The commonality of the substance partakes of its own specific properties."

Oṃ. Upavarṣa stated that in the sense of the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the threefold aggregate consisting of the deity, the object, and the casting of the offering constitutes the meaning; because there is no renunciation of the object (*karman*) by the deity or the substance, the use of the accusative case in connection with *juhoti* would be untenable, and thus he declared it to express the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*).

Su. pṛ. 632. Oṃ. Upavarṣa stated that since a subordinate element (*guṇa*) independent of the meaning of the verbal root serves as the delimiter of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), it functions as the means for achieving the result through the act of oblation (*homa*).
Oṃ, and likewise there is a deprecation.

Having prescribed the Vāravantīya, Yajñāyajñīya, and Vāmadevya Sāmans for the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), a deprecation—that is, a censure—of the chanting of Sāmans is made in the passage: "The fires of one who chants the Brahma-sāmans at the establishment of the fires become 'upavīta'.
The term *upavīta* means "lacking luster" or "dim."

"Brahma" means the Brāhmaṇa priest, specifically the Udgātṛ; this is a censure. Like the prohibition of taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup mentioned in the section "But having taught [the rule], there would be a prohibition" (10.8.13.6), this should serve as an option. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an option regarding the singing of the *Sāman* at the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*).
If it is argued that action [is required] because of a prohibition;
He raises an objection: there is no option regarding the singing of the Sāmans at the fire-consecration (ādhāna); rather, it is non-performance—that is, they are simply not to be sung at all.
At the fire-consecration, the Sāman must not be sung.
"If one chants the *brahmasāmans* at the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*), the first oblations of this [sacrifice] become worn-out," because of this prohibition of chanting the *sāmans*.
If this is argued, we say:
no, because [the rule] is based on the authority of the sacred word (*śabda*).
The proponent (siddhāntin) says: There is no absolute prohibition of Sāman-chanting at the fire-installation (ādhāna),
because a prohibition is preceded by a scriptural injunction.
And thus, because of both the injunction and the prohibition, there is indeed an option regarding the fast (*upavāsa*). [This concludes] the section on the censure (*upavāda*), sūtra 1166.
Oṃ. The section on censure. At the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the singing of the *Sāman* chants is optional.
The same applies to the *upavādya*. The Commentary states: "Its establishment [is as follows].
Regarding this, they recite: 'He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya'; 'He who, knowing thus, sings the Yajñayajñīya'; 'He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya.'"

In this regard, the following is recited: "Those for whom the Brahman priest chants Sāmans at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) become, as it were, those who wear the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*upavīta*), even though they are [actually] *acirāgni*s.
In this matter, the meaning is subject to doubt: is this a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), or is it an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), or is it an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)?
What is established? It is not a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), because Brahman is not [otherwise] established [as a subject].
A statement concerning that which does not exist serves the purpose of an *arthavāda* (eulogistic or explanatory passage).
For example: "Prajāpati alone existed; he cut out his own omentum."
This being the case, we reply:
no explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning Brahman can serve as a basis for any [inferential] purpose; nor does any explanatory passage situated in another sentence have any utility whatsoever.
Therefore, the censure is similar to that.
To what is it like? It is as if, having enjoined "One takes the ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra," there were a prohibition;

for how could the statement serve the purpose of prohibiting the knowledge of the Brahman-sāman when the singing by the Brahman-priest has not even been established? Thus, the statement cannot be intended as a prohibition of the knowledge of the Brahman.

Therefore, the mention of "Brahman" is not intended [as a specific object]. This must simply be a piercing [of the heart] as obtained through the Sāman chant. If it is argued that the word "Brahman" is a scribal error, this is not so.
The designation "Udgātṛ" will apply because he is a Brāhmaṇa.
[Objection: "If it is argued that it is not a ritual act because of its prohibition"—the Commentary states: "If this is seen, it is merely a censure of the singing of the Sāman."
There is no performance of the *sāman* chanting;
for that which is censured should not be performed.
No, because it is based on scripture (*śabda*).
The Commentary: This is not so.
For just as it is understood from the censure that [something] should not be done, so too it is understood from the instruction that it should be done.
Furthermore, no other injunction is postulated for which this censure would serve as a glorification by stating that "something else should be done."
Therefore, there is an injunction (*vidhi*) for performance and a prohibition (*upavāda*) for avoidance.

Regarding *soma*—the connection [of this example] is due to its arising as before (i.e., as an illustrative instance). Even though in the sentence cited from the Commentary—"The fires of him whose *brahmā* sings the *sāmans* at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) become, as it were, invested with the sacred thread (*upavīta*)"—it is stated thus:
The prefix *upa* expresses proximity. *Vītāḥ* means "gone."
The meaning is that they pass away without delay.
And thus, in that context, only censure (*nindā*) is heard, not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).

For this very reason, even in the Sūtra, the word *upavāda*, which signifies censure, is employed; nevertheless, it should be understood that this is cited with the intention that a prohibition is implied by the censure.
In the passage "The Brāhmaṇa does not sing the Sāmans," the word *brahma* refers to the Brāhmaṇa caste and thus serves as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Udgātṛ priest.
Consequently, the phrase "he should not sing" prohibits singing itself in its essential form.
Since the prohibition concerns singing, the word *brahma* is a restatement of the fact that, in reality, the Brāhmaṇa is the Udgātṛ.
The meaning is that it is something other [than the previous case] because it is mentioned in the Sūtra as well.
As for *ci*: "The prohibition of both is prescribed as a praise of the enjoined;
or it is optional, just as in the case of the height of the sacrificial post (*vapotsedha*), there is also the term *sūti*."
If the injunction were from another source, then the *brahman* priest would perform the *stotra*;
in that case, because the thing to be enjoined is identical, an option (*vikalpa*) is held here, as in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
The singing of the Udgātṛ is subject to option (*vikalpa*) due to two injunctions and prohibitions concerning the same object.
According to the Bhāṭṭas: In the context of the Fire-laying (*ādhāna*), the Sāmans are enjoined thus: "He sings the Vāravantīya," "He sings the Vāmadevya," and "He sings the Yajñīya.
Subsequently, it is heard in scripture: "The Brahman priest does not sing the Sāmans."

In this regard, this is neither a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) nor an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the Brahman priest's agency, because since there is no injunction (*vidhi*) for the Brahman, there is no prior application (*prāpti*) of that role which would require such a negation.

For in the case of the *ādhāna-sāmans*, since they are prescribed by the Yajurveda, the rule governing their application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) dictates that, according to the principle of the *svaras* (melodic accents), the Adhvaryu alone would logically be the performer; nevertheless, the textual statement (*vacana*) establishes the Udgātṛ as the performer, not the Brahman. Therefore, following the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "Brahman" as "one who belongs to the Brāhmaṇa [class]," the word "Brahman" refers to the Udgātṛ himself, and the prohibition is simply of his singing. Thus, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the singing itself.

Even when, according to the *Kalpasūtras*, Brahmā is also prescribed as an optional alternative together with the Udgātṛ, even then, since the option for Brahmā is established by that very [prescription], this [text] does not constitute a prohibition of Brahmā, as that would be redundant.
Therefore, it should be understood that even in that case, this is merely a prohibition of singing (gāna) for the purpose of establishing that option.
Maṇḍana states: "There is an option regarding the Sāmans in the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*)."

Śaṅkara says: "And as for the Sāman in the Agnyādheya [rite], it is there obligatory. However, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, fasting does not have the function of necessitating the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) or the potsherds (kapāla).
Fasting (upavāsa), [entry number] 1167; the sacred thread (upavīta) [is associated with] fasting (upavāsa).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the fasting of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) is enjoined by the rule: "All the ṛtvij fast. This is based on the maxim: "Better to blink than to miss [the opportunity]. (Bhāṣya 10.6.15.5).

In this context, the word *vara* is used in the neuter gender as a general term. Just as the desire for fasting is superior to that for alms—even though both produce affliction—because fasting is desired as being more meritorious despite causing greater suffering; so too, this [rule] applies where it is taught that, according to the relative degree of affliction, that which causes less suffering is superior (*vara*) when compared to that which causes much suffering.

And likewise, for those common folk (*pāmara*) to whom the great knowledge born from mahāvākyas such as "That thou art" does not ascend to the intellect—even though heard repeatedly—due to some obstacle, they must, according to the present reasoning, perform the ritual action (*karman*) prescribed by the supreme tradition; from that, they must certainly practice the meditation on the qualified (*saguṇa*) [Brahman].

Then, when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) becomes purified, knowledge indeed arises. Thus it is stated in the *Pañcadaśī* treatise: "Just as alms are better than fasting, so meditation is better than anything else," and so forth.
This is the courageous one's [view].

The austerity consisting of fasting is a duty for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), not for the officiating priest (*ārlijya*). This is the section concerning austerity (*tapa-adhikaraṇa*). Bhāṣya 8.1.13.9–11.
The *upavīta* is to be worn eight times.
Bhāṣya 10.4.1.1, Section 1: *Upavīta*. The *upavīta*, which is merely a particular arrangement of the garment by the performer, constitutes a subordinate element (*guṇa*).

3|1|1|121: The *upavīta* (sacred thread) is prescribed throughout the entire context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), not only in connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses.
The *upavīta* is an integral part of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Vi. 3|4|2: The *upavīta* is used in rites dedicated to the gods (*daivika*).
3|4|1. The *upavīta*—enjoined by the *smṛti* as "one should always wear the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder" (*nityayajñopavītī*)—is for the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
*Upavīta* means the *yajñopavīta*.
It is one way [of wearing] the *upavīta*, and another way [of wearing] the *yajñopavīta*.
For *upavīta* is merely the arrangement of the garment by the agent, whereas *yajñopavīta* is a specific arrangement of the sacred thread (*sūtra*).

That [arrangement of the garment] is established by general custom as being for the purpose of all ritual acts; however, *upavīta* [as the term here] pertains only to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) due to the context. Since there is no contradiction with the *yajñopavīta*, there is a combination of both. This is because it was stated by the author of the Vārttika in the *Dupaṭīkā*: "In the case of doubt, there would be a syntactical split of the sentence" (3.1.1.121), and furthermore: "And for the agent, that which is called *upavīta* is merely a quality consisting of the arrangement of the garment" (p. 733).

Since this was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, the *brahmasūtra* is not enjoined by the word "he wears" (*upavyayate*). Furthermore, its status as being based on Śruti is established by the passage in the section on the two-fold distinction (*dvidhākopa*) at Sūtra 1.3.16: "He who wears the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītī*) should study, teach, or perform sacrifices."

Regarding the *upavīta* (sacred thread): "For one wearing the *yajñopavīta* milks for the gods"—this is the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that serves as the basis for the rule "one should milk while wearing the *prācīnāvīta*," which pertains to the *pretāgnihotra* rite.
"The wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) should be a duty for all [classes], because of the observation of indicative marks.
Starting from this sūtra, a group of six sūtras has not been commented upon by the authors of the Bhāṣya,

In the *Vistara* and other works, this second section (*adhikaraṇa*), consisting of these two initial sūtras, is as follows:

Or rather—since it is already established that ritual acts (*karma*) are integrated with other ritual acts, the *upavīta* is now cited as an example to determine whether the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) or the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) is the more effective means of application (*viniyojaka*).

Just as subsidiary sentences (*aṅgavākya*), which possess their own complete meanings, enter into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the sentence concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) without abandoning their own nature, so too the subsidiary productive operations (*aṅgabhāvanā*)—complete in their own subsidiaries—are connected to the supreme productive operation (*paramabhāvanā*); it is not by way of deficiency that their own specific properties (*svadharma*) cease to exist.
Furthermore, since a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) has the *apūrva* as its purpose, it requires the means for its accomplishment and thus enters the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Even in the case of a visible result, there exists an internal context because it requires the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) for the sake of accomplishing the unseen merit of the restrictive rule (*niyamādṛṣṭa*).
"Even when the visible fruit is present, that [desire] does not fail to arise;
however, even when it is present, it is turned away by some means or other.

However, since the optional rites (*kāmyāḥ*) are understood from scripture itself as being for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*), they are not included within the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses; thus, the section concerning the sacred thread (*upavīta-adhikaraṇa*) does not apply to them.

If, however, the *nivid*s were subsidiary (*aṅga*) [to the sacrifice], then, by the principle of the *godohana* vessel, because they would be grasped through their dependence on a substratum, there would still be a continuation of the context (*prakaraṇa*) even in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*). Even if they were subsidiary to the optional rites, we might somehow determine—through a connection similar to that of the mantras for the *pūya* offering—that the context is not sublated; yet neither of these conditions exists. Therefore, in the absence of an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), the *nivid*s serve all purposes by virtue of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*).

Now, if optional ritual procedures (*kalpa*) are heard in a context that has been interrupted, then [the question arises]: "One should effect stability by means of twenty-one [verses]—by what are they supported? Since the requirement for a support is being sought through the context (*prakaraṇa*), incompleteness results because of the resulting expectancy.

Alternatively, if the support is brought forward by the syntactical connection (*vākya*), then, since the ritual act is already established, the sentence would suffer from a split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the establishment of two distinct relationships.

In that case, if a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) were admitted, or if it were somehow avoided, then in the cases of the *revatī*, *vāravantīya*, and *saubhara* hymns as well, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) would be lost because the context (*prakaraṇa*) would likewise provide the substratum (*āśraya*) by means of the sentence itself. If, on the other hand, the context continues to apply somehow due to the availability of a substratum, then the *upavīta* (the sacrificial thread) would also obtain [its application] in exactly the same way; thus, this is a dilemma in every respect. It is said in reply:

Therefore, one should accomplish "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth by means of the recitation (*anuvacana*) qualified by "twenty-one" and the other attributes.

Conclusion: Regarding the general injunction (anārabhyavidhi) stating "one should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses in a similar manner," there is a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) by the rule for the *sāmidhenīs* in cases of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) and so forth, according to the principle: "That which is prescribed as fifteen-fold applies to cases of deficiency and so forth."
10|8|19|17–19. Conclusion: The restriction of what is generally obtained to a specific case. (A general rule that is unclear should be restricted by a specific one;

Vārttika, p. 977. An *anārabhyavidhi* (unattached injunction) is a general rule, whereas an injunction found within the context of the *Mitravindā* sacrifice and others is a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*).
Mīmāṃsā:
Repetition for the purpose of a conclusion is powerful, because it is improper for many [repetitions] to be otherwise.
Parākrama: For in a conclusion, there is a restriction from what has been obtained in a general sense to a particular one.

If it is argued that—just as the fourfold division, which applies to the *puroḍāśa* in general according to the rule "one divides the *puroḍāśa* into four," is restricted to the *āgneya* cake by the rule "one divides the *āgneya* into four"—[the author states the refutation offered by the *Nyāyasudhākāra*: this is because restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) serves the purpose of restricting [a rule] to that specific instance alone.

[To refute that, he states the traditional view: Others, however, maintain that restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) consists in the logical restriction of a prescription—which has been established in a general sense—to a particular case.

What is the meaning of "restriction to that alone" (*tanmātrasaṃkoca*)? Is it a restriction to the *āgneya* [cake] alone, or is it a restriction to a specific instance of what was previously established as a general rule? In the first case, there would be no subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) of the rule taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) by the sentence located within the context of the *Mitravindā* and other sacrifices, because there would be no restriction to the *āgneya* alone. In the second case, just as the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), which applies to all sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) in general, is restricted to the *āgneya*, so too, since the rule applies generally to both the *anuyāja* and non-*anuyāja* offerings, its restriction to the *anuyājas* would indeed constitute a subsumption. (Therefore, that is not the case).

*Mīmāṃsā*, pp. 456–57: On account of the strength of the concluding portion (*upasaṃhāra*), there is no determination that dahara and the others are Brahman; rather, it is by the principle of favoring the majority (*bahunugrahanyāya*).

*Parākrama*: 571, the connection of a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*) that has already attained self-sufficiency through the strength of its conclusion is not logical. 4312: Prohibition in the form of a conclusion (*upasaṃhārarūpa*) is of many kinds.
Furthermore, the method of sublation (*upasaṃhāra*) is of various kinds.
All of this, along with examples, should be examined in the extensive treatise titled *Vidhirdvividhaḥ?*, which is intended for beginners.

A rule occurring in the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) is set aside by one occurring in the introduction (*upakrama*), just as the words "Ṛk" and so forth in the injunction "one recites the Ṛks loudly" are superseded by the introductory statement regarding the Vedas.
*Bāla.*, p. 140: For the purpose of a summary (*upasaṃhāra*).
Regarding defects and so forth, the repeated mention of the *sāmidhenī* verses for the *sādana* is for the purpose of summarizing the *sādana* taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*).
