The Fourth Section.
The fourth section:

The division into four parts belongs only to the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni, not to that dedicated to Agni-Soma and others. However, the remnant, being associated with the subordinate qualities, should be understood as common [to all], because of their mutual connection.
Commentary: Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is stated generally: "He divides the cake dedicated to Agni into four parts.

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the division into four apply everywhere—to the cake for Agni, the cake for Agni-Soma, and the cake for Indra—or only to the cake for Agni? What is the prima facie view? The division into four applies to all; for the term "cake for Agni" (*āgneyam*) is understood as a general designation connected with the quality of the deity.
It should apply to the offering to Agni-Pūṣan as well as to the offering to Indra;
why?
Because those two are also [offerings] to Agni.
That for which Agni is the deity, and nothing else, is *āgneya*.
Just as, for example, the mother of both Ḍittha and Ḍittha belongs to Ḍittha, so it is here as well.
If there were no mutual relationship between the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni and that dedicated to Agni-Soma, then the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) would be restricted to the *āgneya* alone.
But there is indeed a connection;
therefore, there is no fixed restriction.

Just as, according to the rule, "Having divided the head of the Āgneya [offering], he cuts off the portions," the eating of the *prāśitra* portion is performed from all [the cakes], so too is the fourth division (*caturthākaraṇa*).
Or rather—the determination of the meaning has been stated according to the connection (*saṃyoga*).
However, the inquiry is whether that connection occurs even by way of a single part, or only by way of the whole.
Furthermore, in the injunction regarding the fourth preparation (*caturthākaraṇa*), is the two-deity offering (*dvidevatya*) included by the word *āgneya*, or not?
We say that it is grasped. Why? Because it is possible for [an offering] to have two deities.
He was to be perceived by her alone,
as Agni is in the *manotā* hymn during the union with Agni and Soma.
Even though Agni is not a deity, he is not non-integrated [with the sacrifice].
And it is the state of being integrated that is the cause for being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), not the status of being a deity.
Furthermore, Agni here is not connected with the ritual action (*kārya*) in such a way that—
It is not absolutely respected.
What then? It is for the purpose of indication (*upalabdhyārtha*).

Furthermore, the secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇāni*) are not adopted in their ritual applications exactly as they are heard—such as the two *puroḍāśa* cakes which serve to indicate the time between the *upāṃśuyāja*—but rather according to their indicative function.
Likewise, because it is employed for Patnīvat, that [offering] is independent;
likewise, "the mother of the one about to give" means the mother is [the giver] of both the object to be given and the wealth to be spent.
(Regarding words denoting what is to be protected, since they have the sense of a characteristic mark, by that very reason of being perceived, [the word] *taddhura* [is used]).
Because there is no mutual relationship between the characteristic mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the action (*kārya*), there is commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*).

However, the Commentator, having attached this very term "non-injunction" (*acodanā*) from the sūtra "Proximity is not an injunction" (3.1.24), has stated: "Because of the lack of connection among them, it would be an injunction."

And for such things, there is indeed commonality; thus, it is said that "the *prāśitra* is cut off" (meaning the remnant in the form of the *prāśitra*-portion, though connected with the quality of fire, is common).

Or rather, there is a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) due to the connection with a specific purpose; the mention of the quality is for the sake of indicating the relationship of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) with its object.

Commentary: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. Or rather, the fourth act is restricted to the Āgneya sacrifice alone; it cannot be common to both. Why? Because of its connection with the specific purpose.
The connection with Agni as the deity applies to that which has Agni alone as its deity, not to that which has two deities, such as the Agnīṣomīya or the Aindrāgna.
Why? Because for that which has Agni-Soma as its deity, the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is made qualified by both attributes;
in that case, Agni is a deity only insofar as it depends upon Soma, not independently.
Furthermore, when fire (agni) has Soma as its expectant deity, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is not produced from that [compound],
for it is said to be applied only to those [compounds] that are semantically independent (*samartha*); and that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*) is not semantically independent.
Therefore, by means of a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, there is the designation of the two-deity offering as having Agni as its deity independently.
Consequently, the employment of the fourth case (*caturthī*) occurs only where Agni is the independent deity;
for the connection of the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix with the deity-sign occurs through semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), and not when such capacity is absent.
Now, as for the argument that just as the cutting off of the *prāśitra* portion is performed by all [the priests], so too should the fourth act be performed;
this may well apply to the cutting off of the *prāśitra*, but there the connection is not made in that way, namely: "The *prāśitra* of the cake dedicated to Agni is cut off."
How then? The head of the *āgneya* [cake] is divided.
One portion is designated as "he cuts off the *prāśitra*," and the second is "having divided the head of the *āgneya*.
In that case, it is understood that he cuts off from the head of the *āgneya*.
It is another [cup] that should not be taken from the head of one [deity] for another;

however, if the name *kevalāgni-devatya* (dedicated solely to Agni) were not present there, then even a cup dedicated to two deities (*dvidevatya*) would have been accepted in order to avoid its becoming purposeless.
As for the argument that it belongs to the mother of the one intended to be given, that is appropriate in that case.
The mother is the primary cause (*mātṛla*).
From her he is born; by this much connection she is called "mother.
Nothing else is required here.

And since such a relationship exists there, it is appropriate to say that [the cup] is the mother of what is intended to be given. Or rather: "Just as the cups are not characterized by the state of being *prahita*, so too there would be no characterization by the state of being dedicated to two deities (*dvidevatya*) in the case of the *āgneya*."
It has been stated that what is being uttered is indeed intended to be expressed.
However, the Agniṣomīya and Aindrāgna offerings do not possess the character of being dedicated to Agni alone (*āgneyatva*).
For in these cases, it is not the mere generality of "Agni" that serves as the defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).
What then? It is the status of being a deity (devatātva) as conveyed by the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita).
Agni, moreover, is its qualifier. That toward which a substance is offered when prompted [by a scriptural injunction] is the deity.

Furthermore, that which belongs to two deities is not offered by designating Agni alone; for a cognition directed toward multiple objects is not designated by a single term. It is not said that the offering to Agni-Soma, Agni, or Indra-Agni is the same as that to Agni alone.

In this context, the gender is determined by the secondary derivative (taddhita) suffixes and so forth; for a secondary derivative occurs with words that are semantically connected, while a compound occurs with words that are not [separately] connected, and the secondary derivative *ām* also exists in the place of a compound.

The term *āgneyaḥ* refers to that which has Agni as its deity independently; it does not apply when Agni is a deity in conjunction with another. Therefore, this *taddhita* suffix is said to be excluded from cases such as *āgnīṣomīya*, and thus it does not express the deific status of that [conjoint] meaning.
But where that deity is independent, it can be called "belonging to Agni" (āgneya). As for the argument that it is "like the *prāśitra*," it is replied:
in this case, the scriptural mention of the quality of belonging to Agni is for the purpose of indicating a specific location.

Since the general rule would apply the *prāśitra* portion everywhere, this specific statement—"this [portion] is for the head"—is intended to establish a special exception regarding the head; thus there is a discrepancy.
However, once the formal topic (*adhikaraṇa*) is established, it is further countered as follows:
"Or rather, both [portions are taken], because of the lack of distinction," based on the hearing of the Kātyāyana injunction.
Kātyāyana has stated here, having seen the Śatapatha Śruti:
"Having divided that cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass. To this it is replied: "It is true that there is a scriptural statement which is seen without qualification."
But that [knowledge] is established as distinct by means of another scripture, which is eternal.
If it is argued that the same applies to the *prāśitra* (the portion for the Brahman priest), we say no; because it serves a secondary purpose (*guṇārthatvāt*).
Since the statement "having divided the head" is intended to convey a specific quality (*guṇa*), a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*) cannot be restricted by it.
However, this [other] repetition, being devoid of such qualities (*nirguṇa*), is capable of establishing the general rule within its own domain.
If it is argued that its inclusion is impossible because of its distance, we say no; for "whatever has a semantic connection with something else [is connected] with it, even if it is distant;
indeed, proximity is merely the cause for those things that lack such a connection."
(Thus ends the remainder of the verse) according to the maxim:
"Therefore, the universal necessarily moves toward the particular."
And as soon as it has gone, it is certainly established by him in a state of excellence.

Alternatively, because it is obtained specifically, the general rule is restated for the purpose of enjoining the making of the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) matting. This [making of the matting] is also already established; therefore, it must be stated that the mention [of the number] is for the sake of the sequence. Consequently, it is established that the fourth making belongs to the *Āgneya* sacrifice alone.

"But if, in that case, Agni alone had not been the deity," this [Bhāṣya] is an explanation of precisely that portion of the Sūtra (3.1.25), namely, "the mention of the quality is for the purpose of indication" (*lakṣaṇārthā guṇaśrutiḥ*).
For if there were no deity consisting solely of Agni, then— as in the case of the *manotā*— the word "Agni" would have to indicate both [deities],
or the mention of the quality would have to be for that purpose.

However, there is one that has a single deity; therefore, the fourth [act of] making belongs to that alone. Even though the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) is not connected to the function, nevertheless, it is impossible to grasp what is not characterized by it; thus, it is established that only that which has a single deity is to be grasped. As the Śāstra says: "Agni would be the secondary characteristic of the substance merely by virtue of the connection."
And since the relationship is not distinct, it serves as an indicator for all of them.
This being the position reached, we reply: "In our view, that secondary derivative suffix denotes only the cause;
it is not capable of expressing a deity associated with a name through conjunction."

Soma: Having concluded the discussion regarding the connection with the restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*) as it pertained to the application of that rule, we now consider whether the connection itself is partial or total; this is the logical connection (*saṃgati*). Although a general statement does not result in a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) merely by the presence of a specific statement—otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of restricting the general statement "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa" by the specific statement "One should not kill an Ātreya"—nevertheless, where a general statement, having granted permission, requires a specification, there a restriction occurs upon that specific case.

In the present context, since the fourth preparation (*caturthakaraṇa*)—being of the nature of a ritual disposal (*pratipatti*)—is required by all [offerings], it is logical that the general statement (*sāmānyavacana*) applies the performance of the fourth preparation to the *puroḍāśa* alone; thus, because there is no further need for a specific requirement regarding its performance, a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) based on a specific statement is not possible. Nevertheless, in this case, the general statement does not enjoin the fourth preparation itself, but rather, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it enjoins either the mere state of being placed upon the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣadatva*) or the sequence (*krama*).

Therefore, since there is no restatement for the sake of establishing a fourth [function], it results in having a specific scope in accordance with the statement regarding the *āgneya* (dedicated to Agni) that has been obtained.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), which is connected with a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) acting as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of another, is understood to be common to the *agnīṣomīya* and other sacrifices, because indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) and qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) cannot coexist with one another.
Vi— "The fourth function is stated to be: 'The cake (*puroḍāśa*) is dedicated to Agni'."
The fourth performance is either the remainder of all [the offerings] or only that which belongs to Agni.
Since the indicative mark (upalakṣaṇatā) is appropriate in the Āgneya [rite], it follows that it applies as a supplement to all;
for this reason, the Agniṣomīya and Aindrāgna [rites] possess the character of being Āgneya.
The status of being dedicated to Agni (āgneyatva) is not primary for those two [offerings], because they do not depend solely on Agni;
therefore, the fourth preparatory act (caturthākaraṇa) resides in only one of the two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa).

Bhaṭṭa: In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the injunction "He makes the cake for Agni fourfold," the property of having Agni as the deity and being an oblation (*haviṣyatva*) is not the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if both were intended as qualifiers of the object. Rather, it is simply the status of being an oblation denoted by the *taddhita* suffix.
Or, in some way, it is simply the status of being an oblation related to Agni.
Furthermore, there is a connection with Agni even in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and others.

Alternatively, because of the concluding statement, "He makes the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) fourfold," that [fourfold division] applies only to the *puroḍāśa* connected with Agni, and not to the clarified butter (*ājya*). Or, even if this restriction is somehow intended, nevertheless, in a sacrifice to two deities, Agni alone possesses the status of the deity (*devatātva*) here.

Since the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) heard at the end of a copulative compound (*dvaṃdva*) is connected with each member individually, it follows that all [deities] are the fourth [offering]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because of its primary application, the secondary derivative suffix—which is capable of denoting deityhood alone—is incapable of indicating a mere relationship.
First of all, there is no establishment of [Agni] as being conjoined with [Soma].

Nor does deityhood belong to each individually in a dual-deity (dvidevatya) offering; for, since the conjunction is intended by the dual compound (*dvandva*) prescribed in the sense of mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), deityhood is accepted as a property residing distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) only in the two deities joined together.

Therefore, one should understand that this applies wherever conjunction is intended as the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), based on the traditional rule beginning with "at the end of a *dvandva*," and so forth.

Therefore, a secondary derivative (taddhita) produced from the word *agni* alone is not capable of conveying the intended meaning of "divinity" without depending on the subsequent member [of the compound], because that would result in the subversion of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). As for the claim that the divinity of *agni* is not intended to be expressed, that is not correct.

In the state of *tathatva* (being such), the mere substance under discussion cannot denote an unprecedented means (*apūrvasādhana*), because it has not been stated as being a deity (*devatātva*) or the like.
Nor can it denote the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣyatva*), because that is untenable without the cognition of its status as a deity.

For there is no restrictive rule in the Smṛti stating that "deity-status exists only when the sacrificial oblation is to be expressed," since the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) exists even when expressing a general relationship, including the relationship with a deity.

Therefore, the deityhood that has arrived first possesses the status of being the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatva*) [of the sacrifice]. However, because that [deityhood] requires a correlative (*anuyogin*) and a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the principle of restrictive application (*upasaṃhāranyāya*)—as in the case of the *havirārti* rule or the statement "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*)—applies to the desired state of having Agni as the deity, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [This applies] to the *upasads*, as far as stated.
The status of being the delimitor of the intended object (*uddeśyatā-avacchedakatva*) is established.
By means of this, there is a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*) of the general statement, "He makes the *puroḍāśa* fourfold.
Therefore, the making fourfold applies only to the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*).
Maṇḍana: "For it must indeed be the fourth Āgneya. 194. Śaṅkara: "It should indeed be the fourth Āgneya. 15. The Principle of Recapitulation (Upasaṃhāranyāya).
When a general injunction is specified by a particular instance, its restriction to that instance is logical, as in the case of the *sātatya* (continuous performance).

However, the restriction of the *sātatya* taught outside the context of the ritual commencement (*anārambhādhīta*) does not result merely from the mention of a particular instance; rather, it results from its lack of clarity.
For instance, the *sātatya* of the *sāmidhenī* verses was stated [in the Brāhmaṇa] outside the context of the ritual commencement.

Just as one begins to assume that [the *sāmidhenī* verses] apply to all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) by way of the *sāmidhenīs*, even at that point, in the case of the *Mitravindā* and other such rites, the *arthāpatti* (presumption) is exhausted by the contextual statement (*prakaraṇa*) which connects them with a specific sacrifice; it does not postulate a connection with other sacrifices. Thus, because the connection is not clearly established, there is a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) to the *Sātatya* [rite].

(With this passage, the nature of the principle of *upasaṃhāra*—namely, "A general rule that is unclear should be restricted by a specific one"—is explained); *Parākrama*, 371–2. The nature of the principle of *upasaṃhāra* is expressed as: "A general rule that is unclear should be restricted by a specific one" (*Vārttika* 3.4.14.21, p.
977). However, the exception to this is the principle of the "Uttarārddhaka": "In the case of a clear rule, there is no assumption of restriction by others."

By considering such statements as "There are exactly three *upasads* for the *Sādyaska*," the application of the *upasad* rites is understood to form a single syntactical unit across both the forenoon and afternoon sessions.
Su. p. 787. The *upasad* consists of the three sacrifices to Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu, which are repeated during both the forenoon and afternoon.

Among the three *upasad* rites prescribed for the *jyotiṣṭoma*, each has as its constituent part an initial *upasat* dedicated to Agni, which is enjoined by the sentence "the *abhimanika* [is the first].
Consequently, there are three [such rites] for Agni;
likewise, there are three for Soma and three for Viṣṇu.

Upasad: There are twelve in the Ahīna and the Dvādaśāha; three in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other Ekāhas; and six in the Agnicayana. Regarding the Upasads: starting from the passage "With two [verses] he cuts out the hair," the text shows that the state of having twelve Upasads is a characteristic of the Dvādaśāha applied to the Gavāmayana (Bhāṣya 8.1.17–19). Upasad: Vi. 4.2.13. The term *upasadaḥ* refers to the oblations to be performed on the two days following the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, prior to the pressing of the Soma.
3|3|13. When the *sāmicis* have been performed, there are six *upasads*.
Since the three *upasads* obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) are established in their own respective positions, the number six must be accomplished.
Thus, the first [day] plus the first, the second plus the second, and the third plus the third constitute the number six.
But it is not [the case that] first, second, third; again, first, second, third—thus there would be six. (Ke. 5.3.13).
By the delimitation through the name of the *upasad*s, there is a threefold [repetition].
(Su. p. 690). The performance of the *upasad*s and the *dīkṣā*s in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) follows the rule of their own respective positions.
*Tupū.* 1|14|5|18: Since the twelve-day period (*dvādaśāha*) prescribes the performance of the *upasad* rites collectively (*tantra*), they are performed together over the twelve days.

*Vi.* 9|1|9: Before the *upasad*s, the *saumya* animal sacrifice is to be performed; between them, the *khāṭ* [animal]; and after them, the *aiḍa* animal sacrifice. However, these do not possess the specific characteristics (*dharma*) of the *upasad*s.
Conjunction;
in the Rājasūya sacrifice,
Bhāṣya 4.4.15–16, the number six for the Upasads applies to all [the rites] collectively, not individually, as in the case of the Cayana.
5|3|11-2. In the Upasad rites, in the animal sacrifice for Agniṣṭoma, and in the Ātithyā ceremony, there is only one single sacrificial grass (barhis).
Among these, it is prepared at the Ātithyā;
by that very preparation, its utility is established by extension (prasaṅga) for the Upasads and the Agniṣṭoma animal sacrifice.

VI. 1.2.1.9. In the *upasads*, the *ātithyā*, and the *abhīṣṭomīya* [sacrifices], the mantra for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is repeated because of the distinctness of the locations. Bhāṣya 1.2.1.20–44: Regarding the *subrahmaṇyā* that is performed during the *upasads* and at the end of the *ātithyā* (in the *pañcadaśarātra*), there is a differentiation of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) according to the respective deity; there is no single recitation of the procedure. Therefore, both *subrahmaṇyās* must be invoked.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 1.2.122: "In the *upasads*, one should recite in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
This accentuation is prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the *upasads* themselves, not by the *apūrva* of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
In the *jyotiṣṭoma*: [text continues]
Bhāṣya 9.1.12–13, Section 2: In the *upasads* and the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is exclusively Vedic.

7.4.12–12: In the *upasads*, the sprinkling of the sacrificial grass (*barhis-prokṣaṇa*) is accomplished through *prasaṅga* (extension of application) by means of the sprinkling of the sacrificial grass at the *ātithyā* ceremony.
1.2.1.9.13–44: In the *upasads*, there should be no action beyond what is expressly stated.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are offerings called the Upasads.
In those Upasads, during the performance of the Upasads, only that which is explicitly stated should be performed;
otherwise, the archetypal elements obtained through the *codaka* rule would not be part of the ritual action.

*Karma* means that which is performed; in the context of the *upasads*, it refers to whatever has been prescribed as fit to be done during the *upasad* period, such as the recitation of the *upasandhyāya*.
"Neither action nor non-action;
everything else is not to be performed"—
thus the established doctrine (siddhānta) itself has been stated.
Or rather, because it is not a quality (*aguṇatvāt*), there would be a prohibition of the remainder.
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of refuting the previously stated position.
How, then, is the determination made? That is now stated.

"One pours with a ladle" (suveṇāghārayati); thus, the pouring (āghāra) performed with a ladle is "made of a ladle" (sauva). This is heard [in the scripture]; the first pouring is that which is performed with a ladle.
And that [Aruṇa] is indeed heard [in scripture] as being without qualities (*aguṇa*).
That which has no non-existent, unprecedented quality is "without qualities.
For it is heard as being merely archetypal (*prākṛta*), devoid of any unprecedented quality.

And thus, because the *āghāra* (libation) to be performed with the *sruva* ladle is not an accessory (*guṇa*), and because the original (*prākṛta*) procedure is what is heard in the scripture, there would be a prohibition of all other unknown remnants of the original procedure—distinct from that first *āghāra* performed with the *sruva*—by means of that *sruva*-performed *āghāra*.
Since even that which was obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) is restated here, this constitutes an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Everything else is thereby excluded by this exclusive specification.
Therefore, another position is that some mark distinct from the first substratum must be made;
or else, it is not prohibited, because after being prohibited, there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the alternative position.
The statement "He pours with the *sruva* ladle" is not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Why? Because it is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to a prohibition.

Having prohibited the general act of offering by saying "One should not offer any other oblation," prior to the principal offerings of the *upasads*, the text then provides a counter-exception for the *āghāra* poured with the *sruva* by stating, "He pours with the *sruva*."
Therefore, this is a re-inclusion (pratiprasava), not an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā).
Consequently, everything archetypal (prākṛta) that is not prohibited—excluding the prohibited elements such as the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and so forth—must be performed.
This is the alternative view.
Or rather, there is no offering of the remnant, because the principal deity has not been offered to.
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of rejecting the alternative view of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
The statement, "One should not offer another oblation; one pours [the butter] with the *sruva* ladle," is not a counter-exception to a prohibition.

However, by the phrase "not another," having stated that no other deity is to be worshipped as the primary one, it is indicated that the primary deity, Agni—the specific recipient of the Soma—is not to be worshipped before [the main offering]; for this is expressed by the statement: "One should not offer another oblation before [the one to Agni]," meaning one should not offer to Agni prior to the oblation dedicated to Agni.
And therefore, this is not a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).

Consequently, regarding the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)—that which is distinct from the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice and belongs to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rite—there is "non-sacrifice" (*anijyā*), meaning the absence of the nature of a sacrifice (*yāgatvābhāva*).
The meaning is that the remainder is not to be performed.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *upasads* are independent rites (*apūrva karma*), and they are to be performed exactly as prescribed. Regarding the *upasads*, the oblation-mantras (*homamantra*) are recorded as follows: "O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the wood, most excellent, dwelling in the depths—may it drive away our fierce [enemy]; may it drive away your brilliant word, Svāhā! "O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the dust... "O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the fire... In this context, the initial portion of the first mantra, beginning with "that body, most excellent," is to be appended (*anuṣajjanīya*) to the latter parts of both the second and third mantras.
VI. 2|1|16. The invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā at the time of the Upasad is a common feature (*tantra*) in a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*).

Bhāṣya 1|1|3|123: Regarding the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā at the time of the Upasad, in the formula "Come to the Soma-pressing on the fourth day," the specific days of the Soma-pressing should not be indicated by changing the form to "Come on the fourteenth day," "Come on the thirteenth day," and so forth; rather, the formula is to be used without modification. This applies to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

The *upasad* and other rites are the exclusive marks of the Soma sacrifice. According to the Vārttika, on the middle *upasad* day, the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) is prescribed as something to be constructed.
Saṃkarṣa 2.1.26: The Agnihotra [is performed] only on the days of the Upasads, but not before them.
The properties of the Upasads are employed only as preceded by the Upasads, and not as employed by the supreme apūrva of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
VI. 9|1|2, Section 2: In the case of the piercing (*vitti*) of the *upasad* days, the completion of the higher number is achieved by piercing at their own respective positions (*svasthāna*).

Bhāṣya 5|3|13: By the principle of piercing at the position of the *upasad* (5|3|13), for the sake of establishing the eleven *prayāja* offerings, when there is piercing at their own positions, the final *prayāja* must be repeated thrice.
VI. 5|3|14: The piercing of the *upasad*.
Upasads: [the rites] are new (apūrva).
In the Upasads, there should be only as much ritual action as has been prescribed.
Commentary: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

In this regard, it is traditionally taught: "Six *upasad* rites are performed. With reference to these, they further declare: "They are without *prayāja*s and without *anuyāja*s. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is everything else that is not prohibited to be performed, while only that which is specifically prohibited is excluded; or is only that which is explicitly mentioned to be performed, while everything else is not to be performed; or rather, are these *upasad*s entirely new and independent rites?
What is established? Regarding the Upasad offerings,
according to the principle of the Upasads, one should not perform anything beyond what has been explicitly stated.

Having performed the prohibition of the *prayājas* and *anuyājas* by means of the statement, "They are without *prayājas* and without *anuyājas*," the word has fulfilled its purpose and does not exclude the remaining elements obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).
Therefore, everything [prescribed] should be performed.
Alternatively, there would be a prohibition of the remainder because of the non-mention of the *sauviṣṭakṛt*.

Commentary: This is not the case; it is not that everything must be performed except for what is prohibited. Rather, this [prohibition] is what must be performed. By means of the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice as the basis (*ādhāra*), everything else is excluded (*parisaṃkhyāyate*).
For this inherent substratum is restated without distinction;
no specific quality is heard there.
Therefore, that [quality] is excluded by that [restatement].
Or it is not prohibited; or having been prohibited, it is reconsidered after deliberation. 45.
The Commentary states: It is not the case that only what has been explicitly mentioned must be performed while the remainder is not;
rather, everything must be performed with the exception of what is prohibited.
For it is heard in scripture: "They are without fore-offerings (aprayāja) and without after-offerings (anunayāja)."
Having thus performed the prohibition, the word has fulfilled its purpose and cannot serve as a sublater of anything else.
As for what was stated— that it is "devoid of qualities" and "like its own substratum"—
this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Thus it is heard:

"The existence of the meaning of prefixes is not distinct from the verbal root, nor is there an impossibility of difference based merely on that [distinction], because [prefixes] are not distinct from nominal suffixes; this is according to the principle of the injunctions for spreading [the sacrificial grass] and so forth."
Nor should it be argued that there may be a connection with the ground (*bhūtala*) through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) in the sense of something other than a pot;
for some maintain that this is because the cognition of difference as a qualifier is a matter of direct experience (*ānubhavika*).

Others, however, hold that just as the presence or absence of a prefix (*upasarga*) is the cause for the existence of primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) within a verbal root (*dhātu*), it is more appropriate to assume that prefixes possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) itself, rather than assuming a power of indication (*dyotakatva-śakti*), due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).

Thus, the demonstration of the expressive power (*śakti*) of the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) in the case of the particle *eva* and others, as well as [the power] of similarity and so forth in the case of the particle *iva* and others, is logically established.

For this very reason, the usage in the Vedic text, "For here indeed they sow, and for here indeed they reap," as well as the worldly usage, "He comes to that very place" and "He turns back from this very place," are justified.
Therefore, they say that [these particles possess] denotative power (*vācakatva*).
Maṇi, pp. 169–170. ✱ The existence of the meaning of a prefix is weaker than the existence of the meaning of the verbal root because its meaning is more remote from the meaning of the suffix.

Therefore, the prescription of the existence of the meaning of a prefix is sublated by the prescription of the existence of the meaning of the verbal root. [As in the example: "They sing approaching for the sake of falling."

Commentary 1014|51. *Upasarjana* (the subordinate element). Sometimes a meaning that has become a prefix (*upasarga*) is intended as the subordinate element, while the primary element is the subject of restatement (*anuvāda*).
For example, in the word "daṇḍī" (staff-bearer), the word is understood as having the staff as its subordinate element and the person as its primary referent.

Sometimes, when a person has already been established [as the subject], a statement is made for the purpose of prescribing an attribute of the staff, such as: "The one with a staff or one with a staff-pole recites.
Or, for example: "The priests proceed wearing red turbans.

In the same way here also (in the case of *aruṇayā*), if the quality of redness (*aruṇa*) is subordinate and the kāraka is the primary element, then the statement is appropriate for the purpose of prescribing the quality of redness when the cause [the substance] has not yet been mentioned.

Bhāṣya 3.1.6.12, p. 687. *Upasarjana*: Regarding this technical designation "upasarjana" for a constituent part—namely, the rule "that which is designated by the nominative case in a compound is the upasarjana"—it serves solely to establish its position as the first member, according to the rule "the upasarjana is placed first"; it does not, however, serve to designate it as a distinct grammatical category (*padasaṃjñā*) relative to other words. Ṛjuvimalā, p. 71. *Although the upasarjana is [governed] by objects and so forth, it nevertheless connects with the qualifier.*
For that which is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) situated within a compound is connected with qualifiers;

however, when situated in a sentence, it is seen to be connected [with another word], as in the example "the man of the wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). (Vārttika 3.4.14.3, p. 938). *The subordinate member situated in a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) is not connected with another word.*

Ratnākara, p. 346. ✱ That which has its meaning eclipsed by a subordinate term (*upasarjana*) does not connect with other qualifiers. Furthermore, in the case of the word *indra* which functions [as a compound] for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there would be vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows—as in the word *mahendra*. Greatness belongs to the substance [it qualifies], not to a connection with a subordinate term.

It would be "Mahendra" [as a single compound], and greatness would not be an attribute of Indra. Vākyapadīya 2.1.1.16, p. 419. For a subordinate term (*upasarjana*) does not connect with another word [outside the compound], just as in the case of "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*). Bṛhatī, p. 70. [Regarding] the subordinate term.

For it is not logical for that which is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) to have a connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.4.143, p. 937). Furthermore, the state of being a subordinate element is characterized by being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) that provides assistance without requiring [anything else], and it is also characterized by providing assistance to a single [principal].

Su. Pṛ. 1378: *The status of being a subordinate (*upasarjanatva*)—even when the meaning is already established in the primary [word] within the mantra—does not take on another; and when its own predominance (*svaprādhānya*) is possible, it does not assume the status of being subordinate to another. Vā. 3.1.7.14, Pṛ. 832. *In grammar, the status of being a subordinate is well-known as "quality" (*guṇatva*). Su. Pṛ. 1422. *The status of being a subordinate is not established without a relationship.

Page 828. ✱ *Upasādana* (the placing down) is the purpose for the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used in the performance of the Veda-strewing. Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.4.147. ✱ *Upastaraṇa* (spreading the base) and *abhighāraṇa* (sprinkling with clarified butter) are not to be performed in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* (gold pieces). Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.2.13–12. ✱ *Upastaraṇa*, when performed in the *iḍā* vessel, is merely a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) of the *iḍā*.
Two.

Regarding the rule for the various types of oblations prescribed therein—namely, the two-fold division (*dvaidhaṃvidha*)—in the view that this is merely a prescription of number, there is no distinction based on parsimony or prolixity. Even if "two-fold division" prescribes an *avadāna* (cutting) qualified by that number, since prescribing the *avadāna* independently would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), it must be prescribed as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) by way of being the commencement of the offering (*pradāna*). Thus, because the *avadāna* is to be enjoined in that very manner, the sequential performance (*anusamaya*) ending with the offering mentioned in the fifth [chapter] is justified. Furthermore, if the sentence concerning the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) were to enjoin an oblation (*homa*) qualified by the cut portion, then by accepting the number four as an injunction, the cutting of four portions from the sacrificial material (*havis*) would not be required; consequently, the constant double-cutting (*dviravadāna*) of the sacrificial material taught in this section would be established. Therefore, both views are approved by the author of the Vārttika.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Since the cake (*puroḍāśa*) exists for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), there is a fourfold cutting (*caturavadāna*) of the primary substance, the cake; for, by virtue of its connection with the oblation, that which is to be offered is understood to be cut four times. However, the clarified butter (*ājya*) is not equal to the cake and is therefore additional; thus, the required number is not completed by means of the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). This is stated because [the butter] is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) due to being intended for a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*). Nor does such an excess of number contradict worldly usage, since we observe an excess of number through subordinate elements such as case-endings in expressions like "Devadatta, who is separate."
Attainment [of the number] is due to the equality of the count.

In the case of the *śatakṛṣṇalacarū* sacrifice, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the spreading of butter (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling over (*abhighāraṇa*) should not be performed with clarified butter, the statement regarding attainment—“He cuts four *kṛṣṇala* seeds; having poured out four times”—is presented as the supporting evidence.
Its meaning is that the requirement of “fourfold pouring” is accomplished by means of the four *kṛṣṇala* seeds.

Furthermore, having set forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) must be performed, the proponent of the prima facie view explains the meaning of the word "attainment" (*āti*):
*āti* means reaching, accomplishment;
the mention of "attainment" is justified because of the equality of number—that is, because of its identity with, or equivalence to, the number [of the butter portions].

In the *avadāna* (cutting-off), there is the number four; likewise, in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* (black-gram seeds), there is also the number four. Thus, there is equality in both cases by way of the number.
This is merely a praise of the number four;
therefore, there is no cessation of the acts of spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*).
The statement regarding the attainment (*āpti*) of the two existing [acts] would be purposeless.

The word "but" (*tu*) is used by the proponent (*siddhāntin*) to set aside what was stated by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*)—namely, that the statement regarding attainment is intended as a praise of the number four.
Since the spreading out (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring (*abhighāraṇa*) already exist, the statement regarding attainment would be redundant if it were merely for the sake of praise.
For there is no praise whatsoever for that which already exists. If "attainment" (*āti*) is said to mean "becoming what was previously non-existent," then the praise would be "possessing qualities.
Therefore, the statement regarding the attainment of the two existing things—the spreading out (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*)—is meaningless.
Therefore, regarding what must be performed, there is an option among them because of the status of being a single portion (*ekāvadāna*).

In the *caru* of one hundred *kṛṣṇala* grains, the cessation of the acts of under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and over-pouring (*abhighāraṇa*) is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the scriptural statement: "He cuts four *kṛṣṇalas*; having poured [butter] four times... Just as it is understood [there], so too, because of the status of being a single portion—specifically from the indicative mark of the statement that "the four *kṛṣṇalas* constitute a single portion"—the non-cessation of under-sprinkling and over-pouring is understood.

"Four *kṛṣṇala* seeds constitute one primary portion (*mukhya-avadāna*), and having established four [portions], the performance of the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) must be carried out.

This being the case, there would first appear to be a contradiction between two indicative marks (*liṅga*). Therefore, there should be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the under-spreading and the sprinkling, rather than their absolute exclusion (*nivṛtti*).
Thus says the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).
The word "tu" (but) serves to indicate a distinction, implying that there might be an option (*vikalpa*).
However, in the case of all modifications, the other oblation would be for the sake of repetition (*abhyāsa*).
Having stated the fault of an option in the preceding sūtra, the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) again establishes his own position.
The word *tu* (but) is for the purpose of refuting the alternative view.

When it is stated, “Four *kṛṣṇala* seeds constitute one portion (*avadāna*),” if there were a modification of the whole—that is, if in place of the fourfold offering (*caturavatta*) there were a single portion consisting of four *kṛṣṇalas*—then the repetition of the second portion of the other oblation by means of further scriptural injunctions regarding the *kṛṣṇalas*, namely, “He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas* each for prosperity,” would be rendered meaningless. This is because, in the case of a modification of the whole, there would be no second portion at all.
Therefore, it is not a modification of everything.
And thus, through practice, the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) is accomplished by means of four *kṛṣṇala* seeds each for the double-portioning, the under-sprinkling, and the over-sprinkling.
Alternatively, it should apply to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, because for any other [application] it would be improper.

In the deliberation as to whether or not the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) should be performed for the sacrificial cake (*caru*) consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇala* grains, it was argued that the repetition expressed in the text, "He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas* each," would occur in view of a second portioning. The word "or rather" (*api vā*) is intended to refute that view.
Rather, the repetition would be for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, serving the purpose of the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Because it is improper for the other [act] to have the purpose of being a second cutting;
for even without repetition, the second cutting is already accomplished by the very nature of the act of cutting.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) remains that the spreading [of butter] and the sprinkling [of butter] must be performed.
Alternatively, let there be a single sūtra for both cases.
In that regard, the meaning is as follows: by means of the word *tu* (but), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) sets aside the alternative and establishes his own position.

In the case where all modifications apply—that is, when the modification consists of taking four portions (*catur-avadāna*) from the hundred *kṛṣṇala* seeds instead of the two portions taken from the original material—the injunction "he cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas* each" would be rendered meaningless under the view that all modifications apply, because there would be no second portion to take.

It establishes precisely its pointlessness, for since repetition would have to be performed either for the sake of the other oblation in the form of the second cutting (*avadāna*), or else for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—
but both of these are improper,
because these two alternative positions are unjustifiable.

First, regarding the view that it is a modification of everything (*sarvavikārapakṣa*), since there would be no second portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, there would be an absence of its context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, the view that it is a modification of everything is indeed untenable.
Consequently, the repetition of the four *kṛṣṇala* seeds is solely for the purpose of constituting a second portion.

By means of one *kṛṣṇala* and so forth, there is a fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) consisting of two portions for the cutting (*avadāna*) and two for the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). “He cuts four *kṛṣṇalas*, thereby attaining the fourfold portion,” [referring to] the under-layering and the sprinkling. This is the principle of the secondary oblation (*upahoma-nyāya*).
This statement regarding the *āti* (clarified butter) must be accepted for the purpose of establishing an equality of number.
Therefore, the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) should be performed.
Alternatively, they are not part of the ritual action because their purpose has ceased once the mixing is achieved; therefore, the *āti* possesses the capacity [to serve as a measure].
The word "vā" (or) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Regarding the *caru* offering consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇala* grains, at the time of its performance, the acts of spreading the base-butter (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring the libation-butter (*abhighāraṇa*) are not to be performed;
they are not to be done.
Because it is intended to prevent contact:

the spreading of clarified butter (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over it (*abhighāraṇa*) are performed so that there may not be a "contact"—that is, a sticking together—of the constituent parts of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other such offerings.
However, in the case of *kṛṣṇala* berries, such contact is simply impossible.
Thus, because the purpose of the mixing has ceased—that is, because it no longer exists—the spreading [of clarified butter] and other such acts need not be performed.
And in this way, the statement, “He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas* each, thereby effecting the fourfold cutting,” achieves its efficacy and its correct meaning. That too is logical; such is the sense.

Since the four *kṛṣṇala* seeds constitute two portions (*dviravadāna*), the requirement of the four-fold portion (*caturavatta*) is fulfilled by that alone, even without the preliminary spreading of butter (*upastaraṇa*) and the subsequent sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇalas*, the spreading and sprinkling are not to be performed.
Ke.

The *upasthāna* (ritual attendance) of the *āhavanīya* fire is performed by taking it from the *gārhapatya* and placing it in its own place; it is not [performed] while it remains as the *gārhapatya* itself. (*Saṃkarṣa.* 3.2.8). In a specific modification [of the sacrifice]—namely, on the tenth day of the *dvādaśāha* prior to the *mānasastotra*—the *upasthāna* of the *āhavanīya* is performed with the very same verse used for the *praṇayana*, namely: “*Ayaṃ sahasramānavaḥ*. (*Bhāṣya* 9.2.8.29–30, *varṇaka* 2). The *upasthāna* is obligatory, even for one who maintains the *upasthāpaka* view.
Su. Pṛ. 1202: An *upasthāna* (ritual attendance) must be performed by standing in the immediate proximity of the person for whom it is intended, and not otherwise.
Tūpū. 7.2.14.36: The *upasthāna* at the *sadyovirdhāna* and the *maṇḍapa* should be performed in sequence with the *aindrī* and *vaiṣṇavī* verses respectively, according to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Vi. 3.18: In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the application of the archetypal mantras belongs to the *āgnīdhra* during the *upasthāna*.
VI.3.18. Regarding the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Gārhapatya fire, the mantra "kadācana" [is used] because of the superior authority of the Śruti.

Since the Āhavanīya fire is also included within the Gārhapatya during the worship and other rites for the noble ones (*ārya*), its presence at that location remains possible even when it is not being directly observed.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since words such as "ādi" (and so forth) denote those fires situated in their respective locations just as they do for the *āhavanīya*, and since they must maintain that same external status (*tāṭasthya*) in all functions other than the oblation (*homa*), the worship must be performed only after having drawn out [the fire from its place].

*Saṃkarṣa* 3.2.8: The qualification for the *upasthāna* (ritual attendance) and other rites belongs to the male alone, not to the female. *Vivaraṇa* 6.1.6: The *upasthāpana* (presentation) is obligatory; it is the side that must be presented. *Sūtra-pṛṣṭha* 1202: Since there is no evidence for abandoning what is already present, the priority of the *savanīya* [offering] is established when the three animals are perceived together after the *āśvina-graha*.
Ke. 5|1|6|13: In the Upahavya sacrifice, the scripturally enjoined horse as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) sets aside the archetypal sacrificial fee consisting of *kṛṣṇala* seeds.

The Commentary states: Furthermore, the quality of the interval is heard in scripture as being for the sake of the principal rite—the Upāṃśuyāja—[in the sense that] "one should benefit the Upāṃśuyāja by means of the interval.

The *upāṃśuyāja* mentioned in connection with the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) would apply even to a full moon sacrifice that has only one sacrificial cake (*ekapuroḍāśā*), because it is still a full moon sacrifice; and since it is prescribed as being "in between," it would also apply when there is no interval. in the statement "He places the potsherds with the *upaveṣa*," it is understood that "whenever there is an *upaveṣa*, then he acts with it."
In the same way here as well, when there is an interval, it will occur in that interval.

The Commentary says: It is replied: Now, although the *upāṃśuyāja* is heard [in the scripture] as being in the interval, and thus its performance would be appropriate if an interval existed, it does not bring about the result in the case of the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice when there is only one *puroḍāśa*, because of the resulting deficiency;
therefore, it is not performed.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the question of whether the *upāṃśuyāja* performed on the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) should occur only when there are two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), or whether—given the absence of an offering to Indra-Agni for the sake of the *āgneya* cake prior to the Soma sacrifice or the *āgneya* cake following the *aindrāgna*—it should also occur when there is only one cake; in this inquiry, since the intermediate time is defined by the two cakes occurring before and after it, that [time] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only as qualified by its definers. Therefore, in the absence of those [cakes], that [time] cannot be obtained. Furthermore, although the full-moon day and so forth constitute the time, just as in the case of "in the afternoon on the new-moon day" (*amāvāsyāyām aparāhṇe*), the specific [full-moon day] is not an auxiliary to the other [new-moon day]. Thus, the performance of the *upāṃśuyāja* occurs only when there are two cakes.

This being the case, since the two *puroḍāśas* serve as the purpose for the ritual procedure (*kalpa*), they are not inherently known as the *upāṃśuyāja*; furthermore, if they were taken as qualifiers of time, there would result the fault of a complex injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi-gaurava*). Thus, they are understood merely as indicators of time (*kāla-upalakṣaṇa*). Moreover, in common worldly usage—as in the expression "one should arrive at the time of the conch-blast"—even in the absence of the specific indicator mentioned, the arrival is easily established by other indicators such as direction, action, or other observations; likewise, even in the absence of an indicator in the form of another *puroḍāśa*, it is logical that the action is indicated by the very *puroḍāśa* [in question].
Even in the case of a single *puroḍāśa* offering, the performance of the *upāṃśuyāja* is established by virtue of the presence of the *āgneya* [offering].

Consequently, there is no sublation here of the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and so forth through a restriction by the intermediate time (*antarālakāla*). However, when it is considered that the word "intermediate" (*antarāla*) prescribes the sequence itself—specifically that which follows the *āgneya*—since this is not obtained from the order of the mantra recitation (*mantrapāṭhakrama*), or if it is understood as being set aside (*anyuta*), then upon the omission of the subsequent ritual element (*uttarapadārtha*), there is the omission of the preceding ritual element (*pūrvapadārtha*).

Thus, since [the objection] is simply irrelevant, the *upāṃśuyāja* must indeed take place. Therefore, the injunction as thus determined is either an original rule (*vidhi*) or a restrictive one (*bādha*).

[Reply: It is said in response: From the wording of the mantra (*mantravarṇa*), the status of the deity exists there; therefore, the injunction is distinct (*vyaktacodana*). Pū. 8|1|31.

Commentary: There is a doubt concerning the deity in relation to the *upāṃśuyāja*: is there no fixed rule, or is there a fixed rule?
What is established? Just as there was no restriction regarding the substance in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section, so too there is no restriction regarding the deity.
[Objection: But isn't it Agni and Soma who are enjoined?
[Reply: It is said in response:
This is of the nature of a *purākalpa* (ancient narrative), not of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*).
In that case, the deities are enjoined by such [passages] as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently."
It is said:
these are explanatory passages (arthavādas) intended for the purpose of prescribing the performance of the closest possible kinship (uttamajāmi).
Therefore, there is no restrictive rule.
Because of the context of those [mantras] being the means of leading [the offering].
The Commentary states: "Indeed, a sacrifice does not take place with a different deity;
nor is there a deity without a scriptural statement."
Furthermore, a deity prescribed for one [rite] cannot be logically applied to another.
Therefore, we shall understand the deity by forming a single syntactical unit with any one of the deities belonging to the primary rites that are present;
and since the purpose is accomplished by means of one, it may be any deity whatsoever that is required.

Regarding *soma*: as before, since there is no desire for a restrictive rule (*niyamakāma*) here, it is stated that there is no sublation (*bādha*) of another deity who is obtained through the sense of the text; this is the connection (*saṅgati*). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: just as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the preceding section there was no restriction regarding the substance (*dravya*), so too there should be no restriction regarding the deity (*devatā*).
[The commentary] says: "In that case, whichever deity it may be—whether Tantric or otherwise—it would be the first."

Because there is no distinction [otherwise], the *tāntrika* (the rule pertaining to the ritual procedure) is restricted here by the context (*prakaraṇa*). The term "*tāntrika*" refers to that which is recited within the framework of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual, because it serves as the basis for the spreading of butter (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). The statement regarding the spreading and sprinkling is not a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the fourfold portioning (*caturavatta*), unlike the case where one says "one should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," and thus in the *Mitravindā* and other sacrifices one recites seventeen; it is not the same here with the fourfold portioning.

How so? [One might think] that one should spread the under-layer (upastṛṇīyāt) and pour the libation over it (abhighārayet). How then? One should offer the substance connected with the fourfold portioning; one should spread the under-layer upon the sacrificial oblation (havis) and pour the libation over it.

Where the offering, while being under-layed and while being poured over, constitutes a presentation involving the fourfold portioning, there the fourfold portioning is not to be taken from the primary substance itself.

Furthermore, where it is impossible to obtain four portions from the principal substance without [taking] from the subsidiary substance, there one must take four portions from the principal substance.
What is intended here is that what constitutes the "four-fold portion" (caturavatta) is to be offered, not that four portions must be taken from this or that specific substance.
Therefore, even in the Upāṃśuyāja, the four-fold portion must be performed.

Soma: The connection [with the previous section] is stated as follows: because it depends upon the rule regarding the portions (*avadāna*) from the preceding topic, this is an injunction of the manner [of performance]. Vi: "In the *Upāṃśuyāja*, would there not be four portions?
It would, since there is no restriction; nor is there a repetition, for that is established by the sentence."
From the sentence "He offers with four portions" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*), it follows that there are four portions (*caturavatta*) in the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Bhaṭṭa: When the number four is also included within the scope of the qualifier for the object of the injunction, and thus a rule prescribing four portions is formulated, then one considers—by way of a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*)—whether or not there are four portions in the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Furthermore, this should be understood as a separate hypothetical inquiry based on the premise that there is a specific injunction for taking four portions (*caturgṛhīta*) in the *upāṃśuyāja*.

In that context, because the fourfold number required for the constituent parts of the *avadāna* (cutting-off) has been accomplished through the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) of the two portions of clarified butter for the animal sacrifice, and because the under-sprinkling and over-sprinkling are omitted from the *upāṃśuyāja* since their purpose is lost there, the fourfold cutting-off (*caturavatta*) is also omitted.

This being the position reached, since the prescribed number four is established by the rule "he cuts off twice from the sacrificial oblation" (*dvirhaviṣo 'vadyati*), even though in the case of the *auṣadha* and *sāṃnāyya* offerings this might be accomplished—as in the case of animal sacrifices—by means of the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), there is no authority for such a restriction. Consequently, because the same [number] applies to the *upāṃśuyāja* as well, it would follow that it must be accomplished with the sacrificial oblation itself; and since there is no authority for its omission, the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) must indeed be performed.

In reality, however, since the offering is prescribed specifically with the delimited portion as its objective according to the previously stated method, the number four does not enter into the category of the objective delimiter; thus, it is not itself that which is enjoined. Consequently, even though the spreading under (*upastaraṇa*) and sprinkling over (*abhighāraṇa*) are omitted in the *upāṃśuyāja* due to the absence of a purpose for them, the injunction "he cuts twice from the sacrificial oblation" (*dvir haviṣo 'vadyati*) establishes only the act of cutting (*avadāna*). Furthermore, because the statement "he takes four portions of clarified butter" (*catura ājyasya gṛhṇāti*) occurs within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*, this sentence prescribes the four-fold taking (*caturgṛhīta*) by means of the ladle (*sruc*) for the sake of the *upāṃśuyāja*. Therefore, the *upāṃśuyāja* is performed by that very [clarified butter], and the disposal (*pratipatti*) of that same [substance] is the act of throwing it into the fire.

As for the statement "he offers with four ladlings" (*caturgṛhītaṃ juhoti*), which is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), by that [statement] there is an injunction of the four-ladling in reference to the offering for breaking [the vessel] (*bhedanahoma*) and similar acts where a specific substance has already been mentioned; however, it does not apply to the *upāṃśuyāja*, because there is no evidence for the word *juhoti* to indicate a sacrifice (*yāga*), and because, since the taking of portions (*avadāna*) is already applicable for that [sacrifice] by virtue of the general rule of three portions within its context, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting that very rule by the independent injunction of the four-ladling.

Therefore, the injunction of the four-ladling applies there only from the sentence recited within the context of the *upāṃśuyāja*, as recorded in the commentary on the section beginning with "And from the clarified butter, because of the connection with all [substances]" (*ājyācca sarvasaṃyogāt*).
And it is established that the pouring of that [milk] into that very [offering] constitutes its disposal (*pratipatti*).
